Can be used alone for emphasis or to draw attention (Aquí tenemos.). Tone can be formal or casual depending on context.
target_language_example: Aquí tenemos a los invitados de honor.
native_language_example: Here we have the guests of honor.

meaning: here for the whole (day/period).
additional_notes: Used before a time period (noche, semana, mañana) to say someone stays or was somewhere for the entire period. Common patterns: 'estar/estaré/estuve/he estado/llevar/ llevamos/me quedaré' + aquí toda la + [noche/semana/mañana]. Time word must match gender/number (toda la noche, toda la semana, toda la mañana).
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme aquí toda la tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay here the whole afternoon.

meaning: here every (as in 'here every day/week/etc.')
additional_notes: Used to say that someone goes to or does something at this place on a regular, repeated schedule. Usually completed with a time word (días, lunes, meses): aquí todos los días = here every day. Word order: 'aquí' (here) + 'todos los' + time noun. If the time word is plural masculine (días, lunes) use 'todos los'; for feminine plural use 'todas las' (aquí todas las semanas).
target_language_example: Vengo aquí todos los días para estudiar.
native_language_example: I come here every day to study.

meaning: here and there; all around; in various places.
additional_notes: Used to indicate things located or happening in multiple places (scattered or around). Can be literal (physical locations) or more general (various times/situations). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Hay hojas aquí y allá por toda la calle.
native_language_example: There are leaves here and there all along the street.

meaning: rainbow
additional_notes: Refers to the multicolored arc in the sky that appears when sunlight shines through raindrops. Often used literally; can appear in idioms (e.g., 'buscar el final del arco iris' — seeking something impossible). The phrase is two words in Spanish.
target_language_example: Después de la lluvia vimos un arco iris sobre el río.
native_language_example: After the rain we saw a rainbow over the river.

meaning: a weapon in/at (indicates location or possession: 'a weapon in/at/on/with').
additional_notes: This is not an idiom but the combination of arma (weapon) plus a preposition indicating where it is placed or held. Common patterns: 'arma en la cintura' (a weapon at the waist), 'arma en la mano' (a weapon in the hand), 'apuntar con un arma en este momento' (pointing a weapon at someone right now). Use with locations (en la mesa, en el suelo) or body parts (en la mano, en la cintura).
target_language_example: Encontraron un arma en el coche.
native_language_example: They found a weapon in the car.

meaning: weapons of / ...-made weapons / weapons for (depends on context).
additional_notes: armas = weapons. 'armas de' introduces what kind of weapons (e.g., 'armas de fuego' = firearms, 'armas de metal' = metal weapons) or possession/source ('traficante de armas' = arms trafficker). Translate based on the following noun: 'armas de fuego' = firearms/guns; 'traficante de armas' = weapons dealer/arms trafficker. Word order: in Spanish the type or material follows 'armas de'.
target_language_example: Encontraron armas de fuego en el coche.
native_language_example: They found firearms in the car.

meaning: weapons for / weapons to (used before an infinitive or noun to indicate purpose or recipient)
additional_notes: Commonly appears when talking about preparing, providing, or possessing weapons for a specific purpose (e.g., 'to kill', 'to shoot') or for someone. 'Para' can mark purpose (followed by an infinitive) or indicate the intended recipient/target (followed by a noun). Context decides whether it means 'in order to' or 'for [someone/something]'.
target_language_example: Preparó armas para defender la ciudad.
native_language_example: He prepared weapons to defend the city.

meaning: in harmony with; in agreement or peaceful relationship with
additional_notes: Used to describe peaceful coexistence, agreement, or alignment between people, ideas, or things (e.g., nature, truth, classmates). Often appears with 'estar' or 'vivir' (estar en armonía con, vivir en armonía con).
target_language_example: Debemos vivir en armonía con el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: We must live in harmony with the environment.

meaning: to fix/repair my (something).
additional_notes: Common verb phrase meaning to repair or make something work again. 'Arreglar' can also mean 'to tidy/arrange' in other contexts, but with possessions (auto, radio, reloj) it means 'to repair' or 'to have repaired.' When followed by a direct object, you may see 'llevar a arreglar mi [objeto]' meaning 'to take my [object] to be repaired.'
target_language_example: Necesito arreglar mi teléfono esta semana.
native_language_example: I need to fix my phone this week.

meaning: arrested for (followed by the reason or crime).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone was arrested for a specific offense. 'Por' introduces the reason or crime (e.g., 'por robo', 'por conducir ebrio'). Context or an explicit agent (e.g., 'por la policía') clarifies whether 'por' means 'for' (reason) or 'by' (agent). Can appear in passive constructions (Fue arrestado por...).
target_language_example: Fue arrestado por conducir ebrio.
native_language_example: He/He was arrested for driving drunk.

meaning: he/she risked his/her (life/neck/other possession).
additional_notes: Past tense of arriesgar + possessive su. Commonly used with 'la vida' (to risk one's life) but can be used with other nouns (arriesgó su cuello, arriesgó su reputación). Context determines gender of possessor. In English often translated 'risked his/her life' or 'put his/her X at risk.'
target_language_example: Arriesgó su reputación por defender la verdad.
native_language_example: He risked his reputation to defend the truth.

meaning: abstract art (art that uses shapes, colors, and forms rather than realistic depictions).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the art style/movement known as abstract art. Can describe paintings, sculpture, and other visual arts that emphasize non-representational elements. Commonly used in galleries, museums, and art discussions.
target_language_example: Me interesa el arte abstracto porque me gustan los colores y las formas.
native_language_example: I'm interested in abstract art because I like the colors and shapes.

meaning: martial art; a system or tradition of combat and self-defense.
additional_notes: Used to refer to organized fighting systems (karate, judo, taekwondo, sumo, etc.). Singular 'arte marcial', plural 'artes marciales'. Commonly used in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: El sumo es un arte marcial japonés.
native_language_example: Sumo is a Japanese martial art.

meaning: modern art (art produced from the late 19th century to present, often experimental or non-traditional).
additional_notes: Refers to artworks and art movements considered 'modern'—includes abstract, avant-garde, and contemporary styles. Used as a general noun phrase (el arte moderno). Common in museums and art discussions.
target_language_example: Me interesa mucho el arte moderno de ese museo.
native_language_example: I'm very interested in the modern art at that museum.

meaning: an artist who works in/with a specific field or of a certain rank ("artist of" / "artist in").
additional_notes: Used to say what kind of artist someone is (artista de mangas, artista de circo) or to indicate rank/quality (artista de segunda categoría) or to refer to an artist 'of' a generation/size. 'De' is followed by a noun or noun phrase describing the field, category, or group.
target_language_example: Es un artista de teatro muy respetado.
native_language_example: He is a very respected theater artist.

meaning: article (in/of) — used to refer to a newspaper/magazine piece or an item belonging to a source.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say an article that appears in or belongs to a particular source: 'artículo de periódico' (newspaper article), 'artículo de la página dos' (the article on page two), or 'artículo de [publication/person]'. The preposition 'de' links the article to its source or location. Word order: 'artículo de + source' or 'artículo de + page/section'.
target_language_example: Leí un artículo de El País sobre medio ambiente.
native_language_example: I read an article in El País about the environment.

meaning: 'the article is' — a simple subject + verb phrase used to describe an article.
additional_notes: This combines artículo (article/item/short piece of writing) with the verb ser (es = is). Use to state characteristics of a written article or a physical item. Context determines meaning of artículo: in journalism it means 'article'; in stores it can mean 'item' or 'product'. Adjectives following 'es' must agree in gender/number with artículo (artículo is masculine singular).
target_language_example: El artículo es interesante y bien investigado.
native_language_example: The article is interesting and well researched.

meaning: 'the murder of' or 'the assassination of'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the victim or target of a killing. 'Asesinato' means murder; when followed by 'de' + noun it specifies who or what was killed (person, animal, etc.). Can refer to criminal murders or famous political assassinations. For everyday speech 'asesinato' is formal/neutral; for animals people may also say 'matanza' (slaughter) depending on context.
target_language_example: El libro cuenta el asesinato de la reina en 1831.
native_language_example: The book tells of the assassination of the queen in 1831.

meaning: seat in / seat on (used to say where a seat is or that someone has a seat in a place).
additional_notes: Asiento means 'seat'. Combined with en it indicates location or assignment (a seat in/on a specific area: en el tren, en la sección, en mi mesa). Can also appear in commands about a seat (e.g., poner el asiento en posición vertical). Use definite/article with places: 'un asiento en la sección de no fumadores', or possessive: 'su asiento en el tren'.
target_language_example: Reservé un asiento en la fila 12.
native_language_example: I reserved a seat in row 12.

meaning: he/she nodded with the (head); used to describe nodding in agreement or acknowledgement, followed by a body part or gesture.
additional_notes: Asintió is the past tense of 'asentir' (to nod/agree). Commonly followed by 'cabeza' ('asintió con la cabeza') to mean 'he/she nodded'. The phrase can also be completed with other parts (e.g., 'con la mano' = waved/gestured) but the most frequent and natural completion is 'con la cabeza'. Used to indicate silent agreement or acknowledgement.
target_language_example: Ella asintió con la cabeza antes de salir.
native_language_example: She nodded with her head before leaving.

meaning: they attended / were present at (something).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) third-person plural of asistir a. Use to say people attended events, meetings, classes, etc. 'Asistir' takes the preposition 'a' when referring to attending something. For English 'attend', word order and preposition match closely.
target_language_example: Muchas personas asistieron a la conferencia.
native_language_example: Many people attended the conference.

meaning: 'the matter/issue is' — used to introduce or describe what the situation or topic is.
additional_notes: Asunto means 'matter', 'issue', 'case' or 'topic'. When followed by 'es' it presents or summarizes the key point, condition or quality of that matter. Common in formal and informal speech. Can introduce a factual description (Este asunto es controvertido) or a personal point (Pues el asunto es que te quiero).
target_language_example: El asunto es que no tenemos suficiente tiempo.
native_language_example: The thing is that we don't have enough time.

meaning: like this before; in this way previously.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has or hasn't happened in the same way at an earlier time. Common with verbs in past perfect (había visto, había sentido) or simple past (sentí). Can appear as 'así antes' or split (e.g., 'antes así') depending on emphasis. Emphasizes manner ('like this') plus prior time ('before').
target_language_example: Nunca había reaccionado así antes.
native_language_example: I had never reacted like this before.

meaning: 'like', 'just as', or 'as well as' depending on context.
additional_notes: Very versatile phrase. Use 'así como' to compare or equate things ('just as' / 'like'), to add items ('as well as'), or to emphasize that something happened in the way just described ('that's how'). Context and word order determine the exact English equivalent.
target_language_example: Así como te lo dije, así ocurrió.
native_language_example: Just as I told you, that's how it happened.

meaning: just like that; without much thought or without permission
additional_notes: Used to say something is done suddenly, casually, or without justification. Often negative: implies you cannot do something 'just like that' or replace someone 'so easily'. Can also stand alone as an exclamation meaning 'just like that' (implying surprise or disapproval).
target_language_example: No puedes dejar el trabajo así como así.
native_language_example: You can't quit the job just like that.

meaning: used to indicate degree or manner: 'this/that (much)'; 'so' or 'this/that (way)'.
additional_notes: Commonly used before adjectives, adverbs, quantities or demonstrative measurements to show degree or manner. Context determines translation: e.g. 'así de alto' = 'this tall/that tall', 'así de sincero' = 'that (so) sincere', 'hablas así de rápido' = 'you speak that/so quickly'. It can be colloquial and often emphasizes how much or how (in what way) something is.
target_language_example: No lo sabía; es así de simple.
native_language_example: I didn't know; it's that simple.

meaning: it/that/he/she/thing used to be like that; that's how it/they/he/she was.
additional_notes: Used to describe how someone or something was in the past or to confirm a remembered state or characteristic. Context determines subject (it/that/he/she/they). Common in recollection or agreement: 'Así era antes' = 'That's how it used to be.'
target_language_example: Así era mi abuelo cuando era joven.
native_language_example: That's how my grandfather was when he was young.

meaning: that's how it goes / that's how it will be / that's how it's going to be.
additional_notes: Used to explain or confirm the way something will happen or how something works. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'va a ser', 'va a funcionar') and can express resignation, explanation, or realization depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Así es como va a funcionar el sistema.
native_language_example: That's how the system is going to work.

meaning: That's life; such is life — a resigned comment about how things are.
additional_notes: Used to express acceptance or resignation about an unpleasant or inevitable situation. Can be said alone or after a statement. Tone ranges from neutral to slightly philosophical; often equivalent to English "that's life" or "such is life."
target_language_example: Se rompió la taza favorita; así es la vida.
native_language_example: My favorite mug broke; that's life.

meaning: 'that's how it is' / 'that's better like this' (depending on context and tone).
additional_notes: Used to comment on the current state or the result of a change. Can express acceptance ('that's how things are') or approval that something is improved ('that's better like this'). Common in everyday speech; tone and context determine nuance.
target_language_example: Así está mejor.
native_language_example: That's better like this.

meaning: so / thus (used to refer to something said, done, or believed in that way).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before or after a verb to refer back to a statement, action, belief, or opinion: 'así lo dijo' = 'he/she said it that way'; 'así lo creo' = 'I believe that to be true.' Often used to emphasize that something is exactly or generally that way. Can be translated depending on context as 'that way,' 'so,' 'thus,' or 'as such.'
target_language_example: Si ellos dicen que funciona, así lo aceptaremos.
native_language_example: If they say it works, we'll accept it as such.

meaning: that's better / this way is better.
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, arrangement, or way of doing something is improved or preferable. Common in spoken Spanish to approve a change or solution. Can refer to present action ('Do it like this, it's better') or to a result already achieved ('Now it's better'). Tone can be neutral or approving.
target_language_example: Si cierras la ventana, así mejor.
native_language_example: If you close the window, that's better.

meaning: so
additional_notes: Used to introduce a result, conclusion, or next step: the second part follows from what was said before. At the start of a sentence, it often works like English "so..." when continuing a conversation or drawing a conclusion.
target_language_example: No tenía paraguas, así que me mojé.
native_language_example: I didn't have an umbrella, so I got wet.

meaning: so this / therefore this (used to introduce a conclusion or comment about 'this')
additional_notes: Combines 'así que' (so/therefore) with 'esto' (this). Used to draw a conclusion, emphasize or introduce what follows about a situation or object close in discourse. Common in spoken Spanish to react to information or to present the next point. Tone can be neutral; not idiomatic beyond literal sense.
target_language_example: Así que esto es lo que quieres para tu cumpleaños.
native_language_example: So this is what you want for your birthday.

meaning: so we have (to) / therefore we must
additional_notes: As a phrase, 'así que' means 'so' or 'therefore'. When followed by 'tenemos' (we have), it introduces a conclusion or necessary action for 'us' (we). Often appears as 'así que tenemos que + infinitive' = 'so we have to... / therefore we must...'. Useful to express consequences, plans, or obligations.
target_language_example: Así que tenemos que practicar todos los días.
native_language_example: So we have to practice every day.

meaning: 'like this' or 'this is how' (used to describe a way something is done or how someone/something is called)
additional_notes: Common phrase that often appears before passive/reflexive verbs (e.g., 'así se hace', 'así se llama') to describe how something is done or how something/someone is referred to. Can point to a demonstration ('like this') or a statement about naming ('this is what it's called' or 'this is how he/she/they call themselves'). Context and the following verb determine the exact translation.
target_language_example: Así se prepara la receta, paso a paso.
native_language_example: This is how the recipe is prepared, step by step.

meaning: so be it
additional_notes: Literally uses the subjunctive of ser: 'may it be so.' It is used to express a wish, hope, or acceptance. After verbs like esperar or ojalá, it often corresponds to 'I hope so' or 'that’s the case.' In expressions like 'que así sea,' it means 'so be it.'
target_language_example: Ojalá así sea.
native_language_example: I hope so.

meaning: that's how (they/they are); that's the way things are.
additional_notes: Used to state that something is the way it is—either describing current circumstances, typical behavior, or explaining an unchangeable fact. Context determines subject: 'así son las cosas' = 'that's the way things are'; 'así son los perros' = 'that's how dogs are (usually)'. Can be used resignedly or matter-of-factly.
target_language_example: No podemos cambiarlo; así son las cosas.
native_language_example: We can't change it; that's the way things are.

meaning: attacked by (someone or something).
additional_notes: Passive construction: 'atacado por' indicates that the subject receives an attack and names the attacker after 'por'. Use with people, animals, groups, or causes (e.g., insects, surprise). Combine with appropriate verb tense and subject (e.g., 'fue atacado por...' = 'was attacked by...').
target_language_example: El perro fue atacado por varios gatos callejeros.
native_language_example: The dog was attacked by several stray cats.

meaning: heart attack (myocardial infarction).
additional_notes: Used to describe a sudden medical event when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked. Common in medical and everyday contexts. You can also say 'infarto' (shorter) in Spanish. Often used with verbs like 'tener' (to have) or 'sufrir' (to suffer).
target_language_example: Tom nunca tuvo un ataque al corazón.
native_language_example: Tom never had a heart attack.

meaning: panic attack (a sudden episode of intense fear or anxiety).
additional_notes: Used to describe a sudden, intense episode of fear or anxiety with physical symptoms (racing heart, shortness of breath, dizziness). Can be framed in present, past, or progressive tenses (tener, tener/estar teniendo). Common in medical and everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Tuve un ataque de pánico en el avión.
native_language_example: I had a panic attack on the plane.

meaning: 'traffic jam' (literally 'jam of') — used to describe being stuck in traffic or a blockage.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'atasco de tráfico' (traffic jam). 'Atasco' alone can mean any blockage (e.g., a clog, jam or bottleneck). Use with 'estar' to say you are stuck: 'estamos en un atasco de tráfico'.
target_language_example: Estoy en un atasco de tráfico y llegaré tarde.
native_language_example: I'm in a traffic jam and I'll be late.

meaning: attention to what (someone says or to what happens).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the phrase 'prestar atención a lo que...' meaning 'to pay attention to what...' followed by a clause. 'Lo' here is a neutral pronoun referring to an idea, statement, or situation (equivalent to English 'what' or 'what ...').
target_language_example: Debes prestar atención a lo que te explican en clase.
native_language_example: You should pay attention to what they explain to you in class.

meaning: to cross the river (by going through it).
additional_notes: Common neutral phrase meaning to go from one side of a river to the other. Can describe any method (walk, swim, boat) but in the example sentences it specifically refers to swimming across (a nado / nadando). Use 'atravesar' for crossing through something (river, street, forest).
target_language_example: Tuvimos que atravesar el río para llegar al pueblo.
native_language_example: We had to cross the river to get to the village.

meaning: 'dare to' or 'I dare to' (to have the courage to do or say something).
additional_notes: Used with verbs to express having (or not having) the courage or boldness to do something. Commonly appears with first-person 'me atrevo a...' (I dare to...) or 'no me atrevo a...' (I don't dare to...). Followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., decir, hablar, abordar, adivinar).
target_language_example: No me atrevo a decírselo porque tengo miedo de su reacción.
native_language_example: I don't dare to tell him/her because I'm afraid of their reaction.

meaning: behind the (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate location behind something feminine (la + noun). Often interchangeable with 'detrás de la' (more common). 'atrás' can stand alone (atrás de + noun) or be followed by 'de la/el/los/las' to match the noun's gender/number.
target_language_example: El perro está atrás de la puerta.
native_language_example: The dog is behind the door.

meaning: behind the / at the back of (followed by a masculine singular noun or contraction 'de + el').
additional_notes: Used to indicate position or location behind something. 'Atrás de' + noun is the basic form; when the noun is masculine singular and uses the article 'el', it contracts to 'atrás del' (atrás de + el → atrás del). Can also appear in phrases like 'la parte de atrás del...' or 'atrás de la/las/...'.
target_language_example: El coche está aparcado atrás del edificio.
native_language_example: The car is parked behind the building.

meaning: back/behind in order to; 'back' + purpose ('so as to...')
additional_notes: Commonly appears when describing someone or something being positioned 'behind' (atrás) for a purpose introduced by 'para' (to/in order to). Often used in contexts like going back to fix something (volver atrás para...) or having someone at the rear to perform a task (tener a alguien atrás para cubrir...). Word order: 'atrás para' usually follows a verb or noun phrase (e.g., 'volver atrás para...' or 'tener a alguien atrás para...').
target_language_example: Volvió atrás para recoger su mochila.
native_language_example: He went back to pick up his backpack.

meaning: 'even so' or 'nevertheless' (introduces a contrast or unexpected result).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting idea or to emphasize that something remains true despite what was said before. Often interchangeable with 'sin embargo' or 'no obstante' in many contexts. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence: 'Aun así, ...' or '..., aun así, ...'.
target_language_example: Estaba cansada; aun así, salió a correr.
native_language_example: She was tired; even so, she went out for a run.

meaning: 'although she' or 'even though she'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or unexpected fact about a female subject. 'Aunque' can be followed by indicative (fact) or subjunctive (uncertainty or concession); here examples use indicative. In English, translate as 'although she' or 'even though she'.
target_language_example: Aunque ella trabaja mucho, siempre tiene tiempo para sus hijos.
native_language_example: Although she works a lot, she always has time for her children.

meaning: 'even if' or 'although' used with 'you' (informal singular), or with a verb referring to you.
additional_notes: Aunque introduces a concession ('even if' / 'although'). When followed by te + verb (or te + object), it refers to the second person singular familiar (tú). In many cases the verb after te is omitted because it's understood from context (e.g., 'aunque te duela' = 'even if it hurts you'). Can be used with present, past, or subjunctive depending on nuance. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Te lo diré aunque te moleste.
native_language_example: I'll tell you even if it bothers you.

meaning: northern lights; natural colorful light display in the sky near the Arctic.
additional_notes: Refers specifically to the atmospheric light phenomenon seen in high northern latitudes (Aurora Borealis). Used as a noun phrase; feminine (la aurora boreal). Spanish word order places 'aurora' (dawn/aurora) before 'boreal' (northern).
target_language_example: Siempre quise viajar al norte para ver la aurora boreal.
native_language_example: I've always wanted to travel north to see the northern lights.

meaning: 'auto' = car; 'se' is a reflexive or passive/impersonal pronoun used with verbs (e.g., 'se detuvo' = it/ste car stopped).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase. 'Auto' is a common short form of 'automóvil' (car). The pronoun 'se' combines with verbs to form reflexive actions (el auto se detuvo = the car stopped), accidental/impersonal constructions (se quedó sin combustible = it/they ran out of fuel), or passive-like statements (se encontró con = met/encountered). Translate depending on context: sometimes 'se' means 'itself' (reflexive), sometimes it's part of a passive/impersonal structure, and sometimes it signals that something happened to the car.
target_language_example: El auto se apagó en el semáforo.
native_language_example: The car shut off at the traffic light.

meaning: the noun 'auto' (car) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and); used in sentences like 'auto y ...' where 'y' connects actions or items—literal meaning: 'car and'.
additional_notes: In Spanish, auto is a common short form for automóvil (car). The examples show 'auto' used with verbs of getting in/out, parking, or actions involving the car. 'Y' simply means 'and' and connects ideas; here it often links the car to another clause (e.g., 'auto y apuntó...' = 'the car and he pointed...'). However, in natural English you would usually translate the whole phrase differently (e.g., 'he got out of his car and...' or 'he opened the car window and...').
target_language_example: Ella dejó las bolsas en el auto y cerró la puerta.
native_language_example: She left the bags in the car and closed the door.

meaning: the bus arrived / the bus came (arrived at a place).
additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) or simple statement: 'autobús llegó' appears in full sentences as 'El autobús llegó...' followed by timing or reason (e.g., 'llegó tarde', 'llegó con retraso', 'llegó adelantado'). Use 'llegó' for a completed arrival in the past. Common modifiers: 'tarde' (late), 'con X de retraso' (with X delay), 'adelantado' (early), 'a causa de' or 'por' to give reasons.
target_language_example: El autobús llegó con cinco minutos de retraso.
native_language_example: The bus arrived five minutes late.

meaning: uses of 'autobús' (bus) with the reflexive/pronominal 'se' in different constructions (e.g., actions done by or to the bus, passive/impersonal uses, or reflexive-like phrasing).
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed phrase but the noun 'autobús' combined with the pronoun 'se'. 'Se' can mark different structures: 1) pronominal reflexive/reciprocal (rare with vehicles), 2) accidental/anticausative (El autobús se detuvo = the bus stopped), 3) passive/impersonal (En este autobús se puede ir al aeropuerto = you can go to the airport on this bus), 4) perfect just happened with 'acabar de' + 'irse' (El autobús se acaba de ir = the bus has just left), 5) result of an action (El autobús se lo llevó por delante = the bus ran him over). Translate depending on context; treat 'se' as a functional particle, not part of the noun.
target_language_example: El autobús se fue sin avisar y tuve que esperar otro.
native_language_example: The bus left without warning and I had to wait for another one.

meaning: cars to/for (used before a destination or purpose)
additional_notes: This looks like a short phrase where 'autos' means 'cars' (plural of 'auto') and 'a' is the preposition 'to/at/for'. It's not a fixed phrase on its own; you'll typically see it as part of a longer phrase, for example 'autos a venta' (cars for sale) — though correct Spanish would be 'autos en venta' — or 'autos a Málaga' (cars to Málaga). Watch word order and preposition choice: common natural phrases use 'coches' or 'autos' plus prepositions like 'en', 'para' or 'hacia' depending on meaning. 'Autos a' by itself is compositional and literal but incomplete.
target_language_example: Hay muchos autos a la venta en esa calle.
native_language_example: There are many cars for sale on that street.

meaning: cars in / cars on (used to indicate cars located in or involved in something).
additional_notes: Autos = cars (common in Latin America; España often uses 'coches'). 'En' is a preposition meaning 'in', 'on', or 'at' depending on context. Together they appear when talking about the number of cars inside/at a place (autos en el estacionamiento) or cars participating/remaining in an event (autos en esta carrera). Word order is typical: noun + preposition + place or situation.
target_language_example: Hay cuatro autos en el garaje.
native_language_example: There are four cars in the garage.

meaning: to be ashamed of; to feel embarrassed about someone or something (used with the reflexive verb avergonzarse).
additional_notes: Usually appears with the reflexive form (se avergüenza de, me avergüenzo de, etc.). Followed by a noun, pronoun, or a clause (infinitive/gerund or subordinate clause) introduced by 'de' (e.g., 'de haberle mentido', 'de su comportamiento'). Expresses shame or embarrassment about actions, qualities, situations, or people. Not a literal separable phrase; it's part of the reflexive verb avergonzarse + de.
target_language_example: Harry se avergüenza de haberle mentido a Sally.
native_language_example: Harry is ashamed of having lied to Sally.

meaning: I am embarrassed/ashamed of (someone or something).
additional_notes: Avergonzarse de is a reflexive verb phrase: 'me avergüenzo de...' = 'I am ashamed/embarrassed of...'. Use the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) to match the subject. Common with people, actions, or things. Can express shame (stronger) or embarrassment (weaker) depending on context.
target_language_example: Me avergüenzo de mis errores.
native_language_example: I am ashamed of my mistakes.

meaning: 'planes are' (the subject 'aviones' + verb 'son' = 'planes are').
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'aviones' (planes) followed by the verb 'son' (they are). Use to state general facts or opinions about planes (e.g., qualities, comparisons, safety, price). Remember subject–verb agreement: 'aviones' is plural, so use 'son'. In everyday speech you might also see 'los aviones son' when specifying 'the planes'.
target_language_example: Los aviones son rápidos pero caros.
native_language_example: Planes are fast but expensive.

meaning: paper airplane (a toy plane folded from paper).
additional_notes: Common phrase for the small toy made by folding a sheet of paper into a plane shape. Used literally; can also be used playfully or metaphorically (e.g., something fragile or makeshift).
target_language_example: Mi hermano y yo hicimos un avión de papel y lo lanzamos por la ventana.
native_language_example: My brother and I made a paper airplane and threw it out the window.

meaning: the plane arrived / the airplane arrived.
additional_notes: Used to say that a flight or airplane has arrived (often followed by where, when, or with what delay). Common constructions: 'el avión llegó a [lugar]' (arrived at), 'el avión llegó con [retraso/adelanto]' (arrived with a delay/early), or 'el avión llegó a las [hora]'. 'Avión' is masculine, so full sentence usually uses 'el avión'.
target_language_example: El avión llegó al aeropuerto con una hora de retraso.
native_language_example: The plane arrived at the airport an hour late.

meaning: yesterday at (used before a time-of-day phrase, e.g., 'ayer a la noche' = yesterday at night)
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a time-of-day noun (la mañana, la tarde, la noche) to indicate when something happened the previous day. In many regions Spanish speakers also say 'anoche' (instead of 'ayer a la noche') or 'ayer por la mañana/tarde/noche.' Word order: 'ayer a la + [mañana/tarde/noche]' or 'ayer por la + [mañana/tarde/noche]'.
target_language_example: Ayer a la tarde fui al cine con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Yesterday in the afternoon I went to the cinema with my friends.

meaning: yesterday when / (it) was only yesterday that...
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause referring to something that happened yesterday or to express that something feels like it happened very recently. Common in narrative or reflective phrases: 'Ayer cuando...' = 'Yesterday when...'. Can also appear in more emotional sentences like 'Fue ayer cuando...' or 'Parece que sólo fue ayer cuando...' meaning 'It feels like it was just yesterday that...'.
target_language_example: Ayer cuando llegué, ya se habían ido.
native_language_example: Yesterday when I arrived, they had already left.

meaning: yesterday in the (afternoon/evening) — used as part of time expressions like 'ayer por la tarde/noche'.
additional_notes: Incomplete alone: normally followed by a time-of-day noun (tarde, noche, mañana) or a specific hour (e.g., 'ayer por la mañana', 'ayer por la noche', 'ayer por la 1'). Used to indicate an approximate time during yesterday (more vague than 'ayer a las').
target_language_example: Ayer por la noche fuimos al cine.
native_language_example: Last night we went to the movies.

meaning: 'help (to)'; used with verbs like pedir, ofrecer, dar to indicate who receives or is asked for help.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs: pedir ayuda a (ask someone for help), ofrecer ayuda a (offer help to), dar ayuda a (give help to). The preposition 'a' introduces the person or group receiving the help. When using pronouns, indirect object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, os, les) often replace or accompany 'a + noun' (e.g., le pedí ayuda a María → le pedí ayuda / I asked María for help).
target_language_example: Voy a pedir ayuda a mi profesor.
native_language_example: I'm going to ask my teacher for help.

meaning: help from a (masculine) — 'help from a/one'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something provides assistance; 'un' is the masculine indefinite article and agrees with a masculine noun (e.g., 'intérprete', 'amigo'). Often appears in phrases like 'con la ayuda de un...' (with the help of a...). For feminine nouns use 'ayuda de una'.
target_language_example: Pude terminar el proyecto con la ayuda de un amigo.
native_language_example: I was able to finish the project with the help of a friend.

meaning: to help him/you (formal) to + verb (i.e., to assist someone in doing something).
additional_notes: Combines the verb ayudar (to help) + object pronoun lo (him/you formal) + the preposition a introducing an infinitive. Use 'ayudarlo a + infinitive' to say you'll help someone do a specific action. If the person is feminine use 'ayudarla a'; for plural 'ayudarlos/as a'. In casual speech you may also hear the pronoun placed before the conjugated verb (e.g., 'lo ayudaré a...').
target_language_example: Voy a ayudarlo a terminar su tarea esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to help him finish his homework this afternoon.

meaning: to help you with / to help you in (doing something).
additional_notes: Common way to offer or describe assistance. Often followed by a noun, infinitive, or phrase (e.g., 'en lo que necesites', 'en otra ocasión', 'en todo'). 'Ayudarte' is the infinitive 'ayudar' + object pronoun 'te' (to you). Replace 'te' with other pronouns as needed: 'ayudarme', 'ayudarlo', 'ayudarles', etc.
target_language_example: Puedo ayudarte en la mudanza este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I can help you with the move this weekend.

meaning: you help
additional_notes: "Ayudes" is the tú present subjunctive form of ayudar. It often appears after que in sentences like quiero que / necesito que, where it means "(that) you help." The a may introduce an infinitive (ayudes a huir = help escape) or a person (ayudes a Tom = help Tom).
target_language_example: Quiero que me ayudes a estudiar.
native_language_example: I want you to help me study.

meaning: blue and (used to connect 'blue' with another item or color)
additional_notes: This is simply the adjective 'azul' (blue) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). It appears when listing two colors or items, e.g. 'azul y blanco' (blue and white) or 'azul y rojo' (blue and red). Word order follows noun: camisa azul y pantalones blancos (blue shirt and white pants). Pronunciation: /aˈθul i/ or /aˈsul i/ depending on dialect. Not idiomatic on its own — it's a compositional phrase.
target_language_example: Compró una camisa azul y una chaqueta negra.
native_language_example: He bought a blue shirt and a black jacket.

meaning: 'the sugar is' or 'sugar is' — simple subject + verb phrase used to describe sugar (taste, quality, etc.).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's the noun azúcar (sugar) followed by the verb ser (es). Use to make general statements about sugar: its taste, properties, or to define it. Remember: azúcar can be used with or without the article (el/lo/todo) depending on whether you mean 'the sugar' (specific) or 'sugar' in general. Example sentences show both 'El azúcar es...' (the sugar is...) and 'Todo azúcar es...' / 'Todo el azúcar es...' (all sugar is / all the sugar is ...).
target_language_example: El azúcar es muy dulce en este café.
native_language_example: The sugar is very sweet in this coffee.

meaning: a year later / one year after.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens one year after a previously mentioned time or event. Often appears as 'un año después' (a year later) but can drop the article depending on context (e.g., 'año después' in headlines or informal narration). Can be followed by a comma when starting a sentence.
target_language_example: Un año después volvimos al mismo lugar.
native_language_example: A year later we returned to the same place.

meaning: the year when / the year in which (something happened).
additional_notes: Use to refer to a specific year when an event occurred. Commonly followed by a clause with a verb (e.g., 'el año en que nací' = 'the year I was born'). Interchangeable with 'el año en que' and sometimes with 'el año en el que' or simply 'el año que' in informal speech.
target_language_example: Ese fue el año en que conocí a mi mejor amiga.
native_language_example: That was the year when I met my best friend.

meaning: school year; the academic year.
additional_notes: Refers to the period when schools are in session (grades K–12, primary/secondary, or equivalent). Used to talk about when classes start or end, custody arrangements during the school year, and other timing tied to the academic calendar.
target_language_example: El año escolar comienza en septiembre en mi país.
native_language_example: The school year begins in September in my country.

meaning: New Year (the new calendar year; also the holiday 'New Year's').
additional_notes: Used to refer to the start of the next calendar year or the holiday period around January 1. Can be used in greetings (e.g., "Feliz Año Nuevo") or when talking about goals, wishes, or the beginning of the year.
target_language_example: Feliz Año Nuevo a todos; espero que este año nuevo sea mejor.
native_language_example: Happy New Year everyone; I hope this new year is better.

meaning: 'next year'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the year following the current one. Interchangeable with 'el año que viene' (more common in some regions). Often appears with definite article 'el' (el año próximo).
target_language_example: El año próximo viajaré a España.
native_language_example: Next year I will travel to Spain.

meaning: 'years before' — indicates a number of years earlier than a referenced time or event.
additional_notes: Used after a number (e.g., 'dos años antes') or with a quantity omitted when context provides it. Common in past-tense narratives to say how many years earlier something happened relative to another event or moment. Can follow the time expression it modifies (e.g., 'Dos años antes, ...' or '...dos años antes de...').
target_language_example: Dos años antes había empezado a estudiar medicina.
native_language_example: Two years before he had started studying medicine.

meaning: for (a) ... years in/on/at the (used to say how long someone spent somewhere or doing something).
additional_notes: Commonly appears with a number (dos años, diez años, muchos años) to indicate duration. The preposition after 'años' can change depending on the location: 'años en el' or 'años en la' for masculine/feminine places (en el mar, en el campo, en el extranjero). Sometimes Spanish uses 'por' (por tres años) or 'durante' (durante muchos años) to express the same idea. Use 'vivir' or 'estar' with it to say someone lived or was somewhere for that period.
target_language_example: Viví cinco años en el extranjero.
native_language_example: I lived five years abroad.

meaning: for X years in/at (a place or institution).
additional_notes: Used to say how many years someone spent studying or staying at a place (e.g., colegio, universidad, cárcel, Siberia). The number usually appears before 'años' (e.g., 'tres años en la universidad'). 'En la' agrees with a feminine noun that follows (la universidad, la cárcel). For masculine nouns you'd use 'en el' (e.g., 'dos años en el colegio').
target_language_example: Estuve dos años en la universidad.
native_language_example: I spent two years at the university.

meaning: older than (by a number of years).
additional_notes: Used after a number to say someone is older than someone else. Structure: [number] años mayor que + person. Commonly appears with 'es' (he/she is) or other verbs. Can also be used with fewer words: 'es mayor que' (older than) without specifying years.
target_language_example: Ella es tres años mayor que su hermano.
native_language_example: She is three years older than her brother.

meaning: …years younger (than).
additional_notes: Used after a number to compare ages: X años menos (que Y) = X years younger than Y. Common in spoken and written Spanish. The word 'que' often follows to introduce the person being compared (puede omitirse if context is clear).
target_language_example: Mi primo tiene cinco años menos que yo.
native_language_example: My cousin is five years younger than me.

meaning: ‘... years older/younger than’ — expresses an age difference (X has Y years more than Z).
additional_notes: Used to compare ages: X años más que Y means X is Y years older. Can refer to exact numbers (cinco años más que) or vague amounts (un par de años más que = a couple of years older). Context determines direction: usually the subject before "tiene/era" is the older one. Common structure: [Person] tiene [número] años más que [otra persona].
target_language_example: María tiene dos años más que Juan.
native_language_example: María is two years older than Juan.

meaning: 'years that' / 'years when' — used to refer to a span of years or particular years related to an action or state.
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about how long something lasted (a period of years), years in which something happened, or years to be recovered/compensated. Often appears with a number (cinco años que...) or with a verb clause (años que viví...). Not a fixed idiom; literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Pasaron muchos años que no pude ver a mi familia.
native_language_example: Many years passed that I couldn't see my family.

meaning: used after a number of years to add extra time (e.g., 'years and X' — 'years and months' or 'years and more'), or as part of time expressions meaning 'years and' (to connect a time quantity with another unit or continuation).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in two ways: 1) as a connector in exact durations: 'cuatro años y tres meses' = 'four years and three months'; 2) as a loose continuation after a number or phrase: 'tengo veinte años y...' or 'hace tres años y desde entonces...' — often followed by another time unit, clause, or continuation. Not a standalone idiom; its meaning depends on the words that follow. In sentences like 'veinte años y conozco…' the 'y' links the duration to a consequence or additional information ('and ...').
target_language_example: Vivimos aquí cinco años y seis meses.
native_language_example: We have lived here five years and six months.

meaning: still can / may still (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is still possible or someone still has the ability/option to do something. 'Aún' = 'still' (can also be written 'aun' in some contexts, but 'aún' with accent emphasizes time). 'Puede' is the third-person singular of 'poder' (can/may). Common in statements about possibility or ability.
target_language_example: Aunque ha perdido fuerza, aún puede caminar unos metros.
native_language_example: Even though he has lost strength, he can still walk a few meters.

meaning: 'still has' or 'still has (something/some quality)'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone continues to possess something, have a quality, or be in a certain state. Aún can also be written with tilde as 'aún' (meaning 'still'/'yet') and is commonly placed before the verb. Context determines whether the object is concrete (book, guitar) or abstract (followers, feelings, work to do).
target_language_example: Ella aún tiene la carta que le escribiste.
native_language_example: She still has the letter you wrote her.

meaning: to make/see someone dance; 'bailar a' marks the person being danced or made to dance (direct object introduced by a).
additional_notes: In Spanish, when the direct object is a person, the preposition 'a' (personal a) is used after the verb. With 'bailar a' this can mean either 'to see someone dance' (ver bailar a alguien), 'to make someone dance' (hacer bailar a alguien), or going to a place to dance (bailar a + place in some dialects). Context determines whether it's seeing, causing, or going to dance. Not all uses require 'a' (e.g., 'bailar' alone means 'to dance').
target_language_example: Fui al festival y vi bailar a mi hermana en el escenario.
native_language_example: I went to the festival and saw my sister dance on stage.

meaning: 'to go down to' or 'to go downstairs to' (movement downward toward a specific place or to do something).
additional_notes: Used when someone descends (physically) to a lower level or goes down to a particular location to perform an action. Common with verbs of motion or followed by an infinitive/noun indicating purpose (e.g., bajar a cortar el pastel = go down to cut the cake). Can also be used to tell someone to bring people down (bajar a todos aquí abajo).
target_language_example: Voy a bajar a buscar las llaves.
native_language_example: I'm going to go down to look for the keys.

meaning: to lower one's head; to accept something reluctantly or submit (sometimes figurative: to give in)
additional_notes: Can be literal (physically lowering your head) or figurative (accepting defeat, yielding to someone or something). Context determines whether it means simple movement or submission/acceptance. Common in expressions like "no voy a bajar la cabeza" (I won't give in).
target_language_example: Después de la discusión no quiso bajar la cabeza y siguieron sin hablar.
native_language_example: After the argument he refused to back down and they kept not speaking.

meaning: to go down / to carry something down (feminine plural object).
additional_notes: Literal verb phrase: bajar = to go down, to lower, to take down. When followed by 'las' it refers to a feminine plural noun (e.g., las escaleras, las maletas). Can mean 'to go down the (stairs)' or 'to bring/carry the (items) down' depending on context. Common constructions: 'bajar las escaleras' (to go down the stairs), 'bajar las maletas' (to bring the suitcases down).
target_language_example: Ayúdame a bajar las maletas, por favor.
native_language_example: Help me take the suitcases down, please.

meaning: Literally 'low of'; commonly used to mean 'lower than' (in comparisons) or 'low/down in' (mood, level, etc.).
additional_notes: Used in two common senses: 1) Comparisons: colloquial variant in phrases like "más bajo de lo que..." to indicate 'lower than' (e.g., a price or ranking). Formal Spanish often prefers "más bajo que" or "más bajo de lo que..." depending on structure. 2) Describing state or position: with nouns like "ánimo" or "nivel" to mean 'down' or 'at a low level' (e.g., "bajo de ánimo", "nivel más bajo de la aldea").
target_language_example: El precio real era más bajo de lo que yo había pensado.
native_language_example: The actual price was lower than I had thought.

meaning: under lock and key; kept locked and safe.
additional_notes: Used to say something is locked up or securely stored (physically or figuratively). Common with doors, containers, valuables. Can be used literally (locked in a safe) or figuratively (kept hidden or inaccessible).
target_language_example: Guardo los documentos importantes bajo llave.
native_language_example: I keep the important documents under lock and key.

meaning: underground; below the surface of the ground.
additional_notes: Used literally to say something is under the ground (buried, or located below ground level). Can describe objects, buildings, or people (e.g., buried or dead). Context determines whether it means physically below ground (literal) or simply 'underground' as in below surface level. Not informal.
target_language_example: El refugio está bajo tierra para protegerse del incendio.
native_language_example: The shelter is underground to protect from the fire.

meaning: he/she/it lowered, took down, or went down the (past simple of bajar + definite article).
additional_notes: Bajar is a versatile verb: it can mean 'to lower' (something), 'to take down' (from a shelf), 'to descend' (go down), or 'to travel down' (a river). With an object after the article (el + noun) the meaning depends on the noun: e.g. bajó el precio (lowered the price), bajó el arma (took the gun down/put it down), bajó el libro (took the book down), bajó el río (went down the river). Context decides the sense. This entry shows the past tense (él/ella/usted bajó).
target_language_example: Ella bajó el cuadro de la pared.
native_language_example: She took the picture down from the wall.

meaning: 'balance of' / 'balance' or 'the balance of' (depending on context)
additional_notes: Can mean physical balance or equilibrium (e.g., balance of a photo, balance while driving) and also financial balance (amount owed on an account). Translate according to context: physical/social balance = 'balance' or 'equilibrium'; financial = 'balance' as in 'amount due' or 'account balance'. Often followed by a noun (balance de la vida, balance de la tarjeta).
target_language_example: El balance de la caja al final del día no cuadra.
native_language_example: The cash register's balance at the end of the day doesn't add up.

meaning: blue whale (the very large marine mammal).
additional_notes: Refers specifically to the species Balaenoptera musculus, the largest animal on Earth. Used as a noun phrase (feminine: la ballena azul). Not idiomatic—it's the literal name of the animal.
target_language_example: Vimos una ballena azul desde el barco durante la excursión.
native_language_example: We saw a blue whale from the boat during the tour.

meaning: sandbank; a raised area of sand in water that can ground a boat.
additional_notes: Used to describe a natural underwater or exposed ridge of sand in rivers, seas or lakes. Often causes boats to run aground (encallar). Can be singular or plural (bancos de arena). Not slang.
target_language_example: La embarcación chocó contra un banco de arena y quedó varada.
native_language_example: The vessel hit a sandbank and became stranded.

meaning: "bank in" or "bench in" (depends on context) — 'banco' can mean bank (financial) or bench (seat); 'en' means 'in' or 'on'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's simply the noun banco followed by the preposition en. Meaning depends on which sense of banco is intended: 1) banco = bank (financial institution): 'banco en [lugar]' → 'bank in [place]'. 2) banco = bench (seat): 'sentarse en un banco en [lugar]' → 'sit on a bench in [place]'. Pay attention to context (financial vs. physical seat). Word order is typical: banco en + location.
target_language_example: Nos sentamos en un banco en el parque.
native_language_example: We sat on a bench in the park.

meaning: the word 'banco' (bank/bench) followed by 'y' (and) — not a fixed phrase; just the noun 'banco' joined to another idea with 'y'.
additional_notes: This is not a single idiomatic expression. 'Banco' can mean a financial bank or a bench/seat depending on context. 'Y' simply means 'and' and connects 'banco' to the next part of the sentence. Pay attention to context and articles/verbs to know which meaning of 'banco' is intended. Examples: 'sentado en el banco y…' = sitting on the bench and…; 'entró en el banco y…' = entered the bank and….
target_language_example: Se sentó en el banco y esperó a su amiga.
native_language_example: He sat on the bench and waited for his friend.

meaning: a phrase used to indicate a specific bar/place associated with someone or something ("the bar of/at").
additional_notes: Used to specify which bar you mean by attaching a name, description, location or characteristic after de: e.g. 'bar de Harry' (Harry's bar), 'bar de la esquina' (the corner bar), or 'bar de karaoke' (karaoke bar). Can be neutral or carry negative tone depending on the noun that follows (e.g. insulting phrases). Common in spoken Spanish to point out ownership, type, or location.
target_language_example: Vamos al bar de Marta esta noche.
native_language_example: Let's go to Marta's bar tonight.

meaning: 'the ship/boat was' (simple past description using 'estar').
additional_notes: This combines barco (ship/boat) with the imperfect/past form estaba of estar, used to describe a state, location, or ongoing/past condition of the boat. Use estaba for past descriptions (location, condition, ongoing situation). If you want 'the ship was' as a completed event or to describe where it ended up, context may require estuvo (preterite) instead. 'Barco' is masculine: 'el barco estaba...'.
target_language_example: El barco estaba en el puerto cuando llegamos.
native_language_example: The ship was in the harbor when we arrived.

meaning: 'the ship/boat is' — simple present description of a boat's state or location.
additional_notes: A basic subject + verb phrase: 'el barco' (the ship/boat) + 'está' (third-person singular of estar). Use 'está' for temporary states, locations, or conditions (e.g., location, condition, being full, attached). For permanent characteristics you'd use 'es' instead. Replace 'el barco' with other subjects as needed.
target_language_example: El barco está en el puerto porque esperan cargas.
native_language_example: The ship is in the port because they are waiting for cargo.

meaning: literally 'ship and' — the noun barco (ship/boat) followed by the conjunction y ('and').
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's simply the word barco used together with the conjunction y to connect it to another word or clause (e.g., 'barco y carro' = 'boat and car', or 'llegó en barco y se marchó en avión' = 'he arrived by boat and left by plane'). Useful to know: barco means 'boat' or 'ship' depending on size and context; y is the common word for 'and'.
target_language_example: Llegó en barco y se quedó una semana en la isla.
native_language_example: He arrived by boat and stayed a week on the island.

meaning: database (a collection of organized information stored electronically).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an electronic system or file where data is stored and can be searched, updated, or uploaded. Common in tech, office, and everyday contexts when talking about lists, records, or stored information.
target_language_example: Guarda el archivo en la base de datos.
native_language_example: Save the file in the database.

meaning: literally 'trash of' or 'trash from'; used to indicate the source/type of trash or to describe something as '...'s trash' (often informal/pejorative).
additional_notes: Combines basura (trash) with de (of/from). Use to say what the trash is made of (e.g., bolsa de basura de plástico = plastic garbage bag) or to criticize something as 'trash from' a source (e.g., basura de los turistas = tourists' trash). Can also appear in colloquial expressions to insult a company or brand (basura de Visa). Word order and meaning depend on context: when followed by a material it describes composition; when followed by an agent it indicates possession or origin.
target_language_example: Hay mucha basura de las fiestas en el parque.
native_language_example: There is a lot of trash from the parties in the park.

meaning: literally 'trash in' — used to say 'trash in/at' a place or 'turn trash into' when followed by a noun.
additional_notes: This is a combination of the noun 'basura' (trash/garbage) and the preposition 'en' (in/on/into). Context determines meaning: 1) 'la basura en [lugar]' = 'the trash in [place]' (e.g., 'the day for trash in England'); 2) 'tirar basura en [lugar]' = 'throw trash in/on [the street]'; 3) 'convertir la basura en [algo]' = 'turn trash into [something]'. Pay attention to preposition use: 'en' can mean 'in', 'on', or be part of 'convertir ... en' meaning 'into'.
target_language_example: En mi ciudad reciclan para convertir la basura en energía.
native_language_example: In my city they recycle to turn trash into energy.

meaning: the battery of (something) — indicates possession: the battery belonging to a device.
additional_notes: Use 'batería del' + [device] to say a device's battery (del = de + el). Common devices: teléfono, auto/coche, control remoto, transmisor. Often appears with verbs like 'acabarse' (to run out), 'estar muerta' (to be dead), 'cargar' (to charge).
target_language_example: Se me olvidó cargar la batería del teléfono.
native_language_example: I forgot to charge the phone's battery.

meaning: 'baño' = bathroom; 'y' = and. Together they are simply the noun 'baño' followed by the conjunction 'y' (and).
additional_notes: This looks like a fragment where 'baño' (bathroom; bath) is immediately followed by 'y' to connect to the next idea. 'Baño' can mean: 1) a bathroom or restroom (place), 2) a bath (the act of bathing). Use context to tell which. The combination 'baño y' itself has no special idiomatic meaning — it's just the word plus 'and'.
target_language_example: Voy al baño y vuelvo en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I'm going to the bathroom and I'll be back in five minutes.

meaning: to drink a (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Beber = to drink. 'Una' is the feminine singular indefinite article (a / an) and agrees with a following feminine noun (taza, cerveza, poción). Use 'beber un' before masculine nouns (un vaso). Common in everyday speech; can be used reflexively in casual contexts (acabar de beberse una = to finish drinking one).
target_language_example: Voy a beber una taza de té.
native_language_example: I'm going to drink a cup of tea.

meaning: drinking water (is/are drinking water).
additional_notes: Present progressive: 'estar + gerundio' indicates an action happening right now. 'Bebiendo' is the gerund of 'beber' (to drink). Can be used with different subjects (él/ella/usted/nosotros etc.). If you want to say 'drinking (some) water' you can add 'algo de' or a quantity: 'está bebiendo algo de agua', 'estoy bebiendo un poco de agua.'
target_language_example: Él está bebiendo agua ahora.
native_language_example: He is drinking water now.

meaning: 'drank a' (past tense, third person singular).
additional_notes: Past simple (pretérito) of beber for he/she/it: bebió. Followed by an indefinite article (una/uno) and a noun: bebió una taza de café = he/she drank a cup of coffee. Can also appear with reflexive se (se bebió) to emphasize finishing the drink (he/she drank up). Use 'bebió un' before masculine nouns (un vaso, un vaso de agua).
target_language_example: María bebió una copa de jugo.
native_language_example: María drank a glass of juice.

meaning: the baby (with reflexive verb forms) — 'the baby' used as the subject in sentences with reflexive verbs or pronominal constructions
additional_notes: This entry pairs the noun bebé with the reflexive pronoun se that appears when the baby is the subject of a reflexive or pronominal verb (e.g., dormirse, convertirse, ponerse, quedarse, chuparse). In Spanish many verbs are used pronominally (with me/te/se/nos/os) to indicate actions done to oneself, changes of state, or certain involuntary actions. Word order: the reflexive pronoun se usually comes before a conjugated verb (El bebé se durmió) or attached to a gerund/infinitive (se está chupando / está chupándose). For gender: bebé can be bebé (male) or bebé/ la bebé (female).
target_language_example: La bebé se despertó a las seis.
native_language_example: The baby woke up at six.

meaning: the baby has / the baby is (in expressions using 'tener').
additional_notes: Uses the verb tener (to have) with bebé (baby). Common to describe possession, conditions, traits, or states: health issues (tiene intolerancia), physical features (tiene una cara linda), temporary states (tiene un día - colloquial for 'is having a day'). In Spanish, tener is used for many states where English uses 'to be' (e.g., tener hambre → to be hungry). Watch word order: 'El bebé tiene...' or 'Un bebé tiene...'.
target_language_example: El bebé tiene sueño y necesita dormir.
native_language_example: The baby is sleepy and needs to sleep.

meaning: the beauty of (something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the attractiveness, charm, or appealing quality of a person, place, thing, idea, or situation. Followed by a noun or phrase that names what is beautiful. Can also be used more abstractly (e.g., "y esa es la belleza de esto" = "and that's the beauty of this").
target_language_example: La belleza de la ciudad me dejó sin palabras.
native_language_example: The beauty of the city left me speechless.

meaning: the beauty of the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: A phrase used to point to the beauty possessed by a specific feminine noun that follows (e.g., 'belleza de la música' = 'the beauty of the music'). 'La' agrees with the noun that comes after; if the noun is masculine use 'belleza del'. Common in literary or descriptive contexts.
target_language_example: Me conmovió la belleza de la pintura.
native_language_example: I was moved by the beauty of the painting.

meaning: give a kiss to (someone) — used to say to pass on a kiss or to indicate someone kissed another person.
additional_notes: Commonly appears with the verb dar (dar un beso a) or verbs like dar/poner and with indirect object pronouns (le, me, te). Often used to ask someone to give a kiss on your behalf (Dale un beso a X de mi parte = Give X a kiss for me). Structure: dar un beso a + person.
target_language_example: Dale un beso a María de mi parte.
native_language_example: Give María a kiss for me.

meaning: a (type of) kiss; used to specify the kind, purpose, or source of a kiss (e.g., 'kiss of goodnight', 'kiss from').
additional_notes: Beso means 'kiss'. When followed by de + noun or phrase, it describes the type, purpose, origin, or characteristic of the kiss: 'beso de buenas noches' (goodnight kiss), 'beso de despedida' (farewell kiss), 'beso de mi parte' (a kiss from me / give my regards). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., 'beso de la vida' — a life-saving kiss). Word order and preposition are important: 'un beso de [X]'.
target_language_example: Le mandé un beso de cumpleaños por teléfono.
native_language_example: I sent them a birthday kiss over the phone.

meaning: the library of the / the ...'s library (feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is a possessive structure: 'biblioteca' (library) + 'de la' + noun (feminine or feminine-gendered place/organization) that owns or is associated with the library. Use 'de la' before feminine singular nouns (la escuela, la prisión, la orquesta). For masculine nouns use 'del' (de + el).
target_language_example: La biblioteca de la universidad tiene muchos libros digitales.
native_language_example: The university's library has many digital books.

meaning: 'library in' — the phrase 'biblioteca' (library) followed by the preposition 'en' (in/at) used to indicate location or means.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun 'biblioteca' plus the preposition 'en'. Use 'en' to say 'in/at' a place (e.g., 'en la ciudad' = 'in the city') or to indicate means with some verbs (e.g., 'en auto' = 'by car'). For location you usually include an article or place after 'en' (en la ciudad, en cada ciudad).
target_language_example: Voy a la biblioteca en la ciudad mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library in the city tomorrow.

meaning: 'bicycle' (with the verb 'es' = 'is') — used to say what/whose/what kind of bicycle something is.
additional_notes: The core word is bicicleta (feminine noun) meaning 'bicycle.' The examples show simple sentences using the verb ser (es) to identify or describe a bicycle: possession (es mía), age/condition (es vieja), color (es azul), or to identify who is riding it (va en bicicleta -> 'goes by bicycle'). In short, use 'bicicleta' with articles or possessives (la bicicleta, mi bicicleta) and 'es' to state facts or descriptions.
target_language_example: La bicicleta es nueva y roja.
native_language_example: The bicycle is new and red.

meaning: a bicycle for (someone or some purpose).
additional_notes: Bicicleta = 'bicycle'. When followed by para + noun/pronoun, it indicates who the bicycle is for or its purpose (e.g., 'para tu cumpleaños' = for your birthday; 'para su hijo' = for his son). Use para to express recipient, intended use, or comparison with 'como' in similes.
target_language_example: Le compré una bicicleta para su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I bought him/her a bicycle for his/her birthday.

meaning: "bicicleta" = bicycle; "por" is a preposition with several uses (through/around, by, for, because of).
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed phrase. In the example sentences the words appear together but serve different roles: (1–2) montar en bicicleta por + place = to ride a bicycle through/around (a place). Use montar en bicicleta or andar en bicicleta + por + lugar. (3–4) bicicleta por + occasion = in these sentences por means "for" (as in "for your birthday") — note Spanish more often uses "para" for recipients (Te daré/Te regalaré una bicicleta para tu cumpleaños) but "por tu cumpleaños" is also common to mean "on/for your birthday."
target_language_example: Vamos a montar en bicicleta por la playa el domingo.
native_language_example: We're going to ride a bicycle along the beach on Sunday.

meaning: The word 'bicicleta' = 'bicycle/bike'; 'y' = 'and'. Used when 'bicicleta' appears before 'y' in a sentence (e.g., 'bicicleta y ...' = 'bicycle and ...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's the noun bicicleta (feminine) followed by the conjunction y ('and'). Pay attention to gender and articles: la bicicleta. In speech you may also hear bici (informal short form). Examples show common verbs with bicicleta: subirse a (get on), caerse de (fall off), ponerse/quitarse casco (put on/take off helmet).
target_language_example: Me compré una bicicleta y la llevo al parque.
native_language_example: I bought a bicycle and I take it to the park.

meaning: "you'll be fine" or reassurance directed at 'you' (informal).
additional_notes: This pattern combines 'bien' (well/fine) with a pronoun or short clause addressing 'tú' (te) to reassure someone. Common in comforting phrases: 'Vas a estar bien, te... (lo prometo/juro/llevaré a casa)'. The pronoun 'te' marks the person being reassured. Use with familiar/informal 'tú'.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: vas a estar bien, te lo prometo.
native_language_example: Don't worry: you'll be fine, I promise you.

meaning: well to your / well with your (used to say something suits or fits someone/something); or 'know well' when combined with a person (conocer bien a tu ...).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed phrase. 'Bien' can modify verbs (conocer bien a tu hermano = I know your brother well) or adjectives (queda bien a tu camisa = it looks good with your shirt). Note that standard Spanish usually uses 'tu' without an article before a noun: 'tu hermano'. In some dialects or informal speech you might hear 'a tu' after verbs that take the personal object marker 'a' (e.g., 'conozco bien a tu hermano'), but more commonly you'll see 'conozco bien a tu hermano' (with 'a' marking the person).
target_language_example: Conozco bien a tu mejor amigo; es muy simpático.
native_language_example: I know your best friend well; he's very nice.

meaning: used to introduce an example or to mean 'such as' / 'as well as'.
additional_notes: Bien como is less common than simplemente using 'como' or 'así como'. It can appear in lists or to emphasize inclusion: 'bien' here strengthens or clarifies the following 'como' ('for example' / 'as well as'). In many contexts native speakers prefer 'como' or 'así como'.
target_language_example: Trajo fruta, bien como manzanas y naranjas, bien como plátanos.
native_language_example: He brought fruit, such as apples and oranges, as well as bananas.

meaning: well / fine as (in the state that)... (used to say something is good enough or acceptable as it is)
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like 'está bien como está' (it's fine as it is) or 'suficientemente bien como para...' (good enough to...). It can indicate adequacy or that no change is needed. Not a fixed idiom by itself—meaning depends on surrounding words (e.g., 'tan bien como' = 'as well as').
target_language_example: Está bien como está; no hace falta cambiar nada.
native_language_example: It's fine as it is; there's no need to change anything.

meaning: 'as well as I' (used to compare someone else's ability/knowledge to the speaker's).
additional_notes: Common comparative phrase: 'tan + adjective/adverb + como' means 'as ... as'. Here 'bien' = 'well'. Often used to say someone does something to the same degree as the speaker (ability, knowledge). Can be placed after the verb or clause: 'Habla inglés tan bien como yo.'
target_language_example: Ella cocina tan bien como yo.
native_language_example: She cooks as well as I do.

meaning: 'well with' or 'get along with' / 'look good with' (used with people or things).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like llevarse (llevarse bien con = get along with) or quedar/combinar/verse (quedar bien con, combinar bien con, verse bien con = to look good with or match). With people it means to have a good relationship; with clothes/objects it means to match or look good together. Common construction: llevarse bien con + alguien.
target_language_example: Me llevo muy bien con mis compañeros de trabajo.
native_language_example: I get along very well with my coworkers.

meaning: well taken care of; well maintained
additional_notes: Used to describe people, animals, plants, objects, or places that receive good care or maintenance. Can describe appearance (well-groomed) or condition (in good repair). Often follows the noun: un jardín bien cuidado, un perro bien cuidado. Not idiomatic—meaning is literal.
target_language_example: El jardín está bien cuidado durante todo el año.
native_language_example: The garden is well taken care of throughout the year.

meaning: 'well' or 'okay' after (something); feeling or being fine following an event or action.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is fine/okay after a specific event, action, or time (e.g., after sleeping, after a repair, after an incident). Can be followed by a noun, an infinitive, or a clause introduced by 'lo de'. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Estará bien después de descansar un poco.
native_language_example: He/She/It will be fine after resting a bit.

meaning: doing well in (a place, situation, or event) / feeling fine at (a place).
additional_notes: Used to say someone performed well or felt good 'in' a specific context (e.g., en el examen, en el concierto, en el sofá). 'Bien' describes how something went or how someone felt; 'en el' is the preposition + masculine article for the place or event. Change article/gender as needed (bien en la, bien en los, bien en las). Can also be used idiomatically with people (caer bien/mal) or general situations.
target_language_example: Ella estuvo bien en el concierto.
native_language_example: She did well at the concert.

meaning: well/in good condition in (a short time) or thoroughly/closely in (a mirror, trip) depending on context.
additional_notes: This sequence combines 'bien' (well/well enough/thoroughly) + 'en un' (in a [short] time or in a [place/thing]). Common uses: 1) Time expressions: 'bien en un minuto/par de días' = 'completely recovered/finished in about...' or 'I'll be fine in...' 2) With reflexive verbs + mirror/place: 'mírense bien en un espejo' = 'look at yourself carefully in a mirror.' 3) With getting to know someone: 'conocerse bien en un viaje' = 'get to know each other well during a trip.' Meaning depends on the verb and the noun that follows 'un'.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, estaré bien en un rato.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll be fine in a little while.

meaning: well done
additional_notes: Used to praise someone for a good job or correct action ("well done"). Can also describe the quality of a finished task or object ("a job well done" / "done properly"). With intensifier 'muy' it means 'very well done'.
target_language_example: Un trabajo bien hecho siempre dura más.
native_language_example: A job well done always lasts longer.

meaning: when examined closely; on closer look
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reconsideration or new perspective after thinking or looking more carefully. Often placed at the start or middle of a sentence: 'Bien mirado, ...' It is somewhat formal/neutral and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Bien mirado, fue la mejor decisión que tomamos.
native_language_example: On closer look, it was the best decision we made.

meaning: 'well' or 'okay' in choices/alternatives; used in questions/phrases to present alternatives like 'well or not' / 'okay or...'.
additional_notes: Used to offer or check an alternative, to ask if something is acceptable, or to present two possible outcomes (good vs. bad). Often appears in short spoken phrases: 'bien o no' (well or not), '¿estamos bien o...?' (are we okay or...?). Can also appear in conditional warnings: 'pórtate bien o...' (behave or...). Context determines whether it contrasts states (well vs. unwell), accepts/rejects an option, or sets a consequence.
target_language_example: Dime si estás bien o prefieres descansar.
native_language_example: Tell me if you're okay or you'd rather rest.

meaning: good-looking; attractive (usually about a person).
additional_notes: Common adjective phrase describing someone's physical appearance. Often used with ser/estar (es/está bien parecido) or as a standalone description (es un chico bien parecido). Neutral to informal register; can describe men or women but is more frequently used for men in some regions. Does not imply personality—only looks.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que su hermano es muy bien parecido.
native_language_example: She said her brother is very good-looking.

meaning: can mean 'good for' (congratulating or approving), 'well for' (benefit), or 'watch/look out for' in some constructions.
additional_notes: Usage depends on context. Commonly used as an interjection: 'Bien por él/ella' = 'Good for him/her' (approval or mild congratulations). As part of a phrase about benefit: 'bien por sí mismo' = 'well for himself' or 'did well for himself.' With payment: 'pagar bien por' = 'pay well for.' In literal directional sense 'mira bien por dónde vas' = 'look carefully at where you're going' (here 'por' introduces direction/route and 'bien' means 'carefully'). Not a fixed idiom with one meaning—learn by context.
target_language_example: Bien por ti, te lo mereces.
native_language_example: Good for you, you deserve it.

meaning: although / even though (expresses contrast).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause showing contrast. In many examples here Spanish uses constructions like "lo bien que" (how well) or "por lo bien que" (because of how well) — these are related but different: "bien que" alone = 'although'; "lo bien que" = 'how/what a good way that...'. Pay attention to word order and context.
target_language_example: Bien que llueva, iremos al parque.
native_language_example: Although it's raining, we'll go to the park.
