additional_notes: Refers to films from the early era of cinema (or any film without recorded dialogue). Commonly used when talking about the film style, era, or preference. Can be used with verbs of liking/disliking (me apasiona, me apesta, me carga) or with verbs about watching (ver, me veo).
target_language_example: Me encanta ver cine mudo los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I love watching silent films on weekends.

meaning: seat belt; safety belt.
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to the belt in cars (or other vehicles) that keeps passengers secure. Often appears in safety instructions and signs. Use el cinturón (singular) for one belt; poner/se abrochar/abrochárselo are common verbs (ponerse el cinturón, abrocharse el cinturón).
target_language_example: Por favor, abróchese el cinturón de seguridad antes de arrancar.
native_language_example: Please fasten your seat belt before starting.

meaning: plastic surgery (medical surgery to change or reconstruct the body's appearance or function).
additional_notes: Refers to surgical procedures for cosmetic (aesthetic) or reconstructive purposes. Common contexts: cosmetic enhancements (e.g., rhinoplasty, breast augmentation) and reconstructive surgery after injury or illness. Used as a general noun; often preceded by articles (la, una).
target_language_example: Después del accidente necesitó cirugía plástica para reconstruir la cara.
native_language_example: After the accident she needed plastic surgery to rebuild her face.

meaning: 'the city is' — used to describe the location, condition, or state of a city.
additional_notes: This is simply the noun ciudad (city) plus the verb estar (to be). Use 'está' for singular third person. Estar is used for locations (physical position), temporary states or conditions, and certain idiomatic expressions (e.g., 'está maldita' = it's cursed; 'está al corriente' = is up to date/informed). For permanent characteristics use ser instead (e.g., 'La ciudad es grande').
target_language_example: La ciudad está cerca del río.
native_language_example: The city is near the river.

meaning: 'the city was' (passive past: ciudad + fue + past participle)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common passive construction: ciudad (subject) + fue (third-person singular preterite of ser) + past participle (e.g., destruida, abandonada, bombardeada). It means 'the city was ...' (something happened to it in the past). Use when describing an action done to the city in the past. For present passive use 'es' or progressive passive if needed.
target_language_example: La ciudad fue reconstruida después del terremoto.
native_language_example: The city was rebuilt after the earthquake.

meaning: used to emphasize or add clarity, similar to 'and of course' or 'clearly, and...'
additional_notes: This phrase combines claro ('clear' / 'of course') with y ('and') to link or emphasize an additional point. It often introduces a follow-up comment or reinforces agreement: e.g., 'claro, y...' or 'claro y...' depending on speech. Common in spoken Spanish; tone determines strength (friendly, emphatic, or corrective).
target_language_example: Llegaremos a tiempo, claro y traeré los documentos.
native_language_example: We'll arrive on time, and of course I'll bring the documents.

meaning: of course; obviously.
additional_notes: Used to add or emphasize that something is obvious or expected. Often appears at the start or end of a sentence (like 'claro está,' or '..., claro está'). Tone can be neutral or slightly emphatic. Equivalent to 'por supuesto' or 'claro' in many contexts.
target_language_example: No podremos entrar sin invitación, claro está.
native_language_example: We can't get in without an invitation, of course.

meaning: of course
additional_notes: Used to agree or confirm something strongly. Often followed by a clause: claro que sí (of course yes), claro que no (of course not). Can be used alone as a short reply (¡Claro!). Tone can be emphatic or friendly depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Vienes a la fiesta? — Claro que sí.
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party? — Of course.

meaning: Of course I (do). / Sure I (will).
additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or agree with something about the speaker (first person). 'Claro que' adds emphasis ('of course'), and 'me' indicates the action affects the speaker (me). Often followed by a verb: claro que me acuerdo (of course I remember); claro que me iré (of course I will leave). Tone is natural in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Claro que me ayudaré cuando puedas.
native_language_example: Of course I will help when you can.

meaning: Of course not; definitely not.
additional_notes: An emphatic phrase used to reject or deny something strongly. Tone depends on context — can be gentle (with cariño) or firm/irritated (with pues). Often used alone as a short response.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir ahora? — ¡Claro que no, es muy tarde!
native_language_example: Do you want to come now? — Of course not, it's very late!

meaning: of course; sure; definitely.
additional_notes: A strong, affirmative phrase used to agree or confirm something. Can be used alone or followed by a noun/pronoun. Tone ranges from friendly to emphatic. Similar to 'por supuesto' but slightly more conversational. Can be used sarcastically depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: ¿Vienes a la fiesta? — Claro que sí.
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party? — Of course.

meaning: middle class (socioeconomic group).
additional_notes: Refers to people, households, neighborhoods, or social groups with moderate income, education, and lifestyle—between working class and upper/upper-middle class. Can be modified (clase media baja, clase media alta) to specify lower or upper middle class. Used in both neutral and sometimes critical contexts.
target_language_example: María vive en un barrio de clase media.
native_language_example: María lives in a middle-class neighborhood.

meaning: social class; a group's position in society based on wealth, education, or status.
additional_notes: Used to talk about socioeconomic groups (upper, middle, lower class). Can refer to someone's background, group identity, or societal standing. Common in discussions about inequality, culture, and belonging.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay mucha división entre la clase social alta y la clase social baja.
native_language_example: In this city there is a lot of division between the upper social class and the lower social class.

meaning: 'classes/lessons at or in (a place)'; used to say you teach or that classes take place at a location.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dar (dar clases = to give/teach classes) or estar/haber (estar dando clases = teaching; no hay clases = there are no classes). 'En' indicates the place (school, faculty, month as time: 'en agosto' meaning during August). For beginners: think 'teach/hold classes at' or 'classes in/at'.
target_language_example: Doy clases en el centro cultural los sábados.
native_language_example: I teach classes at the cultural center on Saturdays.

meaning: 'the customer is always (right)' — refers to the idea that the customer’s opinion/needs should be prioritized.
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of the common proverb 'el cliente siempre tiene la razón' (the customer is always right). It’s used in service contexts to express that businesses should satisfy customers, even if the customer is mistaken. Not a literal rule—often used as a guideline, slogan, or justification for accommodating customers.
target_language_example: En nuestro restaurante seguimos el lema: el cliente siempre tiene la razón.
native_language_example: In our restaurant we follow the motto: the customer is always right.

meaning: the weather/climate here
additional_notes: Used to talk about the local weather or climate where the speaker is. 'Clima' refers to general climate or typical weather patterns; for immediate weather you might also say 'el tiempo aquí'. Often followed by adjectives (templado, frío, suave) or comparisons (más que...).
target_language_example: El clima aquí suele ser muy agradable en primavera.
native_language_example: The climate here is usually very pleasant in spring.

meaning: literally 'climate/weather and' — the word 'clima' (weather/climate) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and); not a fixed phrase on its own.
additional_notes: This is not a set expression. It appears when 'clima' (meaning 'weather' or 'climate') is followed by 'y' to connect another idea (e.g., 'clima y tráfico'). Depending on context, 'clima' can mean short-term weather (el clima hoy) or long-term climate (el clima de la región). Don't treat 'clima y' as a single vocabulary item; learn 'clima' (noun) and 'y' (and) separately.
target_language_example: El informe incluye el clima y la calidad del aire.
native_language_example: The report includes the weather and the air quality.

meaning: my (family member's) car / the car that belongs to my ...
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession: 'coche de mi + family member' means 'my [family member]'s car'. In natural Spanish it's more common to say 'el coche de mi padre' or use a possessive adjective: 'mi padre' usually requires 'el coche de mi padre' or 'el coche de mi' isn't used alone. Keep the family member after 'mi' (mi padre, mi madre, mi marido, etc.).
target_language_example: Es el coche de mi hermano.
native_language_example: It's my brother's car.

meaning: electric car
additional_notes: Refers to a car powered by electricity (battery or electric motor) rather than gasoline. Commonly used in Spain and many Spanish-speaking countries; 'coche' = car, 'eléctrico' = electric. Can be used in singular/plural: coches eléctricos.
target_language_example: Ella conduce un coche eléctrico para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: She drives an electric car to work.

meaning: ‘the car is’ — used to describe the condition or state of a car.
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: 'coche' = car, 'está' = (he/she/it) is (temporary state). Commonly used to say where a car is (location) or its condition (e.g., damaged, under repair). Remember 'está' (from estar) indicates temporary states or locations, not permanent characteristics.
target_language_example: Mi coche está en el taller desde ayer.
native_language_example: My car has been at the shop since yesterday.

meaning: This is not a fixed phrase in Spanish; it's the noun 'coche' (car) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and).
additional_notes: You won't find 'coche y' as a single expression. In the example sentences it appears because 'coche' (car) is used in different sentences and sometimes followed by 'y' to join ideas (e.g., 'coche y mis padres' = 'car and my parents', or 'se metió en el coche y arrancó' = 'got into the car and started off'). Learn 'coche' = car and 'y' = and separately. Word order: 'coche y ...' = 'car and ...'.
target_language_example: Entró en el coche y cerró la puerta.
native_language_example: He got into the car and closed the door.

meaning: take a / grab a (informal imperative or present tense: he/she/you take/grab a).
additional_notes: From the verb coger (to take, grab). In many Spanish-speaking regions coger is neutral and common; in some countries (e.g., parts of Latin America) it can be vulgar—use 'toma' or 'agarra' instead there. 'Coge un' is followed by a noun: e.g. an object, a number, or an action (take a shortcut = 'coge un atajo'). Context and person matters: 'coge' can be él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal) or informal imperative in some dialects (Spain uses 'coge' as tú imperative less often; 'coge' is standard present for él/ella/usted).
target_language_example: Coge un taxi si llueve mucho.
native_language_example: Take a taxi if it's raining hard.

meaning: to catch/take the first (e.g., the first train, bus, flight).
additional_notes: Common phrase used before a transport noun (tren, autobús, vuelo). 'Coger' here means 'to catch' or 'to take' (transport). In some Spanish-speaking regions (e.g., parts of Latin America) coger can be considered vulgar — in those areas use tomar (tomar el primer tren). Usually followed by the vehicle: 'coger el primer tren'.
target_language_example: Tuve que correr para coger el primer autobús.
native_language_example: I had to run to catch the first bus.

meaning: to pick up the phone; to answer a call.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used when someone physically lifts the handset or answers a ringing phone. In some Spanish-speaking countries (notably parts of Latin America) the verb 'coger' can be vulgar, so speakers there may prefer 'contestar el teléfono' or 'tomar la llamada'. In Spain, 'coger el teléfono' is neutral and very common.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes coger el teléfono? Está sonando.
native_language_example: Can you pick up the phone? It's ringing.

meaning: 'in the line/queue for' or 'in the (something)' (literally 'queue of the')
additional_notes: Used to say someone is waiting in a line or queue for a specific place or service. 'Cola' means 'line/queue' and is often followed by 'del' (de + el) + the place (cine, banco, supermercado, avión). In English you usually say 'in line for the...'.
target_language_example: Estuve en la cola del banco más de una hora.
native_language_example: I was in line for the bank for more than an hour.

meaning: 'colegio' = school; 'y' = and. Together they appear as 'school and...' or in phrases like 'to/from school and ...' (i.e., the word 'colegio' followed by 'y' = and).
additional_notes: This isn't a fixed phrase—it's the noun colegio (school) plus the conjunction y (and). Use 'colegio' to mean primary/secondary school (not university). 'Y' simply connects items or clauses. Pay attention to context: 'ir al colegio' = go to school; 'entre el colegio y la estación' = between the school and the station. Word order and articles (el/mi) matter: 'el colegio y la universidad' = the school and the university.
target_language_example: Los padres esperan fuera del colegio y hablan entre ellos.
native_language_example: The parents wait outside the school and talk among themselves.

meaning: "color is" — simple statement linking a noun 'color' with a description or identification.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the noun 'color' and the verb 'es' (third-person singular of 'ser'). Use to say what color something is or to comment on the color. In Spanish word order: subject (el color / su color) + es + adjective or noun. You can also say 'es de color...' to specify color in another way.
target_language_example: Su color es azul oscuro.
native_language_example: Its color is dark blue.

meaning: 'eat with' or 'eat using' (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate who you eat with (eat together) or what you use to eat (e.g., with hands, fork). Context determines meaning: when followed by a person it means 'eat with someone' (share a meal); when followed by an instrument or body part it means 'eat using' that instrument. Verb is third-person singular of comer (come).
target_language_example: Esta noche come con su familia en casa.
native_language_example: Tonight he/she eats with his/her family at home.

meaning: eats everything; eats a lot (literal: 'he/she/it eats everything').
additional_notes: From the verb comer (to eat) + todo (everything). Used literally to say someone eats all food or figuratively to describe someone who eats a lot or is not picky. Context and subject are provided by conjugation (come = él/ella/usted or present tense with 'it'). To say 'I eat everything' use 'como de todo' or 'me como todo'.
target_language_example: Mi hermano come todo lo que le pones en el plato.
native_language_example: My brother eats everything you put on his plate.

meaning: 'to begin the' or 'to start the' (followed by a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Comenzar means 'to begin/start'. When followed by the definite article 'el' it introduces a specific masculine noun: comenzar el viaje (to begin the trip). Use 'comenzar la' for feminine nouns and 'comenzar' + infinitive for starting an action (comenzar a + infinitive). Commonly interchangeable with 'empezar el'.
target_language_example: Vamos a comenzar el proyecto mañana.
native_language_example: We're going to start the project tomorrow.

meaning: began/the ... began (past tense, third person singular) — 'comenzó' = 'began'; 'el' = the (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used to say that something started at a certain time or event. 'Comenzó' is the preterite (simple past) of comenzar. 'El' is the definite article; together they typically introduce a noun or time phrase (e.g., 'comenzó el incendio', 'comenzó el día'). For other genders/numbers use the matching article (la, los, las) or drop the article if not needed.
target_language_example: Comenzó el concierto a las ocho en punto.
native_language_example: The concert began at eight o'clock.

meaning: '(he/she/it) started the' or '(someone) began the' (past tense, third person singular).
additional_notes: Comenzó is the preterite (simple past) of comenzar (to begin/start). 'La' is a feminine singular definite article referring to a feminine noun that follows (e.g., la clase, la guerra). Use for actions completed in the past. For masculine nouns use 'comenzó el'.
target_language_example: Ella comenzó la reunión a las nueve.
native_language_example: She started the meeting at nine.

meaning: began a / started a (feminine noun follows).
additional_notes: Past tense (él/ella/usted) of comenzar (to begin). Use 'comenzó una' before a feminine noun or event: 'comenzó una discusión', 'comenzó una noche'. In English you can usually translate as 'began a' or 'it began on/one...' depending on context. For time expressions like 'comenzó una mañana de enero' it means 'it began on a January morning.'
target_language_example: La película comenzó una tarde lluviosa.
native_language_example: The movie began on a rainy afternoon.

target_language_multi_word_term: comer a los / dar de comer a los
meaning: 'eat' (used with animals attacking people) / 'feed' (give food to someone/animals)
additional_notes: Two related uses appear in the examples: 1) comer a (los) + people — describes animals attacking and eating people (literal, often violent). 2) dar de comer a (los) + animals/people — to give food to someone or to feed animals. Context and pronouns change meaning (e.g., "te darán de comer a los perros" = 'they will kill you and feed you to the dogs'). "A" marks the person/animal affected. Useful verbs: comer (to eat), dar de comer (to feed).
target_language_example: No lo dejes solo; los coyotes se pueden comer a los pequeños con facilidad.
native_language_example: Don't leave him alone; coyotes can eat the little ones easily.

meaning: to eat here (in this place).
additional_notes: Used to indicate where someone will eat or is trying to eat. Can refer to dining at the current location (restaurant, home, bench, etc.). Often follows verbs like intentar, poder, querer, and ir (van a comer aquí = they are going to eat here).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres comer aquí o llevar la comida?
native_language_example: Do you want to eat here or take the food away?

meaning: to eat like (followed by a comparison), often used to say someone eats in a certain way (e.g. 'eat like a pig').
additional_notes: Used with a comparison after 'como' (e.g., 'como un cerdo', 'como antes', 'como ellos'). Can describe manner, habit, or style of eating. Common in expressions that are informal or colloquial when describing messy or excessive eating.
target_language_example: Antes de la dieta, yo solía comer como un cerdo.
native_language_example: Before the diet, I used to eat like a pig.

meaning: to eat in/at the (feminine place).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone eats when the location word is feminine and definite article 'la' is required (e.g., la ciudad, la calle, la cocina, la oficina). For masculine places use 'comer en el' or just 'comer en'. Can also appear with plural or other articles: 'comer en la despensa' (in the pantry).
target_language_example: Prefiero comer en la cocina cuando estoy en casa.
native_language_example: I prefer to eat in the kitchen when I'm at home.

meaning: junk food; unhealthy, low-nutrition food.
additional_notes: Used to describe food high in calories, fats, sugar, or salt (fast food, chips, sweets). Commonly uncountable in Spanish; often used with verbs like comer (to eat). Can be used in singular or repeated as 'comida basura' regardless of amount.
target_language_example: Trato de evitar la comida basura entre semana.
native_language_example: I try to avoid junk food during the week.

meaning: food in/inside (used to say where food is located).
additional_notes: comida = food. 'en' is a preposition meaning 'in' or 'inside'. Used to indicate the location or container where food is (e.g., en el horno, en la nevera, en la despensa, en lata). Combine with a noun or article after 'en' (en la nevera, en el horno).
target_language_example: Hay comida en el refrigerador para el almuerzo.
native_language_example: There is food in the refrigerator for lunch.

meaning: "the food is" — used to describe food (quality, price, importance, etc.).
additional_notes: Comida = food. Adding 'es' (from ser) states a general characteristic or fact about the food (e.g., price, quality, essential nature). Use 'está' instead of 'es' when describing temporary states or conditions (e.g., tastes good right now). 'La comida' can also mean 'mealtime' depending on context ('la hora de la comida' = lunchtime).
target_language_example: La comida es muy sabrosa en este restaurante.
native_language_example: The food is very tasty at this restaurant.

meaning: ‘more food’ or used in phrases like ‘more + (adjective) food’ (e.g. healthier/more important food).
additional_notes: comida = food/meal. When combined with más it can mean 'more food' (quantity) or form part of comparative expressions: 'comida más + adjective' = 'food that is more + adjective' (e.g. comida más saludable = healthier food). In some contexts 'la comida más importante' means 'the most important meal' when referring to a meal of the day. Word order and article matter: 'más comida' (more food) vs 'comida más sana' (food that is healthier).
target_language_example: Deberías comer comida más saludable.
native_language_example: You should eat healthier food.

meaning: eating a
additional_notes: This is the present participle (gerund) form of comer (to eat) followed by the indefinite article un/una. It appears in continuous/progressive constructions or to describe someone currently eating something: e.g. (estar) comiendo un sándwich = (to be) eating a sandwich. Gender of the article must match the noun (un for masculine nouns, una for feminine: comiendo una manzana). Often used with forms of estar (estoy, estás, está, estamos, están) to form the present progressive.
target_language_example: Estoy comiendo un sándwich ahora.
native_language_example: I am eating a sandwich right now.

meaning: committee of / committee for (used to name a committee associated with a person, purpose, place, or task).
additional_notes: Combine 'comité' (committee) with 'de' + noun to indicate what the committee is about or who it belongs to (e.g., 'comité de campaña' = campaign committee; 'comité de disciplina' = disciplinary committee). In English you may translate it as 'committee on', 'committee for', or 'committee of' depending on context. Word order is 'comité de' + noun.
target_language_example: Organizaron un comité de seguridad para el evento.
native_language_example: They organized a safety committee for the event.

meaning: the committee (with a reflexive/pronominal verb) — 'the committee' as subject when used with verbs that include the reflexive pronoun 'se' (e.g., reunirse, odiarse).
additional_notes: This entry pairs the noun 'comité' with the reflexive pronoun 'se' that appears when the verb is pronominal (reunirse, sentirse, odiarse, etc.). In Spanish the pronoun 'se' goes before the conjugated verb (El comité se reúne) or can attach to an infinitive/gerund (van a reunirse). The meaning depends on the verb: with 'reunir(se)' it means 'to meet'; with 'odiarse' it means 'to hate each other' (if the subject is plural or collective it can imply mutual action). Use agreement: 'El comité se reúne' (singular committee meets) vs 'Los comités se reúnen' (plural).
target_language_example: El comité se va a reunir mañana para decidir el presupuesto.
native_language_example: The committee is going to meet tomorrow to decide the budget.

meaning: 'ate the' (past tense of 'comer' + direct object with personal 'a')
additional_notes: Comió is the third-person singular preterite of comer (to eat). When the direct object is a specific animate being (often a person or animal) Spanish uses the preposition 'a' before it: 'comió al X' = 'ate the X'. In these examples the subject (animal) ate another animal. This structure is literal (not idiomatic).
target_language_example: El zorro se comió al pollo en el corral.
native_language_example: The fox ate the chicken in the yard.

meaning: ate the
additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) third-person singular of comer plus the masculine singular definite article el. Used to say someone or something ate a specific (masculine) noun mentioned or understood from context. In Spanish word order the verb comes before the article + noun (comió el pastel = ate the cake). If the noun is feminine the article would be la (comió la).
target_language_example: Ella comió el sándwich en el coche.
native_language_example: She ate the sandwich in the car.

meaning: ate my (something).
additional_notes: A past simple form (pretérito) of comer + possessive 'mi'. Often used with animals or people to say they ate one of your things. In Spanish you can include a reflexive 'se' with certain verbs (se comió) to emphasize that the action was completed or that the eater consumed the item entirely. Word order: subject + (se) comió + mi + noun.
target_language_example: El gato se comió mi cena.
native_language_example: The cat ate my dinner.

meaning: 'ate all' (he/she/you formal ate everything of something).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of comer (comió) + toda (feminine singular) used to say someone ate all of a specific item (la comida, la torta, la manzana). If the noun is masculine use 'todo' (e.g., comió todo el pan). If reflexive 'se comió toda...' can add emphasis that the person finished it themselves. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Se comió toda la pizza en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: He/She ate all the pizza in five minutes.

meaning: he/she/they ate all of the (something).
additional_notes: This is the pronominal past (pretérito) form of comer with 'todo el' to mean someone ate all of a specific item (masculine singular noun follows: el jamón, el pan). 'Se' here is a reflexive/emphatic pronoun often used to emphasize the action or indicate it happened completely. In English you can translate as 'ate all the...' or 'ate up all the...'. Use 'toda la' for feminine nouns (toda la pizza) and 'todos los' for plural (todos los brownies).
target_language_example: Ella se comió todo el pastel en la reunión.
native_language_example: She ate all the cake at the meeting.

meaning: literally 'I eat and' or 'as and' — the conjunction 'y' (=and) joining 'como' (I eat / as).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the verb 'como' (first-person singular present of comer 'to eat') or the conjunction/comparative 'como' ('as', 'like') followed by 'y' ('and'). Meaning depends on context: in sentences like 'Como y bebo.' it means 'I eat and I drink.' When 'como' means 'as' or 'like', 'como y' connects two clauses (e.g. 'lo que como y asegurar...'). It's compositional and literal — just two separate words used together.
target_language_example: Como y trabajo todos los días.
native_language_example: I eat and I work every day.

meaning: as/like something (used to describe or compare something to a general idea or thing).
additional_notes: Commonly follows verbs like 'ver', 'sonar', 'hacer ver', 'tomar' and introduces a vague or general comparison—often translated as “like something” or “as something.” Can be used to downplay, describe appearance, or express perception (e.g., 'se ve como algo del futuro' = 'it looks like something from the future').
target_language_example: No lo tomes como algo personal.
native_language_example: Don't take it as something personal.

meaning: as friends / like friends
additional_notes: Used to say that people act, behave, meet, or are treated in the role of friends (not romantic partners or enemies). Can describe manner ('like friends') or status ('as friends'). Context decides whether it refers to behavior (acting friendly) or relationship (being friends).
target_language_example: Salimos a cenar como amigos.
native_language_example: We went out to dinner as friends.

meaning: exactly alike; like two drops of water (used to say two people look very similar).
additional_notes: An idiom meaning two people (often relatives) are nearly identical in appearance or behavior. Commonly used for twins or siblings. Can be used with 'ser' (son/son como...) or in short 'son como dos gotas de agua.' Tone: neutral; fits everyday speech.
target_language_example: Estas dos fotos son como dos gotas de agua; apenas hay diferencia.
native_language_example: These two photos are like two drops of water; there's hardly any difference.

meaning: like the wind; very fast, free, or effortless.
additional_notes: A simile used to say someone/something moves very quickly or is free/unstoppable. Can be literal (moving with wind) or figurative (very fast, fleeting, or free-spirited). Common in poetic or emphatic speech: 'corre como el viento' = 'runs very fast'.
target_language_example: Corre como el viento y llega a tiempo.
native_language_example: He runs like the wind and arrives on time.

meaning: like the
additional_notes: Used to compare something to a masculine singular noun. In Spanish, the noun is often left out if it is clear from context: como el tuyo = "like yours" / "like the one you have," como el de Ana = "like Ana's."
target_language_example: Quiero uno como el de la foto.
native_language_example: I want one like the one in the photo.

meaning: 'like in the old days' / 'like old times'.
additional_notes: Shortened form of the full phrase "como en los viejos tiempos." Used to say that a situation matches how things used to be — nostalgic. Common in statements about repeating a pleasant past experience. Can be followed by 'tiempos' or used in context where 'tiempos' is implied.
target_language_example: Nos reunimos y charlamos como en los viejos.
native_language_example: We met and chatted like in the old days.

meaning: know (someone/something) very well; be intimately familiar with
additional_notes: Usually completed as "como la palma de mi mano" (literally "like the palm of my hand"). Used to say you know a person, place, or thing extremely well. Common in everyday speech; can be used with objects, places, or people. Followed by the thing known: e.g. "conozco X como la palma de mi mano."
target_language_example: Conozco este barrio como la palma de mi mano.
native_language_example: I know this neighborhood like the palm of my hand.

meaning: at most; no more than; tops (limits a quantity or time).
additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit (quantity, time, age, etc.). Equivalent to 'at most' or 'no more than' in English; often placed after the number or time (e.g., 'cinco, como mucho') or at the end of the sentence. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Puedo quedarme una hora, como mucho.
native_language_example: I can stay one hour, at most.

meaning: at most; no more than; maximum.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a limit in quantity, time, price, etc. Often placed after the quantity or time (e.g., "dos días como máximo"). Equivalent to English 'at most' or 'no more than'.
target_language_example: Llegaré en una hora como máximo.
native_language_example: I'll arrive in an hour at most.

meaning: at least; minimum requirement or amount.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the smallest acceptable amount, degree, or expectation. Can appear alone as a short answer ("Como mínimo.") or within a sentence (usually followed by a clause or noun). Equivalent to 'at the very least' or 'minimum'.
target_language_example: No iré sin dinero; como mínimo necesito veinte euros.
native_language_example: I won't go without money; at the very least I need twenty euros.

meaning: like children; behaving or treated as if (one were) a child.
additional_notes: Used to compare behavior or treatment to that of children. Can describe someone acting immature, playful, naive, or being patronized by others. Often follows verbs like 'comportarse', 'tratar', or 'ser'. Tone depends on context: can be critical ('act like children') or descriptive ('like children').
target_language_example: A veces te pones a jugar y pareces como niños.
native_language_example: Sometimes you start playing and you seem like children.

meaning: like our / as our (used to compare someone to a role, relation, or function considered 'ours')
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone acts in, resembles, or fills a role associated with 'ours' (e.g., our thief, our expert, our father). Often followed by a noun or used before a noun phrase; context determines tone (affectionate, humorous, literal). Agreement in gender/number may require changing nuestro (nuestro/nuestros/nuestra/nuestras) to match the noun.
target_language_example: Como nuestro ladrón oficial, pensamos que podrías hacer algo.
native_language_example: As our official thief, we thought you might be able to do something.

meaning: like new; as good as new
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone has been restored or recovered to a very good, nearly new condition. Common after repairs, cleaning, rest, or recovery from illness. Often placed after the verb (e.g., 'Quedó como nuevo').
target_language_example: Después de la limpieza, el sofá quedó como nuevo.
native_language_example: After the cleaning, the sofa was like new.

meaning: as part (of); as a component or included portion of something.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is included within, considered a member of, or functions as one piece of a larger whole. Often followed by 'de' + noun (como parte de...) but can also be used before a noun or phrase without 'de' in contexts like roles or benefits.
target_language_example: Recibí formación como parte del programa.
native_language_example: I received training as part of the program.

meaning: as such; in that capacity or in itself.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something just mentioned, meaning 'in that role' or 'considered in itself.' Often follows a noun or clause: 'No es un problema como tal' = 'It's not a problem as such.' Can soften a statement or qualify it.
target_language_example: No es peligroso como tal, pero hay que tener cuidado.
native_language_example: It's not dangerous as such, but you need to be careful.

meaning: like everything / like everyone / as usual (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'like everything' or 'like everyone.' Often used to compare someone's behavior or situation to the general case: e.g., 'Él, como todo, tiene defectos' = 'He, like everyone, has flaws.' In some contexts it can mean 'as usual' when describing something typical. Context determines whether it refers to people in general ('like everyone') or to things in general ('like everything').
target_language_example: Ella, como todo el mundo, quiere ser feliz.
native_language_example: She, like everyone, wants to be happy.

meaning: like a father; in a fatherly way (used to say someone acted as a father figure).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who provided care, guidance, protection, or support similar to a father. Common in sentences expressing gratitude or describing a close, supportive relationship. Can refer to biological or non-biological relationships (mentor, guardian, family friend).
target_language_example: Ella siempre estuvo conmigo, como un padre cuando lo necesitaba.
native_language_example: She was always there for me, like a father when I needed it.

meaning: like a clock; very precise, punctual, or working perfectly
additional_notes: Used metaphorically to say someone or something is exact, punctual, reliable, or runs smoothly. Common in contexts about timing, punctuality, or mechanisms that work without problems. Tone is neutral.
target_language_example: Llegó siempre como un reloj a las nueve.
native_language_example: He always arrived like clockwork at nine.

meaning: crazy; acting wildly or strangely (colloquial).
additional_notes: Informal expression used to say someone behaves oddly, extremely, or foolishly. Often used jokingly or lightly insultingly. Can apply to behavior, smells (very strong/unpleasant), or exaggerated actions. Literal image: 'like a goat.'
target_language_example: Siempre hablas como una cabra cuando estás nervioso.
native_language_example: You always talk like a crazy person when you're nervous.

meaning: 'like an arrow' — quickly, straight, or sharply (often used in similes).
additional_notes: A simile meaning 'like an arrow.' Can describe motion that is very straight or very fast. Common in expressions about speed or direction (e.g., 'go straight as an arrow' or 'time flies like an arrow'). Also used poetically or metaphorically. Literal translation is possible.
target_language_example: Salió de la sala como una flecha hacia la puerta.
native_language_example: He left the room like an arrow toward the door.

meaning: like one
additional_notes: A compositional phrase used to compare or classify someone/something. Very often it appears as como uno de... / como una de... meaning 'like one of...' or 'as one of...,' especially after verbs like considerar, reconocer, tratar, parecerse, and sentirse. The word uno changes for gender and number: una, unos, unas.
target_language_example: Si hablas como uno de ellos, nadie notará la diferencia.
native_language_example: If you speak like one of them, nobody will notice the difference.

meaning: as always; like always.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the same as usual or habitual. Can be placed after a noun, adjective, or clause (e.g., 'Borracho, como siempre.' = 'Drunk, as always.'). Tone can be neutral, teasing, or resigned depending on context.
target_language_example: Llegó tarde, como siempre.
native_language_example: He arrived late, as always.

meaning: literally "how to say"; used to ask or explain the manner of expressing a word, phrase or idea (often appears in the question form "¿Cómo se dice...?" meaning "How do you say...?"), or as part of constructions like "como decir..." meaning "such as saying..." or "like saying..."
additional_notes: When used as a direct question learners should use the full phrase "¿Cómo se dice...?" and include the accent on 'cómo'. In spoken or informal contexts you may hear shortened forms, but the canonical question uses the impersonal "se" (¿Cómo se dice...?). As written here without the accent and without punctuation, "como decir" can also function inside sentences (e.g., "como decir la verdad...").
target_language_example: Me preguntó cómo decir 'libro' en español.
native_language_example: He asked me how to say 'book' in Spanish.

meaning: like her / as she
additional_notes: Can mean 'like her' (comparison) or 'as she' (introducing manner), depending on context. Also appears in constructions meaning 'since/because she' when followed by a verb (more common with 'como' at sentence start). Word order and surrounding words determine sense: e.g. 'como ella' after a noun/pronoun is usually comparison ('as much as she'); 'Así es como ella...' = 'this is how she...'.
target_language_example: Ella estudia español como ella estudia inglés.
native_language_example: She studies Spanish like she studies English.

meaning: 'like them' or 'as they do'
additional_notes: Used to compare actions, qualities, or amounts to those of a group (ellos = they/them). Can appear in comparisons of equality (tan ... como ellos / tanto ... como ellos) or alone as 'like them'. Context decides whether it means 'similar to them' or 'as much/as many as them.'
target_language_example: No quiero comportarme como ellos.
native_language_example: I don't want to behave like them.

meaning: properly; as one should; correctly.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is done in the correct, appropriate, or expected way. Often follows verbs (e.g., comer, cuidar) to emphasize doing something properly. Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Deberías dormir como es debido antes del examen.
native_language_example: You should sleep properly before the exam.

meaning: 'how to be' or 'how (someone) is' depending on context.
additional_notes: This combination can appear in two main ways: 1) as an infinitive construction with 'como' (without accent) meaning 'how to' + infinitive, e.g., 'quiero saber como estar tranquilo' (note: prescriptively should be 'cómo' in indirect questions, but in some contexts 'como' without accent can mean 'as' or be a colloquial spelling). 2) as part of a question or reported speech where 'cómo' (with accent) is used with a conjugated verb: '¿Cómo estás?' or 'me preguntó cómo estaba'. Accent placement matters: 'cómo' with accent is used for direct/indirect questions and exclamations; 'como' without accent typically means 'like/as' or appears in constructions where 'how' is not interrogative. Native speakers rarely use the bare sequence 'como estar' alone; it usually appears inside a larger clause (e.g., 'saber cómo estar' or 'aprender como estar').
target_language_example: Me enseñó como estar en calma durante la tormenta.
native_language_example: He taught me how to be calm during the storm.

meaning: 'like being in' — used to compare a situation to being in a place or state.
additional_notes: Common structure to make comparisons or describe an experience by likening it to being in a specific place or situation. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase introduced by 'el/la/los/las' or no article (e.g., 'el campo', 'el cine', 'el jardín del Edén', 'el mismo cuarto'). Can be used with past or present verbs: 'es como estar en...' (it is like being in...), 'era como estar en...' (it was like being in...).
target_language_example: Cuando empezó la lluvia suave, fue como estar en una película romántica.
native_language_example: When the light rain started, it was like being in a romantic movie.

meaning: 'how' or 'how it/they/was/were' depending on context; used to introduce a description of the way something happened or how something/it was.
additional_notes: Uses of 'como fue' vary by context and punctuation: 1) When describing a past state or situation: 'como fue' = 'as it/was was' or 'the way it was' (e.g., Nunca será como fue al principio). 2) When introducing a factual account: 'te contaré mi vida como fue' = 'I'll tell you my life as it really was'. 3) When asking or explaining the manner of an action, it often appears with an accent on 'cómo' if it's interrogative or exclamatory (¿Cómo fue que...?) but without accent it's a relative/neutral 'how' in statements (Tom explicó como fue que perdió el dinero = Tom explained how he lost the money). Pay attention to context and use of accents: 'cómo' (with accent) marks questions or emphasis; 'como' (no accent) is used in statements meaning 'as' or 'how' in reported descriptions.
target_language_example: Ella me dijo exactamente como fue todo aquel día.
native_language_example: She told me exactly how everything was that day.

meaning: as you like / whichever you prefer
additional_notes: Polite, somewhat formal or courteous phrase used to offer choice or defer to someone's preference. Often appears in contexts like 'como usted guste' or 'como le guste' to address someone respectfully. Can be shortened in casual speech to 'como quieras' (tú) or 'como quiera' (neutral).
target_language_example: Haga la reserva para la hora que como guste.
native_language_example: Make the reservation for whichever time you prefer.

meaning: 'how to (do something)'.
additional_notes: Standard written Spanish uses the interrogative/indirect-question form 'cómo hacer' with an accent on 'cómo'. In informal writing the accent is sometimes omitted as 'como hacer', but this can change meaning ('como' without accent often means 'like' or 'as'). In many spoken or casual contexts people write or say 'como hacer' without the accent when intending 'how to'. Followed by an action or clause to indicate the task or method.
target_language_example: Enséñame como hacer eso.
native_language_example: Teach me how to do that.

meaning: 'how to go' or 'how to get (somewhere)'; used to ask or explain directions or the method of reaching a place.
additional_notes: Often appears in questions or instructions: '¿Cómo ir a...?' or as part of titles/sections such as 'Cómo ir desde X hasta Y'. In direct questions the accent on 'cómo' is required: '¿Cómo...?' In many contexts speakers add modal verbs for politeness or grammaticality (¿Cómo puedo ir...? / Cómo ir en transporte público). Note that in running text without the interrogative accent it may appear as 'como ir' (e.g., headings, informal notes), but the correct written question uses '¿Cómo ir...?'
target_language_example: Cómo ir al museo desde la estación
native_language_example: How to get to the museum from the station

meaning: how (he/she/it) arrived; how (someone) got somewhere (past)
additional_notes: This is the combination of 'como' (how) and the past tense verb 'llegó' (he/she/it arrived or usted arrived). When used in direct questions, 'cómo' typically carries an accent: '¿Cómo llegó...?'. Without the accent, 'como llegó' can appear inside a larger sentence as reported speech or subordinate clause. Context determines whether it asks about manner, route, time, or circumstances of arrival.
target_language_example: Explique cómo llegó el paquete esta mañana; quiero saber si hubo retrasos.
native_language_example: Explain how the package arrived this morning; I want to know if there were delays.

meaning: as / like you (just) called me; used to repeat or comment on how someone referred to the speaker
additional_notes: Often appears when the speaker repeats or quotes how another person addressed them. 'Como' here means 'as' or 'like' and 'me' refers to the speaker (direct or indirect object). Common in constructions like 'como me llamaste' (as you called me) or abbreviated 'como me acabas de llamar' (like you just called me). It signals surprise, objection, or clarification about the way they were called.
target_language_example: No soy un niño pequeño, como me acabas de llamar.
native_language_example: I'm not a little kid, like you just called me.

meaning: indicates degree or purpose: 'so ... that' / 'enough to' / 'as to (be able to)'.
additional_notes: Used after an adjective or adverb to show degree leading to a result or to indicate purpose/intent. Often pairs with comparatives like 'tan ... como para' (so ... as to) or 'lo bastante/lo suficiente ... como para' (enough ... to). Can introduce an action that follows logically (She is not so insensitive as to laugh) or a purpose (breathe deeply, as if to sing).
target_language_example: No soy tan tonto como para confiar en esa oferta.
native_language_example: I'm not so foolish as to trust that offer.

meaning: as you can see; as you can tell.
additional_notes: Used to point out something visible or obvious to the listener. Often appears at the start or middle of a sentence to emphasize evidence or explain a situation. Can be followed by a statement or stand alone as a brief remark.
target_language_example: Como puedes ver, la mesa ya está arreglada.
native_language_example: As you can see, the table is already set.

meaning: as you wish / however you want / in whatever way you want (meaning varies by context)
additional_notes: Used in different contexts: 1) To accept or concede: 'Fine, as you wish' (similar to 'como quieras' for tú). 2) To mean 'however' or 'in whatever way' (e.g., 'Puede llamarme como quiera' = 'Call me however you want'). 3) To express quantity/duration: 'tanto tiempo como quiera' = 'as long as he/she wants'. 'Como quiera' can appear with subjunctive when referring to an unspecified subject (e.g., 'como quiera'). Register is generally neutral; 'como quieras' is the informal tú form while 'como quiera' can be used for usted or impersonal constructions.
target_language_example: Está bien, como quiera.
native_language_example: All right, as you wish.

meaning: since
additional_notes: A fairly formal or literary linking phrase. It is most often used to give a reason, similar to ya que or puesto que. In some contexts it can also have a more literal sense like 'however' or 'in whatever way,' but that use is less common for beginners.
target_language_example: Como quiera que ya es tarde, debemos irnos.
native_language_example: Since it's already late, we should leave.

meaning: as you want / however you want; fine by you (giving someone choice or agreeing reluctantly).
additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom to choose how to do something or to indicate agreement/indifference. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be neutral (allowing choice) or slightly dismissive/resigned ("fine, whatever"). Can be followed by actions (Hazlo como quieras) or used alone to agree (Sí, como quieras).
target_language_example: Decide tú el menú; yo como quieras.
native_language_example: You choose the menu; I'm fine with whatever you want.

meaning: as you know; (used to remind the listener of something they already know).
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to introduce or remind information the listener already knows. Often followed by a comma and a statement. Can be used at the start or mid-sentence: 'Como sabes, ...' = 'As you know, ...' It is not a question; it's a discourse marker. Pronunciation: 'KOH-moh SAH-bes'.
target_language_example: Como sabes, mañana no puedo venir.
native_language_example: As you know, I can't come tomorrow.

meaning: anyway
additional_notes: Used to indicate concession or determination. Can mean 'anyway' (to return to a point) or 'by any means/whatever it takes' (expressing determination). Tone depends on context: neutral when shifting topic ('anyway'), more forceful when giving an instruction ('do it by any means').
target_language_example: Necesitas terminarlo como sea.
native_language_example: You need to finish it by any means.

meaning: as if
additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined, unreal, or uncertain situation: someone acts, speaks, or feels as if something were true. It is very often followed by the imperfect subjunctive or pluperfect subjunctive, for example: como si supiera, como si hubiera pasado.
target_language_example: Me mira como si no me conociera.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if he didn't know me.

meaning: a filler phrase meaning "so to speak" or "as it were"; used to soften or qualify what you're saying.
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken and written Spanish to introduce a figurative, approximate, or explanatory expression. Often follows the clause it comments on. It doesn't change tense or grammar; it's a discourse marker. Equivalent to English "so to speak," "if you will," or "as it were."
target_language_example: Estaba en una isla, como si dijéramos, rodeado de trabajo y sin tiempo libre.
native_language_example: I was on an island, so to speak, surrounded by work and with no free time.

meaning: as if nothing (had happened); acting like nothing is wrong.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone behaving calmly or ignoring a past event or problem. Often followed by a verb in subjunctive (hubiera ocurrido, pasara) when referring to hypothetical or past situations. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ella entró a la sala como si nada hubiera pasado.
native_language_example: She entered the room as if nothing had happened.

meaning: 'as (someone/something) used to (be)'.
additional_notes: Used to compare the present with the past. Usually followed by a verb (e.g., ser, estar, hacer) in infinitive or by a clause. Common in phrases expressing change or nostalgia: 'no es como solía ser' = 'it's not as it used to be.'
target_language_example: Mi barrio no es como solía.
native_language_example: My neighborhood isn't like it used to be.

meaning: 'the way I am' or 'as I am'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about one's character, personality, or habitual way of being. Can appear after verbs (soy como soy — I am how I am) or at the start of a clause with 'como' meaning 'since' or 'because' when followed by a verb (Como soy demasiado bueno... = Because I am too good...). Context decides whether it means 'as'/'the way' or 'because'.
target_language_example: No puedo cambiar; así soy, como soy.
native_language_example: I can't change; that's how I am.

meaning: 'how it sounds' or 'the way it sounds' (often used to express impression of words/ideas or to preface a judgment).
additional_notes: Used to comment on the sound or impression of a word, phrase, idea, or situation. Can mean literal auditory sound or figurative impression (e.g., how something 'comes across'). Often appears in structures like 'me gusta como suena' (I like how it sounds) or 'no me gusta como suena' (I don't like the way that sounds). Can be followed by 'eso', a clause, or stand alone with context. Note: accent on cómo is often omitted here because this is a relative/indirect question/phrase, not an interrogative — 'como' (without accent) is correct.
target_language_example: Su propuesta no es perfecta, pero me gusta como suena.
native_language_example: Your proposal isn't perfect, but I like the way it sounds.

meaning: 'because (he/she/it) had' or 'since (he/she/it) had' — introduces a reason using tener (to have).
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'como' meaning 'because/since' followed by the imperfect of tener (tenía). It gives a reason in the past. Subject is usually clear from context (e.g., 'Tom', 'nosotros'). In English you can translate it as 'because he/she had' or 'since I/we/they had' depending on the subject. Use with imperfect when describing ongoing past situations or background information.
target_language_example: Como tenía hambre, no pude concentrarme en la reunión.
native_language_example: Because I/he/she was hungry, I/he/she couldn't concentrate in the meeting.

meaning: as/since already; introduces a reason or recalls information the listener likely knows.
additional_notes: Used at the start of a clause to give a reason (like 'since' or 'as') or to refer back to something already mentioned or known by the listener (like 'as you know' or 'as I've already said'). Common in everyday and written Spanish. Can be followed by indicative perfects (he dicho), pluscuamperfecto (había visto), or simple statements (era tarde).
target_language_example: Como ya lo sabes, mañana no habrá clase.
native_language_example: As you already know, there will be no class tomorrow.

meaning: at the latest; no later than.
additional_notes: Used to set a deadline or the latest possible time for something. Often follows a time expression: 'las 5 como muy tarde' = 'by 5 at the latest'. It's slightly more emphatic than simply 'tarde' and interchangeable with 'a más tardar'.
target_language_example: Llegaré a las 7 como muy tarde.
native_language_example: I'll arrive by 7 at the latest.

meaning: in comparison with / compared to
additional_notes: Used to compare one thing with another. Often appears in the phrase "en comparación con" (literally "in comparison with") to introduce the thing you're comparing to. Can be followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause (e.g., "con este", "con la otra gente", "con las de Europa").
target_language_example: En comparación con el año pasado, las ventas han aumentado.
native_language_example: Compared to last year, sales have increased.

meaning: to share the (masculine) ... — 'compartir' = to share; 'el' is the masculine definite article.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase: it's the verb compartir followed by the masculine singular article 'el' before a masculine noun (e.g., compartir el resultado, compartir el riesgo, compartir el dormitorio). Use 'compartir la' for feminine nouns and 'compartir los/las' for plurals. Context determines what is being shared (object, risk, pain, space, ride).
target_language_example: Podemos compartir el coche para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: We can share the car to go to work.

meaning: complicated to/for; (used in comparisons) more/less complicated than…
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like "más complicado de lo que..." or "menos complicado de lo que..." to compare how difficult something is. Can be followed by an infinitive, a clause (de lo que + verb), or a noun (complicado de + noun) though "complicado para" is also common when indicating who finds something difficult (complicado para mí).
target_language_example: Es más complicado de lo que pensábamos al principio.
native_language_example: It's more complicated than we thought at first.

meaning: is made up of; consists of
additional_notes: Used to describe what something is formed or composed of. Commonly appears as 'se compone de' (impersonal/passive reflexive) to say 'is composed of' or 'consists of'. Followed by a list or quantity (nouns). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: La mesa se compone de madera y metal.
native_language_example: The table is made of wood and metal.

meaning: 'bought the' (past participle + feminine definite article)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: comprado (past participle of comprar = 'to buy') + la (feminine singular 'the'). It appears in perfect or past-periphrastic constructions (he comprado la = I have bought the / I bought the) or with pluperfect/habitual past (había comprado la = had bought the). The gender of the article matches a feminine noun that follows or is understood from context (la novela, la semana, la pintura, la cámara, etc.).
target_language_example: He comprado la cámara nueva.
native_language_example: I have bought the new camera.

meaning: to buy this (one); to purchase this (item).
additional_notes: "Comprar" means to buy. "Este" is a demonstrative meaning "this" (masculine singular) used for something near the speaker. In spoken Spanish you might also hear "comprar esto" (neutral) or "comprar esta" for feminine nouns. Word order normally is "comprar + object" or in commands "compra este/esta/esto".
target_language_example: Voy a comprar este libro.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy this book.

meaning: to buy oneself a
additional_notes: Reflexive form of comprar used when someone is buying something for their own use or benefit. Una must be followed by a feminine singular noun, as in comprarse una casa or comprarse una moto. The pronoun changes with the subject: comprarme, comprarte, comprarse, etc.
target_language_example: Quiere comprarse una bicicleta nueva este verano.
native_language_example: He wants to buy himself a new bicycle this summer.

meaning: I bought a pair (of...).
additional_notes: Used to say you purchased two of something that naturally come as a pair (shoes, gloves, boots, etc.). Often followed by 'de' + the item: 'compré un par de zapatos'. Can be used reflexively (me compré un par) to emphasize you bought it for yourself.
target_language_example: Ayer compré un par de guantes para el invierno.
native_language_example: Yesterday I bought a pair of gloves for the winter.

meaning: bought me this / (someone) bought this (for me).
additional_notes: Compró is the past (preterite) form of comprar (to buy). 'Compró este' is used when saying that someone bought a specific item (este = this) for the speaker or another person. Often followed by the noun: 'compró este libro', 'compró este sombrero'. If the buyer is named, include it before: 'Mi madre me compró este...'. To specify who received it, add an indirect object: 'me compró este...' (bought me this).
target_language_example: Mi abuela me compró este reloj para mi cumpleaños.
native_language_example: My grandmother bought me this watch for my birthday.

meaning: bought a pair (of ...).
additional_notes: Used to say someone purchased two matching items that form a pair (shoes, gloves, boots, etc.). Usually followed by 'de' + the item: 'compró un par de zapatos'. Context clarifies the item if it's omitted. Past tense (compró) indicates a completed action; you can replace with other tenses (compra un par, compraron un par).
target_language_example: Ella compró un par de botas nuevas.
native_language_example: She bought a pair of new boots.

meaning: laptop; portable computer.
additional_notes: Commonly used in Latin America (computadora) combined with portátil. In Spain you may also hear 'ordenador portátil'. Refers to a personal, portable computer (thin, light, runs an OS like Windows, macOS, or Linux). Use possessive adjectives to show ownership (mi, esta, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi computadora portátil es ligera y tiene buena batería.
native_language_example: My laptop is light and has a good battery.

meaning: 'community of' or 'community for' (a group of people with a shared interest, identity, place, or status).
additional_notes: Used to indicate membership or belonging to a group. Followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., 'los ricos', 'submarinos', 'toki pona'). Can refer to social groups, professional communities, online communities, or communities defined by shared traits or interests.
target_language_example: Quiero ser parte de la comunidad de lectores del club.
native_language_example: I want to be part of the community of readers in the club.

meaning: ordinary; common; nothing special.
additional_notes: Used to describe people or things as average, typical, or unremarkable. Often implies lack of special qualities. Can be used neutrally or slightly dismissively depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ella es una chica común y corriente, pero muy amable.
native_language_example: She is an ordinary girl, but very kind.

meaning: with God; used literally or as a farewell/blessing or to say someone is dead (in Heaven).
additional_notes: Can be literal (physically/spiritually 'with God'), a blessing/farewell equivalent to 'go with God' or 'may God be with you' (common in religious contexts), or a euphemism for 'dead' (e.g., 'ya está con Dios' = 'he/she has passed away'). Context determines meaning and tone.
target_language_example: Vete con Dios y cuídate.
native_language_example: Go with God and take care.

meaning: 'with some' (feminine plural) — used before feminine plural nouns.
additional_notes: Con + algunas is the preposition 'with' plus the feminine plural indefinite adjective 'algunas'. Use 'con algunos' for masculine plural nouns and 'con algún/una' for singular. Common in everyday speech to indicate accompaniment, partial amount, or a few items/conditions/questions.
target_language_example: Voy al mercado con algunas amigas esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to the market with some (female) friends this afternoon.

meaning: 'with some' or 'with a few (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate accompaniment or involvement with an unspecified small number of people or things. Followed by a plural noun (often with de before a noun phrase: 'con algunos de mis amigos' = 'with some of my friends'). Can be used for people or objects. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Fui al concierto con algunos amigos.
native_language_example: I went to the concert with some friends.

meaning: with love; lovingly
additional_notes: Used to say that something is done with love, care, or affection. Common in letters, greetings, instructions, or descriptions of feelings and actions. Can be literal (doing something lovingly) or emotional (expressing love).
target_language_example: Te lo entrego con amor y paciencia.
native_language_example: I give it to you with love and patience.

meaning: charged to; billed to; paid from (an account or budget)
additional_notes: Used in formal, financial, or administrative contexts to indicate that a cost, payment, or expense will be applied to a specific account, department, budget line, or person. Often appears in invoices, receipts, bank/expense records, and official documents: e.g., "con cargo a la cuenta 1234" or "con cargo a gastos de viaje". Equivalent to English "charged to" or "to be charged to."
target_language_example: El pago se hará con cargo a la cuenta de la empresa.
native_language_example: The payment will be charged to the company's account.

meaning: with affection; fondly; lovingly.
additional_notes: Used to express warmth or affection when speaking or writing to someone. Common in letters, messages, or when asking someone to remember or treat something kindly. Tone is gentle and positive.
target_language_example: Te lo digo con cariño: cuida tu salud.
native_language_example: I tell you this with affection: take care of your health.

meaning: with barley (planted/seeded with barley).
additional_notes: Literal phrase: con = with, cebada = barley. Commonly used to say a field, mixture or crop includes or is planted with barley. Use after a verb like sembrar (to sow/plant) or with nouns: 'un pan con cebada' (a bread with barley) or 'campo con cebada' (field planted with barley).
target_language_example: Sembraron la parcela con cebada este otoño.
native_language_example: They planted the plot with barley this autumn.

meaning: 'with food' or 'including food'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something comes together with food or involves/uses food. Can describe a package that includes food, how someone feeds an animal (feeds with a certain kind of food), or that something is filled/served with food. Very literal and common; 'con' means 'with' and 'comida' means 'food'.
target_language_example: El regalo venía con comida incluida.
native_language_example: The gift came with food included.

meaning: with anyone / with just anyone (often: indiscriminately or without selectivity).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is willing to be with or talk to anyone, sometimes with a negative or cautionary tone (e.g., 'with just anyone' or 'with anybody who comes along'). Can be literal ('with any person') or idiomatic to imply lack of selectiveness or poor judgement. Context and tone determine whether it's neutral or critical.
target_language_example: No salgas con cualquiera por la noche.
native_language_example: Don't go out with just anyone at night.

meaning: with pain; feeling pain (physically or emotionally).
additional_notes: Used to describe experiencing pain or sorrow. Can refer to physical pain (e.g., after an injury) or emotional pain/sadness. Often appears in medical contexts or when expressing regret/sadness (e.g., 'con dolor en el corazón'). The construction is simply preposition + noun and can be followed by more details: con dolor de cabeza, con dolor en el pecho, con dolor por la pérdida.
target_language_example: Salió del hospital con dolor en el pecho.
native_language_example: He left the hospital with chest pain.

meaning: with due respect; respectfully (used to preface disagreement or a polite command).
additional_notes: A polite phrase used before disagreeing, offering criticism, or giving an order softly. Often used in formal or courteous contexts (to a person of authority or in polite conversation). Tone can be neutral or slightly ironic depending on context. Can stand alone as a brief polite interjection: "Con el debido respeto."
target_language_example: Con el debido respeto, señor, creo que esa decisión es un error.
native_language_example: With due respect, sir, I believe that decision is a mistake.

meaning: with the dentist / at the dentist (used to say you have an appointment with the dentist).
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like 'tener (una cita) con el dentista' or 'ir con el dentista'. It indicates an appointment or visit to the dentist. In English you often say 'at the dentist' or 'with the dentist' — both are conveyed by 'con el dentista' depending on context.
target_language_example: No puedo cenar hoy porque tengo cita con el dentista.
native_language_example: I can't have dinner tonight because I have an appointment with the dentist.

meaning: in order to; with the purpose of.
additional_notes: Formal way to express purpose or intention. Often followed by an infinitive verb (con el fin de + infinitive) or a noun phrase. Similar to 'para' or 'con el propósito de' but slightly more formal and explicit.
target_language_example: Viajó a la ciudad con el fin de mejorar su inglés.
native_language_example: He traveled to the city in order to improve his English.

target_language_multi_word_term: el uno con el otro / con el otro
meaning: with each other; to one another (reciprocal action between people).
additional_notes: Used to indicate reciprocal actions or relations between two or more people. Common variants: "el uno con el otro" (masculine/plural), "la una con la otra" (feminine), "unos con otros" / "unas con otras" (plural). Can also appear as "con los demás" (with the others). Often follows the verb or phrase it refers to: "hablar el uno con el otro", "ser sinceros el uno con el otro".
target_language_example: Debemos confiar el uno con el otro para que el equipo funcione.
native_language_example: We must trust each other for the team to work.

meaning: with the passing of (time); over time.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something changes or happens gradually as time goes by. Commonly followed by 'tiempo' (con el paso del tiempo) but can imply the passing of days/years in context. Equivalent to 'over time' or 'as time passes' in English.
target_language_example: Con el paso del tiempo, mi confianza en mí misma creció.
native_language_example: Over time, my self-confidence grew.

meaning: with time; over time; eventually (gradual change or eventual result).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens gradually or will happen after some time passes. Common in everyday speech to reassure (e.g., healing, learning) or describe gradual changes. Can mean 'in time' or 'over time' depending on context.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, con el tiempo te sentirás mejor.
native_language_example: Don't worry, with time you'll feel better.

meaning: with desire/enthusiasm; wanting to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone feels motivated, eager, or enthusiastic about an activity. Often followed by 'de' + infinitive (con ganas de + infinitive) to express wanting to do something. Can also be used alone as a short exclamation to show enthusiasm ('Con ganas.' = 'Let's go!' or 'I'm ready!').
target_language_example: Hoy voy a estudiar con ganas para el examen.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to study enthusiastically for the exam.

meaning: 'with pleasure' / 'gladly' / 'willingly'.
additional_notes: Used to accept offers, agree to do something, or indicate willingness and pleasure. Common in formal and neutral contexts (e.g., Aceptamos con gusto) and in everyday speech (e.g., Vendré con gusto). Can be used before or after a verb phrase.
target_language_example: Si necesitas ayuda, con gusto te ayudaré.
native_language_example: If you need help, I'll gladly help you.

meaning: with men / together with men (i.e., in the company of men or involving men).
additional_notes: A simple prepositional phrase: 'con' = 'with' and 'hombres' = 'men'. Used for companionship (e.g., dating, meeting), sexual partners, group inclusion, or to indicate the people affected by something (e.g., a medicine that works with men). Context determines whether it's literal company, sexual context, or inclusion among categories.
target_language_example: Salgo con hombres los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I go out with men on weekends.

meaning: on the condition that; provided that.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a requirement or stipulation for something to happen. Often followed by 'que' + clause. Common in formal and neutral contexts; can be replaced by 'siempre y cuando' or 'a condición de que'.
target_language_example: Te presto mi coche con la condición de que lo devuelvas limpio.
native_language_example: I'll lend you my car on the condition that you return it clean.

meaning: with the window (used to say something is done with the window open/closed).
additional_notes: Often followed by adjectives like 'abierta' (open) or 'cerrada' (closed). Common in sentences about sleeping, letting air in, or leaving a window in a certain state. Literal and straightforward: expresses that an action or state involves the window.
target_language_example: Dormimos con la ventana cerrada porque hacía frío.
native_language_example: We slept with the window closed because it was cold.

meaning: with life; about/related to life (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase is literal in many uses (con la vida = with the life). Context changes meaning: it can appear in expressions about living or existence (e.g., 'seguir con la vida' = to go on with one's life), in phrases meaning 'to take someone's life' when structured as 'acabar con la vida de...' (to end someone's life / kill), or in abstract comments like 'eso pasa con la vida' (that's what happens in life). Translate depending on surrounding verbs and prepositions.
target_language_example: Después del accidente, ella siguió con la vida que conocía.
native_language_example: After the accident, she continued with the life she knew.

meaning: with the
additional_notes: Combination of con + la. It is used before a feminine singular noun: con la profesora = with the teacher. In phrases like con la que, it helps form relative expressions meaning with whom/with which. It can also appear inside fixed expressions, such as salirse con la suya.
target_language_example: Hablo con la vecina todos los días.
native_language_example: I talk with the neighbor every day.

meaning: 'with the' (feminine singular) — a combination of the preposition con + the feminine singular definite article la.
additional_notes: Used when referring to a feminine singular noun after 'with'. Also appears in fixed expressions (e.g., 'salirse con la suya' = 'get one's way') and in contractions with relative pronouns (e.g., 'con la que' = 'with which/whom'). Gender and number must agree: use 'con el' for masculine, 'con los/las' for plurals. Often followed directly by a noun or by a relative clause.
target_language_example: Voy al cine con la chica de la clase.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with the girl from class.

con las manos en la masa

target_language_multi_word_term: con las manos en la masa
meaning: caught red-handed; caught in the act of doing something wrong.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone is discovered while actually committing an offense or wrongdoing (the act is ongoing or evidence is immediate). Common in both formal and informal contexts. Literally means "with the hands in the dough," evoking being caught while baking/stealing. Use to describe being caught in the act.
target_language_example: Lo vimos entrar en la oficina y lo sorprendimos con las manos en la masa.
native_language_example: We saw him enter the office and we caught him red-handed.

meaning: empty-handed; without having obtained anything.
additional_notes: Used to say someone leaves or ends up without getting what they wanted. Common in everyday speech. Often follows verbs like irse, salir, volverse, quedarse. Literal image: having empty hands (no goods, results, or gains).
target_language_example: Llegué al mercado y no encontré nada; me fui con las manos vacías.
native_language_example: I arrived at the market and found nothing; I left empty-handed.

meaning: with milk.
additional_notes: Used to say that a drink or food contains or is served with milk (e.g., coffee, tea, sauces). Very common in menus and everyday speech. Order: 'un/una [bebida] con leche'.
target_language_example: Quiero un café con leche, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a coffee with milk, please.

meaning: with (one's) arms crossed; standing/sitting with arms folded
additional_notes: Describes a body posture (arms folded across chest). Can imply being defensive, closed-off, impatient, or simply relaxed/comfortable depending on context. Use with estar (estaba, está) or sentarse/pararse + con los brazos cruzados.
target_language_example: Ella se quedó con los brazos cruzados durante la reunión.
native_language_example: She sat with her arms crossed during the meeting.

meaning: with tears; showing tears or crying.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is crying or has tears. Commonly follows verbs of seeing, speaking, reading, answering, etc. Can describe tears falling (con lágrimas cayendo/ deslizándose) or just having tears in the eyes (con lágrimas en los ojos).
target_language_example: Ella habló con lágrimas en la voz.
native_language_example: She spoke with tears in her voice.

meaning: 'with tears in (one's) eyes' — describes someone who is crying or about to cry.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person's emotional state; literal and common phrase. Often follows verbs like mirar, ponerse de pie, sentarse. Can refer to present or recent crying and is used for any subject (con lágrimas en los ojos / en los ojos).
target_language_example: Entró en la habitación con lágrimas en los ojos.
native_language_example: He/She entered the room with tears in (his/her) eyes.

meaning: with many (feminine/plural) — used before feminine plural nouns or with feminine abstract nouns.
additional_notes: Literal phrase: 'con' = with, 'muchas' = many (feminine plural). Use before feminine plural nouns (e.g., 'personas', 'cosas', 'victimas', 'chicas') or with feminine abstract nouns used adverbially ('ganas' = desire). If the noun is masculine plural use 'con muchos'. Context determines exact English translation: 'with many people', 'full of many things', 'causing many victims', 'dating many girls', 'left with a lot of desire'.
target_language_example: Llegó con muchas preguntas sobre el proyecto.
native_language_example: He arrived with many questions about the project.

meaning: with a lot / with great (care, skill, etc.).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (often abstract like 'cuidado', 'arte', 'respeto') to mean 'with great' or 'very' in the sense of doing something attentively or skillfully. Common collocations: con mucho cuidado (with great care), con mucho gusto (with pleasure), con mucho respeto (with great respect).
target_language_example: Habla con mucho respeto hacia sus mayores.
native_language_example: He speaks with great respect toward his elders.

meaning: with pleasure; gladly
additional_notes: A polite phrase used to accept a request, offer help, or say you'll do something willingly. Common in formal and neutral situations (e.g., responding to 'gracias' or agreeing to do a favor). Can be used alone as a short reply: 'Con mucho gusto.'
target_language_example: Lo haré con mucho gusto.
native_language_example: I'll do it with pleasure.

meaning: with snow; snowy (lit. 'with snow').
