additional_notes: Reflexive past of 'criar' used to say where someone grew up. Commonly followed by a place (country, city, neighborhood, house). 'Me crié en...' emphasizes upbringing rather than place of birth (compare: 'nací en' = I was born in). Use with past tense 'me crié' for 'I grew up'.
target_language_example: Me crié en una pequeña ciudad costera.
native_language_example: I grew up in a small coastal town.

meaning: “the painting/picture that” — used to introduce a relative clause describing a specific painting or picture.
additional_notes: Cuadro means painting, picture, or frame. 'Que' is a relative pronoun meaning 'that' or 'which.' Together they point to a particular painting being described (e.g., the one on the wall, the one Mary painted). The clause after 'que' gives more information about the cuadro. Agreement (gender/number) is handled by cuadro; que does not change.
target_language_example: Me gusta el cuadro que colgaste en la sala.
native_language_example: I like the painting that you hung in the living room.

meaning: 'which was' or 'which/that was' (used to refer back to a whole idea or fact mentioned before).
additional_notes: Often appears as 'lo cual era' to comment on a preceding clause or situation. It connects a previous statement with a comment about it (e.g., 'which was a lie', 'which was dangerous'). Use 'lo cual' when referring to a whole idea; 'cual' without 'lo' is less common in this fixed phrase. In English it often translates as 'which was' or 'which/that is/was'.
target_language_example: Dijo que no vendría, lo cual era sorprendente.
native_language_example: He said he wouldn't come, which was surprising.

meaning: a connector meaning 'which/which is not' or 'which is/which is not the case', used to introduce a comment about the previous clause (often negative).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of 'lo cual' or 'por cuya/por la cual' constructions. 'Lo cual' refers back to an entire idea or clause and introduces a comment about it (e.g., adding a negation: 'lo cual no era cierto' = 'which was not true'). In 'por la cual/por el cual' it links a reason: 'por la cual no...' = 'for which/reason why... not...'. It's formal/neutral and common in written and spoken Spanish. Don't split 'lo cual' — use the correct article (lo, la, el) depending on context.
target_language_example: Ella mintió, lo cual no ayudó a la situación.
native_language_example: She lied, which did not help the situation.

meaning: in any case; anyway; regardless.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that remains true regardless of previous details or to change the topic. Often appears as 'en cualquier caso' (more common), but 'cualquier caso' can be used in shorter phrases. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: No sé si vendrá, pero en cualquier caso iremos sin él.
native_language_example: I don't know if he'll come, but in any case we'll go without him.

meaning: anything
additional_notes: Used to refer to any object, action, situation, or possibility without specification. Can appear alone (Puedo hacer cualquier cosa = I can do anything) or followed by a clause with que (cualquier cosa que + verb = whatever/anything that...). Common in general statements and hypotheticals.
target_language_example: Puedes pedirme cualquier cosa.
native_language_example: You can ask me for anything.

meaning: any time; at any hour
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something can happen at any time or whenever; often interchangeable with 'a cualquier hora' (with the preposition) in many contexts. Can refer to clock time or more generally 'whenever.' Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Puedes llamarme a cualquier hora si hay un problema.
native_language_example: You can call me at any time if there's a problem.

meaning: when I said / when I said that
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something the speaker said earlier. Common in storytelling or clarification: 'cuando dije...' introduces the moment or the content of a past utterance. If the subject is different (you, he, she), change the verb: 'cuando dijiste', 'cuando dijo', etc.
target_language_example: Cuando dije que necesitaría ayuda, nadie respondió.
native_language_example: When I said I would need help, no one answered.

meaning: when the phone (ringing) / when the phone (did something).
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce an interruption in the past (often with past progressive: estaba ... cuando el teléfono sonó/empezó a sonar). Literally 'when the phone...' — usually followed by a verb like 'sonó' or 'empezó a sonar'. Used to tell what was happening when the phone rang.
target_language_example: Estábamos hablando cuando el teléfono sonó.
native_language_example: We were talking when the phone rang.

meaning: when they (used to introduce a time clause referring to a group of people).
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce temporal clauses about actions or states involving a group of people (ellos). It appears before verbs in the clause and can be followed by different tenses (past, present, future) depending on time relation. In casual speech the subject pronoun 'ellos' is often omitted if context is clear: e.g., 'Cuando llegaron...' instead of 'Cuando ellos llegaron...'.
target_language_example: Cuando ellos salgan, cierra la puerta.
native_language_example: When they leave, close the door.

meaning: when (he/she/it) was
additional_notes: Used to introduce a past-time clause with a third-person subject; 'fue' is preterite of 'ser' or passive 'ser'/'estar' constructions and can mean 'was' or 'became' depending on context (e.g. adopted, kidnapped, notified). Often followed by a past participle (passive) or an adjective/verb phrase.
target_language_example: Ella cambió de ciudad cuando fue mayor.
native_language_example: She moved to another city when she was older.

meaning: 'when I/he/she/you/it was going' or 'when (someone) used to go' — refers to a past repeated or ongoing action of going somewhere.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect tense of ir (iba) used after 'cuando' to describe something that happened while someone was going somewhere or to refer to habitual past actions. Subject is understood from context (yo, él, ella, usted). Common translations: 'when I/he/she/you/they used to go' or 'when I/he/she/you/they was/were going.'
target_language_example: Cuando iba al trabajo, siempre compraba un café.
native_language_example: When I was going to work, I always bought a coffee.

meaning: 'when (to) them' or 'when they/you (formal/plural) ...'
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'cuando' (when) with the indirect object pronoun 'les' (to them / for them). Meaning depends on context: 'cuando les' can introduce a time clause referring to something that happens to them ('when it happens to them' — sentence 1) or a deadline/point in time relative to them ('by the time it reaches them' — sentence 2), or indicate actions directed at them ('when they need/are missing something, they call them' — sentence 3). 'Les' can refer to people or animals (them). Word order is typical in Spanish: 'cuando' + indirect object pronoun + verb or clause.
target_language_example: Cuando les llegue la carta, me avisarán.
native_language_example: When the letter reaches them, they will let me know.

meaning: when (he/she/it/you) arrived at / reached (a place or point).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to describe the moment someone or something reached a physical location or an abstract point (e.g., a stage, age, or conclusion). Usually followed by a noun or verb in past tense (e.g., 'cuando llegó a la estación', 'cuando llegó a los treinta años'). Subject (él/ella/usted) is implied by the verb form 'llegó'.
target_language_example: Cuando llegó a la estación, el tren ya había salido.
native_language_example: When he arrived at the station, the train had already left.

meaning: when I realized / when I became aware
additional_notes: Short for 'cuando me di cuenta' (cuenta = awareness). Used to introduce the moment you understood or noticed something. Often followed by 'cuenta' + a clause, or by a clause describing what happened at that moment. Common in past narratives.
target_language_example: Cuando me di cuenta, había perdido el tren.
native_language_example: When I realized, I had missed the train.

meaning: when least expected; at the most unlikely time
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at a time you didn't expect — similar to 'when you least expect it' or 'just when...'. Often appears with verbs in subjunctive or indicative (e.g., 'cuando menos se espera', 'cuando menos esperábamos').
target_language_example: Justo cuando menos lo esperaba, recibió una llamada.
native_language_example: Just when he least expected it, he got a phone call.

meaning: 'when not' or 'if not' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'when not' to describe a time or condition (e.g., 'when not X, ...') or function like 'if not'/'otherwise' in everyday speech. Context determines whether it's temporal ('when he/she/it had not...') or conditional ('if he/she/it doesn't.../otherwise'). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Las plantas crecen bien cuando no reciben demasiado sol.
native_language_example: The plants grow well when they don't get too much sun.

meaning: whenever (you/he/she/one) wants; when (someone) wants; can also mean 'whenever' in conditional statements.
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate that someone can do something at any time or whenever they choose. In examples with verbs like 'puedo' (I can), it expresses ability to do something whenever desired: 'I can stop whenever I want.' It can also appear in commands or hypothetical statements (e.g., 'When you want to fool the world, tell the truth') where 'quiera' is subjunctive of 'querer'. Subject is understood from context.
target_language_example: Puedes venir cuando quieras.
native_language_example: You can come whenever you want.

meaning: 'when I/he/she was eight (years old)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone was eight years old at the time of an action or situation. Replace the subject or verb as needed (e.g., 'cuando tenía ocho años', 'cuando tenía ocho' is informal shorthand; exact phrase normally includes 'años'). Tense of 'tenía' is imperfect, emphasizing ongoing state or age in the past.
target_language_example: Cuando tenía ocho años, aprendí a nadar en el río.
native_language_example: When I was eight years old, I learned to swim in the river.

meaning: 'when I was your (age)'.
additional_notes: Used to compare the speaker's past (usually their age) with the listener's current age or situation. Complete phrase is usually "cuando tenía tu edad". Common in storytelling or giving advice. The verb can change (tenía, era, estaba) depending on nuance.
target_language_example: Cuando tenía tu edad, trabajaba y estudiaba al mismo tiempo.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I worked and studied at the same time.

meaning: 'when I/he/she/you go' (subjunctive: used for future or hypothetical visits/actions).
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive of ir (vaya). Commonly introduces an action that will happen in the future or is hypothetical/uncertain. Subject can change (cuando vaya = when I go / when he/she goes) — context and verb agreement elsewhere determine the subject. Often followed by a clause describing what will happen or what to do at that time.
target_language_example: Cuando vaya a la tienda, te traigo pan.
native_language_example: When I go to the store, I'll bring you bread.

meaning: when I go
additional_notes: Used to talk about recurring or specific occasions when the speaker goes somewhere or does an activity. 'Cuando' = 'when'; 'voy' is the first-person singular present of 'ir' (to go). Often followed by 'a' + place or an infinitive (e.g., 'a la oficina', 'a ver').
target_language_example: Cuando voy al mercado, compro frutas.
native_language_example: When I go to the market, I buy fruit.

meaning: as soon as possible; as soon after as possible.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency; often placed after a verb or at the end of a sentence. Can be used alone as a short command/response (like "As soon as possible"). Formality: neutral — suitable in both spoken and written contexts.
target_language_example: Necesito el informe cuanto antes.
native_language_example: I need the report as soon as possible.

meaning: 'as for' or 'regarding'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or refer to a particular subject. It is often followed by a noun or pronoun (cuanto a ti, cuanto al tema). In writing you may see the variant 'cuanto a' + noun or 'en cuanto a' (the latter is more common).
target_language_example: Cuanto a la reunión, prefiero que sea el martes.
native_language_example: As for the meeting, I prefer it to be on Tuesday.

meaning: no matter how much
additional_notes: A formal or literary concessive expression, similar to por mucho que or aunque. It introduces a contrast like 'however much...' and is usually followed by the subjunctive. Rare in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Cuanto quiera que lo intentes, no cambiarás su opinión.
native_language_example: No matter how much you try, you won't change his opinion.

meaning: the number 45.
additional_notes: Used to say the numeral 45 in Spanish. Can be used alone or with units (minutos, segundos, años, etc.). Pronunciation: 'kwah-REN-tah ee SEES-ehn-kah' (approx.). Same structure as other compound numbers: 'cuarenta y' + digit.
target_language_example: Tengo cuarenta y cinco años.
native_language_example: I am forty-five years old.

meaning: headquarters (main command center of an organization, especially military).
additional_notes: Used for the main office or command center of a military unit, organization, company, or campaign. Can be literal (military HQ) or figurative (central office or base of operations). Often preceded by a possessive or adjective: 'nuestro cuartel general', 'el cuartel general británico'.
target_language_example: El cuartel general decidió cambiar la estrategia.
native_language_example: The headquarters decided to change the strategy.

meaning: 'room with' — used to describe a room that has or includes something (a feature, people, furniture, etc.).
additional_notes: Cuarto means 'room' (or 'bedroom' in many contexts). 'Con' means 'with'. Together they describe what the room includes (e.g., cuarto con aire acondicionado = room with air conditioning). Can be followed by nouns or noun phrases. Word order: cuarto con + [feature/people/items].
target_language_example: Busco un cuarto con baño privado.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a room with a private bathroom.

meaning: bathroom; restroom; toilet (room for washing and using the toilet).
additional_notes: Common everyday term for the room with a sink, shower/bath and toilet. Used in Spain and many Spanish-speaking countries; alternatives include baño, cuarto de servicio, aseo (often for a small toilet), or lavabo. Can be used with adjectives (privado, público) and in phrases like 'ir al cuarto de baño' = 'go to the bathroom.'
target_language_example: ¿Puedo usar tu cuarto de baño?
native_language_example: Can I use your bathroom?

meaning: literally 'room and' — not a fixed phrase; 'cuarto' means 'room' or 'bedroom', and 'y' means 'and'.
additional_notes: This is not a single idiomatic expression. In your examples 'cuarto y' appears because 'cuarto' (room/bedroom) is followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). Use 'cuarto' to talk about a room or a bedroom (mi cuarto = my room). Remember that Spanish uses 'y' to connect nouns or items in a list: 'tu cuarto, mi cuarto y el baño' = 'your room, my room, and the bathroom.'
target_language_example: Entraron en el cuarto y cerraron la puerta.
native_language_example: They went into the room and closed the door.

meaning: 'four are' or the number four when used in arithmetic sentences (as in 'X and four are Y' or 'four times X are Y').
additional_notes: This phrase appears in basic arithmetic or counting sentences. 'Son' is the third-person plural form of 'ser' used for equals in math (e.g., 'Cinco por cuatro son veinte' = 'Five times four are twenty') or to say 'the four (of them) are...' when describing a group ('las cuatro son lindas' = 'the four are pretty'). Word order and context determine whether it expresses a mathematical result or 'are' to describe people/things.
target_language_example: Los cuatro son mis hermanos.
native_language_example: The four are my siblings.

meaning: literally 'neck of' — used to indicate the neck belonging to or part of something/someone; can also appear in idiomatic or colloquial expressions referring to 'throat' or attacking someone's neck/position.
additional_notes: This is a prepositional phrase: 'cuello' = neck, 'de' = of/from. It's normally followed by a noun (person, object) to show possession or relation (e.g., 'el cuello de la camisa' = the collar/neck of the shirt; 'el cuello de Daphne' = Daphne's neck). In some contexts (especially in fiction or colloquial speech), phrases like 'ir por el cuello de...' or 'cortarle el cuello' mean to go after or attack someone's neck (literal) or to target/defeat someone (figurative).
target_language_example: Arréglate el cuello de la camisa antes de salir.
native_language_example: Fix the collar of your shirt before going out.

meaning: 'neck' followed by a preposition phrase 'en' — used when saying something happened to someone's neck in/at/on (e.g., 'se rompió el cuello en...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself. 'Cuello' = neck. In the example sentences it appears in constructions like 'se rompió el cuello en...'(he broke his neck in...), or literally 'cuello en un clavo' (neck on a nail) when describing the location. For beginners: focus on the structure 'se rompió el cuello en + [evento/lugar]' to say someone broke their neck in/at (an accident, tent, etc.).
target_language_example: Se rompió el cuello en el accidente de coche.
native_language_example: He broke his neck in the car accident.

meaning: 'cuenta' here means 'matters', 'is important', or 'counts'; 'cuenta el' = 'the ___ matters' or '___ counts' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Depending on context, 'contar' can mean 'to count' (numbers), 'to tell' (a story), or 'to matter/be important'. In the phrase 'cuenta el' followed by a noun, it usually means 'the [noun] matters' or 'the [noun] counts'. In imperative contexts (like 'Cuenta el dinero'), it means 'Count the money.' Word order and context determine the meaning.
target_language_example: En esta carrera, solo cuenta el tiempo.
native_language_example: In this race, only time counts.

meaning: '(it) is said that' / 'tells that' / 'reports that' (used to introduce a story, report, or what someone says).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like contar (to tell) in impersonal or narrative contexts: 'La leyenda cuenta que...' = 'The legend says that...'. Can also appear in direct speech or reported speech: 'Cuenta que...' meaning '(he/she) says/reports that...'. Not typically used for counting numbers (use contar/contar hasta).
target_language_example: Mi abuela cuenta que conoció a mi abuelo en una fiesta.
native_language_example: My grandmother says that she met my grandfather at a party.

meaning: countdown (a backward count to zero).
additional_notes: Used for a timed countdown (e.g., to a launch, start, deadline). Commonly appears with verbs like comenzar/iniciar (to start) and detener/para (to stop). Literal elements: cuenta (count/account) + atrás (back/behind).
target_language_example: La cuenta atrás para el concierto empezó anoche.
native_language_example: The countdown for the concert started last night.

meaning: bank account
additional_notes: Refers to an account held at a bank (checking/current or savings). Commonly used when talking about opening, accessing, sharing, or emptying (withdrawals) an account. Often preceded by possessive (mi, su) or verbs like abrir, compartir, vaciar, acceder.
target_language_example: Necesito abrir una cuenta bancaria para recibir el sueldo.
native_language_example: I need to open a bank account to receive the salary.

meaning: aware of what; notice/realize what (someone has done or what is happening).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like 'darse cuenta de' (to realize/notice). The full expression is usually 'darse cuenta de lo que...' and means becoming aware of a fact or action. Commonly appears in subordinate clauses introduced by 'que' (e.g., 'se dará cuenta de lo que hiciste').
target_language_example: Pronto te darás cuenta de lo que necesitas cambiar.
native_language_example: Soon you'll realize what you need to change.

meaning: realized that it was / realized that + clause
additional_notes: This is part of the common reflexive verb phrase 'darse cuenta de que' meaning 'to realize that...'. In sentences the subject is typically followed by 'se dio cuenta de que...' (past) or 'me doy cuenta de que...' (present). The clause after 'que' states what was realized. Do not drop 'de' before 'que' in standard usage.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que era tarde y salí corriendo.
native_language_example: I realized that it was late and I ran out.

meaning: 'realize that there was' or 'become aware that (something had happened)'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of 'darse cuenta de que había...' (or 'me/te/se dimos cuenta de que había...'). It indicates noticing or becoming aware of something that occurred earlier (past perfect). Commonly used with verbs like 'perder', 'olvidar', 'ganar'. In English often translated as 'I realized that I had...' or 'he/she noticed that...' Use appropriate reflexive pronoun (me, te, se, nos) before 'di/dio/dimos'.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había dejado el teléfono en el restaurante.
native_language_example: I realized that I had left my phone at the restaurant.

meaning: 'of his/her/their' as part of the phrase 'darse cuenta de' meaning 'to notice/realize' (literally 'give oneself account of').
additional_notes: This string appears inside the common reflexive phrase 'darse cuenta de' (me doy cuenta de, te diste cuenta de, se dio cuenta de) meaning 'to notice' or 'to realize'. 'Su' is a possessive (his, her, your formal, their) and links what is noticed (e.g., 'su ausencia' = 'his/her absence'). The literal words can be guessed from components, but the full idiom 'darse cuenta (de)' is non-compositional (it means 'realize/notice').
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de su error demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: I realized his/her error too late.

meaning: 'of the' used in the phrase darse cuenta de/ darse cuenta del = 'to realize' or 'to become aware of'.
additional_notes: In these examples 'cuenta del' appears as part of the verb phrase darse cuenta (de/ del) meaning 'to notice' or 'to realize'. Use 'de' before a noun or verb clause; 'del' is the contraction of 'de + el' when the following word is a masculine singular noun (e.g., 'del error', 'del riesgo'). Common forms: 'darse cuenta de' (infinitive), 'me di cuenta de', 'se dio cuenta de'.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta del problema demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: I realized the problem too late.

meaning: 'countdown' (the act of counting down to an event)
additional_notes: Used to talk about the countdown before an event (e.g., launch, New Year, start). Can be used alone as an exclamation ('Cuenta regresiva.') or with estar/entrar ('Estamos en cuenta regresiva'). Often followed by a duration or the thing being counted down to.
target_language_example: Estamos en la cuenta regresiva para el concierto.
native_language_example: We're in the countdown for the concert.

meaning: 'story of' or 'tale about' (used to introduce the topic or subject of a story).
additional_notes: Used before a noun or phrase to indicate what the story/tale is about (cuento de hadas = fairy tale). Can also appear in expressions like 'se cuenta de' but here it's the noun cuento + preposition de. Common in titles and descriptions (cuento de Navidad, cuento de terror).
target_language_example: Leí un cuento de terror anoche.
native_language_example: I read a horror story last night.

meaning: fairy tale; a magical or idealized story.
additional_notes: Used for traditional stories with magic, princes/princesses, and moral lessons. Also used figuratively to describe something idealized or unrealistic (e.g., a 'fairy-tale' romance) or to say an ideal situation has ended ('the fairy tale is over').
target_language_example: Vivieron felices para siempre, como en un cuento de hadas.
native_language_example: They lived happily ever after, like in a fairy tale.

meaning: literally 'rope of' or 'string of'; used to describe a rope/line made of or used for something, or in some dialects part of an expression (colloquial) meaning 'a bunch of/series of'.
additional_notes: Most often appears as part of a phrase describing a rope or clothesline (e.g., 'cuerda de tender' = clothesline) or to say a rope stretched between two points. In some regional or colloquial uses, 'una cuerda de + (insult/description)' can mean 'a bunch of...' (pejorative). Choose the exact meaning from context.
target_language_example: Colgamos la ropa en la cuerda de tender del patio.
native_language_example: We hung the clothes on the clothesline in the yard.

meaning: human body
additional_notes: Refers to the physical body of a human being. Used in general, scientific, or everyday contexts when talking about body parts, functions, or the body as a whole.
target_language_example: El cuerpo humano tiene sistemas como el circulatorio y el nervioso.
native_language_example: The human body has systems like the circulatory and nervous systems.

meaning: 'it costs nothing' / 'it's free' (often used figuratively: 'it's no trouble' or 'there's no harm in...')
additional_notes: Common expression used literally for price but frequently used figuratively to encourage small actions (e.g., saying please, asking a question, doing a favor, or dreaming). Often appears with 'no' before the verb: 'no cuesta nada' = 'it doesn't cost anything / there's no harm in it.' Can be followed by an infinitive: 'No cuesta nada preguntar.'
target_language_example: No cuesta nada ayudar a un amigo cuando lo necesita.
native_language_example: It costs nothing to help a friend when they need it.

meaning: it costs a / it takes a (amount of time/effort); used to talk about price or how long/hard something is.
additional_notes: Commonly used with literal prices (cuesta un dólar = it costs one dollar) and with idiomatic or exaggerative expressions (cuesta un ojo de la cara, cuesta un riñón) to mean very expensive. Also used with time expressions (cuesta un rato, cuesta un tiempo) to mean 'it takes a while.' Context determines whether it's monetary cost or effort/time.
target_language_example: Hacer este proyecto me cuesta un mes.
native_language_example: This project takes me a month.

meaning: it costs a (used to state the price or cost of something).
additional_notes: Common pattern: 'cuesta + (article) + noun' — e.g. 'cuesta una fortuna' = 'it costs a fortune'. 'Cuesta' is the 3rd-person singular of 'costar' (to cost). The noun that follows describes the type/amount (una fortuna, una moneda, una pasta). Use 'cuesta' for singular subjects; use 'cuestan' for plural.
target_language_example: Ese teléfono viejo cuesta una fortuna en el mercado de antigüedades.
native_language_example: That old phone costs a fortune at the antique market.

meaning: downhill; getting worse or going downhill (figurative).
additional_notes: Literally 'down a slope'. Commonly used both literally (walking/driving downhill) and figuratively to say a situation is deteriorating or things are getting worse. Often used with verbs like ir (ir cuesta abajo) or caer (caer cuesta abajo).
target_language_example: Desde que perdimos el contrato, todo ha ido cuesta abajo.
native_language_example: Since we lost the contract, everything has gone downhill.

meaning: a matter/question of time; it's only a matter of time
additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen eventually — inevitable but timing is uncertain. Often appears in sentences like "es (solo) cuestión de tiempo" or "era cuestión de tiempo." Can be used with verbs to indicate future occurrence (e.g., "es cuestión de tiempo que + subjunctive/indicative").
target_language_example: Es cuestión de tiempo que recibas buenas noticias.
native_language_example: It's only a matter of time before you get good news.

meaning: a matter of life or death; extremely urgent or serious.
additional_notes: Used to say something is critical or urgent — literally 'a question/matter of life or death.' Common in both formal and informal contexts to stress importance or danger.
target_language_example: Debemos actuar rápido: esto es una cuestión de vida o muerte.
native_language_example: We must act quickly: this is a matter of life or death.

meaning: 'cave of' or '...’s cave' — used to say what or who the cave belongs to or contains.
additional_notes: A common construction: cueva + de + noun. The noun after de indicates possession, origin, contents, or a characteristic (e.g., cueva de murciélagos = cave of bats; cueva de Gollum = Gollum's cave). Word order differs from English possessive with ’s (English: Gollum's cave → Spanish: cueva de Gollum).
target_language_example: Exploramos la cueva de los osos.
native_language_example: We explored the cave of the bears / the bears' cave.

meaning: careful about / careful in (doing something)
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to pay attention or act with caution regarding an action, choice, or the future. Commonly followed by a noun, a verb phrase introduced by 'lo que' or 'en' + noun (e.g., 'en el futuro', 'en la elección'). Can be used as an adjective with ser/estar (sé cuidadoso, sé más cuidadoso).
target_language_example: Sé más cuidadoso en la elección de tus palabras.
native_language_example: Be more careful in choosing your words.

meaning: 'ass of' or 'butt of' — used to describe someone's butt or as part of insults or expressions.
additional_notes: Culo = butt/ass (vulgar). When followed by 'de' + noun, it can describe possession ('ass of X') or be part of insults and idiomatic phrases. Very informal and often offensive — avoid in polite contexts. Tone can be aggressive, crude, or humorous depending on context. Not grammatical as a standalone fixed expression; its meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: No me hables así, no soy culo de nadie.
native_language_example: Don't talk to me like that, I'm nobody's ass.

meaning: literally 'birthday of'; used to indicate the kind or purpose of a birthday (e.g., 'birthday of sobriety').
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun that describes what the birthday celebrates (sobriedad, jubilación, etc.). In English you might say 'my ... anniversary' or 'my ... birthday' depending on context: 'cumpleaños de sobriedad' = 'sobriety anniversary' (the number of years sober). Word order: cumpleaños (birthday) + de + noun.
target_language_example: Hoy es mi cumpleaños de cuatro años de sobriedad.
native_language_example: Today is my four-year sobriety anniversary.

meaning: to reach (an age) / to turn (a certain number of years).
additional_notes: Used with ages or time limits: 'cumplir' + 'los' + number/years = to reach that age (e.g., cumplir los veinte = turn twenty). Commonly appears with past/future tenses and with phrases like 'antes de' or 'después de' to indicate before/after reaching an age. 'Cumplir' can also mean 'to fulfill' or 'to complete' in other contexts, but when used with 'los' plus an age it specifically means to reach/turn that age.
target_language_example: Acaba de cumplir los veinte.
native_language_example: He/She has just turned twenty.

meaning: 'which/what was the' (used to ask or report what something/someone was)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in indirect questions and reported speech. 'Cuál' = which/what, 'era' = past (imperfect) of 'ser' (was), 'el' = masculine definite article for a following noun (often implied or stated later as 'problema' etc.). Can be used in direct questions (¿Cuál era el problema?) or embedded clauses (No sabía cuál era el problema).
target_language_example: No recuerdo cuál era el horario del tren.
native_language_example: I don't remember what the train schedule was.

meaning: "what is his/her/your name?" (formal or neutral).
additional_notes: Common question phrase used to ask someone's name. "Cuál" contracts with "es" in speech to "¿Cuál es...?" Use "su" for formal 'your' (usted) or to mean 'his'/'her'/'their' depending on context. For informal 'your' (tú) use "cuál es tu nombre" or more naturally "¿cómo te llamas?". In indirect questions, it keeps the same form: "Me pregunto cuál es su nombre."
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es su nombre, por favor?
native_language_example: What is your name, please?

meaning: 'when is' (asks for the date/time of an event or moment).
additional_notes: Use to ask or talk about the timing of a specific event or moment (birthday, wedding, meeting, time to do something). Often followed by a noun or clause: 'cuándo es + [evento]' or 'cuándo es + que...'. In statements it can report knowing or not knowing the time.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes cuándo es la reunión?
native_language_example: Do you know when the meeting is?

meaning: 'how long' (asks about duration or time length).
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the length of time something lasts or will last. Common in questions (¿Cuánto tiempo...?) and indirect questions (Me pregunto cuánto tiempo...). Can be followed by verbs, clauses, or noun phrases.
target_language_example: ¿Cuánto tiempo vas a quedarte en la ciudad?
native_language_example: How long are you going to stay in the city?

meaning: How much does it cost? / How much is it?
additional_notes: Used to ask the price of something. Can be used on its own as a short question (¿Cuánto cuesta?) or within a sentence after verbs like saber, preguntar, or expressions like no tengo idea de. Informal register is fine for everyday situations.
target_language_example: ¿Cuánto cuesta este libro?
native_language_example: How much does this book cost?

meaning: 'How old are you?' (literally: 'How many years do you have?')
additional_notes: Common, everyday question used to ask someone's age. Use 'tienes' for informal tú form. For polite/formal use, ask '¿Cuántos años tiene usted?'. Often preceded by a name or phrase like 'Por cierto' (by the way).
target_language_example: ¿Cuántos años tienes? Yo tengo veintitrés.
native_language_example: How old are you? I am twenty-three.

meaning: 'shut up' (literally: 'shut your mouth').
additional_notes: Very direct, rude command used to tell someone to be quiet. Often appears as 'cállate' alone or as 'cállate la boca' for emphasis. 'La boca' (the mouth) is optional; adding words like 'jodida' makes it more offensive. Use with caution — not appropriate in polite company.
target_language_example: Cállate la boca y deja de gritar.
native_language_example: Shut up and stop shouting.

meaning: in prison for / sent to prison for (a reason or crime).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone was sent to jail because of a specific act or crime. Often appears with verbs like enviar, mandar, ir, estar, or a sentence length (e.g., 'fue a la cárcel por vender drogas'). The preposition 'por' introduces the reason or offense.
target_language_example: Lo condenaron a la cárcel por fraude.
native_language_example: He was sentenced to prison for fraud.

meaning: vicious circle; a self-reinforcing negative cycle
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation where one problem causes another that in turn worsens the first, creating a loop that's hard to break. Commonly used in both social and everyday contexts (economics, habits, fashions, personal problems). Often preceded by verbs like entrar en, caer en, romper, salir de.
target_language_example: Tenemos que romper este círculo vicioso antes de que empeore.
native_language_example: We have to break this vicious circle before it gets worse.

meaning: how do you say (it) / what did you say?
additional_notes: Commonly used to ask how to say a word or phrase in Spanish (often followed by the word to be translated), or as a clarification question meaning 'what did you say?'. Tone and context determine which meaning is intended. When asking for translation, you can follow it with '...?': "¿Cómo se dice 'apple' en español?" For clarification you might hear: "¿Cómo dices?" or more commonly "¿Cómo?" or "¿Qué dijiste?"
target_language_example: ¿Cómo dices 'library' en español?
native_language_example: How do you say 'library' in Spanish?

meaning: 'how is' or 'how are' (formal/singular; asking about state or condition).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's condition or the state of something. When addressing one person formally use '¿Cómo está usted?'. With friends or informal singular use '¿Cómo estás?'. Can also refer to the state of objects or situations (e.g., '¿Cómo está la pista?'). Context determines whether it's about health, mood, condition, or progress.
target_language_example: Buenos días, ¿cómo está usted?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

meaning: 'How are you?' (informal, singular).
additional_notes: Common informal greeting used to ask about someone's well-being. Use 'cómo está' for one person formally, 'cómo están' for plural. Can appear with or without question marks and often preceded by 'hola' or 'y tú'.
target_language_example: Hola, ¿cómo estás?
native_language_example: Hi, how are you?

meaning: how (is someone doing/handling something); asking about someone's well‑being or how they're getting along.
additional_notes: Often appears in questions like '¿Cómo la estás pasando?' or '¿Cómo la llevas?' where 'la' refers vaguely to life, the situation, or a specific thing previously mentioned (e.g., la vida, la situación, la salud). Common in everyday conversation to ask how someone is managing or feeling. Tone is neutral; can be informal depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Amigos, ¿cómo la están pasando con el trabajo nuevo?
native_language_example: Friends, how are you managing/doing with the new job?

meaning: Of course; how could we not; rhetorical 'how/why not' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used in different ways: as a short affirmative reply meaning "of course" or "sure" (Sí, cómo no); in exclamations/questions meaning "how could (we/you) not...?" (¿Cómo no nos dimos cuenta?); or in rhetorical/self-reflective questions (¿Cómo no soy yo mismo?). Tone and punctuation determine meaning—intonation often conveys irony, surprise, or emphasis.
target_language_example: —¿Me ayudas con esto? —Cómo no, cuenta conmigo.
native_language_example: —Will you help me with this? —Of course, count on me.

meaning: 'what is (his/her/its) name?' or 'what is it called?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone's name (formal or neutral) or to ask the name of an object/thing. Literal components: cómo (how) + se llama (is called). Context determines referent (person vs. thing). Can be used with pronouns: ¿Cómo se llama usted? (formal), ¿Cómo se llama tu hijo? (your son).
target_language_example: Disculpa, ¿cómo se llama tu hermana?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your sister's name?

meaning: 'how they/they are' or 'what they are like' (used to ask or state the nature/way of things or people).
additional_notes: Used to describe or ask about the characteristics, behavior, or situation of people, things, or situations. Context determines whether it's present-tense descriptive ('they are like') or an idiomatic comment ('that's how things are'). Often appears in sentences like 'Sabes cómo son' ('You know how they are' / 'You know how things are').
target_language_example: Dime cómo son tus amigos.
native_language_example: Tell me what your friends are like.

meaning: "What is your name?" (informal)
additional_notes: Common, everyday way to ask someone's name in familiar or informal situations (using tú). Use '¿cómo se llama?' for formal or polite situations (usted). The literal translation is 'how do you call yourself.'
target_language_example: Hola, ¿cómo te llamas?
native_language_example: Hi, what is your name?

meaning: 'How's it going?' or 'How are you doing?'
additional_notes: A casual, friendly way to ask about someone's general well-being or progress. Use with friends, acquaintances or informally; context can make it ask about life in general or about a specific task when followed by a clarifier (e.g., "¿Cómo te va con el trabajo?").
target_language_example: Hola Marta, ¿cómo te va últimamente?
native_language_example: Hi Marta, how's it going lately?

meaning: 'how's it going' / 'how is (something) coming along' / 'how does it work'
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's well‑being (Cómo va?) or about progress/status of something (Cómo va el proyecto?). Can also mean 'how things work' or 'how the situation stands' in phrases like 'Ya sé cómo va.' Informal and common in speech. Context determines whether it's general greeting, progress check, or understanding of how something works.
target_language_example: ¿Cómo va la tarea? ¿Necesitas ayuda?
native_language_example: How's the homework going? Do you need help?

meaning: 'how' or 'the way' (with an indirect object pronoun 'le' = to him/her/you formal/it).
additional_notes: Combines the question/relative adverb 'cómo' (how/the way) with the indirect object pronoun 'le'. Used to describe or report the way something happens to or for someone (e.g., how something affected them, how someone beat/saved/reprimanded them, or what they like). 'Le' normally refers to 'to him', 'to her', 'to you (formal)', or 'to it' depending on context. Not a fixed phrase—meanings depend on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Vi cómo le ayudaron cuando lo necesitó.
native_language_example: I saw how they helped him when he needed it.

meaning: 'how we' or 'how us' (depends on grammar); used to introduce the manner or way in which 'we' feel, act, or something happened to us.
additional_notes: Combination of 'cómo' (how) + object pronoun 'nos' (us / ourselves). Often appears in phrases like 'cómo nos sentimos' (how we feel) or 'cómo nos conocimos' (how we met). Word order can change depending on verb: 'cómo nos sentimos' (how we feel), 'cómo nos conocimos' (how we met). Not a fixed idiom—just a common structure.
target_language_example: Explícame cómo nos ayudó ese proyecto.
native_language_example: Explain to me how that project helped us.

meaning: faces onto; opens onto; gives onto (a direction or place).
additional_notes: Used with objects, buildings, windows, rooms, etc., to indicate that something faces, looks out, or opens toward a place or direction. Often followed by a noun or direction (e.g., 'el jardín', 'el este'). Can also be used figuratively with abstract objects (e.g., 'le da al hombre instintos' — 'it gives the man instincts'), but its most common use is spatial.
target_language_example: Mi balcón da al parque.
native_language_example: My balcony faces the park.

meaning: he/she gives the (feminine plural) — 'da' = gives; 'las' = the/them (feminine plural direct object).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a simple verb + direct object construction. 'Da' is the third-person singular present of dar (to give). 'Las' is the feminine plural direct object pronoun or the article 'las' depending on context. In sentences like 'da las nueces' it's 'gives the nuts' ('las' is the definite article). In examples like 'ni siquiera le da las gracias', 'las gracias' is a set phrase meaning 'thanks', so 'da las gracias' = 'gives thanks' = 'thanks'.
target_language_example: Ella siempre da las instrucciones con calma.
native_language_example: She always gives the instructions calmly.

meaning: it's all the same / it doesn't matter / makes no difference
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more options or outcomes are equally acceptable or indifferent to someone. Common in statements (Da lo mismo) and with an indirect object to indicate who doesn't care (A ella le da lo mismo). Can be used with 'si' to introduce alternatives (Da lo mismo si...).
target_language_example: A mí me da lo mismo si cenamos en casa o salimos.
native_language_example: It's all the same to me whether we eat at home or go out.

meaning: 'gives (someone) a strong feeling' — often used to say something causes an emotion (e.g., makes someone happy, scared, pleased).
additional_notes: Common construction with verbs like dar (me/te/le/nos/les) + mucho + noun for an emotion: 'me da mucho miedo' = 'it scares me a lot'. Also used with 'gusto', 'placer', etc. Subject is the thing that causes the feeling; the person who feels it is an indirect object (me, te, le...). Can be translated as 'gives me/you/etc. a lot of ...' or more naturally 'makes me/you/etc. very ...'.
target_language_example: Ese libro me da mucho interés por la historia.
native_language_example: That book makes me very interested in history.

meaning: 'turn (to)' / 'make a turn (toward)'.
additional_notes: Commonly used in directions to tell someone to turn right or left. Often followed by 'la derecha' (right) or 'la izquierda' (left), or by a destination. In many regions you may also hear 'da la vuelta' (turn around) or 'gira a' as alternatives. Imperative form 'da' is informal (tú). For formal commands use 'dé vuelta a' or better: 'dé la vuelta' / 'gire a'.
target_language_example: Da vuelta a la derecha en el semáforo y sigue recto.
native_language_example: Turn right at the traffic light and go straight.

meaning: 'given that' / 'since' / 'because' (introduces a reason or condition).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a cause, reason, or circumstance. Can be formal or neutral; commonly appears at the start or middle of a sentence. Equivalent to 'since' or 'considering that' in English. Often followed by a clause.
target_language_example: Dado que no hay más entradas, cerraremos la taquilla.
native_language_example: Given that there are no more tickets, we will close the box office.

meaning: give him/her/it the... (imperative: tell someone to give something to someone)
additional_notes: Dale is the informal imperative of dar (tú) directed to a third-party recipient (literally 'give to him/her/it'). Combined with el + noun it tells the listener to hand a specific thing to someone. Use context or an indirect object phrase (a + person) to say who should receive it: 'Dale el libro a María.' If you need formal or plural commands use déle/denle or déle usted/denle ustedes accordingly. Pronouns can also attach: 'Dáselo' = 'give it to him/her'.
target_language_example: Dale el mensaje a Juan cuando llegues.
native_language_example: Give Juan the message when you arrive.

meaning: give (her/them) the (thanks). — used to tell someone to say thanks to another person
additional_notes: Imperative + indirect object pronoun: "dale" = give to him/her/it (or 'give them' colloquially). "las" refers to "las gracias" (the thanks) and is feminine plural; speakers often shorten "dale las gracias" to "dale las" when context makes "gracias" obvious. Common in informal and neutral speech when asking someone to pass on thanks.
target_language_example: Por favor, dale las a María cuando la veas.
native_language_example: Please give (her) the thanks when you see María.

meaning: 'ladies and' (part of a phrase meaning 'ladies and ...')
additional_notes: Not a complete phrase by itself — 'damas y' is the start of combinations like 'damas y caballeros' (ladies and gentlemen) or 'damas y señoras' depending on region. Use when addressing or listing women together with others. Remember to complete it with the second element (e.g., 'caballeros').
target_language_example: Damas y caballeros, bienvenidos al espectáculo.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the show.

meaning: ladies and gentlemen (a formal way to address an audience).
additional_notes: Used to get attention or to address a group formally (e.g., at the start of a speech, announcement, or performance). Equivalent to 'ladies and gentlemen' in English; appropriate in public or formal situations.
target_language_example: Muy bien, damas y caballeros, comencemos la presentación.
native_language_example: All right, ladies and gentlemen, let's begin the presentation.

meaning: 'ladies and' (used to begin the phrase 'ladies and gentlemen').
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the fixed phrase 'damas y caballeros' (ladies and gentlemen) used to address an audience formally. 'Damas y' by itself is incomplete — it needs the following word(s) (e.g., 'caballeros'). Common in announcements, speeches, and event introductions.
target_language_example: Damas y caballeros, bienvenidos al espectáculo.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the show.

meaning: Give me a glass (of...). — a direct request asking someone to hand you a glass or a drink in a glass.
additional_notes: Dame is the informal imperative (tú) of dar + pronoun 'me' (give me). Use 'dame un vaso de agua' or 'dame un vaso de leche' to ask for a specific drink. For politeness, add 'por favor' or use the formal imperative 'deme un vaso' when speaking to someone you should address as usted. Word order: 'dame un vaso de + [drink]'.
target_language_example: Por favor, dame un vaso de agua fría.
native_language_example: Please give me a glass of cold water.

meaning: 'we give the' (first-person plural present of 'dar' + feminine singular direct article 'la').
additional_notes: Literally 'we give the...' — used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., 'damos la bienvenida' = 'we give the welcome' → 'we welcome'). The phrase by itself is incomplete; confirm the noun that follows. 'Damos' is first-person plural ('we give' or 'we hand'). Context determines translation (welcome, back, turn, etc.).
target_language_example: Les damos la bienvenida a los nuevos estudiantes.
native_language_example: We welcome the new students.

meaning: literally 'giving the' or 'doing the' — the gerund 'dando' (giving/doing) + feminine singular article 'la'; used as part of verb phrases like 'dando la vuelta' (turning around), 'dando la mano' (shaking/holding the hand), or 'dando la espalda' (turning your back).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself — it appears before a feminine noun to form progressive actions (estar + dando la + noun). Traductions depend on the noun that follows: 'la vuelta' → 'a turn/around', 'la mano' → 'the hand' (give/offer a hand), 'la espalda' → 'the back' (turn one's back). Use with singular feminine nouns; verb agrees with subject (está/están/estoy etc.).
target_language_example: Estoy dando la mano al nuevo profesor.
native_language_example: I am shaking the new teacher's hand.

meaning: giving/doing/going for a (something) — present progressive 'giving/doing' + an indefinite noun.
additional_notes: Part of the present progressive (estar + gerund) used with 'un/una' + noun to say someone is giving or doing a single action: e.g. 'dando un baño' = giving a bath; 'dando un paseo' = taking/going for a walk/ride. Translate the gerund 'dando' as 'giving', 'taking', or 'having' depending on context. Common with everyday activities.
target_language_example: Estoy dando un paseo por el parque.
native_language_example: I'm taking a walk in the park.

meaning: present participle 'giving' or 'having' + an indefinite feminine noun (literally 'giving a' / 'having a').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the gerund (dando) followed by the feminine indefinite article (una) and a noun that completes the idea (e.g., 'dando una ducha' = 'taking a shower' in some dialects, literally 'giving oneself a shower' or 'having a shower'; 'dando una orden' = 'giving an order'; 'dando una fiesta' = 'throwing/holding a party'; 'dando una paliza' = 'giving a beating'). Context and the noun after 'una' determine the exact meaning. Often used with reflexive verbs (me/te/se) to indicate doing something to oneself: 'me estoy dando una ducha' = 'I'm taking a shower.'
target_language_example: Me estoy dando una vuelta por el barrio.
native_language_example: I'm taking a walk around the neighborhood.

meaning: to make known; to announce or reveal information
additional_notes: Used when someone or an organization announces, publishes, or reveals something to the public or a group. Common with announcements, results, reports, decisions, or new information. Often followed by a direct object (what is revealed) or a clause introduced by que. Can be used in various tenses and voices (e.g., darán a conocer, dieron a conocer, fue dado a conocer).
target_language_example: La empresa va a dar a conocer los resultados mañana.
native_language_example: The company will announce the results tomorrow.

meaning: to give birth; to deliver a baby.
additional_notes: Common Spanish expression for childbirth. Used both literally (a woman giving birth) and sometimes metaphorically (to 'bring something into being'). Follows normal verb agreement: ella dio a luz / va a dar a luz. Often appears with ayudar/impedir/antes de, etc.
target_language_example: Ella va a dar a luz mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: She is going to give birth tomorrow morning.

meaning: to give something; to hand something to someone.
additional_notes: Very common verb + object structure. 'Dar' can mean give, hand, offer, or cause (e.g., dar miedo = to cause fear). With a direct object (algo = something) it simply means to give something. Use indirect object pronouns to indicate the recipient: le doy algo (I give something to him/her).
target_language_example: Te voy a dar algo para la fiesta.
native_language_example: I'm going to give you something for the party.

meaning: to disgust; to be gross or revolting (something causes someone to feel disgust).
additional_notes: Used impersonally: the thing or action 'da asco' (gives disgust) to someone. Common in everyday speech to express strong dislike or revulsion. Can be used literally (smell, taste, sight) or figuratively (behavior, idea). Often followed by indirect object pronouns like 'me', 'te', 'le', etc. — e.g. 'Me da asco'. Tone is informal to neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Ese olor me da asco; abre la ventana.
native_language_example: That smell gives me disgust; open the window.

meaning: to work well; to turn out well; to fit properly (clothing/equipment).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe that something functions properly, that a plan or result is successful, or that an item fits/looks good. Context determines nuance: e.g., una máquina 'da bien' = it works well; una camisa 'me da bien' = the shirt fits me well. Often appears in present: 'da bien', past: 'dio bien', or with subjunctive when needed.
target_language_example: Si la prueba da bien, podremos seguir con el proyecto.
native_language_example: If the test goes well, we can proceed with the project.

meaning: to give a high-five (to slap someone's open hand in celebration, greeting, or agreement).
additional_notes: Informal, physical gesture used to celebrate, congratulate, or greet someone. Often used with an indirect object: 'darle cinco a alguien'. Can appear reflexively ('darse cinco') or as 'chocar cinco' in some regions. Common in casual speech and sports contexts.
target_language_example: Después del gol, fuimos a la banca y decidimos dar cinco entre todos.
native_language_example: After the goal, we went to the bench and decided to give each other high-fives.

dar con una frase de quince

target_language_multi_word_term: dar con una frase de quince
meaning: to come up with/find a fifteen-syllable sentence
additional_notes: dar con means 'to find' or 'to come up with' (an idea, solution, phrase). Here it specifically asks someone to produce a sentence that has fifteen syllables. The phrase is compositional: 'dar con' + 'una frase de quince (sílabas)' literally maps to English components. Commonly used with different imperative forms (tú, usted, vosotros, ustedes) as in the examples.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes dar con una frase de quince sílabas para el poema?
native_language_example: Can you come up with a fifteen-syllable sentence for the poem?

meaning: to make one feel weird, uncomfortable, awkward, embarrassed, disgusted, or uneasy; to cause a negative or odd emotional reaction.
additional_notes: Informal, colloquial expression. Often used in spoken Spanish to describe something that elicits an unpleasant or awkward feeling. Structure: dar + cosa (or dar + noun with similar meaning: dar pena, dar miedo, dar asco). Can be followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase. Tone and exact meaning depend on context (awkward, embarrassing, gross, unsettling).
target_language_example: Ese vídeo me da cosa ver cómo habla así.
native_language_example: That video makes me feel awkward watching how he talks like that.

meaning: to realize; to become aware of
additional_notes: Commonly used to express becoming aware of something. Often appears reflexively as 'darse cuenta de' — e.g. 'darse cuenta de que...' = 'to realize that...'. Literally 'to give account of' but in this sense it means 'to notice' or 'to realize'.
target_language_example: Al final no supo dar cuenta de lo que había pasado.
native_language_example: In the end he couldn't realize/understand what had happened.

meaning: to unsubscribe, cancel a service, deregister, or discharge someone (from a service, membership, job, or hospital).
additional_notes: Commonly used for canceling subscriptions, removing someone's registration, or formally discharging someone. The exact nuance depends on context: for services it means to cancel; for employment it can mean to fire or terminate; in medical/military contexts it can mean to discharge. Often followed by the thing being canceled (dar de baja la cuenta / dar de baja a un empleado).
target_language_example: Quiero dar de baja mi suscripción al gimnasio.
native_language_example: I want to cancel my gym membership.

meaning: to feed (someone/an animal); to give food to.
additional_notes: Common Spanish expression used when giving food to people or animals. It requires an indirect object (a la persona/el animal) or can use a direct object with an article (dar de comer al gato). Often appears with verbs like 'tener que', 'poder' or in past tense (olvidó dar de comer).
target_language_example: No olvides dar de comer a los peces esta mañana.
native_language_example: Don't forget to feed the fish this morning.

meaning: to discharge (from hospital) or to remove someone from an active/registered/cared-for status (to give clearance).
additional_notes: Often used in medical contexts to mean 'discharge a patient'. The more common pattern is 'dar de alta' or 'dar el alta a alguien'; all are used interchangeably depending on region and construction. Can also appear in administrative contexts (e.g., removing someone from a registry or ending benefits).
target_language_example: El jefe del hospital decidió dar el alta al paciente esta mañana.
native_language_example: The hospital chief decided to discharge the patient this morning.

meaning: to make the first move; to take the first step (figuratively or literally).
additional_notes: Commonly used figuratively to mean initiating an action, conversation, reconciliation, relationship, or project. Can also be literal (physically taking the first step). Often implies someone must overcome hesitation or fear to begin. Use when one person must start something that others may follow.
target_language_example: Si quieres cambiar las cosas, tienes que dar el primer paso.
native_language_example: If you want to change things, you have to take the first step.

meaning: to make someone feel like (doing something); to cause a desire or urge
additional_notes: Common impersonal construction: usually used as 'dar ganas de + infinitive' (e.g., 'Me da ganas de bailar' = 'It makes me want to dance'). Subject can be a thing, situation, or person. Use indirect object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, os, les) to indicate who feels the urge.
target_language_example: Esa película me da ganas de viajar; dar ganas a todos mis amigos también.
native_language_example: That movie makes me want to travel; it makes all my friends want to too.

meaning: to give thanks; to be thankful (to someone or in general).
additional_notes: Used to express gratitude. Often used with a person or entity after 'dar gracias' + a preposition: 'dar gracias a alguien' (to thank someone) or 'dar gracias por' (to give thanks for something). Can be followed by a reason introduced with 'por' or by the recipient with 'a'. Common in religious contexts (dar gracias a Dios / al Señor) but also used generally.
target_language_example: Debo dar gracias por mi familia cada día.
native_language_example: I should give thanks for my family every day.

meaning: to take pleasure in; to enjoy doing something; to please (someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used in two ways: 1) to say someone will enjoy or take pleasure in doing something (e.g., Me va a dar gusto + infinitive = I'll be glad to...), and 2) to indicate pleasing others (dar gusto a alguien = to please someone). Can be idiomatic — not always literal 'give taste'. Often appears with personal pronouns or impersonal 'se' (No se puede dar gusto a todo el mundo = You can't please everyone).
target_language_example: Me va a dar gusto conocer a tu familia.
native_language_example: I'll be glad to meet your family.

meaning: to not matter; to be all the same
additional_notes: Used impersonally with an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les) or with 'a' phrases: 'me da igual' = it doesn't matter to me / I don't care. Can express indifference or that two options are equivalent. Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Me da igual si vamos al cine o al parque.
native_language_example: I don't mind if we go to the movies or the park.

meaning: to turn one's back on; to ignore, abandon, or refuse to help someone or something.
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically turning one's back) and figuratively (emotionally or socially abandoning or refusing to face an issue). Commonly followed by a person or thing: dar la espalda a alguien / algo. Can imply betrayal, neglect, or deliberate avoidance.
target_language_example: Después del conflicto, ella decidió dar la espalda y no quiso hablar más.
native_language_example: After the conflict, she decided to turn her back on him and refused to speak anymore.

meaning: to feel like (doing something); to want or be in the mood for something (often used impersonally: 'me da la gana' = 'I feel like it').
additional_notes: Common colloquial expression used to express desire or preference. Often appears in the impersonal construction 'me/te/le/nos/os/les da la gana' + infinitive (e.g., 'me da la gana salir' = 'I feel like going out'). Can be direct: 'me da la gana' (I want to) or with an action: 'me da la gana comer pizza' (I feel like eating pizza). Tone can be neutral or slightly brusque depending on context.
target_language_example: Hoy me da la gana salir; dar la gana es lo que importa.
native_language_example: Today I feel like going out; feeling like it is what matters.

meaning: to annoy, bother, or be a nuisance (to someone).
additional_notes: Informal idiom used when someone is causing irritation, making trouble, or being a pain. Often used with indirect object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, os, les) — e.g., "me das la lata". Literal image: "to give the can," but meaning is figurative and non-compositional. Common in everyday spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: No empieces a dar la lata ahora; estoy concentrado.
native_language_example: Don't start bothering me now; I'm concentrating.

meaning: to shake hands; to give one's hand (as a greeting, agreement, or gesture of friendship).
additional_notes: Commonly used for greeting someone, meeting for the first time, or sealing an agreement. Often used with the preposition 'a' before a person: 'dar la mano a alguien'. Can be literal (physically giving one's hand) or figurative (making an agreement). Neutral register — appropriate in most situations.
target_language_example: Le di la mano para saludarlo cuando llegué.
native_language_example: I shook his hand to greet him when I arrived.

meaning: to turn around; to go back; to change direction or reverse course.
additional_notes: Common phrasal expression. Can mean physically turning around, returning the way you came, or reversing a decision/situation (e.g., 'change your mind' or 'back out'). Context tells whether it's literal (movement) or figurative (undo/avoid).
target_language_example: Si te equivocas, puedes dar la vuelta y volver por el camino correcto.
native_language_example: If you make a mistake, you can turn around and go back the right way.

meaning: to say thank you; to give thanks.
additional_notes: Used to express gratitude. Can be used transitively (dar las gracias a alguien = to thank someone) or impersonally (dar las gracias por algo = to give thanks for something). Common in formal and neutral contexts. Note: English uses 'thank' as a verb; Spanish uses the phrase 'dar las gracias' or the single verb 'agradecer'.
target_language_example: Quiero dar las gracias a María por su ayuda.
native_language_example: I want to thank María for her help.

meaning: to give your best / to do your best
additional_notes: Common phrase meaning to put in your maximum effort or perform as well as you can. Often appears as 'dar lo mejor (de mí/ti/etc.)' to specify the person (e.g., 'dar lo mejor de mí' = give the best of myself). Used in advice, encouragement, or self-motivation.
target_language_example: En el examen, solo puedo dar lo mejor de mí.
native_language_example: In the exam, I can only give my best.

meaning: to not matter; to be all the same (to someone).
additional_notes: Used to indicate indifference or lack of preference/importance to the speaker. Commonly used in the impersonal construction with an indirect object pronoun: 'me da lo mismo' (I don't care / it doesn't matter to me), 'te da lo mismo', 'le da lo mismo', etc. Synonyms include 'dar igual' and 'no importar'. Often followed by an infinitive, noun, or subordinate clause (e.g., 'me da lo mismo si vienes' or 'le da lo mismo el color'). Tone ranges from neutral to informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Me da lo mismo si vienes; a mí me da lo mismo.
native_language_example: It doesn't matter to me if you come; it's all the same to me.

meaning: to cause; to give rise to; to lead to (something happening)
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that one action or situation produces a consequence or result. Often followed by 'a' + noun (dar lugar a un problema) or by subordinate clauses introduced with 'que' (dar lugar a que ocurra...). Neutral to formal register; widely used in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: La falta de mantenimiento puede dar lugar a un fallo en la máquina.
native_language_example: The lack of maintenance can give rise to a failure in the machine.

meaning: to give my / to offer my (something belonging to the speaker). Used with a noun after 'mi' to indicate giving or offering that possession or commitment.
additional_notes: Structure: dar + mi + [noun]. Common with literal gifts (dar mi libro), favors (dar mi ayuda), approvals (dar mi aprobación) and figurative or emphatic expressions (dar mi palabra, dar mi vida). The verb is usually conjugated (doy, das, da, damos, dan) while the multi-word base is 'dar mi'. Include the thing being given after 'mi'.
target_language_example: Estoy dispuesto y preparado para dar mi vida por él.
native_language_example: I'm willing and prepared to give my life for him.

meaning: to scare; to be frightening (to someone).
additional_notes: Common Spanish expression used impersonally: the thing that 'gives fear' is the subject. Often conjugated as 'me da miedo' (it scares me / I'm afraid of it), 'te dan miedo' (they scare you), or in other tenses (p. ej., 'me dio miedo', 'me dará miedo'). Can express physical fear or that something is creepy/intimidating.
target_language_example: Esa película suele dar miedo a mucha gente.
native_language_example: That movie tends to scare many people.

meaning: to report, to inform (officially) or to file a report
additional_notes: Commonly used when reporting an incident, accident, problem, or giving an official update to authorities, a supervisor, or an insurance company. Often followed by 'de' + noun (dar parte de un accidente) or 'a' + person/organization (dar parte a la policía). More formal than just 'decir' and implies an official or formal notification.
target_language_example: Tuvo que dar parte del accidente a la policía.
native_language_example: He had to report the accident to the police.

meaning: to give way; to let someone pass or to make room for someone/something; to allow something to proceed (literally or figuratively).
additional_notes: Commonly used when asking someone to move aside, to yield in traffic, or to allow progress in a discussion or process. Often appears as "darle paso a" + noun/person when meaning 'to give way to' or 'to make room for'. Can be both literal and figurative.
target_language_example: Por favor, da paso a los pasajeros que bajan antes de subir.
native_language_example: Please give way to the passengers who are getting off before boarding.

meaning: to cause pity or sadness; to embarrass or make someone feel ashamed (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common Spanish expression used impersonally with indirect-object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/os/les). With people or things as subject it often means 'to make someone feel pity' (Me da pena = It makes me feel sorry). With actions or situations it can mean 'to be embarrassing' or 'to feel ashamed' (Me da pena decirlo = I'm embarrassed to say it). Tone can be sympathetic or mildly embarrassed; register is neutral to informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Ver a niños sin juguetes da pena; eso sí que da pena.
native_language_example: Seeing children without toys makes one feel sorry; that really makes me feel sad.

meaning: to take something for granted; to assume something is true or certain without verifying it.
additional_notes: Used when someone assumes a fact, outcome, agreement, etc., as certain. Often followed by a noun or a que-clause (e.g., dar por hecho algo / dar por hecho que...). Can imply a mistake or oversight if the assumption is incorrect. Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No debes dar por hecho que vendrá si no te lo confirma.
native_language_example: You shouldn't take it for granted that they will come if they don't confirm it to you.

meaning: to take for granted; to assume something will be true or available without appreciating it
additional_notes: Used when someone assumes a person, thing, or situation will always be the same or available and therefore doesn't appreciate or consider it. Commonly used in constructions like 'dar algo por sentado' or reflexively 'dar por sentado que...'.
target_language_example: No debemos dar por sentado el apoyo de nuestros amigos.
native_language_example: We shouldn't take our friends' support for granted.

meaning: to work; to be effective; to yield results
additional_notes: Used to indicate that an action, plan, remedy, method, etc., produced the desired outcome. Can be used intransitively (esto no dio resultado) or with an implicit subject (la medicina dio resultado). Commonly appears in past tense (dio resultado) or negative form (no dio resultado).
target_language_example: Espero que el nuevo tratamiento dé resultado.
native_language_example: I hope the new treatment will work.

meaning: to give (someone) time; to allow time; to let time pass (for something to happen).
additional_notes: Used to indicate allowing more time for someone or something (dar tiempo a alguien para + infinitive) or that a process requires time (dar tiempo para + infinitive). Common constructions: "darle tiempo a alguien" (give someone time), impersonal forms like "hay que dar tiempo" (one must allow time), and reflexive/neutral uses such as "dar tiempo para que...". Context and subject determine whether the speaker is giving time to someone or stating that time is needed. Polite and neutral register; can be used in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Tenemos que dar tiempo para que la herida sane.
native_language_example: We have to give time for the wound to heal.

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a stroll.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you're going out for a short, usually casual walk. Can be used literally (walking for pleasure or exercise) or sometimes figuratively (e.g., sending someone away), but beginners will most often hear the literal meaning. Often used with verbs like ir (ir a dar un paseo) or quedarse (voy a dar un paseo).
target_language_example: Esta tarde voy a dar un paseo por el parque.
native_language_example: This afternoon I'm going to take a walk in the park.

meaning: to take a step back; to withdraw or reconsider; to pause and reassess.
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically stepping back) and figuratively (stepping back from a situation, project, or decision to gain perspective, delay, or withdraw). Common in contexts like discussions, negotiations, work decisions, or when someone needs space. Can be followed by 'en' or 'de' and a noun or clause (e.g., dar un paso atrás en el proyecto / dar un paso atrás y pensar).
target_language_example: Después del problema, decidió dar un paso atrás y revisar todo.
native_language_example: After the problem, he decided to take a step back and review everything.

meaning: to go for a walk/ride/turn; to take a short outing or stroll.
additional_notes: Common idiom used for short, casual trips by foot, bike, car, or simply 'to go out for a bit'. Context tells the mode (caminar, en coche, en bici). Can also mean to go around (e.g., around a block). Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Voy a dar una vuelta por el parque.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a walk around the park.

meaning: to turn (something) over); to flip; to turn around; to take a short walk/drive (dar una vuelta)
additional_notes: Common multi-word verb phrase formed with dar + vuelta. Often appears with article and object (dar la vuelta a X) to mean flip or turn around. Reflexive form darse la vuelta = to turn oneself around. Regional uses include 'dar una vuelta' (to go for a walk/drive). Conjugates with dar.
target_language_example: Voy a dar vuelta la tortilla para que no se queme.
native_language_example: I'm going to flip the omelette so it doesn't burn.

meaning: to give them the (feminine plural) — commonly used as part of 'darles las gracias' = to thank them.
additional_notes: darles = 'to give them' (les = indirect object for 'them'). las is a feminine plural direct object pronoun/article; in the phrase darles las gracias it combines to mean 'to give them the thanks' (i.e., 'to thank them'). You will most often see this exact sequence in the fixed expression darles las gracias. Word order: dar + indirect object (les) + direct article/plural noun (las gracias).
target_language_example: Quiero darles las gracias por su ayuda.
native_language_example: I want to thank them for their help.

meaning: to realize; to become aware
additional_notes: A pronominal (reflexive) expression usually followed by de + noun or de que + clause (darse cuenta de algo / darse cuenta de que...). Expresses becoming aware, often suddenly or unintentionally. Commonly appears in constructions like sin darse cuenta (without realizing). Conjugates like dar with reflexive pronoun: me doy cuenta, te diste cuenta, se dieron cuenta.
target_language_example: Sin darse cuenta se había comido toda la caja de galletas.
native_language_example: Without realizing it, he had eaten the whole box of cookies.

meaning: to realize; to become aware of
additional_notes: A pronominal verb phrase: darse cuenta (de + something). Commonly used to express noticing or becoming aware of facts, mistakes, feelings, or people. Conjugate the reflexive verb darse (me doy, se dio, nos daremos) and follow with 'de' + noun/phrase, an infinitive, or a 'que' clause. Can be negated (no darse cuenta) or used to indicate feigned ignorance (fingir no darse cuenta).
target_language_example: El primer paso consiste en darse cuenta de que se tiene un problema.
native_language_example: The first step is to realize that one has a problem.

meaning: to think one is important; to act self-important; to put on airs
additional_notes: Used when someone behaves as if they are more important or more knowledgeable than others. Often appears in reflexive forms like 'se da importancia', 'me doy importancia', 'se da mucha importancia a...'. Can be critical (pejorative) or neutral (descriptive).
target_language_example: No te des importancia; deja de darte importancia delante de los demás.
native_language_example: Don't think you're so important; stop showing off in front of others.

meaning: to hurry; to hurry up.
additional_notes: A pronominal verb phrase meaning to move or act faster. Conjugate the verb (dar) and include the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) that matches the subject: por ejemplo, me doy prisa, nos damos prisa. Commonly used with tener que/haber que to express obligation (tener que darse prisa = to have to hurry). Informal register: neutral — used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Hay que darse prisa.
native_language_example: We/One has to hurry.

meaning: will realize / will notice (he/she/it will become aware)
additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase 'darse cuenta (de)' meaning 'to realize' or 'to notice'. 'Dará cuenta' is future tense, third person singular (he/she/it will realize). Often used with 'de' + something: 'darse cuenta de X'. Can be negative: 'no se dará cuenta' = 'he/she/it won't notice.'
target_language_example: Ella se dará cuenta de la verdad mañana.
native_language_example: She will realize the truth tomorrow.

meaning: 'I will give the' (feminine singular object) — first person future of 'dar' + feminine direct object article 'la'.
additional_notes: Used when the speaker promises to give or provide something expressed by a feminine singular noun that follows (la orden, la señal, la vuelta, etc.). The exact meaning depends on the noun: 'dar la vuelta' = 'to turn' or 'to go around', 'dar la orden' = 'to give the order'. The phrase is simply the verb form 'dar' in future (daré) plus the article 'la'. Word order and the noun after 'la' determine the full sense. If the object is a pronoun (la, se la), placement can change: 'se la daré' = 'I'll give it to her/him/them.'
target_language_example: Daré la señal cuando estés listo.
native_language_example: I'll give the signal when you're ready.

meaning: I will give (you) what...
additional_notes: Built from the verb dar (to give) in future tense (daré = I will give) plus lo que (what/that which). Used to promise to give someone whatever they ask/want; the rest of the clause completes the idea (e.g., daré lo que quieras = I will give you what you want). Common in offers and promises. Subject can be implied (te daré = I will give you).
target_language_example: Si me lo pides con calma, te daré lo que necesites.
