additional_notes: Used to indicate a starting point in time or place. When followed by a time expression (años, quince años) it means "since (age/date)". When followed by a place (escalones) it means "from the (place)". The article los agrees with the noun that follows (los años, los escalones).
target_language_example: Vivo aquí desde los veinte años.
native_language_example: I've lived here since I was twenty.

meaning: of course; certainly; sure (used to agree, confirm, or emphasize).
additional_notes: Common phrase to express agreement, confirmation, or emphasis. Can be used alone (e.g., "¡Desde luego!") or within a sentence to strengthen a statement (often followed by que + clause). Neutral register — suitable in spoken and written Spanish. Placement can be sentence-initial or mid-sentence.
target_language_example: ¿Vendrás a la fiesta? — Desde luego que sí.
native_language_example: Desde luego, hablas como una chica que ha estado casada.

meaning: since (a very) / from (a very) — used to indicate starting point in time or distance with emphasis (very).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before age expressions (desde muy niño/pequeño) to mean 'since very young' or before distance (desde muy lejos) to mean 'from very far away.' 'Muy' intensifies the following adjective/adverb. Used in spoken and written Spanish; word order: 'desde muy + [noun/adjective/adverb]'.
target_language_example: Desde muy joven, aprendí a cocinar.
native_language_example: Since I was very young, I learned to cook.

meaning: since childhood; from when (someone was) a child.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has been true starting in childhood and continuing to the present (or for a long time). Often used with verbs like conocer, soñar, gustar, luchar. Can be adjusted for gender/number (desde niña, desde pequeños) to match the person(s) referred to.
target_language_example: Lo he querido ser desde niño.
native_language_example: I've wanted to be it since I was a child.

meaning: since
additional_notes: Used to indicate a point in time from which something has been true or has been happening. Commonly followed by a clause (verb). Can translate as “since” (time) or “ever since” for emphasis. Not to be confused with the preposition desde alone (which is followed by a noun or time expression).
target_language_example: No lo veo desde que se mudó a otra ciudad.
native_language_example: I haven't seen him since he moved to another city.

meaning: I wish all / I want all (feminine object) — literal phrase combining 'deseo' (I wish/I want) + 'toda' (all, feminine).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's just the verb deseo followed by the adjective/pronoun toda. 'Toda' agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to (toda la comida = all the food; toda la vida = whole life). Depending on context, 'deseo' can mean 'I wish' (more formal) or 'I want'. For beginners, remember to match toda/todo/todas/todos to the noun.
target_language_example: Deseo toda la información sobre el curso.
native_language_example: I want all the information about the course.

meaning: 'my/your/his/her/their desire is...' — introduces what someone wants or wishes.
additional_notes: Common construction: [Mi/Su/Nuestro] deseo es + infinitive or noun phrase. Used to state a wish, intention, or longing. In some cases Spanish drops the preposition 'de' before an infinitive (Mi deseo es dar...). When followed by a noun, you may see 'es de' (Su único deseo es de volver...) but more natural is 'es volver' or 'es + noun'.
target_language_example: Nuestro deseo es conocer otros países.
native_language_example: Our desire is to visit other countries.

meaning: bachelor party (party for a man before his wedding).
additional_notes: Used for a party or celebration for a groom-to-be. In some regions you may also hear despedida de soltera for a bride's party, or despedida (alone) in casual speech. Often used with possessive (mi/su) or with articles (una/la).
target_language_example: Vamos a organizar su despedida de soltero este fin de semana.
native_language_example: We're going to organize his bachelor party this weekend.

meaning: I woke up from (something) / I woke up feeling (a certain way).
additional_notes: Past tense first-person singular of 'despertar' + preposition 'de'. Used to say you woke up from a physical state (e.g., a dream, a nightmare, a long sleep) or to indicate the mood you had upon waking (e.g., 'de mal humor' = 'in a bad mood'). 'Me desperté de...' is more common and adds the reflexive pronoun; both forms are understood in context.
target_language_example: Me desperté de una pesadilla y no podía dormir otra vez.
native_language_example: I woke up from a nightmare and couldn't sleep again.

meaning: I woke up in/at (somewhere or at some time).
additional_notes: Literally 'I woke up in/at'. Use to say where or when you regained consciousness or woke up. Common constructions: 'desperté en + lugar' (desperté en la cama), 'desperté en + momento/expresión' (desperté en medio de la noche). The subject is often 'me' (reflexive), so full form is 'me desperté en...'.
target_language_example: Me desperté en la playa con el sonido de las olas.
native_language_example: I woke up on the beach to the sound of the waves.

meaning: 'awake (all)'; used with 'toda la noche' to mean 'awake all night'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears when describing staying awake for an entire period, most commonly 'toda la noche' (all night). Grammatically, the full expression is usually 'quedarse despierto toda la noche' or 'me quedé despierto toda la noche'. 'Despierto' is an adjective meaning 'awake'; it must agree in gender (despierto/despierta) if used as an adjective referring to a person. English speakers normally translate as 'stay/was/were awake all night.'
target_language_example: Me quedé despierto toda la noche estudiando.
native_language_example: I stayed awake all night studying.

meaning: after
additional_notes: Used to refer to something happening later than another event or time. It is followed by a noun or pronoun (después de la tormenta, después de mi divorcio) or an infinitive (después de aprobar). Before a full clause, Spanish usually uses después de que.
target_language_example: Nos vemos después de clase.
native_language_example: See you after class.

meaning: after (followed by a clause); used to link events in time.
additional_notes: Introduces a subordinate clause (verb conjugated) to indicate that one action happens after another. When the action is habitual or viewed as factual, use indicative (e.g., "después de que llegó"); when referring to a future or anticipated action, Spanish often uses the subjunctive (e.g., "después de que regrese"). If followed by a noun instead of a clause, use "después de" + noun (no "que").
target_language_example: Saldré después de que termines tu tarea.
native_language_example: I'll leave after you finish your homework.

meaning: after so much / after a long time or much (effort, waiting, talking, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that happens after a lot has occurred (time, effort, talk, work, etc.). Often followed by a verb or clause describing the result or change. Tone can be emotional or emphatic: 'after all that' or 'after so much'.
target_language_example: Después de tanto, por fin llegó el día.
native_language_example: After so much, the day finally arrived.

meaning: after all; in spite of earlier doubt or contrary expectation.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a conclusion or contrast with what was thought before (like English 'after all'). Can introduce a reason, a surprising result, or soften a statement. Often appears at the start or end of a sentence and is followed by a comma when initial.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: después de todo, todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: Don't worry: after all, everything will turn out fine.

meaning: 'afterward' or 'later' + 'me' (marks that the action affects or involves the speaker later).
additional_notes: Combines después (later/afterwards) with the clitic me (me/myself). Used to say that something the speaker will do, will be done to them, or happened to them later. Word order often places the reflexive/object pronoun before a conjugated verb (Después me voy) or before an infinitive/imperative in some dialects (Después me las enseñas = 'Show them to me later'). Translate based on context: 'later I'll...,' 'later they asked me...,' 'later I felt...,' 'later I left...'.
target_language_example: Hablamos ahora; después me llamas para confirmar.
native_language_example: We talk now; later you call me to confirm.

meaning: 'destiny of' or 'fate of' (used to indicate what or whom destiny/fate concerns).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that destiny/fate affects a person, group, thing, or abstract concept. In Spanish the noun destino is followed by de + noun (destino de la nación; destino de un alma). Can be used literally (fate) or more figuratively (future, outcome). Word order: destino de X = the destiny/fate of X.
target_language_example: El destino de la ciudad depende de nuestras decisiones.
native_language_example: The destiny of the city depends on our decisions.

meaning: 'the details of' (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: A common phrase to introduce specific information about something. 'Del' is the contraction of 'de + el' and agrees with a masculine singular noun (e.g., 'el caso', 'el crimen'). For feminine nouns use 'de la' (e.g., 'los detalles de la historia').
target_language_example: Quiero ver los detalles del contrato.
native_language_example: I want to see the details of the contract.

meaning: private detective; private investigator (a person hired to investigate or follow someone).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a professional investigator hired privately (not by the police). Often used when someone wants surveillance, background checks, or to gather evidence. Agreement: detective (m.) / detective (f.) — when describing a woman use 'detective privado' or sometimes 'detective privada'.
target_language_example: Contrataron a un detective privado para investigar el fraude.
native_language_example: They hired a private detective to investigate the fraud.

meaning: behind
additional_notes: Used to indicate position or location (physically behind something) or movement following something/someone. In some contexts it can mean 'after' in a temporal or figurative sense (e.g., reading 'behind the words' = looking deeper). 'De' must follow 'detrás' (never 'detrás' alone when specifying what it's behind).
target_language_example: El gato está escondido detrás de la puerta.
native_language_example: The cat is hiding behind the door.

meaning: behind the door
additional_notes: A spatial phrase used to indicate something or someone is on the far side or at the rear of a door. Common in both literal contexts (physical location) and figurative/literary uses. Use with verbs of position (estar, quedar), movement (colocar, esconder) or place (colgar).
target_language_example: Me escondí detrás de la puerta hasta que se fue.
native_language_example: I hid behind the door until they left.

meaning: behind his/her/its (something belonging to someone).
additional_notes: Combines 'detrás de' (behind) + possessive 'su' (his, her, its, your formal, or their). Use 'su' to indicate the thing/person being stood, hidden, or located behind. Agreement: 'su' does not change for gender/number; the noun that follows may be singular/plural (e.g., 'su madre', 'sus padres'). Context determines whether 'su' means his, her, their, or your — clarify with context or use 'de él/ella/ellos/usted' if ambiguous.
target_language_example: Ella se escondió detrás de su coche.
native_language_example: She hid behind her car.

meaning: stopped (someone) / arrested (someone) — depends on context.
additional_notes: detuvo is the past (pretérito) of detener(se). With a direct object introduced by the preposition a, detuvo a + person usually means 'arrested' or 'stopped (someone)'. When used reflexively (se detuvo) it means 'stopped' (oneself) or 'paused' an action, often followed by an infinitive: se detuvo a + infinitive = 'stopped to (do something)'. Context (police vs. personal pause) determines the meaning.
target_language_example: El oficial detuvo a los sospechosos en la madrugada.
native_language_example: The officer arrested the suspects at dawn.

meaning: 'give the' or the imperative 'give the' (from dar + definite article), used in many set phrases like 'di la vuelta' (turn around) or 'le di la mano' (I gave him/her my hand).
additional_notes: Di la is the second-person singular imperative (di) + feminine definite article (la) or the past tense first-person (di) + la as direct object in statements like 'le di la mano' (I gave him/her the hand). In commands, 'di la vuelta' means 'turn around' or 'go around' (literally 'give it the turn'). In statements, 'le di la...' means 'I gave him/her the...' Use context to know if it's a command (imperative) or past tense (I gave...).
target_language_example: Le di la bienvenida cuando llegó.
native_language_example: I gave him/her the welcome when he/she arrived.

meaning: say the
additional_notes: "di" is the informal singular command of decir ("to say" / "to tell"). "la" here is usually the feminine singular article "the", so this phrase is normally followed by a feminine noun, as in di la verdad ("tell the truth"). On its own, it is incomplete.
target_language_example: Di la respuesta en voz alta.
native_language_example: Say the answer out loud.

meaning: 'to hell with' / 'screw' (to reject or dismiss something strongly)
additional_notes: Used to express strong dismissal, frustration, or rejection of a person, thing, idea, or situation. Informal and somewhat rude—avoid in formal contexts. Often followed by a noun or clause (e.g., "Al diablo con eso" = "To hell with that"). Tone can be angry, dismissive, or decisive.
target_language_example: Al diablo con las reglas, hoy no voy.
native_language_example: To hell with the rules, I'm not going today.

meaning: to draw a (something).
additional_notes: Common verb phrase: 'dibujar' = to draw; 'un' is the masculine indefinite article meaning 'a' or 'an'. Use 'dibujar una' for feminine nouns (dibujar una casa). Can introduce a direct object (what is drawn). Often followed by nouns like pájaro, árbol, mapa, círculo.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes dibujar un perro para la clase?
native_language_example: Can you draw a dog for the class?

meaning: dictionary of / dictionary for (indicates the subject, language, type, or origin of a dictionary).
additional_notes: Use 'diccionario de' to specify what the dictionary is about (language, topic, format, owner, etc.). Follow with a noun or noun phrase: a language (diccionario de latín), a topic (diccionario de los sueños), a qualifier (diccionario de versión reducida), or a source (el diccionario de la estantería). Word order: 'diccionario de' + noun. Capitalization: languages are usually lowercase in Spanish (latín, francés).
target_language_example: Busco un diccionario de cocina para regalar.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a cooking dictionary to give as a gift.

meaning: the phrase 'diccionario es' is the noun 'diccionario' (dictionary) followed by the verb 'es' (is) — used to say what a dictionary is like (e.g., useful, expensive).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression; it's simply the structure 'diccionario es' as in 'Este diccionario es...' (This dictionary is...). Use it to describe a dictionary's qualities with an adjective or adjective phrase. Remember agreement: 'diccionario' is masculine singular, so use masculine singular adjectives (e.g., útil, caro, inútil). To say 'my dictionary is...' use 'Mi diccionario es...'.
target_language_example: Este diccionario es muy útil para estudiar vocabulario.
native_language_example: This dictionary is very useful for studying vocabulary.

meaning: literally 'dictionary to me' — used to say a dictionary is useful or helpful to the speaker (i.e., 'this dictionary is useful to me').
additional_notes: In Spanish the indirect object pronoun me emphasizes who benefits: 'Este diccionario me es útil' = 'This dictionary is useful to me.' More natural alternatives include 'Este diccionario me resulta útil' or 'Este diccionario me ha sido de gran utilidad.' Use 'me' to show personal usefulness or benefit.
target_language_example: Ese diccionario me resulta muy útil cuando traduzco textos.
native_language_example: That dictionary is very useful to me when I translate texts.

meaning: 'dictionary that' — used to introduce a relative clause describing a specific dictionary.
additional_notes: Combines the noun diccionario (dictionary) with the relative pronoun que (that/who/which). Used to specify or identify which dictionary is meant (e.g., the one that... / the same dictionary that...). In Spanish the relative clause can follow immediately and que replaces English 'which' or 'that'. Word order and agreement stay with the noun (no change to que).
target_language_example: Busco el diccionario que usaste ayer.
native_language_example: I'm looking for the dictionary that you used yesterday.

meaning: says something
additional_notes: Commonly used literally to mean 'says something' (something unspecified). In some contexts (sentence 5) it can mean 'conveys/means something' (i.e., the story tells/means something to me). 'Algo' = 'something' — vague/unspecified. Useful for both spoken comments and figurative meanings.
target_language_example: Siempre que hablamos, él dice algo interesante.
native_language_example: Whenever we talk, he says something interesting.

meaning: they say that
additional_notes: A common phrase used to report what others say. 'Dicen' is the third-person plural of 'decir' and can mean 'they say' or the impersonal 'people say.' 'Eso' = 'that' (refers to a statement or idea just mentioned or understood from context). Used for general statements (Everyone says that / That's what people say).
target_language_example: Siempre dicen eso cuando hablamos de política.
native_language_example: They always say that when we talk about politics.

meaning: the thing (that) was said / said what (followed by clause).
additional_notes: Used after a form of decir to refer to the content that was spoken. Often appears in phrases like 'he dicho lo que sé' (I've said what I know) or 'has dicho lo que querías decir' (you've said what you wanted to say). It's a neutral, common structure for referring back to words or information previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Ya te he dicho lo que tenía que decirte.
native_language_example: I've already told you what I had to tell you.

meaning: said that it/he/she/this/that is
additional_notes: Phrase combines the past participle 'dicho' (said/told) with a reported clause starting with 'que' + 'es' (is). Used to report what someone has said. English translation depends on context and the subject referred by 'es' (it/he/she/this/that). Often appears in contexts like 'me han dicho que es...' (they've told me that it is...).
target_language_example: Me han dicho que es caro, así que ahorraré.
native_language_example: They've told me that it is expensive, so I'll save up.

meaning: said that I'm
additional_notes: Combines decir (to say/tell) in a past participle construction with a following clause starting with estoy (+ adjective/state). Common in responses to insistence or to report what you've already told someone (e.g., 'I already said that I'm fine'). Can appear with different auxiliary verbs (he dicho, te dije, le hubieras dicho). The English equivalent often uses 'said' or 'told' + 'that I'm'.
target_language_example: Ya te he dicho que estoy cansado.
native_language_example: I've already told you that I'm tired.

meaning: a phrase used when reporting what someone said with 'that' + 'not it/that' (part of longer reported statements like 'dicho que no lo hice' = 'said that I didn't do it').
additional_notes: This fragment appears in reported-speech constructions with verbs like decir (he dicho, me dijo, etc.) followed by 'que' and a negative clause containing an object pronoun (lo). In English you usually translate the full sentence (e.g. 'he dicho que no lo sé' → 'I've said that I don't know it' or more naturally 'I told you I don't know'). Alone it is incomplete—expect different verbs and pronouns to complete the idea (hacerlo, tenerlo, saberlo, conocerlo).
target_language_example: Ya te he dicho que no lo tengo.
native_language_example: I've already told you I don't have it.

meaning: a construction used to report what someone has said that someone (third person) does or should do; literally 'said that he/she/they...'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'dicho' (said) with a subordinate clause introduced by 'que' and the reflexive/impersonal pronoun 'se' used with a third-person verb. It appears in reported speech: 'He dicho que se vaya' = 'I have said that he/she should leave' or 'I've told them to leave.' Context and verb form after 'se' determine exact meaning (command, habitual action, plan). 'Se' can be singular or plural depending on context and sometimes refers to people in general.
target_language_example: Ya he dicho que se quede tranquilo.
native_language_example: I've already said that he/she should stay calm.

meaning: '(I/they) have said that you...' — introduces reported speech with a command or instruction directed at 'you'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'dicho' (said) plus a subordinate clause starting with 'que' and a reflexive/object pronoun 'te'. It commonly appears in reported speech to relay orders, requests or statements about what someone told 'you' to do (e.g., told you to leave, told you to stay, told you to take off your clothes). The tense and mood in the clause after 'que' vary (indicative or subjunctive) depending on context and whether the speaker reports a past command, a wish, or a factual statement.
target_language_example: Me han dicho que te vayas ahora mismo.
native_language_example: They've told me to make you leave right now.

meaning: 'told (you) everything' or 'said everything'.
additional_notes: Literal past participle phrase: dicho (said/told) + todo (everything). Used to indicate someone has revealed all relevant information. Common in contexts about confessions, explanations, or sharing complete details. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le) or a subject: 'me lo ha dicho todo' = 'he/she has told me everything.'
target_language_example: Ella me lo ha dicho todo sobre el viaje.
native_language_example: She has told me everything about the trip.

meaning: teeth after eating (used to talk about brushing your teeth after meals)
additional_notes: This phrase appears in instructions or routines about oral hygiene. In Spanish you'd usually say 'cepillarse los dientes después de comer' (to brush one's teeth after eating). The literal words are transparent, but the full idea commonly implies brushing. Use with reflexive verb 'cepillarse' and possessive articles (los/mis/tus) as appropriate.
target_language_example: Siempre me cepillo los dientes después de comer.
native_language_example: I always brush my teeth after eating.

meaning: gave to
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of dar (to give). 'Dieron a' is used with an indirect object to indicate who received something; the full sentence often includes an indirect object pronoun (le, les, se) or a noun after 'a' (a Grace, a él). In English you usually say 'gave (something) to (someone)'.
target_language_example: Le dieron a María un regalo por su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: They gave María a present for her birthday.

meaning: they realized / they noticed.
additional_notes: From the pronominal verb 'darse cuenta (de/que)' meaning 'to realize' or 'to notice'. 'Dieron cuenta' is the third person plural preterite (they realized/noticed). Use 'de' + noun (darse cuenta de un ruido) or 'de que' + clause (darse cuenta de que... ). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Al final, se dieron cuenta de la verdad.
native_language_example: In the end, they realized the truth.

meaning: they gave (her/him/it/the) — past tense, third person plural of 'dar' plus a feminine singular direct object article 'la'.
additional_notes: Used to say that 'they' gave or caused something to someone in the past. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article replacing a specific noun (e.g., la carta, la noticia, la oportunidad, la idea). The exact English translation depends on the noun: 'they gave her the news' / 'they gave the idea to me' (note word order differs). Context can also mean 'they caused her to have' (e.g., 'le cambiaron la cara' = 'it changed her face/expressions when they gave her the news').
target_language_example: Me dieron la noticia ayer.
native_language_example: They gave me the news yesterday.

meaning: they considered/declared (something) to be (a certain way); they assumed or pronounced (someone) as (something, e.g., dead, certain).
additional_notes: Common construction: dar por + past participle (dar por + adj/past participle) meaning 'to consider/assume/declare something as...'. Often used to express an assumption (dieron por sentado = they took for granted) or an official/accepted conclusion (lo dieron por muerto = they declared him dead). Subject is who does the considering; the thing/person considered follows 'por'.
target_language_example: Lo dieron por desaparecido después de la tormenta.
native_language_example: They considered him missing after the storm.

meaning: ten thousand.
additional_notes: A cardinal number used to count or quantify (10,000). Used same way as in English: before nouns (e.g., diez mil estudiantes) or alone as an amount. Note spacing: 'diez mil' is two words. In Spanish numbers larger than 999 are grouped by thousands (mil).
target_language_example: Hay diez mil libros en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: There are ten thousand books in the library.

meaning: difference of / difference in (used to talk about how two things differ by X or in X).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the type or measure of a difference (opinion, age, price, etc.). Often followed by a noun (diferencia de opinión, diferencia de edad, diferencia de precio) or by a quantity (diferencia de cuatro años). Can be used for abstract differences (opinions, tastes) and measurable differences (age, price).
target_language_example: La diferencia de temperatura entre hoy y ayer es de diez grados.
native_language_example: The difference in temperature between today and yesterday is ten degrees.

meaning: different from; unlike
additional_notes: Used to compare two things, people, or ideas. Commonly followed by a noun or a clause introduced by 'lo que'/'la tuya' etc. In many regions you may also hear 'diferente de'—both are correct, though usage can vary by country.
target_language_example: Su opinión es diferente a la mía.
native_language_example: His/Her opinion is different from mine.

meaning: different from
additional_notes: Used to compare one group or thing to another. In Spanish, más commonly encontrarás 'diferente de' or 'diferente a' depending on region; both mean 'different from'. Follow with the person/thing being compared (e.g., 'diferentes a nosotros', 'diferentes a ti'). You can also use 'diferentes entre sí' to say 'different from each other.'
target_language_example: Los estudiantes de primero son diferentes a los de último año.
native_language_example: First-year students are different from the seniors.

meaning: different from
additional_notes: Used to compare two or more things, people, ideas, customs, etc. Common pattern: 'X es/son diferentes de Y' or 'maneras diferentes de + infinitive' (different ways of...). In many Spanish dialects you may also hear 'diferente a' or 'diferente que' — all are widely used, though some style guides prefer 'de' or 'a' depending on construction.
target_language_example: Mis opiniones son diferentes de las tuyas.
native_language_example: My opinions are different from yours.

meaning: different in / different at (used to say things or people are different in a place, aspect, or situation).
additional_notes: Often used with a location, time period, or aspect after 'en' (e.g., en cada rincón, en Europa, en los últimos años). Can describe differences between people (different in everything) or different instances/places. Word order: 'diferentes en + [noun/phrase]'.
target_language_example: He conocido culturas diferentes en varios países.
native_language_example: I have encountered different cultures in several countries.

meaning: hard to find / difficult to find
additional_notes: Common phrase used with a noun or clause after it (e.g., difícil encontrar trabajo / difícil encontrar la verdad). Often appears with impersonal 'es' (Es difícil encontrar...) or with verbs like 'me fue/ me resultó' + adjective + infinitive to express personal difficulty (Me resultó difícil encontrar...).
target_language_example: Es difícil encontrar buenos amigos cuando te mudas mucho.
native_language_example: It's hard to find good friends when you move a lot.

meaning: it's difficult to speak / it's hard to talk
additional_notes: A common construction using the adjective difícil + infinitive hablar to express that speaking (in general, about a topic, or in a situation) is hard. Often followed by a complement introduced with en, sobre, de, or by specifying what (e.g., en público, tres idiomas, de ello). English equivalents: "it's hard to speak," "it's difficult to talk (about it)."
target_language_example: Me resulta difícil hablar en público sin ponerme nervioso.
native_language_example: I find it difficult to speak in public without getting nervous.

meaning: hard to solve / difficult to resolve
additional_notes: Used to describe that something (a problem, task, situation) is challenging to solve. Often appears with impersonal or dative constructions: "Es difícil resolver...", "Me fue difícil resolver...", or with adverbs: "demasiado difícil". Can be followed by a noun or a clause (e.g., "resolver el problema", "resolver cómo..." ).
target_language_example: Es difícil resolver este problema sin ayuda.
native_language_example: It's hard to solve this problem without help.

meaning: 'say your' or 'tell your' (formal imperative + possessive).
additional_notes: Combines the formal (usted) imperative of decir—diga—with the possessive su. Often appears in questions or instructions when asking someone formally what they say or to tell something belonging to them (e.g., diga su nombre = 'state your name'). Context determines exact translation. Use 'dime/di tu' for informal (tú).
target_language_example: Diga su nombre, por favor.
native_language_example: State your name, please.

meaning: "you say to your" (subjunctive or imperative form used when telling someone to tell another person something)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself. 'Digas' is the present subjunctive (or negative imperative) of 'decir' for tú, and 'a' introduces the indirect object (the person you tell). Commonly appears in constructions like 'que le digas a tu madre' (that you tell your mother) or 'no digas a tu amigo' (don't tell your friend). Word order and use depend on the clause: e.g. 'Que le digas a tu hermano que venga' (Make sure you tell your brother to come).
target_language_example: Que le digas a tu madre que llego tarde.
native_language_example: That you tell your mother that I'm arriving late.

meaning: say that
additional_notes: A combination of digas (the tú subjunctive / negative-command form of decir) and que. It often appears after triggers like cuando for future situations, or in negative commands: No digas que... = “Don’t say/tell ... that ...”.
target_language_example: No digas que no tienes tiempo.
native_language_example: Don't say that you don't have time.

meaning: say a (single)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in negative commands with 'no' as in 'no digas una (palabra)' meaning 'don't say even one' or 'don't say a single (word)'. Often followed by 'palabra' (word) or another noun. Used to emphasize that not even one instance should occur. Literal translation is possible but English often uses 'a single' or 'even one' for the same emphasis.
target_language_example: No digas una excusa más.
native_language_example: Don't say one more excuse.

meaning: I say what
additional_notes: Used to introduce what the speaker says/expresses. Common in statements like "Digo lo que pienso/veo" = "I say what I think/see." "Digo lo que" is simply the first-person singular present form (digo) + the relative phrase "lo que" (what/that which). Can be followed by a clause (e.g. pienso, veo).
target_language_example: Digo lo que necesito decir en esta reunión.
native_language_example: I say what I need to say in this meeting.

meaning: 'I say that I (verb) you' — part of phrases used to report or emphasize something you tell someone (often followed by querer/amar/imperative).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the first-person singular of decir (digo) plus que and the clitic te (you). It appears in sentences like 'Cuando digo que te amo' (When I say that I love you) or in commands/requests with te before a verb: 'Si te digo que te quedes...' (If I tell you to stay...). Word order can change: 'te digo que...' or 'digo que te...' depending on emphasis. Commonly followed by verbs like amo, quiero, quedes, vayas.
target_language_example: Si digo que te quiero, es verdad.
native_language_example: If I say that I love you, it's true.

meaning: 'I say' or 'I think' (used to give your opinion or emphasize agreement).
additional_notes: Common colloquial tag attached to a statement or used alone to assert one's opinion or agreement. Can stand alone as a short response meaning 'that's what I say' or 'I told you so' depending on context. Often used for emphasis or to reinforce what someone else said (e.g., "Eso digo yo" = "That's what I say"). Not formal but widely used in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Si hace calor, mejor quedarnos en casa, digo yo.
native_language_example: If it's hot, it's better to stay home, I think/I say.

meaning: ‘I said no’ or ‘as I said, no’ (used to repeat or emphasize a previous refusal or statement).
additional_notes: Combines the past-tense verb dije (I said) with no to reiterate a negative response or remind someone of something already stated. Often appears as part of a larger clause: 'Como dije, no...' = 'As I said, no...'. Common in everyday speech for emphasis or clarification.
target_language_example: Como dije, no puedo ir mañana.
native_language_example: As I said, I can't go tomorrow.

meaning: I told her.
additional_notes: Past simple first-person of decir (decir → dije). 'Le dije a ella' emphasizes the indirect object 'her' (le = to her); adding 'a ella' clarifies or contrasts (for example, to distinguish from 'le dije a él'). In speech, 'le dije' alone is often enough; 'a ella' is used for emphasis or clarity. Word order: 'le dije a ella' is more common than 'dije a ella'.
target_language_example: Le dije a ella la verdad ayer.
native_language_example: I told her the truth yesterday.

meaning: 'I told (to) the…' — first-person past of 'decir' followed by the indirect object introduced by 'al' (a + el).
additional_notes: Structure: 'dije' = I said/told (preterite). 'al' is the contraction of 'a + el' and introduces the person or role who received the information (e.g., al policía = to the policeman). Often followed by a noun or title (al reverendo, al Tom, al Mando). In English this is translated as 'I told the…' or 'I told (to) the…' depending on style; you can omit 'to' in natural English: 'I told the policeman.'
target_language_example: Le dije al profesor la verdad después de clase.
native_language_example: I told the teacher the truth after class.

meaning: "I told you this" (used to introduce something the speaker previously warned or predicted).
additional_notes: Common in spoken and written Spanish to remind someone that the speaker already warned about or predicted a situation. Often followed by a clause describing the outcome (acabó en lágrimas, no iba a funcionar, etc.). 'Te dije que esto...' literally = 'I told you that this...', where 'te' = 'to you'.
target_language_example: Te dije que esto iba a pasar, ¿por qué no me escuchaste?
native_language_example: I told you this was going to happen—why didn't you listen to me?

meaning: 'I said that you should stay in' (past reporting of a command/suggestion to stay inside or at a place).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone told another person to do: 'dije que' (I said that) + subjunctive or past subjunctive form depending on context; here 'te quedaras' is the past subjunctive of quedarse (used after a past-tense reporting verb). Often followed by a location (en casa, en la cama, en el trabajo). Can express annoyance or reminder: "I told you to stay in."
target_language_example: Te dije que te quedaras en casa cuando lloviera.
native_language_example: I told you to stay in the house when it rained.

meaning: I said everything that / I told (you) all that
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you have already told all relevant information. Often followed by a clause (e.g., tenía que decir, sé). Can be used with different subjects (te, le) to indicate to whom it was said. Past tense (dije) indicates the action already happened.
target_language_example: Dije todo lo que sabía sobre el accidente.
native_language_example: I said everything I knew about the accident.

meaning: he/she said things; (someone) said things (about...)
additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase used to report what someone said. Often followed by details introduced with sobre (about), que (that), or an adjective (e.g., raras, sin sentido). Can be vague—context tells whether the things were positive, negative, sensible, etc.
target_language_example: Ella dijo cosas bonitas sobre mi trabajo.
native_language_example: She said nice things about my work.

meaning: said (that) was / what someone said was (used to report truth or correctness).
additional_notes: Combination appears in relative clauses: 'todo lo que dijo era ...' = 'everything (that) he/she said was ...'. Used to report or evaluate what someone said (true, correct, etc.). In English you'd often add 'that' or use 'what' depending on structure: 'what he said was true' or 'everything he said was true.'
target_language_example: Lo que ella dijo era importante para la reunión.
native_language_example: What she said was important for the meeting.

meaning: he/she said that it/is (introduces reported statement about identity, quality or state).
additional_notes: Combines the past-tense verb 'dijo' (he/she said) with the connector 'que' and the present verb 'es' (is). Used to report what someone said about a person or thing (identity, trait, status). In English you usually translate it as 'said that he/she/it is...' or 'told me that...'. Subject of 'es' can be a person or an abstract idea; the original speaker is quoted indirectly. Tense in the reported clause can stay present when reporting a general truth or unchanging fact.
target_language_example: Mi hermano me dijo que es responsable del proyecto.
native_language_example: My brother told me that he is responsible for the project.

meaning: Tell me why... (ask someone to explain a reason).
additional_notes: Common spoken prompt used to request the reason for something. It combines the imperative 'dime' (tell me) + 'por' as the start of 'por qué' (why). In natural speech you should say the full question 'dime por qué...' followed by the reason or action. Use 'por favor' to be more polite.
target_language_example: Dime por qué llegaste tarde esta mañana.
native_language_example: Tell me why you arrived late this morning.

meaning: money (amount) every/each (period).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun 'dinero' (money) followed by a frequency expression 'cada' + time period (cada mes, cada semana). Used to say how much money is given, saved or sent on a regular basis. In English you usually say 'money every month/week' or 'money each month/week.' Remember to include the time unit after 'cada'.
target_language_example: Guardo un poco de dinero cada mes.
native_language_example: I save a little money every month.

meaning: 'money' + 'as' — used when comparing or describing money in a specific role ("money as ...", "money like ...").
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the word dinero followed by como to introduce a comparison, role, or example. Como can mean 'as', 'like', or 'such as' depending on context. Watch word order and articles: e.g. "el dinero como medio" (money as a means) or "adoraban al dinero como a un dios" (they worshipped money as a god).
target_language_example: Muchas personas ven el dinero como seguridad.
native_language_example: Many people see money as security.

meaning: easy money (money obtained with little effort, often implying risk or moral issue).
additional_notes: Used to refer to money gained quickly or with little work; can imply illegality, corruption, or hidden costs. Common in everyday speech and media. Context determines whether literal (small effort) or figurative (ill-gotten gains).
target_language_example: No aceptes ese trato: parece dinero fácil pero es una estafa.
native_language_example: Don't take that deal: it looks like easy money but it's a scam.

meaning: the money that (to) him/her/you (formal) — used to refer to money related to someone (given, owed, lent, etc.).
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining dinero (money) with a relative clause using que and the indirect object pronoun le. It appears in contexts like 'the money that I gave him/her', 'the money that he/she owed', or 'the money that was lent to you'. le is an indirect object pronoun (to/for him, her, or you formal). The exact English translation depends on the verb in the sentence (gave, owed, lent, asked for, etc.).
target_language_example: Voy a buscar el dinero que le presté a Ana.
native_language_example: I'm going to get the money that I lent to Ana.

meaning: the money (that) (he/she/I) had
additional_notes: A relative clause describing money someone possessed. "Tenía" is the imperfect of tener, often used to describe possession in the past or an ongoing past state. The subject (he/she/I/you) is understood from context. The phrase often appears with qualifiers like "poco" (little) or "todo" (all).
target_language_example: Gastó todo el dinero que tenía en comida.
native_language_example: He spent all the money he had on food.

meaning: gave (someone) some / gave a little of (something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone gave a small or some amount of something (food, drink, money, etc.). Structure: [person] dio algo de [sustantivo] (or dio algo de [noun] a [persona]). Emphasizes an unspecified, modest amount. 'Algo de' can be used with uncountable nouns (pan, leche, comida, dinero) or to mean 'some' rather than a specific quantity.
target_language_example: El vecino me dio algo de fruta.
native_language_example: The neighbor gave me some fruit.

meaning: gave the
additional_notes: A common sequence of dio (the preterite form of dar, 'to give') + el ('the'). It is used when talking about something someone gave in the past: dio el libro, dio el cheque, dio el poder. English may sometimes use a different verb in fixed expressions, such as dio el primer paso = 'took the first step.'
target_language_example: Juan me dio el libro ayer.
native_language_example: Juan gave me the book yesterday.

meaning: gave (him/her/them) the money.
additional_notes: Past simple (pretérito) of dar + direct object 'el dinero'. Use when saying someone gave money to someone else. Often followed by an indirect object (le, me, nos) or a prepositional phrase with 'a' + person to clarify who received it.
target_language_example: Juan le dio el dinero a su hermana ayer.
native_language_example: Juan gave the money to his sister yesterday.

meaning: gave (her/them) the — (used with feminine plural direct objects like 'gracias' or 'buenas noches').
additional_notes: Dio is the past (preterite) of dar (to give). 'Las' is a feminine plural direct-object pronoun or article used before feminine plural nouns. Common fixed phrases: 'dar las gracias' (to give thanks = to thank) and 'dar las buenas noches' (to say good night). In English you usually translate the whole phrase (e.g., 'thanked me', 'said good night to us').
target_language_example: Ella me dio las gracias por ayudarla.
native_language_example: She thanked me for helping her.

meaning: gave all the / gave all the (something) — indicates someone gave the entirety of a specific thing.
additional_notes: This is the past (preterite) form of dar (dio = he/she/you formal gave) followed by 'todo el' (all the + masculine noun). It appears before a masculine singular noun (e.g., dinero). Use 'dio todo' + feminine noun as 'dio todo el amor' is possible because 'amor' is masculine in Spanish; otherwise adjust article/gender: 'dio toda la' for feminine singular nouns, 'dieron todo el' for plural subjects, etc. Common in phrases meaning someone gave everything they had or everything requested.
target_language_example: Ella le dio todo el dinero que tenía.
native_language_example: She gave him all the money she had.

meaning: hit (someone) with a punch in the (body part).
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning '[he/she] gave a punch in the…'. Use with a body part after 'la' (e.g., 'cara' = face). Conjugate 'dio' for past tense (él/ella/usted gave). For other subjects use appropriate forms: 'di' is not correct — use 'me dio', 'te dio', 'nos dio', or change the verb (pretérito) to match the subject: 'dió' is incorrect spelling—correct is 'dio'.
target_language_example: Ella dio un puñetazo en la mandíbula.
native_language_example: She punched him in the jaw.

meaning: Oh my God; an exclamation expressing surprise, shock, frustration, or admiration.
additional_notes: Commonly used as an interjection in many situations. Tone and context determine whether it's surprise, annoyance, fear, or amazement. Can be shortened to '¡Dios!' or softened to '¡Dios mío y santo!' in emphatic speech. Be aware of religious sensitivity in very formal contexts.
target_language_example: ¡Dios mío, qué sorpresa verte aquí!
native_language_example: Oh my God, what a surprise to see you here!

meaning: email address
additional_notes: Common phrase used to refer to someone's email. 'Dirección' = address; 'correo electrónico' = electronic mail. Can be used in singular or plural (direcciones de correo electrónico). Often shortened in speech/writing to 'correo' or 'email' in informal contexts.
target_language_example: ¿Me das tu dirección de correo electrónico?
native_language_example: Can you give me your email address?

meaning: addressed to; headed to; went toward (past tense, third person).
additional_notes: From the verb dirigirse (to address, to head toward). Context determines meaning: 'dirigió al público' = 'addressed the public' (speak to); 'se dirigió al baño' = 'went toward the bathroom' (moved toward). 'Al' is the contraction of 'a + el'. The phrase shown is past simple (pretérito) for él/ella/usted.
target_language_example: Se dirigió al escenario para dar su discurso.
native_language_example: He headed to the stage to give his speech.

meaning: I'll say what I'm going to (do/say).
additional_notes: Commonly the start of a sentence where the speaker announces an intention or explains future actions. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., 'hacer', 'decir', 'explicar') or a clause that completes the thought: 'diré lo que voy a hacer' or 'diré lo que voy a decir'. It's a neutral, literal phrase used in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Diré lo que voy a hacer mañana: llamaré al médico.
native_language_example: I'll say what I'm going to do tomorrow: I'll call the doctor.

meaning: would say to
additional_notes: Conditional form of decir followed by a before the person or group receiving the words. It is compositional and often appears with an indirect object pronoun inserted, as in le diría a Juan, but this entry focuses on the exact contiguous sequence diría a.
target_language_example: No sé qué diría a mi jefe.
native_language_example: I don't know what I would say to my boss.

meaning: would say a (feminine/singular noun) — conditional 'would say' + the indefinite article 'a'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a feminine noun or phrase to describe what someone would say (or would not say). Equivalent to 'would say a...' in English. Context may omit the noun if understood (e.g., 'diría una' followed by an implied idea), but more often it's followed by a noun like 'persona', 'cosa', 'sirena'. Pronunciation: dir-EE-ah OO-na. Used for hypotheticals, opinions, or moral judgments.
target_language_example: Yo diría una opinión honesta.
native_language_example: I would say an honest opinion.

meaning: 'hard drive' (computer storage device).
additional_notes: Refers to the physical or logical device used to store data on a computer. Can mean internal or external hard drive (disco duro interno / externo). Often used for storage capacity (llenar el disco duro) or for formatting/erasing (borrar el disco duro). In informal or figurative contexts it can be used metaphorically (e.g., 'disco duro supremo').
target_language_example: Necesito comprar un disco duro externo para hacer copias.
native_language_example: I need to buy an external hard drive to make backups.

meaning: to apologize for (something) — literally 'to excuse myself for'.
additional_notes: A reflexive verb phrase using disculpar(se). Use 'disculparme por' when speaking in the first person (I). Replace the reflexive pronoun for other persons (disculparte, disculparse, disculparnos, disculparos, disculparse). Commonly followed by a noun or clause (lo de anoche, eso, todo lo que dije). You can add 'quiero/quería' to soften or make it polite.
target_language_example: Quería disculparme por haber llegado tarde.
native_language_example: I wanted to apologize for having arrived late.

meaning: excuse the... / sorry for the... (polite way to apologize for something specific)
additional_notes: Polite, formal expression used to apologize for a specific inconvenience or delay. Usually followed by a noun: 'demora' (delay), 'molestia' (bother), 'tardanza' (lateness). Can be used alone as a short apology (e.g., 'Disculpe la demora.'). 'Disculpe' is formal (usted); in informal contexts use 'discúlpame' or 'perdón'.
target_language_example: Disculpe la confusión; le envío la información correcta ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry for the confusion; I'll send you the correct information now.

meaning: I apologize for / I'm sorry for
additional_notes: First-person singular present of disculparse: 'me disculpo por' is a formal or neutral way to apologize for something (an action, situation, person, etc.). Use with a noun, clause, or pronoun: 'me disculpo por el ruido', 'me disculpo por lo que dije', 'me disculpo por él' (I'm apologizing on his behalf). For more casual speech you might hear 'lo siento' or 'perdón'.
target_language_example: Me disculpo por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I apologize for arriving late.

meaning: dressed up as / disguised as (someone or something).
additional_notes: Past tense (third person singular) of 'disfrazarse de'. Used to say someone wore a costume or disguise to look like a particular person, role, or thing. To use in other persons/tenses, conjugate 'disfrazarse' (me disfrazo, te disfrazaste, se disfrazarán, etc.). Common with occupations, genders, fictional characters, or objects.
target_language_example: Ella se disfrazó de astronauta para la fiesta.
native_language_example: She dressed up as an astronaut for the party.

meaning: enjoying (something); taking pleasure in.
additional_notes: Present participle of disfrutar + preposition de. Used to describe enjoying an activity, experience, or thing: disfrutando de + noun (disfrutando de la música) or disfrutando de + gerund/phrase. Common in progressive descriptions: 'estoy disfrutando de...' or 'disfrutando de...' as part of a sentence.
target_language_example: Estoy disfrutando de las vacaciones en la playa.
native_language_example: I'm enjoying the vacation at the beach.

meaning: a shot (fired) in the [body part / location]; used to describe a gunshot wound located in something (e.g., 'disparo en la cabeza' = 'shot in the head').
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the start of a phrase indicating where someone was shot. It is followed by a feminine noun (la + noun) naming the body part or place: e.g., 'disparo en la pierna', 'disparo en la espalda', 'disparo en la cara'. In news or reports, you may see it used to describe injuries: 'recibió un disparo en la...' In everyday speech, 'recibió un disparo' (he/she was shot) + location is common.
target_language_example: Recibió un disparo en la pierna durante el robo.
native_language_example: He received a shot in the leg during the robbery.

meaning: to distinguish good from (—); to tell good from (—).
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by 'mal' to form 'distinguir el bien del mal' — 'to distinguish good from evil/ bad'. It expresses the ability to tell right from wrong. Use with subjects (pueden, es fácil, sé) and often appears in moral or evaluative contexts.
target_language_example: Es importante enseñar a los niños a distinguir el bien del mal.
native_language_example: It's important to teach children to distinguish good from evil.

meaning: 'different from' or 'distinct from'.
additional_notes: Used to compare one thing or person with another. Often follows the preposition 'a' (distinto a) or 'de' in some regions (distinto de). Common in spoken and written Spanish to indicate difference or uniqueness. Can describe characteristics, experiences, or identities.
target_language_example: Ella es distinto a los demás en su forma de pensar.
native_language_example: She is different from the others in her way of thinking.

meaning: 'fun' or 'more fun than' when comparing; used to say something is enjoyable or to compare enjoyment.
additional_notes: Divertido means 'fun' or 'entertaining'. When followed by que + clause/noun it often appears in comparisons (más divertido que = more fun than) or in exclamations/remarks about how fun something/someone is (Lo divertido que eras = How funny/entertaining you were). It can modify verbs (hacer algo divertido = to make something fun). Note: divertido is an adjective and must agree in gender/number (divertida, divertidos, divertidas).
target_language_example: Jugar con amigos es más divertido que ver la tele.
native_language_example: Playing with friends is more fun than watching TV.

meaning: twice as (much) as / double than
additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or amounts: it indicates that one thing is two times another. Often appears before adjectives, nouns or verbs when comparing (e.g., "es el doble que...", "tiene el doble que..."). In Spanish it's common to use "el doble de + noun" (el doble de trabajo) or "ser/estar el doble que + clause" (es el doble que yo). Both forms convey the idea of two times as much.
target_language_example: Ella gana el doble que yo.
native_language_example: She earns twice as much as I do.

meaning: 'documents that' or 'the documents which' — introduces a relative clause describing specific documents.
additional_notes: Used to refer to particular documents already mentioned or identified; 'que' is a relative pronoun meaning 'that/which' and links to a clause giving more information about the documents. Word order: documentos que + verb/clause. Can refer to documents you gave, received, or that accompanied someone.
target_language_example: Revisé los documentos que me enviaste.
native_language_example: I checked the documents that you sent me.

meaning: pain in
additional_notes: Use before a body part or area to indicate pain located there. Commonly followed by a noun (dolor de cabeza, dolor de estómago, dolor de espalda). Can be used with ser/estar/tener and verbs of complaining: estoy con dolor de dientes / tengo dolor de cabeza / se quejaba de dolor de espalda. Not idiomatic if used without a body part.
target_language_example: Tengo dolor de garganta desde ayer.
native_language_example: I have a sore throat since yesterday.

meaning: 'headache' (pain in the head).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe physical pain in the head. Can be used with articles and qualifiers: 'tengo dolor de cabeza', 'tengo un dolor de cabeza leve', 'un poco de dolor de cabeza'. Also used figuratively to mean a nuisance or problem (e.g., 'esto es un dolor de cabeza').
target_language_example: Tengo un dolor de cabeza después de trabajar frente al ordenador.
native_language_example: I have a headache after working in front of the computer.

meaning: pain in the (body part).
additional_notes: Used to describe physical pain followed by a body part (e.g., 'dolor en el pecho' = 'pain in the chest'). In informal insults, the phrase 'eres un dolor en el...' (often 'trasero' or 'culo') means 'you're a pain in the ...' or 'you're a nuisance.' Context determines whether it's literal (medical) or figurative (annoyance).
target_language_example: Tengo un dolor en el hombro desde ayer.
native_language_example: I have pain in my shoulder since yesterday.

meaning: 'the pain was' — simple past description of pain or discomfort.
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'el dolor era' using the imperfect tense (era) to describe an ongoing or repeated state in the past: 'the pain was' (e.g., severe, unbearable, intense). You will often see it followed by adjectives (fuerte, insoportable, terrible) or clauses describing how the person felt or reacted. Use 'el dolor fue' (pretérito) if you want to emphasize a completed event rather than an ongoing state.
target_language_example: El dolor era constante y no me dejaba pensar.
native_language_example: The pain was constant and wouldn't let me think.

meaning: 'pain and' — used to link 'dolor' (pain, sorrow) with another noun to express two related states or things.
additional_notes: dolor = physical pain or emotional suffering. 'dolor y ...' is a common pattern to join two nouns (often abstract or negative like muerte, sufrimiento, venganza, enfermedades, compasión). It is compositional and literal: it simply means 'pain and ...'. Context determines whether 'dolor' is physical or emotional.
target_language_example: La noticia dejó dolor y tristeza en la comunidad.
native_language_example: The news left pain and sadness in the community.

meaning: '(someone) had pain in the...' or '...hurt' (past, imperfect).
additional_notes: Dolía la is the imperfect form of doler used to describe ongoing or repeated pain in the past. Spanish uses an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) to indicate who feels the pain, followed by dolía(n) and the definite article + body part (la cabeza, el estómago, la espalda, etc.). Use dolía (singular) for one body part and dolían (plural) for multiple parts.
target_language_example: Ayer me dolía la cabeza después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Yesterday my head hurt after work.

meaning: on Sundays (followed by a time or activity, e.g. 'domingos por la mañana' = on Sunday mornings).
additional_notes: This is a time expression used to say something happens on Sundays at a particular part of the day. It is normally completed with a noun indicating time: 'la mañana', 'la tarde', 'la noche' (domingos por la mañana / tarde / noche). You can also see 'los domingos' alone to mean 'on Sundays' (more general).
target_language_example: Voy al mercado domingos por la mañana.
native_language_example: I go to the market on Sunday mornings.

meaning: a nobody; an unimportant or insignificant person.
additional_notes: Used insultingly or self-deprecatingly to say someone has no importance, influence, or worth. Often preceded by 'eres', 'soy', or 'es'. Tone can be rude or humble depending on context.
target_language_example: Crees que eres importante, pero para muchos eres un don nadie.
native_language_example: You think you're important, but to many you're a nobody.

meaning: where she (is/was/lives/works).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that describes a place related to a female person (ella). Often appears as 'donde ella + verb' or shortened in speech to just 'donde' when context makes 'ella' clear. Common in relative clauses ('the place where she...') and in expressions of location or movement. Word order: 'donde ella vive' = 'where she lives.'
target_language_example: Voy a visitar la casa donde ella creció.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit the house where she grew up.

meaning: where (the) — used to introduce a location or situation, followed by a feminine plural noun.
additional_notes: Combines the relative adverb 'donde' (where) with the feminine plural definite article 'las'. Used to refer to places or situations characterized by the following feminine plural noun (e.g., 'donde las flores', 'donde las cosas'). Common in both literal (places) and figurative (situations) contexts. Word order and gender must match the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Quiero volver a donde las estrellas brillan.
native_language_example: I want to return to where the stars shine.

meaning: where + plural noun (where the ...).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing a place where something (plural) happens or exists. 'donde' = 'where'; 'los' is the masculine plural definite article agreeing with a plural noun that follows or is implied. Common pattern: 'donde los + [noun/verb phrase]'.
target_language_example: Viajamos a un pueblo donde los mercados abren temprano.
native_language_example: We traveled to a village where the markets open early.

meaning: where (one) wants; wherever one wants (literal, rare/uncommon construction)
additional_notes: This combines 'donde' (where) with the infinitive 'querer' (to want). 'Donde querer' is not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish and is uncommon outside specific grammatical contexts (e.g., in literary, rhetorical, or infinitival constructions). Native speakers usually prefer conjugated or subjunctive forms like 'donde quieras' or 'donde quieren'. Use 'donde querer' only when the infinitive is required by the structure; it may sound formal or unusual.
target_language_example: Es difícil imaginar dónde querer estar en un mundo así.
native_language_example: It's hard to imagine where to want to be in a world like that.

meaning: 'wherever' or 'anywhere' (general place, no specific location).
additional_notes: Used to indicate any place or an unknown/unspecified location. Often appears in the phrase 'donde sea que...' + verb (subjunctive) for 'wherever...'. Can be used alone ('donde sea') to mean 'anywhere' or 'wherever you want'.
target_language_example: Puedes mudarte a donde sea y seguiré visitándote.
native_language_example: You can move anywhere and I'll keep visiting you.

meaning: 'where I know' or 'where I am aware (that...)' — used to introduce something the speaker knows about a place or situation
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'donde' (where) with 'yo sé' (I know). It often appears in longer sentences like 'donde yo sé que...' (where I know that...) to introduce information the speaker is certain about. In casual speech the subject pronoun 'yo' is often dropped: 'donde sé' is less common; more natural is 'donde sé que...' or simply 'donde sé' only in limited contexts. Use when pointing out a place or situation you know about.
target_language_example: Hay un restaurante donde yo sé que sirven buena comida.
native_language_example: There is a restaurant where I know they serve good food.

meaning: As far as I know (about him).
additional_notes: Used to limit a statement to the speaker's knowledge or belief. Commonly appears as 'Hasta donde yo sé' alone; adding 'él' specifies that the comment refers to 'him'. It signals some uncertainty and is polite when giving information that might be incomplete.
target_language_example: Hasta donde yo sé, él llegará mañana.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he will arrive tomorrow.

meaning: asleep in
additional_notes: Used to say someone fell asleep or is asleep in/on a place or situation. Often appears with verbs like quedarse (se quedó dormido = fell asleep) or estar (estaba/está dormido = was/is asleep). Choice of 'in' or 'on' in English depends on the noun (e.g., 'in the crib', 'on the bunk'). When used with 'quedarse', it emphasizes the action of falling asleep.
target_language_example: Me quedé dormido en el sofá.
native_language_example: I fell asleep on the couch.

meaning: asleep on/in the (followed by a masculine noun introduced by 'el')
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone fell asleep or is sleeping on or in a specific masculine noun (el sofá, el bus, el tren, el volante, etc.). Adjust article/gender/number as needed (dormida en la, dormidos en los, dormidas en las). Commonly appears with verbs like quedarse, dormirse, estar: 'se quedó dormido en el tren' = 'he fell asleep on the train.' Can describe literal position or where someone dozed off (including inappropriate places like 'en el volante').
target_language_example: Encontramos al chico dormido en el sofá con el libro abierto sobre el pecho.
native_language_example: We found the boy asleep on the sofa with the book open on his chest.

meaning: 'I slept in/on' (dormí en) or 'I fell asleep on/in' (me dormí en).
additional_notes: Used to say where you slept (dormí en) or where you fell asleep (me dormí en). Use dormí en for intentionally sleeping somewhere (past simple). Use me dormí en when you fell asleep accidentally or unexpectedly. Common prepositions: en + place (el sofá, el suelo, el barco, el autobús, el piso, frente al televisor).
target_language_example: Me dormí en el sofá durante la película.
native_language_example: I fell asleep on the sofa during the movie.

meaning: Name of a town (literally 'Two Sisters') — a municipality in the province of Seville, Spain.
additional_notes: Dos Hermanas is a proper noun and refers to a specific place. Do not translate it in most contexts; in English you would still say 'Dos Hermanas'. The literal meaning is 'two sisters', which can help remember the name. Capitalize both words when writing the town name.
target_language_example: Voy a Dos Hermanas este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to Dos Hermanas this weekend.

meaning: two years older than
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Structure: [person] + es/soy/era + dos años mayor que + [other person]. You can change 'dos' to another number (tres años mayor que). For feminine agreement, 'mayor' stays the same (no gender change).
target_language_example: María es dos años mayor que Juan.
native_language_example: María is two years older than Juan.

meaning: two years older than / two years more than
additional_notes: Used to compare ages (or quantities) between two people/things. Structure: [Person A] tiene dos años más que [Person B]. Literally 'two years more than'. Can be used with other numbers (tres años más que, un año más que).
target_language_example: María tiene dos años más que su hermana.
native_language_example: María is two years older than her sister.

meaning: two kinds/types of
additional_notes: Used to say there are two categories or types of something. Common in general statements (e.g., "Hay dos clases de..." = "There are two kinds of..."). Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Neutral register and very common.
target_language_example: Hay dos clases de estudiantes en esa clase.
native_language_example: There are two kinds of students in that class.

meaning: they were two / there were two (of them).
additional_notes: A combination of the number 'dos' (two) and the imperfect form 'eran' (they were). Used to describe that two people or things existed or were present over some time or background context. Context and word order matter: often appears in phrases like 'dos eran...' (Two of them were...) or 'éramos dos' (we were two).
target_language_example: Dos eran muy amigos desde la infancia.
native_language_example: The two of them were very close friends since childhood.

meaning: 'two thousand'.
additional_notes: Used to express the number 2,000. Also appears in years (e.g., dos mil trece = 2013). In Spanish, numbers are written as words in speech and can combine with other numbers (dos mil uno = 2001). Pronunciation: "dos mil" (stress on 'dos').
target_language_example: En 2023 fuimos a un concierto con dos mil personas.
native_language_example: In 2023 we went to a concert with two thousand people.

meaning: two or three; a small, imprecise number (about 2–3).
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate small quantity or number. Common in everyday speech to indicate uncertainty or that exact count isn't important. Can modify nouns (dos o tres semanas) or actions (dos o tres peleas).
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme dos o tres días más.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay two or three more days.

meaning: two or three times; a few times (approximate count).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an approximate small number of repetitions (usually 2–3). Common in everyday speech to mean 'a couple of times' or 'a few times.' Can describe past events, frequency, or planned repetitions (e.g., per month).
target_language_example: He visto esa serie dos o tres veces.
native_language_example: I've watched that series two or three times.

meaning: 'two points' or 'two marks' — often refers to two points in a score or two punctuation marks (colon) depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to mean 'two points' in a score (e.g., in sports, games, or grading). In punctuation, 'dos puntos' is the Spanish name for the colon (:) and can appear in instructions or writing contexts. Context tells which meaning applies (sports/scores vs. punctuation/marks).
target_language_example: En el partido marqué dos puntos en el último minuto.
native_language_example: In the game I scored two points in the last minute.

meaning: twice
additional_notes: Used to indicate something happens two times or on two occasions. Commonly appears with time expressions (por año, en una semana) or with verbs (visita, fui, comprobé). Can be used literally (I did it twice) or in sayings (Solo se vive dos veces — You only live twice).
target_language_example: He mirado el correo dos veces hoy.
native_language_example: I've checked the mail twice today.

meaning: twice per / two times a (followed by a time period or unit).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens two times within a given period. Commonly completed by an article + time unit (día, mes, año) or by a noun phrase: e.g. "dos veces al día" (twice a day), "dos veces al mes" (twice a month). Can also appear in fixed expressions like "un reloj roto tiene razón dos veces al día."
target_language_example: Tomo la medicina dos veces al día.
native_language_example: I take the medicine twice a day.

meaning: I give the (feminine plural) ... (e.g., orders, instructions).
additional_notes: Doy is the first-person singular present of dar (to give). 'Las' is the feminine plural direct object pronoun or article; in these examples it refers to a feminine plural noun like 'órdenes' (orders). Together 'doy las órdenes' = 'I give the orders' or more naturally 'I give the orders here' / 'I'm the one who gives the orders.' Use 'doy los' for masculine plural nouns (e.g., 'los informes').
target_language_example: Yo doy las instrucciones en esta reunión.
native_language_example: I give the instructions in this meeting.

meaning: I give a
additional_notes: First-person singular of dar + un. Usually means "I give a/an," but the exact English translation depends on the noun that follows. In some common expressions, English uses a different verb: doy un paseo = "I take a walk," le doy un baño = "I give him/her a bath."
target_language_example: Cada mañana doy un paseo antes del trabajo.
native_language_example: Every morning I take a walk before work.

meaning: 'I give a' (used with a noun to mean 'I give/offer/do one [something]'), or in reflexive constructions 'I take/have a [something]' (e.g., me doy una siesta = I take a nap).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but the verb dar (to give) + una + noun. Meaning depends on the noun and whether it's reflexive (me/te/se doy una) or ditransitive (te doy una ...). Common uses: me doy una siesta (I take a nap), me doy una ducha (I take a shower), te doy una mano (I give you a hand/help you), te doy una pista (I give you a hint), te doy una orden (I give you an order). Context and pronouns determine whether it means 'give' or 'take/have'.
target_language_example: Me doy una pausa después de trabajar.
native_language_example: I take a break after working.

meaning: don't hesitate to; feel free to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone to take an action. Usually appears as 'no dudes en + infinitive' (negative command + infinitive). Common in polite offers or invitations: 'no dudes en llamarme' = 'feel free to call me.'
target_language_example: Si tienes preguntas, no dudes en escribirme.
native_language_example: If you have questions, don't hesitate to write to me.

meaning: '... hurts' (used with a specific (singular) body part).
additional_notes: Common way to say that a particular (singular) body part causes pain. 'Doler' is conjugated to agree with the subject (the body part) and indirect object pronouns indicate who feels the pain: me duele (it hurts me), te duele (it hurts you), le duele (it hurts him/her). For plural body parts use 'duelen' (me duelen los pies). Include the definite article before the body part: 'me duele el hombro'.
target_language_example: A Tom le duele el hombro.
native_language_example: Tom's shoulder hurts.

meaning: 'the ... hurts' (used with a feminine singular body part)
additional_notes: Duele is the third-person singular of doler (to hurt). Spanish uses an indirect-object construction: literally 'it hurts to the [me/you/him/etc.]'. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article matching a feminine body part (la cabeza, la mano). Common patterns: 'Me duele la cabeza' (My head hurts). For plural parts use 'duelen las' (Me duelen las manos). To indicate who feels the pain, add the appropriate indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) before duele.
target_language_example: Me duele la espalda.
native_language_example: My back hurts.

meaning: An affectionate or playful phrase meaning 'sweet of you' or 'you're sweet' (praising someone's kindness).
additional_notes: Not a standard, common fixed expression in Spanish — it looks like a shortened or colloquial way to say 'qué dulce de tu parte' or 'qué dulce (de tu parte)'. You might hear similar forms in informal speech or messages. Use to compliment someone's kind action or words. If unsure, use the full phrase 'qué dulce de tu parte' to be clear.
target_language_example: ¡Qué dulce de tu parte ayudarme con la mudanza!
native_language_example: How sweet of you to help me with the move!

meaning: '(more) sweet than' or 'sweet that' depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in comparisons: 'más dulce que' = '(more) sweet than'. It can also appear in exclamations or sentences where 'dulce' means 'nice' or 'pleasant' and is followed by 'que' + clause (similar to English 'it's sweet that...'). Watch word order: to compare two things you usually say 'más dulce que'.
target_language_example: Esta fruta es más dulce que la otra.
native_language_example: This fruit is sweeter than the other one.

meaning: 'sweet dreams' — a friendly way to wish someone a good night's sleep.
additional_notes: Used when saying good night. Polite and warm; often said to children, friends, partners, or family. Can stand alone or follow 'buenas noches' or 'que tengas'. Not formal language but neutral and widely used.
target_language_example: Buenas noches, que tengas dulces sueños.
native_language_example: Good night, may you have sweet dreams.

meaning: during the (school/season) holidays of; during the (summer/winter) vacation(s) of
additional_notes: Use this phrase to say that something happened or is done within a holiday/vacation period. Typically followed by a time or type of holiday (e.g., 'verano' = summer, 'invierno' = winter, 'Navidad' = Christmas). 'Vacaciones' is plural in Spanish. Common structure: 'Durante las vacaciones de + [time/season/personal reference]'.
target_language_example: Durante las vacaciones de verano visité a mis abuelos.
native_language_example: During the summer holidays I visited my grandparents.

meaning: for a long time; for a long period.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something lasted or has been the case over an extended period. Can refer to past or ongoing situations depending on context. Commonly placed before or after the verb phrase: e.g., "Viví en Siberia durante mucho tiempo" or standalone as a comment "Durante mucho tiempo."
target_language_example: Lo busqué durante mucho tiempo antes de encontrarlo.
native_language_example: I looked for it for a long time before finding it.

meaning: for more than (a period of time)
additional_notes: Used before a time expression to say that something lasted longer than that amount (durante más de + time). Often followed by 'de' and a duration (e.g., 'durante más de dos horas'). Can appear with present perfect or past tenses.
target_language_example: He vivido aquí durante más de cinco años.
native_language_example: I have lived here for more than five years.

meaning: for so long; for such a long time
additional_notes: "Durante tanto" is used to emphasize duration—often with surprise, regret, or question about how long something lasted. It usually appears before a noun or verb phrase (e.g., "durante tanto tiempo", "durante tanto sin verte"). Alone it feels incomplete; native speakers often add "tiempo", "años", or a clause after it.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué no me llamaste durante tanto tiempo?
native_language_example: Why didn't you call me for so long?

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a limited, unspecified period of time (short or medium length). Can imply temporary continuation or a pause from something. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: No voy a mudarme; me quedaré aquí durante un tiempo.
native_language_example: I'm not going to move; I'll stay here for a while.

meaning: 'hard' or 'hard (adverb) + and' — used when describing someone doing something with great effort, often followed by another quality/action.
additional_notes: duro is an adverb meaning 'hard' or 'hardly' depending on context; here it means 'with effort' (e.g., trabaja duro = works hard). The connector y ('and') links the following action or trait. Common structure: [verbo] + duro y + [another verb/description]. Not to be confused with 'duro' as an adjective meaning 'hard (solid)'.
target_language_example: Trabaja duro y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: He works hard and always helps others.

meaning: to act like / to pretend to be (someone or something); to show off as
