meaning: 'was (it) ...' as part of the expression 'era lo suficiente...' meaning 'was ... enough' or 'was sufficiently...'
additional_notes: In these examples 'era lo' begins the phrase 'era lo suficiente...' (or 'era lo suficientemente...') used to say someone/something 'was enough' or 'was sufficiently [adjective]'. 'Era' is the imperfect of 'ser' (was), 'lo' is a neutral article used before 'suficiente' or 'suficientemente'. Common pattern: 'era lo suficientemente + adjective' = 'was sufficiently + adjective' or 'was ... enough'.
target_language_example: No era lo suficientemente alto para subirse al carro.
native_language_example: He wasn't tall enough to get on the ride.

meaning: was much
additional_notes: This is the imperfect of ser + mucho. In the examples, it usually appears as era mucho más..., where mucho strengthens a comparison: 'was much/far more...', 'was much taller/richer...'. Era can mean 'he was,' 'she was,' or 'it was,' depending on context.
target_language_example: La diferencia era mucho más grande de lo que pensábamos.
native_language_example: The difference was much bigger than we thought.

meaning: 'when (I/he/she/you) was younger' or 'when (someone) was younger'.
additional_notes: Past-tense phrase used to talk about a time earlier in life. 'Era' is the imperfect of 'ser' (was/were). Replace subject as needed: 'cuando era más joven' (when I/he/she was younger), 'cuando éramos más jóvenes' (when we were younger). Often used to describe habits, memories, or differences between past and present.
target_language_example: Cuando era más joven, jugaba al fútbol todos los días.
native_language_example: When I was younger, I played soccer every day.

meaning: 'was ours' or 'was our' (imperfect past of 'ser' + possessive 'nuestro'), used to indicate that something belonged to or was associated with 'us' in the past.
additional_notes: 'Era' is the imperfect past tense of 'ser' (used for ongoing, repeated or background past actions). 'Nuestro' must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies (nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, nuestras). Context determines whether it refers to possession, role, duty, or characteristic. Can be literal (La casa era nuestra) or figurative (Tom era nuestro héroe).
target_language_example: Era nuestro secreto.
native_language_example: It was our secret.

meaning: 'was someone else' / 'was a different person' (used to say you thought someone was a different person or that someone seemed different).
additional_notes: Commonly used to express mistaken identity ('I thought they were someone else') or to describe feeling/acting like a different person (e.g., after a big change). In past tense (era = imperfect of ser), implies a continuing or repeated belief/feeling in the past. Can be used with 'pensé' or 'creí' to say 'I thought they were someone else.'
target_language_example: Cuando la vi desde lejos, pensé que era otra persona.
native_language_example: When I saw her from afar, I thought she was someone else.

meaning: was a police officer.
additional_notes: Past imperfect of ser + profesión: used to say someone used to be (or was) a police officer. It can describe a past habitual condition or a past state/background. Context tells whether it means 'used to be' (habit) or simply 'was' (in a story or statement). You can replace 'era' with other tenses (fue policía = was a police officer [completed action]).
target_language_example: Antes de jubilarse, mi madre era policía.
native_language_example: Before retiring, my mother was a police officer.

meaning: it was only
additional_notes: Past imperfect of ser (era) + sólo (only/just). Used to downplay or limit what something/someone was — e.g., 'it was only X' or 'he/she was just X'. Can refer to things, people, situations. In everyday writing/speech, sólo (with accent) is increasingly written without the accent (solo) — both are understood. Tense/subject is provided by context (era = he/she/it/it was / I used to be in some contexts).
target_language_example: No era sólo una idea, era la verdad.
native_language_example: It wasn't just an idea, it was the truth.

meaning: was one (of them/it).
additional_notes: Past imperfect 'era' (he/she/it was / it used to be) + 'uno' meaning 'one' or 'one of (them)'. Used to identify something as a single item/member among others (e.g., 'one of our problems', 'one of them'). Context determines whether it means 'one (thing/person)' or 'one of'. Often followed by 'de' + noun or implied group.
target_language_example: Ella era uno de los mejores estudiantes.
native_language_example: She was one of the best students.

meaning: 'it was urgent' or 'it was important/pressing'.
additional_notes: Past-tense phrase used to report that something required immediate attention or action. Common in reported speech (said/they said). Can refer to an actual emergency or to something that needed prompt handling (e.g., a deadline). Tone depends on context—literal urgency vs. emphasizing importance.
target_language_example: Me llamó porque era urgente resolver el problema.
native_language_example: He called me because it was urgent to solve the problem.

meaning: 'you were' (polite/formal, past imperfect)
additional_notes: Combines the imperfect past tense of ser (era) with the formal pronoun usted. Used to describe habitual or ongoing past states or to identify someone in the past (often in polite/formal contexts). Word order can vary in questions or emphasis (e.g., Era usted quien... / ¿Era usted...?).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, era usted la que contestaba el teléfono.
native_language_example: When I arrived, you were the one answering the phone.

meaning: were for
additional_notes: Used to say who or what something was for in the past. It often shows the intended recipient or purpose. "Eran" is the imperfect plural of "ser", so it is used with plural things: for example, "las órdenes eran para su protección" = "the orders were for his/her protection."
target_language_example: Esos regalos eran para los niños.
native_language_example: Those gifts were for the children.

meaning: you are the only one / you are the one thing that matters
additional_notes: Used as an affectionate phrase to tell someone they are unique or the most important person/thing to the speaker. Context determines whether it means 'the only one' (literal exclusivity) or 'the only thing that matters' (emotional emphasis). Common in romantic or deeply personal expressions.
target_language_example: Eres lo único que quiero en mi vida.
native_language_example: You are the only thing I want in my life.

meaning: You are much/more (used to emphasize someone's qualities).
additional_notes: Commonly used to emphasize or boost someone: «eres mucho» on its own is rare; usually appears as part of comparisons or complements (e.g. «eres mucho más...», «eres mucho más que...») meaning 'you are much more...' or 'you are far more...'. Can introduce strength, worth, interest, etc. Tone is positive and encouraging.
target_language_example: Eres mucho más valiente de lo que piensas.
native_language_example: You are much braver than you think.

meaning: you are more than / you are nothing more than (depends on context).
additional_notes: Can be used positively to say someone is 'more than' something (greater, worth more) or negatively with 'no' to belittle someone: 'no eres más que...' = 'you are nothing but / just a...'. Context and tone determine meaning. 'Eres más que' is the affirmative form; add 'no' to make the dismissive phrase.
target_language_example: No eres más que un ayudante, no tomas las decisiones importantes.
native_language_example: You are nothing more than an assistant; you don't make the important decisions.

meaning: you are ours / you are one of us (addressing a female).
additional_notes: Eres nuestra combines the verb 'eres' (you are, informal singular tú) with the feminine possessive pronoun 'nuestra' (our/ours for a female). Use to say someone belongs to a group, is the group's favorite/hope/member, or to express affection/possession. Change 'nuestra' to 'nuestro' for a male person, and use 'es' for usted/él/ella or 'sois' for vosotros in Spain if appropriate. Context determines tone: can be affectionate ('you're our favorite'), supportive ('you're our only hope') or exclusionary ('you are not one of us').
target_language_example: Eres nuestra mejor estudiante.
native_language_example: You are our best student.

meaning: 'you are one' (used to say someone is one of a group or one of a kind)
additional_notes: Commonly followed by de + group (e.g., de ellos, de nosotros) to mean 'you are one of them/us'. Can also be used with adjectives or superlatives (e.g., uno de los mejores) to praise someone. Informal or neutral — context and tone determine meaning (inclusion, praise, or identification). The subject pronoun tú is often omitted because the verb form eres already indicates 'you'.
target_language_example: Eres uno de los mejores jugadores del equipo.
native_language_example: You are one of the best players on the team.

meaning: 'mistake' or 'error' followed by where it happened (in/on/at).
additional_notes: Use 'error en' to say there is a mistake in something; it’s followed by a noun or phrase indicating the location or context (e.g., 'en la prueba', 'en la cuenta', 'en esa oración'). Can be used for physical, written, mathematical, or conceptual mistakes.
target_language_example: Encontré un error en el informe.
native_language_example: I found an error in the report.

meaning: 'the mistake that' or 'error that' (introduces a clause describing a mistake)
additional_notes: Combines the noun error (mistake, error) with the relative conjunction que (that). Used to introduce a subordinate clause giving more information about which mistake or what the mistake consisted of. Works with different verbs/tenses after que (e.g., que haya cometido, que traen, que he cometido).
target_language_example: Cualquier error que haya cometido, lo siento y aprenderé.
native_language_example: Any mistake that I have made, I am sorry and I will learn.

meaning: is suitable / is appropriate
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone is suitable or appropriate for a purpose, situation, role, person, or condition. Common with para + noun (e.g., 'adecuado para principiantes') or seguido por 'para' + infinitive. Can describe objects, people, or situations. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Este programa es adecuado para estudiantes con poco tiempo.
native_language_example: This program is suitable for students with little time.

meaning: "it's something that I have (to)" — used to say you must do or have something (often followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the phrase "es algo que tengo que + [infinitive]" meaning "it's something I have to [do]". Used to express obligation or necessity for the speaker. Can be shortened in speech (e.g. "es algo que tengo que hacer" → "es algo que tengo que" + verb). Context often completes the idea with an action.
target_language_example: Es algo que tengo que decirte pronto.
native_language_example: It's something I have to tell you soon.

meaning: is appropriate / suitable (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Used to say something is suitable or fitting for a purpose, situation, person, or age group. The adjective 'apropiada' agrees in gender and number with the noun it describes (apropiado, apropiada, apropiados, apropiadas). Commonly followed by 'para' + purpose or target (e.g., para niños, para ese trabajo).
target_language_example: La ropa no es apropiada para la ceremonia.
native_language_example: The clothing is not appropriate for the ceremony.

meaning: it's (someone's) business / it's a matter concerning (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say that something concerns a particular person or group (e.g., 'es asunto mío' = it's my business) or to tell someone it's not their concern ('no es asunto tuyo'). Common in everyday and formal speech. You usually add a possessive or subject after or before: 'es asunto tuyo / mío / suyo / de Pedro'.
target_language_example: Eso no es asunto tuyo; déjalo.
native_language_example: That's not your business; leave it alone.

meaning: 'it's meat' or 'it is meat'.
additional_notes: A simple statement identifying something as meat (food from animals). Used to describe what an item is (e.g., ham, raw meat, good-quality meat). Can appear with adjectives: 'es carne cruda' = 'it's raw meat'. Common in everyday speech when distinguishing meat from other foods.
target_language_example: Eso no es pescado; es carne.
native_language_example: That's not fish; it's meat.

meaning: it's clear / it is clear
additional_notes: Used to say that something is easy to understand, obvious, or unambiguous. Can be used impersonally (Es claro que...) or to describe a specific noun (El mensaje es claro). When negated (No es claro...) it means something is not clear or is uncertain.
target_language_example: Es claro que necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: It's clear that we need more time.

meaning: it's like in / it's as in (used to compare a situation to a place, movie, show, etc.)
additional_notes: Use to introduce a comparison: describe a situation by referring to something familiar (e.g., 'like in the movies', 'like in the circus'). Common in spoken and written Spanish. Followed by a noun phrase or location (el circo, las películas, Occidente).
target_language_example: Es como en las películas: todo sucede muy rápido.
native_language_example: It's like in the movies: everything happens very quickly.

meaning: it's/that’s how (we/they/I) + object pronoun (it/him/her) — introduces the way something is done or seen.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'Así es como lo...' meaning 'This is how we/they/I do it' or 'This is how I want it.' 'Lo' is a neutral/masculine direct object pronoun (it, him). The construction can change subject/person (e.g., 'Así es como la quiere ella' for 'her'). Often preceded by 'Así' ('like this/this way') but can appear with other words (e.g., 'Es como lo hacía...').
target_language_example: Así es como lo hago cuando tengo prisa.
native_language_example: This is how I do it when I'm in a hurry.

meaning: 'this is how' (introduces an explanation of how something is done or what happens).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the phrase "Así es como se..." or "Esto es como se..." to introduce a step, method, or result. Followed by a verb in third-person singular reflexive/impersonal form (e.g., "se hace", "se fortalecen"). It is impersonal/general—no specific subject is named.
target_language_example: Así es como se cocina la paella.
native_language_example: This is how paella is cooked.

meaning: 'it's/that's how (you) ...' — used to introduce the way something happens to or is experienced by you.
additional_notes: Combines 'es como' (it's/that's how) with 'te' (reflexive/object pronoun 'you'). Common in spoken Spanish to describe how something affects or is done to someone: 'Así es como te atrapan' = 'That's how they trap you.' Word order can vary (e.g., 'Así te atrapan' or 'Es como te dije'). 'Te' refers to the person addressed (informal you).
target_language_example: Es como te prometí: te ayudaré cuando lo necesites.
native_language_example: It's like I promised you: I'll help you when you need it.

meaning: 'it is to become me' / 'it means becoming (me)' (used when describing something as becoming or turning into the speaker in a general statement)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb ser (es) + infinitive convertir + reflexive pronoun me + preposition en. It often appears in sentences like 'Lo importante es convertirme en...' meaning 'The important thing is to become...'. It's not a fixed idiom; it's a grammatical structure used to state that the action of becoming (referring to the speaker) is the thing being described. Replace 'me' with other pronouns as needed (convertirte, convertirse, etc.).
target_language_example: Lo que quiero es convertirme en médico.
native_language_example: What I want is to become a doctor.

meaning: it's of great / it's very (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say something has great [quality] (valor, importancia, ayuda, etc.). Common structure: 'es de gran + [noun]'. Often interchangeable with 'es muy' + adjective (e.g., 'es muy importante'), but 'es de gran' emphasizes the noun and sounds a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Este proyecto es de gran importancia para la comunidad.
native_language_example: This project is of great importance to the community.

meaning: it belongs to him / it's his
additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to or is the responsibility of a male person (él). Can refer to ownership (Ese libro es de él = That book is his) or to responsibility/blame (La culpa es de él = It's his fault). In spoken Spanish the pronoun él may be omitted if context is clear (Es suyo / Es de él).
target_language_example: Ese libro es de él.
native_language_example: That book is his.

meaning: that is; i.e.; in other words (used to clarify or restate).
additional_notes: Use to introduce a clarification, rephrasing, or brief explanation of what was just said. It can start a sentence or appear in the middle. Equivalent to 'that is' or 'in other words' in English. Not informal slang.
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy, es decir, tengo una reunión importante.
native_language_example: I can't go today, that is, I have an important meeting.

meaning: it's too good (can mean 'so good that it's unlikely', 'better than someone/something deserves', or 'excessively/beyond what's appropriate').
additional_notes: Used both literally and figuratively. Common uses: express skepticism (es demasiado bueno para ser cierto), indicate someone/something is better than deserved (es demasiado bueno para mí/para ti), or say no one is exempt from something (Nadie es demasiado bueno para eso). Word order can change in longer phrases (demasiado bueno para ser cierto). Tone varies by context; can be neutral, admiring, or skeptical.
target_language_example: Es demasiado bueno para ser cierto.
native_language_example: It's too good to be true.

meaning: it's Sunday / today is Sunday (or 'it is Sunday').
additional_notes: Common way to say the day of the week. Used with 'hoy' (today) or 'mañana' (tomorrow) to specify which day: 'Hoy es domingo' = Today is Sunday. Structure: 'Es' (it is) + weekday. Neutral, everyday phrase.
target_language_example: Hoy es domingo y no tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Today is Sunday and I don't have to work.

meaning: literally “is two years”; used to indicate duration or age but is less common than alternatives (e.g., «tiene dos años», «hace dos años»). Can appear in stylistic or elliptical contexts.
additional_notes: Grammatical notes: This phrase on its own is unusual in standard Spanish. For age, Spanish normally uses tener: «Tiene dos años.» For duration/elapsed time, prefer «Hace dos años» or «Son dos años» or «Lleva dos años». Uses of «es dos años» occur in elliptical or colloquial responses (e.g., answering a question with a shortened clause), in some regional speech, or in constructions like «Es dos años desde que...» (though the more natural form is «Hace dos años desde que...»). Avoid using «es dos años» as a beginner; choose the more idiomatic alternatives listed above.
target_language_example: —¿Cuánto tiempo llevan casados? —Es dos años.
native_language_example: —How long have they been married? —It's been two years.

meaning: it's the day when / it's the day on which
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that specifies which day something happens. Often appears as part of the full phrase "es el día en que" or "es el día en el que" (both are common). Can be followed by a verb clause (e.g., "en que va a morir", "en que la gente va a la iglesia"). Equivalent to English "the day when/on which".
target_language_example: Mañana es el día en que empiezan las vacaciones.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is the day when the vacation starts.

meaning: 'it's the book' / 'this is the book'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to identify or point out a specific book. Often appears with a demonstrative (este/ese) or as an answer: 'Es el libro que...' + relative clause. Can be used to say possession (el libro de X) or to introduce which book someone means. Grammar note: 'es' is the third-person singular of 'ser'; use with singular noun 'libro'.
target_language_example: Este es el libro que te presté la semana pasada.
native_language_example: This is the book I lent you last week.

meaning: is the gift / is a gift (used to say something is a gift or blessing).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb 'ser' (es) + noun 'el regalo'. Often used figuratively to call something a gift, blessing, or precious thing (e.g., 'X es el regalo más grande'). Common in statements valuing something someone has or gives. Word order and article matter: 'es regalo' without 'el' is less common; use 'es un regalo' to mean 'is a gift' non-specifically.
target_language_example: Tu amistad es el regalo que más valoro.
native_language_example: Your friendship is the gift I value most.

meaning: it's the only animal / is the only animal
additional_notes: A phrase used to say that something (often a species, organism, or sometimes a person used figuratively) is the sole animal in a certain context. 'Es' is the third-person singular of 'ser'. Use with singular nouns. Can be part of longer sentences: 'Es el único animal que...'.
target_language_example: Este pájaro es el único animal que visita nuestro jardín por la noche.
native_language_example: This bird is the only animal that visits our garden at night.

meaning: ‘is the one I like the most’ (used after a noun to say which option/person/item you prefer).
additional_notes: Common structure: [subject] + 'es el que más me gusta' or shortened 'es el que más me' in context. 'Me' is the indirect object pronoun for 'to me' and 'gusta' (implied) means 'pleases' → 'I like'. Often used pointing to a specific choice among several. You can replace 'me' with other pronouns (te, le, nos) to change the experiencer.
target_language_example: De todos los colores, el azul es el que más me gusta.
native_language_example: Of all the colors, blue is the one I like the most.

meaning: is hope / is (just) hope
additional_notes: A simple predicative phrase using the verb ser (es) + esperanza. Often used to say that something amounts to or consists only of hope/optimism — e.g. “all that's left is hope.” It can follow different subjects (la vida, lo único, etc.). Tone is neutral; context decides if it’s poetic or resigned.
target_language_example: Después de perder el trabajo, lo único que me queda es esperanza.
native_language_example: After losing the job, all I have left is hope.

meaning: 'is to study' or 'it/this/that is to study' — expresses that studying is the important/desired action or goal.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after expressions like 'es', 'mi sueño es', 'mi ilusión es' or 'mi deseo es' to state what someone wants, dreams of, or what is necessary/important. Literally 'es' = 'is' + 'estudiar' = 'to study'. The phrase itself is not idiomatic; it's simply the verb infinitive used as a noun (a verb phrase functioning as the subject or complement).
target_language_example: Mi plan para el próximo año es estudiar en el extranjero.
native_language_example: My plan for next year is to study abroad.

meaning: 'it's no excuse' / 'that is not an excuse'.
additional_notes: Used to reject a reason or justification someone gives. Often appears in sentences like 'Eso no es excusa' or 'Que X no es excusa' to say the reason doesn't justify the behavior. Can be softened with tone or additional words (e.g., 'no es excusa, pero...').
target_language_example: Eso no es excusa para llegar tarde.
native_language_example: That's no excuse for being late.

meaning: is strange / is odd (feminine).
additional_notes: Adjective phrase: extraña agrees in gender with a feminine noun or subject. Use 'es extraño' for masculine subjects. Can describe people, situations, stories, or life in general. Tone can be neutral (unusual) or negative (weird), depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Esa película es extraña pero interesante.
native_language_example: That movie is strange but interesting.

meaning: 'is faithful' or 'is loyal' (to someone, something, or to principles).
additional_notes: Used to describe loyalty, faithfulness, or accuracy. With people it means loyal/faithful (e.g., to a partner, country, or principles). With translations or representations it means accurate/faithful to the original. Common prepositions: 'a' or 'al' before the object (fiel a algo / fiel al original).
target_language_example: Ella es fiel a sus amigos.
native_language_example: She is loyal to her friends.

meaning: 'is to win' or 'is winning' (structure using the verb ser + infinitive ganar).
additional_notes: This is the construction ser + infinitive (es + ganar) used to state that something's purpose, goal, or essence is 'to win' or that 'winning' is the important thing. Context determines translation: can mean 'is to win', 'is winning', or 'the point is to win'. Common in slogans or statements of intent (e.g., "La meta es ganar").
target_language_example: Para este equipo, es ganar cada partido.
native_language_example: For this team, it's to win every match.

meaning: 'is fat' / 'is thick' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Literal meaning: describes someone or something as fat, overweight, or (for objects) thick/bulky. Used for people, animals, and things (e.g., a thick book). Can be neutral, descriptive, or rude depending on context and tone — avoid using about someone unless appropriate. For masculine subjects use 'gordo'; for feminine subjects use 'gorda' (e.g., 'es gorda').
target_language_example: Tu perro es gordo; deberías darle menos comida.
native_language_example: Your dog is fat; you should give it less food.

meaning: is skillful / is skilled / is good at (something).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who has skill, dexterity, or competence. Often followed by a skill or area introduced with 'en' (e.g., 'es hábil en el inglés') or by a tool/part with 'con' (e.g., 'es hábil con sus manos'). Neutral, suitable for formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Él es hábil con la computadora.
native_language_example: He is skilled with the computer.

meaning: is incapable (of); cannot (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is unable to do something or lacks the ability/permission. Common structure: 'es incapaz de + infinitive' (es incapaz de mentir). Often comments on moral inability (can't lie) or physical/mental inability (can't care for themselves). Can be negative or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Ella es incapaz de abandonar a su familia.
native_language_example: She is incapable of abandoning her family.

meaning: is fair / is just.
additional_notes: Used to describe something (la decisión, la ley, la vida, etc.) as fair or just. Agreement: 'justa' is feminine singular; use 'justo' for masculine nouns (e.g., 'es justo'). Common in statements and opinions about fairness.
target_language_example: La decisión es justa para todos.
native_language_example: The decision is fair for everyone.

meaning: it's justice / it is fair (it is what justice requires).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is fair, deserved, or what justice demands. Can refer to legal justice or a moral sense of fairness. Context determines nuance: e.g., 'es justicia de la calle' (street-level justice/folk justice) vs. 'es justicia' as a short comment meaning 'that's only fair.' Common in statements about giving someone their due or acknowledging a fair outcome.
target_language_example: Si lo condenaron por corrupción, es justicia.
native_language_example: If they convicted him for corruption, it's justice.

meaning: it's just / it's exactly / it's fair (depending on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'it's exactly' or 'it's just' (to emphasize precision) or 'it's fair' (judgment). In the example, 'justo' means 'exactly'/'precisely' before a noun phrase. Word order matters: 'es justo' + noun = 'it's precisely...'; 'es justo que' + clause = 'it's fair that'.
target_language_example: Es justo la película que quería ver.
native_language_example: It's exactly the movie I wanted to see.

meaning: it's exactly the/that (one); he/she/it is precisely the (person/thing) I mean.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something or someone is the exact one wanted or needed. Follows a noun (el/la/los/las) and can be adapted to gender/number: 'es justo la', 'son justo los', etc. Often translates as 'this/that is exactly the...' or 'he's exactly the...'.
target_language_example: Este es justo el regalo que quería.
native_language_example: This is exactly the gift I wanted.

meaning: it's exactly/precisely the (thing).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is exactly the thing being referred to. Often followed by a noun or a clause introduced by que (e.g., es justo lo que necesito = it's exactly what I need). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Ese regalo es justo lo que quería.
native_language_example: That gift is exactly what I wanted.

meaning: 'it is the/the letter' or 'this is the letter' (identifying a specific letter or card).
additional_notes: Used to identify or point out a particular 'carta' (which can mean a written letter, a menu in some countries, or an emergency document depending on context). The subject (implicit or explicit) can be 'esto/esta/esta es' or another noun; the phrase often appears in sentences like 'Esta es la carta...' If referring to a menu, regional variation may apply.
target_language_example: Esta es la carta que me enviaste ayer.
native_language_example: This is the letter you sent me yesterday.

meaning: it's the house in which / that (someone) lives or lived.
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a relative clause: 'es la casa en la que...' introduces information about 'la casa' (the house) and is followed by a verb referring to who lives/lived there. 'En la que' = 'in which' (feminine singular to match 'casa'). You can also say 'es la casa donde...' (more colloquial) or 'es la casa en que...'. Use 'en el que' for masculine nouns.
target_language_example: Es la casa en la que crecí.
native_language_example: It's the house in which I grew up.

meaning: 'is the kind/type (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe the kind or type of person, thing, or situation. Common structure: 'es la clase de + [noun] + (que + clause)' meaning 'is the kind of ____ that...'. In English often translated as 'is the kind of' or 'is the sort of'.
target_language_example: No es la clase de película que veo dos veces.
native_language_example: It's not the kind of movie I watch twice.

meaning: is the (the) mountain that is the most ... (used to form superlative descriptions of mountains).
additional_notes: This phrase is used to say a mountain has the highest degree of some quality (usually altura = height). It combines the verb 'ser' (es) + noun 'la montaña' + 'más' to create a superlative: 'es la montaña más alta (de ...)' = 'is the tallest mountain (in/of ...)'. Replace 'alta' with other adjectives as needed (ej. 'peligrosa', 'famosa'). If the mountain name already includes 'El' or 'Monte', you may see variations like 'El Everest es la montaña más alta...' or 'Ésa es la montaña más alta del mundo.'
target_language_example: El Aconcagua es la montaña más alta de América del Sur.
native_language_example: Aconcagua is the tallest mountain in South America.

meaning: 'is the reason why' or 'is the reason for (which)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the cause or explanation for something. Often appears as part of the full phrase 'es la razón por la que...' (or 'esa/es la razón por la que...') meaning 'that is why' or 'the reason why'. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Followed by a clause (por la que + verb) or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Esa es la razón por la que vine hoy.
native_language_example: That is the reason why I came today.

meaning: 'is long' (feminine singular)
additional_notes: Used to describe the length of a feminine noun (e.g., falda, pollera). 'Es' = 'is' (3rd person singular of ser); 'larga' is the feminine form of 'largo'. For masculine nouns use 'es largo'. Can describe physical length or figurative duration depending on context.
target_language_example: La falda es larga y llega hasta las rodillas.
native_language_example: The skirt is long and reaches the knees.

meaning: 'is to wash' or 'is washing' (used to say someone's job or duty is to wash something).
additional_notes: Combines the verb ser (es) + infinitive lavar. Commonly used to describe someone's task, job, or what must be done: 'Su trabajo es lavar...' or 'Lo único que tienes que hacer es lavar...'. The infinitive after es expresses a general action or duty. Pronunciation tip: 'es' sounds like /es/ and 'lavar' like /laˈβar/.
target_language_example: Su trabajo es lavar la ropa todos los sábados.
native_language_example: His job is to wash the clothes every Saturday.

meaning: is ... enough
additional_notes: By itself, es lo is not usually a fixed standalone expression. In these examples, it appears in the pattern es lo suficientemente + adjective + para + infinitive, which means 'is [adjective] enough to ...'. The key part of the meaning comes from lo suficientemente.
target_language_example: El niño es lo suficientemente alto para montar solo.
native_language_example: The boy is tall enough to ride alone.

meaning: 'it's/that is what they (want/say/etc.)' — introduces what 'they' do or want.
additional_notes: Used to report or summarize actions, opinions, desires or statements of other people (ellos = they). Can appear with different demonstratives: 'eso/esto/es' + 'lo que ellos' (e.g., 'Eso es lo que ellos quieren' = 'That's what they want'). The verb after may change (quieren, dicen, etc.).
target_language_example: Eso es lo que ellos quieren.
native_language_example: That's what they want.

meaning: it's what (is/are); that's what (is/are) — points out something that is the case or explains a situation
additional_notes: Commonly used to identify or explain a cause, state, or defining characteristic. Often appears in longer sentences (e.g., 'Es lo que está pasando' = 'That's what's happening'). Can introduce an explanation or conclusion about a situation. Neutral register.
target_language_example: No es culpa mía; es lo que está sucediendo ahora.
native_language_example: It's not my fault; that's what's happening now.

meaning: 'that's what needs to be done' / 'that's what there is to do' (expresses necessity or what must be done)
additional_notes: Used to state the necessary action or the thing that must be found out or done. Often follows esto/eso/eso + clause: 'Esto/eso es lo que hay (que hacer/que averiguar)'. Can be neutral or matter-of-fact; sometimes implies resignation ('that's how it is' in context of necessity).
target_language_example: Eso es lo que hay que decirle al jefe.
native_language_example: That's what needs to be told to the boss.

meaning: 'it's/that is what I have' + past participle (present perfect) — used to introduce something the speaker has done, noticed, heard, etc.
additional_notes: This phrase is part of the present perfect construction (he + past participle). 'Es lo que he...' or 'Eso es lo que he...' introduces what the speaker has done, heard, noticed, asked, etc. In English it's usually translated as 'that's what I have (done/been doing/heard/asked)'. The exact meaning depends on the past participle that follows (buscado, intentado decirte, oído, preguntado). 'Es' or 'Eso es' can both be used; 'eso' is slightly more demonstrative.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que he estado buscando todo el mes.
native_language_example: That's what I have been looking for all month.

meaning: 'it's what the' (part of a larger sentence)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own. 'Es lo que' means 'it's what' or 'that is what', and is followed by a noun phrase introduced by an article and plural noun (here 'los'). You'll usually see it as part of a full sentence: e.g. 'Es lo que los niños necesitan' = 'That's what the children need.' Remember agreement: 'los' signals a masculine plural noun that follows.
target_language_example: Es lo que los estudiantes querían.
native_language_example: That's what the students wanted.

meaning: 'this/that is what I want (someone) to (do/think)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing the action, opinion, or result you want someone else to carry out or have. It is followed by a verb in the subjunctive when referring to someone else's action or thought (e.g., 'que hagas', 'que piense'). The demonstrative can be 'esto', 'eso', or 'así que esto/eso', depending on context.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que quiero que hagas mañana.
native_language_example: That's what I want you to do tomorrow.

meaning: "it's/that is what is going to" (introduces what will happen or what someone will do).
additional_notes: Use to point out or emphasize a future event or action. Often appears in clauses like "eso es lo que va a pasar" (that's what is going to happen) or in questions asking what will change. Follows a demonstrative (eso/esto/eso/lo) or noun and introduces a subordinate clause with "va a + infinitive" to express near future.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que va a ocurrir si no cambias de opinión.
native_language_example: That's what is going to happen if you don't change your mind.

meaning: 'that's what we're going to (do/learn/etc.)' — introduces what will be done or discovered next.
additional_notes: Used to state or confirm a planned action or outcome. Follows a demonstrative (eso/éso/eso) or subject, and is typically completed by an infinitive verb (hacer, averiguar, decir, etc.). Common in spoken and written Spanish to emphasize intention or next steps.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que vamos a hacer mañana.
native_language_example: That's what we're going to do tomorrow.

meaning: 'this/that is what you are going to (do)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce or point out an action or plan someone will do next. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., 'es lo que vas a hacer') or left implied. Common in instructions, explanations, or when emphasizing a future action.
target_language_example: Escucha con atención: esto es lo que vas a hacer mañana.
native_language_example: Listen carefully: this is what you are going to do tomorrow.

meaning: it's magic; it's amazing or inexplicable.
additional_notes: Used literally to say something is supernatural, or figuratively to praise something that works surprisingly well or seems inexplicable. Tone can be playful or emphatic. Common in expressions like "¡Es magia!" or "Eso no es magia".
target_language_example: Cuando la receta sale perfecta sin esfuerzo, es magia.
native_language_example: When the recipe turns out perfect with no effort, it's magic.

meaning: 'is to maintain' or 'is to keep' (used to say the main action or purpose is to preserve, continue or keep something in a certain state).
additional_notes: Common construction: 'La idea/La mejor estrategia/Lo importante/Mi trabajo/Nuestra obligación es mantener...' — followed by what should be kept or preserved. 'Mantener' covers keeping, maintaining, preserving, or keeping up (e.g., a name, a low profile, control, order, cleanliness). Use infinitive after 'es' to state the intended action or purpose.
target_language_example: Nuestra meta es mantener buenas relaciones con los vecinos.
native_language_example: Our goal is to maintain good relations with the neighbors.

meaning: is larger/greater than the (feminine noun that follows).
additional_notes: Used to compare quantities (population, area, etc.). 'Mayor' = 'greater' or 'older' depending on context; here it means 'larger' or 'greater'. The structure compares a feminine noun phrase: 'X es mayor que la de Y' — the 'la' replaces a feminine noun mentioned earlier (e.g., 'población', 'superficie'). For masculine nouns you'd see 'es mayor que el'.
target_language_example: La población de México es mayor que la de Colombia.
native_language_example: Mexico's population is larger than Colombia's.

meaning: 'is better than' (used in comparisons, often followed by 'lo que' + clause or a noun/phrase)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in comparisons: 'es mejor de lo que...' = 'is better than I/you/he/etc. thought' or 'is better than...'. Can also be followed by a time/place phrase (e.g. 'es mejor de noche' = 'it's better at night'). In many regions speakers prefer 'es mejor que' for direct comparisons (es mejor que + noun/clause), but 'es mejor de lo que' is natural when comparing to a clause ('than what').
target_language_example: La película es mejor de lo que dijeron los críticos.
native_language_example: The movie is better than what the critics said.

meaning: It's my book, not his/yours/theirs — used to contrast ownership.
additional_notes: A short contrastive phrase to insist that the item belongs to the speaker, followed by a possessive phrase or pronoun (de usted, de ustedes, suyo, tuyo, vuestro, etc.). Common in spoken and written Spanish to correct or clarify ownership. The full sentence normally includes a possessive after "no el" (e.g. "no el suyo" or "no el de usted").
target_language_example: Este es mi libro, no el tuyo.
native_language_example: This is my book, not yours.

target_language_multi_word_term: es muy amable de su parte
meaning: that's very kind of you / that's very kind of him/her/them.
additional_notes: Polite phrase used to thank or acknowledge someone's kindness or offer. Formal/neutral register; often followed by 'pero...' to decline politely. 'su parte' literally means 'on your/their part' and indicates who performed the kind action. Can be used addressing someone directly (usted/usteded) or speaking about a third person.
target_language_example: Gracias por la ayuda, es muy amable de su parte.
native_language_example: Thanks for the help, that's very kind of you.

meaning: that's very kind of you / you're very kind.
additional_notes: Used to thank someone or acknowledge a kind action or comment. Commonly appears as 'es muy amable de tu parte' (including 'parte') but speakers may shorten it to 'es muy amable de tu'. Followed by 'que' + verb phrase when specifying the action: 'es muy amable de tu parte que me ayudes.'
target_language_example: Es muy amable de tu parte ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: It's very kind of you to help me with the move.

meaning: it's very kind of (someone) to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to thank or acknowledge someone's kindness or polite action. Followed by 'tu parte' (informal you) or 'su parte' (formal you / his/her/their). Often completes the sentence: 'Es muy amable de tu parte' = 'It's very kind of you.'
target_language_example: Es muy amable de tu parte ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: It's very kind of you to help me with the move.

meaning: is more
additional_notes: Literal third-person singular 'is more'. It is used in comparisons, usually with an adjective or adverb, often followed by que: es más alto que... = 'is taller than...'. In English, it may be translated either with 'more' or with a comparative adjective ending in '-er'.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es más joven que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is younger than me.

meaning: 'is prettier' or 'is more beautiful'.
additional_notes: Comparative phrase: es (third-person singular of ser/estar) + más (more) + bonita (feminine adjective). Used to compare feminine nouns. For masculine nouns use más bonito or another adjective form. Can also use estar (está más bonita) to emphasize temporary appearance.
target_language_example: La playa es más bonita en verano.
native_language_example: The beach is prettier in summer.

meaning: is more expensive
additional_notes: Comparative phrase using 'más' (more) + adjective 'caro' (expensive). Used to compare two things; often followed by 'que' (than) or implied context. Agreement not required because 'caro' here describes the noun compared. To say 'is cheaper' use 'es más barato'.
target_language_example: Este restaurante es más caro que aquel.
native_language_example: This restaurant is more expensive than that one.

meaning: is not... at all / is nothing (used to emphasize a negative quality).
additional_notes: Used after 'ser' to strongly negate an adjective or description: 'no es nada + adjective' means 'is not ... at all' or 'is nothing (like that)'. Common in Spanish to emphasize a lack of a trait. Structure: subject + no + ser + nada + adjective/noun. Not used alone without 'no'.
target_language_example: Su trabajo no es nada fácil.
native_language_example: His job is not easy at all.

meaning: 'is the work (of)' / 'is the doing (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the result or creation of someone or something (a person, God, fate, etc.). Common structure: 'Esto es obra de + agent' or 'es obra tuya' (it's your doing). Often used to attribute cause, credit, or responsibility.
target_language_example: La mejora es obra del equipo.
native_language_example: The improvement is the team's work.

meaning: 'is something/someone else' or 'is different/more complicated' (used to contrast two things).
additional_notes: Common in comparisons: after stating one thing, 'es otra' (often with 'una cosa' before) contrasts a second, different matter. Can mean 'it's a different matter', 'it's another story', or 'it's different on the inside.' Context determines nuance (literal 'another thing/person' vs. idiomatic 'that's another matter').
target_language_example: Leer un libro es una cosa; entenderlo es otra.
native_language_example: Reading a book is one thing; understanding it is another.

meaning: it's for the / it's because of the (him/it/the)
additional_notes: A short phrase combining 'es' (it is) + 'por' (for/because of) + the masculine singular article 'el'. Meaning depends on context: 'por el bien' = 'for the good (of...)', 'por el olor' = 'because of the smell'. The referent after 'el' can be a noun or a masculine pronoun (el = him/it) if context makes identity clear.
target_language_example: Es por el bien de los niños.
native_language_example: It's for the good of the children.

meaning: 'it's for your own' (usually followed by a noun like 'bien' = 'good' or 'benefit').
additional_notes: Used to justify an action as being in someone's best interest. Commonly completed as 'es por tu propio bien' (it's for your own good) but can attach other nouns (e.g., 'interés'). Tone can be reassuring or paternal. Often said when doing something the other person may not like.
target_language_example: Lo hago así porque es por tu propio bien.
native_language_example: I do it this way because it's for your own good.

meaning: it's because of a / it's for a (a reason or purpose introduced by 'un')
additional_notes: Used to explain cause, reason, purpose, or motivation and followed by a noun phrase beginning with the indefinite article 'un' (masculine). Can mean 'it's for a [thing/person]' or 'it's because of a [thing/person]'. Context determines whether it's purpose (for) or cause (because of). Replace 'un' with other articles/pronouns as needed (e.g., 'es por una', 'es por el').
target_language_example: Es por un regalo que no pude asistir a la fiesta.
native_language_example: It's because of a gift that I couldn't attend the party.

meaning: it's because you/they (do something to you) — introduces the reason related to 'you' (te).
additional_notes: A short phrase combining 'es' (it is), 'porque' (because) and the indirect/direct object pronoun 'te' (you). Used to give a reason that involves the person 'you' (e.g., they admire you, they saw you). Word order: 'es porque te + verb...'. Context determines whether 'te' is direct or indirect object. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Eso es porque te ayudaron desde el principio.
native_language_example: That's because they helped you from the start.

meaning: 'it is probably' or 'is probably' (indicates likelihood)
additional_notes: Used to express that something is likely or probable. 'Probablemente' is an adverb meaning 'probably'; 'es' is the third-person singular of 'ser' (to be). You can replace 'es' with other forms (soy, eres, está, será) depending on subject and nuance. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Es probablemente la mejor opción para nosotros.
native_language_example: It is probably the best option for us.

meaning: it's deep / it's profound.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that has depth—literally (e.g., water, hole) or figuratively (e.g., an idea, emotion, or conversation). Context tells whether it's physical or abstract. For physical depth you might also hear 'muy profundo' or a specific measure ('dos metros de profundidad'). For abstract depth, similar phrases: 'es muy profundo', 'es interesante y profundo'.
target_language_example: La discusión fue larga y es profundo en sus ideas.
native_language_example: The discussion was long and it's profound in its ideas.

meaning: it's just that
additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation, reason, or excuse, especially in conversation. It often softens what follows, as in answering a question or correcting a misunderstanding. It is not always translated word-for-word.
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy; es que tengo mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: I can't go today; it's just that I have a lot of work.

meaning: a way to introduce or explain something about someone: 'it's that you are...' or 'the thing is, you are...'
additional_notes: Used to give a reason, explain, or emphasize a comment about someone's trait or behavior. Often appears at the start of a sentence to justify/clarify (Es que...) followed by eres + adjective/noun. Tone can be neutral, critical, or explanatory depending on context. Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Es que eres muy trabajador, por eso te contrataron.
native_language_example: The thing is, you are very hardworking, that's why they hired you.

meaning: a conversational filler meaning 'it's that…' or 'the thing is…' used to introduce an explanation relating to something being (in a certain state).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish. 'Es que' is a discourse marker used to give a reason, explanation, or to soften/justify a statement; when followed by 'está' it introduces an explanation about the current state or location of someone/something (e.g., 'it's that it is…' → 'the thing is it's…'). Often used informally to respond or clarify. Tone and context determine whether it's justification, emphasis, or pointing out condition/location.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, es que está cerrado hoy.
native_language_example: Don't worry, it's just that it's closed today.

meaning: 'it's that (to him/her/you formal/it)'; used to introduce an explanation or reason referring to an indirect object (le).
additional_notes: Es que is a common spoken phrase meaning 'it's that' or 'the thing is' used to give an explanation. When followed by le, it indicates the explanation concerns someone (le = to him/to her/to you formal) or something affecting them. Context decides whether le is indirect object ('to him/her') or a dative of interest. Often used in everyday conversation to soften or justify a statement.
target_language_example: No vino hoy, es que le surgió un problema familiar.
native_language_example: He didn't come today; it's that a family problem came up for him/her.

meaning: it's just that I don't know / the thing is I don't know
additional_notes: A conversational filler used to introduce or excuse uncertainty, hesitation, or lack of information. Often appears at the start or middle of a sentence to soften an answer (similar to 'well, I don't know' or 'it's just that I don't know'). Tone and context determine politeness; common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: No puedo ayudarte esta vez, es que no sé qué decir.
native_language_example: I can't help you this time; it's just that I don't know what to say.

meaning: used to introduce an explanation, excuse, or background reason (often 'it's that...' or 'the thing is that...').
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase. 'Es que' introduces a reason; the following 'se' may be part of a reflexive/impersonal verb or pronominal construction in the clause that follows (not part of a fixed phrase). In many examples 'es que' softens or justifies what comes next. Translate the whole sentence naturally (e.g. "It's just that..." or "The thing is that...").
target_language_example: Es que se me olvidó el libro, por eso no fui.
native_language_example: It's just that I forgot the book, that's why I didn't go.

meaning: used to introduce an explanation or excuse about oneself ("it's that I am..." / "the thing is I'm...").
additional_notes: Common filler phrase in Spanish to give a reason, explanation, or self-description. Often follows a statement or question and softens or explains why something is the case. Literally 'it's that I am' but in natural English you'd say 'the thing is...' or 'it's just that I'm...'.
target_language_example: No puedo venir, es que soy alérico a los mariscos.
native_language_example: I can't come; it's just that I'm allergic to shellfish.

meaning: 'it's that I have' — used to introduce an explanation or excuse starting with 'I have...'
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase to preface a reason or clarification. Often appears in responses: 'Es que tengo...' + noun (e.g., 'tengo fiebre') or verb phrase (with que + verb) after context. Tone can be neutral or slightly defensive/explanatory. Not a fixed idiom beyond its literal words.
target_language_example: No puedo ir, es que tengo una reunión a las cinco.
native_language_example: I can't go; it's that I have a meeting at five.

meaning: 'is only for' or 'is just for' (indicates restricted intended audience or recipient).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is intended exclusively for a person or group. Match the subject pronoun and audience: 'para ti' (you informal singular), 'para usted' (you formal), 'para vosotros' (you informal plural, Spain), 'para ustedes' (you plural). 'Solo' (without accent) means 'only' or 'just' — can also be written 'sólo' in older texts but accent is now optional in Spanish. If describing a noun, keep agreement: e.g. 'Este evento es solo para adultos.'
target_language_example: Este regalo es solo para ti.
native_language_example: This gift is only for you.

meaning: 'is sufficiently' or 'is enough/adequately (adjective/adverb)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has an adequate degree or amount of a quality. Often followed by an adjective, adverb, or a clause introduced by 'como para' (as to/so that). Common in everyday and formal speech. Can be shortened to 'suficientemente' without 'es' when used with other verbs.
target_language_example: La sopa es suficientemente caliente para comerla.
native_language_example: The soup is sufficiently hot to eat.

meaning: it's only the / it's just the
additional_notes: Used to downplay something as merely the beginning or a small part of a larger situation. Commonly followed by a noun (e.g., "principio") or phrase. 'Sólo' = 'only/just' (accent optional in modern Spanish), 'es' = 'is', 'el' = 'the'.
target_language_example: Es sólo el comienzo de la historia.
native_language_example: It's just the beginning of the story.

meaning: is as tall (feminine) — used to compare height, meaning 'she/it is as tall'.
additional_notes: es tan alta is the feminine singular form of the structure 'ser + tan + adjective + como' used for equality comparisons: 'as ... as'. Change gender/number or verb as needed: es tan alto (masculine), son tan altas (plural). For negative comparisons use 'no ... tan ... como' (e.g., 'no es tan alta como...').
target_language_example: Ella es tan alta como su hermana.
native_language_example: She is as tall as her sister.

meaning: it's all (that)
additional_notes: Usually followed by a relative clause with que + verb (e.g., "es todo lo que quería"). Used to say that something is everything needed or everything someone wanted/needed to know/hear. Common in sentences like "Es todo lo que quería saber" = "That's all I wanted to know."
target_language_example: Es todo lo que necesitaba escuchar.
native_language_example: That's all I needed to hear.

meaning: it's all that I (have/need/care about) — introduces what remains or what matters to the speaker.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is everything left to someone (e.g., what remains, what they have) or that something is all that matters to them. The rest of the clause (e.g., queda, importa) completes the meaning: "es todo lo que me queda" = "it's all I have left"; "es todo lo que me importa" = "it's all that matters to me." Common in both emotional and material contexts.
target_language_example: Mi familia es todo lo que me queda.
native_language_example: My family is all I have left.

meaning: it's all because of / that's all for (depending on context).
additional_notes: This phrase can mean two main things: 1) 'Es todo por hoy/ahora' = 'That's all for today/now' (used to end an activity or meeting). 2) 'Es todo por + [reason/person]' = 'It's all because of [reason/person]' or 'This is all due to [someone/something]'. Context (especially presence of time words like hoy/ahora or a reason/agent) tells you which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Eso es todo por hoy; nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: That's all for today; see you tomorrow.

meaning: she/it is calm; (it) is quiet/peaceful.
additional_notes: Uses the verb ser (es) + adjective tranquila (feminine). Use es tranquila for feminine singular subjects (ella, la habitación, la oscuridad). For masculine subjects use es tranquilo. Can describe personality (Ella es tranquila = she is calm) or a place/thing (La habitación es tranquila = the room is quiet). For temporary states you might instead hear está tranquila.
target_language_example: La plaza es tranquila por la mañana.
native_language_example: The square is peaceful in the morning.

meaning: is three years older (than someone).
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Structure: [Subject] + es + tres años + mayor + que + [person]. 'Mayor' means 'older'; use 'más joven' or 'menor' for 'younger'. You can change the number (dos, cuatro, etc.). Verb 'es' agrees with third-person singular; for plural subjects use 'son'.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es tres años mayor que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is three years older than me.

meaning: is a very (language).
additional_notes: Used to describe a language (idioma) with an adjective that follows (e.g., difícil, bonito, interesante). Literal structure: 'es' (is) + 'un idioma' (a language) + 'muy' (very) + adjective. Common for giving opinions about languages.
target_language_example: El italiano es un idioma muy melódico.
native_language_example: Italian is a very melodic language.

meaning: is a player of / plays (a sport).
additional_notes: Used to say someone plays or is a player of a sport. Followed by the sport name (de + sport). Can indicate profession (professional player) or general participation. For female players use the feminine form (es una jugadora de). Agreement in gender and number applies to the article and noun (un/una, jugador/jugadora).
target_language_example: Bill es un jugador de béisbol.
native_language_example: Bill is a baseball player.

meaning: it's a lot / it's a huge amount
additional_notes: Used to say there is a large quantity, degree, or intensity of something. Can refer to physical amounts (a lot of things), time (a long time), effort, or importance. Common in everyday speech. Often followed by a noun or used after ser with an implicit noun: 'Es un montón de trabajo' or simply 'Es un montón' (meaning 'It's a lot').
target_language_example: Ese proyecto es un montón de trabajo para una sola persona.
native_language_example: That project is a lot of work for one person.

meaning: is a branch (of) / is a field of
additional_notes: Used to say that one subject or discipline is a subfield or part of a larger area (e.g., 'X is a branch of Y'). Common in academic or formal contexts when classifying fields of study, sciences, arts, etc. Followed by 'de' + the larger category.
target_language_example: La biología es una rama de la ciencia que estudia la vida.
native_language_example: Biology is a branch of science that studies life.

es una de las ciudades más

target_language_multi_word_term: es una de las ciudades más
meaning: is one of the most (used to compare a city among others, e.g., 'is one of the most important/large cities')
additional_notes: This phrase introduces a superlative comparison for cities. After 'más' add an adjective (grandes, importantes, turísticas, caras, etc.) and often 'de' + group (del mundo, de España, de la región). Common structure: [City] + es una de las ciudades más + [adjective] + (de + [group]).
target_language_example: Barcelona es una de las ciudades más turísticas de España.
native_language_example: Barcelona is one of the most touristic cities in Spain.

meaning: is one / it/he/she is one (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'es' (is) + 'uno' (one). Used for numbers, quantities, or to identify someone/something as a single unit. Context determines translation: can mean 'is one' (four divided by four is one), 'it's one and a half' (when part of a larger phrase), or 'he is one' (identifying a person as one of a group). Watch gender/number agreement: 'uno' can change form (un, una) before nouns.
target_language_example: Dos más uno es uno más dos.
native_language_example: Two plus one is one plus two.

meaning: 'it's true that' / 'it is true that'.
additional_notes: Use to introduce a fact or concede a point before adding more information or contrast (often followed by pero 'but' or a statement). Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Es verdad que tenemos tiempo, pero mejor salir ahora.
native_language_example: It's true that we have time, but it's better to leave now.

meaning: 'is true' or 'is real/authentic'
additional_notes: Used to state that something is true, accurate, or genuine. Can refer to facts (es verdadero que...) or to qualities like genuine feelings (amor verdadero). Common in both factual and emotional contexts. Often appears as part of a longer clause (es verdadero que...) or alone as a short answer (Es verdadero.).
target_language_example: Es verdadero que llegaron ayer.
native_language_example: It is true that they arrived yesterday.

meaning: 'it's yours' (plural, familiar/formal in Spain) — says that something belongs to you (plural).
additional_notes: Vuestra is the feminine/neutral plural possessive pronoun used with vosotros/vosotras (you all, informal in Spain). Use 'vuestro' for masculine singular nouns (e.g., 'es vuestro libro'), 'vuestra' for feminine singular nouns (e.g., 'es vuestra llave'), and 'vuestros/vuestras' for plural nouns. In Latin America, vosotros is rare; speakers usually use 'su' or 'ustedes' instead (so they'd say 'es suya' or 'es de ustedes').
target_language_example: Es vuestra decisión.
native_language_example: It's your decision.

meaning: it's that one
additional_notes: Used to identify or point out a specific person or thing previously mentioned or indicated. 'Ése' is a demonstrative pronoun meaning 'that one' (masculine). In informal speech accents on demonstratives are often omitted (ese). Depending on context it can mean 'that's the one' or 'that is him/that person'.
target_language_example: ¿Quién rompió el vaso? — Es ése.
native_language_example: Who broke the glass? — It's that one.

meaning: 'that direction' or 'that address' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to mean 'that direction' (where to go or look). Can also mean 'that line of inquiry' (e.g., investigation) or literally 'that address' (postal). Demonstrative 'esa' = 'that' (feminine) + 'dirección' = 'direction' or 'address'. Use for something not very close to the speaker.
target_language_example: Siga esa dirección hasta el final de la calle.
native_language_example: Follow that direction to the end of the street.

meaning: That's a different matter / That's another (story/thing).
additional_notes: Used to say something is a different issue or to change the subject. Often follows a statement to contrast or dismiss it and introduce a new topic. Tone can be neutral or dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Podemos discutir el precio, pero la calidad, esa es otra.
native_language_example: We can discuss the price, but the quality, that's another matter.

meaning: 'the staircase/ladder is' — the phrase uses the noun escalera plus the verb es (third-person singular of ser) to state what the staircase/ladder is or is like.
additional_notes: Escalera means either 'staircase' (built stairs) or 'ladder' (portable). Use es (from ser) to describe inherent characteristics, identity, material, or general statements (e.g., 'es de metal', 'es símbolo de mala suerte'). For temporary/location descriptions you might use estar instead (e.g., 'la escalera está rota'). Word order: subject + es + complement.
target_language_example: La escalera es de madera y tiene veinte peldaños.
native_language_example: The staircase is made of wood and has twenty steps.

meaning: hid in the (masculine singular place).
additional_notes: Past tense of esconder(se) + preposition 'en' + masculine definite article 'el'. Used to say someone or something hid inside or within a specific masculine noun (e.g., el cajón, el ático, el porche, el hueco). For feminine places you'd see 'escondió en la'.
target_language_example: El gato se escondió en el armario.
native_language_example: The cat hid in the wardrobe.

meaning: to write with (using something or someone as the instrument).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the tool, instrument, or body part used to write (e.g., bolígrafo, mano). Followed by a noun or pronoun introduced by con. Common in simple statements about ability or preference: 'escribir con la mano derecha', 'escribir con un lápiz'.
target_language_example: Puedo escribir con este lápiz sin problemas.
native_language_example: I can write with this pencil without problems.

meaning: to write my / to write (followed by 'my' + noun).
additional_notes: escribir = to write. When followed by a possesive like mi (my) it means 'to write my [something]'. In Spanish the noun comes after mi (e.g., escribir mi nombre = to write my name). Common uses: escribir mi nombre, escribir mi informe, escribir mi apellido. Verb must be conjugated to match the subject (puedo escribir, olvidé escribir, he vuelto a escribir).
target_language_example: No puedo escribir mi dirección en el formulario.
native_language_example: I can't write my address on the form.

meaning: to write one's own (e.g., name, address).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say that someone writes something themselves (often 'nombre' = name). 'Su' can refer to 'his/her/their/your (formal)' depending on context; possessive agrees with the possessor, not the thing written. Common in basic statements about ability (saber/es capaz de/no poder).
target_language_example: Ella puede escribir su propio nombre sin ayuda.
native_language_example: She can write her own name without help.

meaning: 'wrote on' or 'wrote in' (past tense, he/she/it wrote on/in).
additional_notes: Es la forma de pasado (pretérito) del verbo escribir + la preposición en. Se usa para indicar dónde o en qué soporte alguien escribió algo (en la pizarra, en la libreta, en la pared, en su celda, etc.). Traduce como 'wrote on' cuando habla de superficies (la pared, la pizarra) y como 'wrote in' para contenedores o textos (mi cuaderno, su libreta, su celda). Contexto y sustantivo determinan la mejor traducción.
target_language_example: Ella escribió en la libreta todas las direcciones.
native_language_example: She wrote in the notebook all the addresses.

meaning: wrote his/her/its/their (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of escribir + the possessive adjective su. 'Su' can mean his, her, its, their, or your (formal). Use context to know whose thing it is. Commonly followed by words like nombre (name), tesis (thesis), cuaderno (notebook), etc.
target_language_example: Ella escribió su nombre en la lista.
native_language_example: She wrote her name on the list.

meaning: wrote a
additional_notes: escribió is the third-person singular preterite (past) form of escribir (to write). 'un' is the masculine singular indefinite article (a/an). Together they begin a past-tense statement like 'he/she/it wrote a...' or the formal usted wrote a. Use 'escribió una' before feminine nouns. For first- or third-person plural or other tenses you would use different forms (e.g., 'escribimos un', 'escribían un').
target_language_example: Ella escribió un correo electrónico esta mañana.
native_language_example: She wrote an email this morning.

meaning: written in (a language or place)
additional_notes: Used to say that something (a text, book, letter, etc.) was written in a particular language or written at/on a particular place/time. Often appears in passive constructions (está escrito en…) or with past participle + preposition (escribiste/escribió en). When referring to contacting someone, escribir a alguien uses 'a' (escribí a María), while escribir en usually indicates language, place, or topic.
target_language_example: El artículo está escrito en español claro.
native_language_example: The article is written in clear Spanish.

meaning: 'written by' (indicates the author/agent of a written work).
additional_notes: Used to indicate who wrote a text (book, poem, article). Commonly appears in passive constructions with ser/estar/haber + escrito. Use 'por' to introduce the author/agent. Agreement: 'escrito' must agree in gender/number if using past participles that function adjectivally (e.g., 'los textos escritos por...').
target_language_example: El libro fue escrito por Giannis.
native_language_example: The book was written by Giannis.

meaning: have/has written a (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle 'escrito' (written) with the indefinite article 'un'. Commonly appears after the auxiliary 'haber' (he/has/ha/han) to form the present perfect: 'ha escrito un libro' = 'has written a book'. Use 'una' for feminine nouns (ej. 'ha escrito una carta').
target_language_example: Ella ha escrito un artículo sobre música.
native_language_example: She has written an article about music.

meaning: written a (feminine singular noun follows, e.g., 'a novel', 'a letter').
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'escrito' (written) used with an article 'una' to indicate that someone has written one of something (feminine). It appears in perfect constructions (ha escrito, he escrito) and conditional perfect or pluperfect contexts (habría escrito, hubiera escrito). The object after 'una' must be a feminine noun: una carta, una novela, una canción.
target_language_example: Ella ha escrito una carta muy emotiva.
native_language_example: She has written an emotional letter.

meaning: a desk; 'en' = 'in' or 'on' used to show location (desk in/on ...).
additional_notes: escritorio = desk (piece of furniture or a workspace). The example phrase 'escritorio en' combines the noun with the preposition en to indicate location (e.g., 'escritorio en la oficina' = 'desk in the office' or 'sobre mi escritorio' = 'on my desk'). Use definite/indefinite articles and possessives as needed: 'un escritorio en esta habitación' (a desk in this room), 'mi escritorio' (my desk).
target_language_example: Hay papeles sobre el escritorio en la sala.
native_language_example: There are papers on the desk in the living room.

meaning: The phrase consists of the noun 'escritorio' (desk) followed by the verb 'es' (is). Used to make simple descriptions or statements about a desk.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression; it's simply the noun 'escritorio' plus the verb 'es' (third-person singular of 'ser'). Use 'es' to describe essential or general characteristics (material, size, ownership, comparisons). For location or temporary states, Spanish often uses 'estar' (e.g., 'El escritorio está en la esquina'). Word order: subject ('este/mi escritorio') + 'es' + complement.
target_language_example: Mi escritorio es de roble y muy grande.
native_language_example: My desk is oak and very big.

meaning: 'the desk is' (used to describe the desk's state, location, or condition).
additional_notes: A subject (el escritorio) plus the verb estar. Estar is used for temporary states, location, ongoing conditions, physical characteristics (when describing material or current condition), and resulting states (e.g., covered with dust). Use 'está' for third-person singular. For permanent characteristics you might use 'es' instead (e.g., 'El escritorio es de madera' also common).
target_language_example: El escritorio está junto a la ventana y está limpio.
native_language_example: The desk is next to the window and is clean.

meaning: 'listen with' — used to tell someone to listen using a particular attitude or quality (e.g., attention, care, all your being).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'escucha con + [sustantivo]' (escucha con atención, escucha con cuidado, escucha con todo su ser). It instructs the listener how to listen (with attention, with care, with feeling). Often used in commands or requests: 'Por favor, escucha con atención.'
target_language_example: Escucha con atención lo que te voy a decir.
native_language_example: Listen with attention to what I'm going to tell you.

meaning: 'listen to my' (imperative or statement + possessive), used to ask or say that someone listens to something of mine (voice, plan, prayer).
additional_notes: Combines the verb escuchar (to listen) in the imperative or present tense with the possessive pronoun mi (my). In spoken requests use a polite form with por favor or a polite imperative (escuche mi) when addressing usted. Mi is invariable and precedes the noun: escucha mi voz, escucha mi plan. Context determines whether it's a direct command (Listen to my...) or a statement about someone listening.
target_language_example: Escucha mi consejo antes de decidir.
native_language_example: Listen to my advice before deciding.

meaning: 'to listen to' or 'to hear' when directly followed by the masculine singular definite article 'el' (introducing a specific masculine noun)
additional_notes: Escuchar means 'to listen' or 'to hear'. When followed by 'el' it introduces a specific masculine noun (e.g., escuchar el latido, escuchar el sonido). Use 'escuchar a' before people or animals to mark a human/animal object (Escucho a mi profesor). Verb form must agree with subject (escucho, escuchó, escucharé, etc.).
target_language_example: Ella posó su cabeza sobre mi pecho para escuchar el latido de mi corazón.
native_language_example: She laid her head on my chest to listen to the beating of my heart.

meaning: 'to hear' or 'to listen to' (followed by a masculine plural noun).
additional_notes: Escuchar means to listen to or hear something intentionally or passively. When followed by the definite article + plural masculine noun (los), it introduces a specific plural object: e.g. escuchar los latidos (to listen to the heartbeats), escuchar los consejos (to listen to the pieces of advice). Use escuchar + a (person) when specifying a person (escuchar a alguien).
target_language_example: Necesito escuchar los consejos de mi profesor.
native_language_example: I need to listen to my teacher's advice.

meaning: to listen to his/her/its/their (something).
additional_notes: escuchar = to listen (to). su is a possessive that can mean his, her, its, your (formal), or their depending on context. Together 'escuchar su' is followed by a noun (nombre, consejo, música, voz, concierto). For English, translate as 'listen to his/her/their + noun.' In Spanish, the preposition 'a' is often used before a person (e.g., 'escuchar a Tom'), but when using a possessive like 'su' the 'a' is usually omitted: 'escuchar su consejo.'
target_language_example: Deberías escuchar su opinión antes de decidir.
native_language_example: You should listen to his/her opinion before deciding.

meaning: to listen to you (informal 'you')
additional_notes: This sequence is nonstandard in written Spanish. When referring to the pronoun 'you' as a direct object, Spanish normally uses either a clitic attached to an infinitive (escucharte) or the clitic before a conjugated verb (te escucho). 'Escuchar tu' could only be grammatical if 'tu' is the possessive adjective (tú -> tu) followed by a noun (e.g., escuchar tu voz). As shown here, 'escuchar tu' by itself is generally incorrect or incomplete.
target_language_example: No quiero escuchar tu versión de los hechos si vas a decir 'escuchar tu' en vez de 'escucharte'.
native_language_example: I don't want to hear your version of the facts if you're going to say 'escuchar tu' instead of 'escucharte'.

meaning: 'heard the' (past tense, third person singular + feminine singular direct object).
additional_notes: Escuchó = from escuchar (to hear/listen) in the preterite, third person singular (he/she/you formal heard). La is the feminine singular definite article or a feminine direct-object pronoun depending on context. Together they often mean 'he/she heard the...' (feminine noun) or 'he/she heard her.' Word order and meaning depend on the sentence: if 'la' precedes a noun it's the article (escuchó la noticia = he/she heard the news); if 'la' replaces a noun it functions as a direct-object pronoun (la escuchó = he/she heard her), though when used as a pronoun it usually comes before the verb (la escuchó) — post-verb forms like 'escuchó la' + noun are most common.
target_language_example: Cuando llegó a casa, escuchó la radio toda la tarde.
native_language_example: When he got home, he listened to the radio all afternoon.

meaning: language school; a place where languages are taught.
additional_notes: Commonly used for private language institutes, university language centers, or commercial schools that teach foreign languages. Can refer to the institution itself or the business. Plural: escuelas de idiomas.
target_language_example: Trabajo en una escuela de idiomas enseñando inglés.
native_language_example: I work at a language school teaching English.

meaning: 'school starts' (the school begins / classes start)
additional_notes: Common way to say when school or classes begin. Often followed by a time (a las nueve) or a time expression (el lunes que viene). In Spanish the verb 'empezar' agrees with the subject: 'La escuela empieza...' (the school starts). To say 'classes start' you can also use 'las clases empiezan'.
target_language_example: La escuela empieza el lunes a las ocho.
native_language_example: School starts on Monday at eight.

meaning: to go to school by bus / school by bus
additional_notes: Used to say someone travels to school using a bus. Common word order: 'ir a la escuela en autobús' (to go to school by bus).
