Common uses: • describe manner or quality: 'francés con soltura/fluidez' = 'French with ease/fluency' • describe accent: 'francés con acento inglés' = 'French with an English accent' • describe the person you speak with: 'hablar francés con Tom' = 'speak French with Tom'. Word order: con + noun (con fluidez, con acento, con Tom). Use el or no article before francés depending on dialect and formality (hablar francés / hablar el francés both occur).
target_language_example: Hablo francés con confianza y sin miedo a equivocarme.
native_language_example: I speak French with confidence and without fear of making mistakes.

meaning: ‘French at the…’ — refers to studying or using the French language in a particular place (e.g., at school, in class).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the subject (francés = the French language or French class) with a location introduced by 'en el' (in the + masculine singular noun that follows, e.g., instituto, aula). Beginners will often see it when saying where they studied or must speak French. The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows: 'francés en el instituto' = French at (or in) the secondary school; 'francés en el aula' = French in the classroom.
target_language_example: Aprendí francés en el instituto el año pasado.
native_language_example: I learned French at the school last year.

meaning: Not a common fixed phrase; likely part of a larger expression meaning 'French in the ...' or 'French on the ...' (literal).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom in Spanish. It looks like the adjective 'francés' (French) followed by a prepositional phrase beginning with 'en la' ('in the' or 'on the', feminine). You will usually see it as part of a sentence specifying location or context, e.g. 'francés en la mesa' (awkward) or more naturally 'francés en la clase' = 'French in the class' (meaning the French language class). Make sure the noun after 'la' is feminine; if it's masculine use 'en el' instead. For referring to the language you can say 'el francés' or 'en francés' (in French).
target_language_example: Ella habla francés en la clase de idiomas.
native_language_example: She speaks French in the language class.

meaning: "(the) French is" or used to say someone speaks or something is French (language).
additional_notes: ‘Francés’ refers to the French language or something/someone French. In sentences the article can be included ('El francés es...') to mean 'French (the language) is...'. Without the article ('Francés es...') it's less common but can appear in titles or informal statements. 'Tu francés' means 'your French' (your ability in French). Verb 'es' is the 2nd-person singular formal (usted) or 3rd-person singular of ser — translated here as 'is'.
target_language_example: Mi francés es básico, pero practico todos los días.
native_language_example: My French is basic, but I practice every day.

meaning: better French (improved ability or quality of French)
additional_notes: Phrase is the adjective 'francés' (French) followed by 'mejor' (better). Normally used within a sentence (e.g., 'Mi francés es mejor' or 'Hablo francés mejor' or 'Tengo francés mejor que antes'). Using 'francés mejor' standalone is uncommon; prefer a full clause for grammaticality. Context: comparing skill, progress, or the quality of French instruction.
target_language_example: Creo que tengo el francés mejor que antes.
native_language_example: I think I have better French than before.

meaning: ‘the French (man/person) who’ or 'French that' — a noun (francés) followed by a relative clause (que).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause giving more information about a French person or things in French. 'Francés' can mean a French man/person or the French language depending on context; 'que' functions as the relative pronoun 'who/that/which'. Word order: 'el francés que...' = 'the Frenchman who...'.
target_language_example: El francés que trabaja aquí habla tres idiomas.
native_language_example: The Frenchman who works here speaks three languages.

meaning: 'French and' — the adjective/noun 'francés' (French) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and).
additional_notes: Used to list 'French' together with another item. 'Francés' can be a noun (the French language) or an adjective (French [something]). 'Y' connects items in a list. Word order: item + y + next item (e.g., 'francés y español'). Pronunciation note: 'y' is pronounced like the English /i/ (ee).
target_language_example: Estudio francés y alemán este semestre.
native_language_example: I study French and German this semester.

meaning: literally 'phrase is' — used to say that a phrase/sentence has a certain property or state (e.g., language, length, condition).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it combines 'frase' (phrase/sentence) with the verb 'estar' to describe a temporary state or property of the phrase (written in X, formed by X letters, free of errors). In English you would normally say 'this sentence is...'. Use 'está' for conditions, locations, or states; use 'es' (from 'ser') for more permanent identity traits.
target_language_example: Esta frase está escrita en español.
native_language_example: This sentence is written in Spanish.

meaning: used to say that something is not a (useful/true/appropriate) phrase or sentence; literally 'phrase no' (rare/uncommon construction).
additional_notes: This exact pairing 'frase no' is not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish. You might encounter it in contexts like correcting someone (e.g., 'No, frase' or 'frase, no') or in fragments of speech where a speaker rejects a suggested wording. More natural ways to express rejection are: 'no es una buena frase', 'esa frase no sirve', 'no me gusta la frase', or simply 'no'. Use full sentences to be clear.
target_language_example: No, esa frase no funciona en este texto.
native_language_example: No, that sentence doesn't work in this text.

meaning: 'phrases of' or 'phrases about' — used to introduce what the phrases are about or belong to.
additional_notes: A simple prepositional phrase: 'frases' (phrases/sentences) + 'de' (of/about). Commonly followed by a noun or clause (e.g., 'frases de amor' = 'phrases about love', 'frases de la película' = 'lines from the movie'). Can indicate topic, origin, or possession. Use 'frases sobre' to emphasize 'about' a topic. Agreement: 'frases' is plural, so verbs and adjectives referring to it should be plural.
target_language_example: Quiero leer frases de motivación.
native_language_example: I want to read motivational phrases.

meaning: frequency of; how often something happens or occurs.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how often events occur. Often followed by a noun or a time expression (e.g., 'frecuencia de terremotos', 'frecuencia de uso'). Can also appear in comparative expressions ('con más frecuencia') where 'de' may be omitted ('con más frecuencia de lo que crees' is less common than 'con más frecuencia de lo que crees' — note: in sentence 3 the structure is idiomatic).
target_language_example: La frecuencia de llamadas ha aumentado este mes.
native_language_example: The frequency of calls has increased this month.

meaning: 'in front of', 'facing', or 'opposite (to)'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical position (standing in front of something or opposite it) or facing someone/something. Can also mean 'in the face of' or 'when confronted with' in more abstract contexts (e.g., frente a una amenaza). Commonly followed by a noun or pronoun.
target_language_example: Me senté frente a la ventana para leer.
native_language_example: I sat in front of the window to read.

meaning: in front of the (feminine noun) / the front of the
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to indicate location ('in front of') or to talk about the front part of something ('the front of the...'). Spanish articles must match the noun: 'frente del' is for masculine ('de el' → del), 'frente de la' for feminine. Often followed by a noun (e.g., 'frente de la casa').
target_language_example: El coche está frente de la farmacia.
native_language_example: The car is in front of the pharmacy.

meaning: to frown; to knit one's brows (to show displeasure, concern, or concentration).
additional_notes: Describes bringing the eyebrows together, creating wrinkles on the forehead. Can indicate anger, confusion, worry, concentration, or disapproval. Used in both literal and figurative contexts. Common in everyday and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Ella comenzó a fruncir el ceño al leer el informe.
native_language_example: She began to frown when reading the report.

meaning: "cold" (feminine singular) used before a noun or phrase introduced by 'en' — literally 'cold in/at/on'.
additional_notes: Fría is the feminine form of the adjective 'frío'. Here it appears before nouns or prepositional phrases with 'en' (e.g., 'fría en la mesa', 'fría en un día caluroso', 'fría en la cara'). Use 'frío' for masculine nouns (un día frío), 'fríos'/'frías' for plurals. The adjective typically agrees in gender and number with the noun it describes. Context determines whether 'en' means 'on', 'in', 'during', or 'at'.
target_language_example: Había una bebida fría en la mesa.
native_language_example: There was a cold drink on the table.

meaning: cold (something) to (do/use) — used to say you want a cold drink or cold item for a purpose.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like "algo frío para beber" (something cold to drink). "Frío" is an adjective meaning cold; "para" introduces the intended use or purpose (to drink, to eat, etc.). Word order: adjective after noun is normal in Spanish (algo frío). You can replace "algo" with a specific noun: "una bebida fría para beber" (a cold drink to drink) or more naturally "una bebida fría". Often used when asking for a cold thing because you're thirsty/hot.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes algo frío para beber? Tengo mucho calor.
native_language_example: Do you have something cold to drink? I'm very hot.

meaning: it's cold here / it's chilly here.
additional_notes: Common way to say the current temperature where you are. Often used with Hace (Hace frío aquí) to describe weather or room temperature. Can be modified: 'Hace mucho frío aquí' (very cold), 'Hace un poco de frío aquí' (a little cold). Useful for reporting how you feel or asking for a blanket/heater.
target_language_example: Hace frío aquí; ¿puedes cerrar la ventana?
native_language_example: It's cold here; can you close the window?

meaning: 'cold in' or 'cold at' — used to say that a place or part of the body is cold.
additional_notes: Common structure: hacer frío en + place/time (Hace frío en invierno; Hace frío en la ciudad). Also used with tener frío + en + body part to say a specific part feels cold (Tengo frío en las manos). 'Frío en' itself is not a standalone verb; it's part of phrases describing temperature or sensation.
target_language_example: Hace mucho frío en la playa por la noche.
native_language_example: It's very cold at the beach at night.

meaning: used to compare temperatures: 'colder than'.
additional_notes: Often appears in comparative constructions with más (más frío que) to say one time/place/person is colder than another. Can refer to past, present, or general comparisons (e.g., Ayer hizo más frío que hoy = Yesterday was colder than today). Word order: [más + frío + que + comparison].
target_language_example: Esta mañana ha hecho más frío que ayer.
native_language_example: This morning it was colder than yesterday.

meaning: cold and — used to link 'cold' with another state or action (e.g., 'cold and wet', 'cold and sad').
additional_notes: frío is an adjective meaning 'cold'. When followed by y (and) it connects frío to another adjective, verb, or clause describing an additional condition. Agreement: frío agrees in gender/number with the noun it describes (fría, fríos, frías) when used with a noun; in many of the example sentences frío describes a person (está frío → feels cold). Common pattern: 'tener frío' (to be cold) plus y + another phrase: 'tiene frío y está cansado.'
target_language_example: Tenemos frío y tenemos hambre.
native_language_example: We are cold and we are hungry.

meaning: went home
additional_notes: Used to say that someone went home. fue is a past form of ir ('to go'). In the examples, se fue a casa is more common and often suggests the person left and went home.
target_language_example: Ana fue a casa después de clase.
native_language_example: Ana went home after class.

meaning: he/she/it went to his/her/its (somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone going to a place that belongs to them (home, room, office). Fue is the past (preterite) of ir (to go). 'Su' is a possessive (his/her/its/your formal/their) and depends on context. Common structure: [Subject] + fue a su + [place].
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, ella fue a su oficina.
native_language_example: After the meeting, she went to her office.

meaning: went to / was meant for / was to (depending on context).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the past tense of ir/ser (fue) with para. Its meaning depends on the verb and context: with ir (to go) it can mean 'went to' + destination (fue para África = went to Africa); with purpose/instrument it can mean 'was for' or 'was meant to' (fue para quedarme aquí = was intended for me to stay here). In some literary/older uses, it can appear with reflexives or substitutions (fue para ti = was for you). Pay attention to surrounding verbs to choose the right English translation.
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la universidad, fue para Londres.
native_language_example: When he finished university, he went to London.

meaning: he/she/they left early; went to bed early (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common phrase using the reflexive verb 'irse' (to leave/go away). 'Pronto' here means 'early' (soon/earlier than others or earlier than usual). With places like 'a la cama' it specifically means 'went to bed early'. Subject is expressed elsewhere (se fue = he/she left).
target_language_example: Después de la cena, ella se fue pronto porque estaba cansada.
native_language_example: After dinner, she left early because she was tired.

meaning: was punished (passive voice).
additional_notes: Used to say someone received punishment. 'Fue' is the past (pretérito) of 'ser' used to form the passive voice with the past participle 'castigado'. Can refer to discipline, legal punishment, or temporary penalties (e.g., 'fue castigado por tres semanas' = 'was punished for three weeks'). Replace 'fue' with other tenses/persons to change time/subject (e.g., 'es castigado', 'fueron castigados').
target_language_example: El perro fue castigado por romper la cama.
native_language_example: The dog was punished for chewing the bed.

meaning: it was something
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'it was something.' Used both literally (to say that something existed or happened) and idiomatically as a vague or emphatic comment: to downplay, emphasize, or qualify an event (e.g. 'it was pretty/quite something,' 'that was something,' or 'maybe it was something I did'). Often followed by an adjective (fue algo increíble = it was something incredible) or used alone as a summing-up (Eso fue algo = That was something). Context decides nuance.
target_language_example: No esperaba su reacción; fue algo inesperado.
native_language_example: I didn't expect their reaction; it was something unexpected.

meaning: it was (happened) two [units of time] ago
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened two (days/weeks/months/years) ago. The phrase combines the past tense (fue) with 'hace dos' + time unit (años, días, meses, semanas). Native speakers often omit the subject: 'Fue hace dos años.'
target_language_example: Eso fue hace dos años.
native_language_example: That was two years ago.

meaning: it was three (units) ago — used with time expressions (años, días, semanas, etc.).
additional_notes: Common structure: Fue/eso fue + hace + number + time unit. Equivalent to English 'It was three years ago' or 'That was three days ago.' Use 'fue' (past tense of ser) or 'eso fue' to refer to a past event or moment. Replace 'tres' with other numbers as needed (uno, dos, cuatro...).
target_language_example: Eso fue hace tres semanas.
native_language_example: That was three weeks ago.

meaning: it/that was (happening) (time) ago — used to say how long ago something happened.
additional_notes: Common structure: [evento] + fue/hace + cantidad de tiempo. Often shortened to 'fue hace un/una...' or simply 'fue hace [tiempo]'. 'Hace' expresses 'ago'; 'fue' (past of 'ser') or context may omit 'fue'. Use 'hace' alone with present: 'Hace un año que vine' (I came a year ago).
target_language_example: Eso fue hace un año.
native_language_example: That was a year ago.

meaning: it was the best night (of my life / ever).
additional_notes: Common way to say an evening or night was excellent. Often followed by 'de mi vida' (of my life) to emphasize it's the best ever. 'Fue' is past (simple) of 'ser' — used to describe a completed past event. You can change time words (anoche, esa, esta) or person (fue → fue nuestra) depending on context.
target_language_example: Anoche fue la mejor noche que he pasado en mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: Last night was the best night I've had in a long time.

meaning: 'was' + neutral pronoun used in fixed expressions like 'fue lo suficientemente...' (was ... enough).
additional_notes: Combines the past tense of ser/ir (fue = he/she/it was, or went) with the neutral pronoun lo to form phrases like 'fue lo suficiente...' or 'fue lo suficientemente...' meaning 'was ... enough' or 'was so ... that...'. Commonly appears in comparisons or comments about someone/something being 'enough' (rápido, estúpido, afortunado, etc.). Context determines whether fue = 'was' (most likely) or 'went'.
target_language_example: Ella fue lo bastante valiente para hablar.
native_language_example: She was brave enough to speak up.

meaning: was ours / was our (singular, feminine or neutral context).
additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) of 'ser' + possessive 'nuestra' (our). Use when saying that something (feminine noun or abstract idea) belonged to or was associated with 'us' in the past. If the noun is masculine use 'fue nuestro'. If plural use 'fueron nuestros/nuestras'. Context can be literal possession or figurative (e.g., 'was our promise', 'was our fault', 'was our only weapon').
target_language_example: Esa decisión fue nuestra y la asumimos.
native_language_example: That decision was ours and we take responsibility.

meaning: 'it was for your' (followed by a noun) — used to explain a reason or motive concerning the listener (e.g. 'for your own good', 'for your mother')
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of phrases like "fue por tu propio bien" (it was for your own good) or "fue por tu madre" (it was because of/for your mother). "Fue" is the past (preterite) of "ser/ir" here meaning 'it was'; "por" introduces the reason or motive; "tu" is the informal possessive 'your' (without accent — for 'yours' possessive adjective). If addressing someone formally, use "su" instead of "tu". Often used to justify an action done for the listener's benefit or because of someone/something related to them.
target_language_example: Fue por tu seguridad que cerramos la puerta.
native_language_example: It was for your safety that we locked the door.

meaning: 'it was only' or 'it was just' (used to downplay or limit what something was).
additional_notes: Used to minimize or limit the importance/nature of something in the past. Common with nouns like 'un sueño' (a dream), 'una aventura' (an adventure), 'un ejemplo' (an example), or abstract ideas like 'una conjetura'. In Spanish, 'solo' here means 'only/just' (not 'alone'); accent (sólo) is optional in modern orthography. Context determines whether it's dismissive, explanatory, or consoling.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, fue solo un malentendido.
native_language_example: Don't worry, it was only a misunderstanding.

meaning: 'it was only' or 'it was just'.
additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something in the past (pretérito: fue). Can introduce a noun, phrase, or explanation: e.g. 'fue sólo un sueño' = it was only a dream. If referring to a person, context may change (e.g. 'no fue sólo por mí' = it wasn't just because of me). 'Sólo' (with the accent) is increasingly written as 'solo' without an accent in modern Spanish; both are understood.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, fue sólo un malentendido.
native_language_example: Don't worry, it was just a misunderstanding.

meaning: that was all
additional_notes: Fue is the preterite of ser ('was'). It is often used in phrases like eso fue todo = 'that was all' or 'that's it.' Before a noun phrase, todo can add emphasis meaning 'entirely' or 'completely,' as in Fue todo culpa suya = 'It was entirely his/her fault.'
target_language_example: Le hice una pregunta y eso fue todo.
native_language_example: I asked him one question, and that was all.

meaning: was one (of them/one of the...)
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something belonged to a group or category in the past: 'was one of my ...' or 'was one of the ...'. Often followed by 'de' + noun phrase (e.g., de los míos, de mis amigos, de los supervivientes). Past tense (pretérito) of 'ser' + numeral/indefinite 'uno'.
target_language_example: María fue uno de los voluntarios en la campaña.
native_language_example: María was one of the volunteers in the campaign.

meaning: to set fire to / to burn (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used with prender/poner/echársele etc. + fuego a + direct object (often preceded by an indirect object pronoun when the person affected is specified: le prendió fuego a su casa). Common verbs: prender fuego a, poner fuego a. Can be literal (burning) or figurative. Word order: verb + fuego a + thing/person.
target_language_example: Prendieron fuego a la bodega abandonada.
native_language_example: They set fire to the abandoned warehouse.

meaning: firework (singular) — an explosive pyrotechnic device used for celebrations.
additional_notes: Used for single fireworks or as a general term for fireworks displays. Plural is fuegos artificiales. Can also refer to fireworks collectively (los fuegos artificiales). Common in contexts like fiestas, New Year's, Independence Day, and celebrations.
target_language_example: Anoche vimos un fuego artificial espectacular en la plaza.
native_language_example: Last night we saw a spectacular firework in the square.

meaning: crossfire; figuratively, being caught between opposing sides.
additional_notes: Literally 'crossed fire.' Used for literal gunfire between two sides or figuratively when people/objects get caught between conflicting groups, decisions, or consequences. Common in news, warnings, and metaphorical speech.
target_language_example: No quiero que los niños queden en el fuego cruzado.
native_language_example: I don't want the children to be caught in the crossfire.

meaning: “fire in” — used to say there is a fire at/in a place or figuratively a spark/ardor in something.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe a physical fire located somewhere (fuego en + place). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., 'fuego en los ojos' = passion, intensity). Word order: 'fuego en + lugar'. For physical fires, Spanish often uses 'un fuego en...' or 'el fuego en...'.
target_language_example: Hay un fuego en la cocina; llama a los bomberos.
native_language_example: There is a fire in the kitchen; call the firefighters.

meaning: 'the fire' + reflexive/pronominal verb marker — appears with verbs that describe what the fire does (e.g., extinguishes, spreads, starts).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun fuego ('fire') followed by a reflexive pronoun attached to a verb (se apagó, se desató, se propagó). In Spanish, many intransitive verbs use the pronoun 'se' to indicate that something happens to itself or that an event occurs. Useful verbs with 'fuego' include: apagarse (to go out), iniciarse (to begin), desatarse (to break out), propagarse (to spread), convertirse en (to turn into).
target_language_example: El fuego se apagó antes de que llegara el bombero.
native_language_example: The fire went out before the firefighter arrived.

meaning: 'fire and' — the conjunction 'and' following the noun 'fuego' (fire).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's simply the word 'fuego' (fire) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). It appears in lists or poetic expressions (e.g., 'fuego y agua' = 'fire and water'). Pronounce the 'y' as /i/. Depending on context, 'fuego' can be literal (flame) or figurative (passion, destruction).
target_language_example: Fuego y agua no pueden mezclarse en este cuento.
native_language_example: Fire and water cannot mix in this tale.

meaning: outside of
additional_notes: Common prepositional phrase. Usually means physical location 'outside of' or 'not in' (fuera de la casa = outside the house). Can also be used figuratively to mean 'apart from' or 'except for' (fuera de lo ordinario = apart from the ordinary). Use with nouns or pronouns; when referring to persons or places it indicates exclusion or separation.
target_language_example: No puedo vivir fuera de este país.
native_language_example: I can't live outside of this country.

meaning: out of control; not under control or unmanageable.
additional_notes: Used to describe situations, people, or things that are chaotic, uncontrollable, or beyond someone's ability to manage. Commonly follows estar (estar fuera de control). Can be used for events (la situación), behavior (él/ella está), or objects/processes.
target_language_example: La reunión se volvió fuera de control cuando comenzaron a gritar.
native_language_example: The meeting got out of control when they started shouting.

meaning: out of place; inappropriate; not where it belongs.
additional_notes: Used both literally (something physically not in its proper place) and figuratively (feeling awkward or describing comments/behavior that are inappropriate). Common collocations: 'estar fuera de lugar' (to be out of place), 'comentario fuera de lugar' (inappropriate comment).
target_language_example: Me sentí fuera de lugar en la fiesta porque no conocía a nadie.
native_language_example: I felt out of place at the party because I didn't know anyone.

meaning: out of service; not working or unavailable.
additional_notes: Used to say a machine, device, system, or service is broken, turned off, or temporarily unavailable. Common on signs (e.g., 'Fuera de servicio') and in reports. Can refer to individual staff only in specific contexts (e.g., 'personal fuera de servicio' meaning staff not on duty), but most often describes equipment or systems.
target_language_example: El cajero automático está fuera de servicio; use la sucursal de la esquina.
native_language_example: The ATM is out of service; use the branch on the corner.

meaning: extremely upset, distraught, or out of control (emotionally).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is emotionally overwhelmed, furious, shocked, or not acting like their normal self. Can refer to strong anger, grief, panic, or general loss of composure. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Cuando recibió la noticia, se quedó fuera de sí de la rabia.
native_language_example: When he received the news, he was beside himself with anger.

meaning: subjunctive form meaning 'went to' or 'go to' (imperfect subjunctive of ir + article 'la'); used in subordinate clauses to talk about someone going to a feminine place (e.g., la Policía, la reunión) or hypothetical/uncertain actions.
additional_notes: Fuera is the imperfect subjunctive of ir (to go) and can be used for past hypotheticals, wishes, doubts, or after verbs that require the subjunctive (e.g., aconsejar, querer, intentar). 'A la' combines the preposition a + feminine definite article la. The full phrase depends on the noun that follows (e.g., 'fuera a la Policía', 'fuera a la reunión', 'fuera a la guerra'). English equivalents: 'that (he/she) went to', 'that (he/she) would go to', 'if (he/she) were to go to'.
target_language_example: Si fuera a la reunión, podría explicar mi idea.
native_language_example: If I/they/he/she were to go to the meeting, I/they/he/she could explain my/ their idea.

meaning: go to the
additional_notes: Here, fuera is the imperfect subjunctive of ir ('to go'), followed by al ('to the' = a + el). It often appears after que with verbs of doubt, suggestion, hope, or reminders, and in si clauses. In this phrase, fuera does not mean 'outside'; it is a verb form of ir.
target_language_example: El profesor recomendó que fuera al museo el sábado.
native_language_example: The teacher recommended that he go to the museum on Saturday.

meaning: If I were you / in your shoes.
additional_notes: Used in conditional sentences (often with 'si yo' omitted in casual speech) to give advice or say what one would do in the other person's situation. The full structure is 'Si yo fuera tú,...' (subjunctive 'fuera' because it's hypothetical). Can be softened with commas or modal verbs (e.g., 'yo que tú').
target_language_example: Si yo fuera tú, hablaría con tu jefe antes de decidir.
native_language_example: If I were you, I'd talk to your boss before deciding.

meaning: 'if I/he/she/it were a' — the start of a hypothetical conditional using the imperfect subjunctive (si + fuera) plus an indefinite noun.
additional_notes: Used to introduce unreal or hypothetical situations (contrary-to-fact) with si + imperfect subjunctive (fuera). Followed by a noun phrase introduced by 'un/una' (a/an). The result clause usually uses the conditional (condicional simple), e.g. 'lo habría...' or 'volaría'. Depending on context, 'fuera' can refer to different subjects (I/he/she/it); the subject is understood from context or stated elsewhere.
target_language_example: Si fuera un cantante, viajaría por el mundo.
native_language_example: If I were a singer, I would travel the world.

meaning: the imperfect-subjunctive form 'you were' + indefinite article (you would be / that you were a... in hypothetical, doubt, emotion, or non-factual contexts).
additional_notes: Fueras is second-person singular imperfect subjunctive of ser (tú fueras). Often used after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., expresar duda, deseo, emoción, hipótesis): si (if), esperaba que, no sabía que, temía que, basta de actuar como si. The article 'un' begins a noun phrase (a/an). In English this is translated depending on context: 'if you were a...', 'I didn't know you were a...', 'I feared you might be a...'.
target_language_example: Si fueras un libro, ¿cuál serías?
native_language_example: If you were a book, which one would you be?

meaning: they went (to do something / to a place).
additional_notes: Uses the verb ir in preterite (ellos/ustedes form) + 'de' to indicate going somewhere or going to do an activity (fueron de pesca = they went fishing; fueron de vacaciones = they went on vacation). With reflexive 'se fueron de' it emphasizes that they left or departed from a place (se fueron de casa = they left home). Can be followed by a noun (pesca, vacaciones, excursión) or by 'las manos' in idiomatic uses (se fueron de las manos = got out of hand).
target_language_example: Fueron de viaje a México el mes pasado.
native_language_example: They went on a trip to Mexico last month.

meaning: they went by / they went in / they set out (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with transportation: 'fueron en + medio' (bus, tren, automóvil) = 'they went by ...'. Used with purpose or direction: 'fueron en busca de...' = 'they went in search of... / set out to find...'. Also appears in reflexive form 'se fueron en ...' meaning 'they left in/on (the middle of the night)' or simply 'they left.' Context determines translation.
target_language_example: Fueron en tren a la ciudad para ver la exposición.
native_language_example: They went by train to the city to see the exhibition.

meaning: 'they were' or 'were the' (third-person plural past of 'ser' with a feminine plural noun or feminine plural context).
additional_notes: Fueron is the preterite (past) third-person plural of ser (to be) or ir (to go) depending on context; with 'las' it functions as 'they were the...' referring to feminine plural nouns already mentioned or understood. Common in sentences like 'Fueron las apuestas...' (It was the bets...) or 'No fueron las flores...' (It wasn't the flowers...). Word order can vary: 'Fueron las...' = 'It was the...' or literally 'They were the...'.
target_language_example: Fueron las dudas las que me detuvieron.
native_language_example: It was the doubts that stopped me.

meaning: 'stronger than (you/it) think(s) or appear(s)'.
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say someone or something has more strength (physical, emotional, etc.) than is believed or visible. Commonly appears in phrases like "eres más fuerte de lo que crees" (you are stronger than you think). Structure: más/ mucho más + fuerte + de lo que + verb/clause.
target_language_example: Eres más fuerte de lo que piensas.
native_language_example: You are stronger than you think.

meaning: 'strong for' or 'be strong for (someone)'; used to say you stay emotionally strong on behalf of someone else. Also appears in a different structure meaning 'a strong reason for'.
additional_notes: Most commonly used in emotional contexts: 'ser fuerte por + alguien' means to endure or show strength for someone else (e.g., a family member). In sentence 4 it appears in a different construction: 'motivo fuerte por el cual...' meaning 'a strong reason for which...'. Context determines whether it's about personal strength or a strong cause/reason.
target_language_example: Voy a ser fuerte por mi hermana durante su hospitalización.
native_language_example: I'll be strong for my sister during her hospitalization.

meaning: 'stronger than the' (used in comparisons).
additional_notes: This is part of the comparative structure 'más fuerte que el...' meaning 'stronger than the...'. You'll usually see 'más' before the adjective: 'más fuerte que...'. The definite article (el/la/los/las) matches the noun compared (el odio, la roca). Can be used for physical or figurative strength (e.g., love, materials, people).
target_language_example: La amistad es más fuerte que el miedo.
native_language_example: Friendship is stronger than fear.

meaning: an informal word order where 'fuerte' (strongly/hard) is placed before a determiner + noun or pronoun ('el') to indicate that something is done forcefully or intensely; effectively equivalent to 'fuerte' modifying the action or the noun phrase (e.g., 'apretar fuerte el nudo' = 'tighten the knot hard').
additional_notes: This is a colloquial arrangement in Spanish where 'fuerte' functions adverbially and appears before the noun phrase introduced by 'el'. It's common in spoken Spanish and regional varieties. More neutral alternatives: 'aprieta fuerte', 'muy fuerte', or 'aprieta el nudo con fuerza'. 'Fuerte el' is compositional (meaning derives from its parts) and not a fixed idiom; word order may vary. Not a false cognate. Register: informal/colloquial but widely understood.
target_language_example: Aprieta fuerte el nudo para que no se suelte con el viento.
native_language_example: Tighten the knot hard so it doesn't come loose in the wind.

meaning: the strength/force of the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to say 'the force/strength/power of the ...' (e.g., fuerza de la naturaleza = force of nature). 'Fuerza' is feminine, so phrase matches feminine nouns; English translations vary (force, power, strength, influence) depending on context.
target_language_example: La fuerza de la naturaleza es impresionante.
native_language_example: The force of nature is impressive.

meaning: willpower; strength of will.
additional_notes: Refers to a person's ability to control impulses, persist, or resist temptation. Used in positive and negative statements (tener/ no tener fuerza de voluntad). Common collocations: 'tener fuerza de voluntad', 'falta de fuerza de voluntad', 'con/por su fuerza de voluntad'.
target_language_example: Con fuerza de voluntad, dejó de fumar.
native_language_example: With willpower, he quit smoking.

meaning: 'strength/power of the' (masculine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: A short phrase meaning 'the strength/power of' someone or something. 'Fuerza' is feminine, but when followed by 'del' it indicates possession/relationship with a masculine singular noun (de + el = del). Use 'de la' for feminine nouns, 'de los'/'de las' for plurals. Common in literary or descriptive contexts.
target_language_example: La paciencia es la fuerza del maestro.
native_language_example: Patience is the strength of the teacher.

meaning: strength/power in (used to say something has strength, intensity, or influence in a place, situation, or context).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'con fuerza en' or 'fuerza en' within a sentence to indicate where or in what context the strength, intensity, or emotional support exists. Can refer to physical intensity (e.g., light shining strongly in a place), emotional/mental strength, or influence/power in a domain. Word order and prepositions may vary (e.g., 'brillar con fuerza en...' or 'fuerza en el mundo').
target_language_example: La música tiene mucha fuerza en este concierto.
native_language_example: The music has a lot of power at/in this concert.

meaning: This appears to be the pronoun 'se' combined with the noun 'fuerza' in different contexts — usually 'fuerza' = 'force' or 'strength', and 'se' is a reflexive/impersonal pronoun or part of a passive/impersonal construction.
additional_notes: These example sentences show different uses: 'fuerza' can mean physical force, power, or strength. 'Se' can be: (1) part of a passive/impersonal construction ('contra la fuerza se puede encontrar...' — roughly 'against force one can find...'), (2) a reflexive pronoun indicating something happens to itself ('se ha ido' = 'has gone away'), or (3) used with verbs to form intransitive/passive meaning ('con fuerza se romperá' = 'if you do it with force it will break'). The two-word sequence 'fuerza se' is not a fixed phrase; learners should treat 'fuerza' and 'se' separately and learn the common patterns (passive/impersonal se, reflexive se).
target_language_example: Con más fuerza se abre la puerta.
native_language_example: With more force the door opens.

meaning: the armed forces; the military (all branches).
additional_notes: Refers collectively to a country's military organizations (army, navy, air force, etc.). Common in formal contexts and news. Use when talking about military service, institutions, or actions by the military.
target_language_example: Mi hermano sirvió en las fuerzas armadas durante cinco años.
native_language_example: My brother served in the armed forces for five years.

meaning: 'escape from' or 'leak of' depending on context.
additional_notes: Can mean an escape (fuga de la prisión, fuga de la ley) or a leak/loss (fuga de aire, fuga de gas). The preposition 'de' links what is being escaped from or what is leaking. Choose meaning from context: with people/places/abstract (escape), with substances (leak).
target_language_example: Hubo una fuga de gas en la cocina, llamamos al servicio de emergencia.
native_language_example: There was a gas leak in the kitchen; we called emergency services.

meaning: I went with (someone).
additional_notes: Past-tense first-person singular of ir + the preposition con. Use to say you went somewhere accompanied by someone or that you went to see/meet someone (context can show destination). Common in everyday speech: 'Yo fui con...' or simply 'Fui con...'.
target_language_example: Fui con mi hermana al médico.
native_language_example: I went with my sister to the doctor.

meaning: I was the
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun or description to say who or what someone was in the past: for example, el primero, el mejor, el único, el responsable. Here fui is from ser (“to be”), not ir (“to go”). For feminine forms, use fui la.
target_language_example: Fui el último en llegar.
native_language_example: I was the last to arrive.

meaning: 'I was the' (feminine).
additional_notes: Combination of the past tense of 'ser/ir' (fui = I was/went) plus the feminine definite article 'la' before a noun or adjective. Here it introduces a description identifying the speaker as the only one who had a certain experience: 'Fui la única...' = 'I was the only one...'. Context determines whether 'fui' is from 'ser' (to be) or 'ir' (to go); with descriptions it's 'ser'.
target_language_example: Fui la primera en llegar a la oficina.
native_language_example: I was the first to arrive at the office.

meaning: 'I was a' (feminine singular) — simple past (preterite) first person of 'ser' with an indefinite article, used before a feminine noun or adjective.
additional_notes: Used to state a past identity, role, characteristic, or behavior about the speaker (female). 'Fui' is the preterite of 'ser' (to be). The feminine article 'una' agrees with a following feminine noun or adjective (e.g., buena madre, persona solitaria). For masculine subjects you'd say 'fui un'. Can describe a one-time or completed state in the past; context may imply duration (e.g., 'hasta los trece fui una buena chica' = until thirteen I was a good girl).
target_language_example: Fui una estudiante muy aplicada en la universidad.
native_language_example: I was a very hard-working student in college.

meaning: 'we went' (used with an activity or destination; literal: 'we went of/to').
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of 'irse'/'ir' with 'de' + noun phrase. Common constructions: 'fuimos de + activity' (fuimos de compras = we went shopping), 'fuimos de + destino' or 'nos fuimos de + lugar' (we left a place). Context determines whether it means 'we went (to do something)', 'we went on (an outing)', or 'we left'.
target_language_example: El verano pasado fuimos de excursión a las montañas.
native_language_example: Last summer we went on a hike to the mountains.

meaning: 'you were the' (past tense, singular informal 'you')
additional_notes: Combination of the preterite second-person singular of ser/ir (tú fuiste) plus the masculine definite article el. Used to describe a past state, role or characteristic of 'you' (informal). If referring to a feminine noun, use 'fuiste la'. For formal you (usted) use 'fue el/la'. Context determines whether the verb is 'ser' (to be) or 'ir' (to go); most examples here use 'ser' (to be).
target_language_example: Fuiste el mejor amigo que tuve en la universidad.
native_language_example: You were the best friend I had in college.

meaning: to smoke in the (female noun) — used to say smoking is allowed or prohibited in a specific place.
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by a feminine location noun (la oficina, la escuela, la estación, la terraza). Use 'fumar en el' for masculine places (el restaurante). Commonly appears in rules and signs: 'No se permite fumar en la ...' or 'Prohibido fumar en la ...'.
target_language_example: No se permite fumar en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: Smoking is not allowed in the library.

meaning: "smoking is bad for the" (usually completed as "salud" = health).
additional_notes: A fixed phrase used to state that smoking harms something, most commonly 'la salud' (health). In examples it's often part of fuller sentences like 'fumar es malo para la salud.' Useful for warnings or general statements. The fragment here ends with 'la' because the noun that follows is feminine (la salud).
target_language_example: Fumar es malo para la salud y para la de quienes te rodean.
native_language_example: Smoking is bad for your health and for the health of those around you.

meaning: 'how this (works)'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how a particular thing, system, job, business, etc. operates. Often appears as 'cómo funciona este/esta + [noun]' or in clauses like 'Así es como funciona este negocio.' The verb 'funciona' comes from 'funcionar' (to work/function). Pronunciation note: 'cómo' carries an accent when used in questions or indirect questions.
target_language_example: No sé cómo funciona este programa, ¿me lo explicas?
native_language_example: I don't know how this program works, can you explain it to me?

meaning: 'it works' / 'how it works' (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun (la + noun) or after 'cómo' to ask/explain the way something operates or behaves. 'Así funciona la...' = 'This is how the ... works.' 'Cómo funciona la...' = 'How the ... works.' Replace 'la' with 'el' for masculine nouns. Common in descriptions, explanations, and demonstrations.
target_language_example: ¿Me explicas cómo funciona la cafetera?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me how the coffee maker works?

meaning: founder of — someone who started or established something.
additional_notes: Used to state who started an organization, company, movement, city, religion, etc. 'Fundador' is masculine; use 'fundadora' for a female founder. Followed by 'de' + the thing founded (company name, place, movement). Often preceded by a name or a subject pronoun.
target_language_example: Bill Gates es el fundador de Microsoft.
native_language_example: Bill Gates is the founder of Microsoft.

meaning: literally 'future and' — used as part of phrases linking 'futuro' (the future) with another idea; not a fixed idiom on its own.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's simply the noun futuro ('the future') followed by the conjunction y ('and'). In the example sentences it appears as part of larger thoughts (e.g., 'futuro y me olvido…' where 'y' links clauses, or 'futuro y una novia' where it links two nouns). Use it whenever you need to join 'futuro' with another element. Watch word order: 'mi futuro' means 'my future.'
target_language_example: Pienso en mi futuro y en mis metas cada semana.
native_language_example: I think about my future and my goals every week.

meaning: as easy as / as ... as (used to compare ease).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say something is as easy as something else (or not). Often appears in structures: 'tan fácil como' (as easy as) or 'lo suficientemente fácil como para...' (easy enough to...). When negated, it expresses that something is not as easy as expected. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Aprender a tocar la guitarra no es tan fácil como parece.
native_language_example: Learning to play the guitar isn't as easy as it seems.

meaning: easier than (what) / than it seems or than someone thinks
additional_notes: Used to compare actual ease to someone's expectation or appearance. Commonly appears in comparisons like "más fácil de lo que..." (easier than you/he/she/they think/expect/appear). The clause after "de lo que" can be a verb or phrase (cree, parece, pensaban, pensé, había esperado). If referring to the speaker's past expectation use past tense (pensé, había esperado).
target_language_example: Aprender estas frases fue más fácil de lo que imaginaba.
native_language_example: Learning these phrases was easier than I imagined.

meaning: used to compare ease; 'easier than' or 'so easy that'.
additional_notes: Often appears in comparisons (más fácil que = easier than). Can also introduce a result with 'tan fácil que' (so easy that). Watch spelling: 'más' (with accent) when meaning 'more'. Context determines whether it's comparative ('than') or result ('that').
target_language_example: Aprender a andar en bicicleta es más fácil que aprender a conducir.
native_language_example: Learning to ride a bike is easier than learning to drive.

meaning: American football (the sport played with helmets and an oval ball).
additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to American-style football (not soccer). In Spanish, 'fútbol' alone often means soccer, so 'fútbol americano' distinguishes the U.S. sport. Can be used as a noun (verbo jugar al fútbol americano) or to describe a game/event (partido de fútbol americano).
target_language_example: Voy al estadio a ver un partido de fútbol americano.
native_language_example: I'm going to the stadium to watch an American football game.

meaning: sunglasses
additional_notes: Common plural noun in Spanish (always used in plural: 'las gafas de sol'). Used to refer to protective or fashion eyewear for bright sunlight. Can be used with verbs like 'llevar' (to wear), 'poner(se)' (to put on), or 'quitar(se)' (to take off).
target_language_example: Me compré unas gafas de sol nuevas para el verano.
native_language_example: I bought new sunglasses for the summer.

meaning: 'earns/gets a (masculine singular noun)'; third-person singular of ganar + indefinite article
additional_notes: Gana is the third-person singular present of ganar (to win/earn/get). When followed by un it introduces a masculine singular noun (e.g., gana un profesor = 'a ... earns...'? note: in sentence 1 the structure is 'cuánto gana un profesor' = 'how much a PE teacher earns'). Can mean 'earns' (salary) or 'wins/gets' (prize), depending on context. Use with other articles/words as needed (gana una, ganas un, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi primo gana un buen sueldo cada mes.
native_language_example: My cousin earns a good salary every month.

meaning: 'won the first' (masculine, singular) — used to say someone or something has won the first [place, match, prize, etc.]
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining the past participle ganar (ganado) with the article and ordinal adjective el primer. It requires a noun after primer (e.g., primer puesto, primer premio, primer partido). The subject before this phrase is typically the winner (e.g., Él ha ganado el primer puesto). In Spanish you will more often see the full phrase (ganó el primer puesto / ha ganado el primer premio). Agreement: if the noun after primer is feminine use primera (ganado/a + la primera ...), and the participle form may change depending on sentence structure (ganó vs. ha ganado).
target_language_example: Ella ha ganado el primer premio.
native_language_example: She has won the first prize.

meaning: to win the
additional_notes: Ganar is a verb meaning 'to win' or 'to earn'. When followed by a feminine singular noun (la + noun), ganar la means 'to win/earn the [feminine noun]'. The exact English verb depends on context (e.g., ganar la carrera = to win the race; ganar la confianza = to earn the trust). Not a fixed phrase on its own—it requires the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Ella quiere ganar la carrera este domingo.
native_language_example: She wants to win the race this Sunday.

meaning: to buy time; to gain extra time (delay or create more time to act).
additional_notes: Used when someone wants to delay, postpone a decision, or create more time to prepare or act. Can be literal (saving time) in contexts like faster travel, but often idiomatic meaning is 'buy time'—to stall or delay. Common with actions taken to 'ganar tiempo' (measures, excuses, tactics).
target_language_example: Dijo que necesitaba consultar para ganar tiempo.
native_language_example: He said he needed to check to buy time.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living (by working).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone gets money to support themselves. Often followed by a gerund or a noun describing the activity (e.g., 'ganarse la vida pescando', 'ganarse la vida como...'). Common everyday phrase; neutral register.
target_language_example: Se mudó a la ciudad para ganarse la vida enseñando inglés.
native_language_example: He moved to the city to earn a living by teaching English.

meaning: This appears to be the noun garganta (throat) followed by y (and). Used in sentences where garganta is part of different expressions; 'y' simply connects to the next phrase.
additional_notes: 'garganta' means 'throat' and is used both literally (physical throat, illness, clearing throat) and figuratively in violent expressions (threats, being held at someone's throat). The example strings show garganta used in different constructions — e.g. 'aclararse la garganta' (clear one's throat), 'doler la garganta' (throat hurts), 'poner un cuchillo en la garganta' (hold a knife to someone's throat), and violent colloquial threats that mention the throat. The 'y' after garganta is just the conjunction 'and' joining the next idea; it has no special idiomatic meaning when attached to garganta.
target_language_example: Me aclaré la garganta y comencé a hablar.
native_language_example: I cleared my throat and began to speak.

meaning: 'spends a lot' (used with money, time, or other resources).
additional_notes: From the verb gastar (to spend) + mucho (a lot). Commonly used with dinero (money) or tiempo (time). Subject determines what is being spent; include the thing spent after gastar (e.g., gastar mucho dinero / gastar mucho tiempo).
target_language_example: Ella gasta mucho tiempo aprendiendo idiomas.
native_language_example: She spends a lot of time learning languages.

meaning: 'cat in' (literal combination: gato = cat; en = in/at).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom—it's simply the noun 'gato' (cat) followed by the preposition 'en' (in/at). In Spanish word order, 'gato en' will usually be followed by a noun or phrase indicating location (e.g., 'gato en la caja' = 'cat in the box'). Remember to use the correct article and agreement after 'en' (el/la/una, etc.) depending on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: El gato en la ventana mira la calle.
native_language_example: The cat in the window is looking at the street.

meaning: Persian cat (a long-haired cat breed).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the Persian breed of domestic cat. Adjective follows the noun in Spanish (gato persa = Persian cat). Can be singular/plural (gatos persas). Common in everyday speech; not slang.
target_language_example: Mi vecina tiene un gato persa muy cariñoso.
native_language_example: My neighbor has a very affectionate Persian cat.

meaning: 'to give someone gato por liebre' = to trick someone; to substitute something inferior for what was promised (to pass off a bad thing as a good one).
additional_notes: This is part of the idiom 'dar (a alguien) gato por liebre' meaning to deceive or cheat someone by substituting an inferior item. The literal words ('cat for [a] hare') are vivid but used idiomatically. Outside the idiom, 'por' can mean 'by' or 'by the' in physical expressions (e.g., 'coger al gato por la cola' = 'grab the cat by the tail'). Pay attention to context: with 'gato por liebre' it's an idiom (deception); in physical contexts 'por' is literal.
target_language_example: No compres eso; podrían darte gato por liebre.
native_language_example: Don't buy that; they might trick you (sell you a bad substitute).

meaning: 'a cat that...' — used to introduce a relative clause describing the cat
additional_notes: Combine the noun gato (cat) with the relative pronoun que to add information about the cat: who/that/which + verb or description. In English this corresponds to 'a cat that...' or 'the cat that...'. The clause after que gives more detail (e.g., what the cat does or which cat you mean). Word order and verb agreement follow normal Spanish rules.
target_language_example: Vi un gato que dormía en la ventana.
native_language_example: I saw a cat that was sleeping on the windowsill.

meaning: literally 'cat and' — the word 'gato' (cat) followed by 'y' (and); used when listing or linking 'cat' with another noun or in the phrase 'gato y ratón' (cat and mouse).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's simply the noun gato plus the conjunction y. Common collocations include 'gato y ratón' (cat and mouse), which can refer to the animal pair or the figurative 'cat-and-mouse' game (a chase or tactical back-and-forth). Use 'gato y' whenever you want to say 'cat and ...'. Remember Spanish uses 'y' (and) unchanged, but pronunciation can change before words starting with 'i' sound (no spelling change).
target_language_example: Tenemos un gato y un perro en el patio.
native_language_example: We have a cat and a dog in the yard.

meaning: '(to) cats (they) — used in impersonal/cleft constructions to say that cats like or are affected by something.'
additional_notes: This chunk comes from the structure 'A + (definite/possessive) + [noun] + les + verb' used to express what someone/what things like or experience. 'A los gatos les gusta...' = 'Cats like...'. The double-marking (A los gatos + les) is common in Spanish to emphasize who is affected; the verb agrees with what is liked (gusta/gustan). Use 'les' for third-person plural (they).
target_language_example: A los gatos les encanta dormir en cajas.
native_language_example: Cats love sleeping in boxes.

meaning: literal: 'cats can' — used to state abilities or possible behaviors of cats.
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the noun 'gatos' (cats) and the verb 'pueden' (they can). Commonly introduces general facts, abilities, or claims about cats (e.g., what they are capable of). In Spanish sentences you may add verbs or clauses after 'pueden' (e.g., 'pueden ver', 'pueden ser').
target_language_example: Los gatos pueden trepar árboles con facilidad.
native_language_example: Cats can climb trees easily.

meaning: 'cats have' — the phrase 'los gatos tienen' means 'cats have' or 'cats possess'.
additional_notes: This is the third-person plural present form of tener (ellos/ellas tienen) used with 'los gatos' (cats). Use it to state traits, possessions, abilities, or idiomatic beliefs about cats (e.g., 'tienen cuatro patas', 'tienen siete vidas'). Word order: subject + tienen + object/complément. For negatives use 'no tienen' (they don't have).
target_language_example: Los gatos tienen buen oído y olfato agudo.
native_language_example: Cats have good hearing and a keen sense of smell.

meaning: kind/nice of (someone) to do something.
additional_notes: Used with a person expressed as 'de mi/tu/su parte' to say that an action or gesture was kind of them. Common construction: 'Es muy generoso de + [mi/tu/su/nombre] + parte' or shortened 'de tu parte'. Can be followed by a clause: 'Es muy generoso de usted ofrecer ayudar.'
target_language_example: Es muy generoso de tu parte ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: It's very kind of you to help me with the move.

meaning: 'genius of' (someone brilliant in a field) or 'genie of' (spirit associated with something), depending on context.
additional_notes: Two common meanings: 1) 'genio' = a very talented person; 'genio de + [campo]' = 'a genius in/at [field]' (e.g., genio de las matemáticas). 2) 'genio' = 'genie' (magical being) often appears in phrases like 'el genio de la lámpara' (the genie of the lamp). Use context to know which meaning is intended. Word order: 'genio de + noun'.
target_language_example: Ella es un genio de la música.
native_language_example: She is a genius in music.

meaning: 'people believe' or 'people think'.
additional_notes: A simple subject-verb phrase: gente (people) + cree (believe/think). Used to express what many people generally believe or think. Often followed by 'que' + clause. 'Gente' is a singular collective noun but commonly used with third-person singular verb forms (la gente cree).
target_language_example: Mucha gente cree que las vitaminas lo curan todo.
native_language_example: Many people believe that vitamins cure everything.

meaning: the people from here / the local people
additional_notes: Refers to people who live in or are from the place being talked about (locals). Can be used neutrally, descriptively, or with a positive or negative opinion depending on context (e.g., friendly, suspicious, dislike). 'Aquí' means 'here' (this place).
target_language_example: La gente de aquí siempre saluda por la mañana.
native_language_example: The people from here always greet in the morning.

meaning: 'people should' or 'people must' (general recommendation or obligation)
additional_notes: A combination of 'gente' (people) + the modal verb 'deber' in third-person singular ('debe'). Used to express what people in general ought to do. Tone can be softer ('should') or stronger ('must') depending on context and speaker. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., 'debe aprender').
target_language_example: La gente debe cuidar el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: People should take care of the environment.

meaning: 'people say' or 'people say that...'
additional_notes: Used to report general opinions or rumors. Often followed by que + clause (gente dice que...) or a direct phrase (gente dice + noun/phrase). It refers to people in general (not specific individuals).
target_language_example: La gente dice que la película es muy buena.
native_language_example: People say that the movie is very good.

meaning: people in / people at (indicates there are many or some people present in a place).
additional_notes: Gente = people (singular collective noun). Combined with a preposition like en (in/at), it describes how many people are present at a location. Commonly used with adjectives like mucha/mucha(s) (a lot of) or demasiada(s) (too many). Agreement: gente is treated as singular, so use verbs in third person singular (había mucha gente). To specify number, use expressions (poca gente, mucha gente, demasiada gente).
target_language_example: Hay mucha gente en la plaza hoy.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people in the square today.

meaning: people in the (place).
additional_notes: Use 'gente' to refer to a group of people (uncountable; no plural). Follow with 'en' + definite article + place (e.g., 'en la fiesta', 'en la playa'). If the place is masculine use 'en el' (e.g., 'gente en el parque'). To say 'there are people' use 'hay gente en...' or past 'había gente en...'.
target_language_example: Hay gente en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: There are people in the library.

meaning: people were (doing something) — past continuous describing what people were doing or feeling.
additional_notes: Combines 'gente' (people) with the imperfect progressive 'estaba' + gerund or complement. Common to describe ongoing past actions or states of a group. In Spanish, 'gente' is singular grammatically but takes verbs like 'había' or 'estaba' in third person singular when followed by an adjective or verb phrase (often with a gerund: 'estaba llorando', 'estaba esperando'). You can also say 'mucha gente estaba...' to emphasize quantity.
target_language_example: Mucha gente estaba celebrando en la plaza.
native_language_example: Many people were celebrating in the square.

meaning: 'people were' — the noun 'gente' (people) plus the past imperfect of 'estar' (to be).
additional_notes: Used to describe the state, condition, or location of a group of people in the past. 'Gente' is singular in Spanish grammatically but refers to a plural concept; however verbs commonly agree with the implied plural idea in natural speech (more common is 'la gente estaba...'). Use with adjectives (hambrienta, contenta) or prepositional phrases (a la merced de, allí).
target_language_example: La gente estaba preocupada por la lluvia.
native_language_example: The people were worried about the rain.

meaning: people are (doing something).
additional_notes: Combines 'la gente' (people) with the present progressive 'está + gerund' to describe actions happening now or general ongoing states. Often used with a verb in gerund (e.g., 'está intentando', 'está esperando'). In spoken Spanish you may also hear just 'gente' + verb without the article: 'gente está' is grammatically fine when context supplies 'la'.
target_language_example: Mucha gente está aprendiendo español en línea.
native_language_example: Many people are learning Spanish online.

meaning: "people (talk/speak)" — literally 'people speak' or 'people talk'.
additional_notes: This combines the noun 'gente' (people) with the verb 'habla' (he/she/it speaks or you formal speak). In natural Spanish you'd usually say 'la gente habla' (people talk) or 'la gente habla de...' (people talk about...). 'Gente' is singular grammatically (so verbs use third person singular: 'habla'). Use with context to indicate what people say or that people generally do something.
target_language_example: La gente habla mucho sobre la nueva película.
native_language_example: People talk a lot about the new movie.

meaning: older people; elderly people.
additional_notes: Refers to older adults or the elderly in a general, respectful way. Common in everyday speech to talk about seniors as a group. Can be used with verbs like tener, ser, cuidar, temer, and expressions like "la gente mayor suele..."
target_language_example: Debemos escuchar a la gente mayor y aprender de sus experiencias.
native_language_example: We should listen to older people and learn from their experiences.

meaning: 'people died' or 'many people died' (plural idea: people + died).
additional_notes: Literal combination of 'gente' (people) and the past tense 'murió' (he/she/it died). In Spanish, 'gente' is grammatically singular but refers to a group; when you want to emphasize many people, speakers often add quantifiers (mucha gente, un montón de gente). Use 'murió' (singular) after 'gente' even though the meaning is plural. To explicitly use a plural verb you can rephrase (la gente murió / muchas personas murieron).
target_language_example: Mucha gente murió en el terremoto.
native_language_example: Many people died in the earthquake.

meaning: people need / people require
additional_notes: A simple phrase combining 'gente' (people) and the verb 'necesitar' (to need). Commonly used to make general statements about what people as a group require or want. In Spanish, 'gente' is singular in form but refers to a plural idea; verbs are usually used in singular or plural depending on emphasis — here examples use singular verb form 'necesita' (la gente necesita) or plural 'necesitan' can be heard in some regions. For beginners, translate as 'people need' and use with a noun or infinitive (e.g., 'gente necesita agua' or 'gente necesita descansar').
target_language_example: Mucha gente necesita tiempo para descansar.
native_language_example: Many people need time to rest.

meaning: 'people think that' or 'people believe that'.
additional_notes: Used to report a common belief or opinion held by many people. Often appears with quantifiers like 'mucha gente', 'la mayoría de la gente', or without when context implies 'people' in general. Followed by a clause that states the belief (subordinate clause introduced by 'que').
target_language_example: Mucha gente piensa que aprender un idioma es difícil, pero con práctica mejora rápido.
native_language_example: Many people think that learning a language is difficult, but with practice it improves quickly.

meaning: 'people used to' (they did something habitually in the past).
additional_notes: Combines 'gente' (people) with the imperfect + 'soler' construction. In Spanish you often see 'la gente solía + infinitive' to describe past habitual actions or behaviors that no longer happen. Equivalent to 'people would' or 'people used to' in English. Use the imperfect 'solía' for repeated past actions; you can also say 'la gente solía + infinitive' or simply 'la gente + imperfect' (e.g., 'la gente hablaba').
target_language_example: Antes, la gente solía comprar en tiendas pequeñas del barrio.
native_language_example: Before, people used to buy in small neighborhood shops.

meaning: people are going to (do something); indicates a future action by people
additional_notes: Combines 'la gente' (people/the people) with the periphrastic future 'va a' (is going to). Use 'la gente va a + infinitive' to say what people will do, think, or say. In spoken Spanish 'la' is often included: 'La gente va a...'.
target_language_example: La gente va a protestar mañana.
native_language_example: People are going to protest tomorrow.

meaning: people go to / people go (to).
additional_notes: Common phrase combining gente (people) with the verb phrase 'va a' (goes to). Used to talk about where people typically go or what they do (e.g., 'la gente va a la playa', 'la gente va a la iglesia', 'la gente va a la cama'). Subject is impersonal—'gente' is singular in form but refers to a group. 'Va a' must be followed by a place or an infinitive/action (e.g., 'va a la playa', 'va a buscar').
target_language_example: Por la tarde, la gente va a pasear al parque.
native_language_example: In the afternoon, people go for a walk in the park.

meaning: 'people live' (the combination of gente + vive; 'gente' = people, 'vive' = (he/she/it) lives or 'you live' formal) — used to say where people live or how they live.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun 'gente' (people) followed by the verb 'vive' (from vivir). In most contexts 'vive' refers to 'people live' in general (impersonal idea) or to 'he/she/it lives' when talking about a specific group understood as singular. Spanish often treats 'gente' as singular grammatically (la gente vive...). Use 'mucha/poca gente' to say many/few people. To be more explicit you can say 'la gente vive en...' (people live in...).
target_language_example: Mucha gente vive cerca del río.
native_language_example: Many people live near the river.

meaning: a hit/blow on (a part of the body) or a knock at (a place).
additional_notes: Used to describe receiving or giving a physical hit to a specific body part (golpe en + body part). Can also mean a knock or bang on an object or place (e.g., puerta). Context determines whether it's physical violence or a sound/impact. Common verbs: dar (dar un golpe en = to hit), recibir/sentir/oir (to receive/feel/hear a hit).
target_language_example: Le dio un golpe en la pierna durante el partido.
native_language_example: He gave him a hit on the leg during the game.

meaning: hit/knocked the table with his/her/its
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a sentence describing someone striking a table using a body part or object (commonly 'puño' = fist). 'Golpeó' is past (preterite) of 'golpear' — 'he/she/it hit'. 'Con su' agrees in gender/number with the possessor (su = his, her, its, your formal, their). Commonly followed by a noun: 'puño', 'mano', 'codo', etc.
target_language_example: Ella golpeó la mesa con su puño.
native_language_example: She hit the table with her fist.

meaning: by the grace of; thanks to (usually followed by a noun or clause indicating cause or source).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened because of someone's kindness, favor, or divine help. Often appears in expressions like "por gracia de" or "gracia de Dios". In everyday Spanish, "gracias a" is more common for 'thanks to' when indicating cause; "gracia de" is more formal or literary and frequently used in religious or formal contexts.
target_language_example: Todo salió bien, gracia de Dios y al trabajo del equipo.
native_language_example: Everything went well, by the grace of God and the team's work.

meaning: thank you for what / thank you for (what) you did or said.
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific action, thing they said, or help—often followed by a clause (dijiste, hiciste) or more detail. It's a natural way to express gratitude for something already mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Gracias por lo que me ayudaste ayer.
native_language_example: Thank you for what you helped me with yesterday.

meaning: Thank you for your help.
additional_notes: A polite, formal way to thank someone for assistance. Use 'su' for formal or when speaking to one person respectfully or to a group; use 'tu' (gracias por tu ayuda) for informal/familiar situations. Can be shortened to 'gracias' or strengthened with 'muchas' (Muchas gracias por su ayuda).
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por su ayuda con el informe.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help with the report.

meaning: 'thank you for your help.'
additional_notes: A polite way to thank someone for assistance. You can vary intensity: gracias / muchas gracias / muchísimas gracias. Use 'por su ayuda' for formal situations or when addressing usted; 'por tu ayuda' is informal (tú). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda con el proyecto.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help with the project.

meaning: thanks to
additional_notes: Used to indicate cause or credit — can be positive or neutral. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or phrase (e.g., 'gracias a ti', 'gracias a la lluvia', 'gracias a que + clause' in some varieties). Tone is usually neutral; when emphasizing blame, English 'because of' works better.
target_language_example: Hemos ganado gracias a ti.
native_language_example: We won thanks to you.

meaning: thank God; fortunately.
additional_notes: Used to express relief, gratitude, or that something positive/fortunate happened. Common in everyday speech; can be followed by a clause (e.g., 'gracias a Dios que...') or stand alone. Tone ranges from casual to sincere depending on context.
target_language_example: Gracias a Dios que viniste a ayudarme.
native_language_example: Thank God you came to help me.

meaning: thank God; fortunately.
additional_notes: Used to express relief, gratitude, or that something good/fortunate happened. Can stand alone (Gracias a Dios.) or introduce a clause (Gracias a Dios que... ). Tone ranges from casual to formal and can be religious or simply idiomatic.
target_language_example: Gracias a Dios que llegaste a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thank God you arrived on time.

meaning: degrees below (zero); used to say temperatures under zero (Celsius).
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'cero' as 'grados bajo cero' (below zero) or with a number: 'diez grados bajo cero' = −10°C. In everyday speech you can also hear 'grados bajo' followed by 'cero' omitted if context is clear. Works with numbers and verbs like 'hacer', 'estar' or 'descender'.
target_language_example: Esta noche hará ocho grados bajo cero.
native_language_example: Tonight it will be eight degrees below zero.

meaning: graduated from (a school, university, program).
additional_notes: Used to say someone completed studies at an institution. Commonly appears with the institution: se graduó de + [escuela/universidad/programa]. In many Spanish varieties you may also hear 'se graduó en' or 'se licenció en' depending on country and level of study. The subject form changes with person/number (me gradué, te graduaste, se graduó, nos graduamos, se graduaron).
target_language_example: Ella se graduó de la universidad el año pasado.
native_language_example: She graduated from university last year.

meaning: department store; a large retail store with many types of goods.
additional_notes: Used for big multi-department retail stores (like Macy's or El Corte Inglés). 'Gran' is an apocopated form of 'grande' used before a noun (grande → gran). Can refer to an individual large store or the concept/category of department stores. Plural: 'grandes almacenes'.
target_language_example: Compré un abrigo nuevo en el gran almacén del centro.
native_language_example: I bought a new coat at the downtown department store.

meaning: 'a big deal' or 'something important/significant' (can be positive or sarcastic).
additional_notes: Used to say something is important or noteworthy (Es una gran cosa = It's a big deal). Often used sarcastically or minimising with negation (No es gran cosa = It's no big deal). In plural or with people it can mean someone thinks highly of themselves (creerse la gran cosa = to think you're hot stuff / to be full of yourself).
target_language_example: No es gran cosa, puedo ayudar.
native_language_example: It's no big deal, I can help.

meaning: 'a large number of' or 'many'.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to indicate a large quantity of people or things. Formal/neutral register; common in written and spoken Spanish. Can be followed by 'de' + noun (gran número de personas). Verb agreement: often treated as plural (e.g., 'un gran número de estudiantes luchó' can also be 'lucharon'), but plural agreement is more common in everyday usage.
target_language_example: Un gran número de vecinos asistió a la reunión.
native_language_example: A large number of neighbors attended the meeting.

meaning: a big step; an important advance or major progress
additional_notes: Used figuratively to describe significant progress, achievement, or an important stage in a process. Common in sentences like 'Es un gran paso (para mí/nosotros)' meaning 'This is a big step (for me/us)'. Not typically literal (walking) unless context specifies.
target_language_example: Con este acuerdo hemos dado un gran paso hacia la paz.
native_language_example: With this agreement we have taken a big step toward peace.

meaning: “a great pleasure to be (here/with you)”; used to say you're happy/honored to be somewhere or with someone.
additional_notes: Common polite phrase for greetings or introductions. Often followed by a location (aquí) or a pronoun (contigo, con usted, con vosotros/as). Use 'con usted' for formal singular, 'contigo' for informal singular, and 'con vosotros/as' or 'con vosotras' for informal plural in Spain. Can be shortened to 'es un placer estar...' or simply 'es un placer' in many situations.
target_language_example: Es un gran placer estar con ustedes en este evento.
native_language_example: It's a great pleasure to be with you all at this event.

meaning: 'great life' or 'big/beautiful life' (a very good, fulfilling life).
additional_notes: Used to describe a very good, fulfilling, or ideal life. Can be literal (a long, large life) but usually means 'a wonderful life' or 'a great life' in a general, positive sense. Common in wishes (Espero que tengas una gran vida) and descriptions. 'Gran' is placed before a feminine noun when shortened from 'grande'.
target_language_example: Te deseo una gran vida llena de salud y alegría.
native_language_example: I wish you a great life full of health and joy.

meaning: phrase used in comparisons meaning 'the ... of the' when indicating size/degree within a specific group (e.g. 'the biggest of the')
additional_notes: Commonly appears with definite article and plural noun (los/las) to refer to a specific group: 'el más grande de los X' = 'the biggest of the X'. Can be used in comparisons among many or between two ('el más grande de los dos'). Word order often: 'el/la/los/las + más/menos + adjective (grande) + de + (article) + noun/phrase.' Here 'grande de los' is the core sequence when the adjective is 'grande' and the following article is 'los'.
target_language_example: Es el más grande de los artistas vivos.
native_language_example: He is the biggest of the living artists.

meaning: 'big/large in' or 'largest in' when comparing size within a place or context.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that is large relative to a location, category, or medium. Often appears as 'más grande en' for comparisons ('bigger in' or 'biggest in'). In many cases English uses 'in' the same way: e.g. 'largest in the city' = 'más grande en la ciudad'. Can also appear without 'en' when followed by a direct noun ('lago más grande de Suiza' is also common).
