Use plural 'haya' + 'unos' or 'haya' + plural noun when needed (e.g., "que haya unos..."), and for feminine nouns use 'una' ("que haya una...").
target_language_example: Espero que haya un médico disponible esta noche.
native_language_example: I hope there is a doctor available tonight.

meaning: there is a
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression, but a common fragment. Here, haya is the subjunctive form of hay, used before a singular noun. It often appears after words or phrases that express doubt, possibility, desire, or uncertainty, such as puede que, quizá, esperan que, antes de que, and sometimes cuando when talking about a future or uncertain event.
target_language_example: Puede que haya una farmacia cerca.
native_language_example: There may be a pharmacy nearby.

meaning: have finished
additional_notes: Present perfect subjunctive form used in subordinate time clauses (often after cuando, hasta que, después de que) to refer to an action that will be completed before another future action. Typically follows 'cuando' or similar connectors: 'cuando hayas terminado' = 'when you have finished'. The subject is usually 'tú'.
target_language_example: Avísame cuando hayas terminado la tarea.
native_language_example: Tell me when you have finished the homework.

meaning: do exactly the (thing) — an informal command fragment used to tell someone to do something precisely
additional_notes: This is the imperative form (tú) of hacer + adverb exactamente + direct object pronoun lo. It is usually followed by a verb, clause, or implied action: e.g., "Haz exactamente lo que te dije." Alone it feels like a fragment: "do exactly the…" Use with context or complete it: "haz exactamente lo que..."
target_language_example: Haz exactamente lo que te dije y todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: Do exactly what I told you and everything will be fine.

meaning: 'do whatever you want' — an imperative giving someone freedom to choose (can be neutral, resigned, or dismissive depending on tone).
additional_notes: Commonly used to tell someone they can decide for themselves. Tone matters: can be helpful/encouraging, indifferent, or annoyed. 'Haz' is the informal (tú) imperative of hacer; for formal or plural use 'haga lo que quiera' (usted) or 'haced/ hagan' depending on region. The phrase is literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Haz lo que quieras, pero avísame si cambias de idea.
native_language_example: Do whatever you want, but let me know if you change your mind.

meaning: 'do what you have to (do)'.
additional_notes: A colloquial imperative phrase telling someone to take whatever necessary action. Often completed as 'haz lo que tengas que hacer' but can be shortened as here. Tone can be neutral or slightly commanding; used to give permission or urge decisiveness. Common with informal tú commands.
target_language_example: Haz lo que tengas que hacer y luego descansa.
native_language_example: Do what you have to do and then rest.

meaning: 'do what you have to' or 'do what you must'.
additional_notes: A common imperative phrase telling someone to carry out necessary or expected actions. Often completed as "haz lo que tienes que hacer" (do what you have to do). Can be used to encourage, order, or reassure someone to focus on the task. Informal tone (tú form).
target_language_example: Haz lo que tienes que hacer y luego descansa.
native_language_example: Do what you have to do and then rest.

meaning: 'I have gotten used to' or 'I have become accustomed to'.
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (he + acostumbrado) to say you have become used to something in the recent past or over time. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., trabajar) or a noun/phrase introduced by 'a' (e.g., a su forma de hablar). Spanish more commonly uses 'me he acostumbrado a...' (with the reflexive pronoun) — the provided phrase omits the reflexive pronoun in the term itself but in actual use include 'me' (Me he acostumbrado a...).
target_language_example: Me he acostumbrado a levantarme temprano para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: I have gotten used to getting up early to go to work.

meaning: I've messed up / I've screwed up (I made a big mistake).
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar. Used to admit a serious mistake or error; often followed by apologies. 'La he cagado' literally references a feminine object/situation ('la') but is idiomatic — you can also say 'lo he cagado' depending on what was messed up. Use only in casual contexts and avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Lo siento, la he cagado con las entradas.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I messed up with the tickets.

meaning: have told (to) — the present perfect of 'decir' used with an indirect object ('to someone').
additional_notes: Used to say that you have told (or not told) something to someone. Spanish often uses an indirect-object pronoun (le, les, se) plus 'he dicho' and may repeat the indirect object as a noun or phrase introduced by 'a' (e.g., 'le he dicho a mi madre'). Common in negative sentences: 'No le he dicho a nadie' = 'I haven't told anyone.'
target_language_example: No le he dicho a nadie sobre el plan.
native_language_example: I haven't told anyone about the plan.

meaning: I've said everything (that)...
additional_notes: This is the start of a clause meaning 'I have said everything that...' and is followed by a subordinate clause (e.g., 'que tenía que decir' or 'que sé'). Commonly used to indicate there is nothing more to add. Verb is present perfect (he dicho).
target_language_example: Ya he dicho todo lo que tenía que decir.
native_language_example: I've already said everything I had to say.

meaning: I have fallen in love (with).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'me he enamorado de [alguien/alguna cosa]'. Use the reflexive pronoun 'me' (me he enamorado) to mean 'I have fallen in love'. Followed by 'de' + person or thing. In everyday speech native speakers often omit 'me' in some fragments, but the correct full form is 'me he enamorado de...'. Past participle 'enamorado' is used with 'haber' to form the present perfect.
target_language_example: Me he enamorado de mi mejor amiga.
native_language_example: I have fallen in love with my best friend.

meaning: I have waited a long time (for something).
additional_notes: Present perfect (he + past participle) expressing that the speaker has been waiting up to now or for a long time; often followed by 'para' or 'por' + noun/infinitive to indicate what was waited for (e.g., 'para conocerte', 'por esto'). Can stand alone to mean 'I've waited a long time.'
target_language_example: He esperado mucho para verte de nuevo.
native_language_example: I have waited a long time to see you again.

meaning: I have been looking (for) everywhere
additional_notes: This is the present perfect progressive (he estado buscando) + 'por todas (partes)' meaning 'everywhere'. In natural Spanish you'd usually say "por todas partes" or simply "por todas" in casual speech. The direct object pronoun (la, le, lo, los, te) comes before the verb: e.g. "Te he estado buscando por todas partes." Use to emphasize continuous searching up to now.
target_language_example: Te he estado buscando por todas partes.
native_language_example: I have been looking for you everywhere.

meaning: I haven't heard anything / I haven't known anything (about someone or something).
additional_notes: This phrase uses the present perfect (he sabido) with a negative nada to say you haven't received news or information. Commonly followed by de + person/thing (e.g., de ella). In natural speech Spanish more often uses No he sabido nada de... or No he sabido nada sobre... to mean 'I haven't heard from...' or 'I haven't heard anything about...'.
target_language_example: No he sabido nada de mi hermano desde el viaje.
native_language_example: I haven't heard anything from my brother since the trip.

meaning: I've (never) seen (it/him/her) in my (life/experience).
additional_notes: Used with verbs in perfect tense (he visto = I have seen) plus 'en mi vida' to express that you have (or have never) seen something in your life — often equivalent to English 'I've never seen...' or 'I have not seen...'. Commonly appears with 'nunca' or 'no' to negate: 'No la he visto en mi vida' = 'I've never seen her in my life.' Can be followed by direct object pronouns (la, lo, te).
target_language_example: No lo he visto en mi vida.
native_language_example: I have never seen it in my life.

meaning: 'here is' or 'here are' (used to present or show something).
additional_notes: Formal or literary way to introduce or point out something (similar to 'aquí está' / 'aquí están'). Often used in writing, speeches, or to draw attention to an example or explanation: 'He aquí...' = 'Here is/are...'.
target_language_example: He aquí la razón por la que llegaste tarde.
native_language_example: Here is the reason why you were late.

meaning: made of
additional_notes: Used to say what material something is made from. Agreement: 'hechas' is feminine plural past participle of 'hacer' and must match the gender/number of the noun it modifies (e.g., hechas de, hecho de, hechos de, hecha de). Can often be translated as 'made of' when material is visible (madera, vidrio) and 'made from' when material is transformed (paper from wood).
target_language_example: Las ventanas están hechas de vidrio.
native_language_example: The windows are made of glass.

meaning: made by hand; handmade.
additional_notes: Used to describe objects crafted manually rather than by machine (e.g., ropa, joyas, muebles, alimentos artesanales). Common label on products to emphasize craftsmanship. Can be used attributively (un bolso hecho a mano) or predicatively (este collar está hecho a mano).
target_language_example: Este suéter fue hecho a mano por mi abuela.
native_language_example: This sweater was made by my grandmother.

meaning: done (at a) ... ago / done ... ago (with a time expression).
additional_notes: Combines the past participle hecho (done) with hace to indicate that an action was completed a certain time ago. Common constructions: (deberías/habrías) haberlo hecho hace + time (e.g., hace mucho tiempo, hace días, hace un momento). Word order can vary: Lo hice hace... / Lo he hecho hace... / Deberías haberlo hecho hace....
target_language_example: Deberías haberlo hecho hace una semana.
native_language_example: You should have done it a week ago.

meaning: done what
additional_notes: A compositional pattern: hecho is the past participle of hacer ('done/made') and lo que means 'what' or 'that which'. In sentences like has hecho lo que..., he hecho lo que..., or hubiera hecho lo que..., it means 'have/has/had done what...'. It introduces the thing that someone did.
target_language_example: No he hecho lo que me pediste.
native_language_example: I haven't done what you asked me to do.

meaning: done very well; well done (referring to an action/result).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone's action or result. Appears after verbs like 'has hecho' or 'han hecho' (present perfect). Can be used alone as short praise (e.g., '¡Lo has hecho muy bien!').
target_language_example: Has hecho muy bien en el examen.
native_language_example: You did very well on the exam.

meaning: 'ever' used with a past participle to mean 'ever (done something)' or 'never' when negated (e.g. 'have/has never done')
additional_notes: Appears after a past participle (hecho = done). In questions or positive statements with 'mejor' it means 'ever' (the best ... I have ever done). With negation (no ... nunca / nunca ...) it means 'never'. Word order can vary: 'he hecho nunca' is less common than 'he hecho jamás' in some regions; more natural forms are 'he hecho nunca' in comparative sentences ('lo mejor que he hecho nunca') or 'no lo he hecho nunca' for 'I have never done it.'
target_language_example: Es la película mejor que he hecho nunca.
native_language_example: It's the best movie I've ever made.

meaning: done for me / done by me (depending on context); here usually 'done for me'.
additional_notes: Literal components: hecho (done), por (for/by), mí (me). In most of the example sentences it means 'done for me' — something someone else did benefiting the speaker. Context determines agent: with passive/agent omitted it often means 'done for me' (by someone). If you want 'done by me' (I did it), use 'hecho por mí' with emphasis or clearer phrasing (e.g., 'lo hice yo' is more natural).
target_language_example: Gracias por todo lo que has hecho por mí.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything you have done for me.

meaning: literally 'made/ done a' — part of verb phrases meaning 'I/you/they have made/done a (something)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the combination of a past participle (hecho = made/done) plus the indefinite article 'una' and a feminine noun. It appears in perfect tenses (he hecho, has hecho, nos hubieran hecho, te he hecho) followed by an object: una elección, una promesa, una reserva, una pregunta, una señal. Choose the noun after 'una' to complete the idea.
target_language_example: Te he hecho una propuesta honesta.
native_language_example: I have made you an honest proposal.

meaning: the fact is that / the truth is that
additional_notes: Used to introduce a factual statement or to emphasize the real situation. Often follows 'El' as in 'El hecho es que...' and is followed by a clause explaining the fact. Common in spoken and written Spanish to correct, clarify, or state a blunt truth.
target_language_example: El hecho es que no tenemos suficiente dinero.
native_language_example: The fact is that we don't have enough money.

target_language_multi_word_term: hechos el uno para el otro
meaning: made for each other; meant to be together (about two people).
additional_notes: Used to say two people are a perfect match or well-suited romantically. Literal components: hechos (made), el uno para el otro (one for the other). Commonly used with plural conjugations (están, estamos, estaban). Can refer to couples in general; tone is neutral to affectionate.
target_language_example: Creo que estamos hechos el uno para el otro.
native_language_example: I think we are made for each other.

meaning: 'the facts are' or 'facts are (that...)'.
additional_notes: A simple phrase used to state or emphasize what the facts are. Often appears in sentences like 'Los hechos son...' followed by a description or conclusion. It is literal and neutral/formal; frequently used to insist that reality or evidence matters (e.g., 'Los hechos son los hechos' = 'Facts are facts').
target_language_example: Los hechos son claros: no estuvo en la escena.
native_language_example: The facts are clear: he wasn't at the scene.

meaning: a wound caused by (something); 'wound from' or 'wound by'.
additional_notes: Used to specify the cause or instrument of a wound. Followed by a noun indicating the cause (e.g., guerra, bala, flecha, espada). Common in medical, forensic, and descriptive contexts. Word order in Spanish: "herida de + [cause]" (not "de + herida").
target_language_example: Tiene una herida de bala en la pierna.
native_language_example: He has a bullet wound in his leg.

meaning: "wound/injury" followed by a negation — literally 'wound not' but used as part of phrases like 'the wound does not...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun 'herida' (wound, injury, sore) appearing next to the negation 'no'. Useful patterns: 'la herida no + verb' (the wound does not ...), 'si no veo la herida...' (if I don't see the wound...). 'Herida' can refer to physical wounds or emotional hurts depending on context.
target_language_example: La herida no se está infectando, pero debemos limpiarla.
native_language_example: The wound is not getting infected, but we should clean it.

meaning: wounded/injured in (something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone suffered an injury as a result of an event or while in a place. Commonly appears with verbs like 'estar', 'resultar', 'quedar' or in participial constructions (e.g., 'estaba herido en el suelo', 'resultó herido en el accidente'). Can describe degrees of severity (e.g., 'gravemente herido').
target_language_example: El soldado yacía herido en el suelo.
native_language_example: The soldier lay wounded on the ground.

meaning: 's sister of mine / the sister of my ...' (used to indicate someone is the sister of a person related to the speaker)
additional_notes: This structure combines hermana (sister) + de + a possessor phrase (mi, mi madre, mi padre, mi primo). In context, 'la hermana de mi madre' = my mother's sister (i.e., my aunt). When used as 'saluda a tu hermana de mi parte' or 'dile hola a tu hermana de mi parte', 'de mi parte' means 'from me' (give my regards) — note that 'de mi' alone is incomplete; typically it's 'de mi parte' or followed by the person who owns the sister (e.g., 'de mi madre').
target_language_example: La hermana de mi hermana vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: My sister's sister lives in Madrid.

meaning: 'my/your/etc. sister in the' (fragment used before a place or location).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a fragment: hermana (sister) + en el (in the). It appears before a masculine noun indicating a place (e.g., parque, cajón). For complete sentences you need the place: 'mi hermana en el parque' = 'my sister in the park'. Pay attention to possessives (mi, tu, su) and gender/number agreement of the noun that follows 'el'.
target_language_example: Encontré a mi hermana en el parque ayer.
native_language_example: I found my sister in the park yesterday.

meaning: my/someone's sister is a… / (someone's) sister is a…
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the structure noun (hermana) + verb (es) + indefinite article (una) used to describe or classify a sister (e.g., age, appearance, role). Depending on context, the subject can be first person (mi hermana es una...), third person (su hermana es una...), etc. Replace the noun/adjective after 'una' to say what kind of sister she is.
target_language_example: Su hermana es una médica muy competente.
native_language_example: Her sister is a very competent doctor.

meaning: my sister got married
additional_notes: Literal structure: hermana = sister; se casó = (reflexive) past of casarse, 'to get married'. Used to say someone married (usually indicates ceremony and change of marital status). To include spouse: 'se casó con ___'. Time can be added: 'hace unos años' = a few years ago.
target_language_example: Mi hermana se casó con su novio el verano pasado.
native_language_example: My sister got married to her boyfriend last summer.

meaning: 'my sister works' (literal: 'sister works')
additional_notes: Common structure: <subject> + trabaja (present tense of trabajar = 'to work'). In the examples the subject is 'mi hermana' ('my sister'), but the pattern applies to any noun/pronoun (e.g., 'mi hermano trabaja', 'ella trabaja'). Often followed by a workplace or job introduced with 'en' (in/at) or 'como' (as). 'Trabaja' is used for él/ella/usted.
target_language_example: Mi hermana trabaja en una escuela como profesora.
native_language_example: My sister works at a school as a teacher.

meaning: 'my/your/his/her/their brother is' + (doing something) — present progressive/state
additional_notes: Combines hermano (brother) with the verb estar. Used to describe what a brother is doing right now (present progressive: "está + gerund", e.g., está regresando, está trabajando, está viendo) or to state his current condition/location (está llegando). Word order can change (Mi hermano está... / Su hermano está...) depending on the possessor. For simple present actions without gerund, Spanish often repeats articles or shortens words (ver la tele / ver tele).
target_language_example: Mi hermano está estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: My brother is studying for the exam.

meaning: literally 'brother lives' — used as part of a sentence to say 'my/your/his/her brother lives (somewhere)' or 'a brother is alive'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; it's the verb phrase 'hermano' (brother) + 'vive' (he/she/it lives). You will usually see it with a possessive or subject context, e.g. 'Mi hermano vive en Madrid' (My brother lives in Madrid) or as a statement that a brother is alive: 'Mi hermano vive.' Remember verb agreement: 'vive' matches él/ella/usted. For 'my brothers live' use 'mis hermanos viven'.
target_language_example: Mi hermano vive en Barcelona.
native_language_example: My brother lives in Barcelona.

meaning: used to link 'brother' with another noun (e.g., 'brother and sister').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's simply the noun hermano ('brother') followed by 'y' ('and'). In examples it's part of a coordination: 'hermano y hermana' = 'brother and sister'. Pay attention to pluralization and gender: e.g. 'él tiene un hermano y dos hermanas' = 'he has one brother and two sisters.'
target_language_example: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
native_language_example: I have a brother and a sister.

meaning: 'beautiful and' — the adjective hermosa (feminine) followed by the conjunction y (and).
additional_notes: Used when describing a feminine noun or person and adding another quality or item. 'Hermosa' agrees in gender with the noun (feminine). If the subject is masculine use 'hermoso y' (though native speakers often reorder adjectives or omit repetition). Can appear in lists (e.g., 'joven, hermosa y...') or in short phrases ('Hermosa y obstinada').
target_language_example: Ella es hermosa y amable.
native_language_example: She is beautiful and kind.

meaning: 'beautiful' (used before a clause introduced by que) — often part of superlative or comparative expressions (e.g., "the most beautiful that...").
additional_notes: Hermoso is an adjective meaning 'beautiful.' When followed by que and a clause, it links the adjective to what is being described (often in constructions like "lo más hermoso que..." or "el regalo más hermoso que..."). Native speakers commonly use "lo más hermoso que..." for "the most beautiful thing that..." Use gender and number agreement (hermoso/hermosa/hermosos/hermosas) with the noun.
target_language_example: Es lo más hermoso que he recibido en la vida.
native_language_example: It's the most beautiful thing I've received in my life.

meaning: 'I hurt (my) ...' or 'I injured (my) ...' (used with a body part).
additional_notes: Common way to say you injured a specific body part. Often used in the first person: me hice daño en + [la/el + body part]. The verb phrase is reflexive (hacer(se) daño). Use definite article with body parts (me hice daño en el pie). Can refer to minor or more serious injuries depending on context.
target_language_example: Me hice daño en la mano mientras cortaba verduras.
native_language_example: I hurt my hand while cutting vegetables.

meaning: I did what I had to (do).
additional_notes: Used to say you acted out of necessity, duty, or self-preservation. Often completed as 'hice lo que tenía que hacer.' Tone can be neutral or defensive depending on context (e.g., justifying an action).
target_language_example: Hice lo que tenía que para proteger a mi familia.
native_language_example: I did what I had to do to protect my family.

meaning: 'I did (it) because...'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or motive for an action in the past. 'Hice' is the first-person preterite of 'hacer' (to do/make). Often followed by a clause starting with 'porque' (because). Can be shortened to 'Lo hice porque...' when referring to a specific action.
target_language_example: Hice porque quería ayudar, no por reconocimiento.
native_language_example: I did (it) because I wanted to help, not for recognition.

meaning: 'I did it' (with emphasis on 'I')
additional_notes: Combine the preterite verb hice (I did) with the pronoun yo to stress that the speaker — not someone else — performed the action. Common in spoken Spanish for emphasis or contrast (e.g., after someone else claimed credit). You can use other persons similarly (lo hiciste tú, lo hizo él). Often the object (lo/los/la/las) appears before the verb: Lo hice yo.
target_language_example: No fue ella; lo hice yo.
native_language_example: It wasn't her; I did it.

meaning: 'did with' / 'made with' / 'got hold of' (depends on context)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past tense verb 'hicieron' (they did/made) with 'con' (with). Meaning changes by context: 1) 'hicieron con él' can mean 'what did they do with him' (what happened to him) or 'what did they do to him' when used with people/objects taken by others; 2) with instruments/materials it means 'were made with' or 'done using' (e.g., made using funds); 3) in passive/reflective constructions like 'se hicieron con' it means 'they seized/gained control of' or 'took possession of.'
target_language_example: Los ladrones lo hicieron con su teléfono y sus documentos.
native_language_example: The thieves did something with his phone and his documents.

meaning: 'we did (it) in/at' — indicates something we did and the place where it happened.
additional_notes: Hicimos is the first-person plural past (pretérito) of hacer: 'we did'. When followed by en + place, it specifies the location or context where the action occurred (e.g., en la escuela, en Nueva York, en la clase). The object pronoun lo/los/las is often placed before hicimos (Lo hicimos en...).
target_language_example: Lo hicimos en el parque el fin de semana pasado.
native_language_example: We did it in the park last weekend.

meaning: what you did was
additional_notes: Used to comment on or evaluate an action someone performed. Often appears in the structure "Lo que hiciste fue + [adjective/phrase]" to state an opinion or judgment about that action.
target_language_example: Lo que hiciste fue muy valiente.
native_language_example: What you did was very brave.

meaning: you did for me / what you did for me (past tense, informal 'you')
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of hacer (hiciste) + por mí = actions someone did on your behalf or to help you. Used to thank or refer to a specific past favor or action. 'Hiciste' is the informal singular 'you' (tú). For formal 'you' (usted) use 'hizo por mí'.
target_language_example: Nunca olvidaré lo que hiciste por mí aquel día.
native_language_example: I will never forget what you did for me that day.

meaning: literally 'daughter of the' — used to show family relationship or as part of expressions like 'X is the daughter of Y' (often figurative: 'wisdom is the daughter of experience').
additional_notes: This phrase combines the noun hija (daughter) + de la (of the). Use it to indicate someone is the daughter of a named female or a concept: e.g., 'la hija de María' or figuratively 'la hija de la experiencia'. Word order and gender must match (hija is feminine). If referring to a male parent use 'hija del' (de + el = del). When followed by a possessive or adjective, structure may change (e.g., 'su hija').
target_language_example: La hija de la profesora llegó tarde.
native_language_example: The teacher's daughter arrived late.

meaning: an insult meaning 'son/daughter of a bitch' or 'bastard' (very offensive).
additional_notes: Strong vulgar insult used to attack someone’s character; can be directed at a person ('Es una hija de puta') or yelled alone as an exclamation. Extremely offensive—avoid in polite conversation. Tone and context determine severity; among friends it may be used jokingly in some groups, but it remains vulgar.
target_language_example: ¡No vuelvas a hablarme así, hija de puta!
native_language_example: Don't speak to me like that again, you son of a bitch!

meaning: son of God (religious title).
additional_notes: Used primarily in religious contexts to refer to a divine son (most commonly Jesus in Christianity). Can be used literally in theology or figuratively to indicate a person considered favored by God. Capitalization: 'Dios' is capitalized in monotheistic religions.
target_language_example: En la iglesia se habló sobre Jesús como el hijo de Dios.
native_language_example: At church they talked about Jesus as the son of God.

meaning: son of my (used before a family relation: e.g., 'hijo de mi hermana' = 'my sister's son').
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'hijo' (son) + 'de' (of) + a possessive phrase starting with 'mi' (my). It is followed by a family noun (hermana, amigo, hijo, etc.). For natural English word order, translate as 'my [relative]'s son' or 'the son of my [relative]'.
target_language_example: Es el hijo de mi hermano mayor.
native_language_example: He is my older brother's son.

meaning: insult meaning 'son of a bitch' (very rude).
additional_notes: Strong vulgar insult used to call someone cruel, dishonest, or contemptible. Can be used alone as an exclamation or directed at a person. Highly offensive — avoid in polite contexts. Tone and intent depend on context; sometimes used jokingly among close friends but risky.
target_language_example: ¡No vuelvas a hablarme así, hijo de perra!
native_language_example: Don't talk to me like that again, you son of a bitch!

meaning: insult: 'son of a bitch' or 'motherfucker' — a strong, offensive insult directed at someone.
additional_notes: Very vulgar. Used to express anger, contempt, surprise, or as a strong exclamation. Can be directed at someone (you hijo de puta), used vocatively, or uttered about someone nearby. Tone and context matter: among friends it can sometimes be joking (in very informal groups), but in most situations it is highly offensive and should be avoided. Literal literal translation is 'son of a whore', but the idiomatic meaning matches strong English insults.
target_language_example: ¡Cállate, hijo de puta!
native_language_example: Shut up, you son of a bitch!

meaning: son of a (masculine) — used to say someone's father or origin.
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'son of a...'. Followed by a noun (e.g., profession, social status, or relation). Can indicate lineage, background, or origin. Use 'hija de una' for feminine, or change article/gender as needed (e.g., 'hijo de la' if specific). In sentence 3 the structure 'un hijo de un matrimonio anterior' means 'a son from a previous marriage' and uses 'de' to indicate source/relationship.
target_language_example: Ella es el hijo de un médico.
native_language_example: She is the son of a doctor.

meaning: 'my/your/your (pl.) son was' — the noun hijo (son) + the imperfect of ser (era).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a simple combination: hijo (son) + era (imperfect of ser = "was"). Use era to describe past states, characteristics, habitual actions or ongoing past contexts. Replace hijo with mi/tu/vuestro/etc. to match the possessor (e.g., mi hijo era = my son was).
target_language_example: Mi hijo era muy tímido cuando era pequeño.
native_language_example: My son was very shy when he was little.

meaning: our/your/their son died / (the) son died.
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining hijo (son) + murió (he/she/it died). Used to say that a (male) child or son has died. Verb murió is the third-person singular preterite of morir (to die). Subject can change (nuestro, su, etc.). This is a plain, formal/neutral statement—sensitive topic; use gently.
target_language_example: Nuestro hijo murió en un accidente el año pasado.
native_language_example: Our son died in an accident last year.

meaning: 'my son' used as a familiar or affectionate address (like 'my dear' or 'my boy').
additional_notes: Commonly used by a parent or older relative to address a son or a young male; conveys affection, concern, or emphasis. Can sound tender, protective, or mildly reproachful depending on tone. Literal translation is 'son of mine.'
target_language_example: Ten cuidado, hijo mío.
native_language_example: Be careful, my son / my dear.

meaning: 'son who/that' — used to introduce more information about a son (relative clause).
additional_notes: Common structure: hijo + que + verb or clause. It links 'hijo' with a description, profession, name, or defining info (e.g., 'hijo que es dentista' = 'a son who is a dentist'). Can be used for non-defining or defining relative clauses depending on context. Not an idiom; literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Tengo un hijo que vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: I have a son who lives in Madrid.

meaning: my/your/their son wants (to)...
additional_notes: Combines hijo (son) + quiere (wants). Used to say what a son desires or intends to do. Change hijo to mi/tu/su/nuestro as needed; verb querer is followed by an infinitive (quiero ir) or a noun (quiere un coche). For female child use hija quiere.
target_language_example: Mi hijo quiere estudiar medicina el próximo año.
native_language_example: My son wants to study medicine next year.

meaning: 'my/your/their/etc. son too' — indicates that a son is included in what was just said.
additional_notes: Combine 'hijo' (son) with 'también' (also/too) to say that a son shares or is included in a previous statement. In English word order you often say 'my son also…' or 'my son, too…'. 'También' can appear before or after the verb (e.g., 'mi hijo también se dedica…' or 'mi hijo se dedica también…').
target_language_example: Mi hijo también viene a la reunión.
native_language_example: My son is coming to the meeting too.

meaning: 'only son' (a male who has no siblings).
additional_notes: Used to describe a male who has no brothers or sisters. For a female, use 'hija única'. Can be used literally (no siblings) or to imply sole heir/responsibility in context.
target_language_example: Soy hijo único y vivo con mis padres.
native_language_example: I am an only son and I live with my parents.

meaning: sons of
additional_notes: Literally 'sons of'. Often appears as the start of an insult (e.g., hijos de puta = sons of whores / sons of bitches). Strong vulgar language — avoid in polite conversation. The phrase by itself is incomplete; it normally requires a following noun or expletive to form the insult. Can be used angrily to refer to people (plural).
target_language_example: Esos tipos son unos hijos de puta.
native_language_example: Those guys are sons of bitches.

meaning: 'children and' — the plural noun hijos (sons/children) followed by y (and).
additional_notes: Hijos means 'children' or more literally 'sons' but in modern usage it commonly refers to children of both sexes unless specified. The construction 'hijos y ...' is just the noun plus 'and' used to connect another noun (e.g., hijos y nietos = children and grandchildren). In examples like 'tenemos dos hijos y dos hijas' the word 'hijos' refers specifically to sons while 'hijas' refers to daughters; when listing family members you may see both forms. There is nothing idiomatic about this phrase — it's compositional and literal.
target_language_example: Quiero tiempo para mis hijos y mi familia.
native_language_example: I want time for my children and my family.

meaning: literally 'sons and one (feminine)'; used as part of a phrase to say there are X sons (or children) and one daughter/wife/etc.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in sentences like 'tengo dos hijos y una hija' ('I have two sons and one daughter') or 'dos hijos y una esposa' ('two sons and one wife'). The word 'una' is feminine and must match the feminine noun that follows (e.g., hija, esposa). By itself this fragment is incomplete; it's normally followed by a feminine noun. Use the correct number and gender: 'hijos' can mean 'children' or specifically 'sons' (or mixed-sex children), and 'una' signals one feminine person or thing.
target_language_example: Tenemos dos hijos y una hija.
native_language_example: We have two sons and one daughter.

meaning: 'thread' or 'train (of thought)'; used metaphorically to mean the thread/line of a story, argument, or conversation.
additional_notes: Commonly used in expressions like 'perder el hilo' (to lose the thread) meaning to lose track of what's being said or the logical sequence. 'Seguir el hilo' means to follow or keep track. Often followed by 'la conversación', 'la historia', 'la argumentación', etc.
target_language_example: No me interrumpas; necesito seguir el hilo de la explicación.
native_language_example: Don't interrupt me; I need to follow the thread of the explanation.

meaning: national anthem
additional_notes: Refers to the official patriotic song of a country, often sung at official events, sports matches, and ceremonies. 'Himno' = anthem/song; 'nacional' = national. Used in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Antes de la ceremonia, todos se pusieron de pie para escuchar el himno nacional.
native_language_example: Before the ceremony, everyone stood to listen to the national anthem.

meaning: 'the story of' or 'the history of' (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Common phrase used before a noun to indicate a story, account, or history about something or someone. 'Del' is a contraction of 'de' + 'el' and requires a masculine singular noun (e.g., 'del accidente', 'del horror', 'del Trío Ternura'). Can mean a literal historical account or a colloquial 'story' (possibly invented).
target_language_example: No te creas la historia del vecino; es exagerada.
native_language_example: Don't believe the neighbor's story; it's exaggerated.

meaning: 'the story was' (past imperfect/description) or 'his/her story was'.
additional_notes: Combines historia (story; tale; account) with era (third-person singular imperfect of ser: 'was' used for descriptions, ongoing past states, or habitual past). Use to describe how a story/claim or someone's tale was in the past. If referring to 'history' as a subject, context matters, but here it usually means 'story' or 'account.'
target_language_example: La historia era increíble, todos querían escucharla de nuevo.
native_language_example: The story was incredible; everyone wanted to hear it again.

meaning: 'the story is' — a common phrase to describe the state or qualities of a story.
additional_notes: Combine historia (story, history) with está (third-person singular of estar) to say how a story is (e.g., based on, full of). Use for temporary states or descriptions (estar), not for defining what a story is in general (use ser for permanent traits).
target_language_example: La historia está basada en hechos reales.
native_language_example: The story is based on real events.

meaning: used to add emphasis before an adjective describing a story (e.g., 'the most ... story' or 'what a ... story').
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish to emphasize an adjective about a story. Often appears as 'es la historia más + adjective' ('it's the most + adjective story') or as an exclamation 'Qué historia más + adjective' ('What a ... story!'). The word order places 'más' before the adjective (not after). Use to compare (superlative) or to express surprise/criticism.
target_language_example: Qué historia más sorprendente me contó ayer.
native_language_example: What a surprising story he told me yesterday.

meaning: "story that" — used to introduce or refer to a story, account, or narrative (often followed by a clause).
additional_notes: Commonly appears when describing a story, memory, or version of events. The word 'que' links 'historia' to a relative clause (e.g., 'historia que nos contamos' = 'the story that we tell ourselves'). Can be used for true or imagined accounts. Word order is natural in Spanish; English often requires 'that' or a relative clause.
target_language_example: Ésa es la historia que siempre cuenta mi padre.
native_language_example: That's the story that my father always tells.

meaning: 'such a ... story' or 'a story so ...' (used to emphasize the adjective describing 'historia').
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'historia' (story) with 'tan' (so/that) to intensify an adjective that follows (e.g., tan triste = so sad; tan interesante = so interesting). In Spanish word order the pattern is: 'historia tan + adjective' or exclamatory 'Qué historia tan + adjective'. Use 'tan' for degree (can be followed by que + clause to show result: 'tan ... que ...').
target_language_example: Qué historia tan increíble; me dejó sin palabras.
native_language_example: What an incredible story; it left me speechless.

meaning: literally 'made to his/her/its' — part of a construction where 'hizo' (he/she/it made/did) is followed by a prepositional phrase starting with 'a su' (to his/her/its).
additional_notes: This sequence appears when describing someone/something making or causing something for or to a person or thing: e.g. 'hizo a su alrededor' or in older/poetic uses. By itself it's incomplete; you need an object or clause after it (e.g. 'hizo a su amigo un favor' would more naturally be 'le hizo un favor a su amigo'). In modern conversational Spanish, direct use 'hizo a su' is uncommon — Spanish typically uses indirect-object pronouns (le/les) or places 'a + person' after the verb phrase.
target_language_example: Le hizo a su madre un regalo por su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: He made/gave his mother a gift for her birthday.

meaning: 'pretended' or 'acted as if' (he/she/it did as if).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe someone pretending, feigning, or behaving as though something were true (often followed by 'que' + clause). Can also mean 'did as instructed' in some contexts (e.g., 'lo hizo como le dijeron' = 'he did it the way they told him'). Tense/subject changes: 'hace como' (does/acts as if), 'hice como' (I pretended), etc.
target_language_example: Ella hizo como que no me conocía cuando entré.
native_language_example: She pretended she didn't know me when I came in.

meaning: he/she/it (or someone) acted as if / pretended (that)...
additional_notes: Used to describe someone behaving in a way that suggests a false appearance or pretense. Often followed by a subjunctive clause when the action is hypothetical or contrary to fact (e.g., 'hizo como si no supiera'), but in casual speech you may also hear the indicative. Can refer to actions or expressions (looks, gestures, words).
target_language_example: Ella hizo como si no me conociera.
native_language_example: She acted as if she didn't know me.

meaning: 'did/made ... for' (indicates purpose or beneficiary in the past).
additional_notes: Combination of 'hizo' (past of hacer: he/she/it did or made) + 'para' (for, in order to, for the benefit of). Use 'hizo para' when describing why something was done (purpose: 'hizo para salvar su vida' = 'he did it to save his life') or for whom something was done (beneficiary: 'hizo para su hermana' = 'he made it for his sister'). Word order: 'lo/la/él/ella' often appears before 'hizo'.
target_language_example: Ella lo hizo para ayudar a su amigo.
native_language_example: She did it to help her friend.

meaning: did it for / did it because of (indicates motive, reason, or benefit).
additional_notes: Used to state the reason, motive, cause, or benefit behind an action. The full verb phrase is typically [subject] hizo [algo] por [razón/beneficio]. Common constructions: 'por obligación' (out of obligation), 'por sí mismo / por sí solo' (by himself), 'por dinero' (for money). 'Por' introduces the reason or motivation.
target_language_example: Ella lo hizo por amor.
native_language_example: She did it for love.

meaning: made (someone) feel
additional_notes: Combination of the verb hacer (in past tense hizo = he/she/you formal made) + sentirse (to feel oneself). Used to say that someone caused another person to experience a feeling. The indirect object pronoun (le, lo, etc.) or a named person indicates who felt that way. Can be used with different subjects (tú, usted, él/ella, ustedes) depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu comentario le hizo sentirse más seguro.
native_language_example: Your comment made him/her feel more confident.

meaning: 'my/your/etc. hobby is...' — used to say what someone's hobby is.
additional_notes: Common structure: [Possessive] + hobby + es + [activity]. Borrowed word 'hobby' is used in Spanish (often pronounced like English). You can replace 'hobby' with 'pasatiempo' for a fully Spanish alternative. Use a possessive (mi, su, tu, nuestro) before 'hobby' to indicate whose hobby it is.
target_language_example: Nuestro hobby es viajar los fines de semana.
native_language_example: Our hobby is traveling on weekends.

meaning: 'home is' (used to start a sentence that defines or describes what 'home' means).
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'hogar' (home) followed by the verb 'es' (is). Commonly used in proverbs or definitions (e.g., 'hogar es donde...') or simple sentences like 'mi hogar es...'. Use 'mi/tu/nuestro hogar es...' to say 'my/your/our home is...'.
target_language_example: Mi hogar es donde están mi familia y mis recuerdos.
native_language_example: My home is where my family and my memories are.

meaning: literally 'sheet/leaf in' — not a fixed phrase; likely the start of a phrase such as 'hoja en blanco' (blank sheet) or 'hoja en Excel' (sheet in Excel).
additional_notes: Alone, 'hoja en' is incomplete in Spanish. 'Hoja' means 'sheet' (paper) or 'leaf' (of a plant) and is often combined with a preposition to specify location, format, or context: e.g. 'hoja en blanco' (blank sheet), 'hoja en Excel' (sheet in Excel), 'hoja en papel' (sheet of paper). For beginners, recognize 'hoja' as 'sheet/leaf' and that 'en' means 'in' or 'on' and will be followed by the place or format.
target_language_example: Necesito una hoja en blanco para escribir la nota.
native_language_example: I need a blank sheet to write the note.

meaning: one-on-one; man-to-man (direct, face-to-face confrontation or comparison)
additional_notes: Used to describe direct competition, confrontation or comparison between two people (often in sports or debates). Can imply an honest, straightforward encounter. Gendered literal wording — context may use 'uno a uno' or 'cara a cara' for neutral alternatives.
target_language_example: En el partido fue hombre a hombre y ganó por habilidad.
native_language_example: In the match it was one-on-one and he won by skill.

meaning: a good man; a kind, moral, or decent man.
additional_notes: Used to describe a man who is morally good, kind, honest, or decent. Context can mean morally upright, compassionate, or simply a nice person. Common in both formal and informal contexts; can be used respectfully (usted) or familiarly (tú). Word order is normal adjective after noun in Spanish.
target_language_example: Mi vecino es un hombre bueno: siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: My neighbor is a good man: he always helps others.

meaning: businessman; a man who works in business or commerce.
additional_notes: Used to describe a man involved in business, commerce, or entrepreneurship. Can imply experience, success, or professionalism depending on context. For a gender-neutral term use "persona de negocios" or "empresario/empresaria" (empresario is common for 'business owner' or 'entrepreneur').
target_language_example: Él es un hombre de negocios muy respetado en la ciudad.
native_language_example: He is a very respected businessman in the city.

meaning: a man should / men should (ought to).
additional_notes: Combines 'hombre' (man) with the conditional verb 'debería' (should/ought to). Depending on context, it can refer to a specific man ('ese hombre debería...') or to people in general using 'hombre' or 'ningún hombre' (no man). For general statements about people, Spanish often uses 'todo hombre' (every man) or 'ningún hombre' (no man). The gendered noun can be replaced with neutral/plural forms (la gente, nadie, la persona) if desired.
target_language_example: Ningún hombre debería sufrir tanta injusticia.
native_language_example: No man should suffer so much injustice.

meaning: literally 'man in the' — used as the start of phrases like 'a man at/in the [place]' or figuratively 'our man at/in [place]'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the beginning of phrases such as 'hombre en la puerta' (a man at the door) or 'nuestro hombre en la embajada' (our man at the embassy). Can be literal (a man located somewhere) or figurative (a representative, contact, or important person in an organization or situation). Pay attention to the noun and article that follow (la/ el) and agreement/context.
target_language_example: Tenemos un hombre en la oficina que puede ayudar.
native_language_example: We have a man in the office who can help.

meaning: ‘man is the only animal’ — a fixed phrase used to make general statements about humans vs. animals.
additional_notes: Often followed by a verb or clause describing a uniquely human trait (e.g., capaz de..., que puede..., sujeto a...). Commonly used in generalizations or philosophical statements. 'Hombre' here means 'humankind' or 'man' in a general sense. Structure: 'El hombre es el único animal + [que/ capable de + infinitive]'.
target_language_example: El hombre es el único animal que puede crear herramientas complejas.
native_language_example: Man is the only animal that can create complex tools.

meaning: a segment meaning 'man is a' used to start descriptions about a man.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the sequence 'hombre es un' (man is a) used to describe or classify a man (e.g., 'El hombre es un lobo...' = 'Man is a wolf...'; 'Este hombre es un huésped' = 'This man is a guest'). For beginners: remember Spanish word order uses noun + verb + article + noun here. Choose the correct article (un/una/el/la) and adjective/agreement as needed.
target_language_example: Ese hombre es un buen amigo.
native_language_example: That man is a good friend.

meaning: ‘man/ humans are animals’ — a general statement that people are (by nature) animals with certain traits (social, rational, habitual, political).
additional_notes: Used to express a general, often philosophical observation about human nature. Context determines whether 'hombre' means 'man' (male) or 'humankind/people' (more general). Common continuations add adjectives: 'social', 'racional', 'de costumbres', or 'político'. Not an idiom—literal meaning applies.
target_language_example: El hombre es un animal social por naturaleza; necesita vivir en comunidad.
native_language_example: Man is a social animal by nature; he needs to live in community.

meaning: the man is / that man is (followed by a description or state).
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'hombre' (man) with the verb 'estar' (to be) to describe a temporary state, condition, location, or emotion. Use 'el hombre está' for 'the man is' and 'ese/este hombre está' for 'that/this man is'. Not used for permanent characteristics (use 'ser' instead). Word order can change: 'ese hombre está' or 'está ese hombre' (less common).
target_language_example: Ese hombre está cansado después del viaje.
native_language_example: That man is tired after the trip.

meaning: the man was
additional_notes: A short sequence combining the noun 'hombre' (man) and the past passive/preterite auxiliary 'fue' (from ser or ir). In these examples 'fue' is passive ('was') to form passive voice (e.g., 'was accused', 'was found'). Not a fixed idiom—it's simply 'the man was...' and will be followed by a past participle or past action. Subject–verb agreement: for plural use 'hombres fueron'.
target_language_example: El hombre fue herido en el accidente.
native_language_example: The man was injured in the accident.

meaning: literally 'dead man'; used figuratively to mean someone doomed, finished, or in serious trouble
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to say someone is 'a dead man' (doomed or in trouble). Context can be literal (a dead man) but in many everyday uses it means the person has no chance, will be punished, fired, defeated, etc. Common in phrases like 'eres un hombre muerto' or 'soy hombre muerto.'
target_language_example: Si lo descubren, eres hombre muerto.
native_language_example: If they find out, you're a dead man.

meaning: literally 'man is not' — used to say what a man (or person) is not or to introduce a general statement about what a man/people are (or aren't).
additional_notes: This phrase is part of sentences that negate or define 'un hombre' (a man) and often leads into a general truth or definition (e.g., 'A man is nothing more than...'). In English you might say 'a man is not...' or 'a man is nothing but...'. The exact meaning depends on the rest of the sentence. 'No es sino' is a more formal/literary variant meaning 'is nothing but' or 'is only'.
target_language_example: Un hombre no es solo lo que posee; también son sus acciones.
native_language_example: A man is not just what he owns; he is also his actions.

meaning: literally 'man or' — used as part of a choice 'man or ...' (i.e., 'man or woman', 'man or thing').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the noun 'hombre' followed by the conjunction 'o' ('or'). It appears when listing alternatives (e.g., 'hombre o mujer' = 'man or woman'). Word order and agreement are normal: you can replace 'hombre' with another noun. Beginners should treat it as two separate words: 'hombre' (man) + 'o' (or).
target_language_example: ¿Es un hombre o una mujer?
native_language_example: Is it a man or a woman?

meaning: 'a man can' or 'a man may' (used to state what a man is able to do or experience).
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'hombre' (man) with the verb 'poder' (to be able to). In sentences it's usually part of a larger phrase: 'un hombre puede...' (a man can...), 'lo que un hombre puede...' (what a man can...). Use 'un hombre' for the general idea of 'a man'; 'el hombre' can mean 'the man' or 'humankind' depending on context. Word order and articles matter: 'hombre puede' alone is uncommon without an article or pronoun.
target_language_example: Un hombre puede aprender algo nuevo cada día.
native_language_example: A man can learn something new every day.

meaning: literally 'man has' — shows possession or a state for 'the man' or 'a man'.
additional_notes: This is the combination of the noun 'hombre' (man) and the verb 'tiene' (he/it has). Use 'el hombre tiene' for 'the man has' and 'un hombre tiene' for 'a man has'. 'Tiene' can indicate possession (tiene una caja), physical states/needs (tiene hambre = he is hungry), characteristics (tiene mala fama), or quantities (tiene diez dedos).
target_language_example: El hombre tiene un sombrero nuevo.
native_language_example: The man has a new hat.

meaning: men of the / the men from the (used before a feminine noun phrase).
additional_notes: This is a fragment meaning 'men of the...' and must be followed by a feminine noun (la + noun) like 'aldea', 'arena', 'constructora', or a proper name with feminine article. It indicates belonging, membership, origin, occupation, or association. For masculine nouns you'd say 'hombres del' (de + el = del) or 'hombres de los' for plural. Word order: 'hombres de la' + feminine noun.
target_language_example: Los hombres de la aldea ayudaron a reparar el puente.
native_language_example: The men of the village helped repair the bridge.

meaning: men in the/men on the (depending on context).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the plural noun 'hombres' (men) with the prepositional phrase 'en el' (in the/on the + masculine singular definite article). Meaning depends on the noun that follows (e.g., 'hombres en el auto' = 'men in the car'; 'hombres en el agua' = 'men in the water'; 'en el campo' = 'men in the field' or 'on the field'). Use 'en la' if the following noun is feminine, and 'en los' / 'en las' for plural definite articles.
target_language_example: Hay tres hombres en el techo.
native_language_example: There are three men on the roof.

meaning: the phrase combines 'hombres' (men) with the indirect object pronoun 'les' meaning 'to them' or 'for them'; used in Spanish impersonal/cleft-like constructions to mark who is affected (e.g., 'to men' or 'men like/are affected by...').
additional_notes: In the examples, 'A los hombres les...' or 'A estos hombres les...' is a common Spanish structure used to say what men (as a group or specific men) like, lack, or are affected by. The full pattern is 'A + (article + noun) + les + [verb/phrase]'. The 'les' is an indirect object pronoun referring back to 'hombres'. English normally translates this with 'men (like...)', 'men are ...', or 'I trust these men with my life.' Include the article (los/estos) in natural Spanish: 'A los hombres les gusta...' Note: word order in Spanish often puts 'A los hombres' at the start for emphasis.
target_language_example: A los hombres les gusta jugar al fútbol.
native_language_example: Men like to play soccer.

meaning: used to introduce a superlative about men (e.g., 'one of the most ___ men').
additional_notes: Appears after a modifier to form expressions like 'uno de los hombres más + adjective' (one of the most + adjective + men). 'más' means 'more' or 'most' depending on context; here it's part of a superlative (the most). Ensure agreement and correct article/number: 'uno de los hombres más poderosos', 'uno de los hombres más ricos'.
target_language_example: Él es uno de los hombres más inteligentes que conozco.
native_language_example: He is one of the most intelligent men I know.

meaning: men are equal / all men are equal (used to say people have equal rights or worth).
additional_notes: Often appears in legal, religious, or general statements about equality. In Spanish you'd more commonly say 'todos los hombres son iguales' or 'los hombres son iguales'. Context determines whether it means 'men (male people) are equal' or the broader idea 'all people are equal' (use 'todas las personas' for gender-neutral).
target_language_example: La constitución declara que todos los hombres son iguales ante la ley.
native_language_example: The constitution states that all men are equal before the law.

meaning: 'honesty is' — used to state a quality or describe what honesty represents or leads to.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun, adjective, or phrase that defines honesty's role or value (e.g., 'la razón principal', 'una virtud', 'la base del éxito'). It's a simple way to make general statements about honesty. Use 'la honestidad' (the noun) with 'es' (it is).
target_language_example: La honestidad es esencial en cualquier relación.
native_language_example: Honesty is essential in any relationship.

meaning: 'honest that' — appears when describing honesty in comparative, explanatory, or clause-introducing constructions (e.g., 'más honesto que...', 'tan honesto que...').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; combines adjective 'honesto/a' with conjunction 'que' to introduce comparisons or result/explanatory clauses. Remember gender/number agreement (honesto/honesta/honestos/honestas). Common in phrases like 'es más honesto que...', 'es tan honesto que...', or 'lo más honesto que...'.
target_language_example: Es más placentero ser honesto que mentir.
native_language_example: It is more pleasant to be honest than to lie.

meaning: 'the honor of' — used to express that someone is given the privilege, distinction, or reputation to do or receive something.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in set phrases like 'tener el honor de' (to have the honor of...) to politely announce a privilege (e.g., meeting, presenting). Can also refer to reputation or dignity ('el honor de la familia' = the family's honor). Tone can be formal or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Tengo el honor de presentar a la ganadora del premio.
native_language_example: I have the honor of introducing the prize winner.

meaning: an honor for; used to say something/someone is a privilege or honor to someone.
additional_notes: Commonly used in phrases like "es un honor para mí/nosotros/esta institución" to express that meeting, hosting, or having someone is a privilege. Often follows "es" or "sería" and is usually followed by "mí", "nosotros", "nuestra escuela", etc. Formal and polite; appropriate in speeches, introductions, and thank-you remarks.
target_language_example: Es un honor para mí presentar a la ganadora.
native_language_example: It is an honor for me to introduce the winner.

meaning: the decisive moment; the moment of truth.
additional_notes: Used to say that a crucial, revealing, or decisive moment has arrived — when the real outcome will be known. Common in formal and informal contexts. Often preceded by 'es' or 'llegó' (it's/has come).
target_language_example: Ha llegado la hora de la verdad: vamos a presentar el proyecto.
native_language_example: The moment of truth has arrived: we're going to present the project.

meaning: it's time for us to (do something) / it's time that we (do something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a suggestion or statement that now is the appropriate time for a shared action. Follows the impersonal expression 'es hora de que' + subjunctive verb (e.g., vayamos, conozcamos). The 'nos' indicates the action involves 'us' (we/us). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Es hora de que nos vayamos a casa.
native_language_example: It's time for us to go home.

meaning: it's time for you to / time that you (should)...
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a larger construction usually followed by a subjunctive verb: "Es hora de que te ..." Meaning: it's time that you do something (often expresses necessity or recommendation). In everyday speech speakers may also say "Ya es hora de que te vayas" or shorten to "es hora de irte" (infinitive). Use the subjunctive after "que" when a specific subject follows.
target_language_example: Es hora de que te prepares para la entrevista.
native_language_example: It's time for you to get ready for the interview.

meaning: 'time to (do something) again' or 'it's time to return to (a place/state)'.
additional_notes: Used to say it's time to resume an action, go back somewhere, or return to a previous state. Followed by an infinitive verb (volver a + infinitive) to mean 'do again' or by a noun/place to indicate returning somewhere (often with 'casa', 'tiempos', etc.). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Creo que es hora de volver a intentar.
native_language_example: I think it's time to try again.

meaning: an hour later / one hour after
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens one hour after a reference time or event. Often appears as "una hora después" (feminine "una" matches "hora"). Can be used with or without a comma: "Una hora después, ..." or within a clause: "una hora después de la medianoche."
target_language_example: Salimos a las ocho y una hora después llegamos a casa.
native_language_example: We left at eight and an hour later we arrived home.

meaning: overtime (extra working hour); also extra time (in sports).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to paid extra work hours (tener/dar horas extras). In sports, plural 'tiempo extra(s)' or 'hora extra' can mean extra period but 'prórroga' is more common. Use singular when referring to one extra hour or the concept in general: 'trabajar horas extras'.
target_language_example: Hoy voy a trabajar una hora extra para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to work one extra hour to finish the project.

meaning: one more hour; an additional hour
additional_notes: Used to indicate one extra hour of time (e.g., staying, waiting) or to form phrases like "la hora más oscura" (the darkest hour) where "más" modifies the noun to mean 'most' or 'more' depending on context. Context determines whether it means 'one more hour' (additional time) or 'the ...est hour' when part of a superlative phrase.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes esperar una hora más?
native_language_example: Can you wait one more hour?

meaning: an hour to/for (time available or allotted for something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a period of about one hour that is available, allotted, or necessary for an action. Can mean 'an hour to do X', 'about an hour until X', or simply 'it's a good time to...' depending on context. 'Una hora' can be approximate ('around an hour'). 'Ya es buena hora' is an idiomatic use meaning 'it's a good time/right time' (not a literal hour).
target_language_example: Tengo una hora para terminar el informe.
native_language_example: I have an hour to finish the report.

meaning: rush hour; busiest time with heavy traffic or crowds.
additional_notes: Used to refer to peak travel times (morning or evening) when roads, public transport, or places are most crowded. Often appears in the phrase 'hora punta' or 'las horas punta'. Can be used for traffic (tráfico) or workplace/customer peaks.
target_language_example: Salimos antes de la hora punta para no quedarnos atascados.
native_language_example: We left before rush hour so we didn't get stuck in traffic.

meaning: the hospital is / the hospital + (estar) — describes the hospital's state, condition, or location.
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'hospital' with the verb 'estar' (to be). Use 'está' for temporary states (open/closed, under construction) or to indicate location (near). For permanent characteristics use 'es' instead. Common constructions: 'está abierto/cerrado' (is open/closed), 'está cerca' (is nearby), 'está a punto de' (is about to).
target_language_example: El hospital está abierto todos los días.
native_language_example: The hospital is open every day.

meaning: 'hospital' with the conjunction 'y' ('and'); not a fixed phrase—it's just 'hospital' followed by 'and' connecting clauses or items.
additional_notes: This is not a single idiom. In the examples, 'hospital y' appears when 'hospital' is followed by 'y' to link another idea (e.g., 'está en el hospital y...'). Use 'hospital' for 'hospital' and use 'y' to join it to the next clause or phrase. Remember Spanish uses accents (está). Pronunciation: [ospiˈtal i].
target_language_example: Está en el hospital y necesita muchas visitas.
native_language_example: He is in the hospital and needs many visits.

meaning: nowadays; today; these days.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the present time or current habits/situations. Can mean 'today' (this specific day) or more commonly 'nowadays'/'these days' when referring to general current trends. Register: neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Hoy día mucha gente trabaja desde casa.
native_language_example: Nowadays many people work from home.

meaning: nowadays; these days; in the present time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current era or present situation, often to contrast with the past. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence. Formality: neutral — appropriate in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Hoy en día muchas personas compran por internet.
native_language_example: Nowadays many people shop online.

meaning: today in the (time of day).
additional_notes: Used to specify a part of today (e.g., hoy en la mañana, hoy en la tarde, hoy en la noche). Followed by a time-of-day noun (mañana, tarde, noche). Common in everyday speech to indicate when something happens today.
target_language_example: Hoy en la tarde tengo una reunión a las 3.
native_language_example: This afternoon I have a meeting at 3.

meaning: today was
additional_notes: Used to state how today was (a day, an event, or an experience). 'Hoy' = today; 'fue' is past (pretérito) of 'ser' (to be) and describes a finished event or general quality of the day. Common with adjectives (peor, bueno, inolvidable) or noun phrases (un día divertido, la lectura de hoy).
target_language_example: Hoy fue un día muy productivo.
native_language_example: Today was a very productive day.

meaning: I had (a...) today; used to say how you spent the day (often followed by an adjective: bien, genial, fatal...).
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a common Spanish structure 'Hoy me lo pasé + [adjective]' meaning 'I had a [good/bad/great] time today' or 'I spent today [feeling ...]'. Literally: 'today I passed it to myself,' but idiomatically it refers to how enjoyable (or not) the day/event was. Common completions: 'hoy me lo pasé muy bien' (I had a great time today), 'hoy me lo pasé fatal' (I had a terrible time today).
target_language_example: Hoy me lo pasé muy bien en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I had a great time at the party today.

meaning: today (emphasizing immediacy or 'right away' today).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something will happen or should happen today, often implying urgency or immediacy (equivalent to 'this very day' or 'today itself'). Common in both spoken and written Spanish. Can be used alone (¿Puedes venir hoy mismo?) or with verbs (Lo haré hoy mismo).
target_language_example: Te llamo hoy mismo para confirmar.
native_language_example: I'll call you today to confirm (I'll call you later today).

meaning: today we / today us (used to start sentences about something happening to or done by 'us' today).
additional_notes: Combines 'hoy' (today) + 'nos' (we/us). 'Nos' can be a subject in reflexive/reciprocal constructions (nos encontramos = we meet/meet each other), a direct/indirect object (nos acompaña = accompanies us), or part of a pronominal verb (nos vamos = we leave). Common in spoken and written Spanish to introduce events or actions occurring today.
target_language_example: Hoy nos vamos de excursión al parque.
native_language_example: Today we're going on an outing to the park.

meaning: today I want (to)... — expresses a desire or intention for today
additional_notes: Use 'hoy quiero' to state what you want or plan to do today. It's followed by an infinitive verb (hoy quiero comer), a noun (hoy quiero el dinero), or a clause (hoy quiero que hablemos). Polite/softened alternatives include 'hoy me gustaría' or 'hoy quisiera'.
target_language_example: Hoy quiero aprender unas frases nuevas en español.
native_language_example: Today I want to learn some new phrases in Spanish.

meaning: today I have (to)... — used to say you must or need to do something today.
additional_notes: Combine 'hoy' (today) + 'tengo' (I have) typically followed by 'que' + an infinitive verb: 'Hoy tengo que + [infinitive]'. Common for stating obligations, plans, or things you need to do today.
target_language_example: Hoy tengo que estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: Today I have to study for the exam.

meaning: ‘today we go’ — used to say what we are doing today or where we are going today.
additional_notes: Hoy (today) + vamos (we go / we are going). Commonly used to introduce plans or actions for today: 'Hoy vamos a...' followed by an infinitive or destination (e.g., 'Hoy vamos a la playa' or 'Hoy vamos a estudiar'). In casual speech the 'a' + verb or destination is often included; 'Hoy vamos' alone can imply 'we're going (somewhere) today' when the place or activity is clear from context.
target_language_example: Hoy vamos a cenar con mis padres.
native_language_example: Today we're going to have dinner with my parents.

meaning: I'm going (to) today / today I will.
additional_notes: Used to say you will do something today. Usually followed by an infinitive verb (voy a + [infinitive]). Common in everyday speech to state plans or intentions for the same day. Tone can be neutral; meaning depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Hoy voy a comprar pan después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to buy bread after work.

meaning: 'there were/was' in conditional or hypothetical clauses (imperfect-subjunctive + article 'una')
additional_notes: Hubiera is the past (imperfect) subjunctive form of haber used to talk about hypothetical or counterfactual situations (often introduced by si/antes de que/sería bueno si). Combined with an indefinite article (una) it means 'if there were/was a...' or 'that there was a...'. Common in conditional sentences and formal/written registers; can also appear in past subjunctive subordinate clauses.
target_language_example: Si hubiera una oportunidad, la aprovecharía.
native_language_example: If there were an opportunity, I would take it.

meaning: there was a big / there was a great (used to report a large event or incident)
additional_notes: Hubo is the preterite of haber used impersonally to report that something happened. Use 'hubo un gran...' to describe a single past event (earthquake, fire, celebration, problem). For ongoing or repeated events you would use other forms. 'Gran' before a noun means 'big' or 'great' and shortens from 'grande' when placed before singular nouns.
target_language_example: Hubo un gran apagón anoche en el barrio.
native_language_example: There was a big blackout last night in the neighborhood.

meaning: fingerprint (the unique pattern on a fingertip).
additional_notes: Used for identification, security, or forensic contexts. Often appears in phrases like 'tomar la huella dactilar' (to take/scan a fingerprint) or 'huella dactilar digital' (digital fingerprint/scan). Formal and neutral term.
target_language_example: La policía tomó la huella dactilar del sospechoso.
native_language_example: The police took the suspect's fingerprint.

meaning: 'eggs of' or 'eggs from' — literal possessive/partitive phrase used to describe origin or type of eggs (e.g., 'huevos de gallina' = 'chicken eggs').
additional_notes: This is a compositional, literal phrase: huevos = eggs, de = of/from. Commonly used to indicate the source, species, preparation style, or ingredient (huevos de codorniz = quail eggs; huevos de la granja = farm eggs). In some contexts 'de' can introduce what the eggs are made with or used for (huevos de chocolate = chocolate eggs). Not a fixed idiom by itself — it needs a noun after 'de'.
target_language_example: Compré huevos de gallina y huevos de codorniz.
native_language_example: I bought chicken eggs and quail eggs.

meaning: eggs in the (feminine noun that follows, e.g. 'la heladera', 'la caja', 'la cesta').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's simply the plural noun 'huevos' ('eggs') followed by the preposition 'en' and the feminine definite article 'la' before another noun. The final noun (la heladera, la caja, la cesta, la arena, etc.) tells where the eggs are. Change 'la' to 'el' if the place is masculine (e.g. 'huevos en el refrigerador').
target_language_example: Hay huevos en la mesa.
native_language_example: There are eggs on the table.

meaning: 'is human' or 'human ... is' (phrase combining adjective 'humana' + verb 'es')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two separate words: 'humana' (feminine form of 'humano' = 'human') and 'es' (third-person singular of 'ser' = 'is'). They appear together when describing a feminine noun: e.g. 'la historia humana es...' ('the human history is...'), 'la vida humana es...'. Adjust gender (humano/humana) and number (es/son) to match the noun.
target_language_example: La experiencia humana es compleja.
native_language_example: The human experience is complex.

meaning: humans (do) not — negative statement about people.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the plural noun 'humanos' (humans) followed by the negation 'no'. It appears in sentences to say that humans do not or cannot do something. Word order is flexible in Spanish: often 'los humanos no' (the humans do not) or 'los humanos no pueden' (humans cannot). 'No' negates the verb that follows or the clause.
target_language_example: Los humanos no entienden todo lo que ocurre.
native_language_example: Humans do not understand everything that happens.

meaning: in the mood for (something) / not in the mood for (something).
additional_notes: Used with estar (estoy/estaba) + de humor para + noun or verb (infinitive) to say you feel like doing something or not. Commonly negative (no estoy de humor para...) to refuse or avoid activities. Can express temporary mood; often followed by a specific activity: una pelea, una fiesta, hablar, salir.
target_language_example: No estoy de humor para cocinar hoy.
native_language_example: I'm not in the mood to cook today.

meaning: sank into / sank in (past tense of 'hundirse' with 'en' + place or state).
additional_notes: Used with 'hundirse' (to sink, to submerge, or to collapse) in the past third person singular. Followed by a place (el mar, el horizonte, Génova) to mean 'sank into' or by a state (un sueño profundo) to mean 'sank into' figuratively. Context determines whether it's physical (a ship, bridge) or figurative (sinking into sleep, thought).
target_language_example: El barco se hundió en la tormenta.
native_language_example: The ship sank in the storm.

meaning: 'was going to the' or 'used to go to the' (imperfect past of ir + definite article 'la').
additional_notes: Iba is the imperfect form of ir (to go). Depending on context, 'iba a la' can describe a habitual past action ('used to go to the') or an ongoing past action ('was going to the' / 'was on the way to the'). The phrase must match the feminine singular noun that follows (la). For masculine nouns you'd see 'iba al' (a + el). If followed by an infinitive, 'iba a' + verb (without 'la') means 'was going to [do something]'.
target_language_example: Iba a la biblioteca todas las tardes.
native_language_example: I used to go to the library every afternoon.

meaning: 'was going to' / 'used to go (to/for)' or part of expressions meaning 'was about/was wearing/was acting like' depending on context.
additional_notes: Iba de is the imperfect form of ir + de. It combines 'was going' with 'to/for' or is used in idiomatic phrases: "ir de compras" (to go shopping), "ir de paseo" (to go for a walk), "ir de rosa" (to be dressed in pink) or "ir de + role" (to act like / pretend). Context determines whether it's literal movement, habitual action, clothing/appearance, or figurative role.
target_language_example: Ayer iba de compras al centro comercial cuando me encontré contigo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was going shopping at the mall when I ran into you.

meaning: 'round trip' (a journey that goes there and back).
additional_notes: Commonly used for travel tickets (train, bus, plane) to indicate a return ticket. Can also describe any two-way movement. Often shortened to 'ida y vta.' in tickets or writing.
target_language_example: Compré un boleto de ida y vuelta a Madrid.
native_language_example: I bought a round-trip ticket to Madrid.

meaning: an idea/suggestion for (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a proposal or suggestion aimed at a project, plan, thing, or person. 'Para' shows purpose or recipient: idea para el proyecto (for the project), idea para ti (for you). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Tengo una idea para la fiesta de cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I have an idea for the birthday party.

meaning: ideas/opinions in (someone's head) or ideas about (a topic).
additional_notes: Used after 'meter(le) ideas en la cabeza' meaning 'to put ideas into (someone's) head' — often negative (influencing someone). Also used as 'ideas en [tema]' meaning 'ideas about [topic]' (e.g., 'ideas en educación'). Context determines whether it refers to someone's mind or a subject. Common collocations: 'meter ideas en la cabeza', 'tener/ponerse ideas en la cabeza'.
target_language_example: No le metas ideas en la cabeza a los niños.
native_language_example: Don't put ideas in the kids' heads.

meaning: foreign language
