native_language_example: I go to school with María every day.

meaning: the ... school of / the school for ... (used to specify the type, owner, or specialty of a school)
additional_notes: Common pattern: 'la escuela de + noun' can indicate ownership (la escuela de tu padre), specialization (la escuela de arte = art school), the field (la escuela de ingenieros = engineering school) or the purpose (la escuela de conducir = driving school). Word order and preposition may change in English (e.g., 'school of business' or 'business school'). 'La escuela' can also appear with other prepositions (ir a la escuela = go to school).
target_language_example: Estudia en la escuela de medicina desde hace tres años.
native_language_example: He has been studying at the medical school for three years.

meaning: 'the school in' or 'school in' (a phrase fragment used before a place or context)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself but a fragment: la escuela (the school) + en (in). It's used when specifying location or context for a school, e.g. la escuela en mi barrio (the school in my neighborhood) or la escuela en Madrid (the school in Madrid). Make sure to include the noun after 'en' (a place, time, or context). Word order: la escuela + en + [place/context].
target_language_example: La escuela en mi barrio abre a las ocho.
native_language_example: The school in my neighborhood opens at eight.

meaning: at the corner of the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate location: something is located at the corner of a place. 'La' agrees with a feminine noun that follows (e.g., la plaza, la calle, la habitación, la pieza). For masculine nouns use 'la esquina del' (la esquina del parque). You can also say 'en la esquina' alone when context supplies which corner.
target_language_example: Hay una tienda en la esquina de la calle principal.
native_language_example: There is a shop at the corner of the main street.

meaning: to the station at (a specific time).
additional_notes: This combines a location (la estación = the station) with the time expression 'a las + [hour]' meaning 'at [hour]'. Used to say arriving at, going to, or picking someone up at the station at a given clock time. Replace 'las' with 'la' only for 1:00 (a la una).
target_language_example: Voy a la estación a las ocho para tomar el tren.
native_language_example: I'm going to the station at eight to catch the train.

meaning: the station + 'by/ in/at' depending on context; here 'en' is a preposition meaning 'by' (transport) or 'in/at' (time/season).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the noun 'la estación' (the station or the season) with the preposition 'en'. 'En' has several uses: with modes of transport to mean 'by' (ir a la estación en taxi = go to the station by taxi); with time expressions to mean 'in' or 'within' (llegará a la estación en quince minutos = will arrive at the station in fifteen minutes); and with seasons to mean 'in' (la estación en que = the season in which). Context determines the translation.
target_language_example: Fui a la estación en tren y llegué en veinte minutos.
native_language_example: I went to the station by train and arrived in twenty minutes.

meaning: to the party with (someone or something).
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'la fiesta' (the party) plus the preposition 'con' (with). Used to say who or what someone attends the party with (a person, an item of clothing, etc.). Word order: ir/venir + a la fiesta con + [companion or thing].
target_language_example: Voy a la fiesta con mi hermano.
native_language_example: I'm going to the party with my brother.

meaning: the final (the last match/round of a competition or the final stage)
additional_notes: Used to refer to the last game, match, or round in a tournament or competition. Can mean 'the final' as an event (la final del campeonato) or a specific match (jugar/ir a la final). Gender is feminine (la final).
target_language_example: La final será el domingo en el estadio central.
native_language_example: The final will be on Sunday at the main stadium.

meaning: the flute (musical instrument).
additional_notes: Refers to the woodwind instrument. Used like other definite-noun phrases in Spanish (la + noun). Can mean the specific flute in context (e.g., 'the flute' or 'bring me the flute').
target_language_example: ¿Puedes enseñarme a tocar la flauta?
native_language_example: Can you teach me to play the flute?

meaning: the people (who/whom/that)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to people. 'A la que' combines the preposition 'a' (used with certain verbs like llevar, perseguir, robar — when the verb takes a direct object that is a person) + the relative pronoun 'la que' (feminine singular to agree with 'gente'). Often translated as 'who' or 'whom' depending on English grammar. If 'gente' is modified by a prepositional phrase with a pronoun (e.g., 'a la que le pagamos'), the structure stays the same.
target_language_example: La gente a la que ayudamos está agradecida.
native_language_example: The people whom we helped are grateful.

meaning: 'the room without' (phrase fragment used before specifying what the room lacks).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase on its own; it's the noun phrase 'la habitación' (the room) followed by 'sin' (without). You will normally see it followed by a noun or clause explaining what's missing: e.g. 'la habitación sin ventana' (the room without a window) or 'la habitación sin baño' (the room without a bathroom). Adjust agreement and word order as needed: 'sin' is followed by a noun (no preposition).
target_language_example: Buscamos la habitación sin balcón porque es más barata.
native_language_example: We're looking for the room without a balcony because it's cheaper.

meaning: 'the daughter'.
additional_notes: Definite article + noun: 'la' marks feminine singular. Used for someone's female child or in idiomatic/metaphorical expressions (e.g., 'la hija mayor' = the eldest daughter, or 'La prudencia es la hija mayor de la sabiduría' = prudence is the eldest daughter of wisdom). Use 'el hijo' for son, and possessive forms (mi, su, la hija de...) to specify whose daughter.
target_language_example: Su hermana es la hija del profesor.
native_language_example: Her sister is the professor's daughter.

meaning: a strong slang expression meaning 'awesome/amazing' or (depending on context) 'very, a lot'; can also be an expletive meaning 'damn' or refer to 'a hit' (vulgar).
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar in many contexts. Literally 'the host' (the consecrated bread in Catholic Mass), but used colloquially to express strong surprise, admiration, intensity, or anger. Tone and meaning depend on context and intonation: here it mostly means 'awesome' ('this is amazing'). Avoid in very formal or religious settings.
target_language_example: Esta película es la hostia, tienes que verla.
native_language_example: This movie is amazing, you have to see it.

meaning: to the left on / turn left on (used for directions).
additional_notes: Common phrase in giving directions. Often appears in commands like 'gira a la izquierda en...' or 'gire a la izquierda en...' followed by a place (la próxima calle, la esquina, la tercera intersección). Can also describe staying on the left side of the road (e.g., 'se mantienen a la izquierda en...'). Use 'a la izquierda en' before a location or point in the route.
target_language_example: Gira a la izquierda en la próxima calle.
native_language_example: Turn left on the next street.

meaning: 'the long' (feminine singular) — used before a feminine noun to mean 'the long (something)'.
additional_notes: La palabra larga es un adjetivo que concuerda en género y número con el sustantivo que acompaña. Aquí aparece en femenino singular (la larga) porque modifica un sustantivo femenino implícito o explícito: la larga oscuridad, la larga guerra, la larga sequía. Use 'el largo' para sustantivos masculinos y plural forms ('las largas', 'los largos') según corresponda.
target_language_example: Recuerdo la larga espera en la estación.
native_language_example: I remember the long wait at the station.

meaning: 'the milk' (the dairy liquid) or used literally to refer to milk.
additional_notes: Most often refers to cow's milk or milk in general. It's a simple noun phrase: definite article + noun. Context determines if it's literal (the drink) or part of idioms (not shown here). Use with verbs like beber, tomar, estar, gustar, venir (de), saber, robar. Feminine singular noun.
target_language_example: La leche está en el refrigerador.
native_language_example: The milk is in the refrigerator.

meaning: 'lightly' or 'not seriously' (used in the phrase 'a la ligera' meaning to treat something carelessly or without due thought).
additional_notes: Appears in the fixed phrase 'a la ligera' (not usually used alone). It means to do or treat something superficially, carelessly, or without seriousness. Common with verbs like tomar (tomar a la ligera), usar (usar a la ligera), or tomarlo (no se lo tome a la ligera).
target_language_example: No deberías tomar esa decisión a la ligera.
native_language_example: You shouldn't take that decision lightly.

meaning: the light when/upon (doing something); used in instructions to say 'turn off the light when...'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in commands like "Apaga la luz al salir" = "Turn off the light when you leave." 'Al' is a contraction of 'a' + 'el' and here means 'upon' or 'when (doing)'. The full instruction often omits the action after 'al' because the verb follows (e.g., 'al salir' = 'when leaving').
target_language_example: Apaga la luz al terminar la clase.
native_language_example: Turn off the light when the class ends.

meaning: the way that / the manner in which
additional_notes: Used to introduce how something is done or the manner/way of something. Often appears as 'de la manera que' = 'in the way that' or 'in the manner that'. Can be followed by a verb clause or a clause describing preference or comparison.
target_language_example: Hazlo de la manera que te expliqué.
native_language_example: Do it in the way that I explained.

meaning: 'the sea' (literal) — also an idiomatic intensifier meaning 'very' or 'extremely' in some expressions.
additional_notes: Primary literal meaning: la mar = the sea (poetic/colloquial alternative to 'el mar'/'el océano'). Idiomatic use (common in Spanish): 'la mar de' + adjective/adverb = 'very', 'extremely', 'really' (e.g., 'la mar de bien' = 'very well'). Context decides meaning: if referring to water it's literal; if used before an adjective or past participle it's the intensifier. Register: colloquial, sometimes poetic for literal sea; idiomatic use is informal but widely used.
target_language_example: Hoy estamos la mar de contentos.
native_language_example: Today we're very happy.

meaning: 'the medal' or 'the pendant/medallion' (a small decorated metal piece, often awarded or worn).
additional_notes: Can refer to an award (sports, honors) or a decorative/ religious pendant worn on a chain (e.g., Saint medals). Context decides whether it's a prize or a piece of jewelry. Feminine singular definite article 'la' used when speaking about a specific medal.
target_language_example: Ella recibió la medalla por su trabajo voluntario.
native_language_example: She received the medal for her volunteer work.

meaning: 'the best night' — used to describe a very good or the best evening/ night.
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining la (the) + mejor (best) + noche (night). Use to talk about a particular night that was excellent (e.g., a party, concert, trip). Can refer to a single evening or to a night in general. Commonly followed by a description (la mejor noche de mi vida, la mejor noche del año).
target_language_example: Fue la mejor noche de mi vida.
native_language_example: It was the best night of my life.

meaning: the best night of my life (or existence).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a particular night was (or will be) extremely special or memorable. Commonly completed as "la mejor noche de mi vida" or more formally "...de mi existencia." Can be used as a full sentence/exclamation: "¡La mejor noche de mi vida!"
target_language_example: Anoche fue la mejor noche de mi vida.
native_language_example: Last night was the best night of my life.

meaning: 'the lie' or 'lying' (a false statement or the act of being untruthful).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to a false statement (la mentira) or the concept of dishonesty. Can be used literally (someone tells a lie) or figuratively (living a lie). Feminine noun; plural = "las mentiras."
target_language_example: No quiero vivir en la mentira; prefiero la verdad aunque duela.
native_language_example: I don't want to live in a lie; I prefer the truth even if it hurts.

meaning: the same age as me / I'm the same age (as someone).
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Can refer to a third person (Él tiene la misma edad que yo) or state that someone and the speaker share the same age. You can replace 'yo' with another pronoun or name (la misma edad que tú / que él). In casual speech Spanish sometimes drops 'yo' if context is clear: 'Tiene la misma edad.'
target_language_example: María tiene la misma edad que yo.
native_language_example: María is the same age as me.

meaning: at the same time (the same hour).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens at the same time as another event or repeatedly at the same hour each day. Common in scheduling or routine contexts. Can be shortened in speech to 'a la misma hora' meaning 'at the same time (as before)'.
target_language_example: Quedamos a la misma hora de siempre.
native_language_example: Let's meet at the same time as always.

meaning: the same reason
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a reason already mentioned or implied. Commonly appears in phrases like 'por la misma razón' (for the same reason) to connect explanations or justify actions. Agreement in gender/number: 'la misma razón' (feminine singular); plural would be 'las mismas razones'.
target_language_example: No fui al concierto por la misma razón que tú.
native_language_example: I didn't go to the concert for the same reason as you.

meaning: 'to/for the girl' as part of the Spanish dative/construction that marks the indirect object (often translated with 'to' or 'for' or by using English subject/object order: 'the girl' + verb).
additional_notes: This pattern combines a noun phrase (la niña) introduced by the preposition a plus a clitic indirect object pronoun (le). Spanish often uses both the full indirect object (a la niña) and the clitic (le) together for clarity or emphasis. English usually expresses this with word order and prepositions (e.g., 'they gave the girl a prize' or 'the girl likes bananas'). In sentences with gustar-type verbs, the subject in Spanish is what English treats as the object ('Le gustan los plátanos' = 'She likes bananas').
target_language_example: A la niña le regalaron un libro por su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: They gave the girl a book for her birthday.

meaning: to spend the night here / the night here (as a location).
additional_notes: Used when saying you'll stay overnight at a place. Commonly appears with verbs like pasar (pasar la noche aquí = spend the night here) or quedar/estar. In everyday speech you can also hear Sólo 'aquí' after pasar la noche (e.g., 'puedes pasar la noche aquí').
target_language_example: ¿Quieres pasar la noche aquí conmigo?
native_language_example: Do you want to spend the night here with me?

meaning: spent the night in/at (a place).
additional_notes: Used to say someone spent or will spend the night at a specific location. Followed by a noun with the definite article la (feminine) — e.g., la cárcel, la habitación, la playa. For masculine places use 'la noche en el' (e.g., la noche en el hotel). Common verb is 'pasar la noche' (to spend the night).
target_language_example: Anoche pasé la noche en la playa con amigos.
native_language_example: Last night I spent the night at the beach with friends.

meaning: 'night' with a reflexive/impersonal verb construction—used to say that night is coming, spreading, or as part of impersonal/night-time statements (literally: 'the night itself...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the article + noun (la noche) followed by the reflexive pronoun se used with verbs. It appears in two common patterns: 1) verbs describing changes or movements: 'La noche se acerca' = 'Night is approaching'; 2) impersonal/ambient statements with 'se' to mean 'one can' or 'people can' during the night: 'Por la noche se pueden ver las estrellas' = 'At night one can see the stars.' Pay attention to verb agreement and placement: the verb follows 'se' and agreement depends on the subject (often singular 'la noche' or plural when the true subject is plural in impersonal constructions).
target_language_example: La noche se vuelve más fría.
native_language_example: The night becomes colder.

meaning: 'the notion' / 'the idea' / 'a basic understanding'
additional_notes: Used to refer to an idea, concept, impression, or a basic understanding of something. Often used with verbs like tener (tener la noción), perder (perder la noción), or expresar (dar/exponer la noción). Can describe vague or general knowledge rather than detailed information.
target_language_example: No tengo la noción exacta de cuánto costará.
native_language_example: I don't have an exact idea of how much it will cost.

meaning: the black sheep of the (family/group) — the odd one out or person who doesn't fit in.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone considered different, troublesome, or shameful within a family or group. Usually followed by the group (e.g., 'la familia'). Common idiom in Spanish and similar to English 'black sheep'.
target_language_example: Él siempre fue la oveja negra de la familia.
native_language_example: He was always the black sheep of the family.

meaning: 'the word of' or 'the promise/authority of' (depending on context)
additional_notes: This phrase is the feminine noun 'la palabra' followed by the preposition 'de' (of). Alone it is incomplete and needs a following noun or name (e.g., la palabra de alguien, la palabra de Dios) or can introduce a phrase meaning 'the promise/assurance of...'. It can also appear in expressions like 'dar la palabra' (to give one's word) or 'tener la palabra' (to have the floor/speaking turn) when used with verbs. Translate depending on context.
target_language_example: Tengo la palabra de mi jefe sobre el aumento.
native_language_example: I have my boss's word about the raise.

meaning: 'the [stop/place] of' or 'the ... stop' (used to indicate a stop or station for buses, metro, taxis, etc.).
additional_notes: A common phrase used before a mode of transport or a proper name: la parada de autobús (bus stop), la parada del metro (metro stop), la parada de taxis (taxi rank). Often followed by the vehicle or location. 'La parada' by itself means 'the stop'.
target_language_example: Esperamos en la parada de autobús.
native_language_example: We waited at the bus stop.

meaning: the happiest person
additional_notes: A superlative phrase: 'más' + adjective (feliz) makes 'more/most'. Use 'la' (feminine) or 'el' (masculine) to match gender of the person referred to. Can refer literally to someone's emotional state or be used hyperbolically (I'm the happiest person).
target_language_example: Después de recibir la noticia, me sentí como la persona más feliz del mundo.
native_language_example: After receiving the news, I felt like the happiest person in the world.

meaning: 'to the beach with' or 'at the beach with' (indicates going to/being at the beach accompanied by someone).
additional_notes: This is the noun phrase la playa (the beach) followed by the preposition con (with + companion). Use it to say who you went to or are going to the beach with. Word order: [ir/estar] + a/la playa + con + [person(s)]. In casual speech the article la is often kept: fui a la playa con mis amigos. Pronouns and names follow con (con él, con ella, con Juan).
target_language_example: Voy a la playa con mi hermana este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to the beach with my sister this weekend.

meaning: 'the police stop' or 'the police (something) stop' — but note this is not a fixed phrase; meaning depends on context.
additional_notes: This is not a set phrase. 'La policía' = 'the police'. 'Para' can be a verb form (from parar: 'stops'), a preposition ('for', 'in order to'), or part of a clause ('para que' = 'so that'). Read the whole sentence to know which meaning is intended. Examples above show different uses: 1) 'para' as a verb (stops) — though sentence 1 is vulgar and odd; 2) 'tardó a la policía para llegar' is non‑standard — the correct phrasing is 'a la policía le tomó mucho tiempo llegar' or 'les tomó mucho tiempo a la policía llegar'; 3) 'para que' introduces purpose ('so that the police can help us').
target_language_example: Llama a la policía para que nos ayude.
native_language_example: Call the police so that they can help us.

meaning: the main (feminine singular)
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (explicit or understood) to say that something is the most important, main, or primary one. If the noun is masculine, use "el principal". Can refer to abstract things (la principal razón) or concrete things (la principal atracción).
target_language_example: La principal ventaja es que es más rápido.
native_language_example: The main advantage is that it's faster.

meaning: “the door before” — used to refer to actions or conditions that must occur with respect to the door prior to some other action (i.e., something done before dealing with the door). Often appears as part of phrases like “la puerta antes de…” or in constructions where “antes” relates to an action involving the door.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; meaning depends on context and usual structures: 'antes de' + infinitive (antes de abrir la puerta) or 'antes de que' + subjunctive (antes de que el tren se haya detenido). Native word order often places the noun and 'antes' together when emphasizing timing relative to the door (e.g., 'ponerle llave a la puerta antes de irte'). The fragment 'la puerta antes' can appear in spoken/written sentences but typically attaches to the rest of the clause.
target_language_example: Acuérdate de ponerle llave a la puerta antes de irte a acostar.
native_language_example: Remember to lock the door before going to bed.

meaning: a very strong expletive meaning something like 'f***ing hell' or 'it hurts/it's intense as hell'.
additional_notes: Very vulgar Spanish swear phrase used to express extreme anger, pain, surprise or emphasis. Can stand alone as an exclamation or modify verbs/nouns to intensify (e.g., 'duele la puta madre' = 'it hurts like hell'). Avoid in formal situations; may be highly offensive. Tone and exact translation depend on context (anger, pain, admiration or shock).
target_language_example: ¡Me duele la puta madre después de la caída!
native_language_example: It hurts like f***ing hell after the fall!

meaning: a relative phrase meaning 'the one/that which (that) to you' or 'the reason/way that (affects) you' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence where la/las/lo/los + que introduce a relative clause; te is the indirect or direct object pronoun referring to 'you'. Meaning depends on the noun and verb around it: e.g. 'la razón por la que te...' = 'the reason why (you) ...', 'la manera en la que te lo dijeron' = 'the way in which they told you'. Watch word order: Spanish often places the object pronoun (te) after the relative clause verb.
target_language_example: Esa es la razón por la que te llamé ayer.
native_language_example: That's the reason why I called you yesterday.

meaning: the root; the origin or base of something (literal root of a plant or figurative root/cause).
additional_notes: Used both literally (root of a plant, tooth root, mathematical root) and figuratively (cause, origin, origin of a word). Common in phrases like "la raíz del problema" (the root/cause of the problem). Feminine noun; plural: "las raíces."
target_language_example: Tenemos que encontrar la raíz del problema.
native_language_example: We need to find the root of the problem.

meaning: 'the root of' or 'the source/cause of'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the origin, cause, or main source of a problem, idea, or feeling. Commonly followed by a noun or the phrase 'todo/total' (e.g., 'la raíz de todo mal'). Formal or neutral register; literal meaning 'the root of' (like a plant root) and figurative meaning for causes.
target_language_example: La ignorancia es la raíz de muchos prejuicios.
native_language_example: Ignorance is the root of many prejudices.

meaning: the reputation (someone or something has).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how people view someone's character, abilities, or past actions. Commonly followed by de + noun or que + verb: la reputación de X (the reputation of X) or tener la reputación de + infinitive (to have a reputation for ...). Formal/common vocabulary.
target_language_example: Tiene la reputación de ser honesto entre sus colegas.
native_language_example: He has a reputation for being honest among his colleagues.

meaning: literally 'the blood on/in' — used to describe blood on a surface or as part of expressions mentioning someone being angry or resentful (see notes).
additional_notes: Most often used literally to point out blood on something: 'la sangre en la camiseta' = 'the blood on the shirt'. Word order is 'la sangre en + [place/surface]'. However, some idiomatic uses appear with related phrases (e.g., 'quedarse con la sangre en el ojo' means 'to remain angry or hold a grudge' — not literal). Context tells you whether it's physical blood or figurative.
target_language_example: Vi la sangre en sus manos y llamé a una ambulancia.
native_language_example: I saw the blood on his hands and called an ambulance.

meaning: 'the week that' used in the common expression 'la semana que viene' meaning 'next week'.
additional_notes: On its own 'la semana que' is incomplete; it's typically followed by a verb (viene) to form 'la semana que viene' (next week). It can also be used with other verbs to mean 'the week that...' (e.g., 'la semana que viene' = the week that comes = next week). This is a very common way to talk about next week in Spanish.
target_language_example: Tenemos una reunión la semana que viene.
native_language_example: We have a meeting next week.

meaning: the afternoon with (used to say you spent the afternoon with someone).
additional_notes: Use 'pasar la tarde con' to say you spent the afternoon with someone. Conjugate 'pasar' as needed (pasé, pasó, paso, etc.). You can replace 'la tarde' with other time words (la mañana, la noche). Common structure: [pasar] + la tarde + con + [person].
target_language_example: Pasamos la tarde con mis primos en el parque.
native_language_example: We spent the afternoon with my cousins in the park.

meaning: the sad (one) / the sad [feminine noun].
additional_notes: La frase 'la triste' se usa antes de un sustantivo femenino (por ejemplo, 'la triste noticia' or 'la triste historia') o puede aparecer sola como referencia a algo triste ya mencionado ('la triste (noticia)'). 'Triste' is an adjective; it agrees with the noun in gender and number (la triste, las tristes). Common collocations: 'la triste noticia', 'la triste historia'.
target_language_example: La triste noticia cambió el ánimo de todos.
native_language_example: The sad news changed everyone's mood.

meaning: life
additional_notes: Usually means "life." Spanish often uses the article here even when English just says "life" in a general sense. It also appears in common expressions such as buscarse la vida (to get by / make a living), dar la vida (to give one's life), and hacer la vida difícil (to make life difficult).
target_language_example: La vida en el campo es tranquila.
native_language_example: Life in the countryside is peaceful.

meaning: life is short.
additional_notes: A common proverb-like phrase used to remind someone to enjoy life, act now, or value time. Can be used literally (life is short) or more figuratively (make the most of moments). Suitable in conversations about priorities, mortality, or seizing opportunities.
target_language_example: Vámonos de viaje este fin de semana: la vida es breve.
native_language_example: Let's go on a trip this weekend: life is short.

meaning: the old (feminine)
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to mean 'the old' (e.g., la vieja casa = the old house, la vieja capilla = the old chapel). It describes age or longtime use. In some regions, 'la vieja' alone can colloquially refer to 'the (old) woman' or someone's wife — be cautious; that use can be informal or affectionate and sometimes rude depending on context.
target_language_example: Visitamos la vieja escuela del pueblo.
native_language_example: We visited the town's old school.

meaning: the spitting image of; the exact likeness of (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to say that one person looks exactly like another or that something is an exact likeness. Often followed by a person or noun (e.g., la viva imagen de su madre). Formal but common in everyday speech. Can be used literally (appearance) or figuratively (behaviour).
target_language_example: Es la viva imagen de su abuelo.
native_language_example: He is the spitting image of his grandfather.

meaning: 'the last time that I/she/we saw her' (or 'the last time that + object pronoun').
additional_notes: This phrase is used to refer to the most recent occasion something happened, often followed by a verb clause. 'La' is a direct object pronoun (her/it); the subject and tense vary (vi, vimos, etc.). You can replace 'la' with other pronouns: 'lo' (him/it), 'me' (me), 'nos' (us). Commonly used in storytelling or reports about past events.
target_language_example: La última vez que la vi estaba de vacaciones en Madrid.
native_language_example: The last time I saw her she was on vacation in Madrid.

meaning: the only thing
additional_notes: Used to point out a single important item, action, or fact. Can be followed by a clause introduced with que (…que + verb). Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: La única cosa que quiero es paz.
native_language_example: The only thing I want is peace.

meaning: 'the only reason (that/for)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the sole cause or motive for something. Often followed by 'que' + clause (la única razón por la que...) or by an infinitive/phrase. Common in explanations or emphasis: 'the only reason I/you/he did something'.
target_language_example: La única razón por la que vine fue ayudarte.
native_language_example: The only reason I came was to help you.

meaning: 'the wedding' (a marriage ceremony or wedding event).
additional_notes: Refers to the wedding ceremony or the overall wedding event (ceremony, celebration, or related materials like videos or announcements). Used with articles and possessives (la boda, mi boda, su boda). Common collocations: 'día de la boda' (wedding day), 'el video de la boda', 'anuncio de la boda', 'ser el padrino/la madrina de la boda'.
target_language_example: Vamos a decorar el salón para la boda.
native_language_example: We're going to decorate the hall for the wedding.

meaning: 'people' (general, uncountable — people in general or a group of people).
additional_notes: Used to refer to people collectively (people in general or a group). Treat as singular in Spanish grammar (use third-person singular verbs: la gente es). Can mean 'the public' or 'folks' depending on context. Not used with a plural article (no *las gentes* for general sense).
target_language_example: La gente está preocupada por el cambio climático.
native_language_example: People are worried about climate change.

meaning: the line; the end of the line (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Common noun meaning 'line' (a row, queue, stripe, or printed line). In some contexts (e.g., 'el final de la línea') it means 'the end of the line' or 'the end' (literal or figurative). Gender is feminine: 'la línea'. Can refer to a physical queue (stand in line), a printed line of text, or a route/rail line.
target_language_example: Estoy esperando en la línea para comprar boletos.
native_language_example: I'm waiting in line to buy tickets.

meaning: 'the word' (a single word or term).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific word or term in speech or writing. Common in phrases like 'el significado de la palabra' (the meaning of the word). 'Palabra' is feminine, so 'la palabra'. Can also be used more abstractly (e.g., someone's 'word' or promise) but here it refers to a lexical item.
target_language_example: No encuentro la palabra que necesito para describirlo.
native_language_example: I can't find the word I need to describe it.

meaning: the movie / the film.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific movie (definite article la). Common in everyday speech and writing. Can mean any film shown in a cinema, on TV, or in general. To say 'a movie' use 'una película'.
target_language_example: Vi la película anoche con mis amigos.
native_language_example: I saw the movie last night with my friends.

meaning: the truth; what is true or the real situation
additional_notes: Used to refer to truth in general, a specific true fact, or 'the real situation.' Common in expressions like 'el día de la verdad' (the day of truth). Can be used both literally and more figuratively (e.g., moral or revealed truth). Often preceded by articles or possessives: 'la verdad', 'mi verdad'.
target_language_example: La verdad es que no sé cómo se arregla.
native_language_example: The truth is that I don't know how to fix it.

meaning: the one/belonging to my (feminine noun) — 'la' refers to a feminine thing and 'de mi' marks possession (my).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific feminine noun previously mentioned or understood from context. 'La' is a feminine definite article replacing the noun (like 'the one' or 'the ... of mine'). The structure matches English 'mine' or 'the one that belongs to me' but keeps the gendered article. For masculine nouns you'd use 'el de mi'. Common in short phrases: 'la mía' is a full possessive pronoun; 'la de mi' is often followed by a family member or noun: 'la de mi hijo' = 'my son's (feminine thing)'.
target_language_example: Prefiero la de mi hermana porque es más grande.
native_language_example: I prefer my sister's (one) because it's bigger.

meaning: they are (doing something) to her/it (direct object feminine).
additional_notes: La is the feminine direct object pronoun (her/it). 'Están' is the 3rd-person plural of 'estar' used in the present progressive with a gerund (e.g., la están buscando = they are looking for her). Word order in Spanish often places the pronoun before the conjugated verb (la están buscando) or attached to the gerund (están buscándola). Use 'la' for feminine singular direct objects (a woman, a feminine noun).
target_language_example: La están ayudando con la mudanza.
native_language_example: They are helping her with the move.

meaning: 'makes her' or 'her it makes' (third-person singular: causes or produces an effect on 'her')
additional_notes: Composed of the direct object pronoun la (her/it feminine) + hace (he/she/it makes/does). Used to say that someone or something causes a feeling, appearance or action in a female person or feminine noun. Word order can vary in Spanish (e.g., 'la hace sentir', 'la hace parecer'). In sentence 4 the structure is reversed ('la hace el chef...') and 'la' refers to a feminine noun like 'mejor' or 'mejoría' implied by context.
target_language_example: La noticia la hace muy feliz.
native_language_example: The news makes her very happy.

meaning: I need her/it (feminine object).
additional_notes: Direct object pronoun 'la' (her/it) comes before the verb in neutral statements. Use 'la' for feminine singular nouns (la llave, la ayuda, ella when referring to a person). Word order: subject (optional) + 'la' + verb (necesito). Can be used for people (informally) or things. Negative: 'No la necesito.' For emphasis or after infinitives/gerunds, placement changes (e.g., 'necesitarla' attached to an infinitive).
target_language_example: La necesito para abrir la puerta.
native_language_example: I need it to open the door.

meaning: you (plural, informal Spain) can/are able to (do something) — with feminine direct object 'la'.
additional_notes: Combines the feminine direct object pronoun 'la' (her/it) + the verb 'poder' in the second-person plural informal form 'podéis' (used in Spain: vosotros/vosotras). Use 'vosotros' (masc/mixed) or 'vosotras' (feminine) when speaking to a group of people you address informally. The object pronoun usually comes before the conjugated verb: 'la podéis poner' = 'you (all) can put it/her'. In Latin America, 'ustedes la pueden' is used instead.
target_language_example: Vosotras la podéis dejar en la mesa.
native_language_example: You (all, informal Spain) can leave it on the table.

meaning: ‘can her/it’ or 'can (do something to) her/it' — third-person singular ability with the feminine direct object pronoun 'la'.
additional_notes: This is the verb 'poder' (to be able/can) in third person singular (puede) combined with the feminine direct-object pronoun 'la' (her or it). Word order in Spanish often places the pronoun before the conjugated verb: 'la puede' = 'he/she/it/you(formal) can [do something to] her/it.' Context determines whether 'la' refers to a person (her) or a feminine noun (it). In affirmative commands or with infinitives/gerunds, pronoun placement changes (attached to the end).
target_language_example: Nada la puede detener.
native_language_example: Nothing can stop her.

meaning: 'I can (her/it/that)'; 'I am able to (do something to/with it/her)'.
additional_notes: Combination of direct object pronoun 'la' (feminine singular: her, it, or formal you 'usted' in some contexts) placed before the conjugated verb 'puedo' (I can). Used when the speaker refers to a feminine singular object or person. Word order in Spanish: pronoun + conjugated verb (la puedo + infinitive) or pronoun attached to an infinitive (puedo ayudarla). Context determines whether 'la' means 'her', 'it' (feminine noun), or 'you' formal. In sentences with another verb (e.g., 'puedo ayudar'), 'la' can refer to the object of that action.
target_language_example: No la puedo llamar ahora; está en una reunión.
native_language_example: I can't call her now; she is in a meeting.

meaning: we are going to (do something) to her/it (direct object 'la').
additional_notes: Combination of the direct-object pronoun 'la' (her/it, feminine) placed before the conjugated verb 'vamos' (we go/we are going) and usually followed by an infinitive: 'la vamos a + infinitive' = 'we are going to [verb] her/it.' Used for actions directed at a feminine singular person or feminine noun. Register is neutral; context decides politeness or forcefulness.
target_language_example: La vamos a ayudar mañana por la tarde.
native_language_example: We are going to help her tomorrow afternoon.

meaning: a maze of / a labyrinth of (used to describe a complex, confusing network or tangle of things).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to describe that something is like a maze — e.g., tunnels, mirrors, streets. Often implies complexity, confusion, or many winding paths. Common collocations: 'laberinto de túneles', 'laberinto de calles/callejones', 'laberinto de espejos'.
target_language_example: El casco antiguo es un laberinto de callejones estrechos.
native_language_example: The old quarter is a maze of narrow alleys.

meaning: the positive side; the good side (of a situation or person).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to focus on positive aspects or to describe someone's good side. Common in phrases like "mira el lado bueno" (look on the bright side). Can be used for situations or to contrast traits (e.g., "tiene un lado bueno y uno malo").
target_language_example: Mira el lado bueno: al menos aprendiste algo.
native_language_example: Look on the bright side: at least you learned something.

meaning: the side of the yellow line (usually referring to standing behind the safety line on platforms or marked areas).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position relative to a yellow safety line (e.g., on train/subway platforms, construction zones, or marked pedestrian areas). Often implies staying behind the line for safety. Can be used literally or to give instructions (e.g., 'quédate al lado de la línea amarilla').
target_language_example: Por favor, espera al lado de la línea amarilla hasta que el tren se detenga.
native_language_example: Please wait on the side of the yellow line until the train stops.

meaning: the positive side; the bright side (of a situation).
additional_notes: Used to encourage focusing on good aspects of a situation. Common in imperatives: 'Mira el lado positivo' = 'Look on the bright side.' Can be used generally: 'el lado positivo de las cosas/ de la vida.'
target_language_example: Aunque fallamos, intenta ver el lado positivo: aprendimos mucho.
native_language_example: Even though we failed, try to see the bright side: we learned a lot.

meaning: literally 'barking all (over/through)'; incomplete phrase — likely part of expressions meaning 'complaining/barking the whole time' or 'making noise constantly'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase in Spanish; it looks like the beginning of a larger expression (e.g. 'ladrando toda la noche' = 'barking all night' or 'ladrando todo el rato' = 'complaining/barking the whole time'). Use with a time or duration after it. Context determines if it's literal (a dog barking) or figurative (a person complaining loudly).
target_language_example: El perro estuvo ladrando toda la noche y no pude dormir.
native_language_example: The dog was barking all night and I couldn't sleep.

meaning: 'thief of' or 'thief who steals (something)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who steals a particular thing or from a particular place. Combine with the item stolen (e.g., 'ladrón de bicicletas' = bicycle thief). Often used with definite/indefinite articles and in phrases describing roles (e.g., in movies) or accusations. Grammar: 'ladrón' is masculine noun; for a female thief use 'ladrona de'.
target_language_example: Lo arrestaron por ser el ladrón de coches del vecindario.
native_language_example: They arrested him for being the neighborhood car thief.

meaning: “a thief in” — used to say a thief is located inside/at (a place).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun 'ladrón' (thief) followed by the preposition 'en' (in/at). Use 'un ladrón en...' to report that a thief is in a particular place (room, house, barn, etc.). For full sentences you usually include the location after 'en' (e.g., 'un ladrón en la casa'). If you want to say 'there is a thief in...', use 'hay un ladrón en...'.
target_language_example: Hay un ladrón en la cocina.
native_language_example: There is a thief in the kitchen.

meaning: a thief (used in sentences where the reflexive pronoun 'se' appears with verbs).
additional_notes: The phrase combines the noun 'ladrón' (thief) with the reflexive pronoun 'se' attached to a verb (e.g., se escapó, se llevó, se mezcló). 'Se' here belongs to the verb, not to 'ladrón' itself; it marks reflexive, passive/mediopassive, accidental, or pronominal uses depending on the verb (e.g., 'se llevó' = 'took away', 'se escapó' = 'escaped', 'se mezcló' = 'blended in'). Beginners should treat 'ladrón' as 'thief' and learn common verb+se patterns separately.
target_language_example: El ladrón se llevó la cartera y huyó.
native_language_example: The thief took the wallet and ran away.

meaning: 'the lake is' — a simple subject + verb phrase describing a lake.
additional_notes: This combines the noun 'lago' (lake) and the verb 'es' (third-person singular of 'ser' — to be). Use 'es' for permanent or descriptive qualities (size, depth, color, ownership when used with 'de' or possessive). For location or temporary states, Spanish may use 'está' instead. In many sentences you would see just 'el lago es' rather than the isolated pair 'lago es'.
target_language_example: El lago es tranquilo en verano.
native_language_example: The lake is calm in summer.

meaning: 'lago' = lake; 'se' is a reflexive/impersonal pronoun used with verbs here (e.g. 'se congela' = 'freezes' / 'se ve' = 'looks').
additional_notes: This item combines a noun (lago = lake) with the pronoun 'se' seen in the example sentences. 'Se' is not part of the noun; it is a pronoun used with verbs to form reflexive actions (El lago se congela = the lake freezes), passive/impersonal constructions (Se vende = for sale / Se habla español = Spanish is spoken) or to indicate how something appears (Ese lago se ve como el mar = That lake looks like the sea). For learners, treat 'lago' as a regular masculine noun (el lago, un lago). 'Se' appears with the verb and changes the meaning to reflexive, passive/impersonal, or middle-voice; it does not change the noun.
target_language_example: El lago se ve tranquilo al atardecer.
native_language_example: The lake looks calm at sunset.

meaning: lit. 'the lake has' — a subject + tener construction used to describe attributes or measurements of the lake (size, features).
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'lago' (lake) followed by the verb 'tener' (to have). Spanish often uses tener + noun to state physical characteristics, quantities, or possessions (e.g., 'El lago tiene una anchura de tres millas', 'El lago tiene agua cristalina'). For learners, recognize the pattern: [subject] + tiene + [attribute/measurement]. If you want to say 'the lake is ...' you may instead use 'el lago es/está' depending on the adjective.
target_language_example: El lago tiene muchas islas pequeñas.
native_language_example: The lake has many small islands.

meaning: 'I'm sorry (that) I didn't / that I haven't'.
additional_notes: Used to express regret about something the speaker failed to do or doesn't have. Followed by an infinitive clause (e.g., no haber..., no poder..., no tener...). Common in both formal and neutral speech. You can omit 'que' when introducing an infinitive (lamento no poder...) but use 'que' for subordinate clauses with conjugated verbs (lamento que no pude...).
target_language_example: Lamento no llamarte antes.
native_language_example: I'm sorry I didn't call you earlier.

meaning: long (measuring) — used to describe the length or extent of something, often followed by a measurement or phrase indicating what it's long in.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; typically compositional. 'Largo de' can link an adjective to a measurement or qualifier (e.g., 'largo de dos metros', 'largo de tierra'). In many contexts speakers instead say 'de X de largo' or simply 'largo' with a different word order ('una mesa de dos metros de largo'). Usage and word order can vary by region and register.
target_language_example: La carretera es larga de más de cien kilómetros y se conoce como la carretera larga de la costa.
native_language_example: The road is long — more than one hundred kilometers, and it is known as the long road of the coast.

meaning: 'longer than' (used to compare length or duration).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons with 'más ... que' (more ... than) to say something is longer than something else. Can refer to physical length or to duration/extent in a figurative sense. Also appears with 'tan ... que' to indicate 'so/too ... that'. Watch word order: 'más largo que' for 'longer than', 'tan largo que' for 'so long that'.
target_language_example: Este puente es más largo que el de mi ciudad.
native_language_example: This bridge is longer than the one in my city.

meaning: the goats (feminine plural) — 'cabras' = female goats; 'las' = the (plural).
additional_notes: Literal plural definite article + noun. Use when referring to a group of goats (female or mixed in casual speech). In Spanish nouns are gendered; 'las cabras' is grammatically feminine plural. Could also be a proper name (e.g., a team, place, or nickname) depending on context — then treat as a name rather than the literal animals.
target_language_example: Las cabras están en el campo.
native_language_example: The goats are in the field.

meaning: the flowers
additional_notes: Plural feminine noun: 'las' is the definite article for feminine plural nouns. Use to refer to flowers in general or specific flowers already mentioned (e.g., 'las flores del jardín' = the flowers of the garden). Can also be used metaphorically (e.g., 'oler las flores' — to smell the flowers).
target_language_example: Las flores del balcón están hermosas esta primavera.
native_language_example: The flowers on the balcony are beautiful this spring.

meaning: the change (money) returned after a purchase; short errands or trips; turns/rounds (contextual).
additional_notes: Most commonly used in Spain and many Latin American countries to mean the small amount of money given back after paying (the change). It can also mean running quick errands ('dar las vueltas') or going around/turns depending on context. Gender/plural: 'la vuelta' (singular) = one return/one lap/one errand; 'las vueltas' (plural) = the change or multiple trips. Context determines meaning — in a shop '¿Me das las vueltas?' = 'Can you give me the change?'.
target_language_example: Perdí las vueltas que me dio el cajero; eran veinte pesos.
native_language_example: I lost the change the cashier gave me; it was twenty pesos.

meaning: on the outskirts of the (town/city); just outside the
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is located just outside a town or city. Typically followed by a place: "las afueras de la ciudad" (the outskirts of the city). Can be singular contextually (la afueras is always plural in Spanish: las afueras). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Vivo en las afueras de la ciudad, cerca de un parque.
native_language_example: I live on the outskirts of the city, near a park.

meaning: 'the girls of' / 'the girls who/with/from' (depends on context).
additional_notes: A noun phrase: 'las chicas' = 'the girls'. The preposition 'de' can mean possession (girls of the class), origin (girls from X), characteristic (girls with long hair), age (girls of my age), or introduce a clause (girls who...). Translate depending on what follows. In some sentences 'de' combines with a noun (de la clase, de mi edad) or with a relative idea (de verdad = really).
target_language_example: Las chicas de la escuela ganaron el concurso.
native_language_example: The girls from the school won the contest.

meaning: 'to the girls' (used with verbs like gustar/encantar to indicate who likes something).
additional_notes: This is part of the gustar-style construction: A + indirect object (a las chicas) + indirect-object pronoun (les) + verb (gusta/gustan/encanta). It literally marks 'to the girls' and is followed by what they like. The pronoun 'les' agrees with 'las chicas' and remains 'les' even if the thing liked is singular or plural (the verb changes: gusta vs. gustan).
target_language_example: A las chicas les gusta la nueva canción.
native_language_example: The girls like the new song.

meaning: the largest cities
additional_notes: Used to refer to cities with the greatest size — usually by population but sometimes by area. 'Las' is the feminine plural article matching 'ciudades'. 'Más' is used to form the comparative/superlative 'more/most'. Can appear in different contexts (e.g., 'las ciudades más grandes del país' = the country's largest cities).
target_language_example: Las ciudades más grandes de España son Madrid y Barcelona.
native_language_example: The largest cities in Spain are Madrid and Barcelona.

meaning: the things of the / the things on the (depending on context)
additional_notes: Very general phrase: 'las cosas' = 'the things' and 'de la' is a feminine singular preposition + article ('of the' or 'from the' or 'on the' depending on noun). Meaning depends on the noun that follows (e.g., 'las cosas de la lista' = items on the list; 'las cosas de la mesa' = things on the table; 'las cosas de la naturaleza' = things of nature). Often used to refer to objects, items, or abstract 'things'.
target_language_example: Quita las cosas de la mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Remove the things from the table, please.

meaning: the phrase used to say 'four o'clock', followed by a time-of-day specification (e.g., de la mañana/tarde/noche).
additional_notes: In Spanish you usually say the hour plus a time-of-day phrase: 'las cuatro de la mañana' (4:00 AM), 'las cuatro de la tarde' (4:00 PM). 'De' links the hour to the period of day. If you just say 'son las cuatro' it means 4:00 (context or added phrase clarifies AM/PM).
target_language_example: La fiesta empieza a las cuatro de la tarde.
native_language_example: The party starts at four in the afternoon.

meaning: ten o'clock (10:00).
additional_notes: Used to tell the time or talk about events happening at 10:00. In Spanish, times use the definite article (las for hours except 1:00 which uses la). Can appear with 'a' or 'a las' to indicate 'at ten' (e.g., 'a las diez').
target_language_example: La película empieza a las diez.
native_language_example: The movie starts at ten o'clock.

meaning: the time 'ten o'clock' followed by a period of day (e.g., morning/night).
additional_notes: Used to say 'at ten o'clock' with a specified part of the day: 'las diez de la mañana' (10 AM) or 'las diez de la noche' (10 PM). In Spanish time expressions use definite article(s): 'a las diez' = 'at ten'. 'De la' links the hour to the period of day.
target_language_example: Quedamos a las diez de la mañana en la cafetería.
native_language_example: We meet at ten in the morning at the café.

meaning: used to tell time: 'two o'clock and...' (start of a time like 'two and ... minutes' or 'two thirty').
additional_notes: Combine with a number or palabra for minutes (e.g., 'las dos y diez' = 2:10) or with 'media' for half past (e.g., 'las dos y media' = 2:30). In Spanish, the feminine article 'las' is used for all hours from 1 to 12 except 'la una'. Native speakers often drop 'las' in casual speech when context is clear.
target_language_example: Te espero en el café a las dos y cuarto.
native_language_example: I'll wait for you at the café at 2:15.

meaning: the leaves of the (plural masculine noun).
additional_notes: A common phrase used to talk about leaves belonging to plural masculine nouns (e.g., los árboles). 'Las hojas' is feminine plural; 'de los' indicates possession from a masculine plural noun. You can replace 'los' with other articles/pronouns as needed (de las, del, de la, de mi, etc.).
target_language_example: En otoño caen las hojas de los árboles.
native_language_example: In autumn the leaves of the trees fall.

meaning: part of the phrase 'dar (poner) las manos a' meaning 'to give (put) one's hands to' — used in idioms like 'dar las manos a palmear' or more likely incomplete fragment; by itself it refers to 'the hands to'.
additional_notes: This appears to be an incomplete fragment rather than a standalone fixed phrase. In Spanish, 'las manos a' commonly appears inside larger expressions such as 'poner las manos a' (to put one's hands on/into), 'echar las manos a' (to grab/lay hands on), or 'dar las manos a' (to join hands). Choose the full verb+phrase (e.g., 'echar las manos a algo', 'poner las manos en') to convey a clear action. For beginners: learn complete verb phrases with 'las manos' plus a preposition (a/en/por) depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Echó las manos a la bolsa para buscar su teléfono.
native_language_example: He put his hands into the bag to look for his phone.

las mujeres viven más que los

target_language_multi_word_term: las mujeres viven más que los
meaning: women live longer than (men).
additional_notes: This phrase compares average lifespans: 'las mujeres' (women) + 'viven más que' (live more than) + 'los' (the, typically followed by 'hombres' — men). It's used to state or ask about a general comparison. You can complete the phrase with the group being compared (e.g., 'los hombres').
target_language_example: En mi familia, las mujeres viven más que los hombres.
native_language_example: In my family, women live longer than men.

meaning: 'nine o'clock' (part of a time expression: 'las nueve de la mañana/tarde/noche')
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a time expression. Complete it with mañana, tarde, or noche (or other time words) to indicate AM/PM or context: 'las nueve de la mañana' = 9:00 AM. Use 'las' because reloj hours (except 1:00) are feminine plural in Spanish. For 1:00 use 'la una de la...'.
target_language_example: La reunión empieza a las nueve de la mañana.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at nine in the morning.

meaning: a time expression meaning 'eight o'clock (of the) —' used before specifying morning/evening or a place (e.g., 'las ocho de la mañana').
additional_notes: Commonly completed with words like 'mañana' (morning), 'tarde' (afternoon), 'noche' (night) or a location/part of day. Spanish uses feminine plural 'las' with 'ocho' because 'hora' is feminine (las ocho (horas)). In speech you'll often hear the full phrase 'las ocho de la mañana' or the shorter 'a las ocho' to mean 'at eight.'
target_language_example: La reunión es a las ocho de la mañana.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eight in the morning.

meaning: used to tell time: 'eight and...' as in 'eight and a half' (8:30) or 'eight and [minutes]'.
additional_notes: Common in clock-time expressions. Spanish often uses 'las ocho y media' for 8:30 ('eight and a half') and 'las ocho y cuarto' for 8:15 ('eight and a quarter'). After 'y' you add minutes (e.g., 'las ocho y veinte' = 8:20). When giving full hours without minutes, Spanish uses 'las ocho' (8:00).
target_language_example: La reunión es a las ocho y cuarto.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eight fifteen (8:15).

meaning: 'sunsets' (literally 'the settings' — short for 'las puestas de sol')
additional_notes: In Spanish, 'puesta de sol' means 'sunset'. Speakers often say simply 'las puestas' when context makes clear they mean 'de sol' (sunsets). It's a plural feminine noun phrase: 'la puesta (de sol)' → 'las puestas (de sol)'. Common verbs: amar, encantar, gustar.
target_language_example: Me gustan las puestas (de sol) en la playa.
native_language_example: I like the sunsets on the beach.

meaning: "six o'clock (in the)" — used to say 6:00 with a time of day (morning/afternoon).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'las seis de la mañana' (6:00 AM) or 'las seis de la tarde' (6:00 PM). Spanish uses definite article 'las' for times (e.g., 'son las seis' = it's six o'clock). Followed by 'de la mañana/tarde/noche' to specify time of day.
target_language_example: Nos vemos mañana a las seis de la tarde.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow at six in the evening.

meaning: at three o'clock (used with a time of day like 'la mañana' or 'la tarde').
additional_notes: This phrase combines a specific hour (las tres) with 'de' to introduce the part of the day that follows: 'de la mañana' (AM), 'de la tarde' (PM/afternoon), or 'de la noche' (evening/night). Common in spoken and written Spanish to say when something happens. You can replace 'tres' with any hour: 'las cuatro de la tarde', 'la una de la mañana' (note: use 'la' for 1 o'clock).
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las tres de la tarde en la cafetería.
native_language_example: We'll meet at three in the afternoon at the café.

meaning: 'three o'clock and' used to tell times (e.g., 'las tres y media' = 3:30).
additional_notes: In Spanish, times after the hour are expressed with 'y' (and). Common phrases: 'las tres y cuarto' (3:15), 'las tres y media' (3:30), 'las tres y cinco' (3:05). Use 'las' for plural hours (except 1:00 uses 'la una'). You can also say ranges with 'entre las tres y las cinco' (between 3 and 5).
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las tres y cuarto en la cafetería.
native_language_example: We'll meet at 3:15 at the café.

meaning: a short form meaning 'the ones/of the (feminine) from the...'; refers to feminine plural things belonging to or associated with someone or something mentioned.
additional_notes: Used to avoid repeating a noun. 'Las' marks feminine plural; 'de la' indicates possession or association with a feminine singular noun that follows or is understood from context. English equivalents: 'the ones from the...', 'those of the...'. Context decides the omitted noun (e.g., huellas, recetas, cosas).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres las de la maleta o las de la caja?
native_language_example: Do you want the ones from the suitcase or the ones from the box?

meaning: both (feminine) / the two (feminine).
additional_notes: Used to refer to two feminine people or feminine nouns previously mentioned or understood from context. Can mean 'both' (as a pronoun) or 'the two [of them]'. If referring to mixed-gender or masculine pairs, use 'los dos'.
target_language_example: Las dos hablamos por teléfono anoche.
native_language_example: Both of us spoke on the phone last night.

meaning: there are some
additional_notes: Used to refer back to previously mentioned feminine plural things (las) in an impersonal construction with haber (hay). Often contrasts existence vs. nonexistence: 'aquí no las hay' = 'there aren't any (of them) here'. Can also be used generally: 'las hay buenas' = 'there are good ones'. The gender/number of the article (las) matches the noun being referenced (las for feminine plural; use los for masculine plural).
target_language_example: No quiero esas galletas; aquí no las hay.
native_language_example: I don't want those cookies; there aren't any here.

meaning: to wash one's hands
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase (lavarse) indicating someone washes their own hands. Commonly used literally for hygiene (agua y jabón) and figuratively to mean avoiding responsibility (similar to English "wash one's hands of something"). The reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) agrees with the subject: voy a lavarme, quiere lavarse, lávate, lávense, etc.
target_language_example: Tom usó agua y jabón para lavarse las manos.
native_language_example: Tom used water and soap to wash his hands.

meaning: I wash the
additional_notes: First-person singular present of lavar (to wash) + definite plural masculine article los. Used before a plural masculine noun (e.g., los dientes, los calcetines, los platos). In contexts like 'los dientes' it translates naturally as 'I brush the' in English, though literal meaning is 'I wash the'. The subject can be explicit (yo) or implied; reflexive forms appear with me (me lavo los dientes = I brush my teeth).
target_language_example: Me lavo los dientes antes de salir.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth before leaving.

meaning: 'he/she/you (formal) opened (for/to) him/her/you' — past tense of abrir with an indirect object (le).
additional_notes: Le is an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him/her/you (formal)'. Abrió is the third-person singular preterite of abrir (to open). Together they indicate someone opened something for or to someone, or gave someone access/experience (literal or figurative). Context decides the direct object (puerta, corazón, bata, un mundo). Spanish word order can place the pronoun before the verb (le abrió) or attached to an infinitive/gerund/imperative in other contexts.
target_language_example: Él le abrió la mochila y sacó el libro.
native_language_example: He opened the backpack for him and took out the book.

meaning: I assure you (formal) / I assure him/her/you (formal).
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to give assurance. 'Le' is an indirect object pronoun: can mean 'to you (formal)', 'to him' or 'to her' depending on context. Common in statements like 'Le aseguro que...'(I assure you that...). Use 'te aseguro' in informal situations with 'tú'.
target_language_example: Le aseguro que recibirá una respuesta mañana.
native_language_example: I assure you that you will receive a response tomorrow.

meaning: '(he/she/they) like you' or 'you make a good impression on (him/her/them)'.
additional_notes: From the verb caer bien (to like someone / to get along with someone). 'Le' is an indirect object pronoun referring to him/her/usted/ella/él or a polite/formal subject; 'caes' is the second-person singular (tú) form. Commonly used to say someone likes you (Le caes bien = He/She likes you). To specify who likes you, add a phrase with 'a' + name or pronoun: 'A mi hermano le caes bien.' Negation: 'no le caes bien' = 'he/she doesn't like you.'
target_language_example: A Marta le caes muy bien.
native_language_example: Marta really likes you.

meaning: I gave her/him/them the (feminine) — literal sequence 'le' (to him/her), 'di' (I gave), 'las' (them, feminine).
additional_notes: This sequence looks like three separate pronouns/verb forms that could appear in a sentence but as written together is ungrammatical in standard Spanish. More likely you'd see: 'le di las flores' (I gave him/her the flowers) or the clitic order: 'se las di' (I gave them to him/her). 'Le' is an indirect object pronoun (to him/her), 'di' is the first-person past of 'dar' (I gave), and 'las' is a feminine direct object pronoun (them, feminine). In normal speech the pronouns cannot both appear after the verb as 'di las'; instead you place pronouns before the verb (e.g., 'se las di') or attach to an infinitive/gerund/affirmative command.
target_language_example: Le di las flores a María.
native_language_example: I gave the flowers to María.

meaning: I found him/her / I found for him/her (depends on context).
additional_notes: Spanish uses 'encontré' (I found) with the indirect object pronoun 'le' to mean different things: 'le encontré + gerund' = I found him/her doing something (I came upon him/her). 'Le encontré + noun' can mean I found someone/something for him/her (I obtained/found X on his/her behalf) or I considered him/her to be X (less common). With 'me le encontré' it means 'I ran into him/her' (I found him/her by chance). Context decides whether 'le' is 'him' or 'her' and whether 'encontré' means 'found', 'ran into', or 'found/obtained for'.
target_language_example: Le encontré esperando en la puerta cuando llegué.
native_language_example: I found him/her waiting at the door when I arrived.

meaning: writes to him/her/you (indirect object: 'le' = to him/her/you formal).
additional_notes: Uses the indirect object pronoun 'le' before the verb 'escribe' (from escribir). 'Le' indicates the person receiving the writing (to him, to her, or to you formal). Common structure: [Subject] + le + escribe + a + [recipient] (recipient can be explicit). Often used with people (padre, madre, hijo, tío).
target_language_example: María le escribe a su abuela todos los domingos.
native_language_example: María writes to her grandmother every Sunday.

meaning: he/she/you(formal) wrote (to) him/her/you a (feminine) [letter/note].
additional_notes: This phrase shows indirect object pronoun 'le' (to him/her/you formal) + past of escribir (escribió) + the feminine indefinite article 'una' introducing a feminine noun (commonly 'carta'). In Spanish word order the indirect object pronoun often appears before the verb; the person receiving the action can be repeated after the verb with a phrase like 'a su hijo' for clarity. The exact noun after 'una' is usually specified (una carta, una nota, una carta larga).
target_language_example: El profesor le escribió una nota a la estudiante.
native_language_example: The teacher wrote her a note.

meaning: 'awaits him/her/you/it' or 'is in store for him/her/you/it'.
additional_notes: Combination of indirect object pronoun 'le' (to him/her/you formal) + verb 'esperar' in third person singular. Used to say that something awaits or will happen to someone. Context decides who 'le' refers to (he, she, you formal). Can be translated as 'waits for him/her' when literal or more naturally as 'is in store for him/her'.
target_language_example: No sabe lo que le espera después de la reunión.
native_language_example: He doesn't know what awaits him after the meeting.

meaning: they are (doing something) to you / you are being (done to) — 'le' = indirect object pronoun (to/for him/her/you formal), 'están' = they are (present progressive helper).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a present progressive verb (están + gerund) to say someone is doing something to or for someone (e.g., 'le están esperando' = 'they are waiting for you/him/her'). 'Le' can refer to usted, él, or ella depending on context. Word order in Spanish: indirect object pronoun + estar + gerund. In some regions 'le' may be used as a polite 'you' (usted).
target_language_example: Le están buscando en la oficina.
native_language_example: They are looking for you/him/her in the office.

meaning: 'you are (verb) to him/her/it' — you are doing something to/for him/her/it (present progressive with indirect object pronoun le).
additional_notes: Le is the indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him/her/it' (or sometimes a polite 'you' in some regions). Estás is the second-person singular present of estar. Together they precede a gerund (estás + -ando/-iendo) or a participle/verb phrase to indicate an action directed at that indirect object: e.g. 'le estás haciendo' = 'you are doing (something) for him/her'. Word order can vary (Te lo estás diciendo / Estás diciéndoselo), but 'le estás' commonly appears before the verb.
target_language_example: Le estás contando el secreto a tu amigo.
native_language_example: You are telling the secret to your friend.

meaning: Literal reading (unnatural word order): 'it/her/him is pleasing to her' — likely intended meaning: 'a ella le gusta' = 'she likes (it)'.
additional_notes: The string 'le gusta ella' is not standard Spanish word order. Spanish normally places the indirect object pronoun (le) before the verb and the clarified indirect object (a ella) before the pronoun if used for emphasis: 'A ella le gusta...'. Writing 'le gusta ella' (verb then noun phrase) is unidiomatic and can cause ambiguity; it may be heard in colloquial speech for emphasis or as a fragment, but avoid it in neutral writing. Remember: gustar's grammatical subject is the thing liked, and the person who likes appears as an indirect object pronoun (le/les) often with a prepositional phrase for clarity (a ella).
target_language_example: Le gusta ella la idea, pero no está segura.
native_language_example: She likes the idea, but she isn't sure.

meaning: 'he/she/you (formal) likes it' or 'it pleases him/her/you (formal)'.
additional_notes: This is a combination of the indirect object pronoun le + gusta + the neutral article lo. It's used to say that something (often an idea, action, or unspecified thing) pleases someone. In natural Spanish you will more often see structures like 'le gusta' + a noun ('Le gusta el chocolate') or 'le gusta + infinitive' ('Le gusta bailar'). 'Le gusta lo...' can introduce a clause or noun phrase: e.g. 'Le gusta lo que haces' (He/She likes what you do).
target_language_example: Le gusta lo que dijiste en la reunión.
native_language_example: He/She liked what you said at the meeting.

meaning: he/she likes him (emphatic word order: 'him is liked by her' or 'she likes him').
additional_notes: This is a word-order pattern used for emphasis or clarity: the indirect-object pronoun 'le' indicates 'to him/her' (here meaning 'he' as the person being liked), and the subject is the person who feels the liking (often introduced with 'a + name/pronoun' for clarity). In the examples, 'A ella le gusta él' literally frames it as 'To her, he is pleasing' = 'She likes him.' The structure often appears with 'a + person' to avoid ambiguity (because 'le' can mean 'to him' or 'to her').
target_language_example: A Mariana le gusta él, pero a él le gusta su mejor amiga.
native_language_example: Mariana likes him, but he likes his best friend.

meaning: '(that) you speak to him/her/it/you (polite)'; negative: 'don't speak to him/her/it'.
additional_notes: From the verb 'hablar' (to speak) with the indirect-object pronoun 'le' (to him/her/you formal). 'Le hables' appears in subjunctive or imperative contexts: e.g., 'Necesito que le hables' (I need you to speak to him/her) uses the present subjunctive. In commands or warnings Spanish often uses 'No le hables' for 'Don't talk to him/her' (negative tú imperative uses the subjunctive form). 'Le' refers to an indirect object (to/for someone). If you need to clarify gender or emphasis, Spanish speakers often add 'a él', 'a ella' or 'a usted' after the verb.
target_language_example: Por favor, no le hables así a mi hermana.
native_language_example: Please, don't talk to my sister like that.

meaning: you do to him/her/it
additional_notes: Second-person singular present (tú) of hacer plus indirect object pronoun le. Commonly used to say you cause or do something to someone (e.g., cause an effect, do a favor, make someone have an experience). English translations vary by context: 'you make him/her...', 'you do for him/her', 'you give him/her'. 'Le' can refer to him, her, or a neutral/impersonal 'one' in some dialects (leísmo).
target_language_example: Si le haces una sorpresa, la va a recordar siempre.
native_language_example: If you give him/her a surprise, he/she will remember it forever.

meaning: 'they did to him/her' or 'they did to (someone)'.
additional_notes: Phrase combines indirect object pronoun 'le' (to him/her/you formal) + past tense of 'hacer' (hicieron) + preposition 'a' + the person affected. Used to talk about something done to someone (often something bad). In English you can render it as 'they did to [name]' or 'they did to him/her'. If the person is plural (them) Spanish would use 'les hicieron a'.
target_language_example: No puedo creer lo que le hicieron a María.
native_language_example: I can't believe what they did to María.

meaning: we (caused something) to him/her/you (formal) / we did (something) for him/her/you (formal).
additional_notes: Compound of indirect object pronoun 'le' (to/for him, her, or usted) + preterite 'hicimos' (we did/made). Often used to indicate that we did something affecting that person (e.g., made them feel, gave them something, made them believe). The exact English translation depends on the verb that follows or the implied action. 'Le' can refer to a person; context determines gender and formality.
target_language_example: Le hicimos una sorpresa por su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: We surprised him/her for his/her birthday.

meaning: doesn't care at all (lit. 'it matters to him/her/it a [small/nothing]'), used with colloquial intensifiers like 'bledo', 'pito', 'carajo' to mean 'doesn't care a bit'.
additional_notes: This phrase is used with indirect object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/os/les) + 'importa un' + a colloquial word (bledo, pito, carajo, céntimo, etc.) to express that someone doesn't care at all. Tone ranges from neutral colloquial ('no le importa un bledo') to stronger vulgarity ('no le importa un carajo'). Common structure: 'A + person + le importa un + [word] + (lo que...)'.
target_language_example: A ella no le importa un bledo lo que digan los demás.
native_language_example: She doesn't care at all what others say.

meaning: a good (idea/solution) occurred to him/her — 'he/she had a good idea'.
additional_notes: This phrase is part of the impersonal/semi-impersonal construction 'se le ocurrió (una idea/solución)' meaning 'it occurred to him/her' or 'he/she came up with'. Use 'le' for third person (él/ella/usted) and match the noun: 'una buena idea', 'una buena solución'. Commonly used to say someone suddenly thought of something.
target_language_example: A María se le ocurrió una buena idea para la fiesta.
native_language_example: María had a good idea for the party.

meaning: he/she forgot (something) — with indirect object pronoun showing who forgot.
additional_notes: This construction uses the indirect object pronoun (le) + past tense of olvidar to indicate that something was forgotten by or happened to someone. In Spanish it's common to add 'se' (se le olvidó) to make the verb impersonal or to emphasize that the forgetting occurred to the person (more natural than 'él olvidó' in many contexts). Use se le olvidó + infinitive or noun: se le olvidó llamar / se le olvidó la cita. For different persons change the pronoun: me/te/le/nos/os/les.
target_language_example: A Marta se le olvidó el paraguas y se mojó.
native_language_example: Marta forgot her umbrella and got wet.

meaning: 'seemed to him/her' or 'it seemed to him/her' (used to express someone's impression or opinion)
additional_notes: Impersonal construction using the indirect object pronoun 'le' (to him/her/you formal) + imperfect of 'parecer' (to seem). Common to report opinions, impressions, or perceived durations. Subject can be a noun, adjective, clause, or time expression. For other persons use 'me parecía', 'te parecía', 'nos parecía', 'les parecía'.
target_language_example: A él le parecía una buena oportunidad.
native_language_example: It seemed like a good opportunity to him.

meaning: 'has/has left' or 'has remaining' (something left for someone).
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun (le, les, me, nos, etc.) plus a noun to say how much time, quantity, or items remain for someone. Verb agrees in number with the thing remaining (quedan tres meses, queda un mes). Can also be used with clothing/items to mean 'they fit him/her well' when followed by adverb (e.g., le quedan bien).
target_language_example: A María le quedan cuatro días para el examen.
native_language_example: María has four days left until the exam.

meaning: he/she/it was left with / he/she had (resulting state); or 'had no choice' in set phrases.
additional_notes: Commonly uses the indirect object pronoun 'le' to indicate the person affected. 'Quedar' here expresses a resulting state (e.g., a scar remained, a face was left swollen) or lack of alternatives in expressions like 'no le quedó otra' (he/she had no other option). Can combine with reflexive forms (se le quedó) when describing reactions or physical/mental states left on someone.
target_language_example: Después de la operación, le quedó una cicatriz pequeña.
native_language_example: After the surgery, he/she was left with a small scar.

meaning: I remind him/her/you (formal) / I remember him/her/you (formal) — context-dependent.
additional_notes: Spanish 'recordar' can mean either 'to remember' or 'to remind'. With an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) plus the verb 'recuerdo' the phrase can mean 'I remember him/her/you (formal)' (e.g., 'Sí, le recuerdo' = 'Yes, I remember him/her/you') or 'I remind him/her/you' when used with a direct object or clause (e.g., 'Le recuerdo que...'). Context and presence of a following object/clause tell you which meaning is intended. 'Le' is the indirect object pronoun for 'to him/to her/to you (formal)'.
target_language_example: Le recuerdo que la reunión es mañana a las nueve.
native_language_example: I remind him/her/you that the meeting is tomorrow at nine.

meaning: is going to (for him/her/you formal)
