target_language_example: Estamos en medio de una tormenta emocional.
native_language_example: We are in the middle of an emotional storm.

meaning: 'middle one is' or 'the middle one is' (used to identify something/someone in the middle)
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'el del medio es...' / 'la del medio es...' to say that the middle person/item belongs to someone or has a property. 'Del' is contraction of 'de' + 'el'. Gender (el/la) and possession (mío/mía) must agree with the noun referred to. Often used in contexts like pointing to objects, people in a row, or fingers (e.g., 'el dedo del medio').
target_language_example: La del medio es la más bonita.
native_language_example: The one in the middle is the prettiest.

meaning: halftime (the break between the two halves of a game); also can mean 'half-time' as an adjective/phrase.
additional_notes: Used primarily in sports to refer to the break between the first and second halves (halftime) or anything happening during that break (e.g., a halftime show). Can also appear in contexts describing a 'half-time' duration. Pronounced as two words. Not slang.
target_language_example: El concierto del medio tiempo fue espectacular.
native_language_example: The halftime show was spectacular.

meaning: someone's best friend / the best friend of (someone).
additional_notes: Use this to say who someone's best friend is. It is followed by the person (mi, su, de + name/pronoun). Word-for-word it means 'best friend of'. Common in possessive phrases: 'el mejor amigo de Juan' = 'Juan's best friend.'
target_language_example: Ella es el mejor amigo de Carlos.
native_language_example: She is Carlos's best friend.

meaning: the best of the (feminine plural) / 'the very best' (in comparisons or expressions).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean 'the best of the [group]' or more generally 'the very best'. Often appears in fixed expressions (e.g., 'la mejor de las intenciones' = 'the best of intentions'). Can be used emphatically or rhetorically in comparisons: 'es la mejor de las X, o la peor de las Y.' Agreement matters: 'mejor de los' for masculine plural, 'mejor de la' for singular feminine.
target_language_example: Ella es la mejor de las amigas que tengo.
native_language_example: She is the best of the friends I have.

meaning: 'the best of the' or 'the best (one) of the'
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the best among a group or category. Often followed by a noun or phrase indicating the group (e.g., sueños, dos, cumpleaños, tratamientos). Can be used with definite articles and sometimes with numbers (el mejor de los dos).
target_language_example: Ella tiene el mejor de los recuerdos de su viaje.
native_language_example: She has the best of the memories from her trip.

meaning: the best (of) scenarios; in the best case(s)
additional_notes: Used to describe the most favorable possible outcome. Often appears in phrases like "en el mejor de los casos" (in the best-case scenario). Can be used to contrast with worse possibilities (e.g., "en el peor de los casos").
target_language_example: En el mejor de los casos, llegaremos a tiempo.
native_language_example: In the best-case scenario, we'll arrive on time.

meaning: 'the best of me' — the best effort, qualities, or part of oneself.
additional_notes: Used to refer to giving one's best effort or showing one's best qualities. Common in phrases like dar lo mejor de mí (to give the best of myself). Can be literal (the best part of a person) or figurative (maximum effort). Often appears with verbs like dar, mostrar, sacar.
target_language_example: Siempre trato de dar lo mejor de mí en el trabajo.
native_language_example: I always try to give the best of myself at work.

meaning: best decision
additional_notes: Used to describe the choice judged as the most favorable or beneficial. Common in statements about past choices (e.g., 'was the best decision I made') and as advice or encouragement (e.g., 'make the best decision'). 'Mejor' modifies 'decisión' (comparative/superlative meaning 'better/best' depending on context).
target_language_example: Tomar ese trabajo fue la mejor decisión que pude haber tomado.
native_language_example: Taking that job was the best decision I could have made.

meaning: the best part of (something); the most enjoyable/valuable part
additional_notes: Used to highlight the most positive, enjoyable, or valuable portion of an event, time period, object, or situation. Common in phrases like "la mejor parte del día" (the best part of the day) or "la mejor parte de la experiencia". Can be used literally (part of a competition) or figuratively (a benefit gained). Often followed by a noun or clause introduced by "que".
target_language_example: La mejor parte de la película fue la escena final.
native_language_example: The best part of the movie was the final scene.

meaning: the best (that someone) could (do/experience); 'the best thing that could have...' or 'the best (he/she/they) could do'.
additional_notes: Often appears in full phrases like 'lo mejor que pudo hacer' (the best thing he/she/they could do) or 'lo mejor que pudo haberme pasado' (the best thing that could have happened to me). Used to evaluate an action or outcome as the best possible under the circumstances. Verb form after 'pudo' can be infinitive (hacer) or part of a perfect/periphrastic construction (pudo haber + past participle).
target_language_example: Mudarse fue lo mejor que pudo hacer por su salud.
native_language_example: Moving was the best thing he/she could do for their health.

meaning: nothing better to do (used in negative constructions: 'no tener nada mejor que hacer').
additional_notes: This phrase usually appears in the negative construction 'no tener nada mejor que hacer' meaning someone has nothing more useful or interesting to occupy their time. It can express boredom, idle curiosity, or mild criticism (e.g., implying someone is wasting time). Use with a subject: 'él/ella/yo no tengo...' or with names.
target_language_example: No tenía nada mejor que hacer, así que lo ayudé.
native_language_example: I had nothing better to do, so I helped him.

meaning: better than the (feminine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: Used to compare qualities; 'mejor que' = 'better than'. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article and agrees with a feminine noun mentioned or implied (la arena, la paz, la salud). For masculine nouns you'd hear 'mejor que el'. Can be used with nouns, pronouns, or clauses.
target_language_example: La comida casera es mejor que la de restaurante.
native_language_example: Homemade food is better than restaurant food.

meaning: It's better that (you) not (do/know/see) it; used to suggest someone should avoid something.
additional_notes: Common fixed phrase beginning with 'Es/Será mejor que no lo...' + verb clause. Often followed by a verb in subjunctive (conozcas, hayas hecho, sepa, hagas) to express advice, warning, or preference that someone not do or know something. Can be softened or strengthened with context (e.g., 'Es mejor que no lo sepas' = 'It's better you don't know'). Pronoun 'lo' refers to a masculine or neutral object/idea mentioned earlier.
target_language_example: Es mejor que no lo digas ahora.
native_language_example: It's better that you don't say it now.

meaning: better now; feeling or being improved at this moment.
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone's condition (health, mood, situation) has improved at the present time. Common in responses to illness or problems. Can be used as a short reply ('Mejor ahora.') meaning 'I'm better now.'
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; me siento mejor ahora.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; I feel better now.

meaning: even better; better still
additional_notes: Used to introduce an improved alternative, stronger point, or to emphasize something preferable. Common in both spoken and written Spanish. Can appear at the start or middle of a sentence: 'Mejor aún, ...' or '... , mejor aún, ...'.
target_language_example: No tienes que venir mañana; mejor aún, quédate en casa y descansa.
native_language_example: You don't have to come tomorrow; even better, stay home and rest.

meaning: 'better to leave' / 'better to go (away)'.
additional_notes: Used to suggest that it would be preferable for someone to leave a place or situation. Often appears with an implied subject (es mejor irse / mejor que te vayas) and can be followed by a reason: "mejor irse ahora" (better to leave now). Tone can be neutral or firm depending on context.
target_language_example: Hace mucho frío, mejor irse antes de que empeore.
native_language_example: It's very cold, better to leave before it gets worse.

meaning: better next time (do better on a future attempt).
additional_notes: Used to encourage improvement after a past attempt or to suggest someone should try again and perform better in the future. Often completed with 'vez' (mejor la próxima vez) but can omit 'vez' in casual speech. Common in advice, encouragement, or gentle criticism.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, cantarás mejor la próxima vez.
native_language_example: Don't worry, you'll sing better next time.

meaning: 'the best years' (usually referring to the best years of someone's life or a best period)
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about a period of life or time that was especially happy, productive, or memorable (e.g., 'los mejores años de mi vida' = the best years of my life). Can be used literally for years or figuratively for a peak period. Often appears with de + noun (de mi vida, de su carrera, etc.).
target_language_example: Pasé los mejores años de mi vida en la universidad.
native_language_example: I spent the best years of my life at university.

meaning: minor; underage (a person under the legal adult age).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is below the legal age of majority. Common in legal, official, and everyday contexts. Often follows a verb (ser/estar) or a name. In English 'minor' or 'underage' are natural equivalents.
target_language_example: María aún es menor de edad, no puede votar.
native_language_example: María is still a minor; she can't vote.

meaning: at least; the least that (one) can do / do for someone.
additional_notes: Used in set phrases like 'es lo menos que (puedo/podemos/puede)...' to express humility or that an action is the minimum deserved or possible. Literally 'less than', but here it conveys 'the least' or 'at least' in English. Common with verbs in different persons (puedo, podemos, puede).
target_language_example: Es lo menos que puedo hacer por ti.
native_language_example: It's the least I can do for you.

meaning: 'except' or 'except for' (used to exclude someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate exclusion. Often placed before the excluded person/thing: 'todos, menos a mí' = 'everyone except me.' In spoken Spanish the 'a' may be omitted with things (menos mí), but is kept with persons when the verb requires the personal 'a' before a direct object (e.g., 'invitaron a todos menos a mí').
target_language_example: Invitaron a toda la oficina, menos a mí.
native_language_example: They invited the whole office, except me.

meaning: except for the (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Used to exclude a feminine singular noun or idea from a general statement. 'Menos' means 'except' or 'minus'; the article 'la' specifies a feminine singular noun (e.g., la ensalada, la paciencia). Can appear in similar forms with other articles/genders (menos el, menos los, menos las).
target_language_example: Lo entiendo todo menos la razón por la que se fue.
native_language_example: I understand everything except the reason why he left.

meaning: less than one (a) / fewer than one
additional_notes: Used to indicate an amount, quantity, time, or portion that is smaller than one unit. Often appears before a feminine noun (una) or before a feminine implied noun (e.g., 'menos de una hora' = less than an hour). If the noun is masculine, use 'menos de un' (e.g., 'menos de un día').
target_language_example: Llegó en menos de una hora.
native_language_example: He arrived in less than an hour.

meaning: thankfully; luckily; it's a good thing
additional_notes: Used to express relief that something turned out better than expected or that a negative outcome was avoided. Common in informal speech. Often appears alone ("¡Menos mal!") or with "que" + clause explaining what was avoided.
target_language_example: Menos mal que traje paraguas; empezó a llover.
native_language_example: Luckily I brought an umbrella; it started to rain.

meaning: less than
additional_notes: Used for comparisons. Use 'less than' for quantities, amounts, or comparisons of degree (menos que). Use 'fewer than' when comparing countable items in English. Can also appear in figurative expressions (e.g., 'soy menos que...' = 'I'm less than...').
target_language_example: Tengo menos que tú en la cuenta bancaria.
native_language_example: I have less than you in the bank account.

meaning: text message (SMS) — a written message sent by phone.
additional_notes: Common, neutral term for a text/SMS. Used both as countable (un mensaje de texto) and in phrases like recibir/ignorar/enviar un mensaje de texto. Can refer to single texts or the content of a text.
target_language_example: Te envié un mensaje de texto con la dirección.
native_language_example: I sent you a text message with the address.

meaning: a message in/on (used to say where a message is placed or found).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a location or medium (e.g., 'mensaje en una botella', 'mensaje en mi contestador', 'mensaje en la televisión'). Use 'mensaje' for 'message' and 'en' to indicate 'in', 'on', or 'via' depending on context. For telling where a message was left or found, use this construction + noun. Word order: 'mensaje en + [lugar/medio]'.
target_language_example: Dejé un mensaje en tu buzón de voz.
native_language_example: I left a message on your voicemail.

meaning: open-minded; willing to consider new ideas or opinions.
additional_notes: Literally 'open mind'. Used to describe a person (or group's) attitude toward new, different, or unfamiliar ideas. Commonly appears with verbs like tener (to have) or mantener (to keep) — e.g., 'tener/mantener la mente abierta'.
target_language_example: Trata de mantener una mente abierta durante la reunión.
native_language_example: Try to keep an open mind during the meeting.

meaning: literally 'mind of' — used to indicate who/what possesses a mind or mentality (e.g., 'the mind of...').
additional_notes: Combines mente (mind) + de (of). Common in phrases like 'la mente de un genio' (the mind of a genius) or metaphorical uses ('mente de víbora' — 'viper's mind' or 'malicious mind'). Often followed by a noun or descriptive phrase; can also appear in expressions describing someone's mindset (e.g., 'mente de metal' = a mind like metal). Because it's compositional, beginners can usually translate it word-for-word.
target_language_example: La mente de la niña está llena de preguntas.
native_language_example: The girl's mind is full of questions.

meaning: 'mind on' or 'mind in' — used to say where someone's attention or thoughts are directed.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in constructions like 'poner la mente en' (to put one's mind on/into) or 'tener la mente en' (to have one's mind on). It indicates focus or attention. Use 'la/tu/nuestra mente en' with a topic or state (e.g., 'la mente en calma', 'la mente en otra cosa').
target_language_example: Trata de poner tu mente en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Try to put your mind on the work.

meaning: 'often when (I/he/she) was...' — describes something that happened frequently in the past.
additional_notes: Use with a past tense (imperfect) to say that an action or habit occurred frequently during a past period of life (e.g., cuando era joven / niño / estudiante). 'Menudo' here means 'often' or 'frequently'.
target_language_example: Iba al parque a menudo cuando era niño.
native_language_example: I used to go to the park often when I was a child.

meaning: 'often' used with a reflexive or passive-like verb construction
additional_notes: A menudo = often. When followed by 'se' it commonly appears with verbs that are reflexive, impersonal, or describe habitual actions (e.g., se compara, se saltan, se pintan). Structure: 'A menudo se + [verb]' or 'A menudo + [subject] + se + [verb]'. Use to talk about things that happen frequently. 'Se' here is not a separate word to translate; it marks the verb's reflexive/impersonal/passive sense.
target_language_example: A menudo se olvidan las llaves en la mesa.
native_language_example: Keys are often forgotten on the table.

meaning: This exact phrase is not used; the correct common phrase is 'a menudo' meaning 'often'.
additional_notes: Use 'a menudo' to say 'often' or 'frequently'. It usually stands alone or appears before a clause: 'a menudo, ...' or 'se dice a menudo que...'. The form 'a menudo que' is not standard — if you see 'a menudo que' it likely comes from 'a menudo' followed by 'que' starting a subordinate clause (e.g., 'a menudo que' = 'often that...'), but in Spanish you normally place 'a menudo' and then 'que' begins the clause without joining them as a fixed phrase.
target_language_example: Se dice a menudo que practicar mejora la memoria.
native_language_example: It is often said that practice improves memory.

meaning: black market (illegal market for goods or currency).
additional_notes: Refers to unofficial, illegal buying or selling—often of prohibited goods, controlled items, or currency at unofficial rates. Commonly used in contexts about buying/selling where legality or regulation is bypassed. Can be used as a noun phrase or shorthand (e.g., "Mercado negro").
target_language_example: Compraron las entradas en el mercado negro.
native_language_example: They bought the tickets on the black market.

meaning: deserves the (feminine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: From the verb merecer (to deserve). 'Merece la' is used before a feminine singular noun or a feminine definite phrase (e.g., 'merece la pena', 'merece la atención'). For masculine nouns use 'merece el' or for plural 'merecen las/los'. Common fixed phrase: 'merece la pena' = 'it's worth it'.
target_language_example: Tu ayuda merece la gratitud de todos.
native_language_example: Your help deserves everyone's gratitude.

meaning: deserves a (something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is worthy of or should receive whatever follows (a noun): e.g., un trago, un ascenso, un trato justo. Often followed by a noun phrase. Conjugation: merece (he/she/it deserves); other forms: merezco, mereces, merecen.
target_language_example: Después de tanto trabajo, ella merece un descanso.
native_language_example: After so much work, she deserves a rest.

meaning: one more month / the most (adjective) month (depends on context)
additional_notes: This phrase can mean two different things depending on word order and context: 1) As in 'un mes más' it means 'one more month' or 'another month' (adding time). 2) As in 'el mes más + adjective' it is the superlative construction 'the most ... month' (e.g., 'el mes más caluroso' = 'the hottest month'). Pay attention to articles and adjectives to tell which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Necesito un mes más para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: I need one more month to finish the project.

meaning: month (remaining) until / month to (do something); 'a month left to' or 'a month to' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used when talking about a time period of one month related to a future event or purpose. Often appears with verbs like quedar (to have remaining), esperar (to wait), dar (to give), or followed by an infinitive or a clause introduced by que. English equivalents: 'a month until...', 'give/wait a month for...', or 'this month to (do something)'.
target_language_example: Tengo un mes para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: I have a month to finish the project.

meaning: 'table with' — used to describe a table that has or is acted on by something.
additional_notes: This is the noun 'mesa' (table) followed by the preposition 'con' (with). It can describe possession ('a table with X') or be part of a larger phrase describing an action using the table (e.g., 'golpeó la mesa con el puño' — 'he hit the table with his fist'). Word order and surrounding words determine exact meaning. Not an idiom; fully literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Pusieron el florero sobre la mesa con el mantel azul.
native_language_example: They put the vase on the table with the blue tablecloth.

meaning: ‘table for’ or ‘table to/for (a purpose or destination)’ depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase combines mesa (table) with the preposition para. It can mean 'a table for X' (e.g., mesa para el salón = a table for the living room; mesa para dos = table for two). With verbs, para can indicate purpose or direction: 'mesa para afuera' = take the table outside; 'le di la vuelta a la mesa para arreglarla' = I turned the table over in order to fix it (para + infinitive = 'in order to'). Pay attention to context to choose the correct English translation.
target_language_example: Reservé una mesa para cuatro en el restaurante.
native_language_example: I reserved a table for four at the restaurant.

meaning: mesa (table) + y (and). It's the noun 'mesa' followed by the conjunction 'y' — used when 'mesa' begins a phrase that continues with 'and'.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's simply the word 'mesa' (table) immediately followed by 'y' (and). Beginners may see this sequence in texts where 'mesa' is listed together with other items or followed by another phrase. Pay attention to punctuation and context: in sentence 2 the phrase 'en la mesa y ella abajo' contrasts positions; in sentence 3 'suba a la mesa y baile' uses 'y' to link two verbs (rise to the table and dance).
target_language_example: Puse la planta en la mesa y la lámpara al lado.
native_language_example: I put the plant on the table and the lamp beside it.

meaning: for (a) months in the ... / spent months in the ...
additional_notes: A common Spanish sequence used to say how long someone stayed or spent time in a place: [number] meses en el + location (masculine singular noun or definite article). Use "meses en la" for feminine places (e.g., "meses en la ciudad"). For expressing duration with a specific place, English often uses "for X months in [place]" or "spent X months in [place]."
target_language_example: Pasé dos meses en el sur de España.
native_language_example: I spent two months in the south of Spain.

meaning: 'puts (something) in' or 'sticks (something) in' (3rd person singular, indicative: meter + feminine singular direct object).
additional_notes: From the verb meter (to put, insert, stick). 'Mete la' appears before a feminine singular noun (la) or as part of idiomatic expressions (mete la nariz, mete la mano, mete la pierna). Usage often implies physically placing or inserting something, or intruding (e.g., mete la nariz = sticks his/her nose into). Tone can be neutral or colloquial; context determines meaning and force.
target_language_example: Se mete la chaqueta antes de salir.
native_language_example: He puts on the jacket before leaving.

meaning: 'to put (something or someone) into; to insert; to cause or get someone to do something; to get someone into (trouble)' (depends on context).
additional_notes: "Meter a" + noun usually means to place or put something/someone into or inside a place or container (e.g., meter a la caja = to put into the box). "Meter a" + infinitive can mean to cause or make someone do an action (often colloquial) or to get someone into trouble (e.g., meter a alguien en problemas). It is a verb (meter) followed by the preposition a; the exact meaning depends on the following noun or infinitive and on context. Common in everyday speech; register can be neutral to colloquial depending on phrasing.
target_language_example: Voy a meter a los libros en la caja ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I'm going to put the books into the box right now.

meaning: to make a mistake; to put one's foot in it (to blunder or embarrass oneself).
additional_notes: Informal idiom common in spoken Spanish. Often used in past tense (e.g., 'metí la pata'). Refers to social or general blunders; can describe saying something inappropriate or committing an obvious error.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no quería meter la pata delante de todos.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn't mean to put my foot in it in front of everyone.

meaning: to pick a fight with; to mess with; to bother or get involved with someone (usually negative or threatening).
additional_notes: Commonly used in informal speech. Often appears in prohibitions or warnings (e.g., "no meterse con..."). Can imply verbal or physical confrontation or interference. Tone can range from a light tease to a serious threat depending on context.
target_language_example: Es mejor no meterse con él.
native_language_example: It's better not to mess with him.

meaning: to get into; to enter (physically) or to become involved/interfere in (a situation or someone's affairs)
additional_notes: Literal: 'to put oneself into'. Used for physical entry (meterse en la piscina = get into the pool) and figurative involvement (meterse en problemas = get into trouble; meterse en la vida de alguien = meddle). Context determines whether neutral, positive, or negative. Reflexive verb form: meterse (conjugate the reflexive pronoun).
target_language_example: No deberían meterse en mi vida.
native_language_example: You shouldn't get involved in / meddle in my life.

meaning: something got into (a body part) — used to say an object accidentally entered someone's body part (commonly the eye, nose, or mouth).
additional_notes: Often appears with an indirect-object pronoun and reflexive construction (se le metió algo en el ojo) to indicate that something entered someone's body part unintentionally. Replace 'el ojo' with other masculine body parts (el ojo, el dedo — note some body parts are feminine: la nariz, la boca). The literal subject is 'algo' (something) while the affected person is expressed with pronouns (me, te, se, le, nos, os, les). Used to explain sudden discomfort or irritation.
target_language_example: A ella se le metió algo en el ojo cuando caminaba por la playa.
native_language_example: Something got into her eye when she was walking on the beach.

meaning: put the / placed the (masculine singular object) — past simple (preterite) of meter (to put) plus masculine definite article 'el'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone put or placed a specific masculine noun somewhere. If the verb is reflexive (meterse), it can mean to put something into one's own clothing or to go into/into oneself (context matters); reflexive pronoun appears before 'metió' (e.g., 'se metió el pañuelo' = put the handkerchief into his pocket). The noun must be masculine singular because of 'el' (e.g., el libro, el jamón, el bolsillo).
target_language_example: Ella metió el teléfono en la bolsa.
native_language_example: She put the phone in the bag.

meaning: entered/put (someone or something) into the...
additional_notes: From the verb 'meter(se)' meaning to put or to get into. 'Metió en el' is the past (pretérito) third-person singular of 'meter' + 'en el' (into the). Often used with a place or container: metió en el coche (he/she got into the car), nos metió en el congelador (he/she put us in the freezer). If the subject is reflexive (meterse), it means the person entered: 'se metió en el coche' = 'he got into the car.' Watch word order: 'se metió en el coche' vs 'metió en el coche a Juan' (he put Juan into the car).
target_language_example: Ella metió en el bolso las llaves.
native_language_example: She put the keys in the bag.

meaning: literally 'put/shot a (feminine noun)'; used to say someone inserted, threw, or caused something (often sudden or violent) into/into someone or something.
additional_notes: Metió is the past tense (él/ella/usted) of meter (to put/insert). With 'una' it introduces a feminine noun (una bala, una mosca). Context determines meaning: can be literal (inserted, put in) or idiomatic (sudden occurrence, e.g., 'se me metió una mosca en el ojo' = a fly got into my eye). Often used in passive-like constructions to describe an action done to someone.
target_language_example: Alguien me metió una piedra en el zapato.
native_language_example: Someone put a stone in my shoe.

meaning: I put (something feminine) / I inserted (something feminine) — first-person singular past of meter + feminine direct object article.
additional_notes: Metí is the preterite (past) of meter (to put/insert). La is the feminine singular direct-object pronoun/article — here it likely refers to a feminine noun mentioned earlier (e.g., la carta, la llave). Together they begin a sentence like 'metí la llave en la cerradura' (I put the key in the lock). Word order and context matter: depending on surrounding words, la could be the definite article ('the') rather than a pronoun.
target_language_example: Metí la carta en el sobre.
native_language_example: I put the letter in the envelope.

meaning: The phrase combines 'my grandfather' with the indirect object pronoun 'le' used to mark who feels or experiences something (e.g., is afraid of, loves).
additional_notes: In Spanish, people who experience feelings or states are often marked with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les). 'A mi abuelo' is used for clarity or emphasis; 'le' is the pronoun that agrees with 'a mi abuelo'. This structure is common with verbs like dar miedo (to frighten), encantar (to love/like a lot), temer (to fear), interesar (to interest), etc. You can drop the full phrase 'a mi abuelo' if context is clear and just say 'le' after the verb when the person is already known, but for beginners keep both for clarity.
target_language_example: A mi abuelo le interesan las historias de guerra.
native_language_example: My grandfather is interested in war stories.

meaning: my soul / my spirit (can be literal or used affectionately/emotionally).
additional_notes: Used both literally (the soul or spirit) and figuratively as an emotional or affectionate expression. Short phrases like "Mi alma" can be used as a term of endearment (similar to "my dear" or "my love"), an emotional exclamation ("My soul"), or in religious/spiritual contexts ("save my soul"). Context and tone determine whether it's affectionate, poetic, or literal.
target_language_example: Tu voz calma mi alma cuando estoy triste.
native_language_example: Your voice calms my soul when I'm sad.

meaning: 'my song' — indicates a song that belongs to or is favored by the speaker.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a song that is owned by, associated with, or liked by the speaker. Can mean a literal composition the speaker wrote ('my song') or simply 'my favorite song' depending on context. Commonly appears with adjectives (mi canción favorita) or verbs like tocar, cantar, gustar, pedir.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner mi canción favorita, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you play my favorite song, please?

meaning: my appointment; my date (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a scheduled meeting, appointment (doctor, hairdresser, etc.) or a personal date. Context determines whether it means a formal appointment or a romantic/social date. Common verbs: tener una cita (to have an appointment/date), cancelar, posponer, perder.
target_language_example: Tengo que llamar para cambiar mi cita con el dentista.
native_language_example: I have to call to change my appointment with the dentist.

meaning: literally 'my butt'; used either literally (body part) or informally/emphatically in expressions.
additional_notes: Primarily vulgar/informal. Can refer to the speaker's buttocks literally (body part) or be used figuratively for emphasis, humor, or self-deprecation (e.g., 'my luck', 'I really want/need', or to express strong feeling). Tone varies by context—avoid in formal situations. Pronunciation and register make it common in songs, jokes, and casual speech.
target_language_example: Hoy me duele mi culo después de tanto sentarme.
native_language_example: My butt hurts today after sitting so much.

meaning: 'my address' or 'my direction' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'my postal/address' (where you live or to send something) or 'my direction' (the way toward me). Context clarifies meaning: when talking about giving location or sending mail, use 'direccion' = address; when talking about movement or pointing, it means direction. To specify, you can say 'mi dirección postal' or 'la dirección hacia mí'.
target_language_example: Te dejo mi dirección para que me escribas.
native_language_example: I'll give you my address so you can write to me.

meaning: my pain / my grief (literal: my physical pain or emotional suffering).
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that hurts you physically or emotionally. Context determines whether it's physical pain (e.g., a headache) or emotional sorrow. Not an idiom; can appear in medical or personal contexts. For sympathy, Spanish speakers more often say "me duele" + body part (e.g., "me duele la cabeza") rather than "mi dolor", which can sound more formal or literary when referring to one's suffering.
target_language_example: He hablado con el médico sobre mi dolor de espalda.
native_language_example: I spoke with the doctor about my back pain.

meaning: literally 'my wife and (to)' — part of a Spanish indirect/direct object construction meaning 'my wife and ...' (used when listing people after a/ a la/ a los).
additional_notes: This fragment appears when you list people introduced by the preposition a (used for direct objects who are people and for indirect objects). In full phrases you'll often see 'a mi esposa y a mi hijo', 'a mi esposa y a mí' (with accent on mí when it's the stressed pronoun). When used with verbs like 'encontrar' (to find) or 'buscar' (to look for), the a marks the people as direct objects. With gustar and similar verbs, use 'a mi esposa y a mí nos gusta...' or 'a mi esposa y a mí nos interesa...'.
target_language_example: Encontré a mi esposa y a mi hijo en el parque.
native_language_example: I found my wife and my son in the park.

meaning: 'my experience' — what I have personally observed, learned, or lived through
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal observation, opinion, or lesson learned. Common in sentences like 'En mi experiencia...' (In my experience...) or 'Mi experiencia me dice...' (My experience tells me...). It can refer to a specific experience (with someone/something) or general past experience.
target_language_example: En mi experiencia, practicar todos los días mejora mucho la pronunciación.
native_language_example: In my experience, practicing every day greatly improves pronunciation.

meaning: my party / my celebration
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession: the speaker's party or celebration. Can refer to a specific party (birthday, gathering) or a favorite type of celebration (e.g., 'mi fiesta favorita'). Common in everyday speech. Tone is neutral; context clarifies what kind of celebration.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a mi fiesta el sábado?
native_language_example: Can you come to my party on Saturday?

meaning: my people / my folks (can mean family, close friends, community)
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to refer to a group you belong to or feel loyalty toward: family, close friends, community, coworkers, or supporters. Tone depends on context — can be affectionate, protective, or political. Not literal only; often means 'people like me' or 'those I trust.'
target_language_example: Siempre defiendo a mi gente.
native_language_example: I always stand up for my people.

meaning: The sequence 'mi hijo' ('my son') followed immediately by the preposition 'a', used to mark recipient, destination, direction, or role/relationship in constructions like 'dar algo a mi hijo' (give something to my son) or 'mandar a mi hijo a la universidad' (send my son to university). It's not a fixed idiom but a common syntactic pattern.
additional_notes: Not a single lexical item—it's the noun phrase 'mi hijo' plus the preposition 'a' that introduces an indirect object, destination, direction, purpose, or the start of a subordinate phrase. Word order and meaning depend on the verb and context. Common verbs with this pattern: dar a, dejar a, mandar a, llevar a, enviar a. 'A' can translate as 'to', 'for', 'into', or be part of a larger structure; literal translation varies by context.
target_language_example: Dejo a mi hijo a tu cuidado.
native_language_example: I leave my son in your care.

meaning: 'my young' — a possessive + adjective used to address or describe someone younger or less experienced; often followed by a noun (amigo, aprendiz, dama).
additional_notes: Used to refer affectionately or respectfully to a younger person or someone with less experience. Common in literary, formal, or affectionate contexts. In everyday speech Spanish speakers might instead say 'mi amigo joven' (my young friend) or simply use a name or 'joven' alone when addressing someone directly (e.g., 'Joven, ¿puedo ayudarle?'). 'Mi joven' usually appears before a noun (mi joven amigo) or as a vocative (Mi joven, escucha.).
target_language_example: Mi joven estudiante, practica todos los días.
native_language_example: My young student, practice every day.

meaning: my call (usually a phone call) or my visit/appeal depending on context.
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a phone call (mi llamada telefónica). Can also mean a personal visit or a request/appeal in some contexts, but for beginners treat it as 'my call' (phone). Use with verbs like esperar (to wait for) or querer (to want).
target_language_example: Te dejaré un mensaje después de mi llamada.
native_language_example: I'll leave you a message after my call.

meaning: my best (used before a noun, e.g. 'my best friend' or 'my best show').
additional_notes: mi = my (possessive). mejor = better/best. Together they appear before a noun to mean the speaker's top/closest person or favorite thing. Commonly used with amigo (friend), opción, momento, programa, etc. Gender and number agreement: mejor stays same, but possessive changes (mi, mis). Use 'mi mejor amigo' (male friend) or 'mi mejor amiga' (female friend).
target_language_example: Ella es mi mejor amiga desde la infancia.
native_language_example: She is my best friend since childhood.

meaning: my goal / my aim / my objective.
additional_notes: Used to say what you hope to achieve in the future (short- or long-term). Commonly followed by a verb infinitive or a noun phrase (e.g., "mi meta es ser...", "mi meta en la vida es..."). Polite and neutral — suitable in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Mi meta es aprender inglés fluido este año.
native_language_example: My goal is to learn fluent English this year.

meaning: ‘my computer, if…’ — offers permission to use the speaker's computer, followed by a conditional 'if'.
additional_notes: This sequence combines a possessive noun phrase (mi ordenador = my computer) with the conjunction si (if). In natural speech it introduces a conditional offer or permission: 'You can use my computer if you want.' The subject and verb before or after may change depending on formality (tú/usted/ustedes) and number (singular/plural).
target_language_example: Podéis usar mi ordenador si queréis.
native_language_example: You can use my computer if you want.

meaning: 'my father' plus the preposition 'de' used before a verb or noun phrase (e.g. 'mi padre de dejar...') — this is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the possessive 'mi padre' followed by 'de' to link to another element.
additional_notes: This sequence is simply the noun phrase 'mi padre' (my father) followed by the preposition 'de'. 'De' is used in many ways in Spanish: to introduce an infinitive after verbs that take 'de' (e.g., convencer de + infinitive or convencer a alguien de + infinitive/idea), to indicate removal (sacar a alguien de), to indicate cause/purpose (librar de), or to link possession/relationship. The examples show different constructions: 'convencer a mi padre de ...' (convince my father to...), 'librar a mi padre de ...' (free my father from...), 'sacar a mi padre de aquí' (take my father out of here), and an insult 'quiero a mi padre de regreso' uses 'de' as part of 'de regreso' (back). So learners should treat 'mi padre' as the phrase for 'my father' and learn the various uses of 'de' separately.
target_language_example: Convencí a mi padre de ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: I convinced my father to help me with the move.

meaning: my father likes (something).
additional_notes: This is the Spanish structure used to say that someone likes something: A + person + le + gusta + [noun/infinitive]. The thing liked is expressed with a singular noun or an infinitive verb; use gustan for plural things. 'A mí también' means 'me too.'
target_language_example: A mi padre le gusta escuchar música clásica.
native_language_example: My father likes listening to classical music.

meaning: 'my father' + que (introducing a clause) — used to say 'that/to (my) father' when reporting who is affected or who receives an action or advice.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the possessive noun phrase 'mi padre' followed by the conjunction 'que' which introduces a subordinate clause (often with verbs of telling, advising, suggesting, wanting, etc.). English equivalents: 'that my father...' or 'to my father that...' depending on the main verb. Word order: verb + (a) + mi padre + que + clause (e.g., aconsejó a mi padre que dejara...).
target_language_example: Le expliqué a mi padre que el cambio sería para mejor.
native_language_example: I explained to my father that the change would be for the better.

meaning: my umbrella in/on (used to say where you left or found your umbrella).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'mi paraguas' (my umbrella) with a preposition like 'en' + place (el tren, el taxi, el camión) to say where you left or found it. 'En' can mean 'in' or 'on' depending on the vehicle or context (e.g., 'en el tren' = on the train, 'en el taxi' = in the taxi). Also used with verbs like dejar (to leave), olvidar (to forget), tomar (to take).
target_language_example: Dejé mi paraguas en el autobús por la mañana.
native_language_example: I left my umbrella on the bus this morning.

meaning: my point (what I'm trying to say)
additional_notes: Used to state or emphasize the main idea, argument, or opinion you're making. Can appear as a complete sentence ('Mi punto.') to signal you've finished your argument or to draw attention to the central idea. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Mi punto es que necesitamos más tiempo para terminar.
native_language_example: My point is that we need more time to finish.

meaning: 'my luck' or 'my fate/destiny' (literally 'my luck').
additional_notes: Used to refer to one's luck, fortune, or fate. Context determines nuance: can mean good/bad luck (mi suerte se acabó = my luck has run out), fate (dejarme a mi suerte = leave me to my fate/situation), or affectionally (eres mi suerte = you're my good luck/you're my destiny).
target_language_example: Después de tanto buscar, creo que por fin llegó mi suerte.
native_language_example: After searching so long, I think my luck has finally come.

meaning: 'my train' — refers to the specific train someone is using or expecting.
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession or association with a particular train (the one you intend to take or are traveling on). Can refer to departure/arrival times, being missed, or which train has priority. In spoken Spanish, context clarifies which train (schedule, platform, ticket) is meant.
target_language_example: Mi tren sale en veinte minutos; voy corriendo a la estación.
native_language_example: My train leaves in twenty minutes; I'm running to the station.

meaning: 'my tea'.
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: mi + noun. Used to indicate that the tea belongs to or is intended for the speaker (or the person being referred to). Commonly followed by details about how the tea is prepared (con/sin azúcar, con leche, caliente, frío, etc.). Pronunciation note: té (accent) distinguishes the noun 'tea' from the pronoun 'te'.
target_language_example: Voy a calentar mi té antes de salir.
native_language_example: I'm going to heat my tea before leaving.

meaning: my real / my true (used before a noun, e.g. 'my true name')
additional_notes: Uses 'verdadero' (true/real) to specify the authentic or correct identity of something you own or are called. Commonly appears as 'mi verdadero nombre' (my real name) or 'mi verdadero yo' (my true self). Place 'mi verdadero' before the noun. Tone is neutral and standard.
target_language_example: Mi verdadero nombre es Ana.
native_language_example: My real name is Ana.

meaning: 'my life with you' — used to say you want to spend your life together with someone.
additional_notes: A romantic phrase expressing the desire to share the future with another person. Often appears with verbs like querer (quiero pasar) or amar (te amo). Can be modified with 'el resto de' to mean 'the rest of my life.' Used in declarations of love or marriage proposals.
target_language_example: Te amo y quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo.
native_language_example: I love you and I want to spend the rest of my life with you.

meaning: a colloquial emphatic phrase meaning 'in my life' or 'I've ever' used to stress how strongly you feel about something.
additional_notes: Often appears as part of expressions like 'En mi vida me he...' or 'Nunca en mi vida me...' to emphasize that something has (or has never) happened to the speaker. It is informal and emphatic; 'mi vida' here is not literal 'my life' but a way to stress the personal experience. Common with verbs of feeling or reaction (reír, sentir, matar [figurative]).
target_language_example: Nunca en mi vida me había emocionado tanto.
native_language_example: Never in my life have I been so moved.

meaning: my old (feminine) — used for things (or sometimes people) that are old or former.
additional_notes: Literal feminine form of "mi viejo"; agrees with a feminine noun (casa, bicicleta, espada, guarida). Commonly means "my old [thing]" (the one I used to have or that's aged). In some dialects or contexts, "mi vieja" can informally refer to one's wife or girlfriend, but here examples show possessions and places. Use "mi viejo" for masculine nouns.
target_language_example: Le presté a Marta mi vieja bicicleta hasta que arregle la suya.
native_language_example: I lent Marta my old bike until she fixes hers.

meaning: 'me too' (expresses that the same applies to the speaker).
additional_notes: Commonly used to agree or indicate the same feeling/action applies to the speaker. Typically appears with the preposition 'a' for emphasis (A mí también) and the pronoun 'mí' is usually written with an accent when used after 'a'; however, in informal contexts accents are sometimes omitted in writing. Can be used standalone as a short reply ('¡Mi también!' is nonstandard — prefer 'A mí también') or within a sentence: 'A mí también me gustan...' Informal expletives may follow in casual speech.
target_language_example: A mi también me gustan los pasteles.
native_language_example: I like cakes too.

meaning: fear of (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you are afraid of a person, animal, situation, etc. Often appears with verbs like tener (tener miedo a/de). In Spanish both 'miedo a' and 'miedo de' are heard, but 'miedo a' + noun or infinitive is very common. To negate, use 'no tener miedo a' or 'no tener miedo de'.
target_language_example: No tengas miedo a volar si el avión es seguro.
native_language_example: Don't be afraid of flying if the plane is safe.

target_language_multi_word_term: miedo de su / miedo de su propia
meaning: 'afraid of' or 'fear of (someone or something of one's own)'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is afraid of someone/something. When followed by 'propio/a' it emphasizes that the fear is of one's own (e.g., 'su propio marido' = 'his/her own husband', 'su propia sombra' = an idiom meaning 'very easily frightened'). In Spanish the preposition can be 'de' (tiene miedo de su padre) or the direct object can use 'a' with people (tiene miedo a los perros), but 'miedo de' is common in these examples.
target_language_example: Ella tiene miedo de su propia sombra.
native_language_example: She is afraid of her own shadow.

meaning: lies to (someone)
additional_notes: Verb phrase: miente is the third-person singular present of mentir (to lie). Use 'le' before 'miente a' when indicating 'to him/her/you (formal)' (e.g., 'le miente a Mary'). For plural subjects or other persons change verb form (yo miento, tú mientes, ellos mienten). Commonly followed by the person who is being lied to.
target_language_example: Él le miente a su amigo sobre lo que pasó.
native_language_example: He lies to his friend about what happened.

meaning: 'while she' or 'as long as she'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action or state that happens at the same time as, or during the period when, 'she' does something. Can express simultaneous actions (while she was crying) or a condition/duration (as long as she is here). Verb mood may change: use indicative for factual statements (está, estaba) and subjunctive (esté) when expressing uncertainty, condition, or pending actions.
target_language_example: Puedes entrar mientras ella duerma.
native_language_example: You can go in while she sleeps.

meaning: while I (am) / while I (do something).
additional_notes: Combination of 'mientras' (while) + reflexive pronoun 'me' used with reflexive verbs (ducharse, bañarse, afeitarse, etc.). Indicates two actions happening at the same time: one thing occurs while the speaker is performing the reflexive action. Use the appropriate verb form after 'me' (me ducho, me bañaba, me afeito).
target_language_example: Mientras me ducho, escucho música.
native_language_example: While I shower, I listen to music.

meaning: while / whereas (to contrast two things) or 'while' meaning 'during' in some contexts.
additional_notes: Most often used to contrast two people, situations, or ideas (equivalent to English 'whereas' or 'while' in contrast). It can also mean 'while/during' when introducing an action happening at the same time, but that use is less common for beginners. Use 'mientras' alone for simple 'while' (during) sentences; 'mientras que' emphasizes contrast.
target_language_example: A ella le gusta la playa, mientras que a mí me gustan las montañas.
native_language_example: She likes the beach, whereas I like the mountains.

meaning: meanwhile; in the meantime.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action or situation that happens at the same time as another. Can appear at the start or middle of a sentence and often followed by a comma. Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Prepara la comida; mientras tanto, yo pongo la mesa.
native_language_example: Prepare the food; meanwhile, I'll set the table.

additional_notes: Used in Spanish to mean 1,000,000,000 (long scale). Common in Spain and many Spanish-speaking countries. In some regions, people may also say 'un millardo' but 'mil millones' is far more common. Use with de when counting (e.g., 'mil millones de personas').
target_language_example: Hay mil millones de estrellas visibles en esa imagen.
native_language_example: There are one billion stars visible in that image.

meaning: an emphatic way to say 'millions and (millions)' or 'millions upon millions' — used to stress a very large, often indefinite number.
additional_notes: Often appears in repetition (e.g., "millones y millones") to emphasize enormous quantity or age. Can be used literally (many millions of units) or figuratively (a huge, almost immeasurable amount). In sentences like "vale millones y..." it implies a very high value (millions) followed by more information.
target_language_example: Hay millones y millones de insectos en ese bosque.
native_language_example: There are millions and millions of insects in that forest.

meaning: a gold mine; literally a mine where gold is extracted; figuratively something that yields great profit or value.
additional_notes: Can be used literally for an actual gold-mining site or figuratively to describe a very profitable business, resource, opportunity, or source of useful information. In plural: minas de oro. Stress on 'mi-na de o-ro'.
target_language_example: Ese cliente es una mina de oro para nuestro negocio.
native_language_example: That client is a gold mine for our business.

meaning: lied to (someone).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of mentir (to lie). Use 'le' (or other indirect object pronouns: me, te, nos, les) before the verb to indicate who was lied to, or add an indirect object phrase: 'mintió a María' = 'lied to María'. Can also be used without 'a' when followed by a noun phrase for the person (mintió a la policía).
target_language_example: Él le mintió a su amiga sobre dónde estaba.
native_language_example: He lied to his friend about where he was.

meaning: one more minute; a minute longer
additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate a short extra amount of time. Often appears with words like 'un' (one) or in negative expressions 'ni un minuto más' (not one minute more). Common in requests (Dame un minuto más) and in commands or limits (Ni un minuto más tarde).
target_language_example: Espérame sólo un minuto más.
native_language_example: Wait for me just one more minute.

meaning: a (short) amount of time before doing something; 'a minute to/for' (to allow time to... / time remaining to...).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a brief pause or a small amount of time needed (Déme un minuto para pensar = Give me a minute to think) or time available/remaining for an action (tiene un minuto para formar a la unidad = you have a minute to form the unit). Can also appear in phrases like 'minuto para el impacto' (minute before impact) or 'puntos de último minuto' (last-minute points). 'Minuto' is literal; context decides whether it means an actual 60 seconds or simply 'a moment.'
target_language_example: Dame un minuto para terminar este correo.
native_language_example: Give me a minute to finish this email.

meaning: Watch what you do / look at what you're doing.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to pay attention to their actions—can be a warning, instruction, or complaint. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be gentle advice or sharp reproach. Common in informal spoken Spanish. Literally: 'look at what you do.'
target_language_example: Mira lo que haces antes de tirar eso, podrías romperlo.
native_language_example: Watch what you do before you throw that, you could break it.

meaning: 'was looking at' or 'used to look at' (third person singular imperfect of mirar + feminine singular direct object article).
additional_notes: Miraba is the imperfect tense of mirar (él/ella/usted miraba) and describes a past ongoing or repeated action: 'was looking at' or 'used to look at.' La is the feminine singular definite article (the) and marks a feminine direct object that follows the verb (e.g., la luna, la película, la gente (la used with gente as a whole)). For masculine objects you'd see 'miraba el' or 'miraba lo' for neuter ideas. Word order is verb + article + noun in these examples.
target_language_example: Ella miraba la ventana durante horas.
native_language_example: She was looking at the window for hours.

meaning: a look directed at / gaze fixed on
additional_notes: Used to say someone looks at or fixes their gaze on something or someone. Commonly appears with verbs like fijar (fijó la mirada en), poner, clavar, or tener (una mirada en). Can describe brief glances or an intense, sustained gaze depending on context.
target_language_example: Ella clavó la mirada en la puerta esperando a que entrara.
native_language_example: She fixed her gaze on the door waiting for him to enter.

meaning: looking out for / watching over (feminine noun follows)
additional_notes: This is a fragment of the verb phrase 'mirar por' meaning to look out for, to care for, to watch over. 'La' is the feminine singular direct object or feminine article replacing a feminine noun (e.g., 'la casa', 'la niña'). Context determines whether it's literal (looking through/for something) or idiomatic (taking care of someone). You will often see 'mirando por' followed by a noun or pronoun: 'mirando por la familia', 'mirando por la salud'.
target_language_example: Ella está mirando por la salud de su abuela.
native_language_example: She is looking out for her grandmother's health.

meaning: to look at
additional_notes: Used when specifying the object/person being looked at; 'a' introduces a direct object that is a person or animate being (or sometimes a specific thing). In many contexts it is interchangeable with 'mirar' + direct object without 'a' for inanimate objects, but Spanish often uses 'a' before people. Can also imply watching (e.g., watching children play).
target_language_example: Me gusta mirar a la gente en el parque.
native_language_example: I like to watch people in the park.

meaning: to look someone in the eyes; to make eye contact.
additional_notes: Used literally (to meet/look into someone's eyes) and figuratively (to face someone honestly or confidently). Common in contexts about sincerity, confrontation, or intimacy. If subject is reflexive (mirarse a los ojos) it often means two people look at each other.
target_language_example: Le dije la verdad y me obligó a mirar a los ojos.
native_language_example: I told her the truth and she forced me to look her in the eyes.

meaning: to look around; to look/survey the area or surroundings.
additional_notes: Common phrasal expression used when scanning a place or checking surroundings. Can be used literally (looking with your eyes) or more loosely (glancing around, checking options). Often appears as 'mirar alrededor de' when specifying a place (e.g., 'mirar alrededor de la casa').
target_language_example: Voy a mirar alrededor antes de entrar.
native_language_example: I'll look around before going in.

meaning: to look up (physically) — to direct one's eyes upward.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe the physical action of turning one's gaze toward something above. 'Mirar arriba' and 'mirar hacia arriba' are both used; for searching information Spanish prefers verbs like 'buscar' or 'consultar' rather than 'mirar'. Can be used literally (e.g., 'mirar arriba al cielo') and occasionally figuratively depending on context.
target_language_example: Cuando oímos el ruido, decidimos mirar arriba para ver qué lo causaba.
native_language_example: When we heard the noise, we decided to look up to see what caused it.

meaning: look at the
additional_notes: Common collocation of the verb mirar + the definite article el; means to direct your eyes toward something (look at) or to observe/watch something (watch the). The exact translation depends on the noun that follows (e.g., mirar el mar = look at the sea; mirar el partido = watch the match). Not a fixed idiom — it's compositional.
target_language_example: Me gusta mirar el mar al atardecer.
native_language_example: I like to look at the sea at sunset.

meaning: 'to look at the' (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: Mirar = to look/watch. 'La' is the feminine singular direct object pronoun or article ('the' or 'her/it' depending on context). Together 'mirar la' commonly appears before a feminine noun (la pantalla, la cara, la televisión) or when 'la' replaces a previously mentioned feminine noun. Use 'mirar' for both looking at (brief) and watching (ongoing), though 'ver' and 'observar' have different nuances.
target_language_example: No me gusta mirar la televisión todas las noches.
native_language_example: I don't like to watch the television every night.

meaning: to look at (feminine plural things).
additional_notes: Mirar = 'to look at' or 'to watch'. 'Las' is the feminine plural definite article (the). Use 'mirar las' before feminine plural nouns (e.g., estrellas, montañas, nubes, fotos). For masculine plural nouns use 'mirar los'. You can also use 'mirar' with other determiners (mis/estas/unas) or without an article: 'mirar fotos' or 'mirar las fotos' both possible depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Me gusta mirar las estrellas por la noche.
native_language_example: I like to look at the stars at night.

meaning: to check/see what (something is or will be); to look into what
additional_notes: Used to indicate checking or finding out information about something. Often followed by a clause or question word (e.g., 'qué', 'si', 'cómo') or used colloquially to mean 'let me see' or 'I'll check.' Context determines whether it's an instruction ('look and see what...') or a speaker deciding to check now ('I'll check what...').
target_language_example: Voy a mirar qué opciones hay para el viaje.
native_language_example: I'm going to check what options there are for the trip.

meaning: looked at the (feminine noun) / looked toward the
additional_notes: Past tense of mirar (él/ella/usted). 'Miró a la' is followed by a feminine noun or direction (e.g., 'cara', 'izquierda'). It can mean 'looked at the [thing/person]' or 'looked to/toward the [direction]'. If referring to a person, Spanish often uses 'mirar a' + object (me miró a la cara = he/she looked me in the face). For masculine nouns use 'miró al' (a + el).
target_language_example: Ella me miró a la espalda cuando pasé.
native_language_example: She looked at my back when I walked by.

meaning: my own eyes (emphasizes that you saw something yourself).
additional_notes: Used to stress direct personal observation or eyewitness experience. Often appears in phrases like 'lo vi con mis propios ojos' ('I saw it with my own eyes'). 'Propios' agrees in number/gender with the noun: e.g., 'mis propios ojos' (my own eyes), 'mi propia casa' (my own house).
target_language_example: Lo vi con mis propios ojos.
native_language_example: I saw it with my own eyes.

meaning: 'mission of' or 'mission for' — used to describe the purpose or type of a mission/task.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun that specifies the mission's purpose, type, or target (e.g., entrenamiento, reconocimiento, alto riesgo). Can refer to military, scientific, corporate, or organizational tasks. In English it usually translates as 'mission to/for/of' depending on context; choose the preposition that fits the noun (e.g., 'mission of reconnaissance' → 'reconnaissance mission', 'misión de entrenamiento' → 'training mission').
target_language_example: La tripulación salió en una misión de rescate.
native_language_example: The crew went on a rescue mission.

meaning: 'misma' emphasizes that the subject herself did the action to 'le' (to him/her/you formal).
additional_notes: This is actually two parts: 'misma' (feminine singular of 'mismo') adds emphasis — 'herself' or 'myself' — and 'le' is the indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him/to her/to you (formal)'. Together they highlight that the woman (or speaker, if feminine) personally performed the action for that person. Word order can vary: e.g. 'Ella misma le ayudó' or 'Yo misma le di'. Use 'mismo' for masculine subjects (él mismo, yo mismo).
target_language_example: Yo misma le entregué el paquete a mi vecino.
native_language_example: I myself gave him the package.

meaning: the same room
additional_notes: Used to indicate two or more people or events share a single room or location. 'Misma' agrees in gender with 'habitación' (feminine). Can describe living, sleeping, being present, or events that occur in the same physical room. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Vivimos en la misma habitación desde hace tres meses.
native_language_example: We've been living in the same room for three months.

meaning: the same clothes
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is wearing/repeating identical clothing items as before or as someone else. "Misma" agrees in gender with ropa (feminine). Common in comparisons (que ayer, que llevaba) and negatives (no siempre uso la misma ropa).
target_language_example: Hoy llevo la misma ropa que ayer.
native_language_example: Today I'm wearing the same clothes as yesterday.

meaning: An emphatic construction combining 'mismo' (self/same, used for emphasis) with the neutral direct object pronoun 'lo' ('it' / referring to an idea or statement). It emphasizes that the very person mentioned is the one related to the action or statement (e.g., 'he himself said it').
additional_notes: 'mismo' agrees in gender and number when used adjectivally with nouns (mismo/misma/mismos/mismas), but in emphatic constructions before 'lo' it commonly appears as 'mismo lo' (or with a subject pronoun: 'usted mismo lo', 'él mismo lo'). Word order can vary: subject + 'mismo' + 'lo' + verb (e.g., 'usted mismo lo dijo') or subject + verb + 'mismo' + 'lo' in some contexts. 'Lo' often refers to an idea, statement, or unspecified neuter object. Tone ranges from neutral to emphatic; common in both formal and informal speech depending on context.
target_language_example: Usted mismo lo dijo.
native_language_example: You yourself said it.

meaning: 'the same without' (used to say something/person would not be the same without someone or something).
additional_notes: Combine 'mismo' (same) with 'sin' (without). Common in sentences like 'No sería lo mismo sin ti' = 'It wouldn't be the same without you.' Often appears as part of the phrase 'no (es/era/sería) lo mismo sin...'.
target_language_example: La fiesta no fue lo mismo sin ella.
native_language_example: The party wasn't the same without her.

meaning: the same neighborhood
additional_notes: Used to say two or more people or events are/were located in the same neighborhood. 'Mismo' agrees in sense (not in gender here because barrio is masculine); you can change to 'mismo/a/os/as' to match nouns. Common in everyday speech to talk about where people live or grew up.
target_language_example: Vivimos en el mismo barrio cuando éramos niños.
native_language_example: We lived in the same neighborhood when we were children.

meaning: the same place / the same location
additional_notes: Used to indicate that two or more things or people share the same physical location or source. Can be used alone as a short reply (e.g., "Mismo lugar.") to confirm meeting at the same place. "Mismo" agrees in meaning with "same" and does not change for gender/number when used before "lugar" (singular).
target_language_example: Quedamos en el mismo lugar de siempre.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the same place as always.

meaning: in the same way; similarly.
additional_notes: Used to compare actions or situations, equivalent to 'de la misma manera' or 'igualmente'. Can appear as 'del mismo modo' (more common) or simply 'mismo modo' in context. Often followed by a clause or sentence showing the similar action or result.
target_language_example: Ella resolvió el problema y yo actué de mismo modo.
native_language_example: She solved the problem and I acted in the same way.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a mistaken split of 'mismo' + preposition 'a' or part of a larger construction. It does not form a common, grammatically correct multiword expression by itself.
additional_notes: If you encounter 'mismo a' it is usually a typo, a word break across lines, or part of phrases like 'a mí mismo' (to myself) or 'el mismo a quien' (the same one to whom) where 'mismo' and 'a' belong to different constituents. Prefer correct constructions such as 'a mí mismo', 'lo mismo a', or rephrase (e.g., 'incluso a mí', 'igual a').
target_language_example: No debería haber escrito 'mismo a' separado; debía poner 'a mí mismo' para indicar énfasis.
native_language_example: He shouldn't have written 'mismo a' separated; he should have written 'a mí mismo' to indicate emphasis.

meaning: the same as you
additional_notes: Used to compare equality of things, actions, amounts, or opinions with the person addressed. Often appears with 'lo' (lo mismo que tú) when referring to a thing/idea previously mentioned. Can be used in statements, questions, or short replies (e.g., 'Lo mismo que tú' = 'Same as you').
target_language_example: Yo quiero lo mismo que tú.
native_language_example: I want the same as you.

meaning: the same eyes (same eye color/shape/features).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say two people share identical or very similar eyes (color, shape, expression). Often appears in descriptions of family resemblance. 'Mismos' agrees in gender/number with the noun (mismos ojos = masculine plural).
target_language_example: Tu hija tiene los mismos ojos que tú.
native_language_example: Your daughter has the same eyes as you.

meaning: half of the (feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used before feminine plural nouns to indicate 50% of a group or amount. If the noun is masculine plural use "mitad de los"; for singular use "la mitad de". Often followed by a noun (e.g., ganancias, bananas, veces).
target_language_example: Recibí la mitad de las ganancias.
native_language_example: I received half of the profits.

meaning: half of what (something is or that someone does).
additional_notes: Used to compare amounts, actions, knowledge, or statements to indicate 'half as much' or 'only half of what...'. Often appears with quantifiers (sólo, menos, más) or verbs. Common in comparisons and cautions (e.g., 'only half of what you hear/see').
target_language_example: Ella sabe sólo la mitad de lo que cuenta.
native_language_example: She knows only half of what she tells.

meaning: 'the way' or 'how' (the manner in which).
additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or style of an action or situation. Usually appears as 'el modo en que' or 'el modo en el que' + clause, or shortened in speech as 'el modo en que le hablas' = 'the way you talk to him/her'. Can be followed by 'que' or a relative clause.
target_language_example: No me gusta el modo en que me miras.
native_language_example: I don't like the way you look at me.

meaning: 'one moment, please' / 'please wait a moment'.
additional_notes: Polite request asking someone to wait briefly. Common in phone conversations or when you need a short pause. You can also say just 'un momento, por favor' or the shorter 'un momento' in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Un momento, por favor. Ahora vuelvo con la información.
native_language_example: One moment, please. I'll be back with the information.

meaning: 'the moment when' or 'the moment that' (the exact time something happened).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the specific instant when something occurred. Often appears as 'en el momento en que' or 'desde el momento en que' and is followed by a clause (verb). Common in past and present narratives. Not informal.
target_language_example: Lo entendí en el momento en que lo explicaste.
native_language_example: I understood it the moment you explained it.

meaning: the moment when (her); at the moment that she...
additional_notes: Used to introduce the exact time something happened concerning a female person (la = her). Often appears as part of phrases like "desde el momento en que la conocí" (from the moment I met her). Can be adapted for other subjects: "el momento en que lo vi" (the moment when I saw him).
target_language_example: La reconocí en el momento en que la vi.
native_language_example: I recognized her the moment I saw her.

meaning: the happiest moment of (someone's life, childhood, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to say which point in time was the happiest for someone or something. Usually followed by a noun or possessive phrase (mi vida, mi infancia). Common in past or present: 'fue el momento más feliz de mi vida' or 'este es el momento más feliz de mi vida.'
target_language_example: Ese fue el momento más feliz de mi vida.
native_language_example: That was the happiest moment of my life.

meaning: 'coin in' — used to say a coin is located in or on something (e.g., in my pocket, on the sidewalk).
additional_notes: This is the noun moneda ('coin') followed by a preposition (en = in/on/at). Use 'moneda en' when describing where a coin is found or placed: 'una moneda en mi bolsillo' (a coin in my pocket), 'una moneda en la acera' (a coin on the sidewalk). Preposition can change meaning: 'en' = in/inside or on/surface depending on context. For 'on top of' you can also use 'sobre'.
target_language_example: Encontré una moneda en el sofá.
native_language_example: I found a coin in the sofa.

meaning: literally 'mountain is' — the phrase is just the noun montaña ('mountain') plus the verb es ('is').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression; it's simply the structure 'montaña es' used when describing a mountain (quality, location, etc.). For beginners: montaña = mountain (feminine). Es is the 3rd person singular of ser used for descriptions, identity, origin, or inherent characteristics. Use 'la montaña es...' when speaking generally (la is the definite article: la montaña es...).
target_language_example: La montaña es alta y nevada.
native_language_example: The mountain is tall and snowy.

meaning: literally 'mountain is' — the verb phrase 'está' (is) used with montaña to describe the mountain's current state or condition.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the noun montaña (mountain) plus the verb estar (to be) in the third person singular. Use está to describe temporary states, locations, or conditions of the mountain (e.g., hidden, high, covered in snow). For permanent characteristics you might use es instead of está (La montaña es alta).
target_language_example: La montaña está cubierta de nieve hoy.
native_language_example: The mountain is covered in snow today.

meaning: the mountain is covered
additional_notes: A simple descriptive phrase: 'montaña' (mountain) + 'está cubierta' (is covered). 'Cubierta' is the past participle of 'cubrir' used as an adjective after the verb 'estar' to describe a temporary state (e.g., covered with snow, clouds, vegetation, etc.). To specify what covers the mountain, add 'de' + noun (e.g., 'está cubierta de nieve').
target_language_example: La montaña está cubierta de nieve después de la tormenta.
native_language_example: The mountain is covered with snow after the storm.

meaning: the mountain is covered with/of (something).
additional_notes: Use to describe that a mountain has a covering (snow, trees, clouds, etc.). 'Cubierta de' follows the thing covering it; can be used with definite articles when needed (La montaña está cubierta de nieve / La montaña está cubierta de nubes). For other subjects replace 'montaña' with the noun and adjust agreement (La playa está cubierta de algas).
target_language_example: La montaña está cubierta de nubes esta mañana.
native_language_example: The mountain is covered with clouds this morning.

meaning: a lot of things that / lots of things to (do) — indicates many items or tasks related to something.
additional_notes: Common, informal phrase used to say there are many items, tasks, or matters. Often followed by a verb or clause (e.g., 'que hacer', 'que podemos encontrar'). 'Montón' emphasizes quantity; you can also say 'muchas cosas que'.
target_language_example: Tengo un montón de cosas que preparar antes del viaje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to prepare before the trip.

meaning: bit the (feminine singular body part).
additional_notes: From the verb morder (to bite) in past tense (él/ella mordió) plus the feminine singular definite article la. Used when specifying that someone/something bit a feminine-noun body part (la mano, la pierna, etc.). Word order in Spanish often places the indirect object pronoun or explicit person before the verb (e.g., 'me mordió la mano' = 'he/she/it bit my hand').
target_language_example: El perro me mordió la mano.
native_language_example: The dog bit my hand.

meaning: 'to die of hunger' — used literally or figuratively to mean 'starve' or 'be extremely hungry'.
additional_notes: Can be used literally (to starve to death) or figuratively to express extreme hunger or worry about not having enough to eat/money. Common in phrases like 'a punto de morir de hambre' (about to starve) or in rhetorical questions expressing concern ('¿me voy a morir de hambre?').
target_language_example: Si no encontramos comida pronto, vamos a morir de hambre.
native_language_example: If we don't find food soon, we're going to starve (to death).

meaning: 'a fly in' (literally), used to say there is a fly in/on something (e.g., in your coffee).
additional_notes: This is a literal, common phrase used to report a fly being inside or on food/drink or in a place (e.g., 'una mosca en el café', 'una mosca en la sopa'). Not an idiom here (although 'estar como mosca en leche' in one example is an idiomatic/smaller phrase meaning 'to be out of place' or 'uncomfortable'). Use 'hay una mosca en...' to say 'there is a fly in...'.
target_language_example: Cuidado: hay una mosca en la ensalada.
native_language_example: Careful: there's a fly in the salad.

meaning: I will show the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Future tense of mostrar (mostraré = I will show) followed by the definite article el before a masculine singular noun. Used to promise or offer to show someone something. For feminine nouns use mostraré la; for plural use mostraré los/las or te/les mostraré + noun without article in some contexts.
target_language_example: Te mostraré el museo cuando vengas.
native_language_example: I will show you the museum when you come.

meaning: showed the (feminine singular object) — past tense of 'mostrar'.
additional_notes: Use when someone showed a specific feminine noun (la escuela, la foto, la zona, la carta). 'Mostró' is the third person singular preterite (he/she/you formal showed). If the object is masculine use 'mostró el' (or 'mostró los/las' for plural). Spanish word order can also place the indirect object after with 'a + person' (e.g., 'mostró la foto a todos').
target_language_example: Ella me mostró la foto ayer.
native_language_example: She showed me the photo yesterday.

meaning: for the reason of; because of; due to
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of larger phrases (e.g., 'motivo por el que', 'motivo por...'). Often followed by a clause or noun explaining the cause. Can be singular 'motivo por' or plural 'motivos por' depending on context; standalone 'motivo por' without continuation is uncommon.
target_language_example: El motivo por el que no vino fue la lluvia.
native_language_example: The reason why he didn't come was the rain.

meaning: 'for reasons of' or 'because of' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to explain the reason for an action or situation. Commonly followed by nouns like seguridad, salud, decisión. Formal/neutral register and often used in written or official contexts (por motivos de seguridad, por motivos de salud).
target_language_example: Cancelaron el concierto por motivos de seguridad.
