native_language_example: They cancelled the concert for reasons of safety.

meaning: to move the (feminine) [something]; to cause a feminine noun to change position or location.
additional_notes: Mover is a regular -er verb meaning 'to move'. 'La' is the feminine direct object pronoun or the feminine definite article depending on context. In these examples 'mover la' is followed by a feminine noun (la cama, la pierna, la oficina, la escalera, la caja). When using a direct object pronoun instead of repeating the noun, 'la' can replace a previously mentioned feminine noun: e.g., 'Voy a moverla' (I'll move it). Conjugate mover to match the subject: 'muevo, mueves, mueve, movemos, movéis, mueven'.
target_language_example: Voy a mover la mesa para limpiar.
native_language_example: I'm going to move the table to clean.

meaning: 'good luck' or 'very lucky' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used both as a noun phrase meaning 'a lot of luck' (Tengo mucha suerte = I'm very lucky) and as a short wish 'Mucha suerte' = 'Good luck!'. Common in everyday speech. 'Mucha' modifies 'suerte' (feminine).
target_language_example: Mucha suerte en tu entrevista mañana.
native_language_example: Good luck with your interview tomorrow.

meaning: 'the boy is' (third-person statement about a boy).
additional_notes: Combines the noun muchacho (boy; young male) with the verb es (he/it is). Use to describe or identify a specific boy. Muchacho = boy/lad; can be interchangeable with chico or chaval in some regions. Es is the present tense of ser for él/ella/usted. Grammar: muchacho is the subject + es as the verb.
target_language_example: El muchacho es simpático y estudia en mi clase.
native_language_example: The boy is friendly and studies in my class.

meaning: thank you very much
additional_notes: A common, polite way to express strong thanks in Spanish. Used in formal and informal situations; you can add a name or title after it (e.g., "Muchas gracias, señor"). Can be shortened to "gracias" for a less emphatic thank you.
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help.

meaning: 'many times' or 'often'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens repeatedly or frequently. Can translate as 'many times', 'often', or 'a lot of times' depending on context. Placed before or after the verb (commonly after the verb or at the start of a sentence).
target_language_example: He visitado ese pueblo muchas veces.
native_language_example: I have visited that town many times.

meaning: long before; well before (a time or event).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened or will happen a long time before another event. Can modify past events (e.g., 'mucho antes de...') or future expectations (e.g., 'No pasará mucho antes de...': it won't be long before...). Common in both written and spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Mucho antes de que llegaran, ya había terminado la cena.
native_language_example: Long before they arrived, I had already finished dinner.

meaning: a lot that / very (happy/satisfied) that — used with verbs like alegrarse to intensify emotion about a fact or event.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs of emotion (e.g., alegrarse, sorprenderse) as 'me alegro mucho de que...' meaning 'I'm very glad that...'. It is followed by a subordinate clause introduced by 'que' and then a conjugated verb (often subjunctive). 'Mucho' intensifies the feeling; 'de' links the emotion verb to the 'que' clause.
target_language_example: Me alegro mucho de que hayas aprobado el examen.
native_language_example: I'm very glad that you passed the exam.

meaning: a lot/something has changed or happened since (a specific time or event).
additional_notes: Combines 'mucho' (a lot) with 'desde' (since). Used to say that something or someone has changed, suffered, improved, etc., a great deal compared to a past point in time. Common structures: 'ha cambiado mucho desde...' (has changed a lot since...), 'sufrió mucho desde...' (suffered a lot since...). The time point after 'desde' can be a specific time, event, or phrase (e.g., 'la última vez que...', 'la muerte de...').
target_language_example: He aprendido mucho desde que empecé a trabajar aquí.
native_language_example: I've learned a lot since I started working here.

meaning: "much" or "a lot" + "that (feminine)" — used to say you like or use something a lot, or that something happened a lot on a particular (feminine) noun.
additional_notes: This is the combination of the adverb "mucho" (a lot, much) and the demonstrative adjective "esa" (that, feminine singular). "Esa" agrees with a feminine noun mentioned or understood (esa ventana, esa idea, esa noche, esa costumbre, esa palabra). In English you'd normally say "that ... a lot" or "... a lot that" depending on sentence; typical translations: "I like that X a lot," "That habit has spread a lot," "It rained a lot that night." Word order in Spanish is: verb + mucho + esa + feminine noun.
target_language_example: Me interesa mucho esa película.
native_language_example: I'm very interested in that movie.

meaning: 'a lot' or 'very much' + 'this' (as in 'a lot this week/area/photo') — used when 'mucho' modifies time expressions, places, or demonstratives with 'esta'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the combination of 'mucho' (a lot/much) and 'esta' (feminine singular demonstrative 'this' or part of time expressions like 'esta semana'). Common uses: 'mucho esta semana' means 'a lot this week' (often after a verb: 'He trabajado mucho esta semana' = 'I've worked a lot this week'), and 'mucho esta zona' isn't standard word order — better: 'esta zona ha sido muy afectada' or 'ha afectado mucho a esta zona'. In short, learners will most often see 'mucho' + time phrase with 'esta' as in 'mucho esta semana' or 'me gusta mucho esta fotografía' where 'mucho' modifies liking and 'esta' points to the noun.
target_language_example: He estudiado mucho esta semana.
native_language_example: I have studied a lot this week.

meaning: very cold (weather or temperature).
additional_notes: Used to describe strong coldness in the environment or how someone feels because of low temperature. Common with verbs like hacer (hace mucho frío / hacía mucho frío). Not used to mean 'very cold' as personality; it's about temperature.
target_language_example: Hoy hace mucho frío; ponte un abrigo.
native_language_example: It's very cold today; put on a coat.

meaning: much less; let alone; even less likely.
additional_notes: Used to downplay or exclude a stronger/more extreme possibility. Often follows a negative statement to introduce something even less likely or desirable. Can also be used to express wanting to do something far less (e.g., quiero gastar mucho menos). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No sé cocinar, mucho menos preparar postres.
native_language_example: I don't know how to cook, much less make desserts.

meaning: much taller; a lot taller
additional_notes: Used to compare height (or metaphorically, any degree) with emphasis. Commonly appears in comparisons with 'que' (than) or clauses introduced by 'de' (e.g., 'de lo que'). 'Mucho' adds emphasis to 'más' — 'más alto' = 'taller', 'mucho más alto' = 'much taller' / 'a lot taller'. Word order is fixed: 'mucho' before 'más'.
target_language_example: Ella es mucho más alto que yo.
native_language_example: She is much taller than me.

meaning: 'much' or 'so much' when referring to someone (you) — used in phrases like 'how much I/they...' or 'it's been a long time that... you'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in different constructions. 1) 'Lo mucho que te...' or 'No sé lo mucho que te...' means 'how much I/they/it ... you' (expressing intensity: need, love, etc.). 2) 'Hace mucho que te...' is part of the time expression 'Hace mucho que...' meaning 'It's been a long time that...' or 'I have known you for a long time.' 'Te' is the indirect/object pronoun 'you'. Translate according to context (intensity vs. duration).
target_language_example: No sabes lo mucho que te aprecio.
native_language_example: You don't know how much I appreciate you.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; literally 'much/many see' but normally incorrect on its own. It may appear as a fragment of longer expressions (e.g., 'mucho que ver', 'mucho para ver') or result from a typo.
additional_notes: The two-word sequence 'mucho ver' is uncommon and usually ungrammatical by itself. In natural Spanish you'd say 'mucho que ver' ('much to see' or 'a lot to do with') or 'mucho para ver' ('a lot to see'). If you encounter 'mucho ver' in text, it may be an edited fragment, poetic compression, or an error. 'Mucho' is an adjective/adverb meaning 'a lot' or 'much'; 'ver' is the infinitive 'to see'.
target_language_example: Hay mucho ver en esta ciudad, aunque la forma completa sería 'mucho que ver'.
native_language_example: There is much to see in this city, although the complete form would be 'mucho que ver'.

meaning: Nice to meet you; pleased to meet you.
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used when meeting someone for the first time. Can stand alone or follow a greeting (e.g., "Hola, mucho gusto"). Note: in a different sense, 'tener (buen/mal) gusto' means 'to have (good/bad) taste' — e.g., "Tus amigos no tienen mucho gusto" means "Your friends don't have much taste."
target_language_example: Hola, mucho gusto. Me llamo Ana.
native_language_example: Hello, nice to meet you. My name is Ana.

meaning: a lot of time
additional_notes: Used to talk about either the amount of time spent on something or a long duration. In natural English, it often becomes 'a lot of time' or 'for a long time' depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Paso mucho tiempo estudiando español.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time studying Spanish.

meaning: a lot of work to (be done / do something / ahead).
additional_notes: Usually appears in phrases like "mucho trabajo por hacer" (a lot of work to be done) or "mucho trabajo por delante" (a lot of work ahead). "Por" here introduces what remains to be done or the task-oriented purpose. Common with verbs like hacer or delante; can be used in present or past contexts.
target_language_example: Todavía tenemos mucho trabajo por hacer antes de la entrega.
native_language_example: We still have a lot of work to do before the deadline.

meaning: a lot to talk about / much to discuss
additional_notes: Used after verbs or with impersonal constructions to say there is plenty to discuss or many topics to talk about. Often appears in phrases like "hay mucho de qué hablar" (there's a lot to talk about) or with pronouns/subjects: "tenéis mucho de qué hablar" (you have a lot to talk about). Word order: "mucho de qué" follows forms of 'haber', 'tener', or similar verbs.
target_language_example: Después de la reunión tendremos mucho de qué hablar.
native_language_example: After the meeting we'll have a lot to talk about.

meaning: 'a lot to' / 'much to' (something) — indicates there is a large amount of something to do, say, learn, etc.
additional_notes: Used before infinitives or verbs/activities (mucho para + infinitive) or before nouns/clauses to say there is a lot of something to do, discuss, tell, learn, etc. Common in phrases like 'mucho para decir', 'mucho para aprender', 'mucho para discutir'. Context determines the exact English phrasing (a lot to..., much to...).
target_language_example: Hay mucho para aprender en este curso.
native_language_example: There is a lot to learn in this course.

meaning: many children
additional_notes: A simple quantifier + noun phrase. 'Muchos' agrees in gender/number with the noun (muchas niñas for many girls). Used to describe a large number of children; can refer to people present (Hay/Hubo) or possession/relationship (Él tiene muchos niños).
target_language_example: En la fiesta había muchos niños jugando.
native_language_example: At the party there were many children playing.

meaning: Thank you very much / Thanks a lot.
additional_notes: An emphatic way to express strong gratitude. 'Muchísimas' is the superlative form of 'muchas' (many), so this is stronger than 'muchas gracias'. Common in both formal and informal contexts; can be followed by a reason (por...) or by a short comment. Tone depends on voice and context.
target_language_example: Muchísimas gracias por ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for helping me with the move.

meaning: moved to (someone moved their home to a new place).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of 'mudarse a' meaning to change residence and go live in a different city, neighborhood, or country. Use with a place after 'a' (se mudó a Madrid). For other persons change reflexive pronoun: me mudé a, te mudaste a, nos mudamos a. Common in everyday and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Se mudó a Barcelona el año pasado.
native_language_example: He/She moved to Barcelona last year.

meaning: the clause 'when the ... dies' (subjunctive: 'when the [masculine noun] dies').
additional_notes: This is the present subjunctive form of morir (muera) used in temporal clauses introduced by 'cuando' to speak about a future event that is uncertain. 'El' is the masculine definite article before a noun (e.g., 'el bosque', 'el obispo'). In English we usually say 'when the X dies'. The construction requires the subjunctive because the event is hypothetical/unknown at the time of speaking.
target_language_example: Cuando muera el director, cambiarán las reglas.
native_language_example: When the director dies, they'll change the rules.

meaning: 'very' or 'extremely' used with a noun to express a strong state or feeling (literally 'dead from/of').
additional_notes: Used after a feminine subject (muerto/ muerta vary by gender) plus 'de' + noun to indicate an intense degree of that condition: e.g. muerta de hambre (extremely hungry), muerto de risa (dying of laughter). Common in everyday spoken Spanish. For masculine subjects use 'muerto de'.
target_language_example: Estoy muerta de sueño después del viaje.
native_language_example: I'm extremely sleepy after the trip.

meaning: 'the death of' (used before a masculine noun or title).
additional_notes: Combines muerte (death) + del (contraction of de + el). Use before masculine nouns/titles: 'la muerte del rey' = 'the death of the king'. For feminine nouns use 'de la' (e.g., 'la muerte de la reina'). Often used in news, stories, legal contexts, and expressions of responsibility or cause.
target_language_example: La muerte del autor cambió la publicación del libro.
native_language_example: The death of the author changed the book's publication.

meaning: 'very hungry' or 'starving'.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to say someone is extremely hungry. Literally means 'dead of hunger' but is used informally to emphasize hunger. Can describe people or oneself; often used with estar (estoy muerto de hambre) or deber de (debe de estar muerto de hambre) to guess someone is very hungry.
target_language_example: Después del partido, estaba muerto de hambre y me comí dos bocadillos.
native_language_example: After the game, I was starving and ate two sandwiches.

meaning: 'dead' (physically, emotionally) or 'deserted/quiet at a time' when followed by 'por' plus a time or cause; can indicate time, cause/agent, or idiomatic 'dead inside' sense.
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: with times ('por la noche') it usually means 'deserted/quiet during that time' (e.g., streets, places). With agents/causes it can mark cause ('muerto por la voluntad de...') or emphatic statements about who caused someone's death. In colloquial use, 'muerto por dentro' = 'dead inside' (emotionally numb). Be careful: word agreement matters (muerto/ muerta/ muertos/ muertas) and placement; 'muerto por' must appear exactly as shown when specifying cause/time.
target_language_example: Ese barrio está muerto por las noches, no hay ni un alma en la calle.
native_language_example: That neighborhood is dead at night; there isn't a soul on the street.

meaning: a fragment used in fixed expressions meaning 'dead and...' to join 'dead' with another adjective or participle (e.g., 'muerto y enterrado' = 'dead and buried'); often emphasizes finality or completeness and requires agreement in gender/number with the noun.
additional_notes: This is a multi-word fragment rather than a standalone phrase — it usually appears followed by another word (enterrado, abandonado, arruinado). Pay attention to gender/number: muerto/muerta/muertos/muertas. Can be used literally (someone is dead and buried) or figuratively (a project is dead and buried = finished). The fragment by itself is incomplete in most contexts. Note also common colloquial uses where grammar may be lax (e.g., mistaken plural agreement in some informal speech).
target_language_example: El silencio era tan profundo que el lugar parecía muerto y abandonado.
native_language_example: The silence was so deep that the place seemed dead and abandoned.

meaning: literally 'dead and' — part of a clause where 'muerto' (dead) is linked with 'y' to continue the sentence; shows someone has died and then adds another related idea or contrast.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'muerto y' appears when a clause states that someone has died (ha muerto / había muerto / pensé que habías muerto / que yo hubiera muerto) and the sentence continues with another action, reaction, contrast or consequence. Pay attention to tense of the verb around 'muerto' (past participle used with auxiliary verbs) and to the rest of the sentence that completes the thought.
target_language_example: Pensé que mi abuelo había muerto y me quedé en shock.
native_language_example: I thought my grandfather had died and I was in shock.

meaning: he/she/it shows the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Made of the verb mostrar (to show) conjugated in the present tense (ella muestra = she shows) followed by the masculine definite article el. Used to say someone or something displays or points out a specific masculine noun (el camino, el espejo, el estómago). Context determines whether 'show' means physically display, point the way, or reveal. If referring to a feminine noun, the article would change (muestra la).
target_language_example: Ella me muestra el mapa.
native_language_example: She shows me the map.

meaning: 'woman of' or 'the woman of' (used to link 'mujer' with a following noun introduced by the preposition 'de' / 'del' = de + el).
additional_notes: Del is the contraction of de + el. 'Mujer del' appears before a noun to indicate relationship, possession, role, origin, or a descriptive link (e.g., 'la mujer del capitán' = the captain's wife or the woman associated with the captain). Context determines whether it means 'wife of', 'woman of/about', or simply 'the woman in/with [something]'. If the following word is feminine or requires 'de la' or 'de las', use those forms instead (not 'del').
target_language_example: La mujer del pintor llegó tarde.
native_language_example: The painter's wife/the woman of the painter arrived late.

meaning: a woman in the [place]. (Used with a feminine singular noun for a location: e.g. 'mujer en la tienda' = 'a woman in the store')
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining 'mujer' (woman) + the preposition 'en' (in/at) + the feminine definite article 'la' that introduces a following place noun. It is not a fixed idiom—replace the place noun after 'la' (tienda, iglesia, casa, oficina). If the place is masculine, use 'el' instead (e.g. 'mujer en el parque').
target_language_example: Vi a una mujer en la cafetería leyendo un libro.
native_language_example: I saw a woman in the café reading a book.

meaning: "the woman is very..." — used to describe a woman with an adjective.
additional_notes: This sequence combines the noun 'mujer' (woman) + the verb 'es' (is) + 'muy' (very). It's followed by an adjective (buena, bella, grande, mala, importante, etc.). Use it to give a strong description of a specific woman or 'la mujer' (the woman). Word order: subject (mujer/la mujer) + es + muy + adjective. If you refer to a specific woman, add a determiner (esa, la, mi) before 'mujer' as in the examples.
target_language_example: Esa mujer es muy inteligente y amable.
native_language_example: That woman is very intelligent and kind.

meaning: 'the woman was' — past tense description (woman + imperfect of 'estar').
additional_notes: Mujer = woman. Estaba is the imperfect form of estar, used to describe ongoing, habitual, or background states in the past (e.g., feelings, location, physical condition). Together they start a past description: 'the woman was...' followed by an adjective, location, or verb in gerund/participial constructions. You can replace mujer with otra noun or estaba with other past tenses depending on context.
target_language_example: La mujer estaba cansada después del viaje.
native_language_example: The woman was tired after the trip.

meaning: ‘the woman is’ or 'my/your wife is' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal translation: 'woman is' (mujer = woman/wife; está = is — temporary state or location). In Spanish, context and possessives (mi/tu) determine whether 'mujer' means 'woman' or 'wife'. Use 'está' for temporary states (ready, sick) or locations (arriba, en la oficina).
target_language_example: La mujer está cansada.
native_language_example: The woman is tired.

meaning: 'mujer' = woman/wife; 'ha' = has (auxiliary for present perfect).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's just the noun mujer ('woman' or 'wife' depending on context) followed by the auxiliary verb haber in the third person singular (ha) to form the present perfect (e.g., ha dicho = has said, ha sufrido = has suffered). In many examples 'mi mujer' means 'my wife'. Word order and context determine whether 'mujer' means 'a woman' or 'wife'.
target_language_example: Mi mujer ha llamado para decir que llega tarde.
native_language_example: My wife has called to say she'll be late.

meaning: a woman who is very (…); 'mujer' = woman, 'muy' = very
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'mujer' (woman) followed by the intensifier 'muy' (very) plus an adjective: mujer muy + adjective. It emphasizes a characteristic of a woman (e.g., muy rica = very rich). Word order: in Spanish the adjective usually comes after 'mujer'. Use 'muy' before the adjective, not before 'mujer' (you say 'una mujer muy inteligente', not 'una muy inteligente mujer').
target_language_example: Es una mujer muy amable.
native_language_example: She is a very kind woman.

meaning: "(a) woman is not" — used to negate a statement about a woman or to say something about 'a woman' is not the case.
additional_notes: This phrase is simply the noun mujer (woman) followed by the negation no and the verb ser (es). It appears in contexts denying a quality, role or relevance of a woman (e.g., 'a woman is not enough', 'a woman is not a witch', or 'what my wife does is none of your business'). Word order may vary (e.g., "una mujer no es...") and can refer to 'a woman' or 'my wife' (mi mujer).
target_language_example: Una mujer no es responsable de tus decisiones.
native_language_example: A woman is not responsible for your decisions.

meaning: 'the woman has' (third-person singular: 'the woman' + 'has').
additional_notes: A simple subject-verb phrase: mujer = woman (could mean 'the woman' or 'my wife' depending on context), tiene = has (from tener). Used to state possession, age, feelings, conditions, or qualities. In some dialects 'mi mujer' means 'my wife' while 'la mujer' or 'esa mujer' means 'the/that woman'.
target_language_example: La mujer tiene tres libros en la mesa.
native_language_example: The woman has three books on the table.

meaning: the phrase 'mujer y' is not a fixed expression—it's simply 'mujer' (wife/woman) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and).
additional_notes: Read as two separate words: mujer = 'woman' or 'wife' (context decides), y = 'and'. In sentences the meaning depends on what comes after. 'Mi mujer y yo' = 'My wife and I'. Pay attention to context to know whether 'mujer' means 'wife' (married speaker) or 'woman' (any female).
target_language_example: Mi mujer y mi hermana vienen mañana.
native_language_example: My wife and my sister are coming tomorrow.

meaning: used to mark the indirect object 'to women' or 'women (as a group)'; indicates that women are the people affected or experiencing something (dative clitic + prepositional phrase).
additional_notes: This appears in the dative construction 'a + [noun] + le/les' used with verbs like gustar, encantar, interesar, etc. Spanish often uses both the prepositional phrase ('a las mujeres') and the clitic ('les') for clarity or emphasis. The verb agrees with the thing that is liked or affects them (e.g., gustan, interesa), not with 'mujeres'.
target_language_example: A las mujeres les gustan las rosas.
native_language_example: Women like roses.

meaning: women (who are) more / the most (used in comparisons or superlatives)
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'mujeres' (women) with 'más' to form comparative or superlative expressions. Context determines whether it's a comparative ('more ... than') or part of a superlative ('the most ...'). Often followed by an adjective and optionally 'de' or 'del' + group/place (e.g., 'las mujeres más hermosas del mundo' = the most beautiful women in the world). Agreement: the adjective after 'más' must agree in gender/number with 'mujeres' (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Ella es una de las mujeres más inteligentes de la clase.
native_language_example: She is one of the most intelligent women in the class.

meaning: 'women who' or 'women that'.
additional_notes: A relative phrase: 'mujeres' (women) + 'que' (who/that). Used to introduce a clause that describes or specifies which women you mean. Can be followed by verbs, adjective phrases, or relative clauses (e.g., 'mujeres que hablan', 'mujeres que conozco', 'mujeres que se burlan'). In English, you can translate 'que' as 'who' (for people) or 'that'.
target_language_example: Conozco a muchas mujeres que trabajan en la universidad.
native_language_example: I know many women who work at the university.

meaning: women have / women possess
additional_notes: This is the plural noun 'mujeres' (women) followed by the verb 'tienen' (they have). Use when talking about things women possess, physical traits, or characteristics. Word order is subject (mujeres) + verb (tienen) + object/complement. In Spanish, 'tener' is used for possession, age, certain physical states, and some expressions (e.g., 'tener sed').
target_language_example: Las mujeres tienen muchas ideas creativas.
native_language_example: Women have many creative ideas.

meaning: fantasy world; an imagined or unrealistic world.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is disconnected from reality, daydreaming, or imagining things that aren't real. Can be literal (a fictional fantasy setting) or figurative (someone not accepting real facts). Commonly used with verbs like vivir (to live) — e.g. 'vive en un mundo de fantasía' = 'he/she lives in a fantasy world.'
target_language_example: No puedes tomar esas decisiones viviendo en un mundo de fantasía.
native_language_example: You can't make those decisions living in a fantasy world.

meaning: 'the world of the' (used to refer to a particular field, group, or sphere)
additional_notes: This is a common Spanish phrase pattern: mundo de + definite article + noun (e.g., mundo de los negocios). It points to a domain, profession, social circle, or area of activity. Adjust the noun that follows (los/las/el) to match the gender and number of the group being referred to.
target_language_example: Entró en el mundo de los deportes cuando era niño.
native_language_example: He entered the world of sports when he was a child.

meaning: a (type of) world where... / a situation in which...
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or described world/situation followed by a clause (often subjunctive after verbs of doubt, desire, or negation). Often equivalent to 'a world in which' or 'a world where' in English. Can be literal (physical world) or figurative (a situation, state, or condition).
target_language_example: Quiero vivir en un mundo donde haya paz.
native_language_example: I want to live in a world where there is peace.

meaning: not a fixed phrase by itself; likely part of expressions meaning the world is in a certain state (e.g., 'el mundo está de cabeza' = the world is upside down).
additional_notes: Alone, 'mundo está de' is incomplete — it needs an adjective or noun phrase after 'de' to complete the idea. Common uses: 'el mundo está de cabeza' (things are chaotic), 'el mundo está de fiesta' (the world is celebrating), 'el mundo está de luto' (the world is in mourning). Use 'el mundo está ...' to describe the world's current condition.
target_language_example: El mundo está de cabeza después de tantas noticias sorpresivas.
native_language_example: The world is upside down after so many surprising news.

meaning: the world is full of / the world is full of (people/things).
additional_notes: Used to say that many of something exist in the world (often followed by a noun). Can express a neutral observation (e.g., 'full of creatures') or a negative opinion (e.g., 'full of idiots'). Structure: 'El mundo está lleno de + noun' or 'El mundo está lleno de + gente que + verb'.
target_language_example: El mundo está lleno de oportunidades si sabes buscarlas.
native_language_example: The world is full of opportunities if you know how to seek them.

meaning: 'the world likes him/her/it' or 'everyone likes him/her/it' (literal reading).
additional_notes: This phrase as written is not a natural fixed expression in Spanish. It appears to be a literal combination of mundo (world) + le (to him/her/it) + gusta (likes). A more idiomatic way to say 'everyone likes him/her' is 'a todo el mundo le gusta' or simply 'todo el mundo le gusta' or 'a todo el mundo le cae bien'. Without the article 'todo' or the preposition 'a', 'mundo le gusta' is likely a fragment or a translation error. Use 'a todo el mundo le gusta' for 'everyone likes (it/him/her)'.
target_language_example: A todo el mundo le gusta esa canción.
native_language_example: Everyone likes that song.

meaning: a better world
additional_notes: Used to refer to an improved world or future—often in ideals, goals, or slogans (e.g., for social change, environment, peace). Common in optimistic statements and campaign language. Word order: 'mundo' (world) + 'mejor' (better).
target_language_example: Trabajamos juntos por un mundo mejor.
native_language_example: We work together for a better world.

meaning: 'the world needs' — used to say that something is needed globally or by people in general.
additional_notes: A common phrase: mundo (the world/people in general) + necesita (needs). Used to express that something is desirable or necessary for society or humanity. Can be followed by verbs (infinitives) or nouns. Tone is neutral; context determines emphasis (e.g., moral, practical, humorous).
target_language_example: El mundo necesita más personas que cuiden el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: The world needs more people who care for the environment.

meaning: 'the world is not' — used to state that the world (or life/situation) is not something (as you expect or imagine).
additional_notes: This phrase begins a comparative or descriptive clause and is followed by an adjective, clause, or phrase (e.g., 'lo que era', 'tan dulce', 'como el mío'). It's a general statement about reality or circumstances. Often used to temper expectations or contrast with an imagined/previous state.
target_language_example: El mundo no es siempre justo, pero podemos intentar hacer lo correcto.
native_language_example: The world is not always fair, but we can try to do the right thing.

meaning: the real world; everyday life outside of fiction, theory, or a protected environment.
additional_notes: Used to contrast practical, everyday reality with fiction, theory, online life, school, or sheltered situations. Can imply challenges, responsibilities, or a correction from idealized expectations (e.g., “welcome to the real world”). Often used in phrases like "el mundo real" or "volver al mundo real."
target_language_example: Después de las vacaciones, volveré al mundo real el lunes.
native_language_example: After the vacation, I'll return to the real world on Monday.

meaning: 'the world' used with a reflexive verb or passive-like construction (se) — often part of phrases like "el mundo se..." meaning "the world [does/verbed]" or "the world is..."
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common word combination: mundo (world) followed by the clitic se. Se can mark reflexive actions, impersonal constructions, or passive-like statements. In examples: "el mundo se veía" = "the world looked/appeared (to be)"; "en este mundo se mide" = "in this world things are measured"; "el mundo se está haciendo..." = "the world is becoming..."; "hacer que el mundo se detenga" = "to make the world stop." Useful when you want to talk about what happens to or in the world.
target_language_example: El mundo se está recuperando después de la crisis.
native_language_example: The world is recovering after the crisis.

meaning: 'the world would be' (as part of conditional statements about how the world would be under certain conditions).
additional_notes: Used in conditional sentences (often with si/si no fuera por/sin) to state hypothetical or imagined states of the world. 'Mundo' = world; 'sería' is the conditional form of 'ser' (would be). Common structure: Si + condition, (entonces) el mundo sería + complement.
target_language_example: Si todos ayudaran, el mundo sería un lugar más justo.
native_language_example: If everyone helped, the world would be a fairer place.

meaning: died of
additional_notes: Third-person plural past (preterite or imperfect depending on context) of morir + the preposition de to indicate cause. Used to say people or animals died because of a specific cause (disease, hunger, etc.). In English both "died of" and "died from" are natural; choose "of" for illnesses and "from" for broader causes if desired. Verb tense and subject must agree (murieron = they died).
target_language_example: Muchos pacientes murieron de neumonía.
native_language_example: Many patients died of pneumonia.

meaning: died before (something happened).
additional_notes: Used to say someone died prior to another event (often someone's birth). Often followed by a clause introduced by 'de que' + subjunctive (e.g., 'antes de que yo naciera') or an infinitive construction ('antes de nacer yo'). Both are common; the subjunctive is typical after 'antes de que'.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió antes de que yo lo conociera.
native_language_example: My grandfather died before I met him.

meaning: died in the year (used to give the year someone died).
additional_notes: This phrase is the verb 'morir' (murió = he/she/it died) followed by 'el año' (the year) and is normally completed with a specific year or phrase (e.g., 'murió el año 1999' or 'murió el año pasado'). Common in biographical statements. You will usually hear a year or time expression immediately after it.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió el año 2005.
native_language_example: My grandfather died in the year 2005.

meaning: died (some time) ago — used with a time expression (e.g., un año, un par de años).
additional_notes: Combine with a time expression after 'hace' to indicate how long ago someone died: 'murió hace un año' = 'he/she died a year ago'. 'Hace' + time = 'ago'. If subject omitted, it's understood from context. Use 'murió' (preterite) for completed action.
target_language_example: Mi abuela murió hace un mes.
native_language_example: My grandmother died a month ago.

meaning: 'the museum is' — a simple subject (el museo) + the verb estar used to describe location, temporary states, or conditions.
additional_notes: Use 'está' (from estar) for locations (El museo está en...), temporary states (está cerrado/abierto), opening hours (está abierto de...), or relative descriptions (está a la vuelta de la esquina). For permanent characteristics you would more often use 'es' (El museo es famoso). The phrase is just the noun + verb and changes with the subject (estoy, estás, está, estamos, están).
target_language_example: El museo está junto al parque y hoy está abierto.
native_language_example: The museum is next to the park and today it is open.

meaning: very often; frequently.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens many times or regularly. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence. Slightly more emphatic than just 'a menudo' but interchangeable in most contexts.
target_language_example: Voy al cine muy a menudo los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I go to the movies very often on weekends.

meaning: 'very grateful for' or 'very thankful for'.
additional_notes: Used to express strong gratitude for something someone did. Commonly followed by a noun or a verb in -ing (in Spanish: a noun or an action expressed with 'por' + noun/infinitive). Agreement in gender: 'agradecido' (masculine) / 'agradecida' (feminine). Choose the indirect object/pronoun or possessive according to formality and number: 'Estoy muy agradecido por su ayuda' (formal) / 'Estoy muy agradecido por tu ayuda' (informal).
target_language_example: Estoy muy agradecido por su ayuda.
native_language_example: I am very grateful for your help.

meaning: a polite way to say 'that's very kind of (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used with a possessive or subject phrase after 'de' (e.g., 'de tu parte', 'de usted', 'de él') to thank or acknowledge someone's kindness. Common in expressions: 'Fue muy amable de tu parte' = 'That was very kind of you.' Formal: 'Fue muy amable de su parte.'
target_language_example: Fue muy amable de ustedes ayudarme con las cajas.
native_language_example: It was very kind of you all to help me with the boxes.

meaning: very well
additional_notes: A common, compositional phrase: muy + bien. It can describe doing something well (Habla muy bien), knowing someone well (nos conocemos muy bien), or that something seems good/nice (suena muy bien, está muy bien). At the start of a sentence, it can also mean "all right" or "okay then" to introduce what comes next.
target_language_example: Tu hermano cocina muy bien.
native_language_example: Your brother cooks very well.

meaning: doing/looking/feeling very well in (a specific situation or place).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'muy bien en + [noun/occasion]' or 'muy bien en la/ el + [noun]' to say someone did well, had a good time, or looked good in a situation or place. Also appears in constructions like 'lo pasamos muy bien en la cena' (we had a great time at dinner) and 'se ve muy bien en la foto' (he/she/it looks great in the photo). 'Lo pasamos muy bien' is a fixed phrase meaning 'we had a great time.'
target_language_example: Ella estuvo muy bien en la presentación.
native_language_example: She did very well in the presentation.

meaning: very good
additional_notes: Common adjective phrase modifying nouns (carreteras, ideas, migas, etc.). It intensifies quality: 'muy' = very, 'buenas' = good (feminine plural). Usage changes gender/number to agree with the noun (muy bueno, muy buenos, muy buena). Can also be used colloquially as a short greeting in some Spanish-speaking regions (e.g., '¡Muy buenas!' ≈ 'Hello!'), but in the examples it functions as an adjective phrase.
target_language_example: Tienes muy buenas manos para tocar la guitarra.
native_language_example: You have very good hands for playing the guitar.

meaning: very difficult for (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is especially hard for a person, group, or purpose. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive clause introduced by a pronoun (para mí, para ti, para cualquiera) or by an object/agent. In English you can translate as “very difficult for me/you/anyone to…”. Word order: "muy difícil para + [persona/agent] + [infinitive/gerund/clause]" or "muy difícil para + [persona]" with context.
target_language_example: Es muy difícil para mí aprender ruso.
native_language_example: It's very difficult for me to learn Russian.

meaning: very beautiful (plural, masculine or mixed).
additional_notes: Muy = very (intensifier). Hermosos is the plural form of hermoso (beautiful); use muy + adjective to intensify. Agrees in number and gender with the noun: 'muy hermosos' for masculine plural or mixed groups; use 'muy hermosas' for feminine plural, 'muy hermoso/a' for singular.
target_language_example: Los cuadros en el museo son muy hermosos.
native_language_example: The paintings in the museum are very beautiful.

meaning: it's very important that ... (introduces a clause expressing necessity or strong importance)
additional_notes: Used before a subordinate clause (usually with the subjunctive) to stress that something must happen or be true. Common in advice, instructions, or expressing concern. Followed by 'que' + verb; in formal Spanish the verb often appears in the subjunctive (e.g., cumplas, entienda, hable).
target_language_example: Es muy importante que llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: It's very important that you arrive on time.

meaning: very interested; highly interested.
additional_notes: Used to describe strong interest in a person, topic, offer, job, etc. Can modify a noun (estar muy interesado en algo) or describe someone's attitude toward something. Commonly follows the verb estar (Estoy muy interesado en...) or ser (Es muy interesante → different). Don't confuse with 'interesado' meaning 'self-interested' or 'opportunistic' when used as a noun/adjective about a person; context matters.
target_language_example: Estoy muy interesado en aprender español.
native_language_example: I am very interested in learning Spanish.

meaning: very interested in
additional_notes: Use to express strong interest in a person, activity, topic, opportunity, etc. Often follows the verb estar (estoy/estás/está/estamos/están). Can be negated with no (No estoy muy interesado en...).
target_language_example: Estoy muy interesado en viajar por Sudamérica.
native_language_example: I am very interested in traveling around South America.

meaning: very old (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used before or after a feminine noun (or as a short answer) to say something or someone is very old. 'Muy' = very; 'vieja' is the feminine form of 'viejo'. For masculine nouns use 'muy viejo'. Can describe people, animals, objects, buildings, etc.
target_language_example: La casa de mi abuela es muy vieja.
native_language_example: My grandmother's house is very old.

meaning: 'very well' / 'very good' (used to say something is done well, looks good, or to agree).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to praise quality, appearance, or performance (e.g., 'te queda muy bien' = 'it looks very good on you'), to say someone knows something well ('conocíamos muy bien'), or to acknowledge/agree before speaking ('Muy bien, ...'). Polite and neutral; extremely common in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Muy bien, empecemos la reunión.
native_language_example: Very well, let's start the meeting.

meaning: a doll in/on (used to say a doll is located in or on something).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's the noun muñeca (doll) followed by the preposition en (in/on). Use muñeca en + [place] to say 'a doll is in/on [place]'. Adjust articles (una/la) and possessives as needed: 'una muñeca en la caja' = a doll in the box; 'la muñeca en su cama' = the doll on her bed.
target_language_example: Hay una muñeca en la cesta.
native_language_example: There is a doll in the basket.

meaning: 'doll of' or 'toy of' (used to describe what a doll or figurine represents)
additional_notes: Muñeco means 'doll' or 'figurine'. When followed by de + noun, it indicates what the doll represents or is made of (e.g., muñeco de nieve = snowman, muñeco de acción = action figure, muñeco de peluche = stuffed toy). In Spanish, the full noun phrase usually includes the noun after de. Gender and number of the following noun determine agreement in the sentence.
target_language_example: Le regalé un muñeco de nieve a mi sobrino.
native_language_example: I gave my nephew a snowman (doll).

meaning: snowman
additional_notes: Refers to a figure made of snow, usually with coal/stone eyes, a carrot nose, and sticks for arms. Common seasonal word used in winter and holiday contexts. Singular; plural is 'muñecos de nieve'.
target_language_example: Los niños hicieron un muñeco de nieve en el jardín.
native_language_example: The children made a snowman in the garden.

meaning: sewing machine.
additional_notes: Refers to the device used to stitch fabric automatically. Common household item; often used with verbs like comprar, regalar, usar, reparar. Literal composition: máquina (machine) + de coser (for sewing).
target_language_example: Mi abuela tiene una vieja máquina de coser en el ático.
native_language_example: My grandmother has an old sewing machine in the attic.

meaning: typewriter (a mechanical or electromechanical machine for typing).
additional_notes: Refers to the device used to produce printed characters on paper by pressing keys. Commonly used in past contexts; in modern usage it may refer to vintage or collectible items. 'Máquina' (machine) + 'de' (of) + 'escribir' (to write) is compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Encontré una vieja máquina de escribir en el ático.
native_language_example: I found an old typewriter in the attic.

meaning: time machine (a device that travels through time).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a fictional device that allows travel to the past or future. Common in stories and casual speech about time travel. 'Máquina' = machine, 'del tiempo' = of time, so the phrase is literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Soñaba con construir una máquina del tiempo para ver el pasado.
native_language_example: He dreamed of building a time machine to see the past.

meaning: more about / further information about
additional_notes: Used to refer to additional information or details about a topic. Often appears in phrases like "más acerca de" (more about) or "más acerca del tema". Formal and neutral; common in written and spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Quiero saber más acerca de tu proyecto.
native_language_example: I want to know more about your project.

meaning: later; further on; ahead (in time or space).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a later time (I'll do it later / see you later) or a point further along in space (a bit further down the road). Common in everyday speech. Can be interchangeable with 'después' (later) in many contexts; with commas when at the start of a sentence: 'Más adelante, ...'.
target_language_example: Nos vemos más adelante en la tarde.
native_language_example: See you later this afternoon.

meaning: beyond; further than; (figuratively) besides/aside from
additional_notes: Used both literally (physical location: 'beyond/ farther on') and figuratively (to mean 'apart from' or 'in addition to'). Also appears in the noun phrase 'el más allá' meaning 'the afterlife' or 'the beyond'. Context determines whether it's spatial, figurative, or supernatural.
target_language_example: Más allá de la colina hay un pueblo pequeño.
native_language_example: Beyond the hill there is a small town.

meaning: beyond what (is) / beyond (something) — used to say something exceeds a stated quality or limit.
additional_notes: Followed by an adjective, noun phrase or clause (often introduced by 'que'). Commonly used to emphasize that something surpasses expectations, limits, or a described quality (e.g., más allá de lo esperado / más allá de lo que podemos imaginar). Literal components: 'más allá' = 'further/beyond', 'de lo' links to the quality or clause.
target_language_example: Su generosidad va más allá de lo imaginable.
native_language_example: His generosity goes beyond what is imaginable.

meaning: rather; more like; rather than (used to correct or soften a statement).
additional_notes: Used to modify or correct a previous idea: it can soften a description ("rather" / "quite"), indicate a more accurate alternative ("more like"), or contrast two possibilities ("rather than"). Common in everyday speech. Placement: usually before an adjective, noun, or clause.
target_language_example: No es alto, es más bien bajo.
native_language_example: He's not tall; he's rather short.

meaning: ‘more with you’ — indicates that something (time, attention, laughter, interaction, etc.) occurs to a greater degree involving the person addressed (tú).
additional_notes: Context determines what 'más' modifies (tiempo, atención, risas, conversación). Common in colloquial speech to express increased involvement or focus on the addressee. Can be used neutrally or with jealousy/discomfort depending on tone. Often part of comparative structures (más contigo que conmigo) or standalone after a verb (se ríen más contigo).
target_language_example: Sí, y ahora se ríen más contigo y no me gusta eso.
native_language_example: Yes, and now they laugh more with you and I don't like that.

meaning: more harm; cause more harm than good
additional_notes: Used after a verb to say that something causes harm (often greater than any benefit). Frequently appears in the phrase 'hacer más daño que bien' (to do more harm than good). 'Daño' is uncountable here; 'más' compares degree.
target_language_example: Ese medicamento podría hacer más daño que bien si no se toma correctamente.
native_language_example: That medicine could do more harm than good if it isn't taken correctly.

meaning: too much; more than is normal or appropriate
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something excessively or beyond what's proper/needed (talking, sleeping, drinking, etc.). Often implies negative consequences or disapproval. Literal translation is 'more than the bill/account', but idiomatic meaning is 'too much'.
target_language_example: No comas más de la cuenta; te va a sentar mal.
native_language_example: Don't eat too much; it'll make you feel sick.

meaning: 'after' (telling time) or 'more than the' / 'about' (quantity/partitive).
additional_notes: Most commonly used in telling time: más de las + hour means 'a little past [hour]' or 'it's after [hour]'. Example: 'son más de las siete' = 'it's after seven'. It can also appear in non-time contexts as 'más de' + noun with the article 'las' (feminine plural), meaning 'more than the' or 'over the' (e.g., 'más de las flores' = 'more about the flowers' or 'more of the flowers' depending on context). In casual speech 'más de' alone often means 'about' or 'over' (a number or amount).
target_language_example: Ya son más de las nueve; deberíamos irnos.
native_language_example: It's already past nine; we should leave.

meaning: bigger than (something/someone) expected or than it appears.
additional_notes: Used to compare size or importance to an expectation, appearance, or norm. Usually continues with a clause introduced by 'que' (e.g., 'más grande de lo que pensaba'). Common structure: 'más + adjective + de lo + (que...)'. Can be used literally (size) or figuratively (problem, power).
target_language_example: La casa es más grande de lo que imaginábamos.
native_language_example: The house is bigger than we imagined.

meaning: bigger than the (one).
additional_notes: Used to compare sizes. The phrase ends with 'el' as a short form of 'el/la/los/las' + noun previously mentioned (often omitted). In full sentences you'll often hear: 'más grande que el tuyo' (bigger than yours) or simply 'más grande que el' when the noun is clear from context. For feminine nouns use 'más grande que la' (e.g., 'más grande que la mía').
target_language_example: Mi coche es más grande que el tuyo.
native_language_example: My car is bigger than yours.

meaning: more important than the (feminine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: A comparative phrase used before a feminine singular noun or noun phrase. The structure is: más + adjective + que + article (la) + noun. Example: 'más importante que la reunión' = 'more important than the meeting.' If the following noun is masculine use 'más importante que el'.
target_language_example: Tu salud es más importante que la apariencia.
native_language_example: Your health is more important than appearance.

meaning: younger than (you/it/they) think or than (someone/something) really is.
additional_notes: Used to compare age or appearance: 'más joven de lo que...' = 'younger than what...'. Commonly followed by 'que' or 'que es/que piensas/que parece'. Often used to say someone looks younger than their real age or than someone expects.
target_language_example: Ella parece más joven de lo que dice su pasaporte.
native_language_example: She looks younger than her passport says.

meaning: literally 'more more'; not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish—most often appears as a repetition for emphasis in informal speech or as two instances of 'más' across a sentence (e.g., comparative structures).
additional_notes: Not a common conventional expression. Can occur as emphatic repetition (similar to English 'more, more!') or when 'más' appears twice in comparative constructions (e.g., 'cuanto más... más...'). Use caution: in formal Spanish, emphasis is usually achieved differently; for 'the more... the more...' use 'cuanto más... más...' or 'mientras más... más...'.
target_language_example: — ¡Más, más! —más más— necesito más azúcar.
native_language_example: — More, more! —more more— I need more sugar.

meaning: 'more normal' or 'more usual/typical'.
additional_notes: Used to compare how normal or typical something is (comparative of normal). Can describe behavior, situations, or values that are closer to the usual or expected. Often followed by que + noun/pronoun/phrase (e.g., más normal que) or by a clause.
target_language_example: Para mí, es más normal trabajar de día que de noche.
native_language_example: For me, it's more normal to work during the day than at night.

meaning: never again; no longer ever
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something will not happen again. It is stronger than just 'nunca' in some contexts and often appears in negative statements or promises. Can be used with past or future contexts (e.g., 'Ya no quiero verlo más nunca' = I never want to see him again).
target_language_example: No volveré a ese restaurante más nunca.
native_language_example: I will never go back to that restaurant again.

meaning: 'more or less' / 'approximately'.
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate amount, time, degree, or to soften a statement. Can appear alone (as a short answer) or inside a sentence. Equivalent to 'approximately', 'about', or 'roughly' in English.
target_language_example: Llegaremos en más o menos media hora.
native_language_example: We'll arrive in more or less half an hour.

meaning: most likely (that) / it's most likely that
additional_notes: Used to express probability or likelihood about a situation. Often appears as 'lo más probable es que' + subjunctive (when referring to hypothetical or uncertain actions) or indicative in casual speech. Can be shortened to 'lo más probable' in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Lo más probable es que lleguemos tarde por el tráfico.
native_language_example: It's most likely that we'll arrive late because of traffic.

meaning: more than
additional_notes: Usually used to make comparisons: cuesta más que..., cuenta más que.... In negative expressions like no ... más que, it means 'only' or 'nothing but'.
target_language_example: Este teléfono cuesta más que el otro.
native_language_example: This phone costs more than the other one.

meaning: more than anything/something else
additional_notes: Used to express a stronger preference, feeling, or degree compared with everything or any other thing. Often followed by 'cosa', 'cosa en el mundo', or left trailing in short responses. Can refer to people, things, feelings, or situations.
target_language_example: Te quiero más que cualquier otra cosa.
native_language_example: I love you more than anything else.

meaning: no more than a; just a; only a (downplays importance or limits something).
additional_notes: Used to minimize or limit the scope/importance of a noun that follows. Can appear in negative constructions (no es más que) meaning 'is nothing more than' or without 'no' as comparative emphasis (más que una simple X = more than just a X). Context determines whether it downplays (no es más que = only/merely) or contrasts (más que una = more than one/simple).
target_language_example: No es más que una excusa.
native_language_example: It's nothing more than an excuse.

meaning: more to see / mostly about seeing; often used to say something is primarily visual or that there is more to look at than expected.
additional_notes: Literally 'more than to see.' Commonly used to describe something that is mainly visual (e.g., 'It's more to look at than to use') or to indicate there's a lot to see. Context determines nuance: can mean 'mostly about appearance' or 'there's a lot to see.'
target_language_example: Este museo es más que ver que leer; las obras hablan por sí mismas.
native_language_example: This museum is more to look at than to read; the works speak for themselves.

meaning: "richest in" — indicates someone or something has the greatest wealth or abundance within a particular place, group, or category (can be literal wealth or figurative abundance like resources or cultural richness).
additional_notes: Usually follows a noun or article + noun (e.g., 'el hombre más rico en la ciudad'). Can refer to money/wealth or non-monetary abundance. Often interchangeable with 'el/la más rico(a) de' when the group or place is expressed with 'de' (e.g., 'el país más rico del mundo'). Pay attention to gender/number agreement: más rico / más rica / más ricos / más ricas.
target_language_example: Noruega es el país más rico en el mundo.
native_language_example: Norway is the richest country in the world.

meaning: as fast as I could
additional_notes: Used to say you did something as quickly as possible. Often appears with verbs of motion (correr, llegar, venir) or effort. Literal structure: 'más rápido' (faster) + 'que pude' (that I could). Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Llegué al hospital lo más rápido que pude.
native_language_example: I got to the hospital as fast as I could.

meaning: literally 'knows more'; used to say someone else/another person knows more or to form comparisons about knowledge
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like 'quién más sabe' (who else knows) or in proverbs ('Más sabe el zorro por viejo que por zorro' — 'The fox knows more from being old than from being a fox'). Used to ask who else is informed, or to compare levels of knowledge. 'Más sabe' by itself usually needs context (who knows more / who else knows).
target_language_example: Dime quién más sabe de esto.
native_language_example: Tell me who else knows about this.

meaning: more and more; increasingly.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a gradual increase or intensification over time. Often appears before adjectives, adverbs, or verbs (e.g., más y más alto, más y más difícil, crece más y más). Equivalent to 'cada vez más' and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: La ciudad se hace más y más ruidosa cada año.
native_language_example: The city is getting more and more noisy every year.

meaning: mask of / mask for (used to indicate the type or purpose of a mask).
additional_notes: Used to describe what kind of mask it is or what it's for (e.g., máscara de gas = gas mask; máscara de tigre = tiger mask; máscara de Halloween = Halloween mask). 'De' links the noun 'máscara' to the material, design, function, or subject. Word order: máscara de + [noun or purpose].
target_language_example: Se compró una máscara de carnaval para la fiesta.
native_language_example: He bought a carnival mask for the party.

meaning: the doctor (recommended/advised) to him/her; 'le' is an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him/her/you (formal)'.
additional_notes: This combination shows how Spanish uses an indirect object pronoun (le) with verbs of advising or telling. 'El médico le aconsejó...' = 'The doctor advised him/her/you (formal)...'. The exact English pronoun (him, her, you) depends on context. In Spanish the verb can be followed by an infinitive (aconsejó no fumar) or a subordinate clause with que + imperfect subjunctive (aconsejó que dejara de fumar) when reporting advice.
target_language_example: El médico le dijo que tomara la medicina todos los días.
native_language_example: The doctor told him/her to take the medicine every day.

meaning: 'doctor and' — the noun médico (doctor) followed by the conjunction y (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the word médico (doctor, physician) immediately followed by the connector y (and). You'll see it when listing people, places, actions, or attributes (e.g., 'fui al médico y...' = 'I went to the doctor and...'; 'Tom es médico y también novelista' = 'Tom is a doctor and also a novelist'). Use 'al médico' for 'to the doctor' (a + el = al).
target_language_example: Fui al médico y hablé con la enfermera.
native_language_example: I went to the doctor and I spoke with the nurse.

meaning: used to express contrast/affirmation: 'I (do) / I do like it' or 'as for me, I do'.
additional_notes: Often appears as 'a mí sí' to contrast with someone else's negative statement (e.g., 'No me gusta' → 'A mí sí'). Emphasis on personal preference or disagreement. Common in spoken Spanish; tone and context show contrast. Pronoun 'mí' is stressed after the preposition 'a'.
target_language_example: A mí sí me encanta esa canción, aunque a ellos no.
native_language_example: I do love that song, even though they don't.

meaning: me neither / neither do I (used to agree negatively with someone)
additional_notes: Used to express agreement with a negative statement said by someone else. Common structure: 'A mí tampoco (me/lo + ...)' or simply 'A mí tampoco.' You can also say 'ni a mí' in similar contexts. Do not confuse with 'a mí sí' (me too / I do).
target_language_example: A mí tampoco me gusta esa película.
native_language_example: I don't like that movie either.

meaning: emphasizes that the action happened to 'me' and not to someone else ("me, not ...").
additional_notes: This structure uses a tonic pronoun (mí) with the preposition a plus a contrasting phrase introduced by no a + [other person]. It's used to stress the victim or target of an action: "a mí, no a él/ella" = "to me, not to him/her." Common after verbs of action (pegar, besar, perseguir, etc.). Note the accent on mí (stressed pronoun).
target_language_example: Ella tomó mi bolso a mí, no a mi hermano.
native_language_example: She took my bag from me, not from my brother.

meaning: as for me
additional_notes: Used to add emphasis or contrast to the subject 'yo' (I). Common in Spanish to clarify or stress that the speaker is the one affected or holding the opinion. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause: 'A mí me gusta...' = 'I like...' but emphasizing 'me' (as for me). Can be shortened to 'a mí' or just 'me' in casual speech; word order and duplication (a mí + me) is typical and grammatical.
target_language_example: A mí me encanta viajar en tren.
native_language_example: As for me, I love traveling by train.

meaning: 'to/for me, not' — used to emphasize that something is not true for the speaker or that the speaker is excluded.
additional_notes: This is an emphatic Spanish construction: 'a mí' adds contrast or emphasis (to me), and 'no me' negates the verb for the speaker (they don't do/feel/think/receive something). Common in spoken Spanish to express disagreement, exclusion, lack of payment, or personal opinion. The underlying verb still appears after this phrase (e.g., invitas, pagan, parece, gustó).
target_language_example: A mí no me interesa ese trabajo.
native_language_example: I'm not interested in that job.

meaning: the least/ minimum (that)... — used to say something is the smallest acceptable action or amount someone can do
additional_notes: Often appears in the structure "Es lo mínimo que + [verb phrase]" to express that what follows is the smallest thing someone can do or should do. Can be used with different persons and tenses (puedo, puedes, podíamos, podía). Also used in sentences like "Hago lo mínimo que puedo" meaning "I do the least I can" — sometimes implies obligation, politeness, or mild criticism.
target_language_example: Es lo mínimo que podemos hacer por ustedes.
native_language_example: It's the least we can do for you.

meaning: 'mine, not (someone else's)'. Used to emphasize that something belongs to the speaker and not to another person or group.
additional_notes: Commonly follows the noun as a predicative possessive (e.g., 'El libro es mío, no tuyo'). When contrasting possession, 'no' introduces the other possessor (de ustedes, suyo, tuyo). Match gender and number: mío/mía/míos/mías. Note that 'mío' also appears in fixed expressions (e.g., 'Dios mío', 'amigo mío') where 'no' may be used separately to negate or plead.
target_language_example: Este libro es mío, no de ustedes.
native_language_example: This book is mine, not yours (plural).

meaning: me too; mine too (used to agree or say something also belongs to me)
additional_notes: Mío is a possessive pronoun meaning 'mine'. 'También' means 'also' or 'too'. Together 'mío también' is used informally to agree with someone or to say that something also applies to or belongs to the speaker. More common short replies are 'yo también' (I too) or just 'también'. Use 'mío también' when emphasizing possession (e.g., pointing out something is yours as well).
target_language_example: —Tengo hambre. —Mío también.
native_language_example: —I'm hungry. —Me too.

meaning: look at it from / consider it from (a point of view)
additional_notes: míralo is the imperative tú form of mirar + direct object pronoun lo (‘look at it’). When followed by de + noun/phrase, it introduces a perspective or angle: 'míralo de esta manera' = 'look at it this way' / 'consider it as...'. Common in spoken Spanish to ask someone to consider something from a particular viewpoint.
target_language_example: Míralo de otra manera: fue una lección, no un fracaso.
native_language_example: Look at it another way: it was a lesson, not a failure.

meaning: Look at my (the) ... (imperative: 'look me in the ...').
additional_notes: Commonly used in the set phrase 'mírame a los ojos' meaning 'look me in the eyes.' 'Mírame' is the informal imperative of 'mirar' with the object pronoun 'me' (look at me). 'A los' is the contraction of 'a' + 'los' and will change depending on the noun (e.g. 'a los ojos', 'a la cara'). Use 'míreme' for formal (usted).
target_language_example: Mírame a los ojos y prométeme la verdad.
native_language_example: Look me in the eyes and promise me the truth.

meaning: ‘music is a…’ — a sentence starter to state what music is (e.g., a language, a part of life, a revelation).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the beginning of statements about music. In Spanish word order you often see 'La música es una...' followed by a noun phrase (una lengua, una parte, una revelación). Use it to make general, emphatic statements about the nature or importance of music. Remember to include the definite article 'La' when referring to music in general: 'La música es una...'.
target_language_example: La música es una forma de comunicación sin palabras.
native_language_example: Music is a form of communication without words.

meaning: 'pop music' — popular, mainstream popular-music genre (short for 'popular music').
additional_notes: Used to refer to popular, mainstream music (often catchy, commercial songs). In Spanish, 'música' (music) + 'pop' (from English) — commonly used and understood. You can say 'la música pop' or just 'el pop'. To express likes/dislikes use verbs like gustar: 'Me gusta la música pop.'
target_language_example: A María le encanta la música pop moderna.
native_language_example: María loves modern pop music.

meaning: 'music and' — the noun música (music) followed by the conjunction y (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the word música plus the connector y. You will see it when listing activities, interests, or items (e.g., "música y baile" = "music and dance"). The noun música is feminine and singular. Use y to join words or clauses; it becomes e before words that start with the sound i- (e.g., "música e inglés").
target_language_example: Me gusta la música y el cine.
native_language_example: I like music and movies.

meaning: not good at all; very bad or worrying.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a situation, behavior, or thing is bad or looks bad. Often appears after verbs like 'pintar' (to seem/look), 'estar', or 'venir'. 'Nada' intensifies 'bien' to mean the opposite of 'very good.' Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: La noticia pinta nada bien; deberíamos prepararnos.
native_language_example: The news looks really bad; we should get ready.

meaning: nothing less than; (used to emphasize the importance, size, or surprising nature of something)
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase 'nada menos que' to strongly emphasize or contrast: equivalent to English 'nothing less than' or 'no less than.' Can express admiration, surprise, or the exact amount/degree (e.g., 'no less than three hundred dollars'). In brief introductions like 'Andrés Salgado, nada menos.' it emphasizes the person's importance or notability.
target_language_example: Fue nada menos que una oportunidad única en la vida.
native_language_example: It was nothing less than a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

meaning: 'none of that' / 'nothing like that' (used to deny or reject something mentioned).
additional_notes: Common phrase to deny a statement, dismiss an idea, or say that something is not true or not the case. Depending on context it can mean 'none of that' (as a noun) or 'nothing like that' (as a comment). Often used in short replies: 'No, nada de eso.'
target_language_example: No, nada de eso — nunca dije eso.
native_language_example: No, none of that — I never said that.

meaning: nothing about the galaxy (used to say someone knows nothing about a galaxy)
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining nada (nothing) + de (about/of) + la galaxia (the galaxy). Commonly used to state lack of knowledge about a specific galaxy (e.g., la galaxia de Andrómeda). Can be used with other nouns: 'no sabes nada de la historia' = 'you know nothing about the history.'
target_language_example: No sé nada de la galaxia de Andrómeda.
native_language_example: I don't know anything about the Andromeda galaxy.

meaning: absolutely nothing; not anything at all.
additional_notes: Intensifies 'nada' (nothing). Used for emphasis or to stress total absence. Common in spoken and informal contexts; can be repeated for stronger effect. Translate as 'absolutely nothing' or 'not ... at all' depending on sentence.
target_language_example: No encontré nada de nada en la casa.
native_language_example: I found absolutely nothing in the house.

meaning: 'nothing in the' (used to say there is no/very little of something in a specific place).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to indicate absence or very small quantity of items in a location. Often followed by a noun (casa, cabeza, habitación, caja, heladera, cocina, etc.). Can appear with modifiers like 'casi' (almost) as in 'casi nada en la...' to mean 'almost nothing in the...'.
target_language_example: No queda nada en la nevera.
native_language_example: There's nothing left in the fridge.

meaning: nothing out of (the ordinary); nothing unusual
additional_notes: Used to say that there is nothing abnormal, strange, or unexpected. Often appears in contexts like 'no hay nada fuera' (there's nothing out of the ordinary) or 'nada fuera de lo común' (nothing out of the common). Alone, 'nada fuera' feels incomplete and is usually part of a larger phrase (e.g., 'no hay nada fuera').
target_language_example: No te preocupes, no hay nada fuera.
native_language_example: Don't worry, there's nothing out of the ordinary.

meaning: nothing out of (the) — used in fixed phrases to mean 'nothing unusual' or 'nothing out of the ordinary'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the full expression 'nada fuera de lo común / lo normal / lo ordinario'. It negates surprises or exceptions: 'nothing out of the ordinary'. Common in both spoken and written Spanish. Word order: 'nada fuera de lo común' = 'nothing out of the ordinary'.
target_language_example: No encontré nada fuera de lo común en la casa.
native_language_example: I didn't find anything out of the ordinary in the house.

meaning: as if nothing had happened; as though nothing happened.
additional_notes: Used after 'como si' to describe someone acting or behaving as though an event or problem never occurred. Common in past-subjunctive constructions: 'como si nada hubiera pasado' (formal/past hypothetical). Can follow verbs like 'seguir', 'actuar', 'volver', etc. Tone can be neutral or express surprise/criticism that someone ignores an incident.
target_language_example: Ella entró y sonrió, como si nada hubiera pasado.
native_language_example: She walked in and smiled, as if nothing had happened.

meaning: just
additional_notes: Common multi-purpose phrase. Meanings depend on context: use 'just' or 'only' for limiting statements (1,2); 'as soon as' when followed by an infinitive or clause indicating immediate time (3: "nada más llegar" = "as soon as he/she arrived"); 'nothing else' or 'no more' for negation (4,5). Not formal or slang—widely used in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Nada más hablar con ella, supe la verdad.
native_language_example: As soon as I spoke with her, I knew the truth.

meaning: literally ‘nothing because’; a non-fixed sequence where ‘nada’ (nothing) is followed by ‘porque’ (because) to start or gesture toward an explanation that may be finished, implied or left unsaid
additional_notes: Not an idiom—it's simply 'nada' + 'porque'. Often used when minimizing a problem or declining to elaborate. Speakers may trail off after 'porque' or complete the clause (e.g., 'nada porque estoy cansado'). Intonation and context determine whether it's a full answer or a clipped reply. Typically informal in conversation.
target_language_example: —¿Qué te pasa? —Nada porque no quiero hablar ahora.
native_language_example: —What's wrong with you? —Nothing because I don't want to talk right now.

meaning: to swim with (someone) or to swim regularly/with something (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Most commonly means 'to swim with' (company: someone). In some contexts (example 3) 'nadar con regularidad' uses nadar + adverb/phrase to mean 'to swim regularly' — here 'con' is part of the phrase 'con regularidad' not a fixed partner of 'nadar'. Use 'nadar con' + person to say you swim together with them (e.g., nadar con mamá).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres nadar con tus amigos este fin de semana?
native_language_example: Do you want to swim with your friends this weekend?

meaning: to swim in this (one) — used to talk about swimming in a specific nearby body of water.
additional_notes: Common phrase used with a specific nearby location (este = this). Often followed by a noun (e.g., 'río', 'lago', 'mar'). Can express ability, permission, safety, habit, or intention (e.g., 'Quería nadar en este río', 'No está permitido nadar en este río'). Remember gender/number: use 'este' for masculine singular (este río); 'esta' for feminine (esta playa); 'estos/estas' for plural.
target_language_example: ¿Te gustaría nadar en este lago mañana?
native_language_example: Would you like to swim in this lake tomorrow?

meaning: nobody said / no one said
additional_notes: Used to report that no person expressed something. Often followed by a clause (que ...) or a phrase (nada, eso, nada de ...). Common in negative statements. In Spanish word order, 'nadie' (nobody) comes before the verb. Can negate an idea or deny responsibility.
target_language_example: Nadie dijo que el examen sería fácil.
native_language_example: Nobody said the exam would be easy.

meaning: 'nobody in the' or 'no one in the' (used before a feminine singular place noun).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that a place (house, room, street, etc.) is empty of people. 'Nadie' means 'nobody/no one'. 'En la' is the preposition + feminine article — it will change to 'en el' for masculine nouns (e.g., 'nadie en el coche'). In some sentences 'nadie' can appear with different word order ('no se veía a nadie en la calle').
target_language_example: No había nadie en la cocina cuando llegué.
native_language_example: There was nobody in the kitchen when I arrived.

meaning: nobody's perfect; no one is perfect.
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to excuse or accept someone's mistake or imperfection. Can be used alone as a response (like 'well, nobody's perfect') or followed by a context (e.g., 'en eso'). Tone is informal-to-neutral and widely understood.
target_language_example: Cometí un error, pero nadie es perfecto.
native_language_example: I made a mistake, but nobody's perfect.

meaning: 'nobody was' or 'no one was' (past/ongoing state).
additional_notes: Combines 'nadie' (nobody/no one) with the imperfect past of 'estar' (to be). Used to describe that no person was in a certain state, place, or agreed with something. In many contexts you could also use 'nadie estuvo' (preterite) for a completed action; 'nadie estaba' (imperfect) emphasizes ongoing or background states in the past.
target_language_example: En la fiesta, nadie estaba hablando; todos estaban sentados en silencio.
native_language_example: At the party, nobody was talking; everyone was sitting quietly.

meaning: nobody ever; no one ever.
additional_notes: A strong negative phrase combining 'nadie' (nobody) and 'jamás' (ever/never). Used to emphasize that no person has ever done or experienced something. Often appears before the verb. Equivalent to 'nobody has ever...' or 'no one will ever...'.
target_language_example: Nadie jamás podrá olvidarlo.
native_language_example: Nobody will ever be able to forget it.

meaning: 'nobody/ no one them' — used when saying that no one did something to or with 'them' (los = them).
additional_notes: Combination of the negative pronoun 'nadie' (nobody) and the direct object pronoun 'los' (them, masculine or mixed). Word order: 'nadie' before the verb and object pronoun usually before the verb or attached (e.g., 'nadie los vio'). Use when referring to people or objects previously mentioned. In negative contexts 'nadie' cancels existence or action (nobody ...).
target_language_example: Nadie los encontró en el parque.
native_language_example: Nobody found them in the park.

meaning: no one else; nobody else.
