additional_notes: Used to express that someone has reached their limit (energy, patience, tolerance). Commonly appears as a standalone phrase ('No puedo más' = 'I can't take it anymore' / 'I'm exhausted') or in different tenses (e.g., 'no podía más'). Can be followed by 'de' + noun/verb phrase to specify cause ('no puedo más de cansancio'). Tone ranges from literal fatigue to dramatic complaint depending on context.
target_language_example: No puedo más después de trabajar doce horas seguidas.
native_language_example: I can't take it anymore after working twelve hours straight.

meaning: to not be able to see; to be unable to watch or perceive (physically, visually, or sometimes figuratively).
additional_notes: Literally 'to not be able to see.' Used for physical inability (poor vision, darkness), inability to watch something (e.g., a program), or in some contexts figuratively to express inability to understand or tolerate. Conjugates regularly with poder (e.g., no puedo ver, no podíamos ver, no voy a poder ver). Context determines nuance.
target_language_example: No poder ver la pantalla en la oscuridad me frustra.
native_language_example: Not being able to see the screen in the dark frustrates me.

meaning: we couldn't
additional_notes: Used to say that something would not be possible, often in hypothetical situations introduced by si ('if'). Podríamos is the conditional form of poder for nosotros ('we').
target_language_example: No podríamos hacerlo sin ti.
native_language_example: We couldn't do it without you.

meaning: 'you (plural, informal) cannot' or 'you (plural, informal) must not' depending on context.
additional_notes: Second-person plural (vosotros) form used in Spain. Can indicate inability (cannot) or prohibition (must not / you're not allowed to) depending on the sentence and tone. In Latin America, use 'no pueden' for the same meaning. Verb that must agree with context: infinitive follows (e.g., escapar, nadar).
target_language_example: No podéis entrar sin permiso.
native_language_example: You (plural, informal) cannot/are not allowed to enter without permission.

meaning: I didn't ask.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of preguntar: used to say you did not ask (a question or for information). Can stand alone (No pregunté.) or be followed by a direct object or prepositional phrase: no pregunté la combinación / no pregunté por toda la historia / no pregunté quién.... In everyday speech, context often shows what wasn't asked.
target_language_example: No pregunté dónde estaban las llaves.
native_language_example: I didn't ask where the keys were.

meaning: 'could not' (past/subjunctive form of poder) — expresses inability or impossibility, often in past or in hypothetical/subjunctive contexts.
additional_notes: Pudiera is the imperfect subjunctive of poder (could). With no, no pudiera usually means 'could not' (wasn't able to) in subordinate clauses after expressions of emotion, doubt, wish, or after past verbs. It appears in examples of past inability (Es una pena que no pudiera venir = It's a pity he couldn't come) and in hypothetical or counterfactual/subjunctive uses (Ojalá tuviera una mujer que no pudiera hablar = I wish I had a woman who couldn't speak). In some sentences it conveys purpose with negation (para que no pudiera hablar = so that she couldn't speak).
target_language_example: Me sorprendió que no pudiera terminar el trabajo a tiempo.
native_language_example: I was surprised that he/she couldn't finish the work on time.

meaning: 'cannot' or 'may not be able to' (subjunctive form of poder used after negation or in subordinate clauses).
additional_notes: No pueda is the present subjunctive of poder (yo/él/ella/usted). Common after expressions of doubt, emotion, desire, impersonal phrases, or in clauses introduced by que. Often appears in negative constructions (no pueda) meaning someone/something is unable or may not be able to do something. English translations depend on context: cannot, may not be able to, or (in set phrases) 'that cannot...'.
target_language_example: Es posible que no pueda venir mañana.
native_language_example: It's possible that I/he/she may not be able to come tomorrow.

meaning: 'It can't be' / 'That can't be true' (expresses disbelief or impossibility).
additional_notes: Used to react to surprising, impossible, or unlikely information. Commonly used on its own as an interjection (No puede ser!) or followed by the thing that seems impossible. Can be softened with context (e.g., explaining why something can't happen).
target_language_example: No puede ser, llegaste antes que yo.
native_language_example: It can't be — you arrived before me.

meaning: 'there will not remain' or 'there will be no (thing/person) left'.
additional_notes: Future tense of quedar (quedar + negation). Used to say that something/someone will no longer remain or exist in the future. After no quedará you usually add what will not remain (nada, nadie, nada de mí, de vosotros, etc.).
target_language_example: Después del incendio, no quedará nada de la casa.
native_language_example: After the fire, there will be nothing left of the house.

meaning: may not want to
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive form quiera of querer. It often appears after expressions of doubt, possibility, or uncertainty, such as puede que, tal vez, or no significa que. Depending on context, it can mean that someone might not want something or might be unwilling to do something.
target_language_example: Quizás no quiera venir mañana.
native_language_example: He/She may not want to come tomorrow.

meaning: 'not to break' (used to tell someone to avoid breaking something).
additional_notes: Common construction: 'tener cuidado de no + infinitive' = 'be careful not to...'. 'No' negates the infinitive 'romper' (to break). Use with objects: vasos, jarra, etc. Polite/neutral instruction or warning.
target_language_example: Ten cuidado de no romper mi teléfono.
native_language_example: Be careful not to break my phone.

meaning: 'don't go out' or 'do not leave' (formal command/prohibition).
additional_notes: Polite/formal negative imperative using usted/third-person subjunctive (from salir). Used to tell someone (formal you) or to state that someone should not leave or go outside. Can appear in instructions, warnings, or reported speech (e.g., se le dijo que no salga). For informal tú use say 'no salgas'.
target_language_example: Por favor, no salga de la casa hasta que llegue la policía.
native_language_example: Please do not leave the house until the police arrive.

meaning: don't go out / shouldn't go out (negative command or advice in subjunctive/past tense context)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in reported speech or advice using verbs like decir/advertir and with the imperfect subjunctive (no saliera) after past-tense reporting verbs (e.g., 'le dijo que no saliera'). In everyday spoken Spanish, direct commands use the imperative ('no salgas' / 'no salga'), but 'no saliera' is used when reporting what someone told someone else or giving advice framed in the past.
target_language_example: Mi madre me dijo que no saliera tarde esa noche.
native_language_example: My mother told me not to go out late that night.

meaning: I won't tell (it) to... / I will not tell (someone) about it.
additional_notes: Used to promise or reassure someone that you will not disclose information to a particular person or group. Structure: 'no' (negation) + indirect object pronoun 'se' (to him/her/you formal/them) + direct object pronoun 'lo' (it) + future 'diré' (I will tell) + 'a' + person (often omitted when context makes the person clear or followed by 'nadie' for 'anyone'). In casual speech you may also hear 'no se lo voy a decir' (same meaning, different tense).
target_language_example: No se lo diré a nadie; puedes confiar en mí.
native_language_example: I won't tell anyone; you can trust me.

meaning: to be nothing / to be of no importance or value; used to downplay or minimize something (e.g., say it’s not a problem or not significant)
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Spanish. Context determines nuance: reassurance ('no pasa nada' / 'no es nada'), belittling importance, or literal absence of significance. Can appear in different persons/voices (e.g., «No va a ser nada», «No fue nada»). Tone and context determine whether it's polite, dismissive, or comforting.
target_language_example: No va a ser nada, no te alarmes; probablemente no sea más que un susto.
native_language_example: It’s going to be nothing, don’t be alarmed; it’s probably just a scare.

meaning: will not be
additional_notes: Negative future form of ser. It means that someone or something will not be a certain way, will not have a certain identity, or that something will not happen in the way mentioned. The subject is often omitted in Spanish, so it can mean he/she/it/you formal will not be depending on context.
target_language_example: Mañana no será posible ir contigo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow it will not be possible to go with you.

meaning: 'I'm not like' or 'I am not (the same) as'.
additional_notes: Used to compare the speaker to someone or a group, often to contrast behavior, values, or characteristics. Followed by a pronoun, noun, or clause (e.g., no soy como tú / no soy como ellos / no soy como para hacerlo). Tone can be neutral or defensive depending on context.
target_language_example: No soy como tú; yo prefiero hablar antes que pelear.
native_language_example: I'm not like you; I prefer to talk rather than fight.

meaning: 'it didn't happen' or 'it didn't occur'.
additional_notes: Used to say that an event did not take place. Can be used alone (No sucedió.) or with adverbs/phrases: No sucedió así (it didn't happen that way), No sucedió en realidad (it didn't actually happen), No sucedió nada especial (nothing special happened). Formal neutral register.
target_language_example: Planeamos una fiesta, pero al final no sucedió.
native_language_example: We planned a party, but in the end it didn't happen.

meaning: I don't know
additional_notes: Literally 'I don't know.' It is the 1st-person singular of saber. You can use it by itself as a complete response, or before a noun, infinitive, or clause: no sé los pasos, no sé decirlo, no sé qué es. With de + person, it can mean 'I haven't heard from' or 'I don't know anything about' someone.
target_language_example: No sé qué hacer ahora.
native_language_example: I don't know what to do now.

meaning: I don't know how many (—).
additional_notes: Used when you don't know or can't remember the exact number of something. Often followed by a noun or an implicit noun phrase (e.g., 'no sé cuántos años', 'no sé cuántos libros'). Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Hay no sé cuántos mensajes sin leer en mi correo.
native_language_example: There are I don't know how many unread messages in my email.

meaning: I don't know what
additional_notes: Used to express lack of knowledge about something. Often followed by a clause introduced by que, lo que, más, or a verb. Can be literal ('I don't know what it is') or vague/unspecified ('I don't know what I'll do'). In casual speech it may be shortened or used with a name plus uncertainty (e.g., "Freddy no sé qué" = "Freddy something-or-other").
target_language_example: No sé qué voy a decir en la reunión.
native_language_example: I don't know what I'm going to say in the meeting.

meaning: Don't hold back; go ahead; don't be shy.
additional_notes: Informal command telling someone not to hesitate, be reserved, or be shy about doing or saying something. Used to encourage action or permission. Tone can range from friendly encouragement to strong incitement depending on context (the last example is violent and unacceptable). Commonly followed by the action you want the person to do (e.g., 'No te cortes, dale' = 'Go for it').
target_language_example: No te cortes y pregunta si necesitas ayuda.
native_language_example: Don't hold back and ask if you need help.

meaning: Don't believe me / don't take it seriously (often said after a teasing or joking remark).
additional_notes: Used informally in Spain and many Latin American countries. Commonly follows a playful or exaggerated statement to signal that the speaker was joking or exaggerating. Literally: "don't believe yourself" but functions like English "just kidding" or "don't believe me". Can also be used to downplay a compliment (e.g., "No te creas, no soy tan bueno" = "Don't believe it / I'm not that good").
target_language_example: Me compré un coche nuevo... no te creas, era broma.
native_language_example: I bought a new car... just kidding, I was joking.

meaning: 'you have not' (present perfect negative, informal singular 'tú')
additional_notes: Combination of the negative particle 'no' + indirect/object pronoun 'te' (you, informal singular) + auxiliary verb 'ha' (3rd person singular of haber). Used to form the present perfect (pretérito perfecto compuesto) in negative statements about something that someone/something has or has not done to you. Subject is usually él/ella/usted or an implied third person (e.g., 'él no te ha visto' = 'he has not seen you').
target_language_example: Él no te ha llamado hoy.
native_language_example: He has not called you today.

meaning: a negative polite/subjunctive phrase meaning 'that it hasn't (to) you' or 'I hope it hasn't (done something) to you' (used with past participle).
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect subjunctive (no te haya + past participle) to express hope or concern that something hasn't happened to the person (te = you, informal). Common in sentences like "Espero que no te haya [verbo en participio]" = "I hope it hasn't [verb] you." The subject of the verb is usually third-person or an impersonal event. 'Te' is the object pronoun (familiar singular).
target_language_example: Espero que no te haya causado problemas.
native_language_example: I hope it hasn't caused you any problems.

meaning: don't worry
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone. Common in many situations: comforting (I'm here), declining concern (it's covered), or telling someone not to stress about a decision or outcome. Informal-neutral register; often said with calming tone. If addressing multiple people use "no se preocupen."
target_language_example: No te preocupes, yo me encargo de los boletos.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll take care of the tickets.

meaning: wouldn't have
additional_notes: Negative conditional form of tener. On its own, it means "wouldn't have." Very often it is followed by que + infinitive: no tendría que + verb = "wouldn't have to ..." In some questions or regret contexts, it can sound like "shouldn't ...?" or "shouldn't have ...".
target_language_example: Con más dinero, no tendría que trabajar los fines de semana.
native_language_example: With more money, I wouldn't have to work on weekends.

meaning: we don't have much / we don't have a lot
additional_notes: A simple negative phrase used to say there's little of something (time, money, food, etc.). Context usually clarifies what 'much' refers to; you can add a noun or leave it implied. Common alternatives: 'no tenemos mucho tiempo' (we don't have much time) or 'no tenemos mucho dinero' (we don't have much money).
target_language_example: No tenemos mucho tiempo para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: We don't have much time to finish the project.

meaning: to have no idea; to not know (about something).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you don't know the answer, information, or opinion. Often used with 'de' + noun or an interrogative clause: 'no tengo idea de eso', 'no tengo idea de qué hacer'. The infinitive form 'no tener idea' appears in dictionaries and in constructions like 'Puede que no tener idea...' but in speech it's usually conjugated ('no tengo idea'). For emphasis, speakers often say 'no tengo ni idea'.
target_language_example: No puedo creer no tener idea de lo que pasó.
native_language_example: I can't believe I have no idea what happened.

meaning: to have no idea; to not know at all.
additional_notes: Common informal expression used to say you don't know something. Often appears with personal conjugations (No tengo ni idea; Él no tiene ni idea). The double negative 'no' + 'ni' is typical in Spanish and is emphatic—literally 'to not have even an idea.'
target_language_example: No tener ni idea de qué hacer en esa situación puede causar estrés.
native_language_example: To have no idea what to do in that situation can cause stress.

meaning: to be speechless; to have no words (to express surprise, shock, admiration, etc.)
additional_notes: Used when someone is so surprised, shocked, impressed, or upset that they can't find the right words. Common variants: "no tengo palabras" (I'm speechless) and "me quedé sin palabras" (I was left speechless). Can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on tone.
target_language_example: No tener palabras al ver el desastre fue la reacción de todos.
native_language_example: To have no words when seeing the mess was everyone's reaction.

meaning: to be hopeless / to be beyond remedy or help; to have no solution
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, problem, or person cannot be fixed or changed. Can refer to illnesses, bad habits, situations, or feelings. Often used in everyday speech and can be emphatic: 'no tiene remedio' ('there's no helping them/it').
target_language_example: Mi abuelo fuma desde joven; parece que no tener remedio.
native_language_example: My grandfather has smoked since he was young; it seems there's no helping him.

meaning: I don't have anyone to (do something) with / I have no one who(ever) to ...
additional_notes: This phrase starts a clause meaning you lack a person to do an activity or to talk with. It's typically followed by 'quien' + verb (e.g., 'con quien hablar', 'con quien jugar') or by a verb phrase introduced with 'para' or an infinitive. Common in everyday speech to express loneliness or lack of company/support.
target_language_example: No tengo a nadie con quien salir este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I don't have anyone to go out with this weekend.

meaning: 'I don't have the' (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: Used to say you lack or don't possess a specific masculine singular noun that follows (el). For feminine nouns you'd say 'no tengo la'; for plural 'no tengo los/las'. Common in everyday speech. Word order: 'no' (negation) + 'tengo' (I have) + definite article + noun.
target_language_example: No tengo el permiso para entrar.
native_language_example: I don't have the permit to enter.

meaning: 'I don't have the' (feminine singular object) — used to say you lack something or don't have a particular feeling/intention (when followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Literal: 'I don't have the...'. In Spanish, articles and nouns carry gender; 'la' signals a feminine singular noun (la culpa, la intención, la llave). Many abstract nouns (culpa, intención) use this construction to express 'I don't have the intention/culpability'. For masculine nouns you'd say 'no tengo el'. For general lack without a definite article you might hear 'no tengo' + noun without article (depends on context).
target_language_example: No tengo la experiencia necesaria para ese puesto.
native_language_example: I don't have the necessary experience for that position.

meaning: doesn't look good / doesn't seem right (about a situation, thing, or person’s appearance).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of set phrases like "no tiene buena pinta" (doesn't look good) or "no tiene buena cara" (looks unwell). Used to express a negative impression, suspicion, or that something seems problematic. Often refers to appearance, atmosphere, or the likely outcome. Informal, everyday language.
target_language_example: Esa caja no tiene buena pinta; mejor no abrirla ahora.
native_language_example: That box doesn't look good; better not open it now.

meaning: 'it's pointless' / 'there's no point (in...)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or discussion is useless, won't change anything, or isn't worth the effort. Often followed by an infinitive (no tiene caso + infinitive) or a clause. Tone is neutral; common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: No tiene caso insistir si no van a cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: There's no point in insisting if they're not going to change their mind.

meaning: 'doesn't have the' (used to say someone/something lacks a quality, amount, or interest)
additional_notes: Common construction used with adjectives or nouns introduced by el/los (often with superlatives like "el menor" or phrases like "el más mínimo"). It literally means 'doesn't have the' and is followed by what is lacking: e.g., "no tiene el menor sentido" = 'it makes no sense.' Can be used about people or things lacking interest, sense, value, etc.
target_language_example: Ella no tiene el más mínimo respeto por las reglas.
native_language_example: She doesn't have the slightest respect for the rules.

meaning: 'you don't have a' (singular, informal 'tú' form)
additional_notes: Used with tú (informal you) to say someone lacks or does not possess a singular noun. Followed by a masculine singular noun (un) or sometimes used colloquially before nouns regardless of gender in casual speech; for feminine nouns use "no tienes una." Can imply literal possession or absence of a characteristic/situation (e.g., "no tienes un problema" = you don't have a problem).
target_language_example: No tienes un coche para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: You don't have a car to go to work.

meaning: doesn't work / is not working (he/she/it/you formal doesn't work).
additional_notes: Simple negative present of trabajar (to work). Used to say someone is unemployed, no longer works somewhere, or currently not doing work. Context determines tense/aspect: can mean 'doesn't work' (general), 'is not working right now' (temporary), or 'no longer works/has stopped working' when paired with 'más'. Common with subjects el/la que, quien, names, or impersonal percentages.
target_language_example: María no trabaja desde enero.
native_language_example: María doesn't work / hasn't worked since January.

meaning: had nothing
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'didn't have anything.' Commonly used in two ways: 1) to say someone 'had nothing' (e.g., no money, no time), and 2) idiomatically to say someone 'had nothing to do with' or 'was not involved in' something (often followed by 'que ver con' or 'con' + noun/pronoun). Context determines which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Él no tuvo nada que ver con el accidente.
native_language_example: He had nothing to do with the accident.

meaning: it's no longer acceptable/possible; that's the limit; it's over
additional_notes: Used to say something is finished, unacceptable, or no longer allowed. Can express that a behavior or situation 'can't continue' or that something is 'the last straw.' Context determines nuance: sometimes means 'there's nothing more' (final) or 'this is intolerable.' Common in Spain and Latin America.
target_language_example: Si sigues llegando tarde, no va más: tendrás que buscar otro trabajo.
native_language_example: If you keep arriving late, that's it: you'll have to find another job.

meaning: not worth the (something) / it's not worth the (effort/price/etc.)
additional_notes: This is usually part of a larger phrase like 'no vale la pena' (it's not worth the trouble) or 'no vale la pena hacerlo' and is followed by a noun or clause. Alone 'no vale' can mean 'it's not valid' or 'it's not worth it' depending on context. 'La' here often begins a noun phrase (la pena, la pena, la espera).
target_language_example: No vale la pena esperar tanto por eso.
native_language_example: It's not worth waiting so long for that.

meaning: you're not going to
additional_notes: Usually used as no vas a + infinitive with tú (informal singular 'you') to say someone is not going to do something. In questions like ¿por qué no vas a...?, it can also sound like a suggestion: 'why don't you ...?'
target_language_example: No vas a entender la película sin subtítulos.
native_language_example: You won't understand the movie without subtitles.

meaning: 'you don't go' / 'you're not going' (informal singular)
additional_notes: Second-person singular (tú) present-tense negative of ir (to go). Used to say someone does not go somewhere or will not go. In commands or warnings it can mean 'you're not going anywhere' (i.e., you must stay). Context and intonation determine whether it's a simple statement, a suggestion, or a prohibition. For formal or plural you would use no va (usted) or no van (ustedes).
target_language_example: No vas a la fiesta si no terminas tu tarea.
native_language_example: You won't go to the party if you don't finish your homework.

meaning: don't see
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'don't see' or 'don't watch' used to tell someone not to look at or not to watch something (commands). Colloquially, especially when used alone ('¡No veas!'), it functions as an exclamation meaning 'you wouldn't believe it' / 'wow' to emphasize something surprising or extreme. Can introduce a negative request (No veas la televisión) or warn someone (No veas esas cosas).
target_language_example: No veas eso, que es muy fuerte.
native_language_example: Don't look at that, it's very strong.

meaning: 'doesn't come' or 'don't come' (subjunctive/imperative form of venir).
additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive form of venir. In commands, 'no venga' (usted) is a polite/formal negative command meaning 'don't come' (to one person you address formally). In reported speech or after verbs expressing doubt/possibility (puede que, tal vez, decir que), it expresses that someone may not come: 'may not come' or 'won't come'. Context determines whether it's a negative command or a present-subjunctive referring to possibility.
target_language_example: Dile que no venga mañana si está enfermo.
native_language_example: Tell him not to come tomorrow if he's sick.

meaning: I am not coming / I don't come / I'm not here to (do something) — negative of 'vengo' (venir).
additional_notes: Literal negative of 'vengo' (first person singular present of venir). Used to say you are not coming somewhere, you won't go, or to deny the purpose with 'a' + infinitive (e.g., 'No vengo a arrestarlo' = 'I'm not here to arrest him'). Context determines whether it refers to physical coming, attending, or purpose/motive.
target_language_example: No vengo a molestar, solo quiero hablar.
native_language_example: I'm not here to bother you, I just want to talk.

meaning: 'to be eager to' or 'to can't wait to (do something).'
additional_notes: Used to express strong impatience or excitement about doing something in the near future. It is followed by an infinitive verb (no ver la hora de + infinitive). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No ver la hora de viajar a España este verano me tiene muy emocionado.
native_language_example: I can't wait to travel to Spain this summer.

meaning: 'we didn't see' (simple past — nosotros form of ver with negation).
additional_notes: Used to say that 'we' (nosotros) failed to see something in the past. 'Vimos' is the preterite of ver (to see); adding 'no' before the verb makes it negative. Can be followed by a direct object (nada, a nadie, algo) or a clause. Spanish word order commonly places 'no' before the verb.
target_language_example: Anoche salimos al jardín, pero no vimos a nadie.
native_language_example: Last night we went out to the garden, but we didn't see anyone.

meaning: I didn't come
additional_notes: Literal translation: 'I didn't come'. Commonly used to deny having come for a particular purpose: follow with 'a' + infinitive or 'para' + infinitive/noun to specify the action or reason (e.g., 'no vine a comprar' = 'I didn't come to buy'). Context determines whether it's a simple past negation or part of a contrast ('I didn't come to X but to Y').
target_language_example: No vine a comprar, vine a vender.
native_language_example: I didn't come to buy, I came to sell.

meaning: would not (do something) again / would never (do or experience) again
additional_notes: Conditional form of 'no volver a' (to not do/see/be again). Used to express a past or hypothetical feeling that something will not happen again. Commonly followed by an infinitive (no volvería a verte) or a verb phrase in context. Tone can be regretful or resigned.
target_language_example: Pensé que no volvería a hablarte jamás.
native_language_example: I thought I would never speak to you again.

meaning: 'not ... again' (used to tell or hope that someone/something does not do something again).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the negative 'no' with the imperfect subjunctive form 'volviera' + the particle 'a' + an infinitive (often omitted in examples but implied). It's used in requests, warnings, or wishes about preventing a repeated action: e.g. 'no volviera a llegar tarde' = 'not arrive late again'. Common with verbs of telling, warning, hoping, praying, or commands in reported speech. In many contexts you can also hear 'no vuelvas a' (informal tú imperative) or 'no vuelva a' (formal).
target_language_example: Le pedí que no volviera a mentir.
native_language_example: I asked him not to lie again.

meaning: I didn't return / I never came back (or 'I didn't ... again' when followed by an infinitive: 'I didn't see/learn ... again').
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of volver with negation. Often used alone to mean 'I didn't return' or followed by 'a' + infinitive (no volví a + infinitive) to mean 'I didn't ... again' or 'I never ... again'. Common in storytelling. Context determines whether it refers to physically returning or repeating an action.
target_language_example: Fui a la fiesta una vez y no volví.
native_language_example: I went to the party once and I didn't go back.

meaning: doesn't return
additional_notes: A negative form of volver (to return). Meaning depends on tense/mood and context: can be a simple statement ('doesn't return' / 'won't return') or a possibility using subjunctive with puede que ('may not return'). In commands or idiomatic phrases (e.g. 'Vaya y no vuelva'), it's a strong 'don't come back' / 'go and don't come back'.
target_language_example: Puede que no vuelva a verte.
native_language_example: I may not see you again.

meaning: don't (do something) again; please make sure it doesn't happen again.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone (often firmly) that an action should not be repeated. Appears with a verb in the infinitive after it (e.g., no vuelva a hacerlo = don't do it again). Formal or informal depending on context and tone; 'vuelva' here is subjunctive form of 'volver' (usted/él/ella). For tú commands you'd often hear 'no vuelvas a'.
target_language_example: No vuelva a llegar tarde, por favor.
native_language_example: Don't be late again, please.

meaning: 'we were not' (first-person plural, imperfect tense)
additional_notes: Used to describe past states or situations about 'we' (nosotros/nosotras). Often followed by numbers, descriptions, or clauses (e.g., 'no éramos más de cien', 'no éramos una pareja'). The imperfect tense implies ongoing, repeated, or background actions in the past rather than a single completed event.
target_language_example: No éramos amigos al principio, pero ahora sí.
native_language_example: We were not friends at first, but now we are.

meaning: No, thank you. (polite refusal or declining an offer)
additional_notes: Used to politely refuse offers, invitations, help, or things you don't want. Tone is courteous; you can add a name (e.g., "No, gracias, Andrés") or a short reason. Works in formal and informal situations.
target_language_example: No, gracias por la comida, ya comí.
native_language_example: No, thank you for the food, I already ate.

meaning: noche = 'night'; here shown with conjunction 'y' = 'and'.
additional_notes: noche means the period of darkness between sunset and sunrise. In examples it's followed by 'y' (and) to connect clauses: 'Era de noche, y...' = 'It was night, and...'. Use 'por la noche' for 'at night' and 'esa noche' for 'that night'.
target_language_example: Era de noche, y las calles estaban vacías.
native_language_example: It was night, and the streets were empty.

meaning: wedding night (the night of a couple's wedding).
additional_notes: Refers to the night when a couple gets married — often implies the celebrations and the private time after the wedding. Can be used literally (the actual calendar night) or to refer to the traditional first night as a married couple.
target_language_example: Pasamos nuestra noche de bodas en una pequeña cabaña junto al lago.
native_language_example: We spent our wedding night in a small cabin by the lake.

meaning: a night in/at (used to say where or how someone spent a night).
additional_notes: Common phrase for talking about spending a night somewhere (noche + preposition en + place). Can describe location (en un hotel, en casa) or characterize the night (una noche en un hotel caro). If you want to say 'spend the night' use 'pasar la noche en'.
target_language_example: Pasamos una noche en la playa el verano pasado.
native_language_example: We spent a night at the beach last summer.

meaning: 'the night was' — simple past/imperfect description of the night (used to describe how the night felt or appeared).
additional_notes: This is the structure noche + estaba (imperfect of estar) used to describe conditions or qualities of a particular night (e.g., mood, weather, sound, visibility). In English it's usually translated 'the night was...' or 'that night was...'. Use estaba (imperfect) for ongoing/continuous past descriptions (setting the scene). You can also say 'esa noche estaba' or 'la noche estaba' depending on context.
target_language_example: Esa noche estaba muy tranquila y no escuchábamos nada.
native_language_example: That night was very calm and we couldn't hear anything.

meaning: 'the night was' — simple past description of how the night was.
additional_notes: This is the past tense structure using 'la noche' (the night) + 'fue' (was). Use to describe the quality, mood, or events of a specific night. Can be modified with adjectives or noun phrases (e.g., 'tranquilo', 'fría', 'un completo desastre'). If speaking about 'last night', Spanish often uses 'anoche' or 'la pasada noche' + 'fue'.
target_language_example: Anoche fue una noche tranquila.
native_language_example: Last night was a quiet night.

meaning: 'the most ... night' or 'what a ... night' (used to form superlatives or to emphasize a quality of a night)
additional_notes: Used after an adjective to make a superlative (e.g., 'la noche más larga' = 'the longest night') or in exclamations with inversion: '¡Qué noche más...!' to emphasize a quality (similar to 'what a ... night' in English). Must agree with feminine noun 'noche'. The adjective goes before or after depending on structure: 'la noche más calurosa' (superlative) vs. '¡Qué noche más agradable!' (exclamation).
target_language_example: ¡Qué noche más divertida pasamos anoche!
native_language_example: What a fun night we had last night!

meaning: sense/awareness of time (how you perceive or estimate time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone's ability to judge durations, keep track of time, or understand historical/temporal concepts. Can refer to practical time sense (e.g., being punctual) or a more abstract sense (e.g., historical perspective). Commonly used with verbs like tener, perder, faltar (e.g., 'perder la noción del tiempo').
target_language_example: Con el libro me perdí y perdí la noción del tiempo.
native_language_example: I got lost in the book and lost my sense of time.

meaning: the word 'nombre' (name) used with the preposition 'al' (a + el) — part of phrases meaning 'to (the) name' or 'name someone/something as' or 'give/assign a name to'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but appears when 'nombre' is used with the indirect object introduced by 'a' + 'el' (contracted to 'al'). Common uses: 'decir/poner/le nombre al (bebé/persona/lugar)' = 'tell/give someone a name' or 'conocer de nombre al ...' = 'to know someone by name'. Word order and verbs change meaning: 'conocer de nombre al presidente' = 'I know the president by name'; 'ponerle tu nombre al bebé' = 'to name the baby after you' or 'to give the baby your name'.
target_language_example: Voy a ponerle el nombre al perro.
native_language_example: I'm going to give the dog a name.

meaning: full name (first name(s) + family name(s)).
additional_notes: Used when asking for or giving someone's full legal name. In Spanish-speaking countries, people often have multiple given names and two family names (father's then mother's), so 'nombre completo' may include middle names and both surnames. Common on forms and official documents.
target_language_example: Por favor, escriba su nombre completo en el formulario.
native_language_example: Please write your full name on the form.

meaning: her name (the name belonging to her).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman's name. In everyday Spanish, speakers more often say 'su nombre' (his/her/your formal) or 'el nombre de ella' for emphasis or contrast (to distinguish from someone else's name). 'Nombre de ella' stresses that the name belongs to 'her'.
target_language_example: No recuerdo el nombre de ella, ¿me lo recuerdas?
native_language_example: I don't remember her name, can you remind me?

meaning: given name; first name (the personal name, not the family/surname).
additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to a person's first/given name (e.g., María, Miguel) as opposed to apellido (family name). Common in everyday speech and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Su nombre de pila es Ana, pero todos la llaman Ani.
native_language_example: Her given name is Ana, but everyone calls her Ani.

meaning: the name of a (masculine) / 'the name of a' (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Literally 'name of a'. Used to indicate the name belonging to or assigned to an unspecified or generic masculine noun (un tipo, un oficial, un rival, un personaje). In Spanish articles and gender matter: 'nombre de una' would be used before feminine nouns. Can appear in many contexts (person's name, reputation: 'ensuciar el nombre de…').
target_language_example: Encontré el nombre de un autor en la portada.
native_language_example: I found the name of an author on the cover.

meaning: lit. 'name on' — used to indicate someone's name appearing on or associated with something (e.g., a poster, label, list).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun nombre followed by the preposition en. It commonly appears when saying that a name is written, printed, or used 'on' something (mi nombre en un póster, tu nombre en una etiqueta). Can also be used figuratively (nombre en clave = 'code name'). Word order and articles may vary: 'ver mi nombre en esto', 'poner tu nombre en la lista'.
target_language_example: Pusieron mi nombre en la lista de participantes.
native_language_example: They put my name on the participants' list.

meaning: "name on the" — used to say that a name appears on/was written on something (e.g., the list, the board, the sheet).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common word order: nombre (name) + en la (on the [feminine noun]). The feminine noun that follows (hoja, pizarra, lista, pared) determines what "la" refers to. For masculine nouns you'd see "nombre en el". Often used with verbs like anotar, escribir, ver, oír, poner.
target_language_example: Vi mi nombre en la lista.
native_language_example: I saw my name on the list.

meaning: proper name; a personal name (name of a person, place, or specific thing).
additional_notes: Used to refer to names that identify unique people, places, organizations, etc. In grammar, 'nombre propio' (also often 'nombre propio' vs 'nombre común') is capitalized in Spanish (e.g., María, Madrid, Amazon). It can mean 'first name' in some contexts but generally covers any proper noun.
target_language_example: Mi nombre propio es Ana y vivo en Barcelona.
native_language_example: My proper name is Ana and I live in Barcelona.

meaning: ‘name that’ or 'the name that' — used to introduce or specify a name (often followed by a clause).
additional_notes: Literal combination: nombre (name) + que (that/which). Commonly appears in sentences identifying or describing a name (e.g., "el nombre que busca" = "the name that you are looking for"). Can also be used in titles or fragments (e.g., "Un nombre que resulta familiar" = "A name that sounds familiar").
target_language_example: Ese es el nombre que me dio el profesor.
native_language_example: That's the name the teacher gave me.

meaning: 'we had' / 'it went for us' — often part of expressions meaning how something turned out for us or that something got out of our control.'
additional_notes: A short form of 'nos fue' used to report outcomes (e.g., 'nos fue bien' = 'we did well'). It also appears in constructions with 'se' like 'se nos fue (de las manos)' meaning 'it got out of our hands / out of control' or 'we lost track of it.' Context determines translation: outcome vs. loss of control. 'Nos' marks 'for us' or 'to us.'
target_language_example: En la feria nos fue muy bien con las ventas.
native_language_example: At the fair we did very well with sales.

meaning: we like (something); it's pleasing to us.
additional_notes: Used with verbs (infinitive) or nouns. Structure: nos (indirect object pronoun) + gusta/gustan (third person) + subject (what is liked). Use 'gusta' for singular or verb infinitives, 'gustan' for plural nouns. To state who likes something, use 'a + pronoun/name' for clarity (e.g., A nosotros nos gusta...).
target_language_example: Nos gusta viajar los fines de semana.
native_language_example: We like to travel on weekends.

meaning: 'he/she/it/they look(s) at us' or 'is looking at us'.
additional_notes: A simple present (or present continuous in English) form of mirar with the object pronoun nos (us). Subject is implied by verb ending: mira = él/ella/usted or ello/ella in impersonal uses. Can be used literally (someone looks at us) or figuratively (e.g., a situation 'stares us in the face'). Word order with object pronoun is subject + nos + verb in spoken/written Spanish (Nos mira = 'He/she/it looks at us').
target_language_example: ¿Por qué ese hombre nos mira desde la puerta?
native_language_example: Why is that man looking at us from the door?

meaning: we will think of (something) / something will occur to us
additional_notes: Used to say that a solution, idea, or plan will come to mind later. Common in spoken Spanish as a reassuring or casual way to suggest you'll find something (often followed by 'algo' = 'something'). Structure: 'se nos ocurrirá (algo)'. 'Se' is impersonal/accidental and 'nos' indicates 'to us'.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, ya se nos ocurrirá una solución.
native_language_example: Don't worry, we'll think of a solution soon.

meaning: 'they can (do something) to/for us' — third person plural of poder + object pronoun 'nos' (us).
additional_notes: Combines the indirect/direct object pronoun 'nos' (us) with the verb 'pueden' (they can). Word order can be 'nos pueden + verb' or the pronoun may attach to an infinitive (e.g., 'pueden seguirnos'). Means 'they are able to' or 'they may' do the action to/for us. Context determines exact translation (follow us, manipulate us, find us, etc.).
target_language_example: Los vecinos nos pueden ayudar si llamamos.
native_language_example: The neighbors can help us if we call.

meaning: he/she/it/you (formal) loves/likes us; wants us (depending on context).
additional_notes: Nos is the object pronoun 'us'. Quiere is third-person singular of querer: can mean 'to love' (affection) or 'to want' (desire). Context tells you which: with people (Ella nos quiere) it usually means 'loves us' or 'cares about us'; with situations or God it can mean 'wants us' or 'wishes for us' (Dios nos quiere aquí = God wants us here). Pronunciation: 'nos kyeh-reh'.
target_language_example: Mi familia nos quiere tal como somos.
native_language_example: My family loves us just as we are.

meaning: 'we have to (leave/...)' or 'we must (leave/...)' (used with an infinitive to express obligation for 'us').
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'nos tenemos que' + infinitive (or 'tenemos que' + irnos) to express that the speaker and others must do something (here: leave). 'Nos' is a reflexive/pronominal object meaning 'us' and can indicate 'we must leave' when combined with 'ir' (irse). Common alternatives: 'tenemos que irnos' or 'nos tenemos que ir'.
target_language_example: Nos tenemos que ir antes de que empiece la película.
native_language_example: We have to leave before the movie starts.

meaning: we're leaving
additional_notes: First-person plural reflexive form of irse (irse → to leave/go away). Used to say that we (or you and I) are about to leave a place or are leaving for somewhere. Can be present tense ('we're leaving now') or used with time expressions for future plans ('we're leaving [for]...'). Common in spoken Spanish. Contraction with subject pronoun is normal: "nos vamos" rather than "vamos" when emphasizing leaving/going away.
target_language_example: Nos vamos al aeropuerto a las ocho.
native_language_example: We're leaving for the airport at eight.

meaning: see you
additional_notes: literally means 'we see each other.' It is very commonly used as a casual way to say goodbye, often with a time or place added: nos vemos mañana, nos vemos en el puente. It can also simply mean that two or more people will meet or see each other.
target_language_example: Bueno, me tengo que ir. Nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Well, I have to go. See you tomorrow.

meaning: 'we will see each other' or 'we'll meet'.
additional_notes: Future tense of 'verse' (verse = to see each other). Used to say you'll meet or see someone in the future. Common in farewells or to arrange future meetings: can be followed by place or time (e.g., allí, esta noche). Tone is neutral; can sound final (Ya nos veremos) or reassuring (nos veremos pronto).
target_language_example: Nos veremos mañana en la estación.
native_language_example: We'll see each other tomorrow at the station.

meaning: 'we see each other again' or 'we meet again' (subjunctive, first-person plural).
additional_notes: Used with 'espero', 'quizá', 'hasta que', etc., to express hope or possibility of meeting again. 'Volvamos' is the present subjunctive of 'volver' (to return/meet again) and 'nos' marks a reciprocal action (each other). Often appears as 'nos volvamos a ver' or 'nos volvamos a encontrar'.
target_language_example: Espero que nos volvamos a ver el próximo año.
native_language_example: I hope we see each other again next year.

meaning: we will see each other again / we'll meet again
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb 'volverse a ver' (verse = to see each other). 'Nos volveremos' is future tense (nosotros) and implies a future reunion. Often appears with 'a' (nos volveremos a ver) but can omit it in informal speech. Used to express hope, certainty, or question about meeting again.
target_language_example: Espero que nos volveremos a ver el próximo año.
native_language_example: I hope we'll see each other again next year.

meaning: we two / both of us (emphatic: the two of us)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that exactly two people (including the speaker) are involved. Common in spoken and written Spanish to clarify or contrast 'the two of us' from others. Can appear as 'nosotros dos' (masculine/mixed) or 'nosotras dos' (all-female).
target_language_example: Uno de nosotros dos tiene que quedarse en casa.
native_language_example: One of the two of us has to stay home.

meaning: we go / we are going (we will), usually followed by 'a' + infinitive to mean 'we are going to [do something]'.
additional_notes: Nosotros is the subject pronoun 'we' (often optional in Spanish). 'Vamos' is the present tense of 'ir' (to go). Together, 'nosotros vamos a + infinitive' expresses a near-future action (equivalent to English 'we are going to [do something]' or 'we will [do something]'). In casual speech the subject pronoun 'nosotros' is frequently dropped: 'Vamos a alquilar un coche.' Informal or strong language in the infinitive clause (see example 5) depends on the verb/words used after 'a'.
target_language_example: Nosotros vamos a cocinar esta noche.
native_language_example: We are going to cook tonight.

meaning: 'grades in' (school subjects) OR 'notes on/at/in' depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to talk about school grades: sacar/obtener buenas/malas notas en + subject = to get good/bad grades in [subject]. Can also mean musical notes (las notas en un pasaje) or physical notes left somewhere (dejar notas en la puerta). Context (school, music, or written notes) determines meaning.
target_language_example: Siempre saco buenas notas en historia.
native_language_example: I always get good grades in history.

meaning: news of his/her/your/their (something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific piece of news about someone (su = his, her, your (formal), their). Followed by a noun (embarazo, llegada, muerte, etc.). Common structure: 'la noticia de su + [noun]'. Indicates that people received or reacted to that news.
target_language_example: La noticia de su ascenso alegró a todo el equipo.
native_language_example: The news of his/her promotion made the whole team happy.

meaning: news for / news to tell someone (about something).
additional_notes: Used to say you have information (often important or personal) intended for a specific person or group. Commonly appears in phrases like 'tengo noticias para ti' (I have news for you) or 'tengo malas noticias para...' (I have bad news for...). The preposition 'para' indicates the recipient. Can be followed by a person (ti, usted, vosotros) or by a clause (e.g., 'para decirte...').
target_language_example: Tengo buenas noticias para ti: aprobaste el examen.
native_language_example: I have good news for you: you passed the exam.

meaning: ninety-six (96).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used to state the number 96. Can refer to a year (e.g., 'el noventa y seis' meaning 1996 or 1896 depending on context) or simply the quantity. In spoken Spanish, numbers are usually pronounced without 'y' for tens and units like 'treinta y dos' — here the 'y' is standard. Used in lists, counts, addresses, ages, etc.
target_language_example: En 1996, pero también puedo decir noventa y seis como número.
native_language_example: In 1996, but I can also say ninety-six as a number.

meaning: 'my/your/etc. girlfriend is' (the noun novia + the verb ser 'is')
additional_notes: Novia = girlfriend (or fiancée in some contexts). Here 'es' is the third-person singular of ser (to be). Useful for describing identity, origin, profession, nationality, or characteristics (e.g., 'Mi novia es actriz', 'Mi novia es canadiense', 'Mi novia es muy hermosa'). Replace the possessive (mi/tu/su) as needed: 'Tu novia es...', 'Su novia es...'.
target_language_example: Tu novia es peruana y simpática.
native_language_example: Your girlfriend is Peruvian and friendly.

meaning: ‘my/your/his/etc. boyfriend is…’ — the phrase 'novio' (boyfriend) followed by the verb 'es' (is) to describe someone’s boyfriend.
additional_notes: Used to state or describe a person's boyfriend (gender: male partner). Replace 'novio' with 'novia' for girlfriend. Subject pronoun or possessor (mi, tu, su, etc.) normally comes before 'novio' (e.g., 'mi novio es...'). 'Es' is the third-person singular of 'ser' for permanent or defining traits (profession, nationality, identity, etc.).
target_language_example: Su novio es médico.
native_language_example: Her boyfriend is a doctor.

meaning: literally 'clouds of' — used to describe types or qualities of clouds or used metaphorically (e.g., 'nubes de verano' = summer clouds).
additional_notes: This is a prepositional phrase combining 'nubes' (clouds) with 'de' (of). Commonly followed by a noun that specifies the kind, season, color, or metaphorical quality (nubes de verano, nubes de tormenta, nubes de algodón). In metaphorical uses it can describe how something passes or appears (e.g., 'pasaron como las nubes de verano' = they passed as quickly as summer clouds).
target_language_example: Las nubes de tormenta cubrieron el cielo en minutos.
native_language_example: The storm clouds covered the sky in minutes.

meaning: 'clouds in' — used to talk about clouds being in/over a place or metaphorically having one's mind elsewhere.
additional_notes: Literal use: describes physical clouds located in or over something (e.g., en el cielo, en el suelo as shadows). Figurative use: part of the expression 'tener la cabeza en las nubes' meaning to be daydreaming or distracted. 'Nubes en' itself is just the noun 'nubes' (clouds) followed by the preposition 'en' and must be completed with the location or context (e.g., 'nubes en el cielo', 'nubes en la playa').
target_language_example: Había nubes en el horizonte y parecía que llovería.
native_language_example: There were clouds on the horizon and it looked like it would rain.

meaning: our language; our tongue.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a language shared by the speaker and others (e.g., Spanish, a regional language, or the mother tongue). Can mean 'our way of speaking' or 'our native language' depending on context. 'Nuestra' is the possessive 'our'; 'lengua' = language/tongue.
target_language_example: En nuestra lengua hay muchas palabras para describir la naturaleza.
native_language_example: In our language there are many words to describe nature.

meaning: 'our best' (used before a noun to say something/someone is the best we have or the best option)
additional_notes: Nuestra = 'our'. Mejor = 'best' (comparative/adjective). Combined, they modify a following noun (e.g., nuestra mejor película, nuestra mejor opción). Common with abstract things (opción, defensa) and people (espía). Agreement: mejor does not change for gender/number; use 'nuestro/nuestra' to match the noun's gender.
target_language_example: Esta ruta es nuestra mejor opción ahora mismo.
native_language_example: This route is our best option right now.

meaning: 'our day' — can mean a special day for us, a lucky day, or a planned day/event belonging to us.
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'our day.' Used to say today belongs to us (e.g., it's our big day), that it's our lucky day (good luck), or to refer to a scheduled day/event (nuestro día de campo = our picnic day). Context determines whether it means 'special/important day', 'lucky day', or simply 'the day we planned.'
target_language_example: Hoy es nuestro día: por fin inauguramos la tienda.
native_language_example: Today is our day: we finally open the shop.

meaning: on our side; in our favor
additional_notes: Used to say that people, circumstances, luck, the law, etc. support or favor 'us' (the speaker and their group). Often appears in the phrase 'estar de nuestro lado' or 'tener X de nuestro lado' to mean 'X is supporting us' or 'works in our favor.'
target_language_example: Con todas las pruebas, la ley está de nuestro lado.
native_language_example: With all the evidence, the law is on our side.

meaning: our best (used before a noun or noun phrase); indicates the best one(s) belonging to 'us'.
additional_notes: Combines the possessive nuestro(a/os/as) 'our' with 'mejor' meaning 'best' or 'better'. Agreement: nuestro changes gender and number to match the noun (nuestro mejor amigo, nuestra mejor amiga, nuestros mejores jugadores). Commonly appears in expressions like 'nuestro mejor amigo' (our best friend) and 'hacer nuestro mejor esfuerzo' (to do our best).
target_language_example: Creo que este será nuestro mejor episodio.
native_language_example: I think this will be our best episode.

meaning: new star (literally); can mean a newly discovered star or a rising/new celebrity.
additional_notes: Literally refers to a star that is new or newly discovered in the sky. Commonly used figuratively to describe a new or rising talent/celebrity (e.g., 'la nueva estrella del cine'). Context tells which meaning is intended (astronomy vs. fame).
target_language_example: Han encontrado una nueva estrella en la constelación.
native_language_example: They have found a new star in the constellation.

meaning: 'new to' or 'new for' (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is new in relation to a person, purpose, or place. 'Nueva' agrees in gender with the noun it describes (feminine singular). 'Para' indicates the beneficiary, recipient, intended use, or context. For masculine nouns use 'nuevo para'; plural forms: 'nuevas para' / 'nuevos para'.
target_language_example: Es una idea nueva para mí.
native_language_example: It's a new idea to me.

meaning: New World (the Americas); also can mean a new, unknown, or different world/situation.
additional_notes: Often capitalized as Nuevo Mundo when referring historically/geographically to the Americas after European discovery (the 'New World'). Lowercase can be used figuratively to talk about a new or unfamiliar world or situation (e.g., 'entrar en un nuevo mundo'). Context determines whether it's literal (geographic/historical) or figurative.
target_language_example: Después del viaje, sintió que había entrado en un nuevo mundo.
native_language_example: After the trip, he felt like he had entered a new world.

meaning: never before; not at any previous time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has not happened at any time up to now. Often placed before or after the verb (e.g., 'Nunca antes te había sucedido' or 'Él no ha ido nunca antes'). Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Nunca antes había probado sushi tan bueno.
native_language_example: I had never tried such good sushi before.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) never gave in; never yielded.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of 'ceder' with 'nunca' (never). Used to say someone did not give in, yield, or give up to something (e.g., temptation, pressure, an argument). Subject can be él/ella/usted; context determines the target (he/she/you formal). With different subjects you must conjugate cedió accordingly (yo cedí, tú cediste, nosotros cedimos, etc.).
target_language_example: A pesar de las presiones, ella nunca cedió.
native_language_example: Despite the pressure, she never gave in.

meaning: never say (you/he/she/they should never say); a negative command or advice with 'decir'.
additional_notes: Combines 'nunca' (never) with the imperative or subjunctive form of 'decir'. Most commonly used as advice or a warning: 'Nunca digas...' + clause. Depending on context the verb that follows may be in indicative or subjunctive (often subjunctive after expressions of doubt or emotion). Can be addressed to tú (imperative: 'Nunca digas...') or used descriptively ('Nunca digas eso' = 'Never say that').
target_language_example: Nunca digas que no lo intentaste.
native_language_example: Never say that you didn't try.

meaning: 'never say never' — a warning that something thought impossible might still happen.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to be too sure that something will never occur. Often said after a surprising event or when advising caution. Tone can be casual or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Sé que no te gusta viajar solo, pero nunca digas nunca; podrías cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: I know you don't like traveling alone, but never say never; you might change your mind.

meaning: 'it's never too (something)' — usually completed with 'tarde' to mean 'it's never too late'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as the full phrase 'nunca es demasiado tarde' meaning 'it's never too late' (to do something). Used to encourage action or change; follow with an infinitive (para + infinitive) or a clause. Can be shortened in conversation to 'nunca es demasiado' when context (like 'tarde') is understood.
target_language_example: Nunca es demasiado tarde para intentarlo de nuevo.
native_language_example: It's never too late to try again.

meaning: 'never does' (he/she/it never does something).
additional_notes: Nunca = never. Hace is the 3rd person singular present of hacer (to do/make). Used to describe that someone or something does not do an action habitually or at all. Context determines what follows (e.g., nunca hace lo que se le dice = never does what they're told). Can appear with nada (never does anything) or with clauses.
target_language_example: Ella nunca hace caso cuando le hablo.
native_language_example: She never pays attention when I talk to her.

meaning: never did
additional_notes: Past tense phrase: 'nunca' = never, 'hizo' = he/she/it/you(formal) did (preterite of hacer). Used to say someone did not do something at any time in the past. Watch out for double negatives: Spanish often allows double negatives (e.g., 'Ningún policía nunca hizo...') but in standard Spanish you would normally use either 'ningún... jamás' or 'ningún... nunca' depending on emphasis; literal English typically drops the extra negative.
target_language_example: Él nunca hizo la tarea.
native_language_example: He never did the homework.

meaning: never ever; emphatic never.
additional_notes: A strong, emphatic way to say 'never' in Spanish. Used to stress that something has not happened and will not happen. Often appears in negative statements and can be used alone for emphasis (e.g., '¡Nunca jamás!'). More emotional or dramatic than simple 'nunca'.
target_language_example: Nunca jamás voy a olvidarlo.
native_language_example: I will never ever forget it.

meaning: 'never' + indirect object pronoun 'them' / 'to them' (used to say something never happens to or for people/things)
additional_notes: Combines 'nunca' (never) with the indirect object pronoun 'les' (to them/for them). Used when the action or state does not apply to a group: e.g. 'A mis abuelos nunca les gustaba...' = 'My grandparents never liked...'. 'Les' agrees with third-person plural (ellos/ustedes). Word order can vary: 'Nunca les digas...' (Never tell them...).
target_language_example: A los niños nunca les dieron permiso para entrar.
native_language_example: The children were never given permission to go in.

meaning: never them
additional_notes: A combination of the adverb 'nunca' (never) plus the direct object pronoun 'los' (them, masculine or mixed plural). Used to say that someone never does something to, with, or regarding 'them' (people or masculine/mixed objects). Word order varies: 'nunca los' often appears before or after a verb depending on tense and emphasis (e.g., 'Nunca los vi' or 'No los vi nunca'). In compound tenses with a helping verb, the pronoun usually goes before the conjugated verb ('Nunca los he visto').
target_language_example: Nunca los invité a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I never invited them to the party.

meaning: never again; no more (from now on).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something will not happen again or that someone will not be seen/visited again. Can refer to a single past event that won’t be repeated or to a future refusal. Placement: often follows the verb (e.g., 'la vi nunca más') or comes at the end of the sentence ('nunca más').
target_language_example: Después de esa discusión, decidí no llamarla nunca más.
native_language_example: After that argument, I decided never to call her again.

meaning: a strong negation: 'never anything' or 'never ... anything' (used to emphasize that something never happens or does not exist).
additional_notes: This is a double-negation emphasis common in Spanish: both words are negative but used together for stronger emphasis. In English you'd usually say 'never anything' or rephrase as 'never ... at all' or 'nothing ever'. Word order can change: 'nunca nada' and 'nada nunca' are both possible, but most natural is 'no ... nunca nada' or 'nunca nada' after a verb. Context determines exact translation.
target_language_example: Desde que se fue, nunca nada ha sido igual.
native_language_example: Since they left, nothing has ever been the same.

meaning: you/one never knows; it's impossible to be certain.
additional_notes: Common phrase using 'nunca' (never) + verb 'saber' (to know). Can refer to 'you never know' (general advice) or 'he/she/one never knows' depending on context. Often used to express uncertainty about the future or outcomes (e.g., 'you never know when...'). Subject can be explicit or implied: 'uno nunca sabe', 'uno nunca sabe' → 'one never knows'; 'nunca sabe' after a named subject means 'he/she never knows.'
target_language_example: Nunca sabe si lloverá mañana.
native_language_example: You never know if it will rain tomorrow.

meaning: you never know; it's uncertain
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about the future or outcomes. Common in conversational Spanish to suggest that something unexpected might happen or to justify taking a chance. Can be followed by clauses introduced with cuándo, cuánto, lo que, etc.
target_language_example: Nunca se sabe si mañana lloverá y cancelarán el viaje.
native_language_example: You never know if it will rain tomorrow and they'll cancel the trip.

meaning: 'I never had the...' (start of a sentence about something you never possessed or experienced)
additional_notes: This is a phrase fragment: nunca = never, tuve = I had (preterite of tener), la is a feminine singular direct object or article. It introduces a statement about something feminine you never had or experienced (e.g., la oportunidad, la oportunidad, la suerte, la culpa). Complete the thought with a feminine noun or noun phrase. For masculine nouns you'd use 'nunca tuve el'.
target_language_example: Nunca tuve la oportunidad de viajar sola.
native_language_example: I never had the opportunity to travel alone.

meaning: will never (do something) / is never going to (happen).
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'a' + infinitive (va a + infinitive) to form the near future. 'Nunca' (never) usually comes before the verb: 'nunca va a + infinitive' = 'is never going to ...' or 'will never ...'. Can express certainty about the future; tone can be negative or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Ella nunca va a olvidar ese día.
native_language_example: She is never going to forget that day.

meaning: I never see (or 'I don't ever see').
additional_notes: Nunca = never. Veo is the first-person singular present of ver (to see). Used to say you never see someone or something (can mean 'meet' or 'visit' depending on context). Often followed by a direct object (a mis hijos, a nadie, a mi padre).
target_language_example: Nunca veo a mis amigos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I never see my friends on weekends.

meaning: 'I will never' (start of a sentence meaning 'I will never...')
additional_notes: Common construction: 'Nunca voy a + infinitive' = 'I will never [do something]'. 'Nunca' = never; 'voy' is first-person present of 'ir' used with 'a' to form near future (going to). Used to make strong, definite statements about not doing something in the future.
target_language_example: Nunca voy a rendirme.
native_language_example: I will never give up.

meaning: I never go / I do not ever go
additional_notes: Nunca = never. Voy is first-person singular present of ir (to go). Used to say you never do an activity or never go to a place. Often followed by a destination introduced with a, or by an infinitive with a (voy a + infinitive) to indicate future (but in these examples 'nunca voy a ese restaurante' uses a + noun, not future). 'Nunca voy a' + place = 'I never go to...'.
target_language_example: Nunca voy al cine los lunes.
native_language_example: I never go to the cinema on Mondays.

meaning: telephone number; phone number.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to ask for or refer to someone's phone number. 'Número' = number, 'teléfono' = telephone. Used in formal and informal contexts. Can be shortened in speech to 'número' or 'teléfono' when context makes meaning clear (e.g., '¿Me das tu número?').
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar tu número de teléfono?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

meaning: the second in rank or position; 'number two' (also a nickname for a deputy or second-in-command).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the person or thing in second place, or the deputy/second-in-command. Can be used as a label ("número dos") or in sentences like "es el número dos". Context determines whether it means simple order (#2) or a deputy/vice role.
target_language_example: Ella es el número dos del equipo.
native_language_example: She is the team's number two (the deputy).

meaning: ‘number in’ or ‘number on’ — indicates a number found in/on something or a position number within a list/record.
additional_notes: Used to say where a number appears (e.g., on a piece of paper, in a call history) or to refer to someone's position by their number in a list (número en lista). Often followed by the container: 'número en un papel', 'número en la lista', 'número en el historial'.
target_language_example: Anoté el número en la libreta para no olvidarlo.
native_language_example: I wrote the number in the notebook so I wouldn't forget it.

meaning: favorite number.
additional_notes: Used to say which number you like most. Often appears with verbs 'ser' (es) or 'tener' (no tener here). Word order flexible: 'Mi número favorito es el cuatro' or 'El cuatro es mi número favorito.' 'Número' is masculine; use 'el' with specific numbers.
target_language_example: Mi número favorito es el siete.
native_language_example: My favorite number is seven.

meaning: the number that / the number which (used to refer to a phone number or numeric identifier previously mentioned)
additional_notes: Commonly used in phone and technical contexts to refer to a specific number mentioned or dialed. 'Que' introduces a relative clause describing the number. In English you often translate it as 'the number that' or simply 'the number' + clause.
target_language_example: El número que marcaste no responde.
native_language_example: The number that you dialed does not answer.

meaning: number one; the top / first; the main person or thing
additional_notes: Used both literally (the numeral 1, first in order) and figuratively to mean 'the best', 'the main suspect', or 'top priority/rule'. Common in phrases like "regla número uno" (rule number one) or "sospechoso número uno" (prime suspect). Can appear with articles or alone when addressing someone as 'Number One'.
target_language_example: Ella es la número uno del equipo.
native_language_example: She is the number one on the team.

meaning: 'or two days' — used after a number to indicate an approximate additional amount of time (e.g., 'one or two days').
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a numeral (uno, dos, etc.) to soften exactness: 'uno o dos días' = 'one or two days'. Used to give an estimate, ask for a short wait, or set a short deadline. Often appears in everyday speech and writing; keep number agreement with surrounding words (e.g., 'uno o dos días más').
target_language_example: Necesito uno o dos días para terminarlo.
native_language_example: I need one or two days to finish it.

meaning: 'or that' / 'or so' (used to offer an alternative, suggest a possibility, or sum up briefly).
additional_notes: Common short phrase used after a statement to give an alternative explanation, to soften a claim (like 'or so'), or to conclude a thought. Often follows a clause and can stand alone as a brief reply. Tone depends on context: can be tentative, dismissive, or summarizing.
target_language_example: No era muy alto, o eso recuerdo.
native_language_example: He wasn't very tall, or so I remember.

meaning: 'or (we) will [do something to] him/her' — used to introduce a threat or consequence directed at someone (formal 'usted' object).
additional_notes: Common in threats or warnings: 'o' = 'or' (introduces the alternative/consequence); 'le' is the indirect-object or direct-object pronoun used for 'him/her' (formal). Together they often imply an implied verb like 'vamos a' or a future action: 'Do X, or we'll do Y to him/her.' Tone is aggressive; these examples show violent threats. Not a fixed idiom beyond the literal combination.
target_language_example: Tráeme eso ahora o le diré a la policía.
native_language_example: Bring me that now or I'll tell the police about him/her.

meaning: 'that is', 'I mean', or 'so' — used to rephrase, clarify, summarize, or draw a conclusion.
additional_notes: Very common filler/connector. Use to restate or clarify what you just said (like 'that is' or 'I mean'), to introduce a conclusion ('so'), or to soften/introduce an explanation. Tone can be neutral or informal depending on context; in casual speech it often functions like 'I mean' in English.
target_language_example: No tengo coche, o sea, voy al trabajo en autobús.
native_language_example: I don't have a car, I mean/so I take the bus to work.

meaning: 'or if' — introduces an alternative possibility or hypothesis.
additional_notes: Used to present another possibility, condition, or speculation. Often appears at the start of a clause and can follow a comma or stand alone. In conversational Spanish it can also be used to emphasize surprise or doubt about an alternative scenario.
target_language_example: No sé si vendrá, o si prefieres que cancelemos.
native_language_example: I don't know if they'll come, or if you'd prefer that we cancel.

meaning: 'or else' / 'or (you) will see' (used to warn about a negative consequence); also used simply as 'or' in choices.
additional_notes: Often used in threats or warnings: '... o ya verás' = '...or else you'll see what happens.' In casual contexts it can function as a plain 'or' when offering alternatives (e.g., asking if someone is free or already has plans). Tone can be strong when followed by a consequence; context determines whether it's a warning or a neutral alternative.
target_language_example: Haz la tarea ahora, o ya verás las consecuencias.
native_language_example: Do your homework now, or else you'll see the consequences.

meaning: "objective/goal in (the)..." — part of a phrase meaning someone's goal in life or a target in a context.
additional_notes: This fragment is usually completed by a noun (most often "vida": "objetivo en la vida" = "goal in life"). Depending on context, "objetivo" can mean a personal goal, an intended aim, or a physical target (e.g., "objetivo en la mira" = "target in the sights"). Use the full phrase (e.g., "objetivo en la vida") for clarity.
target_language_example: Mi objetivo en la vida es viajar por el mundo.
native_language_example: My goal in life is to travel the world.

meaning: 'work of art' — a piece created for artistic value (painting, sculpture, performance, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to describe any artistic creation or something considered artistically excellent. Can be literal (a painting) or figurative (praising a performance, design, or creation). Commonly preceded by adjectives like auténtica, hermosa, etc.
target_language_example: Ese edificio moderno es una verdadera obra de arte.
native_language_example: That modern building is a true work of art.

meaning: 'obra' = work (art, book, composition, piece); 'es' = is. Together used as '[the] work is...' or 'your work is...'.
additional_notes: Obra is a feminine noun meaning a piece of art, a literary or musical work, a construction project, or generally someone's output. When combined with the verb es (from ser), it states a characteristic or identity of the work: e.g., who created it, its quality, or its genre. Common structures: 'La obra es de X' (the work is by X), 'Su obra es ficción' (his/her work is fiction), 'Tu obra es excelente' (your work is excellent).
target_language_example: La obra es de un compositor famoso.
native_language_example: The work is by a famous composer.

meaning: masterpiece; an outstanding work of art or achievement.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person's best, most important, or most admired work (art, music, writing, architecture, etc.). Can be literal (a painting, book, composition) or figurative (a project or achievement). Commonly used with possessive pronouns (mi, su) or definite article (la obra maestra).
target_language_example: Su última novela es considerada su obra maestra.
native_language_example: His latest novel is considered his masterpiece.

meaning: literally 'work and' — here part of a larger phrase where obra means 'play/work/project' and y ('and') connects it to something else; used when referring to a play, musical piece, art work, or a workplace plus something else.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; 'obra' commonly means a theatrical play, musical composition, art piece, or construction/worksite. The 'y' simply links 'obra' to another noun or clause (e.g., 'obra y la dirigí' = 'I wrote a play and directed it'). Beginners should treat 'obra' on its own and remember 'y' means 'and'. Word meaning depends on context (theater, music, construction, etc.).
target_language_example: Escribí una obra y la presenté en el teatro.
native_language_example: I wrote a play and presented it at the theater.

meaning: obsessed with; overly preoccupied or fixated on someone or something.
additional_notes: Used to describe a strong, often excessive, interest or fixation. Matches gender/number (obsesionado/obsesionada/obsesionados) to the person. Common with 'estar' (estar obsesionado/obsesionada con) to indicate current state. Can be negative (unhealthy fixation) or neutral/affectionate depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Está obsesionada con esa sonrisa.
native_language_example: She is obsessed with that smile.

meaning: eighty-one (81).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used for age, counts, addresses, scores, etc. In Spanish numbers agree in gender only for some compound forms (not for 'ochenta y uno'); you can also hear 'ochenta y un' before masculine nouns (e.g., 'ochenta y un años'). Often used alone as an answer or call-out (e.g., giving a number).
target_language_example: Mi abuela cumplió ochenta y uno el mes pasado.
native_language_example: My grandmother turned eighty-one last month.

meaning: "eight hours a" — used to say something happens for eight hours per (day, week, etc.).
additional_notes: This phrase appears before a time period word (usually día: "ocho horas al día"). It expresses frequency or duration: how many hours something occurs within each unit of time. Common structure: [number] + horas + al + [period]. In English you can translate it as "eight hours a day/week/etc."
target_language_example: Trabajo ocho horas al día.
native_language_example: I work eight hours a day.

meaning: takes up too much (space).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that an object uses more space than desired. Literally from ocupar (to occupy/take up) + demasiado (too much). Can refer to physical space or, less commonly, time/attention when context allows.
target_language_example: Esa estantería ocupa demasiado en la sala.
native_language_example: That bookshelf takes up too much space in the living room.
