additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone becomes very angry, panicked, or behaves irrationally. Can refer to losing emotional control (anger, fear, love) or making reckless decisions. Tone ranges from informal to neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Cuando vio la deuda en el extracto, empezó a perder la cabeza y llamó a todos sus acreedores.
native_language_example: When he saw the debt on the statement, he began to lose his temper and called all his creditors.

meaning: to lose one's temper; to become very angry or lose control emotionally.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone suddenly gets angry, upset, or behaves irrationally. Common in everyday speech. Literally refers to 'losing the stirrups' (estribos), but the meaning is figurative and not related to riding.
target_language_example: Empezó a perder los estribos cuando le dijeron que tendría que trabajar el fin de semana.
native_language_example: He began to lose his temper when they told him he would have to work on the weekend.

meaning: to lose weight.
additional_notes: Commonly used for reducing body weight through diet, exercise, or temporary measures (e.g., cutting weight for sports). Can be literal (body weight) or figurative in contexts about reducing load. Often used with verbs like 'querer', 'intentar', 'necesitar'.
target_language_example: Quiero perder peso antes del verano.
native_language_example: I want to lose weight before summer.

meaning: you will miss the (something) / you will lose the (something).
additional_notes: Perderás is the future tense (tú) of perder. With "el + noun" it's commonly used to say you'll miss transportation (el bus, el tren) or lose/lose control (el control). Context determines whether 'miss' (e.g., a bus/train) or 'lose' (e.g., control, opportunity) is meant. Often appears in warnings after "o" (or) as in "Date prisa, o perderás el..."
target_language_example: Date prisa o perderás el último autobús.
native_language_example: Hurry up or you'll miss the last bus.

meaning: past participle + preposition used with 'perder' to indicate having lost someone (physically separated, missing, or deceased)
additional_notes: Appears in constructions like 'he perdido a...' or 'había perdido a...'. Used specifically before people (the preposition 'a' marks a person). Context determines whether it means 'lost' as in 'can't find' or 'lost' as in 'died' (formal or emotional contexts often imply death). Conjugate 'perder' as needed; the phrase here shows the participle 'perdido' together with 'a' before the person.
target_language_example: He perdido a mis amigos.
native_language_example: I have lost my friends.

meaning: lost a / lost one (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun or numeral to say that something/someone is lost or has been lost. Context determines exact translation: can mean 'a [thing] is lost' (He perdido un arete = I've lost an earring) or 'a [person] is missing' in announcements (se ha perdido un niño = a child is missing). In some contexts like 'has perdido un paso' it means 'you missed/skipped a step'. Verb tense and pronoun (he/has/se ha) change the subject (I have lost / you have lost / a ... has been lost).
target_language_example: He perdido un libro que tenía en la mesa.
native_language_example: I've lost a book that I had on the table.

meaning: 'lost a' or 'have lost a' (past participle + indefinite article)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a phrase fragment: 'perdido' is the past participle of perder (to lose) and combines with an auxiliary (haber) to form perfect tenses (e.g., 'ha perdido', 'he perdido', 'habíamos perdido'). 'Una' is the feminine indefinite article meaning 'a' or 'one'. Together they indicate that someone or something has lost one (feminine) item or occurrence. The full meaning depends on the auxiliary verb and context (e.g., 'ha perdido una oreja' = 'has lost an ear'; 'he perdido una pelea' = 'I have lost a fight').
target_language_example: He perdido una llave y no puedo entrar.
native_language_example: I have lost a key and I can't get in.

meaning: literally 'losing the' — part of a progressive phrase meaning 'losing the (something)' or 'wasting the (something)'.
additional_notes: Perdiendo is the gerund of perder (to lose). 'Perdiendo el' will normally be followed by a masculine singular noun (el + noun) or by a masculine singular article + noun phrase: e.g. 'perdiendo el tiempo' (wasting time) or 'perdiendo el partido' (losing the match). It appears in continuous (progressive) constructions to show an ongoing action: 'está perdiendo el...' or 'estoy perdiendo el...'.
target_language_example: Estamos perdiendo el partido, hay que reaccionar.
native_language_example: We are losing the match, we have to react.

meaning: 'they lost' or 'they missed the' (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: Perdieron is the past (preterite) third-person plural of perder (to lose; to miss). With 'el' it introduces a masculine singular noun (el tren, el autobús, el juego). Can mean they lost (a game) or they missed (a train/bus). Context tells whether it’s 'lost' (defeat) or 'missed' (failed to catch).
target_language_example: Perdieron el partido por un gol en el último minuto.
native_language_example: They lost the match by one goal in the last minute.

meaning: they lost the / they (fem.) lost the (depending on noun).
additional_notes: Perdieron is the past (preterite) form of perder for 'ellos/ellas/ustedes' — 'they lost'. The article la (the, feminine singular) agrees with a feminine noun that follows (la esperanza, la batalla, la vida). In examples where the lost thing is masculine, la would be replaced by 'el' (perdieron el). 'Perdieron la vida' is an idiomatic way to say 'they lost their lives' / 'they died'.
target_language_example: Después del accidente, perdieron la casa que tanto querían.
native_language_example: After the accident, they lost the house they loved so much.

meaning: lost hope of / gave up hope of (doing or becoming something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone stopped hoping to achieve or become something. Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., volverse, ser) or a noun phrase describing the goal. 'Perder las esperanzas' is the general expression; here it's in the past (perdió).
target_language_example: Ella perdió las esperanzas de ganar la competencia.
native_language_example: She lost hope of winning the competition.

meaning: I lost (someone).
additional_notes: Use 'perdí a' when referring to having lost a person (through death, separation, or disappearance). The preposition 'a' marks a direct object that is a person. Context usually makes clear whether it means 'lost' as in 'died' or 'lost' as in 'lost track of' or 'lost to someone/something'. Commonly followed by a noun or possessive (mi esposa, nuestro hijo, a los míos).
target_language_example: Perdí a mi padre el año pasado.
native_language_example: I lost my father last year.

meaning: I lost track of (the) — commonly used with 'tiempo' to mean 'I lost track of time'.
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun (most often 'tiempo'). Means you stopped being aware of how much time has passed or lost sense/awareness of something. Common in past tense ('perdí') but can be used with other tenses (pierdo, perdí, he perdido).
target_language_example: Perdí la noción del tiempo mientras leía.
native_language_example: I lost track of time while I was reading.

meaning: I lost the / I lost (my) — feminine plural noun(s).
additional_notes: Perdí is the first-person singular past (pretérito) of perder (to lose). Las is the feminine plural definite article, so this phrase is followed by a feminine plural noun (fuerzas, esperanzas, ganas, llaves). In English you can translate as "I lost the..." or more naturally "I lost my..." depending on context (e.g., "perdí las esperanzas" = "I never lost hope" or literally "I didn't lose the hopes").
target_language_example: Ayer perdí las llaves y no pude entrar.
native_language_example: Yesterday I lost the keys and couldn't get in.

meaning: lay low; keep a low profile (stay unnoticed or avoid attention).
additional_notes: Used to say someone wants to avoid attention, publicity, or trouble. Common after verbs like mantener, tener, llevar, or in commands. It's an idiomatic expression but literal words help understand it.
target_language_example: Después del escándalo, decidió mantener un perfil bajo.
native_language_example: After the scandal, he decided to keep a low profile.

meaning: "periódico" = newspaper; "es" = is. Together used in sentences like 'the newspaper is...'/ 'the newspaper is [something]'.
additional_notes: This combines the noun periódico (newspaper) with the verb ser (es = is). Use periódico for a physical or online newspaper. Ser (es) describes identity, origin, material, characteristics, or general facts (e.g., 'es de ayer' = it's from yesterday; 'es gratis' = it's free). For 'what the newspaper says' use 'lo que dice el periódico'.
target_language_example: El periódico es interesante hoy.
native_language_example: The newspaper is interesting today.

meaning: driver's license; driving license.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the official document that allows someone to drive a motor vehicle. Commonly used in Spain and many Latin American countries. Often appears in contexts like showing ID (e.g., police), saying you don't have one, or talking about getting one.
target_language_example: Necesito renovar mi permiso de conducir este mes.
native_language_example: I need to renew my driver's license this month.

meaning: 'don't allow/let (someone) to...' (negative command: tell someone not to allow something)
additional_notes: Second-person singular imperative (tú) in negative commands: 'No permitas que...' means 'Don't let/allow that...'. It introduces a subordinate clause with a verb in subjunctive (e.g., esté, mueran, se vaya). Used to tell someone not to let something happen or not to allow someone to do something.
target_language_example: No permitas que te convenzan de renunciar.
native_language_example: Don't let them convince you to quit.

meaning: a contrastive phrase meaning 'but no' or 'however, no' used to introduce a correction, refusal, or to soften/redirect a previous idea.
additional_notes: Used to oppose or qualify what was just said. Often followed by a clause that corrects, denies, refuses, or changes the topic (e.g., 'but no, it's not like that', 'but no, don't say that'). The comma after 'pero' is common in spoken/written dialogue to mark a pause. Not an idiom—straightforward combination of 'pero' (but) + 'no' (no/not).
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero, no puedo hacerlo ahora.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but no, I can't do it now.

meaning: 'but' + 'for' / 'but as for' — a spoken connector pairing used to introduce a contrast or qualification and then specify purpose, recipient, condition, or point of view.
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed phrase but two common words used together in speech/writing. 'Pero' = 'but' (contrast). 'Para' = 'for', 'in order to', 'to', or 'as for' depending on context. When used together (often with a pause or comma), they introduce a contrast with a following clarification, purpose, condition, or intended recipient: e.g. 'But, as for...' or 'But to (do) ...'. Pay attention to the verb after 'para' — it can mark purpose (para + infinitive) or the beneficiary (para + noun/pronoun).
target_language_example: Pero, para participar en el proyecto, tienes que inscribirte hoy.
native_language_example: But, to participate in the project, you have to sign up today.

meaning: but someone / yet someone (used to introduce an unknown or unspecified person who did something).
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but/yet) with 'alguien' (someone). Used to add a contrasting or unexpected detail about an unspecified person—often to introduce that an unknown person performed an action, spoiled a surprise, left a message, etc. Tone is neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish. The phrase does not identify who the person is.
target_language_example: Quería regalarlo en secreto, pero alguien ya lo abrió.
native_language_example: I wanted to give it secretly, but someone already opened it.

meaning: but that's how it is / but that's the way (things) are.
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge or accept a situation while contrasting it with something else; often follows a statement and softens it. Can translate as 'but like that' or more naturally 'but that's how it is' or 'but it's always been that way.'
target_language_example: Puedes quejarte, pero así es.
native_language_example: You can complain, but that's how it is.

meaning: an interjection like 'well,' 'oh well,' or 'come on' used to react, express surprise, mild disbelief, or to soften a remark.
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Spanish. Tone and context determine meaning: can show surprise ("Well!"), mild annoyance or disbelief ("Come on"), resignation ("Oh well"), or be used to introduce a counterpoint. Often followed by a clause or stands alone. Not strongly formal; fits in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Pero bueno, ¡no me digas que vas a cancelar otra vez!
native_language_example: Well, don't tell me you're going to cancel again!

meaning: but with the (masculine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: A connector phrase used to contrast or add information about something, followed by a masculine singular noun or pronoun (el). Often appears before a noun phrase or before a clause introduced by 'el que' or similar. Context determines exact translation (e.g., 'but with the plan', 'but with him'). If the following word is a verb phrase, speakers may instead use 'pero con' + gerund or another structure.
target_language_example: Quería ir al concierto, pero con el trabajo no puedo.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the concert, but with the job I can't.

meaning: but she (emphasizing contrast or exception)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the pronoun 'ella' (she). Used to contrast a previous idea or to single out a woman as an exception, emphasise her action, opinion, or situation. In spoken Spanish, stress often falls on 'ella' (e.g., 'Pero ella sí' = 'But she does').
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero ella no quiso.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but she didn't want to.

meaning: 'but they' — a contrastive phrase used to introduce or emphasize information about 'them'.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the pronoun 'ellos' (they, masculine or mixed group). Used to contrast, contradict, add exception, or emphasize something about a group. Tone and emphasis can change meaning (e.g., surprise, correction, reinforcement). In spoken Spanish 'ellos' can sometimes be omitted if context is clear, but here it's included for contrast.
target_language_example: Quería ir, pero ellos no pudieron venir.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but they couldn't come.

meaning: but in the (feminine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) + the preposition 'en' (in/on) + the feminine definite article 'la'. Used when contrasting or adding information about something located or happening inside/within a feminine noun (e.g., la casa, la Soyuz). The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Pero en la Soyuz, ellos estarán cálidos.
native_language_example: But in the Soyuz, they will be warm.

meaning: used to introduce an explanation, objection, or strong reason (like "but the thing is" / "it's just that").
additional_notes: Common conversational filler that softens or strengthens a contradiction or provides a justification. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause after a contrasting statement. Tone can be defensive, explanatory, or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Quería ir, pero es que tenía mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but the thing is I had a lot of work.

meaning: 'but I/we/they hope' or 'but I/you/he/she hope(s)'.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) + the verb 'esperar' (to hope). Used to add a contrasting clause that expresses hope or expectation. The subject of 'espero' depends on context (often 'yo' = I). Often followed by 'que' + a clause: 'pero espero que...'.
target_language_example: Vine a estudiar aquí, pero espero volver pronto a casa.
native_language_example: I came here to study, but I hope to return home soon.

meaning: 'but this (one)'.
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) + 'esta' (this, feminine). Used to contrast or introduce a specific thing/situation already in focus. 'Esta' agrees in gender with a feminine noun; 'esto'/'este'/'esta' vary by gender or neutrality. Often followed by a noun or clause: 'pero esta es...' = 'but this is...'.
target_language_example: Quieren ayudar, pero esta es mi decisión.
native_language_example: You want to help, but this is my decision.

meaning: but we are
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction pero (but) + the verb estamos (we are). Used to contrast or add a counterpoint to the previous statement. Tone and meaning depend on the clause that follows (location, state, opinion, condition). Contraction "we're" is common in English equivalents. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Pero estamos listos para empezar.
native_language_example: But we are ready to start.

meaning: 'but these' — a contrastive phrase used to introduce or emphasize specific people/things.
additional_notes: Combine the conjunction pero (but) with the demonstrative estos (these, masculine plural). Used to contrast or add information about particular items or people just mentioned or in view. Gender/number must agree: 'pero estas' for feminine plural, 'pero este/esta' for singular. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Me gusta la idea, pero estos libros están muy viejos.
native_language_example: I like the idea, but these books are very old.

meaning: 'but thanks' — a polite way to refuse or decline something while thanking the other person.
additional_notes: Used to gently reject an offer, invitation, suggestion or compliment. Often appears with short refusals like 'no' or clauses explaining why (e.g., 'no puedo', 'no lo quiero'), and can be followed by 'de todos modos' / 'de todas formas' for extra politeness. Tone is polite and conversational.
target_language_example: No puedo acompañarte, pero gracias por invitarme.
native_language_example: I can't join you, but thanks for inviting me.

meaning: but (he/she) speaks — contrasts a characteristic with the fact that someone speaks a language or speaks in a certain way.
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'pero' (but) followed by the verb 'habla' (he/she/you formal speak). Used to contrast an expected idea with the fact that the person speaks a language (or speaks in a particular manner). Context determines whether it highlights surprise, contrast, or a negative trait (e.g., 'attractive, but talks too much'). Replace 'habla' with other verb forms as needed for different subjects or tenses.
target_language_example: Es tímido, pero habla muy bien inglés con confianza.
native_language_example: He's shy, but he speaks English very well and confidently.

meaning: but the line was (busy / engaged).
additional_notes: Common phrase used when calling someone on the phone to say the line/connection was busy. Often completed with an adjective (e.g., ocupada = busy). 'La línea' refers to the phone line or call connection. You can substitute pronouns/names before this phrase (e.g., 'La llamé, pero la línea estaba ocupada').
target_language_example: Llamé a Carlos, pero la línea estaba ocupada.
native_language_example: I called Carlos, but the line was busy.

meaning: but honestly / but the truth is
additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank opinion, contrast, or clarification. Common in spoken and written Spanish to soften a statement or emphasize honesty. Often followed by a clause (e.g., 'es que...', 'no sé...') or an opinion.
target_language_example: Quería ir a la fiesta, pero la verdad, estoy muy cansado.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the party, but honestly, I'm very tired.

meaning: a combination of 'pero' (but) plus object pronouns 'me' (to me) and 'lo' (it/him) used when contrasting or adding information and referring to something affecting the speaker ('but they told it to me', 'but I smelled it', 'but I had it').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence that appears when 'pero' introduces a contrast and the following clause contains the clitic pronouns 'me' + 'lo' (or part of a verbal construction like 'me lo contaron', 'me lo olía', 'me lo pasé', 'me lo han mandado', 'me lo robaron'). Translate 'me lo' depending on the verb: 'they told it to me', 'I suspected it', 'I enjoyed it', 'they sent it to me', 'they stole it from me'. Word order: in compound tenses and after infinitives/gerunds pronouns attach to the verb (me lo han mandado, me lo robó).
target_language_example: No fui al concierto, pero me lo contaron todo y suena increíble.
native_language_example: I didn't go to the concert, but they told me all about it and it sounds amazing.

meaning: 'but I'm afraid' / 'but I fear' (used to introduce bad news, a problem, or a negative opinion politely).
additional_notes: A polite, slightly formal way to soften bad news or disagree. Often followed by a clause describing the problem or negative information (e.g., 'pero me temo que...'). Can be used in spoken and written Spanish. Tone: apologetic/hesitant.
target_language_example: Quisiera ayudar, pero me temo que no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: I'd like to help, but I'm afraid I don't have time.

meaning: but look / well, look (used to draw attention or emphasize a point).
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to get someone's attention, point something out, or soften what you're about to say. 'Pero' adds contrast ('but' / 'well'), so it often introduces a clarification, objection, or new viewpoint. Can be followed by a demonstrative (esto/eso), a direction (a tu alrededor, dentro), or stand alone as an interjection. Tone and context determine politeness or urgency.
target_language_example: No te enojes, pero mira lo que pasó aquí.
native_language_example: Don't be mad, but look at what happened here.

meaning: 'but you need' or 'but one needs' (contrast followed by a necessity)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the verb 'necesitas' (you need — second person singular, informal). Used to introduce a contrast or exception and then state something necessary. Adjust the verb form for different subjects (necesito, necesitamos, necesita, necesitan). Often followed by an infinitive verb or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Quiero viajar, pero necesitas ahorrar primero.
native_language_example: I want to travel, but you need to save first.

meaning: but not in/from (that way/context); introduces a limitation or exception.
additional_notes: Used to contrast what is true with what is not true, often followed by a noun or phrase indicating the specific aspect being excluded (e.g., 'nombre', 'vista', 'esta manera', 'archivos físicos', 'conciencia'). Common in expressions like 'conozco de nombre, pero no de vista' (I know by name but not by sight). English equivalents: 'but not by/with/in...', 'but not in that sense'.
target_language_example: Lo recuerdo por la historia, pero no de los detalles pequeños.
native_language_example: I remember it for the story, but not for the small details.

meaning: 'but it seems' / 'but it appears'.
additional_notes: Used to add contrast or objection and then present an observation or impression. Often followed by que + clause (pero parece que...) or by a noun/phrase (pero parece X). Softens a statement — it's less direct than saying something as fact.
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero parece que ya resolvieron el problema.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but it seems they already solved the problem.

meaning: 'but I lost' / 'but I missed' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction pero (but) + the past tense yo form of perder (perdí). Used to introduce a negative outcome or contrast: e.g. missing transportation (missed the bus/train), losing interest, or losing someone's trail. Context determines whether 'perdí' means 'missed' (a vehicle/opportunity) or 'lost' (an object, track, or feeling).
target_language_example: Quería verlo llegar, pero perdí la oportunidad.
native_language_example: I wanted to see him arrive, but I missed the opportunity.

meaning: 'but probably' — introduces a contrast and expresses likelihood (softens a statement).
additional_notes: Combines pero (but) + probablemente (probably). Used to contrast a previous idea while indicating that the following clause is likely true. Common in speech and writing; tone ranges from neutral to tentative depending on context. Can appear with affirmative or negative clauses (e.g., "pero probablemente sí" / "pero probablemente no").
target_language_example: Quisiera ir, pero probablemente no podré.
native_language_example: I'd like to go, but I'll probably not be able to.

meaning: but soon; however, shortly after (something happens).
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) with 'pronto' (soon). Used to contrast a current/problematic situation with a quick or imminent positive change or resolution. Common in spoken and written Spanish to indicate that whatever follows will happen shortly.
target_language_example: No veo la solución ahora, pero pronto la encontraré.
native_language_example: I don't see the solution now, but I'll find it soon.

meaning: but it/he/she/they/you know(s) / but it tastes
additional_notes: This phrase combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the verb 'saber'. 'Saber' has two common meanings relevant here: 'to taste' (when referring to food: 'sabe delicioso' = 'tastes delicious') and 'to know' (for facts or information: 'sabe mucho' = 'knows a lot'). Use context to decide which meaning applies. Word order: 'pero' usually comes before the verb or clause it contrasts.
target_language_example: El plato huele raro, pero sabe muy bien.
native_language_example: The dish smells strange, but it tastes very good.

meaning: 'but you know' / 'but (you) know' — a conversational phrase used to introduce or remind someone of a fact or to soften a statement.
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish. Often begins a clause to contrast or add information (like 'but you know...'). Can be followed by a full sentence or a short tag question. Subject 'tú' is usually implied. Tone can be neutral, corrective, or persuasive depending on context.
target_language_example: Pero sabes que no puedo ir mañana.
native_language_example: But you know that I can't go tomorrow.

meaning: but I am
additional_notes: A straightforward combination of pero + soy. It introduces a contrast: something like “however, I am...”. Soy is the first-person singular of ser, used for identity, profession, origin, and more permanent characteristics. For temporary states, Spanish usually uses estoy instead.
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero soy muy malo cocinando.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but I'm very bad at cooking.

meaning: 'but they have' — a contrastive phrase used to introduce something that the subject possesses or experiences despite a previous statement.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction pero (but) + the verb tener in third person plural (they have). Use when contrasting a prior idea with something the same people/things possess, experience, or show. Can begin a sentence or follow a clause. Tener must agree with the subject (pero tengo, pero tienes, pero tiene, etc.).
target_language_example: No son perfectos, pero tienen corazón.
native_language_example: They aren't perfect, but they have heart.

meaning: but you have (to)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the second-person singular present of 'tener' (tienes). Often used to add a requirement or obligation introduced by 'que' + infinitive (pero tienes que + verb) meaning 'but you have to... / but you must...'. Context determines whether it's a soft obligation ('you have to') or stronger ('you must').
target_language_example: Pero tienes que llamar antes de venir.
native_language_example: But you have to call before coming.

meaning: 'but you have' or 'however you have' (contrasts two ideas).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but/however) with the verb 'tienes' (you have). Used to contrast a previous statement and then mention something the listener/subject possesses, feels, or thinks. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Pronoun 'tú' is implied in 'tienes'.
target_language_example: Quieres cambiar de trabajo, pero tienes miedo del cambio.
native_language_example: You want to change jobs, but you are afraid of the change.

meaning: but all that / but everything that
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'pero' (but) with 'todo lo' (everything that / all that). It's not a fixed idiom by itself; you'll usually see it as part of a larger clause, e.g. 'pero todo lo que...' (but everything that...). On its own 'todo lo' needs a following relative word (often 'que') or an adjective (e.g. 'todo lo necesario').
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero todo lo que sabía era insuficiente.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but everything that I knew was insufficient.

meaning: 'but you' (plural) — used to contrast or introduce a point addressed to a group of people.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the plural pronoun 'ustedes' (you all). Commonly used to disagree, contrast, or point out something to a group. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be neutral, corrective, surprised, or emphatic. In Spain, 'vosotros' is often used instead of 'ustedes' in informal contexts; in Latin America 'ustedes' is standard for both formal and informal plural you.
target_language_example: Quieren ayudar, pero ustedes no dijeron nada antes.
native_language_example: You want to help, but you didn't say anything before.

meaning: 'but it's going to' / 'but he/she/it is going to' (contrasting clause introducing a future action or result).
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) with the periphrastic future 'va a' + infinitive to introduce a contrasting future event or outcome. Use when you want to add a contrasting point about something that will happen. Subject (él/ella/usted/eso) is understood from context or stated earlier. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No tengo mucho dinero, pero va a funcionar.
native_language_example: I don't have much money, but it's going to work.

meaning: colloquial filler meaning 'but okay, (let it be)' or 'but fine, (then)'.
additional_notes: This is an informal spoken fragment used to concede a point or accept something reluctantly. Often part of longer phrases like 'pero, vale, la verdad...' or 'pero vale, la dejamos así'. It functions like English 'but okay' or 'alright then' and may be followed by an explanation or the end of the discussion. Not a complete sentence on its own.
target_language_example: No estoy muy de acuerdo, pero vale la dejamos así.
native_language_example: I'm not very happy with it, but okay, let's leave it like that.

meaning: 'but (he/she/it) comes' or the colloquial connector 'but still — it/that/this comes/arrives/occurs'.
additional_notes: Literally 'pero' (but) + 'viene' (comes). Used both literally ('but he/she/it is coming') and colloquially to soften or add a contrasting remark like 'but still' or 'that still applies/holds'. Context determines whether it's about a person arriving, something happening, or introducing an aside. Subject (he/she/it/that) is implied from context.
target_language_example: Llegará tarde, pero viene igual.
native_language_example: He'll arrive late, but he's coming anyway.

meaning: a clause starter meaning 'but he [himself]...'; introduces a contrast involving a male subject and a reflexive/action verb.
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) + 'él' (he) + reflexive pronoun 'se' or start of a verb phrase (e.g., se negó, se quedó, se volvió). Used to contrast what someone else did with what he did (or didn't do). The 'se' is part of a reflexive or pronominal verb and should remain attached to the verb (se negó = he refused). In some examples the 'se' may be omitted if the verb is not reflexive (pero él negó — less common).
target_language_example: Todos salieron a la fiesta, pero él se quedó en casa.
native_language_example: Everyone went to the party, but he stayed at home.

meaning: a dog like (that one) / someone who is (just) like any other (informal, comparative)
additional_notes: Literally 'dog like'. Used to compare a specific dog to another (e.g., 'a dog like that'). In some contexts, calling a person 'un perro como cualquiera' is colloquial and can mean 'an ordinary person' or carry a mild negative connotation (e.g., 'a worthless/typical guy') depending on tone and region. The phrase is compositional (meaning follows from the words) but can be idiomatic when applied to people.
target_language_example: No necesito un perro como ese; prefiero uno más tranquilo.
native_language_example: I don't need a dog like that; I prefer a calmer one.

meaning: 'the dog was' (past progressive: describes what the dog was doing)
additional_notes: Combines the noun perro (dog) with the imperfect progressive estaba + gerund (e.g., cavando, ladrando) to describe ongoing or repeated actions in the past. Use estaba + gerund to say 'was ...-ing'. Subject can change (yo estaba, ella estaba, etc.).
target_language_example: El perro estaba durmiendo en el sofá.
native_language_example: The dog was sleeping on the couch.

meaning: ‘the dog is in/on’ — states where a dog is located (use with a place).
additional_notes: This phrase combines perro (dog) + está (third-person singular of estar, used for location/temporary states) + en (in/on/at). Replace perro with another noun to say where someone or something is. Use estar (not ser) for locations. Commonly followed by a place: la casa, la silla, el garaje, algún lugar, la perrera.
target_language_example: El perro está en el jardín.
native_language_example: The dog is in the garden.

meaning: 'the dog was' (past passive construction: 'was' + past participle follows).
additional_notes: This sequence shows a subject (perro) + the past form of ser/ir (fue) used to form the passive voice with a past participle (e.g., 'fue atropellado' = 'was run over'). In Spanish the full passive usually includes the agent introduced by 'por' (por un auto), but the agent can be omitted. 'Fue' is the third-person singular preterite of ser/ir and here functions as an auxiliary for the passive.
target_language_example: El perro fue rescatado por los vecinos.
native_language_example: The dog was rescued by the neighbors.

meaning: "dog that" or "a dog which" — a noun + relative pronoun phrase used to introduce a clause describing the dog.
additional_notes: Perro = dog. Que here is the relative pronoun meaning "that/which/who" and links a descriptive clause to the noun. Common in defining or descriptive clauses (e.g., a specific dog that did something). Word order is the same as in English: noun + que + verb/clause. If the clause needs a preposition or refers to a person, Spanish may use "que" or "quien" depending on formality and grammar, but with animals "que" is standard.
target_language_example: Vi un perro que corría por la playa.
native_language_example: I saw a dog that was running on the beach.

meaning: literally 'dog always'; used in sentences to say 'the dog always ...' (i.e., expresses a habitual action by a dog).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom—it's the noun 'perro' (dog) followed by the adverb 'siempre' (always). Most natural Spanish orders put the adverb after the verb (e.g., 'mi perro siempre ladra' or 'mi perro está siempre ladrando'), but it's also common to place 'siempre' after the noun for emphasis on the subject ('el perro siempre me ladra' = the dog always barks at me). Can be used with possessive adjectives (mi, tu, su) or general subjects. Not a fixed phrase; meaning depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Mi perro siempre me ladra cuando viene alguien.
native_language_example: My dog always barks at me when someone comes.

meaning: 'dogs, but' — the noun 'perros' followed by the conjunction 'pero' ('but'), used when contrasting liking dogs with something else.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in sentences that contrast preferences: someone likes dogs, but there is a contrasting statement after 'pero' (e.g., they prefer cats or someone else has a different opinion). 'Perros' is simply the plural noun 'dogs'. 'Pero' is a common conjunction meaning 'but'. In natural speech you would not say 'perros, pero' on its own; it's part of a larger sentence: 'A [persona] le gustan los perros, pero...'. Note word order for 'gustar' constructions: 'A [persona] le gustan los perros' = '[Person] likes dogs.'
target_language_example: A mi amigo le gustan los perros, pero no tiene tiempo para cuidarlos.
native_language_example: My friend likes dogs, but he doesn't have time to take care of them.

meaning: the dogs are (…)
additional_notes: Plural subject (perros/los perros) + verb estar. Used to describe temporary states, locations, or conditions of dogs (alive, wet, located somewhere). If you want to say permanent characteristics you would use ser (e.g., "los perros son leales"). Articles like "los" or quantifiers (todos, muchos, varios) commonly appear before "perros".
target_language_example: Los perros están en la terraza.
native_language_example: The dogs are on the terrace.

meaning: 'dogs have' — a subject (dogs) + verb (have) phrase used to say what dogs possess, feel, or experience.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe general characteristics, feelings, or possessions of dogs (physical traits, senses, emotions, personality). In Spanish, 'los perros tienen...' uses plural subject + conjugated tener. Can be followed by nouns, noun phrases, or infinitive phrases with 'miedo a...' (fear of...).
target_language_example: Los perros tienen mucho cariño por sus dueños.
native_language_example: Dogs have a lot of affection for their owners.

meaning: 'dogs and' — the phrase is the beginning of a simple list pairing 'perros' (dogs) with something else (often 'gatos' = cats).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom by itself; it's simply the noun 'perros' (dogs) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). Depending on context it can appear in common expressions (e.g., 'llover perros y gatos' is part of the idiom 'llover a cántaros/perros y gatos' meaning 'to rain heavily'). Alone, 'perros y' signals a list that continues (e.g., 'perros y gatos').
target_language_example: Vi perros y gatos corriendo por el parque.
native_language_example: I saw dogs and cats running through the park.

meaning: the most (used with a person): 'the ...est person' (e.g., the most important person).
additional_notes: Used to form superlatives describing a person. It combines persona (person) + más (more/most). In Spanish you'd usually add an adjective after this phrase (persona más + adjective). Can appear with qualifiers (que conozco, que jamás he conocido). Word order: persona más + adjective + (que + clause).
target_language_example: Es la persona más honesta que conozco.
native_language_example: She is the most honest person I know.

meaning: a person suitable/appropriate for (a role, task, relationship, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the right or best person for something (a job, promotion, partner, task). Often followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., 'la persona para el trabajo', 'la persona para ayudar'). Context determines whether it means 'suitable', 'meant for', or 'right for'.
target_language_example: Ella es la persona para liderar el proyecto.
native_language_example: She is the right person to lead the project.

meaning: a person without (something). Used to describe someone lacking a particular quality, possession, or condition.
additional_notes: Combine 'persona sin' + noun to say 'a person without X' (e.g., sin hogar = homeless, sin estudios = without schooling). It's a neutral, descriptive pattern. The noun after 'sin' can be concrete (hogar, libros) or abstract (corazón, estudios). Word order: persona sin + [noun].
target_language_example: Es una persona sin experiencia, pero aprende rápido.
native_language_example: She is a person without experience, but she learns quickly.

meaning: people here / people (located) here.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the presence or number of people in the current place. Often appears after verbs like 'hay' (there is/are) or in relative clauses describing people who are present. 'Aquí' means 'here' (this location). Word order is normally 'personas aquí' or 'personas que están aquí'.
target_language_example: Hay cinco personas aquí ahora mismo.
native_language_example: There are five people here right now.

meaning: people in / people who are in (a place or situation).
additional_notes: Used to talk about people located in a place or people experiencing a situation. 'Personas' is the plural of 'persona'. When specifying location, 'en' is followed by a noun (e.g., 'en esta habitación'). When describing people with a quality or condition, 'en' may introduce a noun phrase (e.g., 'personas en problemas'). For simple counts use 'Hay' + number + 'personas en...'.
target_language_example: Hay tres personas en la oficina ahora.
native_language_example: There are three people in the office now.

meaning: people in the (followed by a place: room, plaza, meeting, etc.).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the noun personas (people) with the preposition en and the feminine definite article la, so it must be followed by a feminine singular location noun (e.g., sala, plaza, cola, reunión). For other nouns use the matching article: 'personas en el' (masculine) or 'personas en los/las' (plural). Common in descriptions of attendance or presence.
target_language_example: Había muchas personas en la sala durante el concierto.
native_language_example: There were many people in the room during the concert.

meaning: 'people are' — used to make general statements about people.
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'personas' (people) with the verb 'son' (they are, from ser). Common in generalizations or descriptions (e.g., 'Some people are...','People are...'). Can appear with adjectives, comparative phrases, or complements. Use 'las personas' or 'todas las personas' when speaking about people in general. Note: word order is flexible (e.g., 'Las personas son...').
target_language_example: Algunas personas son generosas.
native_language_example: Some people are generous.

meaning: I persuaded (him) to / I convinced (him) to.
additional_notes: Persuadir de + infinitive or persuadir de que + clause: 'persuadir de' is used to indicate convincing someone to do something. The subject (yo) did the persuading; the person persuaded is often marked with 'lo' (him/it). In Spanish you can use an infinitive (persuadí de + infinitive) or a finite clause introduced by 'que' (persuadí de que + clause). Formal register; 'convencer' is a common synonym.
target_language_example: La persuadí de cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: I persuaded her to change jobs.

meaning: despite; in spite of (something masculine or neutral).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast: something happens even though a particular condition exists. 'A pesar del' is followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., 'frío', 'mal tiempo', 'huracán'). For feminine nouns use 'a pesar de la' and for plural use 'a pesar de los/las'.
target_language_example: A pesar del ruido, pude concentrarme.
native_language_example: Despite the noise, I could concentrate.

meaning: to go fishing with my (…)
additional_notes: Literal phrase: pescar = to fish; con mi introduces who you fish with (mi padre, mi amigo, etc.). Commonly used to talk about going fishing together or past habits (ir a pescar con mi padre). Add the person after 'mi' (mi padre, mi hermano). If the person is plural use 'mis' (pescar con mis amigos).
target_language_example: Voy a pescar con mi hermano este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going fishing with my brother this weekend.

meaning: despite; in spite of
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or concession. Can be followed by a noun (pese a la lluvia), an infinitive (pese a ser...), or a full clause with que (pese a que...). Formal register; interchangeable with 'a pesar de' in most contexts.
target_language_example: Pese a la lluvia, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, we went out for a walk.

meaning: 'big fish' — an important or powerful person; a VIP or big shot (idiomatic).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to describe someone with influence, high status, or power in a group or organization. Often used in informal contexts; literal meaning (a large fish) exists but here it refers to a person. Can refer to current or former importance (e.g., 'used to be a big shot').
target_language_example: En la empresa siempre hablan con el pez gordo antes de tomar decisiones.
native_language_example: At the company they always talk to the big shot before making decisions.

meaning: 'piano' (the instrument) + 'and' — used to connect 'piano' with another verb or noun in a sentence.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun piano followed by the conjunction y (and). Used to list instruments, actions or people (e.g., 'piano y guitarra', 'toca el piano y ella canta'). Note word order and articles: 'toca piano y guitarra' (no article) is colloquial; more complete is 'toca el piano y la guitarra' or 'toca piano y guitarra' when listing instruments quickly. Pronunciation: 'piano' (pee-AH-no), 'y' (ee).
target_language_example: Ella toca el piano y la flauta en la banda.
native_language_example: She plays the piano and the flute in the band.

meaning: 'asks (that)' or 'requests (that)'.
additional_notes: Used with a verb clause introduced by que + subjunctive when the speaker expresses a request, command, or desire about someone else's action. The subject doing the asking is usually named before pide. Can be formal or neutral. If negative (no le pide que), still uses que + subjunctive.
target_language_example: Ella me pide que llegue a las ocho.
native_language_example: She asks me to arrive at eight.

meaning: 'they asked (someone) to' or 'they asked (someone) for'.
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of pedir used with an indirect object introduced by a. Use 'pidieron a + person' when saying they asked a specific person to do something or asked that person for something (e.g., their phone number). English may require 'asked someone to' (requesting an action) or 'asked someone for' (requesting an object or information).
target_language_example: Los vecinos les pidieron a los voluntarios que limpiaran el parque.
native_language_example: The neighbors asked the volunteers to clean the park.

meaning: asked his/her/their (asked someone close to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone requested something from a specific person (usually a family member or close person). 'Pidió' is past tense (preterite) of pedir = to ask/request. 'Le' (indirect object pronoun) indicates to whom the request was made; 'a su' introduces the person ('a su esposo', 'a su hermana', etc.). Use with a following clause introduced by 'que' + subjunctive for requested actions (e.g., 'que le ayudara').
target_language_example: María le pidió a su madre que le cosiera un botón.
native_language_example: María asked her mother to sew a button for her.

meaning: asked/requested (of) — used to say someone asked another person (masculine or formal title) to do something.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb pedir (past: pidió) + indirect object preposition 'al' (a + el). Use when someone asked or requested something from a specific person (male or a masculine noun like 'juez', 'presidente', 'hombre', or a general title). If the person is feminine use 'a la' (e.g., pidió a la jueza). Often followed by 'que' + subjunctive when requesting an action.
target_language_example: Ella le pidió al médico que la viera pronto.
native_language_example: She asked the doctor to see her soon.

meaning: asked for some / asked for a little (of).
additional_notes: Common phrase to say someone requested an unspecified small amount or some quantity of something (drink, money, food, etc.). Often followed by a noun: "algo de beber" (something to drink) or "algo de dinero" (some money). Context indicates amount is indefinite and usually modest.
target_language_example: Ella pidió algo de comida para compartir.
native_language_example: She asked for some food to share.

meaning: asked (someone) for advice.
additional_notes: Use when saying someone requested guidance from a specific person. Structure: [Subject] + pidió consejo a + [person]. The indirect object pronoun (le) often appears before pidió (e.g., 'le pidió consejo a su amigo') to mark the person receiving the action. Common with people: amigo, amiga, profesor, nombre.
target_language_example: María le pidió consejo a su madre sobre el trabajo.
native_language_example: María asked her mother for advice about the job.

meaning: asked (me) to (do something) for her/it (female direct object).
additional_notes: This is the verb 'pedir' in past (pidió) + subordinate 'que' introducing a request with a subjunctive verb after it. 'La' is a direct object pronoun referring to a feminine person or feminine noun (her/it). In English structure: 'She asked me to [do something] for her.' The verb after 'que' must be in the subjunctive (e.g., ayudara, despertara, llevara, cuidara).
target_language_example: Mi vecina me pidió que la ayudara con las bolsas.
native_language_example: My neighbor asked me to help her with the bags.

meaning: asked (someone) that you ... / asked me to tell/give you ...
additional_notes: This is part of a reported-request construction using pedir + que + subjunctive. The subject (he/she) asked someone (me) to do something for you. After "pidió que te" you usually see a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., trajera, diera, dijera) or an indirect object phrase (e.g., te lo trajera). It expresses a request made on behalf of or directed to the listener.
target_language_example: María me pidió que te llamara esta tarde.
native_language_example: María asked me to call you this afternoon.

meaning: I ask/request (a)
additional_notes: Combination of the first-person singular present of pedir (pido = I ask/request) + the indefinite article una. Used when the speaker requests one thing or asks for something (often followed by a noun or clause). In English you usually render it as "I ask/request (a) ..." or simply "I ask (for) ...". Context determines whether to translate as "I ask" or "I ask for."
target_language_example: Te pido una respuesta sincera.
native_language_example: I ask you for an honest answer.

meaning: literally 'foot in the/on the' — used as part of expressions referring to a foot or someone standing somewhere (e.g., 'foot on the...', 'standing in/on the...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence that appears in many contexts: physical position (tener el pie en el pasto = to have one's foot on the grass), someone standing (estar de pie en el umbral = to be standing in the doorway), or actions involving a foot (pisó el pie en el tren = stepped on the foot on the train). Choose preposition and article depending on the noun that follows (en el/la/los/las).
target_language_example: Ella estaba de pie en el patio con un pie en el césped.
native_language_example: She was standing in the yard with one foot on the grass.

meaning: lit. 'foot in the' — used as part of larger expressions like 'un pie en la tumba' meaning 'one foot in the grave' (very close to death) or in locutions like 'de pie en la cocina' which implies standing in the kitchen.
additional_notes: 'Pie en la' is not typically used alone; it appears inside multi-word phrases. The most common uses are: 'de pie en la ...' meaning 'standing in the ...' and 'un pie en la tumba' meaning 'one foot in the grave'. Word order and articles matter (e.g., 'de pie en la cocina', 'un pie en la tumba').
target_language_example: A veces como de pie en la cocina.
native_language_example: Sometimes I eat standing in the kitchen.

meaning: literally 'stone in the' — begins phrases referring to a stone located in or on something (depends on the noun that follows).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the start of expressions like 'piedra en el estómago' (a feeling like a stone in the stomach) or literal uses such as 'piedra en el anillo' or 'piedra en el estanque' (a stone in the ring/pond). The full meaning depends on the noun that follows. Use articles and nouns to complete the phrase (el/la + noun).
target_language_example: Tengo una piedra en el zapato y me duele al caminar.
native_language_example: I have a stone in my shoe and it hurts when I walk.

meaning: to throw stones at (someone/something) — literal action; can be used literally or literally describing throwing rocks
additional_notes: Commonly appears with the verb tirar (tirar piedras a = to throw stones at). Use an indirect object or direct object after 'a' to indicate the target (e.g., 'a los cuervos', 'a alguien', 'a los pájaros'). Not an idiom here — straightforward physical action. For beginner learners, focus on structure: [tirar] + piedras + a + target.
target_language_example: Le tiraron piedras a los gatos en el jardín.
native_language_example: They threw stones at the cats in the garden.

meaning: "skin is" — the phrase 'piel es' combines the noun 'piel' (skin) with the verb 'es' (is).
additional_notes: Use 'piel' to talk about the skin as a body part or surface (e.g., skin color, texture, health). 'Es' is the third-person singular of 'ser' and describes inherent or general characteristics (e.g., 'La piel es el órgano más grande'). For temporary or changeable conditions (softness, mood), Spanish often uses 'está' instead of 'es' (e.g., 'Su piel está suave' for a temporary state).
target_language_example: La piel es sensible al sol.
native_language_example: The skin is sensitive to the sun.

meaning: they think about / they are thinking about
additional_notes: Third-person plural present form of pensar + preposition en. Used to say what people are thinking about. Can be about people, ideas, plans, desires, etc. English alternatives: 'they think about', 'they're thinking of'. Context determines whether it's habitual (they usually think about) or current (they are thinking about right now). When reflexive (pensar en sí mismos / cambiarse a sí mismo) it refers to thinking about oneself.
target_language_example: Ellos piensan en mudarse a otra ciudad.
native_language_example: They are thinking about moving to another city.

meaning: what you think about (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to someone's opinion of a person, thing, or topic. Often appears in questions with 'qué' or statements with 'lo que'/'sé lo que'. Common alternatives: 'qué piensas sobre' or 'qué opinas de/sobre'.
target_language_example: ¿Qué piensas de la película que vimos anoche?
native_language_example: What do you think about the movie we saw last night?

meaning: think that
additional_notes: From pensar. Piense is the present subjunctive form (for él/ella/usted) or the formal command form of pensar, so this can mean that someone thinks something, or it can tell someone formally to think/consider something.
target_language_example: No creo que piense que tenemos suficiente tiempo.
native_language_example: I don't think he/she thinks that we have enough time.

meaning: I think a lot (about/of).
additional_notes: First person singular present of pensar (pienso) + mucho (a lot). Used to say you frequently or intensely think about someone or something. Often followed by en + noun/pronoun (pienso mucho en ___) to indicate the topic. Neutral register; common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Últimamente pienso mucho en mis amigos.
native_language_example: Lately I think a lot about my friends.

meaning: 'I think' (used to state the speaker's opinion or agreement).
additional_notes: A way to add or emphasize the speaker's opinion; often placed after the sentence (postposed) for politeness or emphasis. Common in phrases like "eso pienso yo" (I think that too) or following a statement: "Es difícil, pienso yo." Not formal/technical — neutral everyday speech.
target_language_example: Eso no funcionará, pienso yo.
native_language_example: That won't work, I think.

meaning: literally 'feet in'; used in literal and idiomatic expressions about placing/being feet somewhere.
additional_notes: Used as part of phrases describing physically putting feet into or onto a place (e.g., 'meter los pies en la arena') and in idioms meaning to enter or set foot in a place ('poner los pies en'). Also used figuratively in expressions like 'tener los pies en el suelo' / 'poner los pies en la tierra' meaning to be realistic or grounded. The exact meaning depends on the verb and whole expression (meter, lavar, poner, tener).
target_language_example: No vuelvas a poner los pies en mi casa.
native_language_example: Don't set foot in my house again.

meaning: 'feet are' (third-person plural or polite/neutral statement about feet).
additional_notes: Combines the noun pies (feet) with the verb ser (son = they are). Used to describe size, appearance, or characteristics of feet. In full sentences you may have subject pronouns or possessive adjectives before pies (e.g., mis pies, tus pies, sus pies). Word order is flexible: 'Mis pies son pequeños' = 'My feet are small.'
target_language_example: Mis pies son grandes después del verano.
native_language_example: My feet are big after the summer.

meaning: 'and' used after the noun pies (feet) in fixed expressions or lists (literal 'feet and...').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom; it's simply the noun pies ('feet') followed by the conjunction y ('and'). It appears in various contexts: literal lists (pies y manos = feet and hands), poetic expressions (pies y sueños rotos = feet and broken dreams), or part of longer phrases. Pay attention to word order and context—meaning depends on the words that follow. Not a fixed phrase by itself.
target_language_example: Estaba atado de pies y manos.
native_language_example: He was tied by his feet and hands.

meaning: to paint (something) — feminine noun follows (la = the).
additional_notes: This is the verb pintar ('to paint') followed by the feminine definite article la, which indicates the direct object is a feminine noun (la casa, la cocina, la pintura). Beginners should understand 'pintar' is transitive: pintar + [thing]. Word order: pintar la casa = to paint the house. If object is masculine use 'pintar el'.
target_language_example: Voy a pintar la habitación este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to paint the room this weekend.

meaning: 'painting of' or 'painting by' depending on context; generally indicates a painting related to (depicting) or created by someone or something.
additional_notes: Usually 'pintura de' + person/thing means 'a painting of [someone/thing]' (it depicts them). With an artist's name it can mean either 'a painting by [artist]' or 'a painting of [subject] by [artist]' depending on word order and context — Spanish often uses 'una pintura de Andy Warhol' to mean 'a painting by Andy Warhol.' In some contexts 'pintura' can also mean 'makeup' or 'war paint' (colloquial) so 'pintura de guerra' = 'war paint' or 'face paint.'
target_language_example: Compré una pintura de la ciudad para colgar en la cocina.
native_language_example: I bought a painting of the city to hang in the kitchen.

meaning: a painting on/paint on (followed by location) — 'pintura' can mean a painted picture or paint (substance).
additional_notes: Used with a location after 'en' (e.g., 'en la pared' = on the wall). Context determines whether 'pintura' means 'a painting' (a picture) or 'paint' (the substance/coat). Verb phrases often use 'colgar una pintura en...' (to hang a painting on...) or 'mano de pintura en...' (a coat of paint on...).
target_language_example: Colgamos una pintura en la pared del pasillo.
native_language_example: We hung a painting on the hallway wall.

meaning: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the word 'piso' (floor) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and).
additional_notes: 'piso' can mean 'floor' (surface/ground), 'story' or 'apartment' depending on context. In the example sentences the 'y' simply connects 'piso' to the next clause or item (e.g., 'piso y vaya abajo' = 'leave it on the floor and go downstairs'). Do not treat 'piso y' as a single unit—learn 'piso' and 'y' separately. Common uses: 'el piso' (the floor/ground), 'un piso' (an apartment or a building floor), 'el último piso' (top floor).
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en el piso y fui a buscarlas.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the floor and went to look for them.

meaning: a track/area or a clue/hint depending on context (literally 'track of' or 'clue of').
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean a physical track/area (pista de patinaje = skating rink/track; pista de carreras = racetrack; pista de vuelo = runway) or figuratively to mean a lead or clue in an investigation (poner/ponerle a alguien sobre la pista = give someone a lead). English translation depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: La policía encontró una pista de la desaparición.
native_language_example: The police found a clue about the disappearance.

meaning: to be a pleasure to speak (with someone); 'nice to talk to you'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the fixed expression 'fue/ha sido/un placer hablar contigo' or the short 'un placer hablar contigo' used to politely end a conversation. Literally 'pleasure to speak'. Used to show courtesy after a conversation (formal or informal).
target_language_example: Ha sido un placer hablar contigo; hablamos pronto.
native_language_example: It has been a pleasure talking to you; we'll speak soon.

meaning: a pleasure to do business (with someone).
additional_notes: Used as a polite formula after a meeting, deal, or interaction: 'Es un placer hacer negocios con usted/contigo/ustedes.' Variations: Fue un placer..., Ha sido un placer..., or shortened 'Un placer...' Tone is formal to neutral depending on pronoun (usted = formal, contigo/ustedes = informal/plural).
target_language_example: Fue un placer hacer negocios con usted; espero que volvamos a colaborar pronto.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure doing business with you; I hope we work together again soon.

meaning: 'to be a pleasure to do business with' or 'a pleasure doing business with (you)'.
additional_notes: Used to politely express satisfaction after a business interaction. Commonly appears as a full phrase: "Es un placer hacer negocios con usted/ustedes" or shorter: "Un placer hacer negocios con ustedes." Formal when using usted/ustedes. Can be used in writing (emails, letters) or spoken. The literal parts are transparent, but the natural fixed phrase is "Es un placer hacer negocios con..."
target_language_example: Es un placer hacer negocios con usted; espero que trabajemos juntos de nuevo.
native_language_example: It's a pleasure doing business with you; I hope we work together again.

meaning: 'to be a pleasure to work (with/for)' — used to say working with or for someone was enjoyable or agreeable.
additional_notes: This phrase is typically part of the fixed expression "Fue/Ha sido un placer trabajar (con/para + alguien)". Use "con" for working with someone and "para" for working for someone. Common in polite, formal or friendly goodbyes and thank-you messages.
target_language_example: Ha sido un placer trabajar con ustedes este año.
native_language_example: It has been a pleasure working with you all this year.

meaning: ground floor; first level of a building at street level
additional_notes: Common in Spain and Latin America to refer to the level at street/entrance height. In some English dialects this is called the "ground floor"; in U.S. English it may be called the "first floor" (but in Spanish the "primero"/"primer piso" usually refers to the floor above the planta baja). Used for addresses, apartment numbers, and directions inside buildings.
target_language_example: Vivo en la planta baja, junto a la entrada.
native_language_example: I live on the ground floor, next to the entrance.

meaning: 'silver in' — appears as part of the idiom 'nacer con una cuchara de plata en la boca' meaning 'to be born into wealth' or 'to be born with a silver spoon in one's mouth'.
additional_notes: On its own 'plata' means 'silver' or informally 'money'. 'plata en' is not a standalone phrase; it's shown here because it appears in the idiom 'nacer con una cuchara de plata en la boca' (to be born into privilege). The third example uses 'plata' informally to mean 'money' ('hacer humo mi plata' = 'I blew/spent my money').
target_language_example: Ella nació con una cuchara de plata en la boca, nunca tuvo que trabajar.
native_language_example: She was born with a silver spoon in her mouth; she never had to work.

meaning: flying saucer; UFO (an unidentified flying object, typically disk-shaped).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to the stereotypical disk-shaped spacecraft from UFO stories and sci-fi. Used for sightings or imagining extraterrestrial craft. Can be used literally (reporting an unknown object in the sky) or humorously/metaphorically.
target_language_example: Anoche vimos un platillo volador en el cielo.
native_language_example: Last night we saw a flying saucer in the sky.

meaning: literally 'dishes/plates in' — used to say where dishes are or to talk about dishes (platos) in a place or context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun 'platos' (dishes/plates or dishes as in prepared foods) followed by the preposition 'en' (in/at/on). Meaning depends on the noun 'platos' and the location or context that follows 'en'. 'Platos' can mean physical plates/dishes or dishes (recipes/food) depending on context.
target_language_example: Hay muchos platos en la cocina sucia.
native_language_example: There are many dishes in the dirty kitchen.

meaning: 'plates and' — the phrase 'platos y' is the beginning of a list that pairs 'platos' (plates/dishes) with something else.
additional_notes: platos = dishes/plates. 'y' = and. In Spanish, when listing two items you put 'y' between them: 'platos y tazas' = 'plates and cups.' Watch for elision: 'y' becomes 'e' before words that begin with the sound /i/ (e.g., 'platos e invitados' — rare). Agreement: 'los platos' (plural masculine) may require articles: 'los platos y las tazas.'
target_language_example: Los platos y los cubiertos están en la cocina.
native_language_example: The plates and the cutlery are in the kitchen.

meaning: not much; something unimportant or insignificant.
additional_notes: Used to downplay the importance or size of something. Can refer to a small amount (poca cosa de comer = not much to eat) or to something trivial (fue poca cosa = it was no big deal). Often used in everyday casual speech.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, fue poca cosa.
native_language_example: Don't worry, it was nothing / no big deal.

meaning: a few questions; not many questions.
additional_notes: Used to say you have a small number of questions. Often appears with 'unas' (unas pocas preguntas) or 'solo/solamente' to emphasize it's just a few. 'Pocas' agrees in gender/number with 'preguntas' (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Tengo pocas preguntas sobre la tarea.
native_language_example: I have a few questions about the homework.

meaning: seldom; rarely; not often.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens infrequently. Can modify verbs (e.g., 'pocas veces voy al cine') or describe habits. Often interchangeable with 'rara vez' or 'casi nunca', though 'pocas veces' is neutral and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Pocas veces como comida picante.
native_language_example: I rarely eat spicy food.

meaning: little by little; gradually.
additional_notes: Used to describe slow, steady progress or actions done in small steps. Can appear at start or end of a sentence. Common in everyday speech and writing.
target_language_example: Voy aprendiendo español poco a poco.
native_language_example: I'm learning Spanish little by little.

meaning: a little tired (feminine).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone (female) who is slightly tired. 'Poco' means 'a little' or 'not very'; gender agrees with the adjective (cansada for feminine). For a male use 'poco cansado'. Commonly appears with 'estar' or 'sentirse' (estar un poco cansada / se siente un poco cansada).
target_language_example: Después del paseo, ella estaba un poco cansada.
native_language_example: After the walk, she was a little tired.

meaning: a little too; slightly too much.
additional_notes: Used to soften criticism or describe that something exceeds a desirable amount or degree by a small margin. Common in spoken Spanish: can stand alone as a short remark ('Un poco demasiado.') or appear before adjectives/adverbs/verbs ('un poco demasiado grande', 'un poco demasiado picante', 'duele un poco demasiado').
target_language_example: Esta camisa es un poco demasiado grande para mí.
native_language_example: This shirt is a little too big for me.

meaning: shortly after; soon after.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened a short time after a previously mentioned event or time. Can follow the verb or the time expression (e.g., 'poco después, ...' or '... poco después'). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Llegó la invitada y, poco después, empezó la fiesta.
native_language_example: The guest arrived and, shortly after, the party started.

meaning: rare; lightly cooked (meat).
additional_notes: Used mainly to describe how meat is cooked: 'poco hecho' means cooked briefly so the inside is still pink and tender. Can also appear in contexts meaning 'not much done' or 'not very developed', but most common for steak doneness. Opposites: 'medio' (medium), 'bien hecho' (well done).
target_language_example: Quiero el filete poco hecho, por favor.
native_language_example: I want the steak rare, please.

meaning: a little worried; somewhat concerned.
additional_notes: Used to describe mild worry or concern. 'Poco' softens the adjective 'preocupado' (worried). Common in everyday speech to indicate it's not a major problem. You can change gender/number: poco preocupada, pocos preocupados, etc. Often appears with 'estar' (estar un poco preocupado).
target_language_example: Estoy un poco preocupado por el examen de mañana.
native_language_example: I'm a little worried about tomorrow's exam.

meaning: a little late; slightly late; somewhat late.
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone is later than expected or appropriate, but not extremely late. Common with verbs like llegar, comenzar, pensar, decidir. Can modify whole sentence (adverbial phrase).
target_language_example: Llegaste un poco tarde a la reunión.
native_language_example: You arrived a little late to the meeting.

meaning: a little/too late for (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that the time for doing something has passed or is nearly passed. Commonly appears as 'es un poco tarde para...' or 'ya es un poco tarde para...'. Tone can be neutral; context determines whether it's mild (slightly late) or implies it's too late.
target_language_example: Creo que ya es un poco tarde para cambiar de planes.
native_language_example: I think it's a little/too late to change plans now.

meaning: a little of
additional_notes: Most commonly used as un poco de before a noun: un poco de tiempo, un poco de espacio. It refers to a small amount of something. Without un, poco de can sound more negative, like 'little' or 'not much of.'
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco de agua?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little water?

meaning: a little more of / a bit more (amount, time, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to ask for or describe a small extra amount of something (quantity, time, money, care, etc.). Common in requests and conditional sentences (e.g., "If I had a little more..." or "Give me a little more..."). Can appear with nouns (pimienta, tiempo, dinero) and with abstract nouns (cuidado).
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco más de tiempo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more time, please?

meaning: 'a little of that' or 'some of that'.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate a small amount of something previously mentioned or visible (food, drink, an idea, etc.). Common in everyday speech. Can be shortened to 'un poco' when context is clear.
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco de eso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little of that, please?

meaning: a little of this; some of this.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a small amount of something near the speaker or the thing being indicated. Common in offering food, drink, or sampling something. Can be part of the phrase 'un poco de esto, un poco de lo otro' meaning 'a bit of this, a bit of that.'
target_language_example: Prueba un poco de esto, te va a gustar.
native_language_example: Try a little of this, you'll like it.

meaning: a little (bit) of French (language).
additional_notes: Used to say someone knows or speaks a small amount of the French language. Commonly appears with verbs like saber, hablar, aprender, enseñar. You can also say 'un poco de francés' or drop 'un' in casual speech ('sé poco de francés' is less common).
target_language_example: Ella entiende un poco de francés cuando escucha canciones.
native_language_example: She understands a little French when she listens to songs.

meaning: a little English; some basic knowledge of English.
additional_notes: Used to say someone knows a small amount of English or to encourage learning a little. Often appears after verbs like hablar, saber, entender, aprender. 'Un poco de' = 'a little (of)'.
target_language_example: Ella habla un poco de inglés, pero está practicando todos los días.
native_language_example: She speaks a little English, but she is practicing every day.

meaning: a little bit of milk in (something).
additional_notes: Used to say there is a small amount of milk located inside a container (glass, bottle, etc.). Common verbs with this phrase: hay (there is), queda/quedan (there remains). You can change 'leche' to other nouns and 'en' followed by the container: p. ej. 'un poco de agua en la taza'.
target_language_example: Queda un poco de leche en el vaso.
native_language_example: There is a little bit of milk in the glass.

meaning: a little more than / a bit more of
additional_notes: Used to indicate a small additional amount or degree of something. Can appear before a noun (un poco más de dinero) or before a noun phrase expressing quantity/quality. Often used to ask for or describe a small increase (time, effort, quantity).
target_language_example: Necesito sólo un poco más de tiempo para terminar.
native_language_example: I just need a little more time to finish.

meaning: what we can do is / what we can do (is to)...
additional_notes: Common phrase used to introduce a suggestion or solution. Often followed by an infinitive or clause that explains the action: 'Lo que podemos hacer es ...' can be shortened in speech to 'podemos hacer es ...' but the full form is more natural. Use to transition to a proposed option.
target_language_example: Si no hay más mesas, lo que podemos hacer es esperar fuera.
native_language_example: If there are no more tables, what we can do is wait outside.

meaning: 'we can reach' or 'we can arrive' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used with different nouns or phrases after 'a'. With a noun like 'un acuerdo' or 'un arreglo' it means 'we can reach (an agreement)'. With time expressions like 'tiempo' it means 'we can arrive (on time)'. Common in negotiations and everyday talk. Conjugate 'podemos' for different subjects (puedo, puedes, podemos...).
target_language_example: Si nos calmamos, podemos llegar a un acuerdo.
native_language_example: If we calm down, we can reach an agreement.

meaning: 'power in' or 'power of/within' (used to say there is strength/power in something)
additional_notes: Used to express that power, strength or influence exists 'in' or 'within' something (a person, place, idea, action). Common in phrases like 'hay poder en...' ('there is power in...') or 'tomó el poder en mi nombre' (took power in/with my name/on my behalf — note preposition use can vary by context). Not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Hay poder en pedir ayuda cuando la necesitas.
native_language_example: There is power in asking for help when you need it.

meaning: to be able to change; can change
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb poder (to be able to / can) with the verb cambiar (to change). Use to express ability or possibility to change something or to change oneself. Conjugate poder according to subject and tense (puedo cambiar, puede cambiar, podríamos cambiar, etc.). Often appears before an infinitive when indicating the action (e.g., 'puedo cambiarlo' = I can change it), but the bare infinitive phrase 'poder cambiar' is used in contexts like reporting ability or after modal structures.
target_language_example: Creo que puedo cambiar; sólo necesito tiempo para poder cambiar.
native_language_example: I think I can change; I just need time to be able to change.

meaning: 'to be able to cope with' or 'to manage/deal with (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: Used to express whether someone can handle a person, task, situation, or emotion. Often appears in negative form: no poder con (meaning 'can't stand' or 'can't cope with'). Con is followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'con eso', 'con él'). Commonly used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: No puedo poder con tanto trabajo esta semana.
native_language_example: I can't cope with so much work this week.

meaning: to be able to wait; to have the capacity or permission to wait (i.e., 'can wait' or 'to be able to expect' in certain contexts).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to mean having the time, patience, or ability to wait (poder + infinitive). Conjugate 'poder' for person/tense (puedo poder esperar is not used — use puedo esperar, pudiste esperar, podremos esperar, etc.). When referring to waiting for something to happen, it's often followed by 'a que' + subjunctive (No puedo esperar a que llegue). Less commonly used to mean 'to be able to expect' in formal contexts. Context determines nuance.
target_language_example: No puedo poder esperar más en esta fila.
native_language_example: I can't be able to wait any longer in this line.

meaning: to be able to speak
