additional_notes: Combines the verb poder (can/to be able to) + hablar (to speak/talk). Used to express ability or opportunity to speak/talk (with someone, a language, or about a topic). Context determines whether it means ability (I can speak French) or the chance to have a conversation (to be able to talk in private / talk about problems). Often followed by a language, a person (con + alguien), or de + topic.
target_language_example: Quiero poder hablar con mi jefe sobre el proyecto.
native_language_example: I want to be able to talk with my boss about the project.

meaning: to be able to do
additional_notes: A common structure with poder + infinitive. It expresses ability or possibility: 'can do,' 'could do,' or 'be able to do,' depending on the tense. Hacer can mean either 'do' or 'make' depending on context.
target_language_example: Quiero poder hacer más por ti.
native_language_example: I want to be able to do more for you.

meaning: be able to go
additional_notes: A common combination of poder + ir used to say that someone has the possibility, ability, or opportunity to go somewhere. In real sentences, poder is usually the part that gets conjugated, while ir stays in the infinitive: puedo ir, no voy a poder ir, deseo poder ir.
target_language_example: Mañana por fin voy a poder ir al médico.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll finally be able to go to the doctor.

meaning: to be able to hear; can hear
additional_notes: A combination of the modal verb 'poder' (to be able to/can) with the infinitive 'oír' (to hear). Use to express ability or possibility of hearing something. Conjugate 'poder' to match the subject (e.g., puedo oír, puedes oír, puede oír). Often followed by direct objects or subordinate clauses: 'puedo oír música' or 'puedo oír lo que dices.'
target_language_example: No sé si voy a poder oír en la sala grande mañana.
native_language_example: I don't know if I'll be able to hear in the big hall tomorrow.

meaning: to be able to work; can work.
additional_notes: Poder + infinitive expresses ability, permission, or possibility. 'Poder trabajar' can mean having the physical/mental ability, having permission, or having the opportunity to work depending on context. Conjugate 'poder' to match subject and tense (e.g., puedo trabajar, pudieron trabajar). Modal nuances: 'puedo trabajar' = I can work / I'm able to work; '¿puedes trabajar?' = Can you work?; 'no pudieron trabajar' = they could not work.
target_language_example: No sé si podré poder trabajar mañana debido a la lesión.
native_language_example: I don't know if I'll be able to work tomorrow because of the injury.

meaning: 'to be able to come' / 'can come'.
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb poder (to be able to/can) + the verb venir (to come). Used to ask about or state someone's ability or possibility to attend/arrive. Conjugate poder for the subject and keep venir in the infinitive (e.g., ¿Puedo venir? / No podemos venir). Common in invitations, scheduling, or permission contexts.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a poder venir a la reunión mañana?
native_language_example: Are you going to be able to come to the meeting tomorrow?

meaning: to be able to see
additional_notes: Built with poder + ver. It expresses ability or possibility to see something or someone. Very common after para: para poder ver = "in order to be able to see." In context, ver can mean physically seeing, seeing clearly, or seeing/meeting people.
target_language_example: Necesito más luz para poder ver.
native_language_example: I need more light to be able to see.

meaning: to be able to return / to be able to come back
additional_notes: Combines the verb poder (can/to be able to) with volver (to return/come back). Use when talking about having the ability or possibility to go back to a place, situation, or state. Conjugate poder according to subject and keep volver in its infinitive (e.g., puedo volver, podríamos volver). Can also be used with subjunctive after expressions of doubt or desire (e.g., ojalá pueda volver).
target_language_example: Espero poder volver a Madrid el año que viene.
native_language_example: I hope to be able to return to Madrid next year.

meaning: polite conditional of 'to speak' — 'could speak' or a polite 'could I/you speak' (request).
additional_notes: Used to express ability in a hypothetical/conditional sense (I could speak ...) or more commonly as a polite request asking permission to speak with someone: '¿Podría hablar con usted?' = 'Could I speak with you?'. Often appears with conditional 'podría' for politeness. Followed by the language, person, or short time (un minuto).
target_language_example: Perdone, ¿podría hablar con usted un momento?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could I speak with you for a moment?

meaning: 'poem by' or 'poem about' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used before a name to indicate authorship (poema de Pablo Neruda = a poem by Pablo Neruda). Can also introduce the poem's subject when followed by a noun (poema de amor = love poem). Context determines whether it means 'by' (author) or 'about/about the theme'.
target_language_example: Este es un poema de Gabriela Mistral.
native_language_example: This is a poem by Gabriela Mistral.

meaning: literally 'police of the' — used to say which police force or police unit (e.g., police of the bay, police of the mafia).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the start of a noun phrase that specifies a particular police body or jurisdiction: 'policía de la bahía' (police of the bay), 'policía de la mafia' (mafia's police or police dealing with the mafia). In Spanish the definite article (la) agrees with a feminine noun that follows (e.g., 'bahía'). If the following noun is masculine use 'policía del' (de + el). 'Policía' can refer to the institution or an officer depending on context.
target_language_example: La policía de la bahía llegó rápido.
native_language_example: The bay police arrived quickly.

meaning: the police (is/are) + present progressive — 'the police are doing...' or 'a police officer is doing...'.
additional_notes: Policía can mean 'police' (collective) or 'police officer' (individual) depending on context. When followed by está/están + gerund (present progressive), it describes an action in progress: e.g., 'la policía está investigando' = 'the police are investigating'. Use está with singular/individual sense (el policía está = the officer is) and están with plural/collective sense (la policía está is also commonly used when referring to the force as a unit). Verb agreement depends on whether the speaker treats 'policía' as singular (an officer or the institution) or plural (members of the force).
target_language_example: La policía está revisando las cámaras de seguridad.
native_language_example: The police are checking the security cameras.

meaning: ‘the police is/are’ or ‘the police are [doing/located]’ — indicates presence, location, or involvement of the police.
additional_notes: Policía can be singular (el policía = a police officer) or collective/plural (la policía = the police as an institution or the police force). Context and article determine meaning: "El policía está..." refers to a single officer; "La policía está..." refers to the police force or police presence. Use "por todas partes/por todas las calles" to say 'everywhere/in all the streets.'
target_language_example: La policía está vigilando la entrada del edificio.
native_language_example: The police are watching the building entrance.

meaning: the police will arrive / the police are coming.
additional_notes: Policía = police (can be singular collective noun). Llegará is the future tense of llegar (to arrive), used to indicate that the police will arrive soon or at some point in the future. In spoken Spanish, present tense (La policía llega) or present progressive (La policía está llegando) is often used to mean the same thing ('are coming').
target_language_example: No te preocupes: la policía llegará en unos minutos.
native_language_example: Don't worry: the police will arrive in a few minutes.

meaning: This isn't a fixed phrase; 'polvo' = 'dust' and 'se' is a reflexive/impersonal pronoun used with verbs. Together they appear in different constructions (e.g., 'el polvo se había acumulado', 'cuando el polvo se aclare').
additional_notes: Treat 'polvo' as the noun 'dust'. 'Se' can combine with verbs to form passive/impersonal or reflexive constructions (e.g., 'se había acumulado' = 'had accumulated' (impersonal/passive), 'cuando el polvo se aclare' = 'when the dust clears' (reflexive/passive sense)). The two words are not a fixed multiword idiom. Watch verb agreement and tense with 'se'.
target_language_example: Cuando el polvo se asiente, podremos ver los daños.
native_language_example: When the dust settles, we will be able to see the damage.

meaning: to begin to (do something) / to start (doing something); 'poner(se) a' indicates the start of an action. 'Pone a' can also mean 'places/puts' or 'causes (someone) to do something' depending on context.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a verb in the infinitive: 'se pone a + infinitive' = 'he/she/it starts to ...' Often 'se pone a' indicates a spontaneous or habitual start. 'Pone a + noun' can mean 'puts/places (someone/something) (somewhere)' or 'assigns/sets (someone) to (a task)'. Context and reflexive form determine meaning.
target_language_example: Cuando una niña se pone a llorar, nunca sé qué decir.
native_language_example: When a little girl starts to cry, I never know what to say.

meaning: it gets better / (he/she/it) gets better
additional_notes: Third-person singular present of ponerse + mejor. Commonly used to say a situation, person, or thing is improving: 'se pone mejor' = 'it/they become(s) better' or 'it improves'. Can refer to health (someone feels better), mood, atmosphere, or a situation. Context determines whether it's 'gets better' (gradual change) or 'is getting better' (ongoing).
target_language_example: Después de descansar, se pone mejor.
native_language_example: After resting, he/she/it gets better.

meaning: put in/on
additional_notes: A flexible phrasal construction of poner + en. Literal meaning is 'put in/on' (e.g., poner en la muñeca = put on the wrist; poner en una lista = put on a list). When used with 'duda' (poner en duda) it forms an idiom meaning 'to cast doubt on' or 'to question'. With reflexive 'se ponen en' it can mean 'they put themselves in (someone's) place/position' or 'they start to (do something)' depending on context. Conjugation and object(s) follow poner; 'en' introduces the location, list, state, or abstract noun.
target_language_example: Ellos ponen en duda la decisión.
native_language_example: They cast doubt on the decision.

meaning: to test, to put to the test; to try out (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say you are testing a person, plan, object, or situation to check ability, performance, reliability, or limits. Often followed by a noun (poner a prueba tu paciencia / poner a prueba el motor) or reflexive with 'se' for being tested (se puso a prueba).
target_language_example: Quiero poner a prueba este teléfono antes de comprarlo.
native_language_example: I want to test this phone before buying it.

meaning: to pay attention; to focus on something.
additional_notes: Commonly used to tell someone to concentrate or to describe the act of paying attention. Often appears as an infinitive (poner atención) or as an imperative (¡Pon atención!) and frequently in phrases like 'poner atención a' + noun. Synonyms: prestar atención.
target_language_example: Es importante poner atención durante la clase para entender la lección.
native_language_example: It's important to pay attention during class to understand the lesson.

meaning: to annoy, irritate, or get on someone's nerves; to make someone nervous or upset.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression. Typically used with indirect-object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, os, les): e.g., 'me pone de los nervios' = 'it drives me crazy/gets on my nerves.' Often followed by a noun or clause describing the cause. Informal and common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Ese ruido constante me pone de los nervios.
native_language_example: That constant noise gets on my nerves.

meaning: to put/place the finger; to point at or touch something with one's finger. Can also mean to single someone out or indicate/blame someone in certain contexts.
additional_notes: Literally 'to put the finger.' Commonly used for physically pointing at or touching something with a finger (often followed by prepositions: poner el dedo en, sobre, contra). Figuratively, it can imply blaming or singling someone out (e.g., 'ponerle el dedo a alguien'). Register: neutral; can be used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: No debes poner el dedo en la herida.
native_language_example: You shouldn't put your finger on the wound.

meaning: to start, to set in motion, to get (something) started.
additional_notes: Commonly used for starting machines, projects, programs, plans, or initiatives. Can be literal (start an engine or machine) or figurative (launch a program or get a process going). Often conjugated with poner (e.g., pongo, puso, pondré) + 'en marcha'.
target_language_example: Vamos a poner en marcha el proyecto la próxima semana.
native_language_example: We are going to start the project next week.

meaning: to put (someone/something) in danger; to endanger or jeopardize
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or situation creates risk or harm for a person, group, thing, or plan. Commonly followed by the direct object that is endangered (poner en peligro + algo/alguien). Can be used in literal (physical danger) and figurative (reputation, plan, career) contexts.
target_language_example: No quiero poner en peligro la salud de nadie.
native_language_example: I don't want to put anyone's health in danger.

meaning: to set the table (to arrange dishes, cutlery, etc. before a meal).
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used when preparing for a meal. Often followed by what is being set (poner la mesa para la cena) or used with ayudar (ayudar a poner la mesa). 'Poner' here means 'to place' or 'to put' and combines with 'la mesa' (the table).
target_language_example: Voy a poner la mesa mientras cocinas.
native_language_example: I'll set the table while you cook.

meaning: to cheat on someone (in a romantic relationship).
additional_notes: Colloquial expression meaning to be unfaithful or to have an affair. Usually used with the construction 'ponerle los cuernos a alguien'. Informal and can carry a strong emotional or pejorative tone.
target_language_example: Ella descubrió que su novio le había puesto los cuernos.
native_language_example: She discovered that her boyfriend had cheated on her.

meaning: to begin to; to start (doing something)
additional_notes: Used to indicate the start of an action or process. It is followed by an infinitive: ponerse a + infinitive. It is reflexive in form (ponerse) but functions as a semi-auxiliary verb meaning “begin to.” Nuance depends on context (e.g., ponerse a dieta = start a diet; ponerse a trabajar = begin working; ponerse a prueba = put oneself to the test).
target_language_example: Ella intentó ponerse a dieta y bajar cinco kilos.
native_language_example: She tried to start a diet and lose five kilos.

meaning: to catch up (bring oneself up to date); to update someone or oneself on recent information, tasks, or developments.
additional_notes: Commonly used reflexively (ponerse al día) to mean 'get up to date' yourself (e.g., on news, work, studies) and transitively with 'con' or 'en' to indicate catching up with someone or on a topic (ponerse al día con los correos / ponerse al día en el proyecto). Used in everyday and professional contexts. Can refer to catching up after an absence or updating records or status.
target_language_example: Tengo que ponerme al día con los correos después del viaje.
native_language_example: I have to catch up on emails after the trip.

meaning: to agree (with someone); to reach an agreement or come to terms.
additional_notes: Used when two or more people decide on the same thing or make a plan together. Conjugated reflexively: me pongo de acuerdo, nos pusimos de acuerdo, se pondrán de acuerdo. Often followed by 'en' or 'sobre' + topic (ponerse de acuerdo en/sobre qué hacer).
target_language_example: Después de hablar, lograron ponerse de acuerdo sobre la fecha.
native_language_example: After talking, they managed to agree on the date.

meaning: to stand up (to rise from sitting or lying down).
additional_notes: Common reflexive expression used when someone moves from sitting or lying to a standing position. Can be used literally (physical movement) or in formal contexts (e.g., courtroom: asking someone to stand). Conjugate poner + reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) with 'de pie' remaining after. Can appear in infinitive (ponerse de pie), imperative (ponte/ póngase de pie), or other tenses (se puso de pie).
target_language_example: Es hora de ponerse de pie.
native_language_example: It's time to stand up.

meaning: to put on (a specific masculine singular item of clothing, accessory, or safety device) — literally 'to put the ... on oneself'.
additional_notes: 'Ponerse' is a pronominal verb used with reflexive pronouns (me/te/se/nos/os/se). When followed by the masculine singular definite article 'el' + noun it forms constructions like 'ponerse el cinturón', 'ponerse el abrigo', 'ponerse el sombrero'. Use 'ponerse la' for feminine nouns. Can refer to clothing, accessories, makeup (often 'ponerse el maquillaje' though 'el maquillaje' is masculine), and safety items (e.g., seat belt). Context determines register; generally neutral.
target_language_example: Los pasajeros también tienen que ponerse el cinturón.
native_language_example: Passengers also have to put on their seat belt.

meaning: 'to become so' (followed by an adjective) — often used to advise or tell someone not to get too [adjective].
additional_notes: Ponerse is a reflexive verb meaning 'to become' or 'to get.' Tan means 'so' (to the extent of). Common in imperative/advice forms: 'no se ponga tan...', 'no te pongas tan...', 'trate de no ponerse tan...'. The adjective must agree in gender and number with the subject (tenso/tensa/tensos/tensas). Conjugation of ponerse varies with pronoun (ponerse → póngase / pónganse / ponte / pónganse).
target_language_example: Trate de no ponerse tan tensa.
native_language_example: Please try not to become so tense.

meaning: I start to / I put (someone/something) to (do something).
additional_notes: Depends on context and reflexive use. With reflexive 'me pongo a + infinitive' it means 'I begin to [verb]' (Me pongo a leer = I start to read). With a direct object + infinitive (pongo a + infinitive) it can mean 'I cause/put someone or something to [verb]' or 'I set (someone) to [action]'. Word order and reflexive pronouns change the meaning. Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Me pongo a estudiar a las ocho.
native_language_example: I start studying at eight.

meaning: I put on a
additional_notes: Depends on verb: poner. "Me pongo un ..." (reflexive) = "I put on a ..." (clothing, accessories, makeup). "Pongo un ..." (non‑reflexive) = "I put/ place a ..." or "I put in/ invest a ..." (e.g. dinero). Context determines whether it's reflexive (wearing) or transitive (placing/adding). Use "me" for reflexive: me pongo un abrigo = I put on a coat. "Pongo un trapo sobre..." = I put a rag over....
target_language_example: Me pongo un abrigo cuando hace frío.
native_language_example: I put on a coat when it's cold.

meaning: start to / get yourself to (do something).
additional_notes: Imperative form of ponerse + a + infinitive. Used to tell someone to begin an action (often somewhat direct or firm). Common in spoken Spanish: 'Ponte a + infinitive' = 'Begin doing...'. Can be followed by reflexive verbs (ponte a estudiar) or non-reflexive actions.
target_language_example: Ponte a limpiar tu cuarto ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Start cleaning your room right now.

meaning: popular among the (masculine/mixed group).
additional_notes: Use to say that something or someone is well-liked by a specific group. 'Los' matches a masculine or mixed plural group (e.g., los jóvenes, los estudiantes, los americanos). For feminine groups use 'las' (popular entre las). You can also omit the article and say 'popular entre jóvenes' for general groups.
target_language_example: Ese restaurante es popular entre los estudiantes.
native_language_example: That restaurant is popular among students.

meaning: 'Popular in' — indicates that people, things, places or ideas are well-liked, widely known, or commonly used within a specific location or among a particular group.
additional_notes: Used after adjectives like 'popular(es)' plus the preposition 'en' to specify the place or group. 'Populares' agrees in number and gender with the noun it modifies (e.g., popular, populares). Common in sentences with verbs like 'ser' or 'estar' and in descriptive phrases. Can be used with definite articles or possessives (por ejemplo, 'los más populares en la ciudad', 'populares en nuestra clase').
target_language_example: En general los coches japoneses son populares en el extranjero.
native_language_example: In general Japanese cars are popular abroad.

meaning: 'for God's sake' / 'by God' (expresses surprise, plea, emphasis, or that someone/something is from God).
additional_notes: Used both as an exclamation (por Dios = 'for God's sake'/'please', to show shock, frustration, urgency or plea) and literally to indicate divine origin or mission (enviado por Dios = 'sent by God'). Tone and context determine meaning; can be strong so avoid in very formal/professional settings if using as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Por Dios, ayúdame a encontrar mis llaves.
native_language_example: For God's sake, help me find my keys.

meaning: by accident; accidentally
additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally or by chance. Can describe accidental actions (I did it by mistake) or chance encounters (I found/ran into someone by accident). Common in everyday speech; interchangeable with 'accidentalmente' in many contexts.
target_language_example: Dejé caer el vaso por accidente y se rompió.
native_language_example: I dropped the glass by accident and it broke.

meaning: around here / around this area; (also) this way (as a direction).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a nearby area or to indicate movement toward the speaker's location. Can mean 'around here' (location), 'this way' (direction), or idiomatically 'from around here' in expressions like 'no es de por acá' (not from around here). Informal, common in spoken Spanish; tone and exact meaning depend on context.
target_language_example: No vengas por acá tan tarde.
native_language_example: Don't come around here so late.

meaning: in advance; beforehand.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done or given before a future event. Common in polite formulas (Gracias por adelantado = Thanks in advance) and for payments or apologies made early. Neutral register; very common.
target_language_example: Te aviso por adelantado que llegaré tarde.
native_language_example: I'm telling you in advance that I'll be late.

meaning: 'for now' or 'for the time being' (temporary situation).
additional_notes: Used to describe a temporary state, plan, or expectation that may change later. Can indicate current knowledge ('as of now') or a temporary instruction. Often appears with commas when at the start: "Por ahora, ..."
target_language_example: Por ahora voy a trabajar desde casa.
native_language_example: For now I'm going to work from home.

meaning: around
additional_notes: Very common, flexible phrase used to indicate an approximate location (around/around there/somewhere) or to mean 'around' in a vague sense (e.g., doing something here and there, asking around). Context determines whether it refers to physical location (En un chico que ha visto por ahí = a boy he saw around) or to non‑specific actions/people (Preguntaré por ahí = I'll ask around). Can be informal but is widely used in neutral speech.
target_language_example: ¿Has visto mis llaves por ahí?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys around/anywhere?

meaning: for some reason; for something (depending on context).
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) 'for some reason' — explains that there is an unknown or unstated reason (e.g., "por algo preguntas" = "you ask for a reason"). 2) 'for something' — indicates purpose or motive when followed by a noun (often with partitive 'algo de' = 'some [amount] of'). Context determines translation.
target_language_example: Salió temprano, por algo lo hizo.
native_language_example: He left early; he did it for some reason.

meaning: for something to eat/drink; to get or pick up some (food/drink).
additional_notes: Common in everyday Spanish to say you're going to get some food or drink. Often followed by a noun like comer, beber, café. In some regions 'voy por algo de...' or 'salir por algo de...' are both used. It implies a small, unspecified amount (some).
target_language_example: Voy por algo de merienda.
native_language_example: I'm going to get some snack.

meaning: over there / around there (at some place a bit farther away)
additional_notes: Used to point out a location that is not very close to the speaker but visible or known. Slightly less precise than 'ahí' (there) and often implies distance or direction. Can be used with gestures. Common in conversation.
target_language_example: Mira por allá: se ve el parque junto al río.
native_language_example: Look over there: you can see the park by the river.

meaning: around there / that way / over there (indicating a general location or direction).
additional_notes: Used to point to a nearby but not exact place or to indicate a general direction. Can mean 'in that area', 'that way' (give directions), or 'around there' (talking about where someone/something was). Tone is neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Puedes dejar las maletas por allí, junto a la pared.
native_language_example: You can leave the suitcases over there, by the wall.

meaning: 'overlook' or 'miss' (to fail to notice or consider something).
additional_notes: Used with pasar (pasar por alto) to mean overlooking, missing, or neglecting something (a detail, fact, clue, etc.). Common in both formal and informal contexts. Typical construction: 'pasar por alto + [thing]' or 'haber pasado por alto'. Can be followed by 'que' + clause.
target_language_example: Creo que hemos pasado por alto un detalle importante.
native_language_example: I think we have overlooked an important detail.

meaning: an exclamation: 'for heaven's sake' / 'for God's sake' (used to beg, plead, express frustration or surprise).
additional_notes: Common emphatic phrase used to ask someone to do or stop doing something, to express disbelief, annoyance, or urgent pleading. Tone can range from mild (like 'please') to stronger frustration depending on context and intonation. Avoid using too strongly in very formal or religious contexts if you want to be polite.
target_language_example: Por amor de Dios, escucha lo que digo.
native_language_example: For heaven's sake, listen to what I'm saying.

meaning: at that time / back then
additional_notes: Used to refer to a past time already mentioned or understood from context. Common in storytelling or remembering; interchangeable with 'en aquel entonces' and similar to 'at that time' or 'back then' in English. Usually placed at the start or middle of a sentence.
target_language_example: Por aquel entonces yo estudiaba en la universidad.
native_language_example: Back then I was studying at university.

meaning: around here
additional_notes: Used for a nearby area or for a route/direction. With movement verbs, it often means 'through here' or 'this way'; in more general statements, it means 'around here' or 'near here'.
target_language_example: Siéntate por aquí, por favor.
native_language_example: Sit around here, please.

meaning: above; on top; from above (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position or direction: 'on top of' or 'above' (e.g., something is dirty on top), 'from above' or 'over' (movement above something, as in flying), or more loosely 'start at the top' (e.g., begin from the upper part). Can be used alone as a short reply meaning 'above' or 'on top'.
target_language_example: La pintura estaba limpia por arriba, pero sucia por abajo.
native_language_example: The paint was clean on top, but dirty underneath.

meaning: a hedging phrase meaning 'so to speak' or 'as it were'.
additional_notes: Used to soften, qualify, or mark a non-literal or approximate expression. Often placed after the phrase being qualified (comma before it). Useful when giving an image, approximation, euphemism, or indirect description.
target_language_example: Es mi jefe, por así decirlo.
native_language_example: He's my boss, so to speak.

meaning: 'for helping' or 'for (your) help'.
additional_notes: Used after 'gracias' or similar verbs/phrases to thank someone or to express purpose ('esforzado por ayudar' = 'struggled/been making an effort to help'). Commonly follows verbs like 'gracias', 'hacer mucho', 'esforzarse por'. Context decides whether it expresses gratitude ('thanks for helping') or purpose/reason ('made an effort to help').
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with the move.

meaning: willingly, peacefully, without force or trouble (try to get someone to do something 'por las buenas' = by asking nicely)
additional_notes: Often used in the phrase 'por las buenas' or 'por buenas' to indicate doing something by persuasion, calmly, or without coercion. Common in contexts like 'convencer por las buenas' (convince peacefully) or 'dalo por buenas' (accept it without arguing). Informal register; can contrast with 'por las malas' (by force/through trouble).
target_language_example: Traté de convencerlo por buenas, pero no funcionó.
native_language_example: I tried to persuade him peacefully/by asking nicely, but it didn't work.

meaning: by chance; accidentally; unexpectedly
additional_notes: Used to say something happened without planning or intentionally. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Can be used alone or with verbs (e.g., 'lo vi por casualidad'). Equivalent to 'by accident' or 'by coincidence.'
target_language_example: Encontré este libro por casualidad en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: I found this book by chance in the library.

meaning: because of; due to.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the reason or cause of something. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase (por causa del tráfico, por causa de la lluvia). In formal Spanish you may also see 'a causa de' with a similar meaning. If followed by 'de' + article, 'del' = 'de + el'.
target_language_example: Llegué tarde por causa del tráfico.
native_language_example: I arrived late because of the traffic.

meaning: because of; due to; on account of.
additional_notes: Used to give a reason or cause for something. Formal or neutral; interchangeable with 'debido a' or 'a causa de' in many contexts. Followed by a noun or noun phrase (no conjugated verb directly).
target_language_example: Cancelaron el partido por causa de la lluvia.
native_language_example: They canceled the match because of the rain.

meaning: percent; for every hundred (used to express percentages).
additional_notes: Used after a number to indicate a percentage (e.g., 'diez por ciento' = 10%). Often abbreviated as '%' in writing. In spoken Spanish you can also say 'por ciento' or use the symbol when reading numbers aloud ('diez por ciento' or 'diez %').
target_language_example: El veinte por ciento de los estudiantes aprobó el examen.
native_language_example: Twenty percent of the students passed the exam.

meaning: by the way
additional_notes: Used to introduce an incidental remark, change the topic slightly, add emphasis, or remind the listener of something. Often appears at the start of a sentence or after a clause (commonly with commas). Tone can be neutral or conversational.
target_language_example: Por cierto, ¿viste la película nueva?
native_language_example: By the way, did you see the new movie?

meaning: completely; entirely; fully.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is done or true to the fullest degree. Can modify verbs (e.g., cambiar por completo = change completely) or stand alone as a short reply (Por completo.). Common in both formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Cambió su rutina por completo el año pasado.
native_language_example: He changed his routine completely last year.

meaning: for any / because of any (depending on context); 'por' + 'cualquier' expresses 'for/through any' or 'any ... that/which'.
additional_notes: Used before a noun or clause to mean 'for any' (e.g., 'por cualquier problema' = 'for any problem') or to indicate 'anywhere/any side' in some dialects when followed by a noun of place ('por cualquier lado'). With a subordinate clause it can appear as 'por cualquier + [noun] + que + ...' meaning 'no matter what/whichever'. Context determines whether it indicates cause (because of any) or nonspecific choice/placement (any).
target_language_example: Por cualquier duda, envíame un mensaje.
native_language_example: For any questions, send me a message.

meaning: on behalf of; at the expense of; because of (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common prepositional phrase with several uses: 'on behalf of' (doing something for someone), 'at the expense of' or 'paid by' (who covers cost), and sometimes 'because of' or 'due to' in formal contexts. Context and verbs determine the sense. Often followed by a person or organization (por cuenta de ella, por cuenta de la empresa).
target_language_example: Hablo por cuenta de mi jefe en la reunión.
native_language_example: I speak on behalf of my boss at the meeting.

meaning: paid for by the establishment / on the house.
additional_notes: Used when something (a drink, meal, service, etc.) is offered free to the customer because the business or host will pay for it. Common in restaurants, bars, hotels, or when a host treats a guest. Equivalent to "on the house" in English.
target_language_example: La cena de hoy va por cuenta de la casa.
native_language_example: Tonight's dinner is on the house.

meaning: on one's own; independently; self-employed
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something independently (by themselves) or works as a freelancer/self-employed. Context determines whether it means 'by oneself' (alone/without help) or 'self-employed' (having one's own business). Common in both personal actions (hacerlo por cuenta propia = do it on your own) and occupations (trabajar por cuenta propia = be self-employed).
target_language_example: Ahora trabajo por cuenta propia como diseñador gráfico.
native_language_example: Now I work on my own as a graphic designer.

meaning: 'because of' or 'due to' with a sense of blame or fault.
additional_notes: Used to indicate cause while implying someone or something is to blame (fault/responsibility). Often followed by 'de' + noun or a pronoun (e.g., 'por culpa de él', 'por culpa tuya'). Can be neutral in some contexts but usually conveys negative consequence or fault.
target_language_example: Cancelaron el picnic por culpa de la lluvia.
native_language_example: They canceled the picnic because of the rain (implying the rain is to blame).

meaning: because of; due to (often with a sense of blame or fault).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the cause of something, frequently implying blame or responsibility. Can be neutral in some contexts (e.g., weather delays) but often carries a negative tone. Commonly followed by a noun, name, or phrase.
target_language_example: Llegamos tarde por culpa del tráfico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of the traffic.

meaning: to be (something) to fulfill / to have yet to fulfill; 'to be for fulfilling'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun or verb to indicate an obligation, task, goal, or expectation that remains to be completed. Common in phrases like "misión por cumplir" (a mission to be fulfilled) or with verbs: "por cumplir con" + object (to try to meet/fulfill). Not a standalone verb — it marks something pending or intended.
target_language_example: Tenemos muchos sueños por cumplir este año.
native_language_example: We have many dreams to fulfill this year.

meaning: under, below, beneath; also: less than (in amount/level).
additional_notes: Used for physical position (under/below) and for figurative comparisons (below expectations, below someone's level, less than a value). Often followed by a noun or pronoun. Can pair with people, objects, measurements, or abstract things (expectations, weight).
target_language_example: El gato está por debajo de la mesa.
native_language_example: The cat is under the table.

meaning: literally 'so to speak' — used to soften or mark an expression as approximate or metaphorical.
additional_notes: Common filler phrase to signal that what you just said (or are about to say) is not exact, is figurative, or might sound odd. Can appear mid-sentence or alone. Similar to English 'so to speak', 'if you will', or 'in a manner of speaking.'
target_language_example: Es mi forma, por decirlo así, de decir 'gracias'.
native_language_example: It's my way, so to speak, of saying 'thank you'.

meaning: 'ahead of' / 'in front of' / 'before' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used spatially to mean 'in front of' or 'past' (e.g., walked past a place). Used figuratively to mean 'ahead of' someone in position, progress, or priority (e.g., to put something before other things or to be one step ahead). Context determines whether it indicates physical location, movement, priority, or advantage.
target_language_example: Ella siempre pone a su familia por delante de su carrera.
native_language_example: She always puts her family ahead of her career.

meaning: unfortunately
additional_notes: Used to introduce bad or regrettable information. Equivalent to 'unfortunately' or 'sadly' in English; commonly placed at the start of a sentence or clause and followed by a comma.
target_language_example: Por desgracia, no puedo venir a la fiesta mañana.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I can't come to the party tomorrow.

meaning: from behind; at the back; behind (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position or movement coming from the rear. Can be literal (someone grabs you from behind, go to the back of the building) or figurative/colloquial (doing something 'behind' in a secret or alternative way). Common with verbs of movement (venir, ir, agarrar) and with commands (Ve por detrás = Go to the back).
target_language_example: Entraron por detrás para no hacer cola.
native_language_example: They came in from behind so they didn't have to wait in line.

meaning: 'for example' — used to introduce an example or illustration.
additional_notes: Common phrase to give one or more examples. Often placed at the start of a sentence (followed by a comma) or after a clause. Can be used alone ("por ejemplo") or followed by a specific example.
target_language_example: Puedes comer muchas frutas, por ejemplo, manzanas y plátanos.
native_language_example: You can eat many fruits, for example, apples and bananas.

meaning: an exclamation meaning 'for the love of God' used to express strong emotion (urgent plea, shock, frustration).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize urgency, begging, disbelief, frustration or annoyance. Common in informal and formal contexts; can be strong depending on tone—may sound religious but often functions as a general intensifier. Be careful: can be seen as emphatic or impolite in very formal or sensitive situations.
target_language_example: Por el amor de Dios, cierra la ventana, hace mucho frío.
native_language_example: For the love of God, close the window, it's very cold.

meaning: something like that / of that sort / along those lines
additional_notes: Used to indicate approximation or give an example without being specific. Common after examples (e.g., "o algo por el estilo" = "or something like that"). Can negate to mean "nothing like that" ("no dije nada por el estilo"). Informal-neutral, very common in speech.
target_language_example: Tráeme platos, vasos o algo por el estilo.
native_language_example: Bring me plates, glasses, or something like that.

meaning: for the moment; for now; temporarily.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is true right now but may change later. Common in everyday and formal speech. Can often be replaced with 'por ahora' (more casual) or 'de momento'.
target_language_example: Por el momento no aceptamos nuevas suscripciones.
native_language_example: For the moment we are not accepting new subscriptions.

meaning: for the rest of my (life/time).
additional_notes: Commonly completed with a noun (most often 'vida') to mean 'for the rest of my life'. Used to express something that will last until the speaker's life or until a long remaining period ends. Can be followed by 'vida', 'tiempo', etc., but leaving 'vida' implied is natural in colloquial speech.
target_language_example: Te protegeré por el resto de mi vida.
native_language_example: I will protect you for the rest of my life.

meaning: on/along the floor; across the ground; (figuratively) very low or ruined
additional_notes: Commonly describes movement or location along a floor or ground (e.g., caminar por el suelo, rodó por el suelo). Can also be used figuratively to mean 'very low' (e.g., precios por el suelo = very low prices) or to indicate something lying on the floor (estar por el suelo). Context tells whether it's literal (physical floor/ground) or figurative.
target_language_example: La taza se cayó y quedó por el suelo.
native_language_example: The cup fell and ended up on the floor.

meaning: 'over' / 'on top of' / 'briefly/roughly (as in 'go over')', depending on context.
additional_notes: This multiword phrase has several related uses: (1) physical position — 'on top of' or 'over' something (e.g., place a leg over something, walk over water); (2) movement — 'pass over' or 'go across' something; (3) figurative/communication — 'briefly review' or 'give a quick summary' (e.g., 'contar por encima su plan' = give a quick overview). Context determines whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes pasar por encima el informe y decirme lo más importante?
native_language_example: Can you go over the report and tell me the most important points?

meaning: above everything; before anything else; most importantly
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has highest priority or importance. Often placed before or after the thing it qualifies (e.g., 'El deber por encima de todo' or 'Por encima de todo, la seguridad'). Formal or neutral register; common in both speech and writing.
target_language_example: Por encima de todo, cuida tu salud.
native_language_example: Above all, take care of your health.

meaning: in writing; written (rather than spoken).
additional_notes: Used to say that something should be recorded or sent in written form (letter, email, note). Common with verbs like poner, mandar, aplicar, dejar — e.g., 'poner por escrito' = 'to put in writing'. Can refer to formal or informal written communication.
target_language_example: Mándame las instrucciones por escrito, por favor.
native_language_example: Send me the instructions in writing, please.

meaning: that's why
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a reason already mentioned. It often connects two ideas, especially at the start of a sentence, and is very common for explaining a result or consequence.
target_language_example: Está lloviendo; por eso no salgo hoy.
native_language_example: It's raining; that's why I'm not going out today.

meaning: around these
additional_notes: Commonly used as part of phrases like 'por estos días' (around these days), 'por estos lados' (around here/these parts) or 'por estos caminos' (along/through these paths). Meaning depends on context and the noun that follows: with time words (días, tiempos) it means 'around/these days'; with places (lados, sitios) it means 'around/these parts'; with paths or routes it can mean 'along/through these'.
target_language_example: Por estos días hace mucho calor.
native_language_example: It's very hot around these days.

meaning: because of an excess; due to too much (of something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a harmful or excessive amount of something (e.g., speed, work). Commonly appears in phrases like 'por exceso de velocidad' (for speeding) or 'por exceso de trabajo' (from overwork). Often followed by 'de' + noun.
target_language_example: Se enfermó por exceso de trabajo.
native_language_example: He got sick from overwork.

meaning: please
additional_notes: Used to make requests more polite. It can also express pleading or urgency, as in por favor no hagas eso ('please don't do that'). It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Pásame la sal, por favor.
native_language_example: Pass me the salt, please.

meaning: 'please leave' or 'please stop' depending on context.
additional_notes: Por favor = please. Deja is the informal (tú) imperative or present of dejar (to leave, to let, to stop). Combined, it can mean 'please leave (something/someone)' (e.g., 'please leave a message', 'please let my daughter go') or 'please stop' when followed by a gerund/infinitive (e.g., 'por favor deja de reír' = 'please stop laughing'). Use deja when addressing one person informally. For formal/plural commands use 'por favor deje' (usted) or 'por favor dejen' (ustedes).
target_language_example: Por favor deja la puerta abierta.
native_language_example: Please leave the door open.

meaning: finally
additional_notes: Used to express relief or satisfaction that something desired or expected has happened after a delay. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence (e.g., "Por fin terminé" or "Terminé por fin").
target_language_example: Por fin llegó el autobús.
native_language_example: The bus finally arrived.

meaning: 'finally we' or 'at last we' (followed by a verb referring to 'us' or 'we').
additional_notes: Por fin = 'finally/at last'. When followed by nos (the object/pronoun 'us' or reflexive 'ourselves'), it introduces actions or states that happen to or are done by/for 'us' (e.g., conocemos = we meet/know each other; dejará en paz = will leave us alone; mudamos = we move). The exact English structure depends on the verb: 'we finally meet', 'they finally leave us alone', 'we finally moved'.
target_language_example: Por fin nos reunimos para celebrar.
native_language_example: We finally got together to celebrate.

meaning: 'for no good reason' or 'just because / for fun' (doing something without practical purpose or benefit).
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without necessary reason, benefit, or intent—often 'just for fun', 'just because', or 'needlessly'. Can be neutral (doing something for pleasure) or negative (needlessly, pointlessly). Common with actions like criticizing, calling, or helping when there's no gain.
target_language_example: No trabajó en el proyecto por gusto; quería aprender.
native_language_example: He didn't work on the project just for fun; he wanted to learn.

meaning: 'because of doing it' / 'to do it' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase can mean different things depending on context. Often, por + infinitive expresses reason ('because of doing something') as in 'Me preocupé por hacerlo' = 'I worried because of doing it.' It can also appear in idiomatic expressions: 'estar por hacerlo' = 'to be about to do it'; 'morirse por hacerlo' = 'to be dying to do it' (very eager); and 'hacer esperar por hacerlo' indicates being delayed because of someone. Word order and surrounding words change the nuance, so translate based on the whole sentence.
target_language_example: Estoy por hacerlo ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I'm about to do it right now.

meaning: per hour; by the hour.
additional_notes: Used to talk about rates or frequency measured each hour (e.g., pay rate: 'se le paga por hora' = 'he/she is paid per hour'). Can also appear alone as a short response meaning 'for now' in some contexts, but primary meaning is 'per hour'.
target_language_example: Trabajo por hora en la cafetería.
native_language_example: I work for an hourly wage at the café.

meaning: for today; (I'm) done for today.
additional_notes: Used to say that an activity is finished or will stop for the rest of the day. Often follows a verb (e.g., 'Terminé por hoy' = I'm finished for today). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ya he hecho todo el trabajo por hoy.
native_language_example: I've already done all the work for today.

meaning: 'by instinct' or 'instinctively' — because of natural, automatic impulses rather than conscious thought.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something acts without deliberate reasoning, guided by innate tendencies or gut feeling. Common with animals and humans. Can describe a general tendency (Los animales actúan por instinto) or a specific immediate reaction (Por instinto, me aparté).
target_language_example: Por instinto, tomé el paraguas antes de salir.
native_language_example: Instinctively, I took the umbrella before leaving.

meaning: thank you for inviting me to (something / somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to express gratitude for being invited. The structure is: gracias por invitarme a + (place, event, or action). 'Invitarme' is the verb 'invitar' (to invite) with the pronoun 'me' (me). You can change the object after 'a' to a noun (la fiesta), a place (tu casa) or an infinitive/phrase (sentarme a la mesa).
target_language_example: Gracias por invitarme a la cena mañana.
native_language_example: Thank you for inviting me to dinner tomorrow.

meaning: through/out the back door; by a back/side exit. (literally and figuratively)
additional_notes: Used literally to mean entering or leaving via a back door. Also used figuratively to mean doing something secretly, quietly, unofficially, or by an indirect/underhanded way (e.g., avoiding formal process). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Sal de la casa por la puerta de atrás para no despertar a nadie.
native_language_example: Leave the house through the back door so you don't wake anyone.

meaning: generally; usually; in general.
additional_notes: Used to describe what typically happens or is true. Often placed at the start of a sentence or before the verb. Comma after the phrase is optional. Synonyms: 'generalmente', 'normalmente'.
target_language_example: Por lo general desayuno a las siete.
native_language_example: I usually have breakfast at seven.

meaning: at least; at the very least
additional_notes: Used to indicate a minimum amount, number, degree, or to soften/limit a statement (e.g., 'at least' in English). Can appear mid-sentence for emphasis ('eso, por lo menos') or at the start ('por lo menos...'). Common in everyday and formal speech.
target_language_example: Por lo menos tráete una chaqueta.
native_language_example: At least bring a jacket.

meaning: because of which
additional_notes: Commonly used to link a cause or reason to a result ("because of which" / "so"), or to refer back to 'that which' (similar to 'what' in English). Context determines exact translation: in causal sentences it means 'because of which' (e.g., 'offended because of what he said'); in expressions of apology or gratitude it can mean 'for what' / 'for that which' (e.g., 'sorry for what I am' or 'thanks for what you have made possible').
target_language_example: Lo agradezco por lo que has hecho por mí.
native_language_example: I thank you for what you have done for me.

meaning: because of what had (happened/done); for what had…
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action or event in the past (pluperfect: 'había' + past participle). Commonly translated as 'because of what had...' or 'for what had...'. The rest of the clause usually completes the idea (e.g., hecho, pasado, ocurrido). Tone is neutral and suitable for formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Me disculpé por lo que había dicho.
native_language_example: I apologized because of what I had said.

meaning: because of what (someone) did/said to him/her; for what (someone) did to him/her.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action or words that affected a third person (le = to him/her). Often follows a noun or clause that names the person affected: 'Es por Lola, por lo que le hiciste a su padre' = 'It's because of Lola, for what you did to her father.' Can introduce a reason ('por lo que' = 'because of what') or refer to the specific thing someone said/did ('por lo que le dijo/hiciste').
target_language_example: Por lo que le contaste, ahora está molesta con él.
native_language_example: Because of what you told her, she's upset with him now.

meaning: As far as I know; based on what I know.
additional_notes: Used to introduce information the speaker believes is true but not certain. Common in spoken and written Spanish to hedge a statement. Often followed by a clause (por lo que sé, + clause). Can be replaced by 'que yo sepa'.
target_language_example: Por lo que sé, la reunión empieza a las nueve.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting starts at nine.

meaning: therefore; so; consequently.
additional_notes: Used to express a logical conclusion or result from what was said before. Common in both spoken and written Spanish; can appear at the start of a sentence or between clauses, often set off by commas.
target_language_example: No tenía dinero, por lo tanto no pudo comprar el billete.
native_language_example: He had no money, so he couldn't buy the ticket.

meaning: 'apparently' or 'it seems' (based on what is known or reported).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information that the speaker believes to be true based on evidence, reports, or appearance. Common in conversational and written Spanish to soften a statement or report hearsay. Can be followed by a clause or a short response (e.g., "Por lo visto, sí.").
target_language_example: Por lo visto, van a cerrar la tienda mañana.
native_language_example: Apparently, they're going to close the store tomorrow.

meaning: around the years of; roughly in the time period of
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate date or time period (often followed by a decade or specific year). Similar to 'around' or 'in the years of' in English. Common in spoken and written Spanish to indicate approximation (e.g., 'por los años de 1990' = 'around 1990').
target_language_example: Empezaron a construir el edificio por los años de 2005.
native_language_example: They started building the building around the year 2005.

meaning: by the skin of one's teeth; narrowly; just barely.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to say something happened with very little margin — barely succeeding, escaping, or avoiding something. Often used with verbs like aprobar (pass), librarse (escape), salvarse (be saved).
target_language_example: Aprobé el examen por los pelos.
native_language_example: I passed the exam by the skin of my teeth.

meaning: 'by means of' / 'through' / 'via' (shows the instrument, method, or means used)
additional_notes: Used to indicate the method, instrument, channel, or intermediary by which something is done. More formal than 'con' or 'a través de' in some contexts but largely interchangeable with 'mediante' and 'a través de'. Often followed by a noun (por medio de + noun).
target_language_example: Enviaron la información por medio de correo electrónico.
native_language_example: They sent the information by means of email.

meaning: as for me / on my part / from my side (expressing personal stance or responsibility).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the speaker's opinion, attitude, or responsibility. Can indicate personal responsibility (e.g., admitting fault) or simply state that the following comment applies to the speaker alone. Often appears with commas: "Yo, por mi parte,..." or at the start: "Por mi parte,..."
target_language_example: Por mi parte, estoy de acuerdo con la propuesta.
native_language_example: As for me, I agree with the proposal.

meaning: 'for my life' — used to say someone is in danger, fleeing, or very strongly swearing (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Common uses:
- Literal/urgent: expresses fear for one's life or running/fighting to save oneself (e.g., estoy luchando/temo/huí por mi vida = I'm fighting/fear/ran for my life).
- Figurative/colloquial: can be used hyperbolically in song or expression to mean 'with all my energy' (bailo por mi vida) or as a strong oath (te lo juro por mi vida = I swear to you on my life). Context determines whether it's literal danger or emphasis.
Often appears in past participle/verbs of motion (corrí/huí) or verbs of emotion (temo, temo por mi vida).
target_language_example: Corrí por mi vida cuando escuché las explosiones.
native_language_example: I ran for my life when I heard the explosions.

meaning: for moments; occasionally; at times
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens occasionally or in short bursts. Common in phrases like 'por momentos pensé...' (for a moment I thought...) or 'por momentos estuvo nublado' (at times it was cloudy). Tone is neutral and it's frequent in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Por momentos pensé que había perdido mi billetera.
native_language_example: For a moment I thought I had lost my wallet.

meaning: 'for many' / 'because of many' (used before a noun to indicate 'by/through/for many [things/people/reasons]').
additional_notes: Used with a following plural noun (e.g., 'por muchas razones', 'por muchas dificultades', 'por muchas criaturas'). Can mean 'because of many' (giving a cause/reason) or 'by/through many' (indicating being known/experienced by many). The exact translation depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: He cambiado por muchas experiencias a lo largo de los años.
native_language_example: I've changed because of many experiences over the years.

meaning: even if (used with quantities or intensity) / no matter how much
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like "por mucho que..." meaning "no matter how much/however much..." It introduces a concession: something happens or is true despite a large amount or effort. Alone, "por mucho" can precede a noun (e.g., "por mucho dinero") to mean "for a lot of.../despite a lot of..." Common structures: "por mucho que + subjunctive" (contrasting hypothetical or general statements) and "por mucho + noun".
target_language_example: Por mucho que estudies, a veces los exámenes son difíciles.
native_language_example: No matter how much you study, sometimes exams are difficult.

meaning: no matter how / however much (introduces a contrast: despite trying or despite something happening)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession: it emphasizes that even with effort or to whatever extent, the result is (usually) negative or unchanged. Followed by a verb in indicative or subjunctive depending on nuance; in many beginner contexts present indicative or past tense appears. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Por mucho que lo intente, no puedo resolver este problema.
native_language_example: No matter how much I try, I can't solve this problem.

meaning: by/for a long time; 'no matter how' when followed by que + clause; or 'not by much' in short phrases (context-dependent).
additional_notes:
Two common uses:
- As part of 'por mucho que + [subjunctive clause]' it means 'no matter how' or 'however much' (e.g., Por mucho que lo intentó... = However much he tried...).
- In other contexts it can mean 'for/by a long time' (less common) or appear in short responses like 'Ni por mucho' / 'No por mucho' to mean 'not by much' or 'not much (at all)' depending on tone. Context determines meaning; when followed by que it needs the subjunctive in the clause that follows.
target_language_example: Por mucho que practiques, mejorarás si sigues intentándolo.
native_language_example: No matter how much you practice, you'll improve if you keep trying.

meaning: for more than; indicating a duration or amount that exceeds a number or period.
additional_notes: Commonly used before time expressions or quantities (un mes, una hora, treinta años). Equivalent to 'for over' or 'for more than' in English. Use 'por más de' with durations or numeric amounts. Can be followed by a number + noun or a clause.
target_language_example: Vivió en esa ciudad por más de diez años.
native_language_example: He lived in that city for more than ten years.

meaning: for me
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something as a favor or to indicate doing something on one's behalf or for one's benefit. Can also express indifference in contexts like “por mí, como quieras” (for all I care / suit yourself).
target_language_example: Haz esto por mí, por favor.
native_language_example: Do this for me, please.

meaning: for nothing / over nothing / about nothing (depends on context)
additional_notes: Common phrase with different meanings depending on context: 1) 'for nothing' meaning with little or no cost (e.g., vender/comprar por nada). 2) 'for no reason' or 'over nothing' to say someone gets upset easily. 3) in negative constructions it can mean 'about nothing' or 'not need to worry about anything' (e.g., no necesitas preocuparte por nada). Choose sense from surrounding words.
target_language_example: Se enfadó por nada y luego pidió perdón.
native_language_example: He got upset over nothing and then apologized.

meaning: "not for anything in the world" — used to say you would never do something or must not do something under any circumstances.
additional_notes: Strong, emphatic negative expression. Often used with verbs in negative commands or statements (No lo haría por nada del mundo / No lo hagas por nada del mundo). Can stand alone as a short reply meaning 'no way' or 'absolutely not.'
target_language_example: No viajaría sola por nada del mundo.
native_language_example: I wouldn't travel alone for anything in the world.

meaning: nowhere; not anywhere.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is not to be found in any place or that something doesn't appear anywhere. Common in negative sentences. Equivalent to 'en ningún lado' / 'en ningún lugar'.
target_language_example: Busqué por toda la casa, pero no lo encontré por ningún lado.
native_language_example: I searched the whole house, but I couldn't find it anywhere.

meaning: by the work of; through the action of (used to indicate who/what caused something)
additional_notes: Formal or literary phrase used to state the agent or cause of an event or result. Often followed by a person, group, or force (e.g., 'por obra de Juan', 'por obra de la casualidad'). Can be replaced in everyday speech by 'por' or 'gracias a' depending on context. Common in written, historical, or formal contexts.
target_language_example: La ciudad fue restaurada por obra de un comité local.
native_language_example: The city was restored by the work of a local committee.

meaning: on the other hand / furthermore
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting point or an additional remark. Commonly placed at the start or middle of a sentence and often followed by a comma. Similar to 'por otro lado' and 'en cambio'.
target_language_example: Me gusta el trabajo; por otra parte, necesito más tiempo libre.
native_language_example: I like the job; on the other hand, I need more free time.

meaning: on the other hand; alternatively; in another place (literal).
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a contrasting idea (like 'on the other hand'). Can also be literal when talking about a different location ('pasea por otro lado' = 'walk somewhere else'). Often paired with 'por un lado' to present two sides.
target_language_example: Por otro lado, creo que deberíamos esperar.
native_language_example: On the other hand, I think we should wait.

meaning: on behalf of others; for other people
additional_notes: 'Por' indicates acting for or because of someone else. Used when someone answers, speaks, or acts representing other people. Context matters: can mean 'because of others' in some sentences, but common in phrases like 'responder por otros' (to be responsible/answer for others).
target_language_example: No puedo firmar por otros sin su permiso.
native_language_example: I can't sign on behalf of others without their permission.

meaning: by (someone); on the part of; from the side of.
additional_notes: Used to indicate who performed an action, who holds an attitude, or the source/side responsible. Common in formal and neutral contexts: 'por parte de + pronoun/noun'. Can also mean 'from the family of' in kinship phrases (e.g., 'por parte de padre').
target_language_example: Fue un error por parte de la empresa.
native_language_example: It was a mistake on the part of the company.

meaning: in parts; piece by piece; step by step.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done or explained in separate pieces or stages. Common in instructions or when describing something broken into sections. Can be used like 'hacer algo por partes' (to do something in parts) or 'explicar por partes' (explain in parts).
target_language_example: Vamos a resolver el problema por partes.
native_language_example: Let's solve the problem in parts / step by step.

meaning: for losing; because of losing; to lose (depending on context)
additional_notes: Por perder is a phrase built from the preposition por + the infinitive perder. It can indicate a reason ('because of losing'), an aim or consequence ('to lose' — often after verbs like 'arriesgarse por perder' is uncommon), or appear in fixed expressions like 'no hay por perder' (nothing to lose). Context matters: more natural constructions for 'in order to lose' use 'para perder'.
target_language_example: No tenemos nada por perder si lo intentamos.
native_language_example: We have nothing to lose if we try.

meaning: almost; nearly (used to say something almost happened, often with a negative result)
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase. Often followed by verbs in simple past or preterite (cometí, no lo logramos) or used before clauses like "por poco + verb". Can appear as "por poco + no + verb" to emphasize that something almost didn't happen (e.g., "Por poco no lo logramos" = We almost didn't make it). Tone can be dramatic; used in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Por poco pierdo el tren esta mañana.
native_language_example: I almost missed the train this morning.

meaning: for the first time
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened at the initial occurrence. Common with verbs of action (fui, montó, conocí). Can appear anywhere in the sentence but often follows the verb or phrase it modifies. Not formal/slang.
target_language_example: Hoy voy a probar sushi por primera vez.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to try sushi for the first time.

meaning: for the first time in my (life / experience); used to introduce something happening to the speaker for the first time
additional_notes: This is a partial phrase that normally continues with a noun like "vida", "memoria" or "recuerdo" (e.g. "por primera vez en mi vida"). It emphasizes that the event or feeling is novel for the speaker. Can be followed by a verb phrase describing what happened.
target_language_example: Por primera vez en mi vida, viajé solo a otro país.
native_language_example: For the first time in my life, I traveled alone to another country.

meaning: through/by (the) doors; via doorways
additional_notes: A literal prepositional phrase used to indicate movement or passage through doors or entrances. In natural Spanish it's more common to include an article or determiner (por la puerta, por las puertas, por una puerta), but por puertas can appear in contexts emphasizing 'through doors' in general rather than specific ones (e.g., describing multiple exits or a pattern). Word order and articles may vary.
target_language_example: Pasaron por puertas para evitar el pasillo principal.
native_language_example: They went through doors to avoid the main hallway.

meaning: why
additional_notes: Used in direct and indirect questions to ask for the reason. It is written as two words with an accent on qué when it means "why" (compare porque = "because"). It can also appear inside expressions like no tener por qué, meaning there is no reason to or no need to.
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué estás enojado.
native_language_example: I don't understand why you're angry.

meaning: 'to know' in the sense of wanting or being eager to know; part of the phrase 'tener curiosidad por saber' meaning 'to be curious to know'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone verb; usually appears after expressions of interest/curiosity/need (e.g., 'tener curiosidad por saber', 'estaban impacientes por saber'). It introduces the information someone wants to know (what, who, why, etc.). In some contexts 'por saber' can be part of shorter phrases (e.g., 'por saber persuadir' = 'to be good at persuading' or 'for knowing how to persuade'), but for beginners focus on its common use with curiosity/impatience.
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de saberlo; estoy curioso por saber la verdad.
native_language_example: I really want to know it; I'm curious to know the truth.

meaning: separately; apart; individually.
additional_notes: Used to say that people or things are not together or are handled individually. Common with actions (arrive, pay) and with items sold individually. Can appear before or after verbs depending on sentence. Informal/neutral everyday phrase.
target_language_example: Prefiero que las cuentas se paguen por separado.
native_language_example: I prefer the bills to be paid separately.

meaning: 'in case' (to express a precaution or possibility).
additional_notes: Use 'por si' before a clause or phrase that states a possible situation you want to prepare for. Often followed by a verb in indicative or subjunctive depending on speaker's view of likelihood (both are common in speech). Common in everyday Spanish to express precaution: 'por si hace frío, trae una chaqueta.'
target_language_example: Voy a dejar las luces encendidas por si vuelves tarde.
native_language_example: I'll leave the lights on in case you come back late.

meaning: just in case; in case something happens
additional_notes: Used to express precaution or preparation for a possible (but not certain) event. Can appear at start, middle, or end of a sentence. Often followed by a clause or an action (e.g., llevar, poner, llamar). Common in everyday speech and polite instructions.
target_language_example: Voy a llevar un paraguas por si acaso.
native_language_example: I'll take an umbrella just in case.

meaning: forever; for all time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts indefinitely or eternally. Common in both serious (emotions, memories) and playful contexts (songs, slogans). Can be replaced by 'para siempre' — both are correct and largely interchangeable, though 'para siempre' is slightly more common in some regions.
target_language_example: Te querré por siempre.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

meaning: 'on one's own', 'by oneself', or 'independently'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone, independently, or without help. Can refer to living alone, working independently (self-employed), or acting on one's own initiative. Context determines nuance: 'por su cuenta' = alone/independently; 'por su cuenta y riesgo' adds 'at one's own risk'.
target_language_example: Ahora vive por su cuenta y paga sus propias facturas.
native_language_example: Now he lives on his own and pays his own bills.

meaning: luckily; fortunately.
additional_notes: Used to say that something good happened or that luck was on someone's side. Often placed at the start of the sentence but can appear elsewhere. Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Por suerte encontré mi teléfono perdido.
native_language_example: Luckily I found my lost phone.

meaning: of course
additional_notes: A very common fixed phrase used to show clear agreement, certainty, or that something is obvious or expected. It can be used on its own as a reply or inserted into a sentence.
target_language_example: —¿Puedo ayudarte? —Por supuesto.
native_language_example: —Can I help you? —Of course.

meaning: by oneself; on its own; alone (without help or intervention).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that a person or thing acts without assistance or that something happens naturally/automatically. Gender and number can vary in related phrases (e.g., "por sí mismo/a", "por sí solos/as"). Modern Spanish typically writes "solo" without an accent. Context determines whether it emphasizes lack of help, spontaneity, or occurrence without external causes.
target_language_example: El gato se subió al techo de mi casa por sí solo.
native_language_example: The cat climbed onto my house roof by itself.

meaning: by oneself; on one's own; by itself (referring to a thing or person acting without help).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone or something does something without help from others. Agrees in gender/number when used as a pronoun phrase (por sí mismo, por sí misma, por sí mismos, por sí mismas). Can refer to a person deciding/learning alone or to a thing that reveals something 'by itself'.
target_language_example: Aprendió a cocinar por sí mismo.
native_language_example: He learned to cook by himself.

meaning: therefore / consequently
additional_notes: A linking phrase used to draw a conclusion or indicate a result from what was just said. It is slightly formal but common in both spoken and written Spanish. Can appear at the start or middle of a sentence and is interchangeable with 'por lo tanto' or 'por consiguiente'.
target_language_example: No había pruebas; por tanto, decidieron cerrar el caso.
native_language_example: There was no evidence; therefore, they decided to close the case.

meaning: everywhere; all over the place.
additional_notes: Used to say something is present or happening in many places or throughout an area. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Can describe people, objects, noises, smells, rumors, etc. Synonyms: 'por todas partes' ≈ 'en todas partes' or 'por doquier'.
target_language_example: Había basura por todas partes después de la fiesta.
native_language_example: There was trash everywhere after the party.

meaning: for everything
additional_notes: Commonly used to thank someone (gracias por todo = thanks for everything) or to apologize/express responsibility (perdóname por todo = forgive me for everything). Can also mean 'about everything' or 'over every little thing' in contexts like "te preocupas por todo" (you worry about everything). In contexts like "él pagará por todo" it means 'pay for everything' (cover the costs).
target_language_example: Gracias por todo lo que has hecho.
native_language_example: Thanks for everything you've done.

meaning: for everything you have (done).
additional_notes: Common part of the phrase 'por todo lo que has hecho' used to thank someone for actions or help. Often followed by a past participle (hecho). Can be used with 'por mí', 'por nosotros' to specify the beneficiary. Formality: neutral; polite and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Gracias por todo lo que has hecho por mí.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything you have done for me.

meaning: everywhere; all over; everywhere around.
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is in many places or all around a place. Common in everyday speech. Can be followed by a person or thing (Busqué a Tom por todos lados) or a noun (Hay agua por todos lados).
target_language_example: Encontré mis llaves por todos lados, hasta debajo del sofá.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys everywhere, even under the sofa.

meaning: by all means; using every possible way or effort
additional_notes: Used to say someone will do something using every available method or that something should be done at all costs. Can also be a short exclamation meaning "absolutely" or "certainly" (e.g., agreeing with a suggestion). Context usually indicates whether it's about effort or strong agreement.
target_language_example: Debes conseguir el billete por todos los medios.
native_language_example: You must get the ticket by all means / at any cost.

meaning: on one hand; from one point of view
additional_notes: Used to introduce one side of a contrast or argument, often paired with 'por otro lado' or 'por el otro' to present the opposite side. Common in spoken and written Spanish to compare two perspectives or reasons.
target_language_example: Por un lado quiero viajar, pero por otro lado necesito ahorrar dinero.
native_language_example: On one hand I want to travel, but on the other hand I need to save money.

meaning: for a cup (of)... — used to express wanting, exchanging, or going to get a cup (usually of a beverage).
additional_notes: Commonly appears with drinks (e.g., café). Can mean: 1) desire/regret ('I'd give my left arm for a cup of decent coffee' = I'd really want one), 2) to go get something ('Voy por una taza de café' = I'm going to get one), or 3) in exchange ('te lo doy por una taza de arroz' = I give it to you in exchange for a cup of rice). Context determines whether it's desire, movement to fetch, or an exchange.
target_language_example: Voy por una taza de té, ¿quieres una?
native_language_example: I'm going to get a cup of tea, do you want one?

meaning: for once; at least this one time
additional_notes: Used to express that something happens (or should happen) at least this one time, often with impatience, surprise, or criticism. Common in commands or comments to urge someone to do something differently than usual.
target_language_example: Por una vez, haz caso a mi consejo.
native_language_example: For once, listen to my advice.

meaning: 'to be yet to be seen' / 'to be eager to see' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) impersonal expression meaning 'it remains to be seen' or 'that's yet to be seen' (e.g., Eso está por ver; Queda por ver quién gana). 2) with a person, 'morir/estar por ver' or 'tener curiosidad por ver' expresses desire or eagerness to see something (e.g., me muero por ver, tenía curiosidad por ver). Context determines whether it's about uncertainty (future outcome) or wanting to see something now/soon.
target_language_example: Queda por ver si el proyecto funcionará.
native_language_example: It remains to be seen whether the project will work.

meaning: per time; at a time (used in expressions like 'a veces' or 'una por vez').
additional_notes: Alone 'por vez' is seldom used by itself; it appears in phrases such as 'una por vez' (one at a time), 'cada vez' (each time), or 'por vez primera' (for the first time). It indicates repetition or counting of occurrences — how many or how often something happens or is done at once.
