additional_notes: Used in comparisons with 'más' (más rápido de lo que...) to say something happens or is done more quickly than another action, person, or expectation. Often followed by 'que' or 'que + clause' (de lo que + verb/clause). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: La noticia llegó más rápido de lo que imaginábamos.
native_language_example: The news arrived faster than we imagined.

meaning: as fast as I/he/she/you can / as quickly as possible
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase 'lo más rápido que (pueda)' meaning 'as fast as possible' or 'as quickly as one can'. Use 'pueda' (subjunctive) after 'lo más rápido que' to express ability/effort. Can be adapted for different subjects (puedas, podamos, puedan). Common in polite requests and instructions.
target_language_example: Sal de la casa lo más rápido que puedas.
native_language_example: Get out of the house as fast as you can.

meaning: as fast as you can / as quickly as you can.
additional_notes: Usually appears after 'lo más' as in 'lo más rápido que puedas' to tell someone to do something with maximum speed/urgency. Use with verbs (e.g., corre, ven, haz). It's a common fixed phrase for urging; you can also say 'tan rápido como puedas' with similar meaning.
target_language_example: Corre lo más rápido que puedas.
native_language_example: Run as fast as you can.

meaning: laughs at (someone or something).
additional_notes: Common verb phrase: form of 'reírse de' (to laugh at). Use with reflexive pronoun and preposition 'de' before the person or thing being laughed at. Can mean laughing with someone (friendly) or laughing at them (mocking) depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: La gente siempre se ríe de mis chistes.
native_language_example: People always laugh at my jokes.

meaning: they laugh at (someone or something).
additional_notes: Ríen de is the present tense, third-person plural form of 'reírse de' (to laugh at). It requires a preposition 'de' before the person or thing being laughed at: se ríen de mí / de ti / de él. It can express teasing, mockery, or joking. For other subjects or tenses, conjugate 'reírse' accordingly (me río, te ríes, nos reímos, se rieron, etc.).
target_language_example: Siempre se ríen de mi acento cuando hablo inglés.
native_language_example: They always laugh at my accent when I speak English.

meaning: downstream; down the river.
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or location in the direction the river flows. Equivalent to English 'downstream' or 'down the river.' Often follows the noun (e.g., 'río abajo') and can be used alone as an adverbial phrase.
target_language_example: Fuimos en canoa río abajo hasta la playa.
native_language_example: We went downstream by canoe to the beach.

meaning: upstream; toward the source of a river.
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction along a river toward its source (opposite of río abajo). Often placed after the noun (e.g., 'río arriba') or after a preposition ('río arriba del puente'). Can be used literally (boats, fish) and figuratively to mean 'upstream' in a route or sequence.
target_language_example: Vimos una isla río arriba.
native_language_example: We saw an island upstream.

meaning: the word 'río' (river) followed by 'y' (and) — used to connect actions, locations or clauses mentioning the river.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom: it's simply the noun río ('river') plus the conjunction y ('and'). You'll see it when the river is part of a list, a sequence of actions, or a location phrase. Pronounce the two words naturally: 'río' has stress on the first syllable (RÍ-o).
target_language_example: Cruzamos el río y seguimos por el sendero.
native_language_example: We crossed the river and continued along the path.

meaning: 'God knows' — used to say something is unknown or uncertain (like 'who knows' or 'heaven knows').
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression often used to express uncertainty, resignation, or that only God knows the answer. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Can appear on its own (e.g., “¡Sabe Dios!”) or as part of a sentence (e.g., “Sabe Dios por qué...” = “God knows why...”).
target_language_example: Sabe Dios cuándo volverán a abrir el restaurante.
native_language_example: God knows when they will reopen the restaurant.

meaning: depends on context: "knows better" (knowledge) or "tastes better" (sensory).
additional_notes: This phrase uses the verb saber. In contexts about knowledge or understanding, "sabe mejor" means "knows better" (e.g., comparing who has greater knowledge). In sensory contexts (food, drink, smoke), it means "tastes better." Pay attention to subject, formality, and context to choose the correct English sense. The phrase can appear in proverbs and comparisons.
target_language_example: Un cigarrillo siempre sabe mejor después de cenar.
native_language_example: A cigarette always tastes better after dinner.

meaning: 'tastes/knows very' — combination of the verb saber with 'muy' to intensify meaning (depends on context).
additional_notes: Saber is a polysemous verb: it can mean 'to know' (facts, information) or 'to taste' (how food tastes). 'Muy' is an adverb meaning 'very' and modifies saber. Use context to decide the sense: e.g. 'sabe muy poco' = 'very little is known' (knowledge), while 'sabe muy bueno' = 'tastes very good' (taste). Word order: 'sabe muy' is followed by an adjective/adverb ('muy bueno') or an adverb/quantity ('muy poco').
target_language_example: Este pescado sabe muy raro.
native_language_example: This fish tastes very strange.

meaning: 'knows if' or 'one/you/he/she knows whether'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb saber (to know) with the conjunction si (if/whether). Used to introduce a yes/no content clause: 'knows if/whether (something is true)'. Subject can change (sé, sabes, sabe, sabemos, saben) depending on who knows. In English both 'if' and 'whether' can be used; choose 'whether' in formal contexts.
target_language_example: No sabe si vendrán mañana.
native_language_example: He doesn't know if/whether they'll come tomorrow.

meaning: know why
additional_notes: Combines the verb saber (ellos/ustedes form 'saben') + 'por qué'. Used to say 'they/you all know why' or 'everyone knows why'. The subject is usually plural (ellos/ustedes/todos). 'Por' must be followed by 'qué' to form 'why' (por qué).
target_language_example: Todos saben por qué viniste tarde.
native_language_example: Everyone knows why you came late.

meaning: to know how
additional_notes: Used to talk about knowing the way something is done, happens, works, or is. It often introduces an indirect question with cómo, as in saber cómo funciona ('to know how it works') or saber cómo estás ('to know how you are'). It can be followed by an infinitive or a full clause.
target_language_example: Quiero saber cómo funciona este juego.
native_language_example: I want to know how this game works.

meaning: to know about; to have knowledge or information about someone or something (can also mean 'to hear from' when referring to people)
additional_notes: Primary meaning: 'to know about' (information/awareness). With people, it often means 'to hear from' or 'have news about' (e.g., 'no sé de él' = 'I haven't heard from him'). Meaning depends on context and following words (e.g., 'saber de dónde' = 'to know from where'). Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Olvida lo que crees saber de la vida, la amistad, y en especial de ti y de mí.
native_language_example: Forget what you think you know about life, friendship, and especially about you and me.

meaning: to know that (piece of information).
additional_notes: Used when referring to a specific fact or piece of information (eso = that). Common in constructions like 'tienes que saber eso' (you need to know that) or 'me tranquiliza saber eso' (knowing that reassures me). 'Saber' here means 'to have knowledge of' (not 'to know how to' + infinitive).
target_language_example: Es importante saber eso antes del examen.
native_language_example: It's important to know that before the exam.

meaning: to know how to do something; practical skill or know-how.
additional_notes: Used both as a verb phrase (saber + infinitive) meaning "to know how to [do]" and as a noun phrase (el saber hacer) meaning "expertise" or "know-how." Common for describing practical ability, professional skills, or craftsmanship. When used as a noun, it often appears with the article: el saber hacer.
target_language_example: El saber hacer de ese chef se nota en cada plato.
native_language_example: That chef's know-how shows in every dish.

meaning: 'you know what (I mean)' or 'you know what I'm referring to'.
additional_notes: Followed by "me refiero" in the examples, but the full phrase is usually "(tú) sabes a lo que me refiero" or simply "sabes a lo que" as a shortened colloquial way to check understanding. Used in informal spoken Spanish to confirm the listener understands or to hint at something without stating it explicitly. Pronoun tú is often omitted; intonation conveys the question or confirmation.
target_language_example: Si vamos temprano, podemos evitar la fila, sabes a lo que me refiero.
native_language_example: If we go early, we can avoid the line, you know what I mean.

meaning: 'you know what (I mean) / you know what I'm referring to'.
additional_notes: Used to check that the listener understands or to hint at something without saying it explicitly. Often followed by 'me refiero' (I mean). Common in spoken Spanish; tone can be casual or neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Sabes a qué me refiero cuando hablo de esa persona, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: You know what I mean when I talk about that person, right?

meaning: do you know anything / you know something (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal components: sabes = (you) know, algo = something/anything. Used both in questions/conditional sentences meaning 'if you know anything' (Si sabes algo...) and in statements meaning 'you know something' or 'I know you know something' (Sé que sabes algo). Tone is neutral; use 'sabes algo' when asking if someone has any information or asserting they know something.
target_language_example: Si sabes algo sobre la reunión, dímelo.
native_language_example: If you know anything about the meeting, tell me.

meaning: you know that / you know it
additional_notes: Combines the verb saber (to know) in the second-person singular (tú sabes) with the demonstrative eso (that/it). Used to say someone knows a fact or piece of information. Context and tone determine whether it's a question, statement, or mild reproach (e.g., Tú no sabes eso = You don't know that). For polite/formal address use 'usted sabe eso'.
target_language_example: ¿Cómo sabes eso tan rápido?
native_language_example: How do you know that so quickly?

meaning: you know how to do (something) / what you can do
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about someone's skills or abilities. Often appears in commands or encouragements (haz lo que sabes hacer = do what you know how to do). Can be followed by an object or left implied (lo, eso). In questions it asks if someone knows how to do something: ¿sabes hacer X?
target_language_example: Haz lo que sabes hacer y confía en ti.
native_language_example: Do what you know how to do and trust yourself.

meaning: 'you know what that/it (thing)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned; often spoken to remind or emphasize that the listener understands the implication. Common in conversational Spanish. Can be shortened to "ya sabes" or expanded with "lo que eso quiere decir/significa".
target_language_example: Hicimos lo que pudimos, sabes lo que eso implica.
native_language_example: We did what we could, you know what that implies.

meaning: 'you know what you have to (do)'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to tell or remind someone that they already know the necessary action. Often followed by an infinitive verb (hacer, decir, etc.) or left trailing when the action is understood from context. Informal and neutral—used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ya sabes lo que tienes que hacer, así que empieza ahora.
native_language_example: You know what you have to do, so start now.

meaning: you know nothing
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they lack knowledge about something or in general. Often appears in negative constructions with no/ni (e.g., "no sabes nada") — standalone "sabes nada" can occur in rhetorical or philosophical contexts (e.g., "mientras más sabes... no sabes nada"). Tone can be blunt or insulting depending on context.
target_language_example: No sabes nada sobre este tema.
native_language_example: You don't know anything about this topic.

meaning: do you know if
additional_notes: From the verb saber (to know) + si (if/whether). Used to ask or state whether someone has knowledge about a possibility or fact. In questions it becomes "¿sabes si... ?" = "do you know if... ?" In statements it can mean "you (don't) know whether...". Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes si la tienda abre los domingos?
native_language_example: Do you know if the store is open on Sundays?

meaning: 'you know so' / 'you know (something) so (well)'.
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb (e.g., tan bien = 'so well') to compare knowledge or ability. Often appears in comparisons with 'como' (e.g., 'tan... como' = 'as... as') or to emphasize degree. In some examples 'tanto' (so much) contrasts with 'tan' (so/so well). The verb 'sabes' is the tú form of 'saber' (to know).
target_language_example: Sabes tan bien como ella cómo tocar esa canción.
native_language_example: You know so well how to play that song, just like her.

meaning: had known (his/her/its)... — part of a conditional phrase (hubiera/hubiese sabido su...).
additional_notes: Used in past unreal conditional sentences to express that, if someone had known something (su = his/her/its), then a different outcome would have happened. Often appears with si (if) and a conditional/result clause (habría + past participle). 'Su' must match the possessed noun (su nombre, su dirección, su número). English equivalent: 'had known his/her/its...'.
target_language_example: Si hubiera sabido su horario, habría ido a la reunión.
native_language_example: If I had known his/her schedule, I would have gone to the meeting.

meaning: 'didn't know anything' (past tense).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past tense of saber (sabía) plus nada to mean 'knew nothing' or 'didn't know anything'. Common in reported speech or descriptions of ongoing/past states. In neutral Spanish you'd often hear 'no sabía nada' (with the negative particle no before the verb). Word order in examples shows omission of 'no' only when context already negates; learners should use 'no sabía nada' to express 'I/he/she didn't know anything.'
target_language_example: Cuando llegaron, yo no sabía nada de la sorpresa.
native_language_example: When they arrived, I didn't know anything about the surprise.

meaning: 'take/remove someone (or something) out' or 'bring someone out' (imperative/command form of 'sacar a')
additional_notes: From the verb sacar + direct object introduced by the preposition a when the object is a person or pet. In commands it means 'get someone out' or 'remove someone from a place.' It can also be used in idioms like "Un clavo saca a otro clavo" (one nail removes another), meaning one thing replaces or helps forget another. Use 'saca' for tú (informal) imperative; formal usted would be 'saque a'.
target_language_example: Saca a los niños del cuarto, por favor.
native_language_example: Take the children out of the room, please.

meaning: to take something out; to remove or take out an object. Also used idiomatically for actions like taking a photo, obtaining/getting something (e.g., sacar entradas, sacar dinero), or achieving results (sacar buenas notas).
additional_notes: Very common verb phrase. Literal meaning is 'to take something out' — the direct object (algo) is what is taken or obtained. Translation depends on context: sacar una foto = to take a photo; sacar la basura = to take out the trash; sacar dinero = to withdraw money; sacar provecho = to take advantage; sacar buenas notas = to get good grades. Can be used with specific objects in place of 'algo'.
target_language_example: Tengo que sacar algo del coche antes de salir.
native_language_example: I have to take something out of the car before leaving.

meaning: to take out of / to remove from / to get out of (a place, situation, or context).
additional_notes: Common construction: sacar + direct object + de + source. Can indicate physically removing someone/something (sacar a alguien de la habitación), extracting something from a place or context (sacar algo de un bolso), or figuratively getting someone out of a situation (sacar a alguien de problemas). Nuance depends on context and object.
target_language_example: Si nos vas a sacar de aquí, hazlo ya.
native_language_example: If you're going to get us out of here, do it now.

meaning: to annoy or drive someone crazy; to unnerve or make someone lose their composure.
additional_notes: Used when something or someone greatly irritates, frustrates, or unsettles a person. Often used in the form 'me saca de quicio' (it drives me crazy). Not literal—'quicio' originally refers to a door jamb, but the expression is idiomatic.
target_language_example: El ruido constante del vecino me hace sacar de quicio.
native_language_example: The neighbor's constant noise drives me crazy.

meaning: to take advantage of; to make the most of (a situation or resource).
additional_notes: Used when someone benefits from a situation, person, or resource. Can be neutral (make good use of) or negative (exploit). Often followed by 'de' + noun: sacar provecho de algo/alguien.
target_language_example: Ella supo sacar provecho de la oportunidad.
native_language_example: She knew how to take advantage of the opportunity.

meaning: took off the
additional_notes: Literal past tense of sacar + the plural definite article los. Can mean 'took off the' (clothing/items worn, e.g. zapatos, calcetines, anteojos) or 'took out the' / 'removed the' (objects from a container, e.g. huevos). Context (whether the action is removing worn items or removing objects) determines the best English translation. Use with reflexive se (se sacó los ...) to indicate removing something from one's own body (he/she took off their ...).
target_language_example: Se sacó los guantes antes de entrar.
native_language_example: He took off his gloves before going in.

meaning: salt and pepper.
additional_notes: A common phrase used when asking someone to pass or bring the salt and pepper. Often appears with verbs like pasar (to pass/give) or pedir (to ask for). In Spanish the article 'la' before 'pimienta' is normal: 'la sal y la pimienta.'
target_language_example: ¿Me pasas la sal y la pimienta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the salt and pepper, please?

meaning: waiting room (a place where people wait, e.g., in a doctor's office, train station, airport).
additional_notes: Commonly used for any indoor area designated for waiting. Can be found in hospitals, clinics, stations, airports, offices. Use with verbs like 'esperar' (to wait) or 'entrar'/'salir' (to enter/leave).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos en la sala de espera hasta que nos llamaron.
native_language_example: We sat in the waiting room until they called us.

meaning: living room (a room for relaxing and socializing).
additional_notes: Commonly used in Spain and many Spanish-speaking countries to refer to the main sitting room in a house or apartment. Can be shortened to 'sala' or 'salón' in some regions. Used in neutral, everyday speech.
target_language_example: Pasamos la tarde en la sala de estar viendo la televisión.
native_language_example: We spent the afternoon in the living room watching TV.

meaning: 'will be released/published/come out' (future of 'salir' + definite article 'el') or literally 'will come out the' when followed by a time or noun.
additional_notes: saldrá is the future tense of salir (to leave/come out/appear). When used with a time expression (e.g., 'el próximo mes') it means 'will be released/come out' or 'will happen' (e.g., a book, article, event). With natural phenomena (e.g., 'el sol') it means 'will rise/come out.' The article 'el' begins the noun or time phrase that follows. Translate depending on context: 'will come out,' 'will be published,' 'will rise,' or 'will go out.'
target_language_example: La película saldrá el viernes próximo.
native_language_example: The movie will be released next Friday.

meaning: it leaves in (one)... (used for departures, e.g., 'leaves in one hour')
additional_notes: Common phrase to say when a vehicle (avión, tren, autobús) departs after a certain time. Usually completed with a time period: 'sale en una hora' (leaves in one hour). Can also use other numbers: 'sale en veinte minutos'. Subject often omitted: 'Sale en una hora' = 'It leaves in one hour.'
target_language_example: Nuestro tren sale en una hora; tenemos que comprar los billetes.
native_language_example: Our train leaves in one hour; we need to buy the tickets.

meaning: 'comes out through' / 'emerges from' (literal) or 'goes out through' / 'leaves by'.
additional_notes: Used with intransitive verbs like salir to indicate the place, direction, or opening through which something or someone comes out or exits. Can be literal (El sol sale por el este; el aire sale por el techo) or figurative (sale por doquier = it appears/goes out everywhere). Commonly followed by a noun or prepositional phrase (por + place/direction).
target_language_example: La luz sale por la ventana.
native_language_example: The light comes out through the window.

meaning: to resemble
additional_notes:
This multiword phrase has two common uses depending on context:
- "salido a" + person: means "to resemble" or "take after" (e.g., "ha salido a su madre" = "she takes after her mother"). It describes similarity in appearance or behavior inherited from family.
- "salido a" + verb infinitive (or "salir a"): means "to go out to" do something (e.g., "salió a comprar" = "he went out to buy"). In compound tenses you may see "ha salido a" or "había salido a". 
Note: "salido" is the past participle of "salir"; when used for resemblance it's often part of "haber salido a" (ha salido a).
target_language_example: Esta niña ha salido a su abuela; le encanta cocinar.
native_language_example: This girl takes after her grandmother; she loves to cook.

meaning: 'to have dated' or 'to have gone out with' (past participle form of salir + con = 'been out with' someone).
additional_notes: Used to say someone dated or went out with another person. Commonly appears in perfect or pluperfect forms (ha salido con, había salido con). Can also appear in reflexive or idiomatic uses (se salió de sus casillas = 'lost his/her temper' — here salir is part of a different expression and NOT related to dating).
target_language_example: Ella ya había salido con varios chicos antes.
native_language_example: She had already dated several guys before.

meaning: coming out of the / having come out of the (feminine singular noun)
additional_notes: Formed from the past participle 'salido' + preposition 'de' + definite article 'la'. Used to indicate origin or movement out of a feminine singular place or thing (e.g., 'salido de la casa'). Agreement of the participle may change (salido → salida) depending on the gender/role of the noun it refers to. Common in participial phrases and descriptions (e.g., 'un hombre salido de la batalla'). Can be literal (physically leaving) or figurative (originating from).
target_language_example: El agua salió del tubo, saliendo y quedando salido de la boca del pozo.
native_language_example: The water came out of the pipe, coming out and ending up coming out of the mouth of the well.

meaning: to come to light; to be revealed or become public
additional_notes: Used when information, facts, news, or secrets become known or are disclosed. Often used for scandals, discoveries, or newly published details. Can refer to something literally appearing in light but is usually figurative.
target_language_example: Después de la investigación, la verdad salió a la luz.
native_language_example: After the investigation, the truth came to light.

meaning: to get by, to move forward in life, to overcome difficulties and succeed
additional_notes: Common idiom used when talking about overcoming problems, improving one's situation, or managing to cope. Often used encouragingly (Vas a salir adelante = You'll get through this). Can refer to short-term coping or long-term progress.
target_language_example: Después de perder el trabajo, confío en que voy a salir adelante.
native_language_example: After losing my job, I trust that I will get through this / move forward.

meaning: to go out with
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about romantic relationships. In context it means 'to date' or 'to be in a relationship with' someone (e.g., 'salir con alguien' = 'to date someone' or 'to go out with someone'). Can also literally mean 'to go out with' in a non-romantic sense if context makes that clear, but romantic meaning is much more frequent. Requires an object (person): salir con alguien/él/Tom. Verb 'salir' is conjugated as normal.
target_language_example: Ella empezó a salir con Marcos el año pasado.
native_language_example: She started dating Marcos last year.

meaning: 'to be about to leave when the (phone/doorbell/etc.) rang' — describes an action that was about to happen but was interrupted by a sound/event.
additional_notes: This pattern combines a verb of intention (estar a punto de / estar por / ir a) + salir (to leave) + cuando sonó el + [noun]. Commonly used with 'teléfono', 'timbrе', 'portero', etc., to say you were just about to go out when something rang or happened. Tense in the first clause is often imperfect or past (estaba, iba); the interrupting action uses the simple past (sonó).
target_language_example: Estábamos a punto de salir cuando sonó el timbre.
native_language_example: We were about to leave when the doorbell rang.

meaning: to leave
additional_notes: Used for leaving a place, vehicle, institution, or situation. It can be literal (salir de la casa) or more figurative (salir de un problema, salir de rehabilitación).
target_language_example: Tenemos que salir de aquí ahora mismo.
native_language_example: We have to get out of here right now.

meaning: to get out of control; to become unmanageable
additional_notes: Used when a situation, person, or emotion becomes uncontrolled or chaotic. Commonly used for events (una reunión), emotions (la situación), machinery or systems (la situación financiera) and sometimes behavior. Often appears with subject + 'se' (e.g., 'se salió de control') or in infinitive after verbs (e.g., 'empezó a salir de control').
target_language_example: La fiesta empezó a salir de control cuando llegó mucha gente.
native_language_example: The party started to get out of control when too many people arrived.

meaning: to go wrong; to turn out badly
additional_notes: Used to say that a plan, situation, or action fails or has a bad outcome. Common in predictions, warnings, or summaries (e.g., "Todo lo que podía salir mal, salió mal"). Can be used impersonally (Eso salió mal) or with an indirect object (le salió mal a este equipo = it went wrong for this team).
target_language_example: Si no revisas todo, puede salir mal.
native_language_example: If you don't check everything, it could go wrong.

meaning: to go out through / to leave by (a place, route, or time); also used to indicate the exit point or general time/frequency (e.g., salir por las mañanas).
additional_notes: Literal components: salir = to leave/go out; por = through/by/at. Used with locations or routes (salir por la puerta/la bahía), with time expressions to indicate habitual time (salir por las mañanas), or to indicate cause/obstacle in some contexts (e.g., no pudimos salir por la lluvia = we couldn't go out because of the rain). Context determines whether por marks location, route, time, or reason. Common patterns: salir por + lugar, salir por + expresión de tiempo, salir por + causa/obstáculo.
target_language_example: No creo que esté en casa a esa hora, suele salir por las mañanas.
native_language_example: I don't think he'll be home at that time; he usually goes out in the mornings.

meaning: to go out and (then do something); to leave and (do something).
additional_notes: Used to link 'salir' (to go out/leave) with another action. In many sentences it means 'go out and [verb]' (e.g., salir y comprar = go out and buy). It can also appear as 'salir y + past participle' or 'salir y + verb in past' in narration (e.g., 'salir y seguir' = left and I followed). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Voy a salir y comprar pan antes de que cierre la tienda.
native_language_example: I'm going to go out and buy bread before the store closes.

meaning: 'turned out very' / 'came out very' (used to comment on how something turned out, followed by an adjective)
additional_notes: This is the third-person past form of salir (salió) plus the adverb muy. It's commonly used to describe the result or outcome of something (e.g., una fiesta, una foto, una película). Structure: 'Salió muy + adjective'. Context determines whether it's about appearance, success, quality, etc.
target_language_example: La película salió muy buena.
native_language_example: The movie turned out very good.

meaning: he/she/it left through or via (a place); departed because of (context dependent).
additional_notes: salió por is the past (pretérito) of salir + por. Common uses: 'salió por la puerta/ventana' = 'left through the door/window' (movement through an exit). Also used with destinations or routes: 'salió por Talcahuano' = 'set off toward/via Talcahuano'. In some contexts it can indicate reason ('salió por un caso' = left to work on a case) or cause—use context to choose translation.
target_language_example: Ella salió por la puerta principal cuando terminó la reunión.
native_language_example: She left through the main door when the meeting ended.

meaning: to jump out of bed; to get out of bed quickly or energetically.
additional_notes: Often used literally (physically jumping out of bed) or figuratively to mean getting up quickly, sometimes because of urgency or excitement. Common in everyday speech. Use context to choose tense/subject (e.g., 'salté de la cama' = I jumped out of bed).
target_language_example: Esta mañana me desperté tarde y tuve que saltar de la cama.
native_language_example: This morning I woke up late and had to jump out of bed.

meaning: (literally “jumped the/it”) colloquial pronominal use meaning to skip, miss, or (in some contexts) for something to pop up/appear (e.g., skip a meal, miss a step, or a message appearing).
additional_notes: Usually appears in pronominal constructions (se saltó + el/la + noun) when someone omits or skips something, intentionally or unintentionally. In some contexts (especially with electronics/notifications) it can mean that something appeared or came up (e.g., 'me saltó el buzón de voz' = the voicemail came up). Often used in past tense (saltó el / se saltó el).
target_language_example: Así que le llamé al celular y me saltó el buzón de voz.
native_language_example: So I called his cellphone and the voicemail came up for me.

meaning: 'health is' — used to state something about health (often as the subject 'health' followed by 'is ...').
additional_notes: Salud = 'health'. 'Es' is the 3rd-person singular present of 'ser' (to be). Together they form the beginning of sentences that define or describe health (e.g., 'La salud es importante'). Common in proverbs and statements. Use with adjectives, nouns, or clauses: 'La salud es importante', 'La salud es riqueza'.
target_language_example: La salud es la base de una vida feliz.
native_language_example: Health is the foundation of a happy life.

meaning: mental health (the state of a person's psychological and emotional well‑being).
additional_notes: Used to talk about psychological well‑being, mental illness, or professions/services related to mental health (e.g., 'enfermera de salud mental'). Common collocations: 'salud mental y física' (mental and physical health), 'servicios de salud mental' (mental health services).
target_language_example: La salud mental necesita atención y apoyo, igual que la salud física.
native_language_example: Mental health needs attention and support, just like physical health.

meaning: 'health and' — the beginning of a phrase linking health with another noun (e.g., salud y enfermedad = health and illness).
additional_notes: Used to connect 'salud' (health) with another word to form common expressions (salud y seguridad, salud y felicidad, salud y enfermedad). Often appears in set phrases and formal contexts (e.g., vows, workplace safety). Not a complete phrase by itself — expect a noun after 'y' (and).
target_language_example: Cuidamos la salud y seguridad de los empleados.
native_language_example: We take care of the health and safety of employees.

meaning: greeted/acknowledged someone with (a gesture or expression).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun that names the gesture or expression (una sonrisa, la mano, una inclinación, etc.). Use to describe how someone greeted you (how the greeting was made). The verb saludar is past tense here (saludó = he/she greeted).
target_language_example: Me saludó con una sonrisa cuando entré.
native_language_example: He/She greeted me with a smile when I came in.

meaning: to save the (masculine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: Salvar means 'to save' or 'to rescue'. When followed by the definite article el it introduces a masculine singular direct object (e.g., salvar el perro, salvar el día). Conjugate salvar as needed (salvo, salva, salvaron, etc.). If the noun begins with a stressed 'a' or 'ha' sound, Spanish often uses 'al' (contraction of 'a + el') for the preposition 'a' + 'el', but 'salvar el' is simply verb + article and does not contract.
target_language_example: Tenemos que salvar el barco antes de que se hunda.
native_language_example: We have to save the ship before it sinks.

meaning: 'to save the' (feminine noun follows)
additional_notes: Salvar = to save, rescue, or preserve. When followed by the feminine definite article la, it means 'to save the...' and the next word will be a feminine noun (la ciudad, la naturaleza, la Tierra). Commonly used for saving people, places, nature, or abstract things. Use salvar a + person when saving a person (salvar a alguien).
target_language_example: Tenemos que salvar la ciudad antes de que sea demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: We have to save the city before it's too late.

meaning: 'sangre' = blood; 'es' = is — together they form the simple statement 'blood is...' or 'the blood is...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the noun sangre (blood) followed by the verb es (third-person singular of ser). Use it to make general statements about blood (e.g., 'La sangre es roja' = 'Blood is red') or to describe a specific blood (e.g., 'Esta sangre es real' = 'This blood is real'). Remember to include the article (la, esta, mi, su) when referring to blood in Spanish, unless you're making a general statement without an article (e.g., 'La sangre es importante' or 'Sangre es...')
target_language_example: La sangre es vital para el cuerpo.
native_language_example: Blood is vital for the body.

meaning: calmness or lack of emotion under pressure; literally 'cold blood'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who stays calm, composed, and unflustered in stressful or dangerous situations. Can be literal (an animal that is cold-blooded) but most often used figuratively in Spanish to mean 'composure' or 'coolness'. Common phrases: 'tener sangre fría' (to have cool nerve).
target_language_example: Ante la emergencia, mantuvo la sangre fría y llamó a los servicios.
native_language_example: During the emergency, he kept a cool head and called the services.

meaning: 'healthy and' — the adjective 'sano' ('healthy') followed by the conjunction 'y' ('and'), used to link 'sano' with another adjective or noun in a larger phrase.
additional_notes: sano means 'healthy', 'well', or 'wholesome'. 'Sano y' is not a fixed idiom on its own; it appears as part of longer expressions (e.g., 'sano y salvo' = 'safe and sound', 'sano y fuerte'). The phrase will usually be completed by another adjective or noun phrase. Register: neutral; common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Volvió sano y salvo de su viaje.
native_language_example: He returned safe and sound from his trip.

meaning: 'safe and sound' — alive, unharmed, and well.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something arrived or returned without injury or damage. Common after travel, accidents, or searches. Literal words mean 'healthy and unharmed.' Often follows verbs like llegar, regresar, volver, venir, and estar.
target_language_example: Después del viaje, todos llegaron sano y salvo.
native_language_example: After the trip, everyone arrived safe and sound.

meaning: Oh my God; good heavens (an exclamation of surprise, shock, or strong feeling).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection to express surprise, disbelief, annoyance, fear, or strong emotion. Can appear with or without vocative (e.g., addressing someone after it). Tone and context determine intensity—from mild surprise to strong alarm. Religious speakers may use it more solemnly; consider alternatives like "Dios mío" which is more common.
target_language_example: ¡Santo Dios, olvidé las llaves en el coche!
native_language_example: Oh my God, I forgot the keys in the car!

meaning: 'loves oneself' or 'is loved' (reflexive use of amar: to love oneself / to be loved, depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the verb amar in the third-person singular reflexive form (él/ella/usted se ama) or an impersonal/reflexive construction meaning 'one loves oneself' / 'people love themselves.' Spanish reflexive pronoun 'se' indicates the action is directed back at the subject. Context determines whether it's literal (self-love) or general/impersonal (people love). To say 'loves him/her' you'd use 'lo ama' / 'la ama' (not 'se').
target_language_example: En la calma de la mañana, ella se ama tal como es.
native_language_example: In the calm of the morning, she loves herself as she is.

meaning: he/she/it changed (clothes, position, or was changed) or he/she/it swapped/was swapped (reflexive/passive nuance).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb cambiarse. Can mean someone changed their clothes (se cambió la camisa), changed position or seat (se cambió de lugar), or that something was changed/altered with passive meaning depending on context. Subject is third person singular. Context determines whether it's reflexive (did it themselves) or a passive/accidental sense (was changed). Common with clothing and locations.
target_language_example: Se cambió la camiseta antes de salir.
native_language_example: He changed his t-shirt before leaving.

meaning: he/she/they changed the (masculine singular) — reflexive past action: 'changed the... (something masculine)'.
additional_notes: This is the reflexive past (pretérito) form of 'cambiar(se)'. 'Se cambió el...' indicates the subject changed something belonging to themselves; often used with 'nombre' (name) as in the examples. Spanish often omits the noun when context makes it clear (e.g., 'se cambió el' = 'changed his/her/the name'). The gender/number of the noun governs the article: 'se cambió el nombre' (masculine), 'se cambió la ropa' (feminine). For third person singular use 'se cambió', for plural 'se cambiaron'.
target_language_example: Ella se cambió el apellido el mes pasado.
native_language_example: She changed her last name last month.

meaning: fell into / fell on (something).
additional_notes: Reflexive/passive-se form of caer used to say someone or something fell. With 'en' it often indicates where the fall happened (into, on, onto, in). English preposition varies by context: 'fell into' for containers/holes, 'fell on' or 'fell onto' for surfaces, and 'fell in' for spaces like 'in the train' (meaning fell while inside). The subject (él/ella, Tom, algo) can be explicit or omitted. Use past tense (se cayó) for completed falls.
target_language_example: María se cayó en el jardín y se lastimó la rodilla.
native_language_example: María fell in the garden and hurt her knee.

meaning: it closes / is closed (reflexive/passive-like form of 'cerrar').
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that something (a door, store, opportunity, etc.) closes. Spanish uses the reflexive 'se' to form an impersonal or passive construction: 'La puerta se cierra' = 'The door closes' or 'The door is closed.' Context determines if it's a scheduled/automatic action ('se cierra a las nueve') or a general statement. Use with third-person singular/plural depending on the noun (e.g., 'las puertas se cierran').
target_language_example: El museo se cierra a las cinco de la tarde.
native_language_example: The museum closes at five in the afternoon.

meaning: is eaten
additional_notes: This phrase uses the pronoun 'se' to form either a passive/impersonal construction or a reflexive/reciprocal sense depending on context. 1) As a passive/impersonal: 'se come' = 'is eaten' or 'one eats' (general statements about food or what is eaten). Example: 'El cuscús se come con la carne' = 'Couscous is eaten with meat.' 2) As a reflexive/transitive action (less common with food verbs): 'se come una mariposa' = 'the hen eats a butterfly' (here 'se' is part of the verb for third-person reflexive/indirect object). Use context to decide meaning.
target_language_example: En este restaurante se come muy bien.
native_language_example: At this restaurant one eats very well. / The food is very good here.

meaning: they bought (for themselves); they purchased.
additional_notes: Reflexive use of comprar (comprarse) emphasizes that the buyers acquired something for themselves or benefited personally. Common in Spanish to say 'se compraron X' instead of 'compraron X'. Context determines if 'for themselves' is important; often it's just a normal past tense statement about buying. 'Se compraron' is preterite (ellos/ustedes form).
target_language_example: Ellos se compraron un sofá nuevo la semana pasada.
native_language_example: They bought themselves a new sofa last week.

meaning: 'is known' or 'is/are known as' (impersonal or passive construction)
additional_notes: Common impersonal/passive use of the verb conocer. Used to say that something is known, unknown, or called/named in general terms (often followed by a noun, clause, or phrase like 'como' or 'que'). Equivalent to passive voice in English: 'is known' / 'is called'.
target_language_example: Esto se conoce como un mito.
native_language_example: This is known as a myth.

meaning: happens
additional_notes: This reflexive construction has different meanings depending on context. With intransitive verbs like 'dar(se) con facilidad' it often means 'happens' or 'comes about' (something 'se da' = it occurs/takes place). With verbs like 'darse cuenta' it forms a fixed expression meaning 'to realize' or 'to become aware'. The exact translation depends on the verb it accompanies.
target_language_example: Eso se da cuando todos colaboran.
native_language_example: That happens when everyone collaborates.

meaning: they/one must; things should be (passive/impersonal use).
additional_notes: Commonly used in impersonal or passive constructions. With plural nouns or infinitives, 'se deben' expresses obligation or that something ought to be done (equivalent to 'one should', 'they should', or 'must be'). Context determines subject: can be impersonal (general advice), passive (something is owed/earned), or reflexive-like ('se deben ganar' = 'must earn'). Often followed by infinitive or plural noun phrase.
target_language_example: Se deben respetar las reglas del laboratorio.
native_language_example: The lab rules must be respected.

meaning: would/should notice; (subjunctive of darse cuenta) — 'notice' or 'realize' in contexts requiring the imperfect subjunctive.
additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb darse cuenta (to realize/notice) in the imperfect subjunctive (diera). Used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., clauses of doubt, emotion, hypothetical or negative statements, or after 'sin que'). Can also appear in requests when combined with a reflexive action (e.g., 'que se diera la vuelta' = 'that he/she turn around'). Context decides translation: often 'noticed,' 'realized,' 'would notice,' or 'should notice.'
target_language_example: Salió sin que nadie se diera cuenta.
native_language_example: He left without anyone noticing.

meaning: 'dissolves' or 'is dissolved' (something breaks apart, melts, or mixes into a liquid; can be literal or metaphorical).
additional_notes: Reflexive passive/impersonal use of disolver: describes a subject that becomes dissolved or loses its separate form. Common with substances in liquids (e.g., azúcar se disuelve en agua) and metaphorically (e.g., una identidad se disuelve en un papel). Use with preposition 'en' to indicate the medium (en agua, en café).
target_language_example: La pintura se disuelve en la lluvia.
native_language_example: The paint dissolves in the rain.

meaning: 'one/you/it hears' or 'is heard' / 'sounds' (impersonal/passive use)
additional_notes: Common impersonal/passive construction using the reflexive 'se' + escuchar. Used to say that something is heard or 'sounds' a certain way (e.g., 'se escucha divertido' = 'it sounds fun'). Can mean 'you hear' or 'one hears' in general statements. Context determines whether it's passive ('is heard') or impersonal ('people hear').
target_language_example: Desde la calle se escucha música por la noche.
native_language_example: From the street you can hear music at night.

meaning: Spanish is spoken (there is Spanish spoken here/there).
additional_notes: Impersonal passive construction using 'se' + verb to say that Spanish is spoken in a place or by people in general. Common on signs (e.g., 'Se habla español' to indicate staff speak Spanish) and in statements about languages spoken in countries/regions. Literally: 'Spanish is spoken.'
target_language_example: En la oficina se habla español y también inglés.
native_language_example: Spanish is spoken in the office and also English.

meaning: English is spoken (there); English is spoken here/there.
additional_notes: Impersonal/passive construction using 'se' to say a language is spoken in a place. Commonly used on signs or to indicate that people in a country/place speak English. Word order can vary: 'En X se habla inglés' or 'Se habla inglés en X.' Not specifying who speaks it (general statement).
target_language_example: En esta oficina se habla inglés y español.
native_language_example: In this office English and Spanish are spoken.

meaning: they become
additional_notes: Form of hacerse (third-person plural present subjunctive). It often appears after expressions like espero que, ojalá, tal vez, or no es que. By itself, the basic idea is 'they become', but in the very common phrase se hagan realidad it means 'come true'. In other expressions, the translation can change depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Ojalá se hagan amigos pronto.
native_language_example: I hope they become friends soon.

meaning: 'became' or 'turned into' (often with time/weather) ; also 'got/obtained' in colloquial contexts
additional_notes: Has two common uses: 1) reflexive impersonal with time or state: 'se hizo de noche' = 'it became night / it got dark' (English passive/impersonal). 2) colloquial pronominal verb 'hacerse de' meaning 'to obtain/get (for oneself)' — e.g. 'se hizo de todos los bocadillos' = 'he/she got all the sandwiches'. Context tells which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Se hizo de noche antes de que llegáramos.
native_language_example: It got dark before we arrived.

meaning: sank all the way to the (bottom).
additional_notes: Used to describe something sinking completely to the bottom of a body of water (fondo). 'Se hundió' = 'it/one sank' (reflexive passives common in Spanish). 'Hasta el' is followed by 'fondo' (the bottom) or another noun indicating how far it sank. Common with boats, objects, or people failing to stay afloat.
target_language_example: La caja se hundió hasta el fondo del lago.
native_language_example: The box sank all the way to the bottom of the lake.

meaning: used to say someone is very good at or has a natural talent for something
additional_notes: This phrase uses the impersonal/indirect-object construction 'se le da (muy) bien' + verb (infinitive) or noun. 'A [persona] se le da muy bien [actividad]' emphasizes ability or knack—often implies natural talent or ease. You can omit 'muy' to soften (se le da bien). The person is marked by 'a + nombre' and the verb is infinitive: A ella se le da muy bien cantar.
target_language_example: A Marta se le da muy bien dibujar retratos.
native_language_example: Marta is very good at drawing portraits.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) gets up at (a time).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb 'levantarse' used to say someone wakes up or gets out of bed. The pronoun (se) matches third person; use 'me levanto', 'te levantas', 'nos levantamos' for other persons. 'a' introduces the time: 'a las siete', 'a las seis de la mañana'. Can be used without a subject when context is clear: 'Se levanta a las siete.'
target_language_example: Él se levanta a las seis todos los días.
native_language_example: He gets up at six every day.

meaning: was called
additional_notes: Passive/reflexive use of llamar. Can mean 'was called/named' (e.g., a thing or person was given a name). With a person as subject and a direct object reflexive (se llamó a sí mismo) it means 'called oneself' or 'named oneself'. Also used to indicate someone phoned/called (Se llamó al FBI = 'The FBI was called' or 'They called the FBI'). Context determines whether it's passive ('was called') or reflexive/reciprocal. Common in past (pretérito) as shown.
target_language_example: La ciudad se llamó Nueva Villa durante cien años.
native_language_example: The city was called Nueva Villa for a hundred years.

meaning: 'one/you/people arrive' or 'is reached' (impersonal/passive way to say how to get somewhere or that something is reached).
additional_notes: Used impersonally with 'se' to mean 'people/one/you arrive' or 'something is reached' (similar to English 'you get to' / 'one gets to' / 'is reached'). Common in directions: 'Por este camino se llega al museo' = 'This path leads to the museum.' Can also appear with verbs of state/change: 'se llega al poder' = 'one reaches/attains power.' Subject is generic or omitted; agent is not specified.
target_language_example: Desde la plaza se llega fácilmente al parque.
native_language_example: From the plaza you can easily get to the park.

meaning: was getting/used to get (something); or 'got along' (with someone) in imperfect tense.
additional_notes: Form of llevarse in the imperfect (él/ella/usted se llevaba). Can mean: 1) to take/receive (e.g., 'se llevaba una parte' — he was taking/receiving a share), or 2) to get along with someone (llevarse bien/mal). Context determines meaning. Commonly used reflexively (se).
target_language_example: Él se llevaba bien con todos en el vecindario.
native_language_example: He got along well with everyone in the neighborhood.

meaning: tell it to him/her/them (formal negative/command context shown: 'don't tell it to...').
additional_notes: Combination of pronouns and the verb decir in subjunctive/imperative: 'se' (indirect object pronoun replacing le/les when combined with lo), 'lo' (direct object pronoun = it), 'diga' (usted form of decir in subjunctive/imperative). Used when addressing someone formally (usted) or in reported speech: e.g. 'No se lo diga a nadie' = 'Don't tell it to anyone.' The person after 'a' names the person you shouldn't tell (a mi madre, a Pierre).
target_language_example: No se lo diga a su jefe hasta que tengamos más información.
native_language_example: Don't tell it to your boss until we have more information.

meaning: I came up with a good (idea). / A good idea occurred to me.
additional_notes: Used to say that a good idea just came to mind. Commonly completes with idea (idea) but can be followed by a noun or clause (e.g., 'se me ocurrió una buena solución'). 'Se me ocurrió' is a reflexive/impersonal construction meaning 'it occurred to me.'
target_language_example: Se me ocurrió una buena solución para el problema.
native_language_example: I came up with a good solution to the problem.

target_language_multi_word_term: se miraron el uno al otro
meaning: they looked at each other.
additional_notes: A reflexive reciprocal expression used to say two or more people looked at one another. You can change tense/person (se miran, nos miramos, se miró el uno al otro) and number (el uno al otro → entre sí or el uno al otro / la una a la otra to match gender if needed). Common alternative: "se miraron" or "se miraron entre sí."
target_language_example: Los dos se miraron el uno al otro y empezaron a reír.
native_language_example: The two looked at each other and began to laugh.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) looked at himself/herself/yourself (in a mirror) — past tense.
additional_notes: Reflexive past form of 'mirar(se)'. Used when someone looks at themselves (often in a mirror). Subject is third person singular (él/ella) or formal usted; context or name indicates who. In English this is usually translated as 'looked at himself/herself/yourself' depending on subject.
target_language_example: Ella se miró en el espejo antes de salir.
native_language_example: She looked at herself in the mirror before leaving.

meaning: was heard / one heard (something was heard).
additional_notes: Passive/impersonal use of oír (to hear). Common to report sounds/events heard without specifying who heard them. Can mean 'it was heard' or 'a ... was heard' (e.g., a noise, a shot). Often followed by the sound source.
target_language_example: Se oyó música desde la calle anoche.
native_language_example: Music was heard from the street last night.

meaning: he/she/it stuck, hit, or caught (something) — reflexive past form of pegar; exact meaning depends on context (stuck to, collided with, hit oneself, or caught [an illness/habit]).
additional_notes: Peñar is a verb with many senses: 'pegar' can mean to stick/adhere, to hit, to glue, to paste, or to catch (e.g., an illness). With the reflexive pronoun 'se' in the past (se pegó), it often indicates that the subject experienced the action (e.g., 'the sticker stuck' or 'he/ she bumped into something' or 'he caught [a cold]'). Context (object and sentence) determines the precise translation. Common uses: 'se pegó un golpe' (he/she got a bump), 'se pegó a la pared' (stuck to the wall), 'se pegó la gripe' (caught the flu), 'se pegó conmigo' (he/she hit/bumped into me or became attached to me, depending on region).
target_language_example: Se pegó un golpe contra la mesa cuando tropezó.
native_language_example: He bumped his head against the table when he tripped.

meaning: 'it was thought' / 'people thought' (impersonal, past)
additional_notes: Impersonal passive/reflective construction used to express beliefs or opinions in the past without specifying who thought it. Equivalent to 'people thought', 'it was believed', or 'it was thought' in English. Common with clauses introduced by 'que'.
target_language_example: Se pensaba que nadie podía volar, antes de los aviones.
native_language_example: People thought no one could fly before airplanes.

meaning: was missed (by someone) / missed out on (something)
additional_notes: Used when someone missed or lost the chance to see, experience, or obtain something. Often appears with a direct object introduced by 'de' (e.g., 'se perdió de la fiesta', 'se perdió de ver el partido'). Common in spoken Spanish; the reflexive 'se' indicates the person missed it (sometimes implies regret).
target_language_example: Se perdió de la reunión porque llegó tarde.
native_language_example: He missed the meeting because he arrived late.

meaning: “one could” or “it could be said”; polite/impersonal way to suggest possibility or opinion.
additional_notes: Uses impersonal/reflexive 'se' with conditional 'podría' (could). Common when giving a tentative opinion or softening a statement: 'Se podría decir...' = 'One could say...' or 'You could say...'. Can be translated as 'it could be said' or 'you could say' depending on context.
target_language_example: Se podría decir que es una buena idea.
native_language_example: One could say that it's a good idea.

meaning: could (be) / it was possible to (do something) — impersonal or passive-sounding past ability/possibility.
additional_notes: Uses impersonal/passive 'se' with the imperfect 'podía' to describe that something was possible or possible to be done in the past (often translated as 'you/one could' or 'it was possible to'). Common with verbs like ver, entender, andar. Tone is neutral and common in descriptions.
target_language_example: Desde la cima se podía ver todo el valle.
native_language_example: From the summit you could see the whole valley.

meaning: 'was able to' / 'could' (past, impersonal or reflexive-like use).
additional_notes: Commonly appears with verbs to express that something was possible or impossible in the past. The pronoun 'se' here is not reflexive in the normal sense; it often marks an impersonal or passive-like construction (e.g., 'se pudo evitar' = 'it could be avoided' / 'was able to be avoided') or appears with a subject (e.g., 'Tom se pudo haber hecho daño' = 'Tom could have hurt himself'). Context determines whether it's impersonal/passive or refers back to a person.
target_language_example: La puerta se pudo abrir después de mucho esfuerzo.
native_language_example: The door could be opened after a lot of effort.

meaning: a subjunctive form meaning 'can be' or 'be able to' (that/so that it can be).
additional_notes: Combines the impersonal/reflexive particle 'se' with the verb 'poder' in the present subjunctive (pueda). Used in subordinate clauses to express possibility, ability, hope, permission, purpose, or conditions (e.g., 'para que se pueda...'). Often translates as 'can be' or 'be able to' in English. Context determines whether it's passive/impersonal ('that can be done') or reflexive/impersonal ('so that one/people can...').
target_language_example: Haremos cambios para que se pueda usar en cualquier país.
native_language_example: We'll make changes so that it can be used in any country.

meaning: it's possible
additional_notes: Common impersonal expression with se + puede. It is used to say that something is possible or allowed in general, without naming a specific person. Depending on context, it can mean 'it's possible', 'you can', 'one can', or 'it can be done'.
target_language_example: Aquí se puede pagar con tarjeta.
native_language_example: You can pay by card here.

meaning: they began to / they became (doing something or in a certain state) — often part of a larger phrase (e.g., 'se pusieron de acuerdo', 'se pusieron de pie').
additional_notes: This is the reflexive third-person plural of 'ponerse' plus the preposition 'de'. Meaning depends on what follows: common constructions include 'se pusieron de acuerdo' (they agreed), 'se pusieron de pie' (they stood up), 'se pusieron de mal humor' (they became in a bad mood). Use it to describe a change of state or starting an action. Context determines whether it's 'began to' or 'became'.
target_language_example: Cuando llegó el jefe, se pusieron de pie.
native_language_example: When the boss arrived, they stood up.

meaning: 'they love each other' or 'they care for each other' (reflexive reciprocal of querer).
additional_notes: Used for mutual/reciprocal feelings or actions between two or more people: 'se quieren' = they love/care for each other. Context decides nuance: querer can mean 'to love' (romantic/familial) or 'to want'; with 'se' and plural subject it usually means reciprocal (they love each other). Can also appear with infinitives (e.g. 'se quieren casar' = they want to marry each other / they love each other and plan to marry).
target_language_example: María y Luis se quieren mucho desde niños.
native_language_example: María and Luis have loved each other a lot since childhood.

meaning: it's not known what / one doesn't know what will happen.
additional_notes: Used impersonally to express uncertainty about events or outcomes. Often appears as 'no se sabe qué...' followed by a verb clause (va a pasar, pasará, sucederá). Neutral register; common in spoken and written Spanish. The construction is impersonal: subject is unspecified (one/people/it).
target_language_example: No se sabe qué ocurrirá durante la reunión.
native_language_example: It's not known what will happen during the meeting.

meaning: sat near (someone or something).
additional_notes: Reflexive past of sentarse (se sentó) + cerca de = 'sat near'. Used to say someone took a seat close to another person or place. Subject can be omitted in Spanish (Se sentó cerca de él = He/She sat near him). Can refer to physical proximity (seat on bus, chair, etc.).
target_language_example: Él se sentó cerca de la ventana para ver el paisaje.
native_language_example: He sat near the window to see the scenery.

meaning: that (someone) know(s) it / be known (subjunctive phrase expressing concern about knowledge becoming known)
additional_notes: Uses the verb saber in the present subjunctive (sepa) with the impersonal/pronominal se. Common after verbs or expressions of desire, fear, indifference, or negation (que no quiero que se sepa; antes de que se sepa). Often implies 'for it to become known' or 'that people find out.' English equivalents: 'that it be known,' 'that people know,' or more naturally 'that someone finds out.'
target_language_example: No quiero que se sepa la verdad todavía.
native_language_example: I don't want the truth to be known yet / I don't want people to find out the truth yet.

meaning: feels much (better/more) — used to say someone feels a lot more of something, commonly 'much better'.
additional_notes: Usually followed by an adjective (e.g., mejor) to indicate a big change in how someone feels. 'Se siente' is reflexive from 'sentir(se)' meaning 'to feel (oneself)'. For beginners, the most common use is 'se siente mucho mejor' = 'feels much better.'
target_language_example: Ella se siente mucho mejor después de dormir.
native_language_example: She feels much better after sleeping.

meaning: 'is/are supposed to' or 'is expected to' (indicates expectation or assumption).
additional_notes: Used to express an expectation, obligation, or assumption about what should happen or what someone should do. Often appears with an infinitive (se supone + que + subjunctive/indicative) or directly before an infinitive. Tone can be neutral; context decides if it's rhetorical, questioning, or corrective.
target_language_example: Se supone que debes llegar a las ocho.
native_language_example: You are supposed to arrive at eight.

meaning: 'one must' / 'it must be' / 'has to' (impersonal/passive construction)
additional_notes: Used in impersonal or passive constructions with 'tener que' to express obligation or necessity without a clear subject. Often appears as 'se tiene que + infinitive' (equivalent to 'hay que' or 'tiene que' in impersonal sense). Can also be used in passive meaning 'is/has to be [done]'. Context determines whether it's general obligation ('one must') or passive ('it must be done').
target_language_example: Se tiene que terminar el informe antes del lunes.
native_language_example: The report has to be finished before Monday.

meaning: he/she dyed (his/her) ... (past tense reflexive of 'teñir' — to dye).
additional_notes: Used with body parts (commonly 'el pelo') to say someone dyed their hair. 'Se tiñó el pelo' = 'He/She dyed his/her hair.' Often followed by a color: 'se tiñó el pelo de negro' = 'dyed it black.' The construction is reflexive (se) and in the past (pretérito).
target_language_example: Ella se tiñó el pelo de rojo la semana pasada.
native_language_example: She dyed her hair red last week.

meaning: 'one works' / 'people work here' (impersonal/passive use of trabajar)
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal or passive 'se' to talk about work in general or what is done here, without specifying who. Common in signs or general statements: 'Aquí se trabaja' = 'Work is done here' or 'People work here.' Can also be used in proverbs or sayings (e.g., 'Se trabaja como se come').
target_language_example: En esta empresa se trabaja con seriedad.
native_language_example: In this company people work seriously.

meaning: 'what this is about' or 'what this concerns'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or say what the subject, purpose, or issue is. Often appears in the phrase 'de qué se trata esto' (what is this about) or 'sé de qué se trata esto' (I know what this is about). Literally built from 'tratar(se) de' meaning 'to be about'.
target_language_example: No entiendo el problema; explícame de qué se trata esto.
native_language_example: I don't understand the problem; explain to me what this is about.

meaning: 'it's not just about' / 'it's (only) about' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used to say what something concerns or to emphasize that an issue involves more than one thing. Often appears with 'no' to mean 'it's not just about...'. Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'ti' = you). In neutral register.
target_language_example: No se trata sólo de dinero; también importa el tiempo.
native_language_example: It's not just about money; time matters too.

meaning: you/one/people can see the (feminine noun) / the (feminine noun) is visible.
additional_notes: Impersonal/passive construction with 'se' + verb 'ver' used to say that something is visible or can be seen. The article 'la' agrees with a feminine singular noun that follows (e.g., la casa, la luna). In English this is often translated as 'you can see the ...' or 'the ... is visible.' For masculine nouns you'd use 'se ve el'.
target_language_example: Desde la colina se ve la iglesia.
native_language_example: From the hill you can see the church.

meaning: become
additional_notes: Common form of the verb volverse (se vuelve / se vuelva) used with a reflexive pronoun; in examples it appears in the subjunctive (puede que se vuelva) or as a present indicative/imperative context. It often means 'become' (a change of state or condition) or 'turn against' someone (volverse contra). Use depends on context and tense: 'se vuelva' = 'becomes'/'might become'/'turns (against)'.
target_language_example: No quiero que se vuelva una discusión.
native_language_example: I don't want it to turn into an argument.

meaning: 'be that as it may' / 'in any case'.
additional_notes: A formal or neutral connector used to introduce a remark that accepts a previous point but shifts to a different or more important point. Similar to 'de todos modos', 'en cualquier caso' or 'sea como sea'. Often used in speech and writing to close a discussion point and move on.
target_language_example: Sea como fuere, debemos tomar una decisión hoy.
native_language_example: Be that as it may, we must make a decision today.

meaning: whatever it is; whatever happens; no matter what
additional_notes: Used to express resignation, determination, or indifference about what the thing or outcome may be. Commonly appears with subjunctive verb forms (e.g., 'sea lo que sea' as a fixed phrase). Equivalent to 'whatever' or 'come what may' in English.
target_language_example: Haré lo necesario, sea lo que sea.
native_language_example: I'll do what is necessary, whatever it takes.

meaning: 'be very' used in subjunctive constructions (third person singular subjunctive of ser + adverb 'muy').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common combination: the verb ser in the subjunctive (sea) plus 'muy' to qualify something (e.g., 'sea muy lejos' = 'be very far'). It appears in wishes, doubts, or subordinate clauses (Espero que..., Ojalá que..., no creo que...). Use sea/esté depending on whether you need ser or estar.
target_language_example: Espero que no sea muy caro.
native_language_example: I hope it's not very expensive.

meaning: 'maybe/because' or 'it may be because' — used to suggest a possible reason.
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish as a tentative way to introduce a possible cause. Often appears as 'quizá/quizás/ tal vez sea porque...' or 'puede que sea porque...'. 'Sea' is the subjunctive form of 'ser' used after expressions of doubt or possibility. Use when offering a hypothesis, not a certain fact.
target_language_example: Tal vez sea porque no dormiste bien anoche.
native_language_example: Maybe it's because you didn't sleep well last night.

meaning: used in clauses meaning 'whoever (wants) it' or 'no matter who says/does it' (subjunctive, indefinite person).
additional_notes: This is part of the expression 'quien(quiera) sea que...' or 'sea quien sea que...' used to refer to an unknown or irrelevant person; it uses the subjunctive (sea) to express indefiniteness or doubt. Often appears as 'a quien sea que lo quiera' ('to whoever wants it') or 'sea quien sea que lo diga' ('whoever says it'). Formal and informal contexts; the structure can vary (quien sea que, sea quien sea que, a quien sea que).
target_language_example: Dáselo a quien sea que lo necesite.
native_language_example: Give it to whoever needs it.

meaning: 'whoever' or 'whoever it may be' (used to refer to an unknown or unspecified person).
additional_notes: Formal/subjunctive phrase built from the verb 'ser' in the subjunctive (sea) + quien. Commonly appears as 'sea quien sea' or 'sea quien', used to say 'whoever' or 'no matter who'. Can precede an imperative or a clause: 'Sea quien sea, dile...' It expresses indifference or uncertainty about the person's identity.
target_language_example: Sea quien sea, no quiero que entre a mi casa.
native_language_example: Whoever it is, I don't want them to enter my house.

meaning: you be a / that you are a (subjunctive: used to express wishes, opinions, commands, or doubts about someone being something)
additional_notes: Combines the subjunctive form 'seas' of 'ser' with the indefinite article 'un'. Common in Spanish to express wishes (Espero que seas un...), opinions/doubts (No creo que seas un...), commands or admonitions in negative imperative (No seas un...), or descriptions about how someone should be. Tone depends on context: can be polite, critical, or joking.
target_language_example: Espero que seas un buen amigo cuando lo necesite.
native_language_example: I hope you are a good friend when I need it.

meaning: literally 'secret is' — used to start a statement about where or how a secret (or the key to something) lies or is kept.
additional_notes: This phrase combines secreto (secret) with está (is). It's not a fixed idiom by itself but common in sentences like 'El secreto está en...' (The secret is in...) or 'Tu secreto está a salvo (conmigo).' (Your secret is safe (with me)). Use it to state location, condition, or security of a secret. Word order in Spanish is usually 'El secreto está ...' rather than 'secreto está' alone.
target_language_example: El secreto está en la receta de la abuela.
native_language_example: The secret is in grandma's recipe.

meaning: 'to move forward' or 'to keep going' (continue, progress, not give up).
additional_notes: Commonly used to encourage persistence after difficulties or to indicate continuing with a plan. Can be used literally (physically moving forward) or figuratively (emotionally or in projects). Often appears in commands or advice: 'Debes seguir adelante.'
target_language_example: Después del fracaso, decidió seguir adelante con su proyecto.
native_language_example: After the failure, he decided to keep going with his project.

meaning: 'to continue like this' or 'to keep going this way'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something will remain in the same state, behavior, or situation. Often expresses persistence (positive or neutral) or frustration/complaint when describing an undesirable situation. Can be followed by verbs or context explaining how 'this' is.
target_language_example: No puedo seguir así; necesito un cambio.
native_language_example: I can't keep going like this; I need a change.

meaning: 'to continue with' or 'to carry on with' (something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone continues an action, plan, project, or state. Often followed by a noun, verb-ing idea, or clause (e.g., seguir con el plan, seguir con la entrevista, seguir con vida). Can also mean 'to keep going despite difficulties.'
target_language_example: Vamos a seguir con el plan aunque haya problemas.
native_language_example: We'll continue with the plan even if there are problems.

meaning: to follow the (masculine) / to keep up with the (masculine).
additional_notes: Seguir el combines the verb 'seguir' (to follow/continue/keep up) with the masculine singular definite article 'el'. It appears before a masculine noun: e.g., seguir el ritmo (keep up with the rhythm/pace), seguir el camino (follow the path), seguir el plan (stick to the plan). Use 'seguir la' for feminine nouns (seguir la ruta), 'seguir los/las' for plurals. Can mean physically following, keeping pace with, or adhering to something (a plan, rules, schedule).
target_language_example: Si queremos llegar a tiempo, debemos seguir el horario.
native_language_example: If we want to arrive on time, we must follow the schedule.

meaning: to play along; to go along with someone's plan, joke, or pretense.
additional_notes: Used when someone pretends, jokes, or sets up a situation and you either cooperate or don't expose it. Can be literal (keep playing a game) but usually idiomatic: to act as if you agree or accept something for social reasons. Common in casual and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Por ahora conviene seguir el juego y no revelar la sorpresa.
native_language_example: For now it's best to play along and not reveal the surprise.

meaning: 'to remain/stay in' or 'to continue in' (a place, state, activity, or relationship).
additional_notes: Used with a noun or place to mean 'stay/remain in' (seguir en el bosque, seguir en el ómnibus) or with abstract nouns to mean 'continue in' a state or role (seguir en la obra, seguir en contacto, seguir en esta locura). Context determines whether it's physical (location) or figurative (state, relationship, activity). Often followed by articles and nouns or by contact/roles.
target_language_example: Quiero seguir en este proyecto hasta terminarlo.
native_language_example: I want to stay on this project until it's finished.

meaning: to follow my... / to keep up with my... (used before a noun: advice, pace, path, etc.)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; 'seguir' (to follow/keep following) is used with a possessive 'mi' + noun. Common uses: 'seguir mi consejo' (follow my advice), 'seguir mi ritmo' (keep up with my pace), 'seguir mi propio camino' (follow my own path). Use it when telling someone to follow or continue with something that belongs to or is associated with the speaker.
target_language_example: Deberías seguir mi recomendación si quieres mejorar.
native_language_example: You should follow my recommendation if you want to improve.

meaning: 'to continue along' or 'to follow (a route) through/along'.
additional_notes: Used when talking about continuing movement along a path, street, route or topic. Often followed by a place, street name, route, or phrase indicating direction (e.g., seguir por la calle, seguir por la derecha). Can also mean 'to keep doing something by means of' in some contexts, but most common for physical movement.
target_language_example: Tienes que seguir por la avenida principal hasta llegar al parque.
native_language_example: You must continue along the main avenue until you reach the park.

meaning: second-hand; used (referring to items previously owned).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe clothing, furniture, books, cars, etc. Can appear before or after the noun (ropa de segunda mano / segunda mano) and is often used in sales contexts: tiendas de segunda mano = thrift/used stores. Not used to mean 'second hand' as in measuring time on a clock.
target_language_example: Compré una cámara de segunda mano porque era más barata.
native_language_example: I bought a second-hand camera because it was cheaper.

meaning: 'second door' (the door that comes after the first one)
additional_notes: Used to give directions or specify location. Often appears in short phrases like 'la segunda puerta a la derecha/izquierda' or as a stand-alone instruction. Articles (la/segunda) may be omitted in brief signs or spoken instructions: 'Segunda puerta a la izquierda.'
target_language_example: Cuando entres al pasillo, la segunda puerta a la derecha es la sala de reuniones.
native_language_example: When you enter the corridor, the second door on the right is the meeting room.

meaning: 'one more second' or 'a second more' (one additional second of time)
additional_notes: Used to request or emphasize a very short additional amount of time. Often appears in phrases like "un segundo más" (one more second) or in negative constructions with "ni" to mean "not even one more second" (i.e., not staying/doing something any longer). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Espera un segundo más, ya termino.
native_language_example: Wait one more second, I'm finishing now.

meaning: 'security/safety is...' — used to state that safety or security is (something).
additional_notes: This phrase combines seguridad (security, safety) with the verb 'es' (is). It commonly begins sentences that emphasize the importance, priority, or nature of safety/security. Choose the appropriate English translation for 'seguridad' from 'security' (protection, systems) or 'safety' (personal safety, danger) based on context.
target_language_example: La seguridad es nuestra prioridad número uno.
native_language_example: Safety is our number one priority.

meaning: 'sure that there is' or 'certain that there are'.
additional_notes: Used to express confidence that something exists or is happening. Often follows 'estoy' (I'm) or other forms of 'estar/ser' + 'seguro' (sure). The construction is: [estar/ser] + seguro(a) de que + hay + [noun/clause]. 'Hay' is impersonal 'there is/are'.
target_language_example: Estoy seguro de que hay suficientes sillas para todos.
native_language_example: I'm sure that there are enough chairs for everyone.

meaning: sure/certain that he (will / did / will do ...).
additional_notes: Used to express confidence about something related to a male person (él). Often appears with verbs in different tenses (future, past, present) to indicate certainty about actions or events. In everyday speech you can also say "estoy seguro de que" without repeating "él" if context makes the person clear (e.g., "Estoy seguro de que irá" or "Estoy seguro de que lo hará").
