target_language_example: ¿Tienes frío? Puedo cerrar la ventana si quieres porque no me gusta tener frío.
native_language_example: Are you cold? I can close the window if you want because I don't like being cold.

meaning: to feel like (doing something); to want/feel a desire to do something.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: tener ganas de + [infinitive]. Literally 'to have desires' but idiomatically means 'to feel like' or 'to want to.' Can express mild or strong desire depending on context and intonation. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Siempre tengo ganas de viajar cuando veo fotos de otros países.
native_language_example: I always feel like traveling when I see pictures of other countries.

meaning: to feel like; to want to (do something)
additional_notes: Use with an infinitive to say you want or feel like doing that action: tener ganas de + verb. Can also be used with a noun to express desire for something: tener ganas de + noun. Common, neutral-register expression for desire or inclination.
target_language_example: Siempre tengo ganas de viajar cuando veo fotos de otras ciudades.
native_language_example: I always feel like traveling when I see photos of other cities.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck or fortune.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to say someone has luck or things go their way (e.g., winning, succeeding easily). Not about literally having milk. Common in Spain and some Latin American countries; tone is casual. Use context to indicate luck (tener suerte is more neutral).
target_language_example: Siempre parece tener leche cuando juega a la lotería; nunca pierde.
native_language_example: He always seems to have luck when he plays the lottery; he never loses.

meaning: to take place; to happen (an event occurs).
additional_notes: Used to describe when or where events occur. Often appears in passive or impersonal constructions (e.g., 'La reunión tendrá lugar mañana' = 'The meeting will take place tomorrow'). Can be used in various tenses: tuvo lugar, tiene lugar, tendrá lugar. Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: La conferencia va a tener lugar en el auditorio a las diez.
native_language_example: The conference will take place in the auditorium at ten.

meaning: to have my
additional_notes: A combination of the verb tener (to have) plus the possessive adjective mi (my). Used before a noun to express possession or desire to possess something (e.g., tener mi casa = to have my house). Common in phrases expressing wishes or goals (Espero tener mi...). Word order and agreement follow normal Spanish rules: mi is invariable (does not change for gender or number), while the noun that follows does.
target_language_example: Espero tener mi propio coche el próximo año.
native_language_example: I hope to have my own car next year.

meaning: to be afraid
additional_notes: Used to express fear or lack of fear. Commonly follows the verb tener + miedo (literally 'to have fear') in Spanish but translates as 'to be afraid' in English. Can be followed by de + noun or de + infinitive to indicate the object of fear (tener miedo de algo / de hacer algo).
target_language_example: No debes tener miedo del futuro.
native_language_example: You shouldn't be afraid of the future.

meaning: to have a lot of (used before a feminine noun or abstract noun).
additional_notes: Commonly used with qualities or needs (paciencia, hambre, suerte, confianza). Because mucha is feminine, the noun that follows is feminine (mucha paciencia, mucha hambre). For masculine nouns use 'mucho' (tener mucho frío). Often used with 'tener que' + infinitive for obligation (tienes que tener mucha paciencia = you have to be very patient).
target_language_example: Tienes que tener mucha paciencia con los niños.
native_language_example: You have to have a lot of patience with children.

meaning: to be over
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. With ages (tener + number) it means "to be over" a certain age (e.g., tener más de cincuenta años = to be over fifty). In other contexts it can mean "to have more" of something (quantity, information, time). Can also appear in future/idiomatic constructions (tener más sobre esto = to have more on this / to cover more about this).
target_language_example: Debe de tener más de cuarenta años.
native_language_example: He must be over forty years old.

meaning: to have nothing against (someone or something); to not oppose or dislike
additional_notes: In natural Spanish the phrase typically appears with negation as 'no tener nada en contra' (e.g., 'no tengo nada en contra de...'). Used to express lack of objection or ill will. It is followed by 'de' or 'a' depending on the noun/pronoun (e.g., 'no tengo nada en contra de ella' or 'no tengo nada en contra de esa idea'). Without the 'no' it is awkward or ungrammatical in isolation.
target_language_example: No quiero que pienses que quiero tener nada en contra de nadie; realmente me importa.
native_language_example: I don't want you to think that I want to have anything against anyone; I really care.

meaning: to have a flair for writing; to be a good or stylish writer (idiomatic); can also be literal: to have a pen.
additional_notes: Literally 'to have a pen' but commonly used idiomatically to praise someone's writing talent or elegant style. Usage varies by region and is not equally common everywhere; context determines whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: Ella tiene pluma; escribe cuentos con mucho estilo.
native_language_example: She has a flair for writing; she writes stories with a lot of style.

meaning: to consider; to regard (someone or something as); to hold the opinion that
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone regards or considers a person or thing in a certain way. Often followed by a noun or adjective (tener a alguien por + sustantivo/adjetivo) or by que + clause (tener por + que + cláusula). More formal or literary than pensar/creer in some contexts. Examples: Lo tengo por experto; Lo tengo por cierto que vendrá.
target_language_example: La mayoría tiende a tener por líder competente a quien toma decisiones con calma.
native_language_example: Most people tend to consider as a competent leader someone who makes calm decisions.

meaning: to keep in mind; to be aware of; to consider.
additional_notes: Used to remind someone to remember or consider something when making decisions or speaking. Common in advice, instructions, and formal or neutral contexts. Often followed by a noun, clause (que + subj/indic), or infinitive: tener presente X / tener presente que + clause / tener presente + infinitive.
target_language_example: Debes tener presente que el tráfico es peor los lunes por la mañana.
native_language_example: You should keep in mind that traffic is worse on Monday mornings.

meaning: to be wearing (something); to have on (clothing or accessories).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone currently has an item of clothing or accessory on. Common construction: tener puesto + [ropa/objeto]. Often interchangeable with llevar or llevar puesto in everyday Spanish; tener puesto can emphasize the item is placed on the person at the moment. Typically used in present tense for current state (e.g., Él tiene puesto un sombrero).
target_language_example: Ella tiene puesto un abrigo rojo.
native_language_example: She is wearing a red coat.

meaning: to have to
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to express obligation or necessity: tengo que estudiar = "I have to study." The form of tener changes with the subject and tense (tengo que, tienes que, van a tener que, etc.).
target_language_example: Odio tener que depender de usted.
native_language_example: I hate having to depend on you.

meaning: to have to go
additional_notes: Part of the very common pattern tener que + infinitive, which expresses obligation or necessity. Here the infinitive is ir ('to go'). Conjugate tener for the subject when used in a normal sentence: tengo que ir, tienes que ir, etc. In the infinitive, as listed here, it can appear after another verb, as in no quiero tener que ir. Without a destination, it can also mean 'to have to leave.'
target_language_example: No quiero tener que ir mañana.
native_language_example: I don't want to have to go tomorrow.

meaning: to be right
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is correct about something. Literally it means "to have reason," but the usual English equivalent is "to be right." You can also use it with "en" to specify the topic: "tener razón en algo" = "to be right about something."
target_language_example: Creo que puedes tener razón.
native_language_example: I think you may be right.

meaning: to make sense; to be logical or meaningful
additional_notes: Used to state that something is logical, understandable, or has meaning. Commonly appears in inflected forms (empieza a tener sentido, empezó a tener sentido, no tiene sentido). Can express both understanding ('now it makes sense') and lack of meaning ('it doesn't make sense' / 'it has no meaning').
target_language_example: Entonces todo empezará a tener sentido.
native_language_example: Then everything will start to make sense.

meaning: to have sex; to engage in sexual intercourse.
additional_notes: A neutral, straightforward way to say 'to have sex' in Spanish. Common in both spoken and written language. Can be used with pronouns or reflexive constructions (e.g., 'tener sexo con alguien'). Be aware of context—it's explicit and may be considered private or intimate language.
target_language_example: No quiero tener sexo si no hay confianza.
native_language_example: I don't want to have sex if there's no trust.

meaning: to be lucky
additional_notes: Used to say someone experiences good luck or favorable circumstances. Commonly appears with verbs like poder, deber, or esperar (e.g., 'podrías tener suerte' = 'you might be lucky'). Not idiomatic; literal composition (tener = to have, suerte = luck) matches English.
target_language_example: Si te presentas temprano, podrías tener suerte y conseguir una plaza.
native_language_example: If you arrive early, you might be lucky and get a spot.

meaning: to be sleepy; to feel drowsy or ready to sleep.
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener + the noun sueño to express that someone feels sleepy (e.g., Tengo sueño). Common in everyday speech for physical tiredness or need for sleep; not used to mean 'to be bored'. To say 'to make someone sleepy' use other constructions (e.g., dar sueño).
target_language_example: Después de correr cinco kilómetros, suelo tener sueño.
native_language_example: After running five kilometers, I tend to be sleepy.

meaning: to have a job; to be employed; to have work
additional_notes: Used to state that someone is employed or has work to do. Can refer to holding paid employment or having tasks to complete (e.g., "tener trabajo por hacer"). Common in everyday conversation about employment status.
target_language_example: Ella dice que va a tener trabajo a partir del lunes.
native_language_example: She says she will have a job starting Monday.

meaning: 'to have your' (used before a noun to indicate possession/experience belonging to 'you')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's the verb tener (to have) followed by the possessive adjective tu (your). It appears before a noun (tener tu apoyo = to have your support) or before edad to say you had the same age (Yo solía tener tu edad = I used to be your age). Use tu (informal you) for friends/family; for formal or plural you, use su / su(s).
target_language_example: Quiero tener tu confianza antes de empezar.
native_language_example: I want to have your trust before starting.

meaning: to succeed; to be successful.
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about achieving goals, doing well in life, work, projects, etc. Conjugate 'tener' to match the subject (e.g., 'tengo éxito', 'tienes éxito', 'tuvo éxito', 'va a tener éxito'). Often followed by infinitives or context explaining the area of success (tener éxito en algo / tener éxito + gerund/infinitive).
target_language_example: Si trabajas duro, puedes tener éxito.
native_language_example: If you work hard, you can succeed.

meaning: to have you (here/with me); to have someone on/at (a particular side or in a role).
additional_notes: Tenerte de combines the verb tener (to have) plus the object pronoun te. Meaning depends on the rest of the sentence: often used in phrases like 'tenerte de regreso' (to have you back) or 'tenerte de mi lado' (to have you on my side). It's colloquial but neutral; the structure is 'tener + te + de + [noun/phrase]'.
target_language_example: Me alegra tenerte de nuevo en el equipo.
native_language_example: I'm glad to have you back on the team.

meaning: 'have a' used in polite wishes or commands (subjunctive usted/ustedes form).
additional_notes: Common in set phrases to wish someone well: 'Que tengan un buen día' = 'Have a good day' (polite/plural or formal). 'Que' + subjunctive expresses a wish; 'tengan' is the ustedes/ustedes-form subjunctive of 'tener'. Can be used with singular formal usted as 'tenga un'.
target_language_example: Que tengan un feliz cumpleaños.
native_language_example: Have a happy birthday.

meaning: you have to / that you have to (subjunctive form used after expressions requiring subjunctive).
additional_notes: Tengas que is the present subjunctive of 'tener que' (to have to) and appears in subordinate clauses after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., emotion, doubt, commands, negation). It often translates as 'you have to' or 'that you have to' in contexts like 'anything you have to say' or 'whoever you have to tell'. Use when the main clause requires the subjunctive (e.g., 'no quiero oír nada de lo que tengas que decir').
target_language_example: Dime si tienes algo que tengas que decir antes de irte.
native_language_example: Tell me if you have something that you have to say before you leave.

meaning: 'when you have time' (used to ask someone to do something at a convenient moment).
additional_notes: Common phrase using the subjunctive (tener → tengas) after 'cuando' to refer to a future or non-specific time. Polite and flexible—can be used to request calls, visits, signing papers, or reading something. Tone depends on context: can be casual or polite. You can shorten it to 'cuando puedas' for 'when you can.'
target_language_example: Llama mañana cuando tengas tiempo.
native_language_example: Call tomorrow when you have time.

meaning: you have a
additional_notes: Contains tengas, the tú present subjunctive of tener, plus un. It is commonly used after que in expressions of hope, wishes, advice, or possibility: espero que tengas un buen viaje = 'i hope you have a good trip.' In wishes, que tengas... can also work like 'have a...' in English.
target_language_example: Ojalá tengas un buen día.
native_language_example: I hope you have a good day.

meaning: 'have a good day' (wishing someone a good day).
additional_notes: Common polite/imperfect-subjunctive phrase used to wish someone well. Often said after 'que' as a short formula: 'Que tengas un buen día.' Can be used with names or contexts (e.g. 'en la oficina'). Tone is friendly or neutral; works with family, friends, colleagues, strangers. If speaking formally to one person, use same phrase; for plural (you all) use 'tengan un buen día.'
target_language_example: Que tengas un buen día en tu nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Have a good day at your new job.

meaning: 'you have a' (subjunctive) — used when speaking about someone having something, often in wishes, requests, or after certain conjunctions
additional_notes: Tengas is the second-person singular (tú) present subjunctive form of tener. Used after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., querer que, alegrarse de que) and after certain conjunctions (e.g., cuando, una vez que) to refer to a non-realized or anticipated situation. Una simply means "a" (feminine) and agrees with a feminine noun that follows (una duda, una copia, una vida, una paz, una conexión).
target_language_example: Espero que tengas una buena semana.
native_language_example: I hope you have a good week.

meaning: I have (it) here / I have here (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that you possess or are holding something and that it is physically nearby or present. 'Tengo' = I have; 'aquí' = here. Often followed by a direct object or by 'por algún lado' (somewhere around). Tone is neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Lo tengo aquí, en mi bolso.
native_language_example: I have it here, in my bag.

meaning: I have good
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the verb tener (to have) in first person present and the adjective buena (feminine form of "good"). It must be completed by a feminine noun (ropa, memoria, puntería, vista) or a feminine adjective-noun phrase. Use "tengo buen" (masculine) before masculine singular nouns (e.g., "tengo buen amigo"). For beginners: translate as "I have good..." and add the specific noun in English (e.g., "I have good memory" → natural English: "I have a good memory").
target_language_example: Tengo buena memoria.
native_language_example: I have a good memory.

meaning: I'm hot (I feel warm).
additional_notes: Common way to say you feel hot/uncomfortably warm. Literally 'I have heat.' Used for physical temperature (not usually for 'hot' as attractive). Can be used with other feelings: tengo frío (I'm cold), tengo hambre (I'm hungry).
target_language_example: Hace mucho sol y tengo calor.
native_language_example: It's very sunny and I'm hot.

meaning: I have things (to do / to say).
additional_notes: A common informal phrase meaning you have unspecified tasks, matters, or things to say. Often followed by 'que...' + verb (e.g., 'tengo cosas que hacer' = I have things to do) or used alone to imply being busy or having other priorities. Tone ranges from neutral to casual; context clarifies whether it means obligations, plans, or topics to mention.
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora no puedo hablar: tengo cosas que terminar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk now: I have things to finish.

meaning: 'I have (no) place' — used with a negative to mean 'I don't have anywhere (to ...)', e.g. to sleep or stay.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in constructions like "no tengo dónde + infinitive" or "no tengo dónde + verb", and is followed by an action (dormir, quedarme, pasar la noche) or implied context. It literally means "I have where", but Spanish requires the structure to express lack of a place when combined with "no" (No tengo dónde dormir = I don't have anywhere to sleep).
target_language_example: Esta semana no tengo dónde quedarme durante la conferencia.
native_language_example: This week I don't have anywhere to stay during the conference.

meaning: I have a feeling/intuition that...
additional_notes: Used to express a vague sense, intuition, or premonition about something that will or might happen. Often followed by 'que' + clause. Slightly formal/neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Tengo el presentimiento de que todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: I have a feeling that everything will turn out fine.

meaning: I'm hungry
additional_notes: A common way to say you are hungry in Spanish. Uses the verb tener (to have) + hambre (hunger); literally 'I have hunger'. Used for current physical appetite. To say 'not hungry', add no: 'no tengo hambre'.
target_language_example: Ahora sí, tengo hambre — ¿vamos a comer?
native_language_example: Now I am hungry — shall we eat?

meaning: 'I intend' or 'I have the intention (to...)'.
additional_notes: Used to express a plan, purpose, or lack of willingness to do something. Often followed by 'de' + infinitive (e.g., tengo intención de ir). Can be used in negative form 'no tengo intención de...' to say you do not plan or do not want to do something.
target_language_example: No tengo intención de mudarme este año.
native_language_example: I don't intend to move this year.

meaning: 'I have bad (news)'; short for 'tengo malas noticias'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce bad news. Native speakers often shorten 'tengo malas noticias' to 'tengo malas' in casual speech; context implies 'noticias'. Often followed by the bad information. Formal: use full phrase 'tengo malas noticias'.
target_language_example: Tengo malas: el vuelo se canceló.
native_language_example: I have bad news: the flight was canceled.

meaning: I have a wife / I am married (I have a wife).
additional_notes: Literally 'I have wife.' Common way in Spanish to say you are married or that you have a wife. Used in everyday speech; context clarifies whether emphasizing marriage or simply stating family composition (e.g., when listing family members). Note: Spanish often omits the article before kinship terms (no 'una').
target_language_example: Tengo mujer y trabajo los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I have a wife and I work on weekends.

meaning: I have nothing
additional_notes: Usually appears as no tengo nada in standard Spanish. Spanish normally uses no before the verb when nada comes after it. Because tengo means "I have," this phrase is specifically first-person singular.
target_language_example: Hoy no tengo nada que hacer.
native_language_example: Today I don't have anything to do.

meaning: I have no idea (about/of).
additional_notes: Used to say you don't know anything about a topic or question. Often followed by a clause introduced by de, a question word (qué, a qué, cuántos, etc.), or an infinitive. Colloquial and very common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea de cuándo llegará el tren.
native_language_example: I have no idea when the train will arrive.

meaning: I don't have any / I have no ... (used to negate existence of something I possess or experience)
additional_notes: This combination is actually ungrammatical in standard Spanish as written: the correct negative forms are either "no tengo ningún/ninguna..." (with "no" before the verb) or "no tengo ningún...". In the example sentences the intended pattern is "no tengo ningún/ninguna + noun" (e.g., "No tengo ningún plan"). Use "ningún" before a masculine singular noun and "ninguna" before a feminine singular noun. For plural or when not using "ningún/ninguna", Spanish often uses "ninguno/ninguna" or other constructions (e.g., "No tengo tiempo" or "No tengo ningún lugar donde quedarme").
target_language_example: No tengo ningún amigo en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: I don't have any friends in this city.

meaning: I have other (ones); I have other things/options.
additional_notes: Used to say you possess other items, options, tasks, ideas, etc. Often followed by a noun (tengo otras cosas) or a clause (tengo otras formas de...). The gender/number of 'otras' must agree with the noun it refers to: otras (f. pl.), otros (m. pl.). If the noun is omitted, context tells what 'other ones' refers to.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, tengo otras soluciones.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I have other solutions.

meaning: I have no reason to / I don't need to (do something).
additional_notes: Used in negative constructions as 'no tengo por qué + infinitive' to say you have no reason, obligation, or need to do something. Literal parts ('tengo' = I have, 'por qué' = why/reason) help understand it, but the phrase functions as a fixed expression in this structure.
target_language_example: No tengo por qué mentir sobre eso.
native_language_example: I have no reason to lie about that.

meaning: 'I have all' / 'I have the whole' (feminine noun follows)
additional_notes: This is the verb tener (to have) in first person plus the feminine adjective 'toda' that agrees with a following feminine noun. It can mean 'I have all/the whole' (e.g., toda la información, toda la casa) or be part of expressions like 'No tengo toda la...' (I don't have all/the whole...). Context determines whether it refers to quantity ('all of') or entirety ('the whole of'). Use 'todo' before masculine nouns (tengo todo) and 'todas' for plural feminine (tengo todas).
target_language_example: Tengo toda la tarde libre.
native_language_example: I have the whole afternoon free.

meaning: I have everything
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'I have everything' or 'I have all'. Context can narrow it: before a noun or phrase it often means 'I have all the [something]' (e.g., 'tengo todo mi dinero' = 'I have all my money'). In sentences like 'Tengo todo el derecho a/ de...' it’s a fixed expression meaning 'I have every/ full right to...' ('todo el derecho' = 'every/full right'). When followed by an indefinite noun with emphasis ('tengo todo un tren'), it adds intensity: 'I have a whole train (to unload)' = 'I have an entire train'.
target_language_example: Tengo todo mi pasaporte y billetes.
native_language_example: I have all my passport and tickets.

meaning: I have all the / I have everything (followed by a noun or clause).
additional_notes: Incomplete phrase: usually part of a longer sentence such as "tengo todo lo necesario" (I have everything necessary) or "tengo todo lo que necesito" (I have everything I need). "Lo" is a neutral direct object pronoun used before adjectives, past participles, or clauses. After "todo lo" you often see an adjective, past participle, or "que" + clause.
target_language_example: Tengo todo lo que necesito para el viaje.
native_language_example: I have everything I need for the trip.

meaning: 'I have a question.'
additional_notes: Common phrase to indicate you want to ask something or request clarification. Used in formal and informal contexts. Can be followed by the question itself or by a polite pause (e.g., 'tengo una pregunta: ...').
target_language_example: Disculpe, tengo una pregunta sobre el horario.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question about the schedule.

meaning: had time
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of perfect tenses with haber (e.g., 'he tenido tiempo' = 'I have had time', 'no he tenido tiempo' = 'I haven't had time'). Used to say someone was/has been able to spare time for something. Can appear in conditional or pluperfect contexts (e.g., 'hubiera tenido tiempo' = 'had had time').
target_language_example: No he tenido tiempo para leer el correo.
native_language_example: I haven't had time to read the mail.

meaning: table tennis (ping-pong).
additional_notes: Refers to the sport played on a table with small paddles and a lightweight ball. 'Ping pong' is an informal/synonymous term often used interchangeably. Used as both a noun for the sport and in contexts like 'jugar al tenis de mesa' (to play table tennis).
target_language_example: Vamos a jugar al tenis de mesa esta tarde.
native_language_example: Let's play table tennis this afternoon.

meaning: tennis (played) in / at (a place) — 'tenis' = tennis; 'en' = in/at.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the noun tenis (often used with the preposition 'en' to indicate location: 'en el parque', 'en el club') or with the verb jugar (jugar al tenis en ...). In Spanish many speakers say 'jugar al tenis' (using the article + preposition 'a' → 'al'), but you can also see 'juego tenis' followed by 'en' to indicate where. Use 'en' to say where the activity happens (en Francia, en el parque, en el club).
target_language_example: Juego al tenis en el parque los domingos.
native_language_example: I play tennis in the park on Sundays.

meaning: A fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase; literally 'sneakers all the...' or 'tennis/tennis shoes all the...'; requires continuation (e.g., a noun or clause) to be grammatical.
additional_notes: This sequence appears incomplete. 'Tenis' commonly means 'sneakers' (athletic shoes) in many Spanish dialects; 'todos los' means 'all the' and must be followed by a noun (e.g., 'tenis todos los colores' = 'sneakers all the colors' — colloquially 'sneakers in all the colors'). As written ('tenis todos los') is ungrammatical by itself and likely part of a larger phrase. If intended as a verb, the correct form is 'tienes todos los' (you have all the...).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde compraste esos tenis todos los días?
native_language_example: Where did you buy those sneakers every day?

meaning: had good (followed by a noun) — e.g., had good reasons/intentions.
additional_notes: Commonly used with nouns like razones (reasons) or intenciones (intentions). Tenía is the imperfect past of tener (he/she/it/you formal had). Use to describe ongoing or repeated past states or explanations. Word order: tenía + buenas + [noun].
target_language_example: Ella tenía buenas razones para decir la verdad.
native_language_example: She had good reasons to tell the truth.

meaning: had four (used to say someone possessed four of something).
additional_notes: Imperfect past tense of tener (tenía) + the number cuatro. Commonly used to describe past possession or a repeated/state situation in the past (e.g., games, cards, objects). Subject can be explicit or implied (yo, él, ella, etc.).
target_language_example: Ella tenía cuatro libros en su mochila.
native_language_example: She had four books in her backpack.

meaning: had in the (something) — indicates possession or that something was located inside/on a masculine singular container, place, or body part in the past (imperfect).
additional_notes: 'Tenía' is the imperfect of 'tener' and describes an ongoing or repeated past state. The phrase is compositional and can change to tenía en la / tenía en los / tenía en las depending on the gender/number of the following noun. Commonly used with words like bolsillo, maletín, pelo, bus (el bus), coche, etc. Can be translated literally in most contexts.
target_language_example: No puedo haber perdido las llaves otra vez; las tenía en el bolsillo hace un momento.
native_language_example: I can't have lost the keys again; I had them in the pocket a moment ago.

meaning: had (something) in the + noun (e.g., head, mind, face); indicates possession/mental or physical placement inside or on a body part or location.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect past of 'tener' plus the preposition 'en' and the definite article 'la' before a feminine noun (e.g., la cabeza, la mente, la cara). It often appears in phrases meaning 'to have (something) in one's head/mind/face' — i.e., to hold an idea, remember something, or display a facial expression. Context determines whether the object is literal (physical placement) or figurative (thoughts, feelings). If the noun is masculine, you'd see 'tenía en el'.
target_language_example: Siempre tenía en la cabeza la canción del verano.
native_language_example: She always had the summer song in her head.

meaning: 'to have an idea/knowledge of' — used in the negative to mean 'to have no idea (that/of)'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in negative sentences (No tenía idea de...) to say you didn't know something. Followed by a clause introduced with que, de + infinitive, de + qué, de a qué, de por qué, or de qué + subjunctive/conditional depending on sentence. Tense of tenía is imperfect; other tenses possible (no tengo idea de, no tuve idea de).
target_language_example: No tenía idea de que ibas a venir hoy.
native_language_example: I had no idea you were going to come today.

meaning: 'had the' (past tense, third-person or yo formal) — used to say someone possessed or experienced something specific.
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect past tense of tener (tenía = 'he/she/you(formal)/I used to have' or 'was having') plus the feminine singular article la. Commonly followed by a feminine noun (la opción, la aprobación, la sensación, la mirada). Used to describe possession, feelings, states, or tendencies in the past. Subject is determined by context or prior clause.
target_language_example: Ella tenía la llave del armario.
native_language_example: She had the key to the closet.

meaning: 'was afraid of' (past tense: used to say someone felt fear of something or someone).
additional_notes: Imperfect past tense of tener miedo a + noun or pronoun. Commonly followed by a thing or person introduced with 'a' (tenía miedo a los perros, tenía miedo a la oscuridad, le tenía miedo a su padre). Use 'tener miedo de' with verbs (tener miedo de hablar) or 'tener miedo a' with nouns/people. The construction 'le tenía miedo a...' emphasizes fear directed at a specific person/being.
target_language_example: Antes tenía miedo a volar, pero ahora ya no.
native_language_example: I used to be afraid of flying, but now I'm not.

meaning: had nothing / didn't have anything
additional_notes: A combination of the imperfect tense of tener (tenía) plus nada (nothing). Commonly appears in negative statements to say someone didn't have something (often preceded by no: no tenía nada). In affirmative contexts without 'no' the phrase is uncommon; learners should use 'no tenía nada' to express 'I/he/she/they didn't have anything.'
target_language_example: No tenía nada que decir.
native_language_example: I didn't have anything to say.

meaning: had no idea / I had no idea.
additional_notes: Used to say you were completely unaware or didn't know something. Common in past narration (tenía) but can appear as short reply "No tenía ni idea." Equivalent present: "no tengo ni idea." "Ni" here reinforces "idea" (means 'not even an idea').
target_language_example: Cuando me lo explicó, yo no tenía ni idea de qué hablaba.
native_language_example: When he explained it to me, I had no idea what he was talking about.

meaning: had no idea (about/of).
additional_notes: Used to say someone was completely unaware of something. Often followed by 'que' + clause or 'de' + noun/infinitive. Common in past tense (tenía) but can appear with other tenses (no tengo ni idea, no tenía ni idea). 'Ni' emphasizes total lack of idea.
target_language_example: No tenía ni idea de que ibas a venir hoy.
native_language_example: I had no idea you were coming today.

meaning: 'didn't have any' (negative: had no ...)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the imperfect of tener (tenía) with the negative word ninguna to say someone 'had no' something in the past or 'didn't have any'. In standard Spanish you normally need the negative particle no before the verb: no tenía ninguna. Without the initial no (as in the input), it would be ungrammatical or mean something different in context. Ninguna agrees in gender/number with the noun it modifies (ningún before a masculine singular noun: no tenía ningún problema). Common in statements about doubts, reasons, relations, illnesses, etc.
target_language_example: No tenía ninguna duda sobre la decisión.
native_language_example: He had no doubt about the decision.

meaning: didn't have any / had no (something).
additional_notes: This occurs when describing the lack of something in the past using tener (imperfect). In correct Spanish, a negative construction normally uses 'no tenía ningún/ninguna' (note the 'no' before the verb). 'Ningún' agrees in gender and is used before singular masculine nouns; use 'ninguna' for feminine nouns. Common English equivalents: 'didn't have any', 'had no', or 'there was no'.
target_language_example: No tenía ningún libro que leer.
native_language_example: He didn't have any book to read.

meaning: had no other (choice/option)
additional_notes: Context determines meaning. Commonly appears in negative phrases like "no tenía otra (opción/alternativa/elección/salida)" meaning "had no other (choice/option/alternative/way out)." Without "no," as in "tenía otra pregunta," it means "had another (one)" or "I had one more." "Tenía otra" is past imperfect (tener) and often refers to possession or availability in the past.
target_language_example: No tenía otra opción, así que acepté.
native_language_example: I had no other option, so I accepted.

meaning: had/was completely (followed by a noun or abstract noun) — emphasizes totality or completeness.
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns after tenía (imperfect of tener) to say someone possessed or experienced the whole/entire of something. Can modify concrete things (toda la casa), categories (toda clase de herramientas) or abstract ideas (toda la razón = completely right). Word agreement: 'toda' agrees with the noun in gender and number (toda, todo, todas, todos).
target_language_example: Ella tenía toda la información sobre el proyecto.
native_language_example: She had all the information about the project.

meaning: theory of / the theory that (used to name or refer to a particular theory about something).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to name a theory followed by a noun or concept (e.g., 'teoría de la evolución' = 'theory of evolution'). Can introduce formal scientific theories or informal/metaphorical theories (e.g., 'teoría de la bala mágica'). Often followed by 'la', 'el', or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: La teoría de la relatividad cambió la física moderna.
native_language_example: The theory of relativity changed modern physics.

meaning: 'third grade' (school level) OR 'third-degree' (mathematical) OR 'intense interrogation/torture' (idiomatic)
additional_notes:
Has multiple meanings depending on context:
- Education: 'tercer grado' = the third year of primary/elementary school. Example: 'estuvo en tercer grado' (he/she was in third grade).
- Mathematics: describes degree of a polynomial or equation (e.g., 'ecuación de tercer grado' = cubic equation).
- Idiomatic (colloquial, somewhat dated): 'poner a alguien al tercer grado' or 'someter al tercer grado' means to give someone harsh questioning or intense interrogation; comparable to 'the third degree' in English.
Choose the meaning from context. The phrase can be translated literally as 'third grade' when referring to school; for the idiom, English often uses 'the third degree.'
target_language_example: Cuando estaba en tercer grado, aprendí a multiplicar.
native_language_example: When I was in third grade, I learned to multiply.

meaning: 'finish (doing something)'.
additional_notes: Used with a verb in infinitive to say someone finishes or should finish an action (termina de + infinitive). Can be a simple statement (Él termina de hablar) or a command/urging (Termina de comer = finish eating / hurry up and finish).
target_language_example: Termina de leer el libro antes de devolverlo.
native_language_example: Finish reading the book before returning it.

meaning: 'finish the' or 'finish it/the (masculine noun)'.
additional_notes: A command or statement using the verb terminar (to finish) followed by the masculine singular definite article el + noun or implied masculine object. In commands it can be an informal (tú) imperative: "¡Termina el juicio!" = "Finish the trial!" When the noun is omitted, context supplies the masculine thing to finish (e.g., el trabajo, el libro, el filete). Use termina (he/she/it finishes or tú imperative informal) depending on context; for formal commands use termine.
target_language_example: Termina el informe antes de salir.
native_language_example: Finish the report before leaving.

meaning: having finished the + (masculine singular noun) — indicates something is completed
additional_notes: Commonly appears after auxiliary verbs (haber, haber de, tener que) or in participial phrases. 'Terminado' is the past participle of 'terminar' and agrees in gender/number with the noun it modifies (terminado el informe, terminada la tarea, terminados los proyectos). Often used in perfect constructions (ha terminado el informe) or in reduced clauses (Habiendo terminado el trabajo...).
target_language_example: He terminado el informe esta mañana.
native_language_example: I have finished the report this morning.

meaning: 'finished' or 'completed' + feminine singular noun (past participle used with a feminine noun)
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'terminado' used with the feminine definite article 'la' before a feminine noun that follows (e.g., 'la tarea', 'la carrera', 'la tarta'). In Spanish the past participle must agree in gender and number when used in compound verbs with 'haber' it does not change (e.g., 'he terminado la tarea'), but when used with 'ser' or as an adjective it does (e.g., 'la tarea está terminada'). The examples show various compound tenses (pretérito perfecto, pluscuamperfecto, futuro perfecto, conditional forms).
target_language_example: He terminado la tarea, ¿puedo salir ahora?
native_language_example: I have finished the homework, can I go out now?

meaning: 'finish this' or 'complete this' (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: Termin ar = to finish/complete. 'Esta' is the feminine singular demonstrative pronoun/adjective meaning 'this' and agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., historia, conversación, tarea, botella). Use 'terminar este' for masculine nouns. Can be used with objects, tasks, or abstract things like conversations or stories.
target_language_example: Tengo que terminar esta tarea antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I have to finish this homework before sleeping.

meaning: to finish this (something nearby or just mentioned).
additional_notes: Use with a masculine singular noun implied or stated (e.g., 'terminar este trabajo' = 'to finish this job'). 'Terminar' is a common verb meaning 'to finish' or 'to end'. Combine with time expressions (en una semana, para el próximo martes) or complements (proyecto, trabajo). Word order: verb + demonstrative ('terminar este...').
target_language_example: Necesito terminar este informe antes del viernes.
native_language_example: I need to finish this report before Friday.

meaning: to finish/end (something feminine) — 'la' is the feminine direct object pronoun/article.
additional_notes: Terminar means 'to finish' or 'to end'. When followed by 'la' it usually refers to a specific feminine noun mentioned or understood (la misión, la película, la tarea). In speech you might also hear 'terminarla' as one word (infinitive + pronoun) when used with another verb: 'voy a terminarla'. Context tells which feminine thing is being finished.
target_language_example: Tenemos que terminar la tarea antes de cenar.
native_language_example: We have to finish the homework before dinner.

meaning: I finished the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: First-person singular preterite of terminar (to finish) + the masculine definite article el. Used before a masculine noun: e.g., terminé el libro (I finished the book). If the noun is feminine, use terminé la. If no noun follows, you usually say terminé (I finished) without el. Common in everyday Spanish and neutral in register.
target_language_example: terminé el informe anoche.
native_language_example: I finished the report last night.

meaning: finished the
additional_notes: Past tense of terminar (to finish/end) followed by a masculine singular noun or clause starting with 'el'. Used to say that someone or something completed or that something came to an end. Context determines whether translated as 'finished' (an action someone completed) or 'ended' (a state or effect stopped). If subject is reflexive (se terminó), it can mean 'ran out' or 'was used up'.
target_language_example: Ella terminó el informe antes del lunes.
native_language_example: She finished the report before Monday.

meaning: "the text is" (used to describe the state or quality of a text).
additional_notes: A simple subject–verb construction: texto (subject) + es (third-person singular of ser). Use to describe inherent or general characteristics of a text (length, legibility, style, quality). For specific or temporary conditions, Spanish speakers might use estar (el texto está borroso), but for qualities and descriptions 'es' with ser is common.
target_language_example: El texto es confuso y necesita revisión.
native_language_example: The text is confusing and needs revision.

meaning: 'you' (object form) with contrast 'not' — used to emphasize that something is for/because of you and not someone/something else.
additional_notes: Ti is the prepositional/object pronoun for 'you' (informal singular). Paired with 'no' it creates contrast: 'por ti, no por...' or 'a ti, no a...' for emphasis ('for you, not someone else' / 'you, not ...'). Common in emotional or corrective statements. Use 'ti' after prepositions (por, para, a) and not before verbs (use 'te' with verbs).
target_language_example: Lo hice por ti, no por ellos.
native_language_example: I did it for you, not for them.

meaning: 'it's easy for you' or 'for you it's easy'.
additional_notes: Used to point out that something is easy from the other person's perspective—often implies contrast (it's not easy for others or for the speaker). Common in spoken Spanish; can express mild reproach or disagreement when followed by a contrasting clause (e.g., 'para ti es fácil decirlo, pero...').
target_language_example: Para ti es fácil hablar, pero yo trabajo todo el día.
native_language_example: It's easy for you to talk, but I work all day.

meaning: 'you either' or 'not even you' used after a negative to add 'you' as another excluded person/thing.
additional_notes: Used with negatives and often appears as part of the structure 'ni a ti' or 'ni por ti' to emphasize that the negative applies to 'you' as well. In Spanish the pronoun 'ti' follows prepositions (a, por) and 'ni' links items in a negative list: e.g. 'ni a ti' = 'not even to you' / 'nor you'. The two words together without a preposition ('ti ni') are less common; learners will mostly see 'ni a ti', 'ni por ti', or 'ni tú' depending on formality.
target_language_example: No le dije nada, ni a ti ni a nadie.
native_language_example: I didn't tell him anything, not you or anyone else.

meaning: 'to you and to' (used to include the person spoken to plus others or another noun)
additional_notes: A common Spanish phrase used to explicitly include the person addressed (tú/te) and someone or something else. Often follows verbs that take an indirect object (e.g., bendecir, aplicar, visitar). Word order can vary ("a ti y a tu familia" or "a tu familia y a ti"); the repeated "a" marks each indirect object. Use when you want to emphasize inclusion of both parties.
target_language_example: Te daré el regalo a ti y a tu hermano.
native_language_example: I will give the gift to you and to your brother.

meaning: used in expressions meaning 'you and (me/another person)' or 'about you and (me/another person)'.
additional_notes: Appears in phrases like 'se trata de ti y de mí' (it's about you and me) or 'cuando se trata de ti y de mí' (when it comes to you and me). Grammatically, 'ti' is the object pronoun for 'you' (informal singular), and the construction often includes 'de' before the persons after verbs like 'tratar(se) de' or prepositions: 'de ti y de mí' = 'of/about you and me'. In casual speech you might also hear 'de ti y mí' but the standard form repeats 'de' for each pronoun.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar más de ti y de mí.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk anymore about you and me.

meaning: 'for you and' (used to indicate something is for you and someone/something/someone else).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'para' (for) with the stressed pronoun 'ti' (you, informal). In examples it's part of constructions like 'para ti y para ellos' or shortened 'para ti y para mí' meaning 'for you and for them/me'. Native speakers sometimes omit the second 'para' when context is clear: 'para ti y mí' (but correct is 'para ti y para mí' or 'para ti y mí' is heard colloquially). 'Ti' is used after prepositions (not 'tu'). Use 'para usted' for formal 'you'.
target_language_example: Compré este regalo para ti y para Ana.
native_language_example: I bought this gift for you and for Ana.

meaning: time with my (family member or person).
additional_notes: Used to say you spend or want to spend time with a specific person (mi papá, mi familia, mi hija). Often appears in phrases with pasar (pasar tiempo con mi...) or pasar algo de tiempo con. Use the possessive + person after 'mi'.
target_language_example: Quiero pasar más tiempo con mi hermana este verano.
native_language_example: I want to spend more time with my sister this summer.

meaning: part of a larger phrase meaning 'time of the...' or 'time to (do) ...' depending on context
additional_notes: ‘Tiempo de lo’ is not usually a standalone phrase; it appears as the start of expressions like 'tiempo de lo' + noun (e.g., 'tiempo de lo mejor') or within clauses such as 'es tiempo de lo que...' More common and complete constructions are 'es tiempo de...' (it's time to/for...) or 'tiempo de' + noun (time for something). Do not use 'tiempo de lo' alone.
target_language_example: Es tiempo de lo importante: decidir el rumbo.
native_language_example: It's time for the important thing: to decide the direction.

meaning: time in the (somewhere or something); used to talk about spending time in a place or doing an activity.
additional_notes: This phrase is a fragment that combines 'tiempo' (time) with a prepositional phrase 'en el' (in the). It commonly appears before a noun (e.g., 'tiempo en el teléfono', 'tiempo en el país') to say how much time someone spends in or on that thing or place. For beginner learners, remember to adjust the article/gender/number: 'en la' (feminine), 'en los'/'en las' (plural) depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Paso mucho tiempo en el parque los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time in the park on weekends.

meaning: time in/on (a place or situation); used to say how long someone spends somewhere or doing something.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of phrases like 'pasar tiempo en la casa', 'tiempo en la naturaleza', or 'trabajar a medio tiempo en la granja'. 'Tiempo' can mean duration (some time) or a specific amount (part-time: 'medio tiempo' / 'a tiempo parcial'). Preposition and article change with the noun (e.g. 'tiempo en el país', 'tiempo en la ciudad').
target_language_example: Pasé mucho tiempo en la biblioteca estudiando.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of time in the library studying.

meaning: a past description using 'tiempo' (weather or time) + 'era' (was) — 'the weather/time was...'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'tiempo' (which can mean 'weather' or 'time') with the imperfect of 'ser' (era) to describe ongoing past states or habitual situations. Context determines whether 'tiempo' refers to the weather (e.g., 'el tiempo era bueno') or a period/condition ('en aquel tiempo era peligroso'). Use 'hacía + tiempo' or other constructions when talking about duration ('desde hacía tiempo').
target_language_example: El tiempo era soleado y cálido durante las vacaciones.
native_language_example: The weather was sunny and warm during the vacation.

meaning: 'the weather was' or 'time was' depending on context; often used to describe past weather or past situations.
additional_notes: In most examples, 'tiempo' means 'weather' and 'fue' is the past (preterite) of 'ser' → 'the weather was'. In other contexts, 'en un tiempo fue' means 'at one time he/she/it was' (referring to a past state or role). Use 'hizo' or 'estuvo' for some weather expressions (e.g., 'hizo calor', 'estuvo nublado'), but 'el tiempo fue' is acceptable for general statements about past weather or past conditions.
target_language_example: El tiempo fue agradable durante las vacaciones.
native_language_example: The weather was pleasant during the vacation.

meaning: a while / some time (usually part of phrases like 'hace tiempo' meaning 'it's been a while')
additional_notes: Alone 'tiempo ha' is not a common fixed phrase in modern spoken Spanish; it appears in more formal or literary constructions (e.g., 'tiempo ha que...' meaning 'it has been some time since...'). More frequently used is 'hace tiempo' or 'ya hace tiempo' to say 'it's been a while.' Use 'tiempo ha que' to introduce an action that started some time ago.
target_language_example: Tiempo ha que no la veo.
native_language_example: It's been a while since I last saw her.

meaning: free time; spare time (time when you're not working or busy).
additional_notes: Used to talk about time available for leisure, hobbies, rest, or personal activities. Can be singular or uncountable in Spanish: no tengo tiempo libre (I don't have free time). Often used with verbs like tener, pasar, dedicar, or usar (e.g., dedicar mi tiempo libre a...).
target_language_example: En mi tiempo libre me gusta leer y caminar.
native_language_example: In my free time I like to read and walk.

meaning: time for the (masculine noun) / time to be ready for
additional_notes: Literal: 'time for the...' followed by a masculine noun (el + noun). Often used to say you have time to do or be ready for something (e.g., 'tiempo para el primer autobús' = enough time to catch the first bus) or to say there's time available for an activity (negative: 'no hay tiempo para el amor'). The exact English translation depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Llegamos temprano, así que hay tiempo para el postre.
native_language_example: We arrived early, so there's time for dessert.

meaning: time for this; (usually) 'no tengo/tenemos tiempo para esto' = 'I/we don't have time for this'.
additional_notes: Commonly used in negative phrases to say you or a group don't have time or patience for something (e.g., a task, argument, or interruption). Can be literal (not enough minutes) or idiomatic (not willing to deal with it). Often appears with verbs like tener (no tengo/ no tenemos) or he esperado (I have waited) to indicate purpose or expectation.
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo para esto ahora; vuelve más tarde.
native_language_example: I don't have time for this right now; come back later.

meaning: part-time (work or study); not full-time.
additional_notes: Used to describe jobs, studies, or commitments with fewer hours than a full schedule. Common opposite: "tiempo completo" (full-time). Can modify nouns: "trabajo a tiempo parcial", "empleo tiempo parcial" or simply "tiempo parcial" as an adjective.
target_language_example: Trabajo a tiempo parcial los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I work part-time on weekends.

meaning: 'time passes' or 'time goes by'.
additional_notes: Used to say that time moves on, often to express that moments go quickly or that situations change with time. Common in general statements (El tiempo pasa) or with adverbs (muy rápido). Word order in Spanish is usually 'el tiempo pasa' (subject + verb).
target_language_example: El tiempo pasa y hay que aprovechar el presente.
native_language_example: Time passes and you have to make the most of the present.

meaning: "time passed" (the time moved by).
additional_notes: Used to say that time went by/how quickly time went. Commonly appears as "el tiempo pasó" followed by an adverb (rápido, deprisa, muy rápido). It's a simple past statement about time elapsing.
target_language_example: El tiempo pasó volando durante las vacaciones.
native_language_example: Time flew during the vacation.

meaning: lost time; time that was wasted or not used productively.
additional_notes: Used to refer to periods when work or progress was delayed or wasted and now must be made up. Common in contexts like work, study, travel delays, or recovery after setbacks. Often appears in verbs like compensar o recuperar (compensate/make up for).
target_language_example: Tenemos que recuperar el tiempo perdido antes de la fecha límite.
native_language_example: We have to make up for the lost time before the deadline.

meaning: time that
additional_notes: Used to refer to a period or amount of time in which something happens or is available. Often appears in relative clauses (el tiempo que tuvimos = the time that we had) and in set phrases telling someone to take as much time as they need (tómate/tómese el tiempo que quieras/necesite). Can be translated as "time that," "time when," or simply "time" depending on context.
target_language_example: Tómate el tiempo que necesites para resolverlo.
native_language_example: Take the time you need to solve it.

meaning: as long as you want / however long you want
additional_notes: Used after a noun (el tiempo) to indicate unlimited or unspecified duration. Common in invitations or permissions: 'Puedes quedarte el tiempo que quieras' = you may stay for as long as you like. Word order can vary (with or without 'aquí' or dropping 'aquí').
target_language_example: Quédate aquí el tiempo que quieras.
native_language_example: Stay here as long as you want.

meaning: to (go) to the store to buy (something).
additional_notes: This phrase appears in sentences with verbs of motion (ir, fui, voy, tengo que ir) and expresses the purpose of going: to buy items. In natural speech Spanish you would usually say 'ir a la tienda a comprar X' or simply 'ir a la tienda' if context implies buying. Use indefinite article or list the items after 'comprar'.
target_language_example: Voy a la tienda a comprar leche y pan.
native_language_example: I'm going to the store to buy milk and bread.

meaning: has nobody / doesn't have anyone
additional_notes: Used to say someone lacks other people for help, company, or support. Often appears in negative sentences with 'no' (no tiene a nadie) meaning 'has no one.' When combined with a relative pronoun it becomes 'no tiene a nadie a quien...' or 'no tiene a nadie con quien...' (no one to whom / no one with whom).
target_language_example: María está triste porque no tiene a nadie con quien salir.
native_language_example: María is sad because she has no one to go out with.

meaning: 'has water' or 'contains water'.
additional_notes: Commonly used with people/places to indicate possession/supply of water (e.g., 'la gente no tiene agua' = people don't have water) or with objects/containers to mean they contain water (e.g., 'este vaso tiene agua'). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., fuel 'having water' = contaminated). Verb 'tiene' is third-person singular of 'tener' (to have).
target_language_example: La ciudad tiene agua potable para todos.
native_language_example: The city has drinking water for everyone.

meaning: 'looks like' or 'has the face of' (used to say someone or something seems to be a certain type/has a certain expression).
additional_notes: Common colloquial expression followed by a noun or adjective (often introduced with 'de'): 'tiene cara de + [sustantivo/adjetivo]'. It describes someone's appearance or the impression their face gives (e.g., trustworthy, criminal, like a parent). Can be used for people or things (e.g., 'tiene cara de lluvia' = 'it looks like rain').
target_language_example: Esa chica tiene cara de buena estudiante.
native_language_example: That girl looks like a good student.

meaning: has almost / doesn't have much (depending on context).
additional_notes: Casi means 'almost' or 'nearly'. With quantities or ages (tiene casi ocho años) it means 'is almost' that amount. With 'no' or negative contexts (no tiene casi nada) it strengthens the negation to mean 'has hardly any' or 'doesn't have much'. Word order and surrounding words determine the exact translation.
target_language_example: Ella tiene casi veinte libros en su estantería.
native_language_example: She has almost twenty books on her shelf.

meaning: is (of) age / has the appropriate age
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something 'has age' in the sense of being old enough or timeless. Often appears as 'tener edad' with qualifiers: 'tener edad suficiente' (to be old enough) or simply 'no tiene edad' (not old enough). Can also describe things as ageless ('no tiene edad').
target_language_example: Ella tiene edad suficiente para conducir.
native_language_example: She is old enough to drive.

meaning: has family (literally: 'he/she/it has family') — used to say someone has relatives or dependents.
additional_notes: Literal present-tense third-person form of 'tener familia'. Can mean having living relatives in a place (e.g., 'tiene familia en Boston') or having family responsibilities/obligations (dependents). Context determines whether it refers to presence, location, or responsibility. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: María tiene familia cerca, así que la visitamos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: María has family nearby, so we visit her on weekends.

meaning: 'to have an idea of' / 'to know about' (used to ask or say whether someone knows or understands something).
additional_notes: Commonly used in questions: ¿Tienes idea de...? or ¿Tiene idea de...? to ask if someone knows, has a clue, or can estimate something. Can be followed by a noun, clause, or infinitive. Formality depends on tú/usted/usteded forms; here 'tiene' is the usted/él/ella form (he/she/you-formal).
target_language_example: ¿Tiene idea de cuánto cuesta el pasaje?
native_language_example: Do you (formal) have any idea how much the ticket costs?

meaning: has at least / has no fewer than (a minimum quantity).
additional_notes: Used to state a minimum amount or number someone/something has. Often appears in negative constructions (no tiene menos de) to emphasize that the quantity is equal to or greater than the number given. English equivalents: "has at least", "has no fewer than", or "not less than."
target_language_example: Él no tiene menos de cien euros en su cuenta.
native_language_example: He has at least a hundred euros in his account.

meaning: 'has nothing' or part of negation meaning 'there is nothing' / 'doesn't have anything'.
additional_notes: Spanish usually expresses negation with 'no' before the verb: 'no tiene nada' = 'has nothing' / 'doesn't have anything'. In some examples above 'tiene nada' appears after 'no' or in conditional phrases like 'si no tiene nada' ('if you have nothing' / 'if there is nothing against it'). Alone, 'tiene nada' without 'no' is nonstandard for negation. Common uses: describe absence (no tiene nada de especial = it has nothing special) or ask/offer (si no tiene nada en contra = if you have nothing against it).
target_language_example: No tiene nada que perder.
native_language_example: He has nothing to lose.

tiene nada que ver con el

target_language_multi_word_term: tiene nada que ver con el
meaning: has nothing to do with the
additional_notes: A negative expression used to say one thing is unrelated to another. More common, grammatically correct forms are 'no tiene nada que ver con el' or 'no tiene nada que ver con él' (with accent on él when referring to 'him' or 'it' as a pronoun). In casual speech, the initial 'no' is sometimes dropped in clipped fragments, but beginners should include it: 'No tiene nada que ver con...' Follow with a noun or pronoun.
target_language_example: No tiene nada que ver con el problema del mes pasado.
native_language_example: It has nothing to do with last month's problem.

tiene nada que ver con la

target_language_multi_word_term: tiene nada que ver con la
meaning: has nothing to do with the (feminine noun that follows).
additional_notes: Use to say two things are unrelated. Typical structure: no + tener + nada que ver con + (el/la/lo + noun or phrase). In spoken Spanish you may also hear "no tiene nada que ver" (without article) or the masculine form "tiene nada que ver con el...". The example phrase includes "la" because the following noun is feminine (la música, la vida, la verdad).
target_language_example: Eso no tiene nada que ver con la película que vimos ayer.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with the movie we saw yesterday.

meaning: has any (none)
additional_notes: A negative construction used with 'no' before the verb: 'no tiene ningún...' = 'doesn't have any' or 'has no'. Native order: 'no' + verb + 'ningún' + noun. 'Ningún' shortens from 'ninguno' and is used before masculine singular nouns (e.g., ningún valor, ningún sentido).
target_language_example: Esta casa no tiene ningún jardín.
native_language_example: This house doesn't have any garden.

meaning: there's a remedy / it can be fixed; (negated) there's no solution / it's hopeless
additional_notes: Used to say whether a problem or situation can be remedied. Often appears in negative sentences (no tiene remedio) meaning 'there's no cure/solution' or 'it's hopeless'. Can be literal (medical remedy) or figurative (skills, situations).
target_language_example: Mi coche antiguo no tiene remedio; es mejor comprar uno nuevo.
native_language_example: My old car has no fix; it's better to buy a new one.

meaning: 'is completely right' or 'you/he/she is absolutely right' (literally: 'has all the')
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say someone is entirely correct. Often followed by razón (tiene toda la razón). Can be used formally or informally; subject can be usted/él/ella/one's name. In English you usually translate the full idea ('is completely right') rather than the literal words.
target_language_example: Tiene toda la razón sobre el problema del presupuesto.
native_language_example: He is completely right about the budget issue.

meaning: he/she/it has a job; is employed (or 'has work').
additional_notes: Third-person singular of 'tener trabajo'. Used to say someone is employed or has work. Can refer to a steady job (trabajo fijo) or work in general. Context and negatives indicate employment status: 'no tiene trabajo' = unemployed. Pronoun subject is understood from context (él/ella/usted).
target_language_example: Mi vecina tiene trabajo nuevo desde enero.
native_language_example: My neighbor has a new job since January.

meaning: they have until / they have up to (a deadline or limit).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a deadline or time limit someone has to do something (tienen hasta + time/date). In the informal exclamation example (¡me tienen hasta los huevos!) the structure is different: 'tener hasta' expresses being fed up — this is slang and not the same literal meaning.
target_language_example: Tienen hasta el viernes para entregar el proyecto.
native_language_example: They have until Friday to turn in the project.

meaning: they have (followed by a feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb tener (tienen = they have) plus the feminine plural definite article las. Use when describing possession or characteristics of feminine plural nouns (las piernas, las orejas, las vacaciones, las llaves, etc.). Word order: 'tienen' + 'las' + noun. For masculine plural nouns you'd see 'tienen los'.
target_language_example: Ellas tienen las mochilas nuevas.
native_language_example: They have the new backpacks.

meaning: they have a lot
additional_notes: Compositional phrase from tienen (“have”) + mucho (“a lot”/“much”). Tienen is the third-person plural form of tener, so it can mean “they have” or “you all have” (ustedes have), depending on context. It is often followed by que + infinitive or another phrase, as in tienen mucho que aprender (“they have a lot to learn”).
target_language_example: Ellos tienen mucho trabajo hoy.
native_language_example: They have a lot of work today.

meaning: 'you have any idea (about/of)'; often used in negative sentences as 'you have no idea (about/of)'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone's knowledge or awareness of something. Commonly appears in negative form 'no tienes idea de...' meaning 'you have no idea about...' or 'you don't know...'. Can be followed by a clause (cómo..., en qué..., lo que...) or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: No tienes idea de lo difícil que fue para mí.
native_language_example: You have no idea how hard it was for me.

meaning: you only have to / you just have to; you have more than (in some contexts).
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the structure 'no tienes más que + infinitive' meaning 'you only need to / you just have to (do something)'. It can also appear in affirmative sentences meaning 'you have more than' (e.g., 'tienes más que suficiente' = 'you have more than enough'). Context and presence of 'no' determine meaning.
target_language_example: No tienes más que llamarme si necesitas ayuda.
native_language_example: You only have to call me if you need help.

meaning: 'you have nothing' (informal spoken Spanish where negative can appear after the verb)
additional_notes: Literally 'you have nothing.' In standard Spanish, a negation typically requires the negative word before the verb (No tienes nada = You don't have anything / You have nothing). In some colloquial contexts speakers may drop the initial 'no' but the examples here include both 'No tienes nada' and 'Tienes nada' used in speech. Use 'No tienes nada' to be clear. Can be followed by clauses (No tienes nada que hacer = You have nothing to do).
target_language_example: No tienes nada que perder si lo intentas.
native_language_example: You have nothing to lose if you try it.

meaning: You have no idea (how/what/etc.).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone does not understand or cannot imagine the extent/quality of something. Often followed by an adjective + que (e.g., 'lo doloroso que...'), a noun clause introduced by 'que' ('lo que...'), or an infinitive phrase. Tone can be neutral or emphatic/sympathetic depending on context.
target_language_example: No tienes ni idea de lo difícil que fue tomar esa decisión.
native_language_example: You have no idea how hard it was to make that decision.

meaning: 'you have none' or 'you don't have any' (used after negative context)
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a negative word like 'no' (e.g., 'No tienes ninguna...') to say you do not have any obligation/opportunity/reason/possibility. In English we often say 'you don't have any' or 'you have no...'. The noun that follows (obligación, oportunidad, razón, posibilidad) completes the phrase.
target_language_example: No tienes ninguna razón para preocuparte.
native_language_example: You have no reason to worry.

meaning: you have (all/whole) — used to emphasize possession of something (e.g., reason, attention, life).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before feminine nouns (toda la razón, toda la atención) or before expressions like 'toda una vida' to add emphasis. It literally means 'you have all/the whole' and is used to stress completeness or totality. Context determines the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Tienes toda la paciencia del mundo.
native_language_example: You have all the patience in the world.

meaning: solid ground; dry land (as opposed to water or a small boat).
additional_notes: Used when contrasting land with the sea, river, or floating platforms. Common in contexts like sailing, arriving on shore, or saying someone won't step onto land. Can be literal (physical ground) or figurative (stable situation).
target_language_example: Después de horas en el bote, por fin vimos tierra firme.
native_language_example: After hours in the boat, we finally saw solid ground / land.

meaning: informal: 'the guy/that guy' (referring to a man previously mentioned or known).
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken Spanish to refer to a man ('tipo' = guy, bloke). Often followed by a relative clause introduced by 'que' (e.g., 'el tipo del que te hablé' = 'the guy I told you about'). Can be used alone with context: 'el tipo del bar' = 'the guy from the bar'. Tone is informal; not rude but casual.
target_language_example: El tipo del que me hablaste trabaja aquí.
native_language_example: The guy you told me about works here.

meaning: 'tough guy' or 'hard man' — someone who is strong, tough, or tries to seem intimidating.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person (often male) who is physically tough, fearless, or trying to act macho. Can be neutral, admiring, teasing, or slightly critical depending on tone and context. Not highly formal; common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: No seas tan tipo duro, pide ayuda si la necesitas.
native_language_example: Don't act so tough, ask for help if you need it.

meaning: 'that guy/person was' — informal way to say 'the guy was' or 'this person was' (followed by a description).
additional_notes: Tipo here is an informal noun meaning 'guy, person' (similar to 'dude' or 'guy' in English). Era is the imperfect of ser ('was'). Together they introduce a description or characteristic of someone in the past (e.g., 'that guy was an idiot'). Common in spoken Spanish. Use with a clear subject (este/ese/el) or a name.
target_language_example: Ese tipo era muy confiado, pero se equivocó.
native_language_example: That guy was very confident, but he was wrong.

meaning: the guy is / that guy is (used to describe a man's state or situation)
additional_notes: Tipo (colloquial) = 'guy' or 'person'. When followed by está + adjective/phrase, it describes the man's condition, situation, or behavior. Often informal; context determines tone (neutral, negative, emphatic). 'Ese tipo está...' = 'That guy is...'.
target_language_example: Ese tipo está agotado después del viaje.
native_language_example: That guy is exhausted after the trip.

meaning: 'the most ... guy/person' — used to make superlative descriptions about a person (e.g., the smartest guy, the luckiest person).
additional_notes: Combines 'tipo' (guy/person) with a superlative adjective introduced after 'más'. Common in spoken Spanish. Can be used positively or negatively depending on the adjective (brillante, limpio, suertudo, espeluznante, listo). When negated (e.g., 'no es el tipo más listo') it softens or downplays the quality. Followed by an adjective that agrees in gender/number if a different noun is used (e.g., 'la persona más lista').
target_language_example: Es el tipo más amable del vecindario.
native_language_example: He's the kindest guy in the neighborhood.

meaning: types of flowers / kinds of flowers.
additional_notes: A simple, literal phrase used to talk about different varieties or kinds of flowers. Common in gardening and descriptions of what blooms in a season. 'Tipos' means 'types/kinds'; 'flores' means 'flowers'. Plural in Spanish matches English plural.
target_language_example: En el invernadero hay muchos tipos de flores raras.
native_language_example: In the greenhouse there are many types of rare flowers.

meaning: pulls on / pulls (something) from
additional_notes: Commonly used with objects: 'tira de' + noun means 'pull (on) (that object)'. Can be literal (pulling a rope, drawer, zipper) or figurative in some contexts (e.g., 'tira de hilos' = 'pulls strings'). If subject is plural use 'tiran de'. For commands use 'tira' (informal tú) or 'tire' (usted).
target_language_example: Tira de la cuerda para abrir la puerta.
native_language_example: Pull the rope to open the door.

meaning: to throw away, to discard (when followed by a feminine noun); can also mean to pull or to shoot depending on context
additional_notes: Tirar is a versatile verb. When used with 'la' plus a feminine noun (e.g., 'tirar la basura'), it commonly means 'to throw away' or 'to take out.' Context changes the meaning: 'tirar la cadena' = 'flush the toilet', 'tirar la puerta' (rare) = 'to pull/throw the door', 'tirar la toalla' = an idiomatic expression meaning 'to give up' (literally 'to throw in the towel'). Remember the object after 'la' determines the exact translation.
target_language_example: Voy a tirar la basura esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to throw away the trash tonight.

meaning: to fart (colloquial/informal)
additional_notes: Very informal and slightly crude phrase used to say someone passes gas. Literally 'to throw oneself a fart' — common in spoken Spanish. Use with friends or in casual contexts; avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no debería tirarme un pedo en público.
native_language_example: Sorry, I shouldn't fart in public.

meaning: a shot in the (something) / a hit in the (something) — part of a phrase meaning a shot taken inside a specific place or area
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it typically appears as part of a longer expression like "tiro en la pierna" (a shot in the leg) or "tiro en la portería" (a shot on goal). "Tiro" = shot (from a gun or in sports), and "en la" = "in the (feminine noun)". You will need a feminine noun after "la" to finish the phrase (e.g., la pierna, la portería, la cabeza).
target_language_example: Recibió un tiro en la pierna durante el accidente.
native_language_example: He received a shot in the leg during the accident.

meaning: dyed (someone's) hair (a specific color).
additional_notes: Past simple (pretérito) of teñir (to dye). Construction: 'tiñó el pelo de + color' or 'tiñó el pelo de + persona' can mean he/she dyed someone's hair. Often used with a color (ej. 'tiñó el pelo de rojo') or with reflexive/indirect object to indicate who changed hair color (e.g. 'se tiñó el pelo de rubio' = 'he/she dyed his/her hair blonde').
target_language_example: Ella tiñó el pelo de azul para la fiesta.
native_language_example: She dyed her hair blue for the party.

meaning: 'the towel is' (phrase used to describe a towel).
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed expression but the combination of the noun toalla (towel) with the verb es (third-person singular of ser). Use it when describing a towel's qualities (color, texture, size, etc.). Ser (es) is used for inherent or defining characteristics like color or material; for temporary states (e.g., wet) use estar: La toalla está mojada.
target_language_example: La toalla es muy suave y blanca.
native_language_example: The towel is very soft and white.

meaning: to play the violin.
additional_notes: A common verb + noun phrase: tocar + instrumento means 'to play' (a musical instrument). Use tocar el violín for playing the violin; change the instrument after 'tocar' (e.g., tocar el piano). Can be used with modal verbs (puede tocar) and with direct object or with indefinite articles omitted.
target_language_example: Mi hermana aprende a tocar el violín este año.
native_language_example: My sister is learning to play the violin this year.

meaning: to annoy, bother, or pester (strong/informal slang).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar in many Spanish-speaking areas (literally 'to touch the balls'). Used to say someone or something is irritating, getting on your nerves, or making things difficult. Can be directed at people or situations. Use only in casual contexts with friends; avoid in formal settings.
target_language_example: Deja de tocar las pelotas y concéntrate en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Stop messing around/annoying me and focus on your work.

meaning: to touch the
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'to touch' followed by a masculine plural noun (los). Used for physical contact: tocar los + body part or object (e.g., tocar los pies, tocar los cables). Can be reflexive/impersonal in some contexts (Sentí algo tocar los pies = I felt something touch my feet). In informal slang, tocar los huevos (or huevos) means to bother/annoy or to mess around (vulgar). Watch context: can be a warning (No tocar los cables = Do not touch the cables) or sexual/colloquial when referring to body parts.
target_language_example: No tocar los enchufes: peligro.
native_language_example: Do not touch the plugs: danger.

meaning: all one's life
additional_notes: Used to refer to the whole span of a person's life. In everyday speech, it can also be used more loosely to mean 'for a very long time' or 'forever,' depending on context.
target_language_example: Vivió en ese pueblo toda la vida.
native_language_example: She lived in that town all her life.
