meaning: 'all my life' or 'my whole life'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that has lasted for the speaker's entire life or a strong feeling/experience that feels lifelong. Can be used literally (time span) or emphatically (I've wanted this forever). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: He soñado con viajar a Europa toda mi vida.
native_language_example: I've dreamed of traveling to Europe all my life.

meaning: with all his/her/their strength; very forcefully or with maximum effort.
additional_notes: Used to say someone uses their full physical strength or that a group exerts all available power (can be literal physical strength or figurative like military/political force). Gender/number adjusts with possessive (su). Common in past and present actions: 'luchó con toda su fuerza', 'lo levantó con toda su fuerza'.
target_language_example: Ella empujó la puerta con toda su fuerza.
native_language_example: She pushed the door with all her strength.

meaning: 'still was' — indicates that someone/something continued to be in a certain state or condition in the past.
additional_notes: Used with the imperfect tense (era) to talk about an ongoing or repeated past state that continued up to a point. Often followed by age, role, time of day, or a condition (e.g., joven, estudiante, de noche). Common in sentences like 'cuando todavía era...' (when I/he/she was still...).
target_language_example: Cuando me mudé, todavía era estudiante.
native_language_example: When I moved, I was still a student.

meaning: 'still her' or 'still (verb) her' — indicates that someone continues to feel or do something toward a female person.
additional_notes: Todavía = still/yet. 'La' is the feminine direct object pronoun (her). This phrase appears before or after the verb depending on verb form: with conjugated verbs, the pronoun usually goes before the verb (e.g., 'la quiero' = I love her); with infinitives or gerunds it attaches to the verb (e.g., 'seguir buscándola'). Translation into natural English often reorders words: 'I still love her', 'He still needs her.'
target_language_example: Aunque pasó el tiempo, todavía la extraño.
native_language_example: Even though time passed, I still miss her.

meaning: not yet
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase used to indicate that something expected or planned has not happened up to now but may happen in the future. Often placed before the verb (Todavía no ha llegado) or at the start of the sentence. Can be used with present perfect, present, or other tenses.
target_language_example: Todavía no he terminado el informe.
native_language_example: I haven't finished the report yet.

meaning: in any case; regardless; anyway.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a comment that remains true despite what was said before or to move the conversation on. Similar to 'de todas formas' or 'en cualquier caso'. It can appear at the start or end of a sentence: 'Todo caso, ...' or '... todo caso.'
target_language_example: Todo caso, mejor que llegues temprano.
native_language_example: In any case, it's better that you arrive early.

meaning: all day
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens, continues, or is true during the entire day. It commonly goes after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Estuve ocupado todo el día.
native_language_example: I was busy all day.

meaning: everyone
additional_notes: A very common way to refer to all people in general. Although it refers to many people, it usually takes a singular verb in Spanish: todo el mundo sabe, todo el mundo quiere.
target_language_example: Todo el mundo quiere ser feliz.
native_language_example: Everyone wants to be happy.

meaning: all the time; the whole time
additional_notes: Used to say something happens continuously or repeatedly over a period of time. Can mean 'constantly' (habitual action) or 'the entire time' (throughout an event). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Llueve todo el rato en primavera.
native_language_example: It rains all the time in spring.

meaning: all the time
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very often or continuously. In everyday speech, it often means 'constantly' or 'very often,' not necessarily every single second.
target_language_example: Mi hermano habla de fútbol todo el tiempo.
native_language_example: My brother talks about soccer all the time.

meaning: 'all this time' or 'the whole time' (referring to a continuous period up to now).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has been happening or been true throughout a period leading up to the present. Can modify actions, states, or people (e.g., 'he estado...' / 'estuvieron...'). Often appears in contexts of surprise, reproach, or clarification.
target_language_example: Lo has sabido todo este tiempo y no me lo dijiste.
native_language_example: You knew it all this time and you didn't tell me.

meaning: all this
additional_notes: Used to refer to a set of things, ideas, events, or the situation just mentioned or about to be discussed. Can express summary, reaction, or suspicion (e.g., "all this seems..." or "all of this smells like..."). Common in both neutral and emotional contexts.
target_language_example: Todo esto me parece demasiado complicado.
native_language_example: All of this seems too complicated to me.

meaning: everyone
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial way to say "todo el mundo" (the standard phrase). Used to refer to all people in a group or generally. Common in spoken Spanish in many regions.
target_language_example: Todo mundo sabe la verdad.
native_language_example: Everyone knows the truth.

meaning: everything before / everything earlier; 'todo' = everything, 'antes' = before/earlier (meaning depends on context).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the combination of todo (everything/all) and antes (before/earlier). Meaning changes with sentence structure: 1) 'todo antes de + noun/infinitive' = 'everything before [something]' or 'before doing something' (e.g., 'todo antes de recurrir' = 'after trying everything before turning to a specialist'). 2) 'escucha todo antes de...' = 'listen to everything before...'; 3) 'sacarlo todo antes' = 'take everything out first/earlier/first'. For deadlines, 'terminar todo antes del viernes' = 'finish everything before Friday.' Use word order and prepositions to clarify exact meaning.
target_language_example: Lee todo antes de decidir qué comprar.
native_language_example: Read everything before deciding what to buy.

meaning: 'everything' or 'all' (followed by 'control', 'cuidado', etc.) — used in phrases like 'todo bajo control' = everything under control.
additional_notes: This phrase usually appears as part of a longer expression: 'todo bajo + noun' (e.g., 'todo bajo control', 'todo bajo control', 'todo bajo llave'). It means that all things/situations are under the state indicated by the noun (under control, under lock, etc.). Common in reassuring statements. Word order: 'todo' (all/everything) + 'bajo' (under) + noun.
target_language_example: No te preocupes; tengo todo bajo control.
native_language_example: Don't worry; I have everything under control.

meaning: 'everything okay' / 'all good' / 'it's (going to be) fine'.
additional_notes: Used both as a casual greeting (like 'all good?' or 'you okay?') and as a reassuring statement (like 'everything is fine' or 'it will be fine'). Context and intonation decide whether it's a question or an affirmation. Common in everyday spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo bien, ya está solucionado.
native_language_example: Don't worry, all good, it's already fixed.

meaning: everything in/on the (masculine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining 'todo' (everything) + 'en' (in/on) + the masculine singular article 'el' before a noun: todo en el + [noun]. Used to say that all items or everything is located inside or on something (e.g., el porche, el piso, el libro, el mostrador). Agreement is with the implied noun; if the noun is feminine use 'todo en la' (or 'toda' with feminine sense).
target_language_example: Dejé todo en el porche.
native_language_example: I left everything on the porch.

meaning: 'everything' or 'all of it' (followed by a feminine singular noun or place)
additional_notes: A combination of todo (everything/all) + en la (in the). Used when referring to everything being located 'in the' something (feminine noun like maleta, enfermería, tienda, estación, mesa, película). Context determines whether it means 'everything is in the [place]' or 'everything on the [surface]'. If the noun after 'la' is omitted in casual speech, the listener infers it from context.
target_language_example: Está todo en la caja.
native_language_example: Everything is in the box.

meaning: used in phrases like "Lo mejor/peor de todo es que..." to introduce the main point: "the best/worst part is that..."
additional_notes: Not used by itself; appears in fixed expressions such as "Lo mejor de todo es que..." (the best part is that...) or "Lo peor de todo es que..." (the worst part is that...). It introduces the main or most important detail, often followed by a clause explaining that detail.
target_language_example: Lo mejor de todo es que podemos intentarlo de nuevo.
native_language_example: The best part is that we can try again.

meaning: everything is a (single) ...; used to say that everything is characterized by something (often negative or dismissive).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun (chiste, desastre, truco, etc.). Expresses a generalization about the whole situation or life. Tone can be ironic, critical, or resigned depending on context. In English often rendered as “it's all a …” or “everything is a …”.
target_language_example: A veces pienso que todo es un malentendido.
native_language_example: Sometimes I think it's all a misunderstanding.

meaning: 'all that is' / 'all of that is' — used to comment on or describe a whole situation or set of things previously mentioned.
additional_notes: Use to refer back to things already mentioned (todo eso = all of that/all those things). Often followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or clause (e.g., verdad, culpa vuestra, posible para ti). Can express judgment, explanation, or summary. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Todo eso es parte de mi historia.
native_language_example: All of that is part of my story.

meaning: 'all together' or 'everything together' (grouped or at once).
additional_notes: Used to say that items or people are combined/assembled as one group, done at the same time, or not separated. Context decides nuance: can mean physically mixed together, acting as a single unit, or happening simultaneously. Often interchangeable with 'todo junto y mezclado' (all mixed together) or 'todos juntos' (everyone together) depending on number and context.
target_language_example: Puse los platos todo junto en la caja.
native_language_example: I put the plates all together in the box.

meaning: the exact opposite; completely the opposite.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the reverse of what was said, expected, or desired. Can stand alone (¡Todo lo contrario!) or be followed by a noun or clause (es todo lo contrario, todo lo contrario a...).
target_language_example: Pensé que era amable, pero hace todo lo contrario.
native_language_example: I thought he was kind, but he does the exact opposite.

meaning: everything else; the rest (of things or matters).
additional_notes: Used to refer to all other items, concerns, or aspects besides what was already mentioned. Common in everyday speech. Can refer to concrete things or abstract matters (e.g., worries, details).
target_language_example: Preocúpate por lo importante y deja todo lo demás para después.
native_language_example: Worry about the important things and leave everything else for later.

meaning: at most; at best (indicating a maximum or best-case limit).
additional_notes: Used to give an upper limit or to downplay something — similar to 'como máximo' or English 'at most' / 'at best'. Often appears before a number, short time, or a minimal description.
target_language_example: Puedo llegar tarde, todo lo más cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I might be late, at most five minutes.

meaning: as much as possible; everything one can do
additional_notes: Used to say someone is making the greatest effort or doing all they can in a situation. Common with verbs like hacer, intentar, estar (haciendo). Can be followed by a verb (hacer todo lo posible para + infinitive) or stand alone (Haré todo lo posible).
target_language_example: Haré todo lo posible para llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I'll do everything I can to arrive on time.

meaning: everything that
additional_notes: Used to refer to the whole of something, usually followed by a clause: todo lo que + verb. It introduces whatever makes up the complete set: 'everything that...' or 'all that...'.
target_language_example: Todo lo que necesito está aquí.
native_language_example: Everything I need is here.

meaning: everything you must/should (do); all that you owe/should pay (context-dependent).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'todo lo que' (everything that) with 'debes' (you must / you owe). Meaning depends on context: with verbs, it indicates obligations or things one should do (e.g., 'todo lo que debes hacer' = everything you must do). With amounts or debts, it can mean everything you owe (e.g., 'todo lo que debes pagar'). Often appears as part of a longer phrase; by itself it feels incomplete and usually requires additional words to specify what is owed or must be done.
target_language_example: Haz todo lo que debes para aprobar el curso.
native_language_example: Do everything you must to pass the course.

meaning: all I can (do/say)
additional_notes: Used to limit what someone can do or say — often followed by a verb (hacer, decir, etc.). Common in statements explaining limits or abilities: 'Eso es todo lo que puedo hacer' = that's all I can do. Can be shortened in speech to 'todo lo que puedo' without repeating the verb.
target_language_example: Te di todo lo que puedo ofrecer.
native_language_example: I gave you all I can offer.

meaning: 'everything/whatever that I have always (wanted)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to something (often a person or thing) that has been desired or wished for for a long time. Commonly followed by verbs like querer (quise, he querido) or tener. Can be used with different subjects (es todo lo que siempre he querido = it's everything I've always wanted).
target_language_example: Tenerte a mi lado es todo lo que siempre quise.
native_language_example: Having you by my side is everything I always wanted.

meaning: all I have to (do/say); everything I need to
additional_notes: Used to introduce or summarize the things someone must do or say. Commonly followed by an infinitive (hacer, decir, etc.) or a clause. In spoken English it often corresponds to 'all I have to say' or 'all I have to do.' Frequently appears in phrases like 'Eso es todo lo que tengo que decir.'
target_language_example: Eso es todo lo que tengo que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: That's all I have to do today.

meaning: all (that) he/she/they/you have to
additional_notes: Used to introduce a minimal list of required actions or obligations: 'todo lo que tiene que hacer' = 'everything he/she has to do' or simply 'all you have to do'. The verb after 'tiene' often continues with 'que' + infinitive (tiene que hacer = has to do). Subject can be explicit (Tom) or implied by context; English translation may become 'all you have to do', 'all he has to do', or 'everything [name] has to do.'
target_language_example: Todo lo que tiene que hacer hoy es descansar.
native_language_example: All he has to do today is rest.

meaning: 'all or nothing' — a situation with only two extreme outcomes (complete success or total failure).
additional_notes: Used to describe high-stakes situations with no middle ground. Can stand alone as an exclamation (e.g., expressing a risky choice). Equivalent to English 'all or nothing.'
target_language_example: Vamos a intentarlo: es todo o nada.
native_language_example: Let's try it: it's all or nothing.

meaning: 'everything has' (used to start a perfect-tense phrase about everything)
additional_notes: Combines 'todo' (everything) + reflexive pronoun 'se' + auxiliary 'ha' (from haber). It introduces a statement in the present perfect about a change or completed action affecting everything: e.g. 'todo se ha vuelto...' (everything has become...), 'todo se ha ido' (everything has gone). The exact meaning depends on the past participle or verb that follows. Common in neutral and informal speech; can be followed by idiomatic endings like 'ido al carajo'.
target_language_example: Todo se ha vuelto más complicado.
native_language_example: Everything has become more complicated.

meaning: 'everything returns' or 'everything goes back'.
additional_notes: Used to say that things return to a previous state (zero, normality, memory, etc.). Often followed by 'a' + noun or phrase (e.g., 'a cero', 'a la normalidad', 'a su lugar'). Common in both literal and figurative contexts.
target_language_example: Después del problema, todo vuelve a la normalidad.
native_language_example: After the problem, everything goes back to normal.

meaning: every weekend / every end (of something) — usually 'every weekend'.
additional_notes: Commonly used in Spain and Latin America to mean 'every weekend' (short for 'todos los fines de semana'). It can also appear before other nouns (e.g., 'todos los fines del mes') to mean 'every end of [period]'. In casual speech speakers often say the full phrase 'todos los fines de semana' for clarity.
target_language_example: Vamos al cine todos los fines.
native_language_example: We go to the movies every weekend.

meaning: all of them; every one of them.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific group of people or things previously mentioned or obvious from context. Slightly more emphatic or formal than just "todos"; can be used interchangeably with "todos" in many cases, especially before a verb.
target_language_example: No todos ellos querían venir al viaje.
native_language_example: Not all of them wanted to come on the trip.

meaning: literally 'everyone has' — used with a past participle to mean 'everyone has (done something)'.
additional_notes: Combines 'todos' (everyone) with the auxiliary 'haber' in the present perfect (han). Use before a past participle: todos han + [past participle]. Common for recent or relevant past actions (e.g., 'todos han votado' = everyone has voted). Not a fixed idiom — it's a grammatical structure.
target_language_example: Todos han terminado la tarea.
native_language_example: Everyone has finished the homework.

meaning: to everyone (they/people) — used to say that something is liked or applies to everyone.
additional_notes: Common structure: 'A + (indirect object) + les + [verb phrase]'. 'A todos' indicates 'to everyone' and 'les' is the indirect object pronoun referring back to 'todos'. Used with verbs like gustar, encantar, agradar (verbs that take an indirect object). In spoken Spanish you may also hear 'a todos' without repeating 'les' in some regions, but the standard neutral form includes both ('A todos les gusta...').
target_language_example: A todos les interesa la música.
native_language_example: Everyone is interested in music.

meaning: all the
additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean 'all the.' It can refer to a group of men or a mixed-gender group. For feminine plural nouns, use 'todas las.' In some common expressions like 'todos los días,' it is often translated naturally as 'every' ('every day').
target_language_example: Todos los estudiantes están aquí.
native_language_example: All the students are here.

meaning: all of us; every one of us.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker plus other people as a group. Interchangeable with 'todos' or 'todos nosotros' for emphasis. Common in formal and informal contexts. Can be followed by verbs in first-person plural (nosotros).
target_language_example: Todos nosotros iremos al museo mañana.
native_language_example: All of us will go to the museum tomorrow.

meaning: 'we all know why' (used to state that everyone understands the reason for something).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by 'qué' + verb (por qué + ...). 'Todos sabemos por' is often used to introduce a reason that is obvious or shared knowledge. Variations include 'todos sabemos por qué lo hiciste' (we all know why you did it). Formality: neutral; can be used in spoken and written Spanish. The verb that follows may change for number/person (e.g., 'hiciste', 'hicisteis').
target_language_example: Todos sabemos por qué te fuiste tan temprano.
native_language_example: We all know why you left so early.

meaning: 'all of you' (plural you).
additional_notes: Used to address a group of people formally or informally in many Spanish-speaking regions. Equivalent to 'ustedes' but emphasizes 'all' members of the group. In Spain people sometimes use 'vosotros' (informal) instead of 'ustedes'. Verb agreement is third person plural (e.g., 'ustedes son', 'caerán').
target_language_example: Todos ustedes tienen que escuchar.
native_language_example: All of you have to listen.

meaning: 'we all are going to' or 'we're all going to' (future plan/statement about a group including speaker).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a future action or state that includes the speaker and others. Often followed by the infinitive verb or a clause introduced by a conjugated verb (e.g., 'a hacer', 'a estar', 'a buscar'). Common in everyday speech. Note subject 'todos' (all of us) implies plural first-person; you can also hear 'todos vamos a...' shortened in casual speech to 'todos vamos a...' or 'vamos a...' when context already implies everyone.
target_language_example: Todos vamos a salir mañana temprano.
native_language_example: We're all going to leave early tomorrow.

meaning: every single one; each and every one.
additional_notes: Emphasizes that no person or item is excluded. Stronger than just "todos" or "cada uno" alone. Commonly used before a noun or pronoun (e.g., "todos y cada uno de ustedes", "todos y cada uno de los sabores") or on its own for emphasis.
target_language_example: Invité a todos y cada uno de mis amigos a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I invited every single one of my friends to the party.

meaning: has/takes a little (drink/food).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone drinks or takes a small amount of something (often beverages like coffee or wine). 'Toma' is the third-person singular of 'tomar' (he/she/you formal takes) or an imperative (toma = take! for tú). Context shows third-person habitual action ('he/she/you often has a little') or a casual offer/command. Use with de + noun to indicate what is taken (e.g., 'toma un poco de vino').
target_language_example: Él toma un poco de vino después de la cena.
native_language_example: He has a little wine after dinner.

meaning: taken a
additional_notes: A fragment meaning the past participle tomado plus the feminine singular article una. It usually appears with haber, as in he/has/ha tomado una..., and is followed by a feminine noun. With some nouns, English uses a different verb: tomado una decisión is usually translated as made a decision, not taken a decision.
target_language_example: He tomado una decisión importante.
native_language_example: I have made an important decision.

meaning: taking the
additional_notes: A compositional phrase. tomando is the -ing form of tomar, and el means "the" before a singular masculine noun. The exact translation depends on the noun that follows: tomando el autobús = "taking the bus," but tomando el café = "drinking the coffee." It is often used with estar to describe an action in progress.
target_language_example: Estoy tomando el autobús al trabajo.
native_language_example: I'm taking the bus to work.

meaning: taking/doing/having a (masculine singular noun) — progressive action: 'having a' (drink/meal), 'taking a' (class/bath/day off), etc.
additional_notes: Present participle form of tomar + indefinite article un. Used to describe an ongoing action involving a masculine noun: e.g. taking a class (curso), having a drink (trago), taking a bath (baño) or taking time off (días). Can appear without a subject (Tomando un helado) as a clipped caption. Adjust article/gender for feminine nouns (tomando una).
target_language_example: Estoy tomando un café mientras trabajo.
native_language_example: I'm having a coffee while I work.

meaning: 'taking a' (used before a feminine noun), e.g. 'taking a nap' or 'taking a photo'.
additional_notes: Present participle (estar + tomando) means 'is/are taking' or 'taking' in progressive actions. 'Una' is the feminine indefinite article, so the noun that follows should be feminine (una siesta, una foto/una fotografía). In Spanish you can drop the noun if context makes it clear: "Estoy tomando una" can mean "I'm taking one" (e.g., a nap or a photo) when listeners know what's being taken.
target_language_example: Estoy tomando una foto ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I'm taking a photo right now.

meaning: to take a breath; to get some fresh air; to breathe (often briefly step outside to refresh yourself).
additional_notes: Commonly used both literally (to inhale or pause to breathe) and idiomatically (to take a short break, step outside to clear your head). Can be reflexive in some contexts (tomarse un aire/tomar aire un momento). Often used when someone is stressed, upset, or after physical exertion.
target_language_example: Voy a salir cinco minutos a tomar aire.
native_language_example: I'm going out for five minutes to get some fresh air.

meaning: to have/get something (often a drink or a small bite); to take something (from a place).
additional_notes: Common, versatile phrase. Context decides meaning: in social settings it usually means 'to have a drink' or 'grab a bite' (e.g., Vamos a tomar algo = Let's get a drink/something to eat). With a direct object or location it can mean 'to take something' (e.g., tomar algo del auto = take something from the car).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres tomar algo en la cafetería después del trabajo?
native_language_example: Do you want to get something (to drink/eat) at the café after work?

meaning: to take a seat; to sit down.
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used to tell someone to sit down or to describe the action of sitting. Can be used formally and informally (e.g., in instructions, announcements, or everyday speech). Synonyms: sentarse, tomar un asiento.
target_language_example: Por favor, tomar asiento antes de que empiece la reunión.
native_language_example: Please take a seat before the meeting begins.

meaning: to get some fresh air; to go outside for a breath or break.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone is stepping outside briefly to breathe, calm down, or take a short break. Can be literal (fresh air) or imply a short walk to clear one's head. Often used with ir (ir a tomar el aire) or as Voy a tomar el aire.
target_language_example: Voy a tomar el aire un momento.
native_language_example: I'm going to get some fresh air for a moment.

meaning: to tease someone; to joke with someone; to kid someone (often by making them believe something untrue)
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone is joking, teasing, or making fun of another person. Can be light-hearted (teasing) or imply tricking someone. Commonly used in informal contexts. Conjugate the verb 'tomar' as needed (e.g., 'me estás tomando el pelo' or 'no me tomes el pelo').
target_language_example: No me tomes el pelo: sé que no ganaste la lotería.
native_language_example: Don't pull my leg: I know you didn't win the lottery.

meaning: to take into account; to consider or keep in mind
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to consider a factor, opinion, or piece of information when making a decision or judgment. Commonly interchangeable with 'tener en cuenta'. Often followed by a noun or a clause introduced by 'que' (e.g., 'tomar en cuenta que...').
target_language_example: Debes tomar en cuenta el tráfico antes de salir.
native_language_example: You should take into account the traffic before leaving.

meaning: "to take this" or "to take/consider this" depending on context (literal: pick up/ingest; figurative: consider/accept).
additional_notes: Tomar = to take; este = this. Can be used literally (e.g., tomar este jarabe) or figuratively (e.g., tomar este problema en consideración). Conjugate tomar appropriately for person and tense (e.g., toma, toma[n], tomaré, he tomado). Word order and prepositions may vary in extended phrases (e.g., tomar este en cuenta → tomar esto en cuenta).
target_language_example: Debes tomar este jarabe para la tos.
native_language_example: You should take this cough syrup.

meaning: to take this / to accept this / to treat this (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'to take this.' In different contexts it can mean: physically take or pick up something, accept or receive something (e.g., medication, criticism), or treat/consider a matter in a certain way (e.g., 'take this seriously' = consider it important). Context determines whether it's physical (take), figurative (accept), or evaluative (treat/consider).
target_language_example: Debes tomar esto en serio si quieres aprobar.
native_language_example: You should take this seriously if you want to pass.

meaning: to take the floor / to speak (to accept the chance to speak in a conversation or meeting).
additional_notes: Used when someone begins speaking or accepts an invitation to speak. Common in formal contexts (meetings, debates) but also in conversations. Can be equivalent to 'to take the floor' or 'to have the floor' in English. Often used with verbs like 'quiero' or 'voy a' (e.g., 'Voy a tomar la palabra').
target_language_example: Si nadie más habla, voy a tomar la palabra.
native_language_example: If no one else speaks, I'm going to take the floor.

meaning: to take note; to write something down or pay attention to remember it
additional_notes: Commonly used when you want to record information (e.g., in a meeting, lecture, or reminder) or tell someone you're paying attention. Can be literal (writing) or figurative (noting mentally). Often followed by de or que + clause: tomar nota de algo / tomar nota de que + clause.
target_language_example: Voy a tomar nota de tu número de teléfono.
native_language_example: I'm going to write down/take note of your phone number.

meaning: to take by surprise; to catch someone off guard.
additional_notes: Used when an event or action happens unexpectedly to someone. Often used with a person as the object: 'tomar a alguien por sorpresa' or simply 'tomar por sorpresa' followed by the thing that surprised them. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: La noticia vino de repente y nos hizo tomar por sorpresa.
native_language_example: The news came suddenly and took us by surprise.

meaning: 'to take time' — to spend or use time (to do something) or to require time.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that an action requires or consumes time (e.g., "Esto toma tiempo" = "This takes time"). Can be used reflexively as "tomarse su tiempo" meaning "to take one's time" (to not rush). Context decides whether it means 'consume time' or 'allow yourself time'.
target_language_example: Es importante tomar tiempo para practicar cada día.
native_language_example: It's important to take time to practice every day.

meaning: to take a nap (short sleep, usually in the afternoon).
additional_notes: Common in Spanish-speaking cultures to rest after lunch. Usually refers to a short daytime sleep (not overnight). Verbs: 'tomar una siesta', 'echarse una siesta' are both used. Use with reflexive 'echarse' is slightly more colloquial.
target_language_example: Después de comer voy a tomar una siesta.
native_language_example: After lunch I'm going to take a nap.

meaning: to take a vacation / to go on vacation.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone is taking time off work or school to rest or travel. In many Spanish varieties you can also say 'tomarse vacaciones' (reflexive) or use 'ir de vacaciones'. Use with a time period: 'tomar vacaciones por una semana'.
target_language_example: Voy a tomar vacaciones la próxima semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a vacation next week.

meaning: they/you (plural) took a (masculine singular) — used to say someone took something (taxi, plane, drink, break, etc.).
additional_notes: Tomaron is the third-person plural preterite of tomar (also used as second-person plural in Latin America's ustedes). 'Un' is the masculine indefinite article. Together they introduce a masculine singular noun (un taxi, un avión, un trago, un descanso). Use tomaron una for feminine nouns (e.g., tomaron una foto). In many contexts tomar can mean 'take', 'have' (a drink), 'have' (a break), or 'ride' (a taxi, plane).
target_language_example: Ellos tomaron un autobús hacia la ciudad.
native_language_example: They took a bus to the city.

target_language_multi_word_term: tomaré como / me lo tomaré como
meaning: I'll take it as / I'll consider it as (used to accept an action/comment as having a particular meaning).
additional_notes: Used to express that you will interpret someone's words, actions, or events in a certain way (often positively). 'Me lo tomaré como' adds a reflexive/object pronoun meaning 'I'll take it (for myself) as...'. Commonly followed by 'un cumplido' (a compliment), 'un sí' (a yes), 'una señal' (a sign), etc.
target_language_example: Si vas a ayudarme, me lo tomaré como una señal de buena voluntad.
native_language_example: If you're going to help me, I'll take it as a sign of goodwill.

meaning: 'take the' (formal command/subjunctive) or 'he/she takes the' depending on context.
additional_notes: Tome is either the formal (usted) imperative of tomar (take) or the present subjunctive/third-person present (tome). 'Tome la' is followed by a feminine noun (la + noun) as in 'tome la decisión' or by a feminine object like 'la botella'. Context decides if it's a command (¡Tome la siguiente salida!) or part of a clause (que tome la decisión = that he/she make/take the decision).
target_language_example: Por favor, tome la carretera que va al centro.
native_language_example: Please take the road that goes to downtown.

meaning: 'take a' or 'have a' (plural imperative: you all take/have a ...).
additional_notes: Plural formal/informal command (ustedes) telling a group to take, have, or grab something. Common with nouns like 'descanso' (break), 'trago' (drink), 'trozo' (piece), or food items. Use to give instructions or offers to multiple people. If addressing one person use 'toma un' (informal) or 'tome un' (formal).
target_language_example: Tomen un descanso y vuelvan dentro de diez minutos.
native_language_example: Take a break and come back in ten minutes.

meaning: imperative/subjunctive form telling someone to 'take the ...' (e.g., take the bus/metro/plane); often appears in commands or wishes (tú tomes + definite article).
additional_notes: ‘Tomes’ is the present subjunctive (used for commands, wishes, recommendations) or negative imperative for tú (with no pronoun). Here it combines with a masculine noun introduced by the definite article 'el' (e.g., el autobús, el metro, el avión, el mando). Context determines tone: can be a suggestion ('Que tomes el autobús') or a prohibition when negated ('No tomes el avión'). Also appears in idiomatic phrases (No me tomes el pelo = Don't pull my leg / Don't make fun of me).
target_language_example: Por favor, toma el tren, pero no tomes el último vagón; mejor que tú tomes el primero.
native_language_example: Please take the train, but don't take the last car; better that you take the first one.

meaning: 'I take the... (transportation)' or 'I drink the... (beverage)' depending on context.
additional_notes: Tomo is the first-person singular present of tomar. With transport (metro, autobús, tren, tranvía, vuelo) it means 'I take' (I ride or I catch). With beverages (té, café) it means 'I drink' or 'I'll have'. The article (el) agrees with the following noun (el metro, el autobús, el tren). Common in everyday speech to describe daily routines (Tomo el metro todos los días).
target_language_example: Tomo el autobús para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: I take the bus to go to work.

meaning: took from the (feminine noun) / he/she/it took from the (feminine noun)
additional_notes: Compound of tomó (past tense of tomar: 'to take') + de la (preposition 'from the' for feminine singular nouns). Use before a feminine noun: e.g., tomó de la mesa (took from the table), tomó de la caja (took from the box). If the following noun is masculine, use 'del' (de + el) instead: tomó del libro. Context determines who 'took'—subject can be él/ella/usted or it.
target_language_example: Ella tomó de la nevera una botella de agua.
native_language_example: She took a bottle of water from the fridge.

meaning: took the trouble (to do something); made an effort to do something for someone.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who went out of their way or made a special effort—often politely—to do a helpful or considerate action. Typically followed by 'de' + verb infinitive (se tomó la molestia de + infinitive). Can be used sincerely or with mild irony depending on tone.
target_language_example: Se tomó la molestia de dejarme un mensaje cuando llegué tarde.
native_language_example: He took the trouble to leave me a message when I arrived late.

meaning: drank a cup (of something) / took a cup
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of tomar + una taza. Commonly used to say someone drank a cup of coffee, tea, or another beverage (tomó una taza de café). Can also mean physically picked up a cup (took a cup). Context tells whether it refers to drinking or taking. For a more explicit beverage mention, add 'de' + beverage (e.g., tomó una taza de té).
target_language_example: Esta mañana tomó una taza de café antes de salir.
native_language_example: This morning he/she drank a cup of coffee before leaving.

meaning: 'so foolish/so stupid as' (used in comparisons, often with 'tan' to mean 'so ... as to ...')
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'tan tonto como' or 'ser tan tonto como para + (infinitive)' to say someone was foolish enough to do something. It compares degree (tan ... como) or expresses 'foolish enough to' when followed by 'para' + infinitive. Tone is neutral to slightly critical; 'tonto' is an everyday word meaning 'stupid' or 'silly'.
target_language_example: No seas tan tonto como para firmar sin leer.
native_language_example: Don't be so foolish as to sign without reading.

meaning: to run into; to come across (someone or something) unexpectedly.
additional_notes: Used when you meet someone or find something by chance. Often used with people or unexpected situations. Commonly conjugated reflexively (me topo, te topas, se topa, nos topamos, etc.). Synonyms: encontrarse con, encontrarse con. Can be used in both literal (meet) and figurative (encounter a problem) senses.
target_language_example: Ayer me topé con mi vecino cuando iba al trabajo; fue sorprendente toparse con él tan temprano.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my neighbor on my way to work; it was surprising to come across him so early.

meaning: 'I ran into' or 'I bumped into' (met someone unexpectedly).
additional_notes: Used to say you met someone by chance. Commonly conjugated from the verb 'topar (con)' (me topé con, te topaste con, se topó con...). Informal-to-neutral; frequently used in everyday speech. Can be followed by a person or a thing encountered.
target_language_example: Me topé con Ana en la cafetería ayer.
native_language_example: I ran into Ana at the café yesterday.

meaning: I ran into / I came across (someone or something).
additional_notes: Common past tense phrase from 'toparse con' meaning to meet someone unexpectedly or to come across something by chance. Used for people or things (e.g., a person on the street, an object, or a book). In English it corresponds to 'run into', 'come across', or 'bump into'.
target_language_example: Ayer me topé con una antigua profesora en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into an old teacher at the supermarket.

meaning: curfew (an order requiring people to stay indoors at certain hours).
additional_notes: Used to describe an official or imposed restriction that people must be home or off the streets during set hours (often for safety, emergencies, or public order). Commonly used with verbs like declarar, imponer, aplicar, cumplir. Not a casual phrase — usually refers to a legal or official rule.
target_language_example: Anunciaron un toque de queda desde las 22:00 hasta las 06:00.
native_language_example: They announced a curfew from 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM.

meaning: 'storm of' or 'storm (with)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a specific type of storm by adding a noun after 'de' (e.g., 'tormenta de nieve' = snowstorm, 'tormenta de verano' = summer storm, 'tormenta de hielo' = ice storm). Can also be used alone with context as 'the storm' plus a specification. Common in weather reports and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Viene una tormenta de viento esta noche.
native_language_example: A wind storm is coming tonight.

meaning: uses of 'tormenta' with a reflexive/impersonal 'se' to say a storm is doing something (approaching, worsening, turning into...); often expresses that the storm acts or changes on its own (e.g., 'the storm is approaching').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but examples of 'tormenta' followed by the pronoun 'se' plus a verb (se acerca, se empeora, se hizo, se volvió, se dirige). Spanish uses 'se' here to form reflexive/impersonal/medio constructions that indicate the storm undergoes or produces a change or simply 'does' the action. Common verbs: acercarse (to approach), empeorar(se) (to get worse), hacerse/volverse (to become), dirigirse (to head toward). Translate contextually: 'la tormenta se acerca' = 'the storm is approaching.'
target_language_example: La tormenta se dirige hacia la costa esta noche.
native_language_example: The storm is heading toward the coast tonight.

meaning: the phrase combination of 'torta' (cake) plus the preposition 'en' used to say 'cake' and to indicate division or location ('into' / 'in').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun torta (cake) followed by the preposition en. Use 'torta en' when specifying where the cake is (e.g., en la panadería = in the bakery) or how it is divided (e.g., en seis pedazos = into six pieces). For division, English uses 'into' — in Spanish use 'dividir/partir + torta + en + (número)'.
target_language_example: Cortó la torta en cuatro trozos.
native_language_example: He cut the cake into four pieces.

meaning: completely out of (place, fashion, context); totally inappropriate or not fitting.
additional_notes: Used to say something is inappropriate, awkward, not suitable, or not in style/context. Often followed by nouns like lugar (place), moda (fashion), lugar/contexto, or phrases indicating what it's out of. 'Totalmente' intensifies 'fuera de'.
target_language_example: Ese comentario fue totalmente fuera de lugar en la reunión.
native_language_example: That comment was totally out of place at the meeting.

meaning: works for / works because of / works during (depends on context).
additional_notes: The preposition por changes the meaning: 1) 'trabaja por la oferta más alta' = 'works for' (in exchange for; for the highest offer). 2) 'trabaja por el bienestar social' = 'works for' (in favor of / on behalf of). 3–4) 'trabaja por la mañana/por la noche' = 'works during' (in the morning/at night). Context tells whether por indicates purpose/reason, beneficiary, exchange, or time period.
target_language_example: Ella trabaja por la comunidad los fines de semana.
native_language_example: She works for the community on weekends.

meaning: working hard on the (masculine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: This is the gerund phrase 'trabajando duro' (working hard) followed by the masculine singular definite article 'el'. It must be completed with a masculine noun or noun phrase (e.g., 'trabajando duro en el proyecto'). Use 'en la' for feminine nouns. Commonly used to describe effort on a task, project, job, problem, etc.
target_language_example: Estoy trabajando duro en el proyecto de la escuela.
native_language_example: I'm working hard on the school project.

meaning: to work (in/at) — used before a place, age, or with a person/thing being observed doing work
additional_notes: This is the verb trabajar followed by the preposition a. Common uses: 'trabajar a [lugar]' = to go/work in a place (often with motion: ir a trabajar a París), 'trabajar a [edad]' = start working at a certain age, and 'ver/tratar/oir + trabajar a [persona]' = to see someone (person or group) working. Context determines translation; sometimes English omits 'to' or uses 'in/at'.
target_language_example: Ella fue a trabajar a Londres el invierno pasado.
native_language_example: She went to work in London last winter.

meaning: 'to work as' (to perform duties or hold a position in the role of...)
additional_notes: Used with a noun or role (trabajar como + [sustantivo/rol]). Can describe formal paid employment or informal/figurative roles; context determines meaning and register. Can emphasize hardship when used with words like 'esclavos' or 'criada'.
target_language_example: Es terrible verlos trabajar como esclavos en este calor.
native_language_example: It's terrible to see them working as slaves in this heat.

meaning: to work hard; to put in a lot of effort.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to describe making a strong effort at work, study, or any task. Can be used in commands, promises, descriptions of effort and fatigue. Literally composed of trabajar (to work) + duro (hard).
target_language_example: Si quieres mejorar, tendrás que trabajar duro todos los días.
native_language_example: If you want to improve, you'll have to work hard every day.

meaning: to work together; to collaborate.
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people cooperate on the same task or project. 'Trabajar' is the verb 'to work'; 'juntos' means 'together'. Agreement: when the group is all female, you can say 'trabajar juntas'. In formal contexts you might use 'trabajar en conjunto' or 'colaborar'.
target_language_example: Podemos trabajar juntos en la presentación.
native_language_example: We can work together on the presentation.

meaning: 'to work a lot' / 'to work hard' (do a large amount of work or put in a lot of effort).
additional_notes: Used to say someone must put in a lot of time or effort. Can mean long hours (work a lot) or high effort (work hard) depending on context. Common with verbs like tener que, acostumbrarse a, and modal constructions.
target_language_example: Ella tiene que trabajar mucho para terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: She has to work a lot to finish the project on time.

meaning: to work for / to work during (a time) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Can mean 'to work for' someone, something, or a cause (e.g., work in exchange for pay or to support a goal) or 'to work during' a time period when followed by a time expression. Context decides meaning. Common structures: 'trabajar por [persona/causa]' (work for someone/for a cause) and 'trabajar por la mañana/tarde/noche' (work in the morning/afternoon/night).
target_language_example: Algunos no quieren trabajar por ese privilegio; otros sí.
native_language_example: Some do not want to work for that privilege; others do.

meaning: work (job) here; can mean 'a job located here' or 'my/your work here' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a job or to the work/task someone does at the current place. Context decides whether it means 'a job here' (employment) or 'the work I'm doing here' (task completed). Common with verbs like tener, conseguir, hacer, estar (estar hecho = finished).
target_language_example: Tengo un trabajo aquí desde hace dos meses.
native_language_example: I have a job here since two months ago.

meaning: 'job as' / 'work as' — used to indicate someone's job, role, or the act of working in a specific capacity.
additional_notes: Can function as a noun phrase ('un trabajo como...') or appear in descriptions of someone's employment. Often followed by a profession or role (e.g., 'trabajo como ingeniera'). Context determines whether it's describing a position or the act of working in that capacity.
target_language_example: Ella consiguió un trabajo como ingeniera de grabación.
native_language_example: She got a job as a recording engineer.

meaning: teamwork; working together as a group.
additional_notes: Refers to coordinated effort by a group toward a common goal. Used in workplaces, sports, military, school projects, etc. Can describe the concept (el trabajo en equipo) or a specific collaborative task (un trabajo en equipo).
target_language_example: Para terminar el proyecto a tiempo necesitamos trabajo en equipo.
native_language_example: To finish the project on time we need teamwork.

meaning: a phrase meaning 'work/job at/in the' (used before a feminine noun or place).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say where someone works or where a task takes place. 'Trabajo' can mean a job (employment) or a piece of work/task; 'en la' is the preposition + feminine definite article that must agree with the following noun (e.g., 'la oficina', 'la planta', 'la capital'). If the following noun is masculine use 'trabajo en el'.
target_language_example: Ella tiene trabajo en la oficina del centro.
native_language_example: She has a job at the downtown office.

meaning: work/job in a (used in time or place expressions).
additional_notes: This chunk appears in two common uses: 1) trabajo en + time expression (e.g., 'trabajo en un día' = 'work in one day' meaning to finish something within that time), and 2) trabajo en un + place (e.g., 'trabajo en un restaurante' = 'I work in a restaurant'). The exact translation depends on context: for time it means 'in/within one...', for place it means 'at/in a...'.
target_language_example: No puedo terminar todo el trabajo en un día.
native_language_example: I can't finish all the work in one day.

meaning: the work/job is (in a certain state); 'the work is...'.
additional_notes: A simple subject–verb phrase: 'trabajo' (work/job) + 'está' (third-person singular of estar). Use with adjectives or past participles to describe the state or completion of a task (e.g., casi terminado = almost finished; hecho = done). 'Estar' emphasizes current state or condition. For completed actions you can also say 'el trabajo está hecho' or use 'el trabajo está terminado'.
target_language_example: El trabajo está casi terminado.
native_language_example: The work is almost finished.

meaning: 'work' or 'job' + 'very' (used when describing a job or the quality of work).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun trabajo ('work, job, task') followed by the adverb muy ('very'). Use to intensify an adjective that describes work (e.g., trabajo muy bueno, trabajo muy aburrido). Make sure the adjective agrees where necessary (trabajo is masculine singular).
target_language_example: Ella hace un trabajo muy cuidadoso.
native_language_example: She does very careful work.

meaning: "job" or "work" when followed by 'o' meaning 'or' (used in lists/choices).
additional_notes: This shows the noun trabajo used with the conjunction o (or). In Spanish you often see "trabajo o algo" (a job or something) or contrasting alternatives: "trabajo o hijos" (work or children). Also note 'trabajo' can mean 'a job' or 'work' (uncountable). The example "hacer el trabajo o no" uses the full phrase 'o no' (or not) to form a yes/no alternative.
target_language_example: ¿Buscas trabajo o prefieres estudiar?
native_language_example: Are you looking for a job or do you prefer to study?

meaning: 1) 'work due by' or 'work for (a deadline)'; 2) 'a job/task for (someone/organization)'; 3) 'a job for someone' (assigning work).
additional_notes: Depends on context: 'trabajo para + deadline' means a piece of work that must be finished by that time (due by). 'Trabajo para + alguien/entidad' can mean that the work is intended for or performed for someone (e.g., 'para la policía' = for the police) or that someone works for an employer (with 'trabaja para'). With a person as indirect object ('un trabajo para ti') it means a task assigned to that person.
target_language_example: Tengo un trabajo para mañana que debes terminar.
native_language_example: I have a job for tomorrow that you must finish.

meaning: 'work' + 'because' — literally 'work because'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun trabajo ('work' / 'job') followed by the conjunction porque ('because'). Use it when 'work' is the word in the sentence and 'because' introduces the reason. Word order in Spanish is the same as in English: trabajo porque + clause. Examples show meanings like 'at work', 'a job', or 'to be fired from work' depending on context.
target_language_example: Cambié de trabajo porque quería un horario mejor.
native_language_example: I changed jobs because I wanted a better schedule.

meaning: "work" (trabajo) followed by "and" (y) — simply the word 'trabajo' used in phrases joined with 'y'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword idiom; it's the noun trabajo ('work, job, labor') appearing before the conjunction y ('and'). Learn 'trabajo' as a basic noun: meanings include job (employment), work (activity/tasks), and sometimes construction/site. 'Y' just connects items. Pay attention to context to know whether it means 'job', 'work' (uncountable), or 'piece of work.' Examples above show different uses: possession (mi trabajo), activity (salir del trabajo = leave work), and lists (trabajo y dinero).
target_language_example: Salió del trabajo y fue al supermercado.
native_language_example: He left work and went to the supermarket.

meaning: bring (someone) a / bring a (something).
additional_notes: From the verb traer (to bring) in the imperative or present tense (él/ella/usted trae). In commands with tú, use trae (informal) or trae una + noun to ask someone to bring one of something. Can be used to request or say someone brings an item. Context determines whether it's a request (Bring a...) or a statement (he/she brings a...).
target_language_example: Trae una toalla para la playa.
native_language_example: Bring a towel for the beach.

meaning: to bring a (feminine singular object)
additional_notes: Composed of the verb traer (to bring) + the feminine singular indefinite article una. Use when referring to bringing one feminine noun (ej.: una silla, una taza, una linterna, una cosita, una paz). Verb form will change with subject and tense (e.g., 'voy a traer una', 'tráeme una'). Replace una with un for masculine nouns. Common in requests, statements, and descriptions.
target_language_example: No te voy a traer una taza de café; mejor tráeme una botella.
native_language_example: I'm not going to bring you a cup of coffee; better bring me a bottle.

meaning: I brought a / (he/she/you) brought a — past tense of traer + the indefinite article 'un'.
additional_notes: Traté 'traje' is the first person singular (yo traje) or third person preterite (él/ella/usted trajo is irregular but 'traje' is only yo) — actually 'traje' is the preterite form for 'yo' (I brought). In casual speech you may see word order: 'Te traje un regalo' = 'I brought you a gift' or 'Traje un libro' = 'I brought a book.' The phrase 'traje un' must be completed by a noun (masculine singular) like 'regalo', 'libro', or 'ayudante'. Use 'traje una' for feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Te traje un sándwich para el almuerzo.
native_language_example: I brought you a sandwich for lunch.

meaning: 'I brought a' (past tense, first person singular) or 'I brought one/a'.
additional_notes: Traté 'traje' is the preterite of 'traer' (to bring) for 'yo' (I). 'Una' is the feminine indefinite article meaning 'a' or 'one'. Use before feminine nouns (una visita, una muñeca, una cerveza, una cosita). If the noun is masculine, use 'traje un' (e.g., 'traje un regalo'). The phrase indicates you brought something to someone (often as a gift or offering).
target_language_example: Ayer traje una sorpresa para mi hermana.
native_language_example: Yesterday I brought a surprise for my sister.

meaning: 'suit/costume of' or 'the ... suit/costume of' — used to describe the type or owner of a suit/costume/clothing item.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say what kind of suit or costume someone is wearing (traje de pirata = pirate costume) or to indicate possession (el traje de tu padre = your father's suit). 'Traje' can mean formal suit, costume, or outfit depending on context. Use 'de' + noun (role, person, thing) to specify type or owner.
target_language_example: Ella tiene un traje de astronauta para la fiesta.
native_language_example: She has an astronaut costume for the party.

meaning: 'swimsuit' or 'bathing suit' (clothing worn for swimming).
additional_notes: Used for both men's and women's swimwear in Spanish. Context or adjectives clarify type (e.g., traje de baño de una pieza, bikini, bañador). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ella compró un nuevo traje de baño para las vacaciones.
native_language_example: She bought a new swimsuit for the vacation.

meaning: 'brought to' or 'brought (someone/something) to (a place/state)'.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of traer + the preposition 'a' contracted with the article (al = a + el) or used before a place/phrase. Used for physical bringing (e.g., brought to a place) and figurative expressions (e.g., 'brought into the world' = born). Subject and object determine exact translation.
target_language_example: Él me trajo al restaurante anoche.
native_language_example: He brought me to the restaurant last night.

meaning: a trap in the (something) / 'trap in the' (used as part of a phrase referring to a trap located in a specific place)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase but the beginning of a phrase: trampa en el + [lugar] (e.g., trampa en el jardín, trampa en el camino). Use it to say there is a trap located in a particular place. 'Trampa' means 'trap' or 'cheat', and 'en el' means 'in the/the (masculine singular)'. Adjust the article if the following noun is feminine (en la) or plural (en los/las).
target_language_example: Hay una trampa en el jardín junto a la puerta.
native_language_example: There is a trap in the garden next to the door.

meaning: calm/peaceful (while) in; describing someone or something being calm or living peacefully in a place or situation.
additional_notes: Tranquila is the feminine form of tranquilo. Used before or after a place or situation introduced by en (in). Commonly describes a person's state (e.g., 'está tranquila en los terremotos' = she stays calm during earthquakes) or a lifestyle ('vida tranquila en el campo' = peaceful life in the countryside). Adjust gender (tranquilo/a) and number (tranquilos/as) to match the noun.
target_language_example: Quiero estar tranquila en la playa durante las vacaciones.
native_language_example: I want to be calm on the beach during the vacation.

meaning: to turn into; to become; to transform into.
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verb construction (se transforma en) or active (transforma en) to indicate that one thing changes into another (physical change, metaphorical change, or becoming). Common with natural processes (agua se transforma en gas) and figurative uses (la cara se transforma en la de Dios). Followed by the new state or thing introduced by 'en'.
target_language_example: La oruga se transforma en mariposa.
native_language_example: The caterpillar turns into a butterfly.

meaning: public transportation; buses, trains, metros, etc. used by the general public.
additional_notes: Refers to government-run or shared transport services (bus, metro, tram, train) used by many people. Commonly used when talking about commuting, city planning, accessibility, or convenience. Can be singular when speaking generally (el transporte público) or plural with specific modes (los transportes públicos) but the singular is far more common.
target_language_example: Vivo cerca del transporte público, así que no necesito coche.
native_language_example: I live near public transportation, so I don't need a car.

meaning: after another; one after the other
additional_notes: Used to indicate sequence or succession: something happening following something else. Commonly appears as part of phrases like 'uno tras otro' (one after another) or 'vino tras otro' (one came after another). It's neutral register and literal in meaning.
target_language_example: Llegaron uno tras otro y ocupamos todas las mesas.
native_language_example: They arrived one after another and we took all the tables.

meaning: the back of / the rear of (something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the rear side or back portion of an object, vehicle, animal, building, etc. 'Trasera' often appears with 'parte' as 'parte trasera' (the back part). Common preposition: 'de' to indicate what it belongs to (e.g., 'la parte trasera de la casa').
target_language_example: Pusieron la caja en la parte trasera del camión.
native_language_example: They put the box in the back of the truck.

meaning: 'treats (someone/something) as' or 'treat (someone/something) like'.
additional_notes: Second-person singular or third-person singular form of the verb phrase tratar + como. Use with a subject: (él/ella/usted) trata como or (yo/ellos) trato/ tratan como. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause that describes how someone/something is being treated (e.g., 'trata como un niño', 'me trata como si fuera tonto'). Common in both literal and figurative contexts.
target_language_example: Ella me trata como a un amigo.
native_language_example: She treats me like a friend.

meaning: treats (someone) like a (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to say someone treats another person as if they were a certain kind of person or thing. The phrase requires an object before it (e.g., 'me trata...') and a noun after 'un/una' (e.g., 'niño', 'idiota'). Often expresses criticism or complaint. Word order: [person] + trata + como + a + [article] + [noun].
target_language_example: Mi jefe me trata como a un aprendiz, aunque tengo experiencia.
native_language_example: My boss treats me like an apprentice, even though I have experience.

meaning: it's about / it's a matter of (referring to the topic or issue).
additional_notes: Used impersonally with 'se' (se trata de/ del) to introduce the topic or to say what something concerns. 'Se trata del' = 'it's about the' or 'it's a question of the'. Often contrasts what something is or isn't about. Followed by a noun or clause. 'Tratar de' without 'se' can mean 'to try to' or 'to deal with' in other contexts.
target_language_example: No se trata del precio, sino de la calidad.
native_language_example: It's not about the price, but about the quality.

meaning: 'tried to' (past participle + 'to' — indicates an attempt to do something).
additional_notes: From the verb tratar (to try/attempt). Commonly appears as 'he tratado de...', 'has tratado de...', 'traté de...' to say 'I have tried to...' or 'I tried to...'. Use 'de' + infinitive verb. Often followed by actions (hablar, venir, sacar, traducir, ascender).
target_language_example: He tratado de aprender español todos los días.
native_language_example: I have tried to learn Spanish every day.

meaning: to deal with, to handle (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used when talking about handling a person, problem, situation, or task. Can mean 'to cope with' or 'to deal with' depending on context. Commonly followed by a noun or pronoun (tratar con alguien / tratar con esto).
target_language_example: Tengo que tratar con ese problema mañana.
native_language_example: I have to deal with that problem tomorrow.

meaning: to try to
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say someone makes an effort to do something: tratar de + infinitive. Don't confuse it with other uses of tratar, which can mean things like 'to deal with' or 'to be about.'
target_language_example: Voy a tratar de llegar temprano.
native_language_example: I'm going to try to arrive early.

meaning: 'deal done' or 'it's a deal' — used to confirm an agreement.
additional_notes: Common phrase to accept or confirm a proposal; equivalent to 'agreed' or 'deal' in English. Used in spoken and informal/formal contexts. Can stand alone as a reply.
target_language_example: Si me ayudas con la mudanza, yo pago la cena. — Trato hecho.
native_language_example: If you help me with the move, I'll pay for dinner. — It's a deal.

meaning: 'brought something' (I/you/he has brought something to someone).
additional_notes: Past participle form of traer (traído) used with a personal pronoun and auxiliary verb (usually 'he', 'has', 'hemos', 'os he', etc.). Commonly appears in sentences like 'Te he traído algo' = 'I brought you something' or 'I've brought something for you.' The phrase is usually followed by what was brought (e.g., comida, hielo, para leer) or left vague as 'algo' (something).
target_language_example: Te he traído algo de comer porque sé que tienes hambre.
native_language_example: I've brought you something to eat because I know you're hungry.

meaning: I/you/he/she have/has brought a (feminine singular item).
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle 'traído' (brought) with the indefinite article 'una'. Common in sentences like 'Te he traído una X' meaning 'I've brought you a X'. Subject is expressed by the verb conjugation (he, has, ha, hemos, han). The noun following 'una' must be feminine (una foto, una taza, una sorpresa).
target_language_example: Te he traído una chaqueta nueva.
native_language_example: I've brought you a new jacket.

meaning: 'thirty and' — used to form numbers from 31 to 39 (e.g., treinta y uno = 31).
additional_notes: In Spanish number formation, 'treinta y' combines with units (uno, dos, tres, etc.) to make numbers 31–39. When speaking, 'y' (and) is pronounced; in writing there is a space before and after 'y'. For 30 alone, say 'treinta' (no 'y').
target_language_example: treinta y cinco
native_language_example: thirty-five

meaning: thirty-five (35).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used for counting, ages, quantities, etc. Spanish numbers from 31 to 99 are often formed with 'treinta y [número]' (thirty and [number]). Pronunciation: 'TREIN-ta ee SIN-ko'.
target_language_example: Tengo treinta y cinco libros en la estantería.
native_language_example: I have thirty-five books on the shelf.

meaning: 'thirty-two' (the number 32).
additional_notes: Used to state the number 32 in age, quantity, distance, etc. Spanish numbers are formed by joining tens and units with 'y' (e.g., treinta y dos). Pronunciation: ['trein-ta ee dos']. Can appear alone as an answer or as part of a sentence.
target_language_example: Tengo treinta y dos años.
native_language_example: I am thirty-two years old.

meaning: thirty-six (36).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used for counting, ages, distances, years, multiplication results, etc. Spanish numbers use 'y' between tens and units for 21–99 (except round tens). Pronunciation: treinta (TREIN-ta) y seis (SEIS).
target_language_example: Tengo treinta y seis libros en la estantería.
native_language_example: I have thirty-six books on the shelf.

meaning: the train of the (e.g., 'the morning train', 'the afternoon train').
additional_notes: Used to specify a particular train by time or part of day (e.g., 'tren de la mañana' = morning train, 'tren de la tarde' = afternoon train). You must add the time-of-day noun after 'la' (mañana, tarde, noche). If the noun is masculine (e.g., 'tren de la noche' is less common), adjust article if needed: 'tren de la mañana' is standard. Commonly followed by 'primero' (first) or 'segundo' (second) to indicate sequence: 'el primer tren de la mañana'.
target_language_example: Tomaré el tren de la tarde para llegar después del trabajo.
native_language_example: I'll take the afternoon train to arrive after work.

meaning: the train (as subject) + pronominal marker 'se' used with verbs (e.g., se retrasó = the train was delayed / delayed itself).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun 'tren' followed by the reflexive/pronominal clitic 'se' attached to a verb (tren se retrasó, tren se fue, tren se descarriló). In Spanish many verbs use 'se' to form intransitive or passive-like constructions: it often indicates that the action happens to or by the subject (the train) rather than being done by someone. Translate depending on the verb: se retrasó = was delayed, se fue = left, se descarriló = derailed.
target_language_example: El tren se detuvo en la estación durante veinte minutos.
native_language_example: The train stopped at the station for twenty minutes.

meaning: 'the train already (left) / already gone' — used to say the train has already departed.
additional_notes: Ya is an adverb meaning 'already' (or 'yet' in negatives/questions). With 'tren' it indicates the train has departed. Use with compound past (haber + salido/ido) or simple past: 'el tren ya se ha ido', 'el tren ya salió'. In affirmative commands or suggestions, 'ya' can mean 'now' or 'right away' (e.g., 'subir al tren ya' = 'get on the train now').
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, el tren ya se había ido.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the train had already gone.

meaning: the numbers three, four, five (used when counting).
additional_notes: These are ordinal elements of the basic Spanish number sequence. Used in counting, giving combinations, phone numbers, steps, etc. Pronunciation: tres (tres), cuatro (KWA-tro), cinco (SEEN-ko). They are literal numerals and are used just like 'three, four, five' in English.
target_language_example: Cuenta conmigo: uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco.
native_language_example: Count with me: one, two, three, four, five.

meaning: three friends (masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Literal phrase: 'tres' = three, 'amigos' = friends. Use for three male friends or a mixed-gender group. For three female friends, use 'tres amigas'. In Spanish, adjectives and nouns must agree in gender and number.
target_language_example: Fuimos al cine los tres amigos.
native_language_example: The three friends went to the movies.

meaning: three years older/older by three years than
additional_notes: Used to compare ages or ages of things (e.g., cars). Place after the number and unit (años) and before the person or thing being compared. Often implies 'is older by three years' when referring to people or objects.
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene tres años más que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is three years older than me.

meaning: literally 'three things' — used to refer to three specific items, points, or matters.
additional_notes: Direct, literal phrase. Can name three items or be used more vaguely to mean 'a few important things' depending on context. In speech it may introduce a list (e.g., 'Tres cosas: primero...') or summarize reasons ('Lo hice por tres cosas').
target_language_example: Cambié mi rutina por tres cosas que quería mejorar.
native_language_example: I changed my routine because of three things I wanted to improve.

meaning: three thousand (3,000).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used with nouns and standalone. 'Mil' is invariable (no plural 'miles' when combined with a numeral): say 'tres mil metros', not 'tres miles metros'. Can be used alone as an amount: 'Tres mil.'
target_language_example: Compré tres mil boletos para la rifa.
native_language_example: I bought three thousand tickets for the raffle.

meaning: used in phrases like 'tres o cuatro' to mean 'three or (about) four' — i.e., 'three or so / three or four'.
additional_notes: Typically appears as part of the phrase 'tres o cuatro' to give an approximate number (three or four). Used for quantities, durations, frequencies, or counts. In English it corresponds to 'three or four' or more loosely 'three or so'. Can be used alone ('Tres o cuatro.') to mean 'About three.' or 'Three or four.'
target_language_example: Necesito tres o cuatro horas para terminarlo.
native_language_example: I need three or four hours to finish it.

meaning: magic trick; a sleight or illusion performed for entertainment.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific illusion, stunt, or sleight-of-hand performed by a magician or someone showing a trick. Common in casual conversation when learning, showing, or commenting on a trick. Can be singular or plural (trucos de magia).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes enseñarme un truco de magia sencillo?
native_language_example: Can you teach me a simple magic trick?

meaning: 'traffic on' or 'traffic in' (refers to vehicle traffic in a place).
additional_notes: Used to talk about road/vehicle traffic located on or in a specific street, avenue, road, area, or place. Common collocations: 'tráfico en la calle', 'tráfico en la avenida', 'tráfico en todas partes'. 'Tráfico' alone means traffic; 'en' introduces the location.
target_language_example: Hay mucho tráfico en la autopista esta mañana.
native_language_example: There is a lot of traffic on the highway this morning.

meaning: 'your coffee'.
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: tu = your (informal singular), café = coffee. Used to refer to someone's cup or the coffee they made/drank. In formal contexts or when addressing someone politely, use "su café." Pronunciation: tu (like English 'too'), café (stress on the second syllable: ca-FÉ).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres calentar tu café?
native_language_example: Do you want to heat your coffee?

meaning: your day (literally: the day that belongs to you); used to talk about someone's day, luck, schedule, or a special occasion.
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'your day.' Common uses: referring to how someone's day is going (¿Cómo fue tu día?), saying it's someone's lucky or special day (Es tu día de suerte / Es tu día especial), or telling someone today isn't going well for them (Hoy no es tu día). Can refer to a free day (tu día libre) or an event assigned to someone. Tone depends on context (neutral, encouraging, or ironic).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, hoy es tu día de suerte.
native_language_example: Don't worry, today is your lucky day.

meaning: 'your lack (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something someone does not have (a quality, habit, responsibility, etc.). Usually followed by 'de' + a noun: tu falta de paciencia, tu falta de respeto. Can be critical or neutral depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Tu falta de atención causó el error.
native_language_example: Your lack of attention caused the mistake.

meaning: 'your great' or 'your big' (used before a noun to praise or emphasize importance/size)
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: tu = your, gran = shortened form of 'grande' used before singular nouns (gran novela = great/important novel; gran oportunidad = great/big opportunity). It emphasizes praise, significance, or size. Use 'gran' before a singular noun; use 'grande' after the noun for literal size (la casa grande).
target_language_example: Esta puede ser tu gran oportunidad para aprender.
native_language_example: This could be your great/big opportunity to learn.

meaning: your left (side); to your left.
additional_notes: Used to indicate location relative to the listener. Commonly appears with a preposition like 'a' (a tu izquierda = to your left) or with verbs (estoy a tu izquierda = I'm to your left). 'Tu' is informal singular 'your' (use 'su' for formal or plural in some regions).
target_language_example: Mira a tu izquierda: ahí está la puerta.
native_language_example: Look to your left: there's the door.

meaning: your light (often used figuratively to mean guidance, help, or divine illumination)
additional_notes: Commonly found in religious or poetic contexts. When addressed to God or a spiritual figure, it requests guidance, protection, or blessing. Can be literal (someone's physical light) but examples show figurative use. Tone is formal or reverent.
target_language_example: Señor, dame tu luz para tomar la decisión correcta.
native_language_example: Lord, give me your light to make the right decision.

meaning: your mother
additional_notes: A literal possessive phrase referring to the person’s mother. tu is the informal singular form of 'your'. madre is neutral and slightly more formal than mamá ('mom').
target_language_example: Voy a hablar con tu madre mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to talk with your mother tomorrow.

meaning: 'your best' (used before a noun or as part of expressions like 'dar tu mejor esfuerzo' = 'give your best').
additional_notes: Literally 'your best.' Commonly appears in phrases such as 'dar tu mejor esfuerzo' (give your best effort), 'tu mejor amigo' (your best friend), or comparisons like 'tu mejor maestro.' After 'tu mejor' you usually expect a noun (amigo, esfuerzo, maestro).
target_language_example: Siempre da tu mejor esfuerzo en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Always give your best effort at work.

meaning: your fear
additional_notes: Combination of the possessive pronoun 'tu' (your, informal singular) + noun 'miedo' (fear). Used to talk about someone's specific fear or fears. 'Tu' is informal (used with friends, family, or people you address with tú). For formal situations, use 'su miedo'.
target_language_example: No dejes que tu miedo decida por ti.
native_language_example: Don't let your fear decide for you.

meaning: 'your father' + 'that' — the sequence appears when saying 'tell/ask/show your father that...' or making comparisons 'your father than...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the words tu padre (your father) followed by the conjunction que (that) used in different structures: reporting/informing (Dile a tu padre que...), asking/requesting (Pídele a tu padre que...), expressing that someone wanted to show their father something (Le querías demostrar a tu padre que...), or in comparisons where que means 'than' (se parece más a tu padre que tú = he looks more like your father than you do). Translate based on context: que = 'that' (subordinate clause) or 'than' (comparison).
target_language_example: Pídele a tu padre que venga mañana.
native_language_example: Ask your father to come tomorrow.

meaning: 'your leg'.
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'tu' (your, informal singular) + 'pierna' (leg). Used to refer to someone's leg—can indicate location (e.g., put ice on your left leg), condition (injury), or action (move your leg). Use 'su pierna' for formal you or third person, and 'tus piernas' for 'your legs' (plural).
target_language_example: Pon hielo sobre tu pierna derecha.
native_language_example: Put ice on your right leg.

meaning: your point / your opinion (what you mean)
additional_notes: Used in conversations to refer to the idea, argument or perspective someone has made.
