Can be neutral or slightly confrontational depending on tone: e.g. "Tienes tu punto" (You have a point) or "Ese es tu punto" (That's your point). Often follows verbs like tener (tener tu punto), ser (ser tu punto) or aparecer in dialogue.
target_language_example: Tienes tu punto, pero no estoy de acuerdo del todo.
native_language_example: You have a point, but I don't fully agree.

meaning: your type (of person); people like you.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a kind or category of person (often based on personality, appearance, behavior, or social group). Can be neutral, descriptive, or negative depending on tone and context. Commonly appears as 'de tu tipo' (of your type) or 'no soy de tu tipo' (I'm not your type).
target_language_example: No me llevo bien con la gente de tu tipo.
native_language_example: I don't get along with people like you.

meaning: your real / true (used before a noun, usually 'nombre' = name).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'tu verdadero nombre' meaning 'your real name' (as opposed to a nickname, alias, or online username). 'Verdadero' agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies (tu verdadero nombre, tu verdadera identidad). Used to contrast authenticity or truth.
target_language_example: No quiero que uses tu verdadero nombre en Internet.
native_language_example: I don't want you to use your real name on the Internet.

meaning: the grave of / tomb of (used to say whose grave/tomb it is).
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession: 'tumba de + person/place'. Common in literal contexts (actual graves) and in idiomatic expressions (e.g., oaths like 'Lo juro por la tumba de mi madre' = 'I swear by my mother's grave'). 'Tumba' is feminine; the article (la/una) may appear before 'tumba' depending on context.
target_language_example: Fuimos a la tumba de mi abuelo el Día de los Muertos.
native_language_example: We went to my grandfather's grave on Day of the Dead.

meaning: shifts of / turns of (used to talk about work shifts, appointments, or taking turns)
additional_notes: Commonly used with jobs (turnos de mañana/tarde/noche), with services (turnos de atención) or to indicate taking turns (dar turnos de). Often followed by a noun that specifies what type of shift or turn it is. 'Turno' = 'shift' or 'turn'; 'de' links to the kind or time.
target_language_example: Tengo turnos de noche esta semana.
native_language_example: I have night shifts this week.

meaning: with your own eyes (you personally see something).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the person must see something themselves rather than being told about it. Often follows verbs of seeing (ver, mirar) and can be used for both positive and negative surprises or proof.
target_language_example: Tienes que verlo con tus propios ojos.
native_language_example: You have to see it with your own eyes.

meaning: I had nothing to do with it / I wasn't involved.
additional_notes: This is a colloquial Spanish construction meaning the speaker denies involvement or responsibility. More standard/grammatical forms are "no tuve nada que ver" or "no tuve nada que ver con eso." In casual speech, the initial "no" can be dropped in some dialects or contexts when negation is understood, but learners should use the full negative form to be safe. Use with past tense (tuve = I had).
target_language_example: No tuve nada que ver con ese problema.
native_language_example: I had nothing to do with that problem.

meaning: had the
additional_notes: Comes from tener ('to have'). Tuviera is the imperfect subjunctive, often used in hypothetical sentences with si ('if') or after expressions like insistieron en que. The meaning is usually simply 'had the' in English, with the noun after el completing the idea.
target_language_example: Si tuviera el tiempo, iría contigo.
native_language_example: If I had the time, I would go with you.

meaning: 'we had the' (plural past of tener + feminine definite article)
additional_notes: Used to say that 'we' possessed, experienced or had something in the past. The noun that follows is feminine (la oportunidad, la suerte, la barbacoa). Often appears in phrases like 'tuvimos la oportunidad' (we had the opportunity) or 'tuvimos la suerte' (we were lucky / we had the luck). Context determines whether it's literal possession or an idiomatic expression (e.g., 'tuvimos la suerte de...' = 'we were lucky to...').
target_language_example: Tuvimos la oportunidad de viajar este verano.
native_language_example: We had the opportunity to travel this summer.

meaning: 'had more' (literally) or part of expressions meaning 'had no more/other choice' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally 'tuvo más' = 'he/she/it had more'. Commonly appears in phrases like 'no tuvo más alternativa/opción' meaning 'he/she had no other choice' or 'was left with no alternative.' Context determines whether it's simply quantitative ('had more [children]') or part of an idiom about lacking options.
target_language_example: Después del primer hijo, ella tuvo más hijos después de unos años.
native_language_example: After the first child, she had more children a few years later.

meaning: had its/his/her
additional_notes: Combination of the preterite of tener (tuvo = he/she/it had) + the possessive su. Used to indicate possession or that someone experienced/received something at a specific past moment (e.g., had an event, experienced an accident, received a baby). Context decides whether su = his/her/its/their; translate accordingly. Common in phrases like 'tuvo su primer bebé' (had his/her first baby) or 'tuvo su accidente' (suffered/experienced an accident).
target_language_example: Ella tuvo su oportunidad ayer.
native_language_example: She had her chance yesterday.

meaning: had an attack (of something, e.g., asthma, nerves, heart).
additional_notes: Common phrase to describe experiencing a sudden medical or emotional episode. Usually followed by the type: 'tuvo un ataque de asma', 'tuvo un ataque de nervios', 'tuvo un ataque cardíaco'. Often used in past simple (pretérito) for completed events. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Ayer mi abuelo tuvo un ataque de corazón y lo llevaron al hospital.
native_language_example: Yesterday my grandfather had a heart attack and they took him to the hospital.

meaning: 'tea with' — used to say tea served with something (milk, lemon, gas, etc.).
additional_notes: Common phrase followed by the ingredient (e.g., 'té con leche', 'té con limón'). Used to order or describe tea prepared with an addition. Word order is 'té con X'. Pronunciation: té (stress on e).
target_language_example: Quiero un té con miel, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a tea with honey, please.

meaning: 'the tea is' (used to describe the tea's state or quality).
additional_notes: Té (tea) + está (third-person singular of estar) = 'the tea is...'. Use está for temporary states (temperature, taste, readiness, condition). For opinions about taste, Spanish often uses estar (este té está bueno). To say permanent characteristics (less common for food), use ser. You can replace 'té' with other nouns: 'la sopa está caliente.'
target_language_example: El té está demasiado caliente; espera cinco minutos.
native_language_example: The tea is too hot; wait five minutes.

meaning: tea without (e.g., sugar, milk, or lemon).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to order or describe tea served without an added ingredient. You will usually hear a specification after 'té sin' (e.g., 'té sin azúcar' = tea without sugar). Can be used for other drinks with 'sin' (without).
target_language_example: Quisiera un té sin azúcar, por favor.
native_language_example: I would like a tea without sugar, please.

meaning: green tea
additional_notes: Refers to the beverage made from unoxidized tea leaves. Commonly ordered in cafes and restaurants. In Spanish the noun 'té' is masculine (el té) and 'verde' agrees in gender. Can be used alone when ordering: 'Té verde, por favor.'
target_language_example: Un té verde, por favor.
native_language_example: A green tea, please.

meaning: tea and (used to join 'tea' with another item or action).
additional_notes: Literal combination of the noun 'té' (tea) plus the conjunction 'y' (and). Common in lists (e.g., 'té y café') and in sentences describing having tea plus something else (another cup, an activity, or a person). Used exactly like English 'tea and'.
target_language_example: Voy a pedir té y un sándwich, por favor.
native_language_example: I'll order tea and a sandwich, please.

meaning: literally 'my aunt [to] me' — the combination shows actions done by 'my aunt' to or for the speaker (direct or indirect object).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun tía (aunt) plus the clitic pronoun me (to/for me or me as direct object). Use me to indicate the speaker is the recipient or affected person: e.g. 'mi tía me enseñó' (my aunt taught me), 'mi tía me regaló' (my aunt gave me). Word order: subject + me + verb (or subject + me + verb + object). 'La tía me contó' uses la because a specific aunt is referred to.
target_language_example: Mi tía me prestó su coche el fin de semana.
native_language_example: My aunt lent me her car for the weekend.

meaning: great-uncle (the brother of one's grandparent).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a parent's uncle (your grandparent's brother). Can be used with or without an article (el/mi) and also as a direct address (Tío abuelo). In Spanish family terms, 'tío abuelo' is gendered; feminine form is 'tía abuela' for great-aunt.
target_language_example: Mi tío abuelo nos contó historias de la guerra.
native_language_example: My great-uncle told us stories about the war.

meaning: 'the uncle is' (literal) / 'that guy is' (colloquial when tío = guy)
additional_notes: tío primarily means 'uncle'. In everyday spoken Spanish (especially in Spain) tío is also a slang noun meaning 'guy' or 'dude'. With está it simply describes a state or condition (e.g., sleepy, rich, thin, angry, located). Use context to tell whether it refers to a family uncle or to 'that guy'.
target_language_example: Ese tío está muy contento hoy.
native_language_example: That guy (or the uncle) is very happy today.

meaning: 'my/your/his/her uncle died' (simple past statement about an uncle's death).
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining the noun 'tío' (uncle) and the past tense 'murió' (he/she/it died). Spanish subjects are often omitted when clear from context, so 'mi tío murió' = 'my uncle died'. You can replace the possessive (mi, su, tu, etc.) to indicate whose uncle. 'Murió' is the preterite of 'morir' (to die) used for completed past events.
target_language_example: Su tío murió el año pasado.
native_language_example: His uncle died last year.

meaning: you must / you should / you probably (depending on context).
additional_notes: Depends on context: 'debes' + infinitive usually gives obligation ('you must/should do something'). Adding 'de' after 'debes' (tú debes de) can make the phrase softer or express probability/guess about the present (you must be / you probably...). In many regions speakers omit the 'de' for obligation. Use 'tú debes' for clear obligation and 'tú debes de' when suggesting a likely conclusion or a tentative suggestion.
target_language_example: Tú debes de estar cansado después del viaje.
native_language_example: You must (or you probably) are tired after the trip.

meaning: 'you' (singular, familiar) + 'them' (indirect or direct object pronoun) — 'you (to) them' or 'you (do something) to/for them'.
additional_notes: Tú is the singular familiar 'you' subject. Les is a third-person plural object pronoun that can be indirect ('to them' or 'for them') or, in some dialects, a direct object for people (leísmo). Together they appear when addressing one person about actions affecting multiple others: Tú les [verbo] = 'You [verb] them' or 'You [verb] to/for them'. Word order: subject (tú) before pronoun (les).
target_language_example: Tú les das el libro.
native_language_example: You give them the book.

meaning: 'you' (subject) + 'them' (masculine or mixed direct object pronoun); means 'you them' as in 'you [do something to/with] them'.
additional_notes: Combines the subject pronoun tú (you, singular informal) with the masculine/mixed plural direct object pronoun los (them). Used when referring to previously mentioned masculine or mixed plural nouns (e.g., libros, zapatos). Word order: subject (tú) before verb; los usually follows the verb (e.g., Tú los viste = You saw them). In short independent phrases like examples, Tú los emphasizes who did the action and what was affected.
target_language_example: Tú los compraste ayer.
native_language_example: You bought them yesterday.

meaning: yourself (emphatic).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the action refers to the person addressed (tú). Often appears before or after a verb or pronoun for emphasis or to indicate that the person did something personally. Can be used literally ('you yourself did it') or idiomatically ('you asked for it').
target_language_example: Tú mismo lo dijiste en la reunión.
native_language_example: You yourself said it at the meeting.

meaning: 'you or' — used to present 'you' as one option among alternatives.
additional_notes: Used with 'o' (or) to offer choices or contrast between people (often followed by another person/pronoun). Common patterns: 'tú o yo' (you or I), 'tú o María' (you or María). Can appear in statements, questions, or commands. Word order may vary (e.g., 'o tú o yo' for emphasis).
target_language_example: Tú o yo tenemos que llamar al doctor.
native_language_example: You or I have to call the doctor.

meaning: a casual way to ask 'and you?' or 'what about you?' (asking the other person's opinion, action, or knowledge).
additional_notes: Used informally to turn a question back to the listener or to ask what they think/know/do. Often appears in spoken Spanish with rising intonation and may be followed by a verb (¿tú qué piensas?) or stand alone as a quick 'and you?'.
target_language_example: Estoy pensando en salir esta tarde, ¿tú qué opinas?
native_language_example: I'm thinking of going out this afternoon — what about you?

meaning: you too
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that the same statement or action applies to them. Can express inclusion (join me/others), agreement (me too), or pointing out that the person shares a characteristic or experience. 'Tú' is the informal singular 'you' in Spanish — used with friends, family, or people you know well. Word order can vary (e.g., 'tú también', 'también tú') depending on emphasis.
target_language_example: Ven tú también.
native_language_example: You come too.

meaning: you go / you are going (informal singular)
additional_notes: Second-person singular of the verb ir (to go). Used in informal speech with someone you know well (tú). Can be used for present simple (routine) or present progressive meaning 'you are going' when context indicates it. For questions, invert subject and verb: ¿Tú vas...? Often the subject pronoun tú is optional: (Tú) vas al cine = You (are) going to the movies.
target_language_example: ¿Tú vas a la fiesta esta noche?
native_language_example: Are you going to the party tonight?

meaning: you already (emphatic).
additional_notes: Combines the subject pronoun tú (you, singular informal) with ya (already). Used to emphasize that the listener is already aware of or has done something. Common in spoken Spanish; ya can appear before or after object pronouns (e.g., 'tú ya lo sabes' = 'you already know it'). Not a fixed idiom—it's simply the pronoun + adverb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Tú ya conoces la ciudad; no necesitas un mapa.
native_language_example: You already know the city; you don't need a map.

meaning: an accident at/in the (specific place).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something had an accident at a particular location. Complete the phrase with a noun for the place (e.g., 'piso', 'cruce', 'trabajo', 'restaurante'). Depending on context, 'en el' may change to 'en la', 'en los', or 'en las' to match the gender and number of the place noun (e.g., 'un accidente en la cocina', 'un accidente en los exteriores').
target_language_example: Tuvo un accidente en el cruce esta mañana.
native_language_example: He/She had an accident at the intersection this morning.

meaning: a keen/acute sense of (something).
additional_notes: Used to describe a very sharp or highly developed sensory ability (oído, olfato, vista, etc.). Follows with the sense noun (e.g., "oído", "olfato") after "del" (de + el). Common in descriptions of people or animals.
target_language_example: El gato tiene un agudo sentido del oído.
native_language_example: The cat has a keen sense of hearing.

meaning: 'for a year' (indicates a duration of one year up to now, often with Hace ... que)
additional_notes: Used to express how long something has been happening up to the present. Common structure: Hace + (time period) + que + (present tense verb) = 'It has been [time] since/that...'. It can also appear as 'Hoy hace un año que...' meaning 'Today marks one year since...'.
target_language_example: Hace un año que trabajo aquí.
native_language_example: I've been working here for a year.

meaning: a kiss on (followed by a body part or place).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone gives or receives a kiss (e.g., 'un beso en la mejilla' = a kiss on the cheek). Common in physical contexts and in phrases describing greetings or affection. After 'en' you typically use a noun indicating a body part or location. Can appear in descriptions, invitations, or stories.
target_language_example: Me dio un beso en la frente antes de irse.
native_language_example: He gave me a kiss on the forehead before leaving.

meaning: a good day in (some place or for some activity); used to say that a day went well or was enjoyable at a specific location or doing something.
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by a location, activity, or situation (e.g., 'un buen día en la playa', 'un buen día en el trabajo'). It describes that the day was pleasant or successful there. Common in informal and neutral contexts when recounting experiences. Word-for-word translation is literal.
target_language_example: Tuvimos un buen día en la montaña.
native_language_example: We had a good day in the mountains.

meaning: a good end; a good ending; often used to wish someone a good weekend/holiday or to refer to a good outcome
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'a good end.' In everyday Spanish, context determines sense: it can mean a good ending/result (e.g., of a story or project) or be a shortened casual wish like 'que tengas un buen fin de semana' (have a good weekend) when 'fin' stands for 'fin de semana' or a holiday period. Not a fixed idiom on its own—usually appears as part of longer phrases.
target_language_example: Espero que todo tenga un buen fin.
native_language_example: I hope everything has a good ending.

meaning: a (strong) heat; used to comment on hot weather.
additional_notes: Common phrase used with adjectives (horroroso, espantoso, infernal, extraño) to emphasize how hot it feels. Often appears with the impersonal verb hacer: 'Hace un calor...'. Can describe unusual, very intense, or oppressive heat. Use in weather comments; not used to mean 'a heat' in scientific contexts.
target_language_example: Hace un calor insoportable hoy, mejor quedarnos en casa.
native_language_example: It's unbearably hot today; we'd better stay home.

meaning: a vulgar way to say 'nothing' or to emphasize contempt (like 'not a damn/thing' or 'screw that').
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Often used after a negation to mean 'not a thing' (No sé un carajo = I don't know jack). Can stand alone as an exclamation to reject or express anger (Un carajo! / Y un carajo!). Avoid in polite contexts.
target_language_example: No sé un carajo de eso.
native_language_example: I don't know jack about that.

meaning: a center; a place or space for a particular activity (e.g., town center, shopping center, sports center).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to a central place (el centro de la ciudad), a facility (centro comercial = shopping mall; centro deportivo = sports center), or an organization (centro cultural). Definite article changes by gender/number (el centro, los centros). Can be used abstractly (un centro de interés).
target_language_example: Encontramos un centro cultural cerca de mi casa.
native_language_example: We found a cultural center near my house.

meaning: a (hot) chocolate; a cup of hot chocolate
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a serving/cup of hot chocolate in cafés. Context can imply 'a chocolate drink' rather than a chocolate bar. Often used with adjectives (caliente, doble) or with verbs pedir, tomar, necesitar.
target_language_example: Voy a pedir un chocolate con churros.
native_language_example: I'm going to order a hot chocolate with churros.

meaning: a butt; (colloquial/sexual) someone's backside
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar in many contexts. Used to refer to the buttocks (physical attraction or description). Avoid in polite/formal situations; in neutral contexts use 'trasero', 'glúteos' or 'nalgas'. Can be used playfully among friends but may offend.
target_language_example: Tiene un culo grande.
native_language_example: He/She has a big butt.

meaning: 'a priest' (Catholic priest)
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to a Catholic priest. The article 'un' makes it indefinite ('a'). Can appear in comparisons or descriptions (e.g., 'como un cura' = 'like a priest'). Neutral form; not slang. Beware: 'cura' can also mean 'cure' as a noun in some contexts, but with the article and examples here it means 'priest'.
target_language_example: Vi a un cura en la iglesia esta mañana.
native_language_example: I saw a priest at the church this morning.

meaning: 'a director' — a person who leads or manages (films, organizations, orchestras, newspapers, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for someone in a leadership or managerial role. Gender: 'director' is grammatically masculine when preceded by 'un'; female form is 'una directora' (though some women may use 'directora'). Context or modifiers specify the type (de cine, de orquesta, de periódico, de empresa). Can refer to film director, company director, orchestra conductor, newspaper director, etc.
target_language_example: Steven Spielberg es un director de cine.
native_language_example: Steven Spielberg is a film director.

meaning: a gunshot wound to (a body part); 'shot in/on'.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone was shot in a specific body part. Followed by the body part (la rodilla, la cabeza, la espalda). Can describe being hit by a bullet; often appears in news or reports. Not idiomatic—literal meaning.
target_language_example: Le dieron un disparo en el brazo durante el robo.
native_language_example: He was shot in the arm during the robbery.

meaning: sometime soon; one of these days (in the near future).
additional_notes: Used informally to say that something will happen at an unspecified time in the near future. Can be vague — could mean within days, weeks, or an undefined soonness. Often used alone as a short answer or to soften a promise.
target_language_example: Un día de estos te invito a cenar.
native_language_example: One of these days I'll invite you to dinner.

meaning: a Spanish person; (also) the Spanish language (in some contexts).
additional_notes: Most commonly means 'a Spanish person' (a person from Spain). In contexts about language, 'un español' can mean 'a form/variety of Spanish' or 'a (level/style of) Spanish' (e.g., 'habla un español impecable' = 'he speaks impeccable Spanish'). Context tells which meaning fits. Use 'un/una español/a' for nationality and 'el español' when referring to the language in general.
target_language_example: Conocí a un español en la universidad.
native_language_example: I met a Spanish person at university.

meaning: a pimple / a grain (small seed) / a kernel; most commonly 'a pimple' in everyday speech
additional_notes: Depends on context: 'grano' can mean a skin blemish (pimple), a grain/seed (grain of rice), or a kernel/particle. In casual conversation about skin, 'un grano' usually refers to a pimple. Plural is 'granos'.
target_language_example: Me salió un grano en la mejilla.
native_language_example: A pimple appeared on my cheek.

meaning: a pleasure; a liking/taste (for something); used as a short polite phrase meaning 'nice to (have) / meet / see you'.
additional_notes: Has two main uses: 1) literally, 'un gusto por...' means a liking or taste for something (e.g., ice cream). 2) as a polite set phrase, '¡Un gusto!' or 'Fue un gusto conocerlos/verte' means 'It was a pleasure' or 'Nice to meet/see you.' Common in casual and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Fue un gusto trabajar contigo este proyecto.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure working with you on this project.

meaning: an axe (a tool used for chopping).
additional_notes: Refers to a single axe. Used for chopping wood or, in violent contexts, killing/decapitation. Feminine noun 'hacha' begins with stressed 'a' so uses the masculine article 'un' in singular (but adjectives remain feminine: 'un hacha afilada'). Plural is 'hachas' (las hachas).
target_language_example: El leñador cortó leña con un hacha afilada.
native_language_example: The woodcutter chopped wood with a sharp axe.

meaning: 'an egg' (literal) — also used informally to mean 'a lot' or 'a huge amount' in some regions
additional_notes: Primary meaning is the literal egg (bird/reptile egg). Informally and regionally, 'un huevo' (or 'un huevo de...' / 'un huevo que...') can mean 'a lot' or 'tons' (colloquial). Context decides meaning: literal in sentences about size or finding an egg; informal when used to express large quantity or emphasis. Not always appropriate in formal speech when used figuratively.
target_language_example: Compró un huevo de dinosaurio en el museo.
native_language_example: He bought a dinosaur egg at the museum.

meaning: a juice; (a) juice (a serving of juice).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a drink made from fruit or vegetables. Commonly used when ordering or asking for a serving (e.g., 'un jugo de naranja' = an orange juice). In some regions 'jugo' and 'zumo' are interchangeable; 'jugo' is common in Latin America. Can also mean homemade or freshly prepared juice ('hacer un jugo').
target_language_example: Por favor, dame un jugo de manzana.
native_language_example: Please give me an apple juice.

meaning: Move aside / make way, please.
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to step to the side or make room. Common variations: 'A un lado, por favor', 'Hazte a un lado, por favor' (informal singular), 'Hágase a un lado, por favor' (formal singular), 'Háganse a un lado, por favor' (plural). Can be used in crowded places, when someone is blocking a path, or to ask someone to give space.
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿puede hacerse a un lado, por favor?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you move aside, please?

meaning: to set aside; to put to one side (something or someone).
additional_notes: 'Un lado a' by itself is not the most common word order in standard Spanish — the usual phrasing is 'a un lado' or 'poner/guardar a un lado'. 'Un lado a' can appear in some colloquial or regional constructions when combined with verbs (e.g., 'ponerse un lado a' in certain dialectal uses) or in elliptical expressions, but it's less natural standing alone. Prefer 'poner a un lado' to sound idiomatic.
target_language_example: Voy a dejar esto un lado a la hora de decidir.
native_language_example: I'm going to leave this to one side when deciding.

meaning: a book in the (feminine noun) — used before a feminine noun like 'mano' or 'mesa'.
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a prepositional phrase meaning 'a book in/on the ...'. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article and must match a feminine noun (mano, mesa, mochila, etc.). Commonly used with locations or body parts: 'en la mano' = in/held in the hand, 'en la mesa' = on the table. For masculine nouns you would use 'en el' instead (e.g., 'un libro en el bolso').
target_language_example: Llevaba un libro en la mochila.
native_language_example: He was carrying a book in the backpack.

meaning: a book that is very (something) — 'muy' intensifies an adjective describing 'un libro'.
additional_notes: This phrase shows the pattern: article + noun + 'muy' + adjective (un libro muy útil / muy viejo). 'Muy' means 'very' and always goes before an adjective or adverb. You can replace 'libro' with other nouns: 'una casa muy grande', 'un coche muy rápido'.
target_language_example: Es un libro muy interesante.
native_language_example: It's a very interesting book.

meaning: a wonderful (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to say something is wonderful, marvelous, or excellent. Can modify people, events, objects or abstract things. Feminine form is 'una maravillosa'. Common in both formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Fue un maravilloso concierto anoche.
native_language_example: It was a wonderful concert last night.

meaning: for one month (in/at).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something has been in a place or situation for the duration of one month. Often appears with locations (en el hospital) or situations (en el hoyo). Can be part of longer time expressions like 'llevar un mes en...' or 'estar un mes en...'.
target_language_example: Lleva un mes en la oficina sin salir.
native_language_example: He has been in the office for a month without leaving.

meaning: a moment
additional_notes: Literally means "a moment." It can refer to a short amount of time, or be used by itself to ask someone to wait briefly, like "just a moment" or "one moment."
target_language_example: Espera un momento, ya vuelvo.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I'll be right back.

meaning: a time/moment like this; in times like these.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the current situation or a situation similar to the one being discussed (often difficult or significant). Can be used to introduce statements about what people do, feel, or should do 'in a moment like this.'
target_language_example: En un momento como este, necesitamos mantener la calma.
native_language_example: In a moment like this, we need to stay calm.

meaning: a doll; a toy figure (often small or stuffed); can also mean a puppet or figurine.
additional_notes: Commonly used for children's dolls or toy figures. Depending on context, muñeco can refer to a stuffed toy, action figure, puppet, or a snowman (muñeco de nieve). In casual speech it can also be used affectionately for a person (like 'cutie' or 'sweetie'), but that is informal.
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene un muñeco de trapo que siempre lleva a la cama.
native_language_example: My sister has a rag doll that she always takes to bed.

meaning: a father for / a father figure for (someone)
additional_notes: Used to say someone acted (or didn't act) as a father or father figure to a person. Often appears in negative sentences: 'no fue/un padre para...' = 'wasn't a father to...'. Can refer to biological or emotional/role relationship (caretaker, mentor).
target_language_example: Mi tío fue un padre para mí cuando mi padre murió.
native_language_example: My uncle was a father to me when my father died.

meaning: a past; one's past (life/history).
additional_notes: Refers to a person's past experiences, history, or background. Commonly used in phrases about everyone having a past. Can mean 'a past' (a specific past period) or more generally 'one's past'.
target_language_example: No puedo juzgarte: todos tenemos un pasado.
native_language_example: I can't judge you: we all have a past.

meaning: a walk/stroll through or around (literally) — also used figuratively to mean something very easy or relaxed.
additional_notes: Used literally to describe walking around a place (e.g., un paseo por el parque). Figuratively it can describe an easy, pleasant, or relaxed experience (e.g., será como un paseo por el parque = it will be easy). Often followed by a place introduced with por. Tone is neutral; context determines literal vs. figurative meaning.
target_language_example: Dimos un paseo por el barrio después de cenar.
native_language_example: We took a walk around the neighborhood after dinner.

meaning: 'a danger' or 'a hazard'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a threat, risk, or hazardous situation. Common in both literal and figurative contexts (physical danger, risky behavior, or problematic person/situation). "Peligro" is a masculine noun, so use "un" or other masculine determiners (el, este, etc.).
target_language_example: Ese cruce sin semáforo es un peligro para los peatones.
native_language_example: That intersection without a traffic light is a danger for pedestrians.

meaning: a profile (e.g., social media profile; description or summary of a person or thing).
additional_notes: Commonly used for online accounts (perfil en Instagram/Facebook) and also for short descriptions or summaries (e.g., perfil profesional). Can refer to a side view or outline in physical contexts but most learners will encounter it as 'profile' meaning personal/account summary.
target_language_example: He creado un perfil nuevo en la red social.
native_language_example: I created a new profile on the social network.

meaning: a fish (as food or a caught/marketed fish).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a fish, especially as food or a specimen from a market/catch. In some contexts it can describe a dead fish (e.g., 'murió como un pescado' — died limp/passive) or emphasize size/quality ('un pescado enorme', 'un pescado muy bueno'). Not used to mean 'a fish' as a live pet in everyday casual talk — for live animals Spanish often uses 'un pez'.
target_language_example: Compramos un pescado muy fresco para la cena.
native_language_example: We bought a very fresh fish for dinner.

meaning: a weight/amount of; often 'a weight of' or 'a (monetary) sum of' depending on context (literal: 'a weight of').
additional_notes: Literally means 'a weight of' and is used when specifying the weight of something (e.g., 'un peso de 2 kilos') or sometimes informally to indicate an amount/value (less common). For money, Spanish more often uses 'un peso' (one peso) or 'un monto de'/'una cantidad de' for sums. Use with a measurement or number after it.
target_language_example: Compré un paquete con un peso de 3 kilos.
native_language_example: I bought a package with a weight of 3 kilos.

meaning: a little more
additional_notes: Common phrase used to request a small increase in amount, degree, intensity, volume, duration, patience, etc. Context determines translation: e.g. volume ('hablen un poco más alto' = 'speak a little louder'), time/duration ('espere un poco más' = 'wait a little longer'), effort/amount ('un poco más' = 'a bit more'). Polite and neutral register.
target_language_example: Espérame un poco más, ya voy.
native_language_example: Wait for me a little longer, I'm coming.

meaning: a little
additional_notes: A common expression for a small amount or degree. With nouns, it is usually followed by de: un poco de agua = a little water. It can also be used with adjectives, adverbs, or verbs: estoy un poco cansado = I'm a little tired.
target_language_example: Necesito un poco de ayuda con esto.
native_language_example: I need a little help with this.

meaning: a precious / a lovely (depends on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'precious' (valuable) or 'lovely/beautiful' depending on context. Often used before a noun: 'un precioso vestido' = a beautiful dress; 'un precioso sello' = a valuable/rare stamp. Tone can be neutral or affectionate. Not idiomatic; meaning comes from the adjective precioso + indefinite article.
target_language_example: Ella encontró un precioso regalo en la caja.
native_language_example: She found a precious/beautiful gift in the box.

meaning: a point of; a bit/degree of (used to indicate a point, degree, or small amount of something).
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun to indicate a point, degree, moment, or small amount: e.g. 'un punto de vista' (a point of view), 'un punto de sal' (a pinch of salt). It can also start phrases like 'un punto de inflexión' (a turning point). The exact translation depends on context—sometimes 'a bit of' or 'a hint of' works better than 'a point of'.
target_language_example: Solo necesito un punto de azúcar en mi té.
native_language_example: I only need a bit of sugar in my tea.

meaning: a bouquet (of flowers).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a bunch of flowers arranged together (a bouquet). Used when giving flowers as a gift. Can specify type: 'un ramo de rosas' (a bouquet of roses). Not used for a single flower.
target_language_example: Le llevé un ramo de flores a mi profesora.
native_language_example: I brought a bouquet of flowers to my teacher.

meaning: 'a gift for his/her/their' (used with a person phrase after 'a')
additional_notes: This pattern combines 'un regalo' (a gift) with an indirect object introduced by 'a' plus a possessive (su) to indicate who the gift is for: e.g. 'un regalo a su hijo' = a gift for his/her son. In Spanish you often also use an indirect-object pronoun (le/les) before the verb: 'Ella le compró un regalo a su hijo.' The possessive 'su' can mean his, her, your (formal), their, or its depending on context—clarify if needed (e.g., 'su hijo' could be 'his son' or 'her son').
target_language_example: María le compró un regalo a su madre.
native_language_example: María bought a gift for her mother.

meaning: a (watch/clock) of; used to describe the type, brand, material or purpose of a watch/clock.
additional_notes: This phrase is the beginning of a noun phrase: un reloj de + (material/marca/uso). You must finish it with a noun or proper noun (e.g., un reloj de oro, un reloj de pulsera, un reloj de pared, un reloj de marca). In Spanish, 'reloj' can mean either 'watch' (wristwatch) or 'clock' depending on context. Use 'reloj de pulsera' for wristwatch and 'reloj de pared' for wall clock.
target_language_example: Compró un reloj de pulsera nuevo.
native_language_example: He bought a new wristwatch.

meaning: a result; an outcome.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the consequence, outcome, or final result of an action, event, test, or situation. Can be countable (un resultado, dos resultados). Common in both everyday and formal contexts (e.g., exams, experiments, events). Often preceded by adjectives: positivo, inesperado, negativo.
target_language_example: El experimento dio un resultado sorprendente.
native_language_example: The experiment gave a surprising result.

meaning: a noise in / a sound in (somewhere).
additional_notes: Common phrase to report hearing a sound coming from a specific place. Use with locations (la casa, la habitación, la cocina). Often followed by a noun or location introduced by en. Useful for describing unexpected or unfamiliar sounds.
target_language_example: Escuché un ruido en la azotea anoche.
native_language_example: I heard a noise on the roof last night.

meaning: a serious (used before a noun to describe something important, severe, or significant).
additional_notes: Serio is an adjective meaning 'serious' or 'severe.' When used with 'un' (or other articles), it qualifies a masculine singular noun: 'un serio problema,' 'un serio error.' It indicates degree/importance, not necessarily danger (can be illness, mistake, accident, problem). For feminine nouns use 'una seria' (e.g., 'una seria preocupación').
target_language_example: Ella tiene un serio problema con su coche.
native_language_example: She has a serious problem with her car.

meaning: a silence; a quiet or period of no sound
additional_notes: Used to describe a moment or atmosphere with little or no noise. Can be neutral, awkward (un silencio incómodo), eerie (un silencio inquietante), or desired (quiero un silencio completo). Common in narratives and everyday requests.
target_language_example: Después de la noticia, quedó un silencio en la sala.
native_language_example: After the news, a silence fell in the room.

meaning: a dream come true (part of the fuller phrase "un sueño hecho realidad").
additional_notes: Usually appears as the phrase "un sueño hecho realidad" meaning something desired has become real. "Un sueño hecho" by itself is often completed with "realidad" in speech or writing. Used to express strong happiness or amazement when plans, wishes, or goals are achieved.
target_language_example: Ganar la beca fue un sueño hecho realidad.
native_language_example: Winning the scholarship was a dream come true.

meaning: 'somewhat', 'a bit', 'rather' (to a certain degree)
additional_notes: Used to soften statements or indicate a moderate degree. Common in expressions like 'estar un tanto cansado' (to be somewhat tired) or 'me parece un tanto caro' (it seems a bit expensive). Often placed before adjectives or past participles. Formal and neutral register.
target_language_example: Estoy un tanto preocupado por el examen.
native_language_example: I'm a bit worried about the exam.

meaning: for a time; at one time; spent time in (a place).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a period in the past. When followed by 'que' + clause (Hubo un tiempo en que...) it means 'there was a time when...' or 'at one time...'. When used with a place (pasé un tiempo en ...) it means 'I spent some time in...'.
target_language_example: Hubo un tiempo en que vivía en Madrid.
native_language_example: There was a time when I lived in Madrid.

meaning: a pull; a sudden quick movement; (colloquial) all at once / in one go
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'a pull' (from tirar = to pull). Used for a physical tug ('dar un tirón') or to describe doing something quickly or all at once (e.g., 'comerse los bocadillos de un tirón' = eat them in one go). Can also mean a minor muscle strain ('tener un tirón' = have a pulled muscle). Context tells which sense is intended.
target_language_example: Se lo llevó de un tirón; terminó el trabajo de un tirón.
native_language_example: He pulled it in one quick move; he finished the job all at once.

meaning: 'a job at/with' used to introduce the type or schedule of a job (e.g., a job at X time or a job with X conditions).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like "un trabajo a tiempo parcial" (a part-time job) or "un trabajo a media jornada." It can also be used to say giving someone a job: "darle un trabajo a alguien" (to give someone a job). The preposition a links the noun trabajo to the type, schedule, duration, or recipient.
target_language_example: Ella consiguió un trabajo a tiempo completo en la oficina.
native_language_example: She got a full-time job at the office.

meaning: a job that is scheduled for a particular time (often followed by 'completo' or 'parcial').
additional_notes: This phrase is usually completed as 'un trabajo a tiempo completo' (full-time job) or 'un trabajo a tiempo parcial' (part-time job). By itself it implies the job has a time-based schedule. Commonly used when talking about hours or type of employment.
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un trabajo a tiempo parcial para poder estudiar.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a part-time job so I can study.

meaning: a part-time job
additional_notes: Used to describe work with fewer hours than a full-time job. Commonly heard as 'trabajo de medio tiempo' or 'trabajo de media jornada' in some regions. Often shortened in casual speech to 'medio tiempo' or 'part-time' (Spanglish).
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un trabajo de medio tiempo para los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a part-time job for the weekends.

meaning: “a glass of water, please” — a polite request for water.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone (formally or informally) to bring or give you a glass of water. Often appears with verbs like dar, traer, or with just the noun phrase plus 'por favor'. The 'por' in the prompt is short for 'por favor' (please). Use 'Dame' (informal tú), 'Deme' (formal usted), or 'Tráigame' (polite request).
target_language_example: Dame un vaso de agua, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me a glass of water, please.

meaning: a help; an aid; assistance (something that helps).
additional_notes: Refers to help, assistance, or a helpful tool/resource. Can mean physical or practical aid (e.g., humanitarian aid) or a teaching aid/resource. Use article 'una' for a single, countable help/item; plural is 'ayudas'.
target_language_example: Un buen profesor es una ayuda para aprender rápido.
native_language_example: A good teacher is a help for learning quickly.

meaning: a huge amount; awful/outrageous (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used informally. Can mean 'a lot' or 'very much' when referring to quantity or degree (e.g., costs, appetite, liking). Can also mean 'an outrageous or terrible thing' when describing an action or situation. Tone depends on context—positive for emphasis ('me gusta una barbaridad' = I really like it) or negative for shock/criticism ('eso es una barbaridad' = that's outrageous).
target_language_example: Este coche cuesta una barbaridad, pero me gusta una barbaridad.
native_language_example: This car costs a fortune, but I like it a lot.

meaning: 'an age' / 'a stage' / 'a time period' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Can refer to a person's age or stage of life (e.g., 'an age when...') or to a historical period/age (e.g., 'an age past'). Context determines whether it's about years of life or an era. Often followed by a clause describing what is typical at that age or by 'pasada'/'antigua' when meaning a past/historical age.
target_language_example: Mi sobrino ha llegado a una edad en la que quiere más independencia.
native_language_example: My nephew has reached an age when he wants more independence.

meaning: a false (something); a fake or phony (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Una falsa is the feminine form of "un falso" and must match a feminine noun (alarma, sensación, poción). It means that something is not real, genuine, or is mistaken (a false alarm, a fake potion, a misleading feeling). Common collocations: "una falsa alarma" (a false alarm), "una falsa sensación" (a false sense).
target_language_example: Era una falsa alarma, no había ningún incendio.
native_language_example: It was a false alarm; there was no fire.

meaning: a flower in/on (something) — used to say someone has a flower placed on or held in a body part or object.
additional_notes: Followed by a noun (su pelo, la mano). 'En' can mean 'in', 'on', or 'attached to' depending on context: 'en el pelo' = in/on the hair (worn), 'en la mano' = in the hand (held). Used with tener (to have) to describe possession or wearing/holding something.
target_language_example: Ella tiene una flor en la cabeza.
native_language_example: She has a flower in/on her head.

meaning: a (female) idiot; a stupid person (insult).
additional_notes: Feminine singular form of 'idiota'. Used as an insult to call a woman (or to refer to oneself if female) stupid or foolish. Tone is rude/offensive — avoid in formal situations. To refer to a man, use 'un idiota'. Can be used reflexively (Me sentí como una idiota = I felt like an idiot).
target_language_example: No vuelvas a hablarme así, no soy una idiota.
native_language_example: Don't talk to me like that again, I'm not an idiot.

meaning: 'a list of what' or 'a list of the things that...'
additional_notes: Used to introduce a list describing unspecified things or actions (lo que + verb). Common in everyday speech and writing. The full phrase usually continues with a verb clause: "una lista de lo que necesitamos" = "a list of what we need." Note: 'lo' here is a neutral pronoun used with 'que' to refer to an idea or set of things, not a specific noun.
target_language_example: Voy a hacer una lista de lo que vamos a comprar.
native_language_example: I'm going to make a list of what we're going to buy.

meaning: a wonderful (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Adjective phrase: 'maravillosa' modifies a feminine noun (una + noun). Use 'maravilloso' for masculine nouns (un maravilloso). Commonly used to describe experiences, choices, places, people, etc. Tone is positive and slightly formal/neutral.
target_language_example: Fue una maravillosa sorpresa para todos.
native_language_example: It was a wonderful surprise for everyone.

meaning: 'shit' used as an insult or to say something is worthless/very bad.
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to insult a person (You're crap) or to dismiss/denigrate things (it's worthless, nothing). Tone ranges from strong anger to casual contempt. Not appropriate in formal settings. Can be used alone as an exclamation ("Una mierda.").
target_language_example: No quiero esa comida, es una mierda.
native_language_example: I don't want that food, it's shit.

meaning: 'a woman is' (used to state something about women).
additional_notes: Simple subject + verb phrase: 'una mujer' (a woman) + 'es' (is). Used to make general statements or descriptions about women. Can introduce opinions, qualities, or comparisons. Agreement and gender are already built into 'mujer' (feminine singular).
target_language_example: Una mujer es valiente aunque tenga miedo.
native_language_example: A woman is brave even when she is afraid.

meaning: an urgent need; something that requires immediate attention
additional_notes: Used to describe a pressing requirement or priority (for people, resources, actions, medical care, etc.). Common in both formal and everyday contexts. Can modify a noun (e.g., 'una necesidad urgente de dinero') or stand alone to emphasize urgency.
target_language_example: Tenemos una necesidad urgente de suministros médicos en la clínica.
native_language_example: We have an urgent need for medical supplies at the clinic.

meaning: 'amazing' or 'great' (colloquial); can also mean 'a trick' or 'a prank' depending on context.
additional_notes: Informal Spanish expression. Most often used to praise something (La película es una pasada = The movie is amazing). In other contexts, especially with a person as subject (Alguien me jugó una pasada), it means 'a trick/prank' or 'played a dirty trick on me.' Tone and surrounding words determine which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: La fiesta de anoche fue una pasada.
native_language_example: Last night's party was amazing.

meaning: a question for (someone) / a question about (something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce who the question is directed to or what it concerns. Often followed by a person (una pregunta para María) or a topic/thing (una pregunta para el profesor / una pregunta para el examen). Common in spoken and written Spanish to politely signal you're about to ask something.
target_language_example: Tengo una pregunta para el profesor sobre la tarea.
native_language_example: I have a question for the teacher about the homework.

meaning: 'a reservation' (booking for a hotel, restaurant, appointment, etc.)
additional_notes: Common in many Spanish-speaking countries (especially in Latin America). Used to say you have a booked spot/time or reserved room/table. You can specify details after it (para dos noches, en la Suite, para las seis y media). Formal and neutral register.
target_language_example: Tengo una reservación para cenar a las ocho.
native_language_example: I have a reservation to dine at eight o'clock.

meaning: an aunt (female relative).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a female sibling of a parent or a related older woman; can also be used colloquially in some regions to refer to a woman (like 'a lady'), but primary meaning is family relation. Article 'una' makes it indefinite: 'an aunt'.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es amiga de una tía muy simpática.
native_language_example: My sister is friends with a very nice aunt.

meaning: once
additional_notes: Literally means "one time." It often refers to a single occasion in the past ("I once saw..."). It can also introduce a time condition meaning "once" or "when," as in "una vez adentro" = "once inside."
target_language_example: Una vez fui a México con my familia.
native_language_example: I went to Mexico once with my family.

meaning: again; one more time.
additional_notes: Used to indicate repetition — doing or saying something another time. Common in commands, requests, or statements about repeating an action. Can be placed before or after the verb (Les voy a preguntar una vez más / Una vez más, les voy a preguntar).
target_language_example: Dímelo una vez más, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell me that one more time, please.

meaning: again and again; repeatedly.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens many times or is repeated frequently. Can be used for actions, habits, mistakes, dreams, statements, etc. Equivalent to 'repeatedly' or 'over and over' in English.
target_language_example: Me llamó una y otra vez hasta que contesté.
native_language_example: He called me again and again until I answered.

meaning: a/one with (used to indicate 'one that has' or 'one with' something).
additional_notes: Commonly used when referring to a single item/person that includes or has something (e.g., 'una con X' = 'one that has X' or 'one with X'). Can appear in varied contexts: arranging (ask to get one with someone), describing parts of a whole (each one with...), tasting/identifying (one with a flavor), or relationships (one with each). Grammar: 'una' is the feminine singular indefinite article agreeing with a feminine noun implied or previously mentioned; 'con' means 'with'. The implied noun is often omitted if obvious from context.
target_language_example: Quiero una con jamón, por favor.
native_language_example: I want one with ham, please.

meaning: one of
additional_notes: Usually means 'one of' when referring to a feminine noun or to a group: una de ustedes = one of you. It can also refer back to a feminine noun understood from context, as in Hay una de Madagascar = There's one from Madagascar. In time expressions, it appears in longer phrases such as la una de la mañana (1 a.m.).
target_language_example: Una de mis amigas vive en Sevilla.
native_language_example: One of my friends lives in Seville.

meaning: 'one in' (used to express a ratio, probability, or a single item among many)
additional_notes: Used before a noun or phrase to indicate 'one in [number/quantity]' or 'one of' in a probabilistic or distributive sense. Common in expressions like 'una en un millón' (one in a million). Can also appear before places/objects: 'una en el campo' = one (of them) in the field. English often inserts a number after 'in' (e.g., 'one in a million').
target_language_example: Es una en cien que gane la lotería.
native_language_example: It's one in a hundred that she wins the lottery.

meaning: "university in" — used to say a university located in or to indicate being at university in (a place).
additional_notes: Combines the noun universidad (university) with the preposition en (in/at). Use en + place to state location (Hay una universidad en Roma = There is a university in Rome) or en + time (en septiembre) when combined in a sentence. For saying 'at university' in a general sense, Spanish also uses 'en la universidad' or simply 'en universidad' less commonly; include the article la when referring to a specific campus (voy a la universidad).
target_language_example: Estudio en la universidad en Madrid.
native_language_example: I study at the university in Madrid.

meaning: 'the universe is' — a short phrase used to state something about the universe.
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase formed by the noun universo (the universe) plus the verb es (he/she/it is). Use it to make statements about the universe. Structure: 'El universo es + [adjective/noun/clause]'. Note that sujeto + es agrees: 'El universo' (singular) takes 'es'.
target_language_example: El universo es misterioso y hermoso.
native_language_example: The universe is mysterious and beautiful.

meaning: 'one at a' or 'one by one' when followed by a time/measure (e.g. uno al día = one a day)
additional_notes: This construction combines 'uno' (one) with the preposition 'a' contracted as 'al' (a + el) or simply 'a' before a noun. It's used to say how many of something should occur per unit (per day, per person, etc.). More common forms are 'uno al día', 'uno a la vez' (one at a time), or 'uno por día'. Watch for gender/number agreement with the noun that follows (e.g. 'una al día' for a feminine noun).
target_language_example: Toma una pastilla uno al día.
native_language_example: Take one pill one a day.

meaning: one of those days (a day when things go wrong or are unusually difficult).
additional_notes: Used to describe a day characterized by bad luck, stress, mishaps, or general difficulty. Tone can be mildly humorous or resigned. Can refer to past, present or future (e.g., "Ha sido...", "Es...", "Va a ser...").
target_language_example: Hoy no encuentro las llaves y el coche no arranca: es uno de esos días.
native_language_example: Today I can't find my keys and the car won't start: it's one of those days.

meaning: someday; one of these days (at an unspecified near or not-so-near time)
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen at an unspecified time in the future. Can imply expectation, threat, or resignation depending on tone and context. Often interchangeable with 'algún día' but 'uno de estos días' can sound more immediate or colloquial.
target_language_example: Uno de estos días te visitaré en tu nueva casa.
native_language_example: One of these days I'll visit you in your new house.

meaning: one does / people do / you do (general, impersonal)
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal pronoun 'uno' to talk about actions in a general or universal way (like English 'one' or 'you' meaning people in general). Common in sayings and general statements. Verb agrees with 'uno' (third person singular). Can often be replaced by 'se' impersonal or 'la gente' depending on context.
target_language_example: Uno hace lo que puede en tiempos difíciles.
native_language_example: One does what one can in difficult times.

meaning: oneself (reflexive: the same person; oneself as the object of an action).
additional_notes: Used as a reflexive/emphatic pronoun to refer back to the subject (usually general/indefinite subjects like 'uno' or third person). Common in expressions about knowing, helping, harming, or improving oneself. In informal speech 'a uno mismo' can be replaced by 'a sí mismo' when subject is specific (él/ella/usted), and by 'me/te/se/nos/os' for concrete persons.
target_language_example: Hay que perdonarse a uno mismo para seguir adelante.
native_language_example: You must forgive oneself to move forward.

meaning: a very (one/of them) — used to refer back to a single masculine noun (or an unspecified item) described as 'very' + adjective
additional_notes: Common in colloquial Spanish when referring back to a singular masculine noun without repeating it (uno = 'one' or 'one of them'). Paired with an adjective: 'uno muy bueno' = 'a very good one'. If the omitted noun is feminine, 'una muy' is used instead. Can appear after verbs like conocer, encontrar, saber, or as a standalone remark. Tone is generally informal to neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Encontré uno muy interesante.
native_language_example: I found a very interesting one.

meaning: one by one; individually.
additional_notes: Used to indicate items or people done, inspected, or occurring individually and in sequence. Common in both literal (objects) and figurative (events, days) contexts. Can be used with people (pasen uno por uno), objects (sacar los huevos uno por uno), or events (murieron uno por uno).
target_language_example: Entren en la sala uno por uno.
native_language_example: Enter the room one by one.

meaning: 'one after another' or 'one after the other' (things/people in sequence).
additional_notes: Used to describe a sequence where people or things follow each other in order, often implying succession without pause. Can be used for actions (they came one after another), events (they died one after another), or for emphasis when repeated alone. Agrees in gender/number when required (uno tras otro / una tras otra) but the masculine form is commonly used generically.
target_language_example: Llegaron a la fiesta uno tras otro.
native_language_example: They arrived at the party one after another.

meaning: a few; some (a small number of people or things).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an indefinite small number. Can refer to people or things. Often implies not many but more than one. Context determines exact amount and can be slightly informal. When followed by "de" + noun, it means "some of these/those."
target_language_example: Vi unos cuantos en la plaza esta mañana.
native_language_example: I saw a few people in the square this morning.

meaning: a few; some (a small number).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a small, indefinite number of people or things. Common before nouns or alone (e.g., "Sólo unos pocos."). Can be slightly more emphatic than "unos" or "algunos" to stress smallness.
target_language_example: Unos pocos alumnos no entregaron la tarea.
native_language_example: A few students didn't turn in the homework.

meaning: about three; approximately three (people, items, or units).
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate quantity. 'Unos' softens the exact number, similar to 'around' or 'roughly' in English. Can be used with countable nouns: unos tres días, unos tres amigos. Agreement: 'unos' matches plural; phrase remains 'unos tres' regardless of noun gender.
target_language_example: Llegaré en unos tres días.
native_language_example: I'll arrive in about three days.

meaning: about twenty; around twenty (used with units like minutes, years, dollars).
additional_notes: A casual estimate: 'unos' softens the number to mean approximately. Common with time, money, age, distance. Use gender/number agreement with nouns that follow (unos veinte minutos, unas veinte personas).
target_language_example: Llegaron hace unos veinte minutos.
native_language_example: They arrived about twenty minutes ago.

meaning: about two / around two (approximate quantity)
additional_notes: Used to give a rough estimate of quantity or number. 'Unos' before a number softens it to mean 'around' or 'approximately'. Common in spoken and informal contexts but acceptable in neutral language. Context determines whether it refers to people, objects, hours, etc.
target_language_example: Llegaré en unos dos minutos.
native_language_example: I'll arrive in about two minutes.

meaning: use (imperative/command) + feminine plural direct object: 'use the...' (you informal singular).
additional_notes: Usa is the familiar (tú) or polite (usted) form of the verb usar in the imperative for affirmative commands when speaking to one person (informal: usa; formal: use). Las is the feminine plural definite article, so 'usa las' appears before feminine plural nouns (las coordenadas, las manos, las herramientas, las piernas). Common in spoken and written instructions.
target_language_example: Usa las gafas de protección cuando trabajes.
native_language_example: Use the safety goggles when you work.

meaning: to use one's head; to think, be sensible or use common sense.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning to think before acting or to act sensibly. Often used as advice or a mild reprimand (e.g., "¡Usa la cabeza!"). Can be directed at someone ("usa la cabeza") or used reflexively ("usa tu cabeza").
target_language_example: Si vas a invertir tu dinero, tienes que usar la cabeza y hacer investigación primero.
native_language_example: If you're going to invest your money, you have to use your head and do research first.

meaning: I use the
additional_notes: A first-person singular present form of the verb usar + the masculine singular definite article el. Commonly appears before a masculine noun (e.g., el coche, el protector, el tenedor). Can mean habitual action (I use) or present continuous (I am using) depending on context. Word order is verb + article + noun; the noun itself is often omitted in examples when context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Uso el bolígrafo que está en la mesa.
native_language_example: I use the pen that's on the table.

meaning: you (formal) + well / properly — 'usted' is the formal you; 'bien' means well or properly.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the combination of the formal pronoun usted with the adverb bien. Depending on sentence placement it can mean 'are you okay?' (Está usted bien?), 'you do X well' (Usted pelea bien), or emphasize doing something properly (Agarre usted bien la cuerda = hold the rope firmly/properly). Word order can change (No lo sabe usted bien = you don't really know it). Use 'usted' in formal situations or to show respect.
target_language_example: ¿Usted bien descansa después del viaje?
native_language_example: Are you getting enough rest after the trip?

meaning: the pronoun usted ('you' formal) followed by a prepositional phrase starting with 'en la' ('in the' or 'on the'), used to indicate 'you' as the object/location in a place or context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the combination of the formal second-person pronoun usted and the preposition 'en' with the feminine definite article 'la' (for feminine nouns). In correct Spanish, word order normally places 'usted' before prepositional phrases (e.g., 'hablan mucho de usted en la oficina' = 'they talk about you a lot in the office'). Be careful: some example sentences contain nonstandard or incorrect uses (e.g., 'enviaremos usted en la red' should be 'le enviaremos por la red' or 'lo enviaremos a usted por la red'). When speaking or writing formally, object pronouns often use 'le' or 'lo/la' depending on the verb construction (not 'enviar usted').
target_language_example: He dejado un mensaje para usted en la recepción.
native_language_example: I left a message for you at the reception.

meaning: you in a (formal) — literal sequence of words; not a fixed phrase
additional_notes: This is not a set phrase by itself. It's simply the pronoun usted (formal 'you') followed by the preposition en and the indefinite article un. You will see this combination when addressing someone formally and then saying they are 'in a' place or situation: e.g. "Usted en un lugar público..." (You, in a public place...). Remember that usted requires third-person verb forms.
target_language_example: Usted en un restaurante debe pedir al camarero si necesita algo.
native_language_example: You in a restaurant should ask the waiter if you need anything.

meaning: Informal spelling (missing accent) of formal 'usted está' — 'you are' (second-person singular, polite).
additional_notes: Correct spelling includes an accent: 'usted está'. Used to address someone respectfully. Verb agrees as third-person singular. Note: written Spanish requires the accent on 'está'; dropping it is common in informal digital contexts but is orthographically incorrect.
target_language_example: Deje usted esta hoja en blanco. (forms with 'usted' following verb; note 'esta' here should be 'está' if used as 'is' — in this imperative example 'esta' is a demonstrative and correct without accent)
native_language_example: Leave this sheet blank. (polite/formal)

meaning: you are (formal) — the polite/formal second-person singular of 'to be' (estar).
additional_notes: Use 'usted' + 'está' to speak politely or formally to one person. 'Estar' is used for temporary states, locations, feelings, ongoing actions, or conditions (e.g., 'usted está cansado', 'usted está en casa', 'usted está pensando'). Conjugation: usted está. In everyday informal situations with friends or family, use 'tú estás' instead.
target_language_example: Usted está invitado a la reunión mañana.
native_language_example: You are invited to the meeting tomorrow.

meaning: The formal 'you' (usted) combined with the indirect object pronoun 'le' — meaning 'to you' or 'for you' in contexts where an indirect object is required; often used in expressions addressing someone formally where an indirect object is present or implied.
additional_notes: 'Usted' is the formal second-person singular subject pronoun. 'Le' is the third-person/indirect-object pronoun used for 'to him/her' and also for the formal 'you' (usted) as indirect object. Word order varies; 'usted le' commonly appears before a verb (usted le + verb). Spanish sometimes uses an explicit prepositional phrase (A usted) to mark the indirect object: e.g., 'A usted le cae bien'. In advice constructions like 'Yo que usted le pedía perdón', 'le' refers to the person receiving the action ('to him/her'). Context determines whether 'le' translates as 'to you', 'to him/her', or 'for you'.
target_language_example: Usted le cae bien a mi hermana.
native_language_example: You (formal) are liked by my sister / My sister likes you (formal).

meaning: you yourself (formal).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the action or quality applies to the person being addressed formally (usted). Often placed after the verb or noun it refers to: 'Lo hizo usted mismo' = 'You yourself did it.' Can also appear as 'usted misma' when addressing a woman, but 'usted' most often pairs with 'mismo' regardless of gender in everyday speech.
target_language_example: ¿Quiere hacerlo usted mismo?
native_language_example: Do you want to do it yourself?

meaning: a polite form of address using 'usted' with 'muy' to intensify an adjective (e.g., 'you are very...').
additional_notes: Combine 'usted' (formal 'you') with 'muy' + adjective to politely emphasize a quality (e.g., 'usted muy amable' = 'you are very kind'). In correct word order in Spanish, the adjective normally follows and 'muy' directly precedes the adjective: 'usted es muy amable', 'está usted muy alegre'. Examples in the input sometimes omit the verb (elliptical) in spoken or formal contexts, but learners should usually include the appropriate verb (es, está, ha sido). Use with people you address formally (strangers, elders, superiors).
target_language_example: Gracias, está usted muy amable.
native_language_example: Thank you, you are very kind.

meaning: you never (formal).
additional_notes: Combines the formal singular pronoun 'usted' with 'nunca' (never). Used to address someone politely or formally while saying they do not/do not ever do something or have never done something. Word order is subject + adverb (usted nunca + verb). In questions or negative contexts, 'nunca' expresses 'at no time' or 'not ever.'
target_language_example: Usted nunca llega tarde a las reuniones.
native_language_example: You never arrive late to meetings.

meaning: 'you or' (formal) — used to offer an alternative involving the formal 'usted'.
additional_notes: Combines the formal pronoun usted with the conjunction o (or) to present two possible people: 'you or [someone else]'. Used in formal contexts or when speaking politely. Word order is the same as in English: 'usted o [otra persona]'.
target_language_example: Usted o el director debe firmar este documento.
native_language_example: You or the director must sign this document.

meaning: 'you and' (formal 'you' paired with another person)
additional_notes: Used to connect the formal singular pronoun usted with another person (e.g., usted y yo = you and I). Use when addressing someone formally (usted) together with someone else. In everyday speech, 'usted y tú' is uncommon; choose 'tú y...' if speaking informally. Verb agreement follows the combined subjects (e.g., 'Usted y yo somos').
target_language_example: Usted y yo tenemos una cita mañana.
native_language_example: You and I have an appointment tomorrow.

meaning: you two (plural: addressing two people formally or informally in Latin America).
additional_notes: Used to address or refer to two people together. In most of Latin America, ustedes is the standard plural 'you' for both formal and informal situations; 'ustedes dos' emphasizes exactly two people. In Spain, 'vosotros' (or 'vosotros dos') is used for informal plural 'you' and 'ustedes' is formal.
target_language_example: Ustedes dos tienen que venir mañana a las ocho.
native_language_example: You two have to come tomorrow at eight.

meaning: the plural formal/informal 'you' (ustedes) + reflexive pronoun 'se' used with reflexive or reciprocal verbs (you all ... yourselves/each other).
additional_notes: Ustedes is the plural 'you' used in Latin America (and formal plural in Spain). 'Se' is the third-person reflexive pronoun used with ustedes for reflexive verbs (ellos/ellas/ustedes se). It appears with reflexive actions (ustedes se lavan = you all wash yourselves), reciprocal actions (ustedes se conocen = you know each other), commands (quiero que ustedes se queden = I want you all to stay), and pronominal verbs or idiomatic expressions (ustedes se creen gran cosa = you all think highly of yourselves). Word order: subject + se + verb (in many subordinate clauses you may see 'se' before the verb).
target_language_example: Ustedes se ayudaron durante el proyecto.
native_language_example: You all helped each other during the project.

meaning: 'used the' (past tense, third person singular).
additional_notes: Usó is the preterite (simple past) form of usar for él/ella/usted — 'he/she/you (formal) used'. El is the masculine singular definite article 'the'. Together they mean someone used a specific masculine noun (e.g., el baño, el cuchillo, el diccionario). For feminine nouns you'd see 'usó la' (e.g., usó la computadora).
target_language_example: Ella usó el ordenador para escribir el informe.
native_language_example: She used the computer to write the report.

meaning: one goes / someone goes (used in general statements or instructions)
additional_notes: Literally 'one goes' or 'someone goes'. 'Uno' is an impersonal subject meaning 'one', 'you' (general), or 'someone'. 'Va uno' is somewhat formal or literary; in everyday speech Spanish speakers more often use 'se va', 'uno va', 'la gente va', or 'voy/vas/va' with a specific subject. Context determines whether it means a general statement (One goes to the park) or a suggestion/instruction (One should go).
target_language_example: Cuando hace calor, va uno a la playa.
native_language_example: When it's hot, one goes to the beach.

meaning: 'cows are' — a simple subject + verb phrase used to state facts or opinions about cows.
additional_notes: Literal combination of the plural noun 'vacas' (cows) and the present-tense verb 'son' (they are) from 'ser'. Used to make general statements or descriptions about cows (e.g., qualities, classification, or cultural beliefs). In Spanish, 'son' is used for permanent characteristics, identities, professions, classifications, or general truths.
target_language_example: Las vacas son importantes en la agricultura local.
native_language_example: Cows are important in local agriculture.

meaning: 'is worth nothing' / 'is worthless' (used to say something or someone has no value or is useless).
additional_notes: Common informal expression. Often used with third-person singular verb 'vale' (from valer). Can be used literally (monetary value) or figuratively (useless, pointless, or not credible). Frequently appears alone as the short phrase 'No vale nada.'
target_language_example: Ese documento sin firmas no vale nada.
native_language_example: That document without signatures is worth nothing.

meaning: 'is valid for' / 'applies to' / 'counts for'
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is valid or applicable for a person, time period, number of uses, or situation. Context decides whether it means 'is valid for' (tickets, passes), 'applies to' (rules, statements), or 'counts for'. Often follows a noun indicating the beneficiary or extent (e.g., 'dos personas', 'tres días').
target_language_example: El pase vale para todo el fin de semana.
native_language_example: The pass is valid for the whole weekend.

meaning: 'better (that) not' — used to advise or warn that something should not happen
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed expression 'más vale que no' (literally 'it is better that not'). It's a warning or piece of advice meaning it's better if X doesn't happen or you don't do X. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., 'aceptes', 'estés') but can stand alone as a short reply: 'Más vale que no.'
target_language_example: Más vale que no vengas sin avisar.
native_language_example: It's better that you don't come without letting us know.

meaning: It's better that it be / It would be better if it were
additional_notes: Often appears in the fixed phrase "más vale que sea..." meaning "it's better (for you/it) that..." Used to express preference or relief about a hoped-for quality or outcome. Followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or subordinate clause introduced by "que" + subjunctive (e.g., "sea"). Tone can be neutral or mildly advisory/warning depending on context.
target_language_example: Más vale que sea barato, porque no tenemos mucho dinero.
native_language_example: It'd be better if it were cheap, because we don't have much money.

meaning: 'is worth a' or 'is worth one/a'.
additional_notes: Used to state the value or worth of something. Often followed by a quantity or noun (e.g., 'vale un millón', 'vale un beso'). Can appear in comparisons or idiomatic expressions (e.g., 'más vale' meaning 'better to/it is better that...'). Verb 'vale' is from 'valer' (to be worth); subject and number may change (vale/valen).
target_language_example: Esta guitarra vale un ojo de la cara.
native_language_example: This guitar is worth an arm and a leg.

meaning: 'to be worth it' or 'to be worthwhile'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something justifies the effort, time, cost, or trouble. Often followed by an infinitive (valió la pena esperar / vale la pena intentar) or a noun phrase. Common tenses: vale la pena (present), valió la pena (past), valdrá la pena (future).
target_language_example: Puede valer la pena esperar un poco más.
native_language_example: It may be worth waiting a little longer.

meaning: 'value of' or 'worth of' (followed by a masculine noun).
additional_notes: A common Spanish phrase used to talk about the value, price, importance, or worth of something. 'Del' is the contraction of 'de' + 'el', so it must appear before a masculine singular noun (e.g., 'valor del dólar', 'valor del tiempo'). Use 'de la' for feminine nouns (valor de la vida).
target_language_example: Debemos conocer el valor del tiempo.
native_language_example: We must know the value of time.

meaning: value, worth, or courage 'in' (used to say something has value/importance in a particular context, or courage shown in a situation).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: 'valor' can mean 'value' (usefulness/importance) or 'courage/bravery'. When followed by 'en' it links that value/courage to a context (e.g., 'valor en el conocimiento' = value in knowledge; 'valor en la faz de un peligro' = courage in the face of danger). Word order and context determine meaning. For describing a person of high importance on a list, Spanish often uses 'de alto valor en la lista' or better 'de alto valor en la lista de vigilancia' meaning 'high-value'.
