Often followed by adjectives or noun phrases describing weather. Can also be expressed as "hay viento" (there is wind) or with measurements: "la velocidad del viento es..."
target_language_example: El viento es muy frío hoy.
native_language_example: The wind is very cold today.

meaning: The word 'viento' = 'wind'. The added 'se' marks reflexive or impersonal constructions used with verbs (e.g., calmarse, llevarse, ponerse, detenerse) to say that the wind does something to/for itself or that an action happens with the wind as subject.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase. 'Viento' is a noun; 'se' appears because the verbs in the examples are pronominal (verb + se) or use the pronominal/impersonal 'se' to form intransitive actions: 'calmarse' (to calm down), 'llevarse' (to carry away), 'ponerse' (to become), 'detenerse' (to stop), 'tomarse' (to take for oneself). With weather nouns like 'viento' you commonly see verbs conjugated with 'se' to describe changes of state or actions where no agent is explicitly mentioned. Literal translation depends on the verb (e.g., 'El viento se ha calmado' = 'The wind has calmed down').
target_language_example: El viento se levantó por la tarde y se llevó las hojas.
native_language_example: The wind picked up in the afternoon and carried the leaves away.

meaning: Imperfect (past) subjunctive form of ver used before a direct object introduced by the preposition 'a' when that object is a person; used in subordinate clauses expressing doubt, possibility, wishes, advice, or hypothetical situations (English: 'saw', 'might have seen', 'would see', 'should see' depending on context).
additional_notes: 'Viera' is one of the imperfect-subjunctive forms of 'ver' (others: viese). It appears after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., es posible que, aconsejó que, dudaba que). The preposition 'a' is required when the direct object is a specific person: 'viera a alguien/María/mi abogado'. Translation into English depends on tense and context.
target_language_example: Aquella fue la última vez en que cualquiera de nosotros viera a Tom.
native_language_example: That was the last time any of us saw Tom.

meaning: 'on Friday (in the) — used with times of day (e.g., noche) to mean 'on Friday night' or similar.'
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete on its own and is normally followed by a time-of-day word (más común: 'noche' — viernes por la noche). It means 'on Friday (night/morning/afternoon)' and expresses a recurring or specific time. Use 'los viernes por la noche' to say 'on Friday nights' (habitual).
target_language_example: Vamos al cine viernes por la noche.
native_language_example: We’re going to the movies on Friday night.

meaning: they saw (someone).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ver with the personal a before a person: 'vieron' = ellos/ellas/ustedes saw. Use 'a' when the direct object is a specific person or people (la 'a' personal). If the object is not a person, 'a' is not required.
target_language_example: Ayer vieron a la vecina en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday they saw the neighbor at the supermarket.

meaning: we saw the / we watched the
additional_notes: Vimos is the first-person plural (nosotros) past simple (pretérito) of ver (to see/watch). El is the masculine singular definite article 'the'. Together they introduce a masculine singular noun that the speakers saw or watched. Context decides if 'saw' (perceived with eyes) or 'watched' (viewed an event, show, or game) is better in English.
target_language_example: Vimos el atardecer desde la playa.
native_language_example: We saw the sunset from the beach.

meaning: 'we saw (her/him/it) in' or 'we met/ran into (someone) at/in' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literal verb 'ver' in past (nosotros) + preposition 'en'. Can mean 'we saw' (observed) something in a source or place (e.g., 'vimos en el pasado bloque') or 'we saw/met someone at/in (a location)' (e.g., 'nos vimos en la calle' or 'la vimos en el aeropuerto'). Subject and object can change meaning: 'nos vimos en...' often means 'we met/ran into each other at...'; 'la vimos en...' means 'we saw her at/in...'.
target_language_example: Ayer la vimos en el cine.
native_language_example: Yesterday we saw her at the cinema.

meaning: I came; I arrived (from venir in the past tense, colloquial form).
additional_notes: Vine tan appears to be an informal or nonstandard spelling/representation of the first-person preterite of venir (vine) plus tan ('so'/'that') or possibly a colloquial fused phrase. In standard Spanish, 'vine' means 'I came' (pretérito de venir). If the intended phrase is 'vine tan [adjective]' it would mean 'I came so [adjective]' (e.g., 'Vine tan cansado' = 'I came so tired'), though more natural is 'Llegué tan...' or 'Vine tan...'. Without context this looks nonstandard/colloquial. Use 'vine' for 'I came' in neutral situations; avoid 'vine tan' as a fixed phrase unless in a specific dialectal context.
target_language_example: Vine tan cansado que me dormí en el autobús.
native_language_example: I came so tired that I fell asleep on the bus.

meaning: 'they came from' or 'they came to (visit/from)'.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of venir + de. Usually means 'they came from' (origin) or 'they came (to) [for a visit]' when followed by 'visita' or similar. Context determines whether de indicates origin (from a place) or part of the verb phrase 'venir de visita' (to come for a visit). Subject is third person plural.
target_language_example: Ellos vinieron de Madrid la semana pasada.
native_language_example: They came from Madrid last week.

meaning: 'came with his/her/their/your (formal)'.
additional_notes: Vino is the past (pretérito) form of venir (to come) for él/ella/usted. 'Con su' + noun shows the person came accompanied by someone (su = his, her, their, or your formal). Context or preceding info clarifies whose (su) it is. Capitalization and pronoun can change: 'Vino con su hermano' = 'He/She/You(formal) came with his/her/your brother.'
target_language_example: María vino con su amiga a la fiesta.
native_language_example: María came with her friend to the party.

meaning: came by / arrived by (a particular means of transport) or 'came during/in' (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to say someone arrived by a mode of transport: 'vino en coche' = 'he/she came by car'. Can also appear in contexts meaning 'came during' or 'came in (someone's absence)' but that use is less common and can be ambiguous; context and subject pronouns help. 'Vino' is the past (pretérito) of 'venir' (to come).
target_language_example: Ella vino en tren ayer.
native_language_example: She came by train yesterday.

meaning: he/she/it came to (do something) — expresses purpose or destination of coming
additional_notes: Vino para is the past (pretérito) third-person singular of venir + para. It usually indicates why someone came (purpose) or where/which direction (less common). Followed by an infinitive (vino para pelear), a noun/pronoun (vino para acá / para verte), or a clause explaining intent. Context determines whether it's purpose ('came to do X') or movement toward ('came here/there').
target_language_example: Mi hermano vino para ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: My brother came to help me with the move.

meaning: 'came and' (used to link one action with another: someone came and then did something).
additional_notes: Common colloquial structure: vino y + [verb/phrase] or (subject) vino y + [verb]. It links the action of coming (vino) with a subsequent action — often used to narrate events quickly (He came and did X). In some dialects/contexts, 'vino' can be replaced by other past forms (e.g., 'vino y me sacó' = 'he came and took me'). Not formal; used in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Ella vino y comenzó a cantar en la fiesta.
native_language_example: She came and started singing at the party.

meaning: white wine.
additional_notes: Refers to wine made from white grapes or produced in a way that results in a light-colored wine. Commonly used when ordering drinks or talking about preferences. Can appear alone (e.g., when ordering) or with articles/adjectives (el vino blanco, un vino blanco seco).
target_language_example: Quisiera una copa de vino blanco, por favor.
native_language_example: I would like a glass of white wine, please.

meaning: red wine
additional_notes: Common phrase for wine made from red grapes. Used when ordering, talking about drinking, or referring to wine color/type. 'Vino' = wine, 'tinto' = red/dark. Not formal or slang—neutral vocabulary.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres una copa de vino tinto?
native_language_example: Do you want a glass of red wine?

meaning: saw the
additional_notes: Compositional phrase: vio is the preterite (simple past) of ver, and el means "the" before a masculine singular noun. It is used for a completed action in the past. Depending on the object, ver can mean either "see" or "watch."
target_language_example: María vio el perro en el parque.
native_language_example: María saw the dog in the park.

meaning: saw (him/her/it) in the… / saw in the…
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ver: 'vio' = he/she/you(formal) saw. 'En la' begins a location with a feminine noun (la estación, la enfermería, la distancia, la luz). Together it introduces where someone or something was seen. Subject and direct object pronouns may change (lo, le, la) before the verb: 'Ella lo vio en la estación' = She saw him at the station.
target_language_example: Él la vio en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: He saw her in the library.

meaning: 'saw' (past of 'ver') + the (feminine plural).
additional_notes: Vio is the third-person singular preterite of ver (to see). Las is the feminine plural definite article ('the'). Together they mean 'he/she/you(formal) saw the...' followed by a feminine plural noun: e.g. vio las fotos (saw the photos), vio las sombras (saw the shadows). Can appear in neutral, descriptive sentences or in more colloquial/explicit contexts depending on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Ella vio las montañas desde la ventana.
native_language_example: She saw the mountains from the window.

meaning: 'was forced/compelled to' (he/she/it was forced to do something).
additional_notes: Past tense third-person singular of the reflexive verb phrase 'verse obligado a + infinitive'. Used to say someone had no choice but to do something (often for external reasons). Common with verbs like dejar, abandonar, hacer. Translate as 'was forced to' or 'had to (reluctantly)'.
target_language_example: Después del accidente, se vio obligado a dejar su trabajo.
native_language_example: After the accident, he was forced to quit his job.

meaning: 'he/she saw his/her' (past tense: saw + possessive)
additional_notes: Vio = third-person singular preterite of ver (to see). Su = his, her, its, your (formal), or their — context decides which. Together they mean someone saw something belonging to or associated with someone. English pronoun gender/number must be inferred from context. Common in simple past narrative.
target_language_example: Cuando vio su foto, sonrió.
native_language_example: When he/she saw his/her photo, he/she smiled.

meaning: to visit (feminine singular place) — 'visit the ...'.
additional_notes: Visitar = to visit. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article used before feminine place nouns (la Gran Muralla, la Esfinge, la Biblioteca Nacional, la ciudad). Use 'visitar el' for masculine nouns (el museo) or 'visitar los/las' for plurals. Verb can be conjugated as needed (quiero visitar, visitamos, visitó).
target_language_example: Quiero visitar la catedral mañana.
native_language_example: I want to visit the cathedral tomorrow.

meaning: to visit my (followed by a noun: place, person, or thing belonging to the speaker).
additional_notes: A common collocation where visitar (to visit) is followed by the speaker's possessive mi + noun (mi tienda, mi iglesia, mi casa, mi país, mi clase). You must include the noun after mi; 'visitarme' (single word) is also used when the object is a person or implied (visit me). Use visitar + place/person to talk about going to see someone or someplace.
target_language_example: Deberías visitar mi restaurante cuando estés en la ciudad.
native_language_example: You should visit my restaurant when you're in town.

meaning: 'in sight' / 'sight in' depending on context; often part of phrases meaning 'lost sight of' or 'keep one's eyes on'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself — 'vista' = sight, 'en' = in/on. Common uses: 'perder de vista' (to lose sight of) + 'en' to indicate where or when (e.g. 'en la muchedumbre'). Also used literally for vision loss: 'perder la vista en [parte]'. Can appear in commands: 'mantén la vista en [algo]' = keep your eyes on [something]. Word order and surrounding verbs determine meaning.
target_language_example: Mantén la vista en la carretera mientras conduces.
native_language_example: Keep your eyes on the road while you drive.

meaning: 'a look at' or 'a glance at' (used with echar/ echa/ echarle un vistazo a)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase echar(le) un vistazo a (to take a look at / glance at). Used for quick, informal checks or brief looks. Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., echar un vistazo a las fotos / echarle un vistazo a eso).
target_language_example: Echa un vistazo a este informe antes de enviarlo.
native_language_example: Take a look at this report before sending it.

meaning: a look at this; take a look at this.
additional_notes: Commonly used as a request or instruction to ask someone to look at or review something right now. Often appears in the imperative with verbs like echar/echale (Échale un vistazo a esto) or echar un vistazo a esto. Informal, everyday phrasing.
target_language_example: Échale un vistazo a esto cuando tengas un minuto.
native_language_example: Take a look at this when you have a minute.

meaning: 'did you see (someone)?' — second person singular past of 'ver' with a direct-person object marker.
additional_notes: Viste is the tú (informal you) preterite form of ver (to see). When the object is a person, Spanish uses the personal 'a' before the name or pronoun: viste a María / viste a él. Used to ask if someone saw a particular person at a specific time or place.
target_language_example: ¿Viste a Marta en la fiesta anoche?
native_language_example: Did you see Marta at the party last night?

meaning: 'seen something' or 'seen anything' (past participle of ver + something/anything).
additional_notes: Commonly used with haber (he visto algo, había visto algo) to form the present perfect or past perfect: 'I have seen something' / 'I had seen something'. 'Algo' usually means 'something' (affirmative) but in negative contexts or questions it can function like 'anything'. Word order can vary: 'he visto algo', '¿has visto algo?', or 'no he visto nada' (note: 'algo' becomes 'nada' in negatives).
target_language_example: He visto algo en el jardín esta mañana.
native_language_example: I have seen something in the garden this morning.

meaning: seen with
additional_notes: Literally 'seen with'. Often used in perfect constructions with 'haber' + 'visto' to say someone was seen accompanied by someone or something (e.g. 'le he visto con la profesora' = 'I saw him with the teacher'). Also appears in expressions emphasizing direct observation with 'mis/ tus/nuestros propios ojos' ('with my own eyes'). The passive-like sentence 'no puedes ser visto con esto' means 'you cannot be seen with this' (i.e., be seen possessing or using this) — context determines whether it refers to accompaniment or being seen holding/wearing something.
target_language_example: La vi anoche y la he visto con su hermano.
native_language_example: I saw her last night and I saw her with her brother.

meaning: 'seen that' (feminine singular): used when saying you've seen a particular thing or expression before.
additional_notes: Visto is the past participle of ver (to see). Esa is a demonstrative adjective meaning 'that' for feminine nouns. Together they appear in sentences like 'He visto esa mirada' ('I have seen that look'). The noun being referred to is feminine (cara, mirada, técnica, vidriera). Word order in Spanish is usually 'verbo + demostrativo + sustantivo' (e.g., 'he visto esa cara').
target_language_example: Ya he visto esa película.
native_language_example: I've already seen that movie.

meaning: seen this
additional_notes: Common combination of the past participle visto (from ver — to see) plus the demonstrative esto (this) used to say you have seen something. Appears in perfect tenses (he visto esto = I have seen this) or in other contexts with auxiliary verbs. Can also be used with nunca (never) or cantidades (cientos de veces). 'Esto' refers to something close in context; in some dialects or contexts 'esto' might be replaced by 'esto'/'eso' depending on distance.
target_language_example: No puedo creer que ya hayas visto esto.
native_language_example: I can't believe you've already seen this.

meaning: 'never seen' or 'never have seen' (usually part of a larger phrase like 'no lo he visto nunca').
additional_notes: Alone 'visto' is the past participle of 'ver' (to see). Spanish typically places negation before the verb: 'nunca lo he visto' or 'no lo he visto nunca' mean 'I have never seen it.' 'Visto nunca' by itself is not a complete or common standalone phrase; you'll most often encounter it inside sentences with auxiliary verbs (he, has, hemos) or with 'haber' omitted in informal speech ('Nunca visto' is uncommon).
target_language_example: No lo he visto nunca en esta tienda.
native_language_example: I have never seen it in this store.

meaning: given that
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or fact that is taken as already clear or established. It is often a bit more formal or written than everyday alternatives like "porque" or "ya que."
target_language_example: Visto que mañana llueve, mejor nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: Since it's going to rain tomorrow, we'd better stay home.

meaning: 'seen everything' or idiomatically 'I've seen it all' / 'you've seen everything' (used to say one has experienced everything or to express surprise/disbelief about something unexpected).
additional_notes: Literally the past participle 'visto' (seen) + 'todo' (everything). Commonly used in perfect constructions with haber (he visto, has visto, ha visto) to say someone has already seen/experienced everything. Also used idiomatically to react to surprising or outrageous events: 'Ahora ya lo has visto todo' = 'Now I've seen it all' (I can't believe it).
target_language_example: Cuando dijo eso, pensé: ya lo he visto todo.
native_language_example: When he said that, I thought: I've seen it all.

meaning: seen one
additional_notes: A compositional phrase: visto is the past participle of ver ('to see'), and uno means 'one' or 'a/an one,' referring back to a masculine noun mentioned earlier or understood from context. It often appears with forms of haber in perfect tenses, as in he visto uno ('I have seen one') or había visto uno ('I had seen one').
target_language_example: ¿Has visto uno de estos antes?
native_language_example: Have you seen one of these before?

meaning: a perfect likeness; the spitting image (someone or something that looks exactly like another).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person (or sometimes thing) strongly resembles another in appearance or character. Often appears as "la viva imagen de..." or "el vivo retrato de..." Can describe family resemblance or to emphasize health/energy (e.g., "viva imagen de la salud").
target_language_example: María es la viva imagen de su abuela.
native_language_example: María is the spitting image of her grandmother.

meaning: lives with his/her/their (plural noun); indicates someone lives together with the people or things referred to by 'sus'.
additional_notes: ‘Vive’ is the third-person singular present of 'vivir' (to live). 'Con' means 'with'. 'Sus' is a possessive adjective (his, her, your formal, their) used before plural nouns. The exact English possessive depends on context (su/sus can be ambiguous). Use 'vive con sus' when saying someone lives with certain family members, roommates, pets, etc. Example completions: 'vive con sus padres' = 'he/she lives with his/her parents.'
target_language_example: Mi hermana vive con sus dos hijos.
native_language_example: My sister lives with her two children.

meaning: lives in that (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Vive = 'he/she/you (formal) lives'. En esa modifies a feminine noun previously mentioned or understood (esa casa = that house). Use 'ese' for masculine nouns (ese libro), 'esa' for feminine (esa casa), and 'eso' for neutral ideas. Common in statements about where someone lives.
target_language_example: Mi hermana vive en esa casa azul.
native_language_example: My sister lives in that blue house.

meaning: 'lives anymore' / 'lives no longer' (in negative) or 'lives the most' / 'lives closest' (in comparative context)
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context and sentence structure. With a negative (e.g., 'ya no vive más'), it means 'no longer lives' or 'doesn't live here anymore'. In comparative phrases (e.g., 'vive más cerca'), 'más' is a comparative adverb meaning 'more' or 'closer/more (adverb)', so 'vive más cerca' = 'lives closer'. Alone 'vive más' can be ambiguous; pay attention to surrounding words (negation or comparative phrase).
target_language_example: Ella ya no vive más en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: She no longer lives in this city.

meaning: she lives alone.
additional_notes: Vive sola = third-person singular of 'vivir' (to live) + 'sola' (alone, feminine). Use 'vive solo' for a male subject. Can be used with or without mentioning the place: 'vive sola' or 'vive sola en casa/apartamento'.
target_language_example: Mi hermana vive sola en un departamento cerca del centro.
native_language_example: My sister lives alone in an apartment near downtown.

meaning: 'they live longer than the' (used to compare how long groups live)
additional_notes: A comparative phrase: viven (they live) + más que (more than/longer than) + los (the, plural masculine or mixed group). Use with a noun or clause after 'los' (e.g., 'los hombres', 'los gatos'). Agreement depends on the subject (viven) and the article matches the noun being compared. Can also appear as 'viven más que las' when comparing to a feminine plural noun.
target_language_example: Las tortugas viven más que los perros en promedio.
native_language_example: Turtles live longer than dogs on average.

meaning: 'lived happily (ever) ...' — part of the phrase meaning 'lived happily ever after'.
additional_notes: This is the beginning of the common fairy-tale formula 'vivieron felices para siempre' = 'they lived happily ever after'. It is usually used at the end of stories to say that things turned out well. The verb 'vivieron' is past (ellos/ustedes). If you want 'we' use 'vivimos felices para siempre'; 'I' would be 'viví feliz para siempre' (rare).
target_language_example: Se casaron y vivieron felices para siempre.
native_language_example: They got married and lived happily ever after.

meaning: to live with
additional_notes: Used to indicate sharing a home or having to coexist with someone or something (a person, condition, situation). Can be literal (sharing a house) or figurative (having to endure a situation or characteristic). Commonly followed by a person, living arrangement, or noun describing the thing you must 'live with.'
target_language_example: A partir de ahora voy a vivir con mi hermana.
native_language_example: From now on I'm going to live with my sister.

meaning: to live in a big/large (usually city) — starts a phrase like 'vivir en una gran ciudad' (to live in a big city).
additional_notes: This is a fragment meaning 'to live in a big...' Often completed with a noun such as ciudad (city). Used to express opinions or facts about living in large places. 'gran' is the shortened form of 'grande' before a singular noun (gran ciudad = big/important city).
target_language_example: Me gustaría vivir en una gran ciudad algún día.
native_language_example: I'd like to live in a big city someday.

meaning: to live (in order) to; to live long enough to (do/see something).
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) to express purpose or goal (live in order to do something) — vivir para + infinitive or + noun; 2) to say someone lives long enough to reach/see something (often followed by a verb like ver or an age). Context and verb after 'para' determine exact nuance.
target_language_example: Quiero vivir para ver a mis nietos graduarse.
native_language_example: I want to live long enough to see my grandchildren graduate.

meaning: lived a (used to describe the kind of life someone had).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of vivir + the indefinite article una; followed by vida + adjective or noun phrase to describe the person's life (e.g., vida larga, vida tranquila). Common structure to summarize someone's past life or how they used to live.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo vivió una vida llena de viajes.
native_language_example: My grandfather lived a life full of travels.

meaning: 'alive' / 'living' or 'vivid' when used with memories or feelings; here followed by 'en' to indicate where something is alive/vivid (e.g., in someone's memory, in a place).
additional_notes: Depending on context, vivo can mean 'alive' (a person still living) or 'vivid/strong' (a memory, feeling, or tradition that remains). The preposition 'en' specifies where it is alive or vivid: vivo en mi memoria (vivid in my memory), vivo en esas comunidades (alive in those communities). Use 'seguir vivo' to say 'to still be alive' or 'to remain vivid'.
target_language_example: Ese recuerdo sigue vivo en mi mente.
native_language_example: That memory is still vivid in my mind.

meaning: 'alive/ lively because of' or 'alive by/for' depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase can appear in different constructions: 1) 'vivo' as an adjective meaning 'lively' + 'por' meaning 'during/because of' (e.g., 'vivo por las noches' = 'lively at night' or 'has a lively atmosphere at night'); 2) 'devorado vivo por' uses 'vivo' to mean 'alive' (emphasizing that something happened while still alive) followed by 'por' to introduce the agent (e.g., 'devorado vivo por gusanos' = 'devoured alive by worms'); 3) 'me siento más vivo por la noche' means 'I feel more alive at night' (personal state + 'por' indicating time). Pay attention to context to know whether 'vivo' describes liveliness, being alive, or a stronger/emphatic sense.
target_language_example: En verano, el paseo está muy vivo por las tardes.
native_language_example: In summer, the promenade is very lively in the evenings.

meaning: 'vivo' + 'que' used in different senses depending on context: 'alive that' / 'living that' OR 'very vivid/realistic that' OR 'live (broadcast/event) that'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the adjective 'vivo' followed by the relative pronoun 'que'. 'Vivo' can mean: 1) alive (living) — e.g. alguien vivo que...; 2) vivid/realistic — un retrato vivo que...; 3) live (as in live performance/broadcast) — espectáculo en vivo que.... The meaning depends on context and noun it modifies. 'Que' introduces a clause describing the noun.
target_language_example: Conozco a un pintor vivo que trabaja en la plaza.
native_language_example: I know a living painter who works in the square.

meaning: 'flying in' or 'flying over' (something, usually a place or space).
additional_notes: Present participle 'volando' (flying) + preposition 'en' (in/on/over). Used to describe birds, insects, objects moving through a space (e.g., volando en el cielo = flying in/over the sky). English choice (in/over) depends on context: 'en el cielo' usually translates as 'in the sky' or 'over the sky/above the sky'; 'en dirección a' adds direction (toward).
target_language_example: Veo mariposas volando en el jardín.
native_language_example: I see butterflies flying in the garden.

meaning: literally 'flying/going through the' — used to describe moving quickly through or over a place or situation
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase; it usually appears before a noun (e.g., volando por la ciudad, volando por la autopista) to say someone or something is speeding/flying through that place. Can be literal (an airplane flying over) or figurative (moving very fast, doing something quickly). Make sure to complete it with a noun (la ciudad, la casa, la carretera, la vida, etc.). Verb form volando is the gerund of volar (to fly).
target_language_example: Íbamos volando por la autopista cuando empezó a llover.
native_language_example: We were speeding down the highway when it started to rain.

meaning: to fly to (a place).
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about traveling by airplane to a destination: volar a + place (country, city, airport). In some contexts (especially literary or figurative), volar can mean 'to make someone/something fly' or 'to blow up' (with different constructions), but with 'a' it usually indicates direction ('to'). Use 'volar a' for planned flights: Voy a volar a Madrid mañana = I'm flying to Madrid tomorrow.
target_language_example: Mañana voy a volar a Barcelona para una conferencia.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm flying to Barcelona for a conference.

meaning: to ... again
additional_notes: With an infinitive, volver a means 'to do something again': volver a preguntar = 'ask again'. With a place or noun after a, it means 'to return to / go back to': volver a la ciudad = 'return to the city'.
target_language_example: No quiero volver a hablar de eso.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about that again.

meaning: to return to my (place/person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to say you are returning to a place or thing that belongs to you (seat, house, desk, etc.). 'Volver a' means 'to return to' or 'to do again'; here it's followed by a possessive 'mi' + noun. Conjugate 'volver' as needed (e.g., 'debo volver a mi casa', 'voy a volver a mi asiento').
target_language_example: Necesito volver a mi casa antes de la medianoche.
native_language_example: I need to return to my house before midnight.

meaning: 'to return in' (to come back after a specified amount of time).
additional_notes: Used to indicate when someone will return, followed by a time expression (e.g., 'en tres horas', 'en la segunda semana', 'en otro momento'). Common in everyday speech. The construction = volver + en + [time phrase]. Not to be confused with 'volver a' (to do something again) or 'volver' alone.
target_language_example: Puedo volver en otro momento.
native_language_example: I can return in another moment.

meaning: to regain consciousness; to come to (after fainting or being stunned).
additional_notes: Used when someone who was unconscious, fainted or stunned becomes conscious again. Often follows verbs like 'desmayarse', 'perder el conocimiento' or incidents (accidents, shocks). Can also be used figuratively for 'coming to one's senses.'
target_language_example: Después del golpe, tardó unos minutos en volver en sí.
native_language_example: After the blow, it took him a few minutes to come to.

meaning: 'to go crazy' or 'to lose one's mind' (mentally or emotionally); can be used literally or figuratively.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe someone becoming mentally unstable or reacting with extreme emotion or panic. Often reflexive (volverse + adjective) and implies a change of state. Can be used jokingly (informal) or seriously depending on context.
target_language_example: Cuando vio la sorpresa, estuvo a punto de volverse loco de alegría.
native_language_example: When he saw the surprise, he was about to go crazy with joy.

meaning: will return in (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something will come back after a specified amount of time. 'Volverá' is future tense of 'volver' (to return). Follow with a time expression: 'unos días', 'una hora', 'diez minutos', etc. For I/you/we use different forms (volveré, volverás, volveremos).
target_language_example: Volverá en tres horas.
native_language_example: He/She/It will return in three hours.

meaning: I will do (it) again.
additional_notes: Future tense of 'volver a + infinitive' expresses repeating an action. With 'no' it means 'I will not do it again.' Often used to promise or warn about repeating behavior. The pronoun (lo/te/etc.) indicates the object affected.
target_language_example: Lo volveré a hacer si tengo la oportunidad.
native_language_example: I will do it again if I have the chance.

meaning: I'll return/come back earlier or before (something).
additional_notes: Simple future of volver (volveré) + antes (before/earlier). Often used to say you'll come back earlier than expected or before a certain time/event. To specify what it's 'before', add a time expression or clause: volveré antes de las cinco / volveré antes de que empiece la reunión. Can also mean 'I'll be back soon' in casual contexts.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, volveré antes de la cena.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll be back before dinner.

meaning: 'you and' (used to link 'vos' with another person or group)
additional_notes: Vos is a familiar second-person singular pronoun used in some Spanish-speaking regions (voseo) or archaic/formal contexts (older literature). 'Vos y' simply combines that pronoun with 'and' to join it to another noun or pronoun (e.g., 'vos y él' = 'you and him'). In modern standard Spanish, 'tú y' or 'usted y' are more common depending on register and region. Usage in examples shows both contemporary voseo (Argentina, Uruguay, parts of Central America) and older/poetic forms.
target_language_example: Vos y yo iremos al mercado mañana.
native_language_example: You and I will go to the market tomorrow.

meaning: 'I'm going to get married' (literally: 'I am going to marry').
additional_notes: Common colloquial way to say you will get married. Often used with a reflexive pronoun (me voy a casar) meaning 'I am going to get married' or with a person introduced by 'con' (me voy a casar con ella). Uses the periphrastic future 'ir a + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Me voy a casar el próximo verano.
native_language_example: I'm going to get married next summer.

meaning: I'm going to tell (you) what… / I'll tell (you) what…
additional_notes: A common phrase to introduce that you will explain or report something. 'Voy a decir' = 'I'm going to say/tell'; 'lo que' = 'what' or 'that which'. Usually followed by a clause (pasa, pasó, pienso, tienes que hacer, etc.). Used to promise information or give instructions.
target_language_example: Voy a decir lo que pasó anoche.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell (you) what happened last night.

meaning: I'm going to say a (feminine noun) / I'm going to give an example (feminine).
additional_notes: Literal: 'I am going to say a...'. Used before stating a feminine noun, example, idea or opinion. In conversation it often introduces an example or a point the speaker is about to make (e.g., 'voy a decir una cosa' = 'I'm going to say one thing'). If the following noun is masculine, use 'voy a decir un'.
target_language_example: Voy a decir una cosa: necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: I'm going to say one thing: we need more time.

meaning: I'm going to introduce (you) to...
additional_notes: Used when telling someone you will introduce them to a person or group. Spanish requires the preposition 'a' before the person(s) being introduced. The subject can be omitted (Te voy a presentar a...) or changed (Voy a presentar a...). Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Te voy a presentar a mi profesor mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to introduce you to my teacher tomorrow.

meaning: 'I'm going to' or 'I go (to) ...' used to say you are going somewhere or going to do an activity.
additional_notes: Common structure: voy de + noun (activity/place) or me voy de + place. 'Voy de' often precedes a noun indicating purpose (voy de compras = I'm going shopping) or direction (voy de regreso = I'm going back). 'Me voy de' means 'I'm leaving (from)'. Use 'voy a' + infinitive for 'I'm going to (do something)'.
target_language_example: Voy de paseo con mi perro esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going for a walk with my dog this afternoon.

meaning: I'm leaving here / I'm going away from here.
additional_notes: Used to say you're going to leave the current place. Common in everyday speech. Often followed by a time word (ahora mismo) or used with ya to indicate immediate departure. Can be shortened to Me voy (de aquí understood).
target_language_example: Me voy de aquí porque está muy ruidoso.
native_language_example: I'm leaving here because it's very noisy.

meaning: I go [very ... / very ...], used to modify how often or in what state someone goes or is.
additional_notes: Voy is the first-person present of ir (to go). 'Muy' is an adverb meaning 'very' and commonly modifies frequency adverbs (muy a menudo, muy poco, muy rara vez) or adjectives/participles (voy muy retrasado = I'm very late/behind). This construction appears before the frequency phrase or adjective. For frequency, English often places 'very' before the frequency adverb (very often, very rarely).
target_language_example: Voy muy seguido al gimnasio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym very often.

meaning: 'voz es' = 'the voice is' (used to describe someone's voice).
additional_notes: This is the noun 'voz' (voice) followed by the verb 'es' (is). Native speakers normally say full phrases like 'Su voz es...' ('His/her voice is...') to describe qualities of a voice (agradable, débil, bonita, como una nana, la de un dios, etc.). Use 'mi/tu/su/nuestra voz es...' to say 'my/your/his/her/our voice is...'.
target_language_example: Su voz es muy agradable.
native_language_example: His/her voice is very pleasant.

meaning: part of a phrase meaning 'return of the' or 'lap/turn of the' depending on context
additional_notes: Alone 'vuelta de la' is not a complete phrase; it usually appears inside longer expressions such as 'la vuelta de la esquina' (just around the corner), 'la vuelta de la playa' (the return from the beach), or 'dar una vuelta de la manzana' (take a walk around the block). 'Vuelta' can mean return, turn, lap, walk or change. The exact translation depends on the noun that follows. Watch for articles and contractions (de + el → del).
target_language_example: La vuelta de la esquina está cerca; llegamos en dos minutos.
native_language_example: The corner is just around the corner; we'll arrive in two minutes.

meaning: to go for a walk/drive/turn around or to wander around a place (for a while).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like dar (dar vueltas por) to mean walking, driving, or wandering around an area without a fixed purpose. Can imply circling, strolling, or spending time exploring. Followed by a place (por + location). Tense and aspect (dar, di, estaba dando) change duration or repetition.
target_language_example: Di vueltas por el parque antes de volver a casa.
native_language_example: I wandered around the park before going home.

meaning: they/you (plural) return to the + (masculine) place (command/imperative form).
additional_notes: From the verb volver (to return). 'Vuelvan' is the ustedes/ellos/ellas imperative (formal plural) or present-subjunctive form used for commands: 'vuelvan al' = 'return to the' (followed by a masculine noun like trabajo, partido, campamento). If addressing a group informally in Spain you might use 'volved al'. Context determines whether it's a command ('Return to...') or a suggestion ('that they return to...'). 'Al' is the contraction of 'a + el'.
target_language_example: Vuelvan al aula y traigan sus libros.
native_language_example: Return to the classroom and bring your books.

meaning: 'returns with' or 'comes back with' (someone or something); also 'get back together with' in context of relationships.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: volver (to return) + con (with). Common uses: 1) Someone returns accompanied by a person or object: Él vuelve con su amiga. 2) In relationships, it often means 'reconciles' or 'gets back together with' someone: Ella vuelve con su ex. Context determines whether it's physical return or rekindling a relationship.
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, Marta vuelve con su hermano.
native_language_example: After the party, Marta returns with her brother.

meaning: 'becomes more' or 'returns more' depending on context
additional_notes: Phrase uses the verb volver (to return / to become) + más (more). In many contexts volver + adjective/adverb means 'becomes more [adjective]': e.g., 'se vuelve más caliente' = 'becomes hotter'. With a person and a time expression, 'vuelve más tarde' means 'come back/return later' (here 'más' modifies 'tarde' = 'later'). Context determines whether volver means 'become' (often reflexive: volverse) or 'return/come back' (volver without reflexive).
target_language_example: Después de entrenar, se vuelve más fuerte cada semana.
native_language_example: After training, he becomes stronger each week.

meaning: 'I'll be back in...' — used to say you will return after a short amount of time.
additional_notes: Common phrase for telling someone how long you'll be gone. Followed by a time expression (e.g., media hora, dos minutos, un momento, un rato). Often used when leaving briefly and expecting to come back soon.
target_language_example: Vuelvo en diez minutos.
native_language_example: I'll be back in ten minutes.

meaning: ‘whisky with’ — used to say what is mixed with or served with whisky (e.g., whisky with cola).
additional_notes: This is a short, colloquial way to describe a whisky mixed or served together with something else. Common completions: 'whisky con cola' (whisky with cola), 'whisky con hielo' (whisky with ice). In speech you may also hear 'whisky y...' or simply the drink name. Pronunciation of 'whisky' follows English; 'con' means 'with'.
target_language_example: Quiero un whisky con cola, por favor.
native_language_example: I'd like a whisky with cola, please.

meaning: "and me" / "and to me" — used to include the speaker as an additional person affected, included, or emphasized.
additional_notes: Common after mentioning others to add the speaker. The preposition 'a' is used when the verb requires or prefers an indirect object (e.g., gustar, extrañar) or for emphasis/clarity. 'Mí' carries stress when emphasizing inclusion. Can appear with or without 'también' (también adds explicit 'too'). Note orthography: 'mí' has an accent; without it ('mi') means 'my'.
target_language_example: A tu mamá le diste todo lo que quiso y a mí la dejaste sin nada.
native_language_example: You gave your mother everything she wanted and left me with nothing.

meaning: and nobody (cares/knows/does) — used to add that no one is involved or concerned.
additional_notes: Commonly follows a clause to emphasize that no one cares, notices, or will be affected. Often appears with verbs like importar (to care), conocer (to know), ayudar (to help), etc. Tone can be neutral or bleak depending on context.
target_language_example: Está sufriendo en silencio y a nadie le importa.
native_language_example: He is suffering in silence and nobody cares.

meaning: and your (singular) — used to add someone or something belonging to 'you' to a list or sentence.
additional_notes: Combines 'y' (and) + the preposition 'a' + the possessive 'tu'. Common when mentioning people or things that belong to or are associated with the person you're speaking to. 'Tu' is informal singular; for formal or plural you would use 'su' or 'sus' respectively. Word order: 'y a tu X' often introduces an additional item (person or object).
target_language_example: Ella trajo la comida, y a tu hermano también.
native_language_example: She brought the food, and your brother too.

meaning: and him / and to him (used to add or contrast someone else)
additional_notes: Used to add another person into the remark or to contrast treatment/actions toward that person. Often appears with object pronoun clitic later (e.g., «y a él lo llevas…», «y a él lo condenaron…») or alone for emphasis («y a él», «y a él también»). Common in spoken and written Spanish to point out someone else who receives the action or to note that someone else is affected.
target_language_example: Invitas a todos menos a mí, y a él lo invitas siempre.
native_language_example: You invite everyone except me, and you always invite him.

meaning: and (he/she/it) opened
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'y' (and) followed by the past tense verb 'abrió' (from abrir). It appears in narratives or descriptions to connect actions: 'and opened'. Subject is usually third person singular (él/ella/usted) or can be used with nouns (la puerta). Common in storytelling: 'Entró y abrió la puerta.'
target_language_example: Llegó, miró alrededor y abrió la ventana.
native_language_example: He arrived, looked around, and opened the window.

meaning: and (he/she) opened the …
additional_notes: A common short sequence: y (and) + abrió (past tense, 3rd person singular of abrir = to open) + la (feminine definite article). It introduces that someone opened a feminine singular object (la puerta, la caja fuerte, la maleta, etc.). Use with a feminine noun; for masculine nouns use 'y abrió el'.
target_language_example: Ella buscó la llave y abrió la puerta.
native_language_example: She looked for the key and opened the door.

meaning: and that's it; and goodbye; and that's the end of it.
additional_notes: Used to signal finality—ending a conversation, decision, or action. Can be literal (saying goodbye) or figurative (closing a topic, indicating nothing more will be done). Tone can be neutral, curt, or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Lo intenté una vez más y adiós.
native_language_example: I tried one more time and that was it.

meaning: and now (he/she/it) doesn't / and now it's not (possible/visible/etc.).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a new situation or problem that has arisen; often followed by a verb or clause showing something that no longer happens, is not possible, or is not wanted. Tone can be neutral or express frustration/surprise. Context determines exact translation (doesn't, isn't, can't, no longer).
target_language_example: Me ayudó antes, y ahora no quiere saber nada de mí.
native_language_example: He helped me before, and now he doesn't want anything to do with me.

meaning: 'and turn off' (command/request to switch something off)
additional_notes: Used to join two actions: first do something (e.g., 'close the door') and then turn off a device or light. Common in commands or requests. Apaga is the tú (informal) imperative of apagar (to turn off) when addressing someone directly; context may imply polite or familiar tone. If speaking formally, use 'y apague'.
target_language_example: Cierra la ventana y apaga la luz.
native_language_example: Close the window and turn off the light.

meaning: and I learned (or and I learned how to ...).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction y (and) with aprendí (first-person preterite of aprender = to learn). Used to add a new piece of information about something the speaker learned in the past. Often followed by an infinitive (aprendí a + infinitive) or a direct object describing what was learned. Tone is neutral; context determines exact translation (e.g., 'and I learned', 'and I learned that', 'and I learned how to...').
target_language_example: Fui a clases de fotografía y aprendí a usar la cámara manualmente.
native_language_example: I went to photography classes and I learned how to use the camera manually.

meaning: and that (over there) / and stuff like that; used to refer vaguely to other things.
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'esto' as 'esto y aquello' to mean 'this and that' or 'this and those other things'—a vague way to refer to various topics, small items, or miscellaneous matters. Often appears in casual conversation: 'hablar de esto y aquello' = chat about various things. Not formal, but neutral everyday usage.
target_language_example: Nos sentamos a conversar de esto y aquello.
native_language_example: We sat down to chat about this and that.

meaning: and so / and like that / and that's how (something happens or is done).
additional_notes: Very versatile connector. Use 'y así' to summarize or conclude a sequence ('and so'), to indicate 'like that' when showing how to do something, or to introduce the result or manner of something ('and that's how...'). Tone depends on context—can be neutral narrative, colloquial when summarizing, or used to close an explanation. Often followed by a verb or a restatement of the result.
target_language_example: Le expliqué todo, y así decidieron cancelar el viaje.
native_language_example: I explained everything, and so they decided to cancel the trip.

meaning: 'and even' or 'and yet' (used to add emphasis or an additional surprising/contrasting point).
additional_notes: y aun is a connector meaning 'and even' or 'and yet'. It often adds emphasis before a surprising fact or contrasts with what was said before. It can be written with or without an accent on aun: 'aun' (without accent) is common; 'aún' (with accent) typically means 'still' or 'yet' — be careful: when used after 'y' to mean 'and even', it's usually 'y aun' (without accent) or 'y aún' depending on intended nuance. In many contexts 'e incluso' or 'incluso' can be used instead.
target_language_example: Estudió mucho, y aun así suspendió el examen.
native_language_example: He studied a lot, and yet he failed the exam.

meaning: 'and blue' (the conjunction 'and' + the color 'blue').
additional_notes: Very literal combination: used when listing or describing things that include the color blue. 'Y' is the common word for 'and'. 'Azul' means 'blue' and agrees in form for both singular and plural nouns (no gender change for masculine/feminine nouns: e.g., 'casa azul', 'cielo azul'). When listing colors, Spanish uses commas and 'y' before the last item (rojo, blanco y azul).
target_language_example: La camiseta es blanca y azul.
native_language_example: The t-shirt is white and blue.

meaning: 'and dance' — the conjunction 'y' (and) plus the verb 'bailar' (to dance).
additional_notes: Used to connect activities or verbs. 'Y' is the standard word for 'and' in Spanish and is pronounced [ee] except before words starting with the sound /i/ where it may sound like [e] or change to 'e' (e.g., 'e inteligente'). The verb 'bailar' means 'to dance' and is commonly used in infinitive form after verbs like 'gustar', 'querer', 'poder', or verbs of motion (e.g., 'bajar y bailar').
target_language_example: Me encanta escuchar música y bailar con amigos.
native_language_example: I love listening to music and dancing with friends.

meaning: 'and drink' (the conjunction 'y' + the verb 'beber' in the imperative or present forms depending on context).
additional_notes: Commonly appears where two actions are joined: 'come y bebe' = 'eat and drink'. In commands or invitations it can be imperative: 'Come y bebe' (Eat and drink). In statements it links two verbs in present tense: 'La mujer come pescado y bebe vino' (The woman eats fish and drinks wine). Verb form (bebe) can be present indicative (he/she/it or you formal) or imperative in colloquial speech for 'tú' the imperative is 'bebe'.
target_language_example: Relájate y bebe agua después del ejercicio.
native_language_example: Relax and drink water after exercise.

meaning: 'and drink' (connects a previous verb or noun to 'drink')
additional_notes: Common conjunction + verb phrase. Used to link actions (e.g., eat and drink) or items (e.g., cigarettes and drinking alcohol). Works with infinitives (comer y beber) or nouns (fumar y beber). Pronunciation note: the 'y' is pronounced like English 'ee'.
target_language_example: Vamos a comer y beber en la terraza.
native_language_example: Let's eat and drink on the terrace.

meaning: 'and white' (feminine singular).
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'y' (and) followed by the adjective 'blanca' (white) in its feminine singular form. Use 'blanco'/'blanca' to agree with the noun: 'blanco' for masculine nouns (el coche blanco), 'blanca' for feminine nouns (la camisa blanca). If the noun is plural, use 'blancos'/'blancas'.
target_language_example: La sábana es azul y blanca.
native_language_example: The sheet is blue and white.

meaning: 'and beautiful' (used to add 'beautiful' as a descriptor)
additional_notes: Commonly follows another adjective or noun to add the quality 'beautiful' (bonita). 'Y' = 'and'. Used to connect two descriptors (e.g., 'tranquila y bonita' = 'quiet and beautiful') or to add emphasis after a noun ('mi mujer ... es ... y bonita'). 'Bonita' is feminine; use 'bonito' for masculine nouns.
target_language_example: La plaza es antigua y bonita.
native_language_example: The square is old and beautiful.

meaning: a filler phrase meaning 'well' or 'anyway' used to wrap up, transition, or add a resigned comment.
additional_notes: Common spoken filler. Can soften a statement, show resignation, change topic, or politely end a conversation. Tone and context determine meaning: sometimes equivalent to 'well,' 'anyway,' 'so,' or 'oh well.' Often informal but widely used in neutral speech.
target_language_example: Y bueno, no podemos hacer más ahora.
native_language_example: Well, we can't do more right now.

meaning: and each one of / and every one of
additional_notes: Used to add items or people individually after mentioning a group or list. Often followed by a plural noun (e.g., 'los niños', 'ellos', 'los libros') or by a phrase introduced by 'los que'/'las que'. It emphasizes that every single member is included. Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Invitamos a los profesores y cada uno de los estudiantes.
native_language_example: We invited the teachers and each one of the students.

meaning: 'and warmth' or 'and heat'.
additional_notes: A simple connector phrase: y = 'and', calor = 'warmth' or 'heat' depending on context. Used literally (sun gives light and heat) or metaphorically (someone brings life and warmth). Calor can mean physical temperature (heat) or emotional warmth (coziness, affection).
target_language_example: Tu sonrisa trae alegría y calor a la casa.
native_language_example: Your smile brings joy and warmth to the house.

meaning: 'and meat' — the literal conjunction 'and' used with 'carne' (meat); also appears in the idiom 'uña y carne' meaning 'very close (as in inseparable)'.
additional_notes: Most often this is just the simple coordination 'and meat' (e.g., listing foods). However, in the fixed expression 'uña y carne' it means 'very close' or 'inseparable' (literally 'nail and flesh'). Pay attention to context: usually literal when listing items, idiomatic in 'uña y carne'.
target_language_example: Compraron pan, queso y carne para la cena.
native_language_example: They bought bread, cheese, and meat for dinner.

meaning: and almost / and nearly (something happened but didn't).
additional_notes: Combines conjunction 'y' (and) with 'casi' (almost). Used to add a short clause describing an event that nearly occurred. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Can introduce past, present, or subjunctive actions: e.g., 'casi se desmaya' = 'almost faints'. The 'y' often links this near-miss to what was just said.
target_language_example: Estábamos caminando y casi nos perdemos en la noche.
native_language_example: We were walking and we almost got lost in the night.

meaning: and (he/she/it) closed the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is a short sequence often found in narratives or instructions: 'y' = and; 'cerró' = past (preterite) of cerrar (to close) for él/ella/usted; 'la' is the feminine singular direct object pronoun or the feminine definite article before a noun. Most commonly it appears before a feminine noun (e.g., 'la puerta') or as 'la' replacing a feminine noun mentioned earlier ('y cerró la' → 'and he/she closed it').
target_language_example: Entró en la oficina, tomó los papeles y cerró la puerta.
native_language_example: He entered the office, took the papers and closed the door.

meaning: and clearly; (used in the phrase 'alto y claro') loudly and clearly.
additional_notes: Often appears in the fixed expression 'alto y claro' meaning 'loud and clear' or 'clear and unmistakable'. Used to describe speech that is both loud (alto) and easy to understand (claro). Can be used as an adverbial phrase: 'Habla alto y claro.'
target_language_example: Dilo alto y claro para que todos lo oigan.
native_language_example: Say it loud and clear so everyone can hear it.

meaning: 'and (it) begins' or 'and begin(s)'.
additional_notes: y = 'and'; comienza is the third-person singular present of comenzar (to begin) or an imperative/formal suggestion when used with implied subject 'you' in some contexts. Used to join actions or note that something starts right after or as a result of the previous clause. In sentences like 'Tranquilízate y comienza...' it functions like 'and (you) start...' (a suggestion).
target_language_example: Todo está listo y comienza la reunión.
native_language_example: Everything is ready and the meeting begins.

meaning: and tie (used to say someone is wearing a tie or wearing formal/business attire)
additional_notes: Commonly follows clothing items (e.g., 'camisa y corbata', 'traje y corbata') to indicate the person is wearing a necktie; often implies formal or business dress. Translate as 'and tie' or idiomatically as 'in a tie' / 'wearing a tie'. Not an idiom beyond literal clothing description.
target_language_example: Él llegó con camisa blanca y corbata.
native_language_example: He arrived with a white shirt and a tie.

meaning: 'and I grew up' (or 'and grew up' when continuing a sentence).
additional_notes: Commonly used after 'nací' (I was born) to say where you were born and raised. 'Crecí' is the first-person past (pretérito) of 'crecer' (to grow up). Can be used with or without the subject pronoun 'yo' (Yo crecí / (Yo) nací y crecí...).
target_language_example: Nací en Madrid y crecí en las afueras.
native_language_example: I was born in Madrid and grew up in the suburbs.

meaning: 'and when the' (used to introduce a time clause referring to a specific masculine noun).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the conjunction y (and) + temporal connector cuando (when) + the masculine singular definite article el. It's followed by a verb in the past, present, or future to describe what happens once that specific event (the noun) occurs. Use 'y cuando la' for feminine nouns. Common in storytelling or instructions.
target_language_example: Y cuando el tren llegue, subiremos todos.
native_language_example: And when the train arrives, we'll all get on.

meaning: 'and to drink' (used after 'dejar de' or similar verbs to indicate stopping a habit of drinking)
additional_notes: Appears as part of a verb phrase like 'dejar de X y de Y' or 'parar de X y de Y' meaning 'stop doing X and stop doing Y.' Commonly used to list two actions/habits (e.g., smoking and drinking). In some contexts speakers may omit the second 'de' and say 'dejar de fumar y beber', but including 'de' before the second verb emphasizes both verbs as objects of the first verb.
target_language_example: He decidido dejar de fumar y de beber este año.
native_language_example: I've decided to stop smoking and drinking this year.

meaning: 'and let' (imperative/request) or 'and stop' when followed by 'de' + verb.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the conjunction y (and) with the verb dejar in the imperative or infinitive form. Common uses: 'y deje + infinitive' can mean 'and let (someone) do something' or 'and leave/put (something)'; when used as 'y deje de + infinitive' it means 'and stop (doing something)'. Context and punctuation determine whether dejar is allowing/placing or the phrasal 'dejar de' (to stop). Formality is neutral — suitable for polite requests when using verbs like 'deje' (usted form).
target_language_example: Cierra la ventana y deje correr el ventilador.
native_language_example: Close the window and let the fan run.

meaning: 'and tell me' or 'and tell (me)'.
additional_notes: Common conversational connector: 'y' links a previous command or clause to the request 'dime' (tell me). Used to ask for information or confirmation after giving an instruction or prompting someone to look or act. Pronoun 'me' is built into 'dime' (imperative of decir). Can be followed by a question or a clause (e.g., 'y dime qué ves').
target_language_example: Mira eso y dime si te gusta.
native_language_example: Look at that and tell me if you like it.

meaning: 'and address' (used after 'name' to request someone's postal address)
additional_notes: Commonly appears after 'nombre' as 'nombre y dirección' on forms, envelopes, or instructions. Used to ask someone to write both their name and their mailing address. Formal and informal contexts; use 'su' for formal/third-person or 'tu' for informal/second-person.
target_language_example: Por favor, escribe tu nombre y dirección en el formulario.
native_language_example: Please write your name and address on the form.

meaning: 'and let me' (used to ask or tell someone to allow the speaker to do or say something).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction y (and) + imperative or subjunctive of dejar (to let/allow). Common in requests (Déjame terminar = let me finish), commands (Vete y déjame en paz = go and leave me alone), or to introduce a statement the speaker wants to make (Y déjame decir...). Often followed by an infinitive or a clause introduced with que.
target_language_example: Escucha y déjame explicarlo en dos minutos.
native_language_example: Listen and let me explain it in two minutes.

meaning: and I started / and I began
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction y (and) + the first-person singular preterite of empezar (empecé). Used to link a previous action or situation to the start of a new action by the speaker. Common in storytelling to continue events: '..., y empecé a...' (and I started to...).
target_language_example: Le expliqué el problema y empecé a buscar una solución.
native_language_example: I explained the problem and I started looking for a solution.

meaning: and to start / and start (again).
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction y (and) + the verb empezar (to start). Often appears before 'de nuevo' (again) to mean 'and start again' or 'and begin anew.' Used to connect actions or commands (e.g., 'do X and start (over)').
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta, olvida lo ocurrido y empezar de nuevo.
native_language_example: Close the door, forget what happened, and start again.

meaning: and in the (feminine plural) — used to connect ideas and introduce feminine plural nouns or phrases.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a simple combination: 'y' (and) + 'en' (in/on/at) + the feminine plural article 'las'. Commonly appears in phrases like 'en las buenas y en las malas' (through good times and bad times). Choose 'las' when the noun that follows is feminine and plural (e.g., 'circunstancias', 'fuerzas', 'casas').
target_language_example: Siempre estaré contigo y en las circunstancias difíciles también.
native_language_example: I will always be with you and in difficult circumstances too.

meaning: and (he/she/it) turned on / switched on / started (something).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction y (and) with the past tense verb encendió (from encender). Encender means to turn on lights, start an engine, switch on a device, or light something (a stove, a candle). Encendió is third person singular in the simple past (pretérito). Commonly used with objects like la luz, el motor, la televisión, la radio, una vela, etc.
target_language_example: Ella cerró la puerta y encendió la lámpara.
native_language_example: She closed the door and turned on the lamp.

meaning: 'and find' (imperative/command or instruction linking two actions).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction y (and) + the verb encontrar (to find). In the examples it's used to link two commands or actions: first do something, and then find X. Encontrar is in the imperative form (tú) implied in commands like 'revisa... y encuentra...' or in third-person contexts it can be indicative. Use with object after encontrar (la droga, algo, a alguien).
target_language_example: Limpia tu cuarto y encuentra tus llaves.
native_language_example: Clean your room and find your keys.

meaning: and that (one, feminine)
additional_notes: Used to point to or introduce a feminine noun or idea previously mentioned or about to be stated. 'Y' means 'and' or 'and so' when starting a sentence; 'esa' is the feminine demonstrative meaning 'that' (near the listener or previously mentioned). In contexts expressing a conclusion or summary, 'y esa' can be translated more naturally as 'and that's' or 'and that is' followed by a noun or clause (e.g., 'and that's the truth').
target_language_example: Salimos a caminar, vimos el parque y esa es la razón por la que volvimos tarde.
native_language_example: We went for a walk, saw the park, and that's the reason we came back late.

meaning: 'and those things' / 'and stuff like that' — a vague way to add related items or generalize.
additional_notes: Common informal filler used to refer broadly to related topics, items, or ideas already mentioned. Often paired with nouns (cosas, cosas inesperadas) and used to soften or generalize a statement. Equivalent to English 'and stuff', 'and that sort of thing', or 'and so on.'
target_language_example: Hablamos de música, viajes y esas.
native_language_example: We talked about music, travel, and stuff like that.

meaning: 'and write' (imperative/command when giving instructions).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction y (and) with the verb escribir in the imperative tú/usted context depending on sentence. In commands like "Elige uno y escribe una carta" it links two actions: do X and write. In instructions or invitations it often uses the imperative: "Ven y escribe tu nombre" (Come and write your name). Can also appear in narrative/descriptive contexts where escribe is present-tense rather than imperative.
target_language_example: Haz la lista y escribe los números al lado.
native_language_example: Make the list and write the numbers next to it.

meaning: used to introduce a contrasting remark meaning 'and yet' / 'even though' / 'and that's saying something'.
additional_notes: Adds emphasis by pointing out a surprising or contrasting fact that makes the previous statement more notable. Often appears at the start of a clause and can imply 'even though' or 'and yet' (highlighting an unexpected detail). Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Llegó tarde, y eso que no había tráfico.
native_language_example: He arrived late, and yet there was no traffic.

meaning: 'and wait' — used to tell someone to do something and then wait.
additional_notes: Common imperative construction: verb (command) + 'y espera' tells the listener to perform the action and then wait afterward. Can be literal (wait physically) or figurative (be patient). Often used after instructions or commands. 'Espera' is the tú imperative; context may change form (e.g., 'y espere' formal).
target_language_example: Apaga la luz y espera un minuto antes de salir.
native_language_example: Turn off the light and wait a minute before leaving.

meaning: and I will be
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction y (and) with estaré, the future tense 'I will be' of estar. Used to add that the speaker (or implied first person) will be in a state, place, or condition in the future (e.g., present, fine, supportive). Often follows a clause and introduces a future action or state. If context implies a different subject (he/she/it), Spanish would use estará instead.
target_language_example: Te ayudo ahora, y estaré contigo mañana.
native_language_example: I'll help you now, and I will be with you tomorrow.

meaning: and is in / and it/he/she is at (a place or group).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'y' (and) with the verb phrase 'está en' (third-person singular of estar + preposition en). Used to add information about location, membership, or presence. Context decides whether subject is a person or thing (it/he/she). Common in everyday speech to continue a sentence.
target_language_example: Llegó tarde y está en la sala ahora.
native_language_example: He arrived late and is in the living room now.

meaning: and that's it; and done; in and out (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase has several uses. As a closing remark (e.g., 'Cambio, y fuera') it means 'over and out' or 'and that's it' — a finalizing comment. In spatial phrases like 'dentro y fuera' it means 'in and out.' In poetic contexts ('y fuera donde fuera') it can mean 'and wherever (it) was' or 'and out wherever' depending on wording. Context determines whether it’s idiomatic (finalizing) or literal (movement or location).
target_language_example: Terminé la tarea, y fuera — ahora puedo descansar.
native_language_example: I finished the task, and that's it — now I can rest.

meaning: and I went
additional_notes: A simple past connector: 'y' = 'and', 'fui' = first-person preterite of 'ir' (to go). Use before a destination or action introduced by 'a' (e.g., 'fui a correr' = 'I went to run') or with a direct place (e.g., 'fui de compras' = 'I went shopping'). Common in narratives to link sequential actions. Not formal/informal by itself.
target_language_example: Terminé el trabajo y fui a casa.
native_language_example: I finished work and I went home.

meaning: and thank you / and thanks.
additional_notes: A short phrase used to add a thank-you after another remark (often at the end of a sentence or conversation). Common in formal and informal contexts; can be followed by the person or thing being thanked (e.g., 'a ti', 'por todo', 'a los Clifton'). Often used as a closing remark: 'Adiós, y gracias.'
target_language_example: Gracias por venir, y gracias por su ayuda.
native_language_example: Thank you for coming, and thanks for your help.

meaning: 'and we will do' or 'and we'll do'.
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction y (and) + haremos (first-person plural future of hacer). Used to add an action that 'we' will perform. Common in plans, offers, or statements of intent. Can be followed by a noun phrase (hacer + noun) or by a clause describing the action. Pronunciation tip: h is silent, so it sounds like 'ee ah-RE-mos'.
target_language_example: Terminemos esto, y haremos la presentación mañana.
native_language_example: Let's finish this, and we'll do the presentation tomorrow.

meaning: and do it (informal command)
additional_notes: A colloquial combination of y ('and') + haz (informal imperative of hacer, 'do/make') + lo ('it'). Used to tell someone directly to do something previously mentioned. Pronunciation often blends in casual speech: 'ee az lo'. Note: grammatically more standard order is 'y hazlo' (the object pronoun attached to the verb).
target_language_example: Dime qué necesitas, y haz lo cuando puedas.
native_language_example: Tell me what you need, and do it when you can.

meaning: and ice cream.
additional_notes: Simple conjunction 'y' (and) + noun 'helado' (ice cream). Used to connect 'ice cream' to another food or item mentioned. Common in lists or when saying you eat/want something plus ice cream. Pronunciation note: 'y' pronounced like English 'ee'.
target_language_example: Quiero pizza y helado.
native_language_example: I want pizza and ice cream.

meaning: and eggs (the conjunction 'y' + the noun 'huevos')
additional_notes: Used to list eggs together with other items (groceries, ingredients, foods). 'Y' simply means 'and'. 'Huevos' is the plural of 'huevo' (egg). Common in shopping lists and recipes. Pronunciation tip: 'y' is pronounced like English 'ee'.
target_language_example: Voy al mercado a comprar leche, pan y huevos.
native_language_example: I'm going to the market to buy milk, bread, and eggs.

meaning: 'and never' or 'and never again'.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction y (and) with jamás (never/ever). Jamás is a stronger form of nunca — it emphasizes 'never' or 'never again' and is used for dramatic or firm statements. In many cases the y at the start links ideas (e.g., 'and never spoke to him again') or continues a sentence ('...and never returned').
target_language_example: Me fui de la ciudad y jamás volví.
native_language_example: I left the city and never returned.

meaning: and I told him/her/you (formal) — connector plus a reporting verb (past).
additional_notes: Commonly used to link a previous action or statement with what the speaker said next. 'Le' is an indirect object pronoun that can mean 'to him', 'to her', or formal 'to you' (usted) depending on context; gender isn't shown. The verb 'dije' is first-person preterite of 'decir' (to tell/say). Use 'y le dije que…' to report what you told someone.
target_language_example: Salí corriendo y le dije que volvería pronto.
native_language_example: I ran out and told him/her that I would be back soon.

meaning: and that's it / and you're done / that's all.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is finished, complete, or no more needs to be said. Common in spoken Spanish as a quick closing phrase (like “and that's it” or “done”). Can follow a clause or list; tone is often casual. Not formal but widely used.
target_language_example: Arregla la mesa, pon la comida, y listo.
native_language_example: Set the table, put out the food, and that's it.

meaning: 'and (he/it/they) arrive(s)/reaches' or 'and it gets to' — used to connect actions, indicating arrival or that something reaches a place/point.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction y (and) + llega (3rd-person singular present of llegar). Used to link two actions: the first action happens, and then someone/something arrives or reaches a destination or state. Context determines whether translated as 'and arrives', 'and reaches', or 'and it gets to' (e.g., physical arrival, reaching a zone, or a substance reaching the blood). Can also be used imperatively with implied subject (e.g., 'y llega tan pronto como puedas' = 'and arrive/come as soon as you can').
target_language_example: El paquete pasa por aduana y llega mañana por la tarde.
native_language_example: The package goes through customs and arrives tomorrow afternoon.

meaning: and (he/she/it) reached/managed to (do something) / and arrived at
additional_notes: Used to link actions: can mean 'and arrived at' (physical arrival) or 'and managed to / came to (a conclusion or state)'. Often followed by an infinitive (llegó a + infinitive) meaning 'ended up doing' or 'managed to do'. Subject is usually third person. Context determines whether it's literal (arrival) or figurative (achievement, change of state).
target_language_example: Trabajó mucho y llegó a terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: He worked a lot and managed to finish the project on time.

meaning: 'and killed' (simple past: someone/something killed someone/something).
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction y ('and') + the preterite form mató (from matar). Used to connect actions in a narrative: '[subject] did X and killed Y.' Subject may be explicit earlier or implied. mató is third person singular (he/she/it/you formal) in the preterite.
target_language_example: Entró en la casa y mató la luz antes de dormir.
native_language_example: He/she/it entered the house and turned off the light before sleeping.

meaning: and I went to (do something / a place); often used for going to bed or to sleep.
additional_notes: Common colloquial sequence: 'y me fui a + infinitive' (e.g., 'y me fui a dormir') means 'and then I went to [do X]'. With a noun it indicates going to a place ('y me fui a la cama'). Frequently used to narrate simple past actions or routines. Tone is neutral; very common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Terminé la película y me fui a dormir.
native_language_example: I finished the movie and I went to sleep.

meaning: and a half; plus half (used to add 0.5 to a number or quantity).
additional_notes: Placed after a number or noun to indicate adding half (0.5). Common with time, age, measurements, quantities (dos y medio = 2.5). Can appear alone as a short reply ('y medio') meaning 'and a half' or 'about half more' depending on context. Works with years, minutes, meters, etc.
target_language_example: Tengo tres horas y medio para terminar.
native_language_example: I have three and a half hours to finish.

meaning: 'and even less' / 'much less' (used to add a stronger negative or to exclude something/someone)
additional_notes: Used after a negative or restrictive statement to emphasize that a second idea is even less likely, appropriate, or possible. In English it often corresponds to "much less" or "let alone". Common in short replies: "Y menos a usted." = "Much less you." Context determines exact translation.
target_language_example: No voy a discutir, y menos delante de tantos invitados.
native_language_example: I'm not going to argue, much less in front of so many guests.

meaning: and died in/at (a place or event).
additional_notes: Simple past construction combining 'y' (and) + 'morir' in the preterite (murió) + 'en' to indicate place or context where death occurred. Commonly used to state where or during what something/someone died (e.g., in a hospital, in the war, in jail, in the park). Use with locations, events, or settings. Verb agrees with subject (yo morí, él/ella murió, ellos murieron).
target_language_example: Viajó por el mundo y murió en una pequeña isla.
native_language_example: He traveled the world and died on a small island.

meaning: 'and black' — the conjunction 'y' (and) followed by the adjective 'negro' (black), used to add the color black after another color, adjective, or noun phrase (e.g., 'blanco y negro', 'grande y negro').
additional_notes: This is compositional: simply 'y' + 'negro'. Remember adjective agreement: 'negro' changes to 'negra' for feminine nouns (e.g., 'bolsa grande y negra'). In fixed expressions describing contrast or palette (e.g., 'blanco y negro' = 'black and white'), the masculine form is commonly used when the phrase is general or refers to a masculine noun. Word order matters: when describing a noun, adjectives typically follow the noun in Spanish, so you'd see forms like 'bolso grande y negro' or standalone phrases like 'blanco y negro'.
target_language_example: Un bolso grande y negro.
native_language_example: A large, black bag.

meaning: and none / and not one (of them).
additional_notes: Used to add that no one or nothing from a previously mentioned group applies. Commonly follows a list or general statement. Can refer to people or things. In short answers it can mean “and none” as a standalone phrase (e.g., Me gustan todos y ninguno = I like them all and none). Context determines whether it refers to 'none of them' or 'no one else'.
target_language_example: Traje varios libros y ninguno me interesó.
