Can also be followed by a noun (su éxito). Context determines nuance: 'seguro' = sure/certain/confident; not to be confused with 'seguro' meaning 'safe'.
target_language_example: Él está seguro de que pasará el examen.
native_language_example: He is sure that he will pass the exam.

meaning: he is
additional_notes: "Esté" is the present subjunctive of estar. This combination is usually seen in a clause after que, especially after expressions of hope, doubt, possibility, emotion, or preference: espero que él esté..., puede que él esté.... It refers to location or temporary states, and Spanish often omits él unless it is needed for emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Dudo que él esté listo para salir.
native_language_example: I doubt that he is ready to leave.

meaning: 'he speaks like' or 'he talks as/like'.
additional_notes: Used to compare the way a man speaks to someone or something else (e.g., 'él habla como un profesor' = he speaks like a teacher). Often followed by a noun, adjective, clause introduced by 'si' (como si...) or by a quoted style. For comparisons of manner with 'as if' use 'como si' + imperfect subjunctive ('él habla como si fuera otra persona').
target_language_example: Él habla como un experto, pero no tiene experiencia.
native_language_example: He speaks like an expert, but he doesn't have experience.

meaning: 'he speaks as if' — introduces a comparison or a hypothetical/unreal manner of speaking
additional_notes: Used to describe how someone talks, often followed by a subjunctive verb when the situation is hypothetical, doubtful, or contrary to fact (e.g., 'él habla como si supiera todo'). In everyday English it corresponds to 'he talks like' or 'he speaks as if'. The phrase can be adapted with other subjects: 'ella habla como si...', 'hablan como si...'.
target_language_example: Él habla como si fuera el jefe, pero no lo es.
native_language_example: He speaks as if he were the boss, but he isn't.

meaning: he may have
additional_notes: Combination of the subject pronoun él (he) plus the present perfect subjunctive form haya (from haber). Used in subordinate clauses or after expressions of doubt, possibility, emotion or uncertainty (e.g., Puede que él haya...). It expresses possibility about a past action or a subjunctive clause meaning 'that he has' in contexts requiring the subjunctive. Not to be confused with él ha (indicative: he has).
target_language_example: Puede que él haya llegado tarde por el tráfico.
native_language_example: He may have arrived late because of the traffic.

meaning: literally ‘he did it’ but as presented the word order is nonstandard/incomplete in Spanish; correct standard forms are “él lo hizo” (he did it) or “él hizo [algo]” (he did/made [something])
additional_notes: “él hizo lo” is not a grammatical standard standalone phrase in Spanish because object pronouns (lo) normally precede a conjugated verb (él lo hizo). You may encounter “él hizo lo” inside longer spoken constructions followed immediately by a relative clause or informal continuation (e.g., “él hizo lo que pudo” = he did what he could). For learners, remember the normal word order: subject + object pronoun + verb (él lo hizo) or subject + verb + direct object (él hizo un proyecto).
target_language_example: Él hizo lo que pidió el jefe.
native_language_example: He did what the boss asked.

meaning: He likes her (literal word order emphasizing subject and object).
additional_notes: This structure uses the indirect-object construction with 'gustar': 'A él le gusta ella' literally means 'To him, she is pleasing.' In everyday Spanish you'd more commonly hear 'él la quiere' (he loves/her likes) or 'a él le gusta ella' for emphasis. Note the full sentence usually includes the prepositional phrase 'a él' for clarity or emphasis. Word order can vary: 'A ella le gusta él' = 'She likes him.'
target_language_example: A él le gusta ella, pero todavía no se lo ha dicho.
native_language_example: He likes her, but he still hasn't told her.

meaning: Incorrect/ungrammatical attempt to say 'he likes the...' or 'she likes the...' (intended meaning: 'le gusta' = 'likes').
additional_notes: This exact string is ungrammatical in Spanish. The correct structures are: 'A él le gusta ...' or simply 'Le gusta ...' to mean 'He likes ...' For objects: 'A él le gusta la música' = 'He likes music.' For plural objects use 'les gustan' or 'le gustan' with plural noun: 'A él le gustan los libros.' Start the phrase with 'A' + pronoun (A él/A ella) for emphasis or clarity. Do not use 'él le gusta la' as written.
target_language_example: A él le gusta la música clásica.
native_language_example: He likes classical music.

meaning: he likes (something) a lot / he really likes (something).
additional_notes: Use with A + pronoun (A él) to emphasize the person; le gusta agrees with the thing liked (gusta = singular or infinitive). 'Mucho' intensifies the liking. Structure: [A + person] + le + gusta(n) + [thing]. For plural things use 'le gustan mucho'.
target_language_example: A él le gusta mucho viajar por el mundo.
native_language_example: He really likes traveling around the world.

meaning: He likes (plural things).
additional_notes: This is a full-personal construction used to say that 'he' likes multiple items. Spanish uses indirect object pronoun + verb gustar: 'a él' (emphatic/clarifying subject), 'le' (indirect object pronoun), 'gustan' agrees with the plural thing liked, and 'los' is the definite article for masculine plural nouns. For feminine plural use 'las' (e.g., 'a ella le gustan las flores'). You can drop 'a él' if context makes it clear: 'Le gustan los perros.'
target_language_example: A él le gustan los libros de aventura.
native_language_example: He likes adventure books.

meaning: he called / he rang (past tense of llamar).
additional_notes: Past simple (pretérito) of llamar. Can mean 'to call' by phone (llamar a alguien), 'to call for' or 'hail' a taxi (llamar un taxi), or 'to knock/knock on' a door (llamar a la puerta). Context tells the exact sense. Use 'a' before a person or thing when calling someone (Él llamó a María).
target_language_example: Él llamó a su amigo desde la estación.
native_language_example: He called his friend from the station.

meaning: himself (emphatic/reflexive: emphasizing that he did something personally or on his own).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a male person acted personally, without help, or to stress identity (he himself). Often follows the noun or pronoun it emphasizes (e.g., 'Tom lo hizo él mismo' = 'Tom did it himself'). When used with verbs like 'haber' it can add surprise or emphasis about the subject's action. For females use 'ella misma'; for plural, 'ellos mismos'/'ellas mismas'.
target_language_example: Él mismo arregló el coche, sin ayuda.
native_language_example: He himself fixed the car, without help.

meaning: used to emphasize that 'he' doesn't even do/know/feel something; 'he doesn't even...' or 'not even he...'.
additional_notes: Combination of the pronoun él (he) with ni adds strong negation/emphasis. Often appears with omitted main verb or with a following verb in subjunctive/conditional contexts. Equivalent to English 'he doesn't even...' or 'not even he...'. Common in colloquial speech. Context determines exact translation (e.g., 'he wouldn't even...', 'he doesn't even know').
target_language_example: Él ni se enteró de la noticia.
native_language_example: He didn't even find out about the news.

meaning: he has nothing / he doesn't have anything
additional_notes: Common phrase used as the start of different expressions: «él no tiene nada que hacer» (he has nothing to do), «él no tiene nada en común» (he has nothing in common), «él no tiene nada que ver con... » (he has nothing to do with...). The literal words match the English meaning, but the full meaning depends on the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Él no tiene nada que ver con ese problema.
native_language_example: He has nothing to do with that problem.

meaning: he is not going to / he won't (do something).
additional_notes: Common short form of 'él no va a + infinitive' used to say someone will not do or will not be able to do something. 'Va' is the present tense of 'ir' used as a future construction when followed by 'a' + infinitive. 'Él' is often omitted in casual speech unless needed for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Él no va a venir mañana.
native_language_example: He is not going to come tomorrow.

meaning: he thought (past tense of 'pensar').
additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) of pensar used to report a completed thought or opinion in the past. Can introduce reported ideas: 'Él pensó que...' = 'He thought that...'. Subject pronoun él (he) is often omitted in Spanish unless for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Él pensó que la película sería aburrida, pero le gustó.
native_language_example: He thought the movie would be boring, but he liked it.

meaning: he could / he might (conditional or possibility).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional form of poder. Can express possibility (he might be...), hypothetical ability or outcome (he could pass), polite suggestion or criticism (he could at least...), or a tentative statement about someone's identity or action. Context determines whether it means 'might' (possibility) or 'could' (conditional ability).
target_language_example: Él podría llamarte más tarde si tiene tiempo.
native_language_example: He could/might call you later if he has time.

meaning: the one who / he who (used to identify or emphasize the person who did something).
additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize a specific person as the doer of an action. Often appears as 'fue él quien...' (it was him who...), 'es él quien...' (it is he who...). In spoken Spanish the pronoun él may be stressed; 'quien' agrees in meaning (not grammatically) and is invariable here. Can be replaced by 'el que' in some contexts.
target_language_example: Creo que fue él quien rompió la ventana.
native_language_example: I think it was him who broke the window.

meaning: he would like
additional_notes: Conditional form of querer (quisiera) used to express polite wishes, hypothetical desires, or contrary-to-fact situations. Context determines whether it's a polite request ('he would like') or a hypothetical ('if he wanted...'). In spoken Spanish 'quisiera' can be interchangeable with 'querría' for politeness. Subject pronoun él is often omitted unless for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Él quisiera venir, pero no tiene tiempo.
native_language_example: He would like to come, but he doesn't have time.

meaning: he earns/wins/gets the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is a subject + reflexive verb construction: 'ganarse' means to earn, win, or gain something (often through effort or merit). 'La' is a feminine singular direct object (e.g., la confianza, la vida, la confianza). Context decides exact translation: 'él se gana la vida' = he earns a living; 'él se gana la confianza de todos' = he earns everyone's trust. Pronunciation note: the accent on 'él' distinguishes the subject pronoun from the article 'el'.
target_language_example: Él se gana la confianza de sus compañeros con su trabajo duro.
native_language_example: He earns his coworkers' trust with his hard work.

meaning: a colloquial/emphatic way to say 'he doesn't care' or 'he couldn't care less' (depends on verb that follows).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; 'él se la' is part of longer colloquial expressions where 'la' is an unstated object and the verb determines meaning. Common completions: 'se la sopla', 'se la suda', 'se la trae floja' — all mean 'he doesn't care' (rude/informal). With verbs like 'llevó' (Él se la llevó) it can mean 'he took it (away)' depending on context. Tone is informal and often coarse; avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: A él se la suda lo que digan.
native_language_example: He couldn't care less about what they say.

meaning: a set of pronouns used to mark actions affecting 'him' (to/for him) or to introduce what happened to him; literal parts: él (he), se/le (reflexive/indirect object).
additional_notes: This combination appears when describing something that happened to or was done for 'him'. 'Se' can be a reflexive/impersonal marker and 'le' is the indirect-object pronoun (to/for him). Word order with 'a él' is used for emphasis or clarity. Context determines exact meaning: passive-like event (A él se le metió algo en el ojo = something got into his eye), receiving something (se le otorgó = was awarded to him), idea occurring to him (se le ocurrió = it occurred to him), or a reflexive action (Él se le acercó — here 'se le' indicates movement toward someone/thing; this particular sentence is unusual and likely means 'He quietly approached him/it').
target_language_example: A él se le olvidó la cartera en el coche.
native_language_example: He forgot his wallet in the car.

meaning: he would be
additional_notes: Composed of él (“he”) + sería, the conditional of ser (“to be”). It is used for hypothetical situations or to describe what someone would be like. Spanish often omits subject pronouns, so él may be included for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Sin ese apoyo, él sería otra persona.
native_language_example: Without that support, he would be a different person.

meaning: 'he continues' or 'he still (does)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that a male person keeps doing something or remains in a state. Often followed by a verb in gerund (sigue + gerund: sigue comiendo) to mean 'keeps doing', or by an adjective/participle/noun to mean 'is still' (sigue parado = he is still standing). Context determines exact translation.
target_language_example: Él sigue estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: He continues studying for the exam.

meaning: he had
additional_notes: This is the pronoun él + the imperfect form tenía of tener. It usually means "he had" or "he used to have." In the example sentences, it appears as él tenía que + infinitive, which means "he had to." Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so tenía by itself can also mean "he had" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: De niño, él tenía una bicicleta roja.
native_language_example: As a child, he had a red bicycle.

meaning: he has more (than/than he can ...).
additional_notes: Used to say someone possesses a larger amount or quantity. Often followed by a comparison or clause introduced with de/que/del/los que (e.g., 'de lo que...', 'de los que...') to specify than what or than whom. Neutral register; 'él' can be dropped in everyday speech ('tiene más').
target_language_example: Él tiene más tiempo del que cree.
native_language_example: He has more time than he thinks.

meaning: he tried / he attempted (past simple of 'tratar' when used to mean 'try').
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'él trató de + infinitive' (he tried to do something). Can also mean 'he treated' in contexts where 'tratar' means 'to treat' (medical or manners), but in that case context differs and often uses different complements. Pronoun 'él' (he) is optional in Spanish and often omitted: 'Trató de...' is more natural in many sentences.
target_language_example: Él trató de llamar, pero no tenía señal.
native_language_example: He tried to call, but he had no signal.

meaning: he is going
additional_notes: Commonly used as the start of a near-future construction: él va a + infinitive = 'he is going to (do something)'. Can also mean 'he goes' in present simple when followed by an action without 'a' (context required). The subject pronoun él is often optional in Spanish (va alone is frequent) but included for emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Él va a volver mañana.
native_language_example: He is going to return tomorrow.

meaning: he is going to / he goes to
additional_notes: Used to say that a male person goes or is going to a place or is about to do something. With a location, 'a' means 'to' (Él va a la escuela = He goes to the school). With an infinitive (va a + verb) it forms the near future: 'he is going to [do something]' (Él va a estudiar = He is going to study). Note: 'va a por' is used in some regions to mean 'go to get' (Él va a por ello = He's going to get it).
target_language_example: Él va a estudiar esta tarde.
native_language_example: He is going to study this afternoon.

meaning: 'he goes' or 'that he go' (subjunctive form used after verbs/expressions that trigger the subjunctive)
additional_notes: Vaya is the present subjunctive of ir (to go). 'Él vaya' appears in subordinate clauses after verbs or expressions that require the subjunctive (wishes, commands, doubt, purpose, etc.) or in certain relative clauses (e.g., 'adondequiera que él vaya' = 'wherever he goes'). In casual spoken Spanish you may also hear 'que él vaya' as a softened command or suggestion ('let him go' / 'have him go'). Use él to emphasize 'he' (as opposed to another person).
target_language_example: Espero que él vaya al médico mañana.
native_language_example: I hope he goes to the doctor tomorrow.

meaning: 'he sees' or 'he watches' (third-person singular of ver).
additional_notes: Ver means 'to see' or 'to watch' depending on context. In Spanish the subject pronoun él (he) is often omitted because the verb ending -e already shows the subject, but it's used here for emphasis or clarity. Use 've' for actions in the present tense (he sees/he watches).
target_language_example: Él ve la película con sus amigos.
native_language_example: He watches the movie with his friends.

meaning: to him and his (something) — used to refer to a person and something that belongs to them (family, image, companion, etc.).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the prepositional object 'a él' (to him) with 'y a su' (and to his). It appears when mentioning both a person and something or someone associated with them (su + noun). Often used to introduce or refer to both the person and their related noun (ejemplar, familia, imagen, señora, guardaespaldas). In speech the first 'a' can be omitted before 'su' in casual contexts, but including both keeps clarity and emphasis.
target_language_example: Voy a hablar con él y a su abogado mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to speak with him and his lawyer tomorrow.

meaning: literally 'he and the/that' — used to join 'él' (he) with another noun or pronoun preceded by the article 'el'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's just the pronoun él ('he') plus the article el ('the') used before a masculine noun or nickname (el niño, el gobierno, el otro tipo). Context determines the second referent. Make sure to pronounce/mark the accent on 'él' to distinguish it from the article 'el'.
target_language_example: Él y el niño pasearon por el parque.
native_language_example: He and the boy walked through the park.

meaning: 'he and his' (used to link a male person with something/person that belongs to him)
additional_notes: Used to join a male third-person subject (él) with something or someone that belongs to him (su). Common in descriptions: 'él y su esposa' = 'he and his wife'. 'Su' is gender-neutral and can mean his/her/their depending on context, but here it refers to 'his'.
target_language_example: Él y su perro pasearon por el parque.
native_language_example: He and his dog walked through the park.

meaning: 'we were a' (past imperfect of 'to be' + indefinite article)
additional_notes: Used to describe what a group (we) used to be or how it was characterized in the past. Éramos is the first-person plural imperfect of ser (we were); una is the feminine singular indefinite article and agrees with a following feminine noun (una familia, una pareja, una piña). If the noun is masculine, use 'éramos un'.
target_language_example: Éramos una familia unida y alegre.
native_language_example: We were a close, happy family.

meaning: 'once upon a time' (used to start fairy tales or stories).
additional_notes: Formulaic phrase used to open a story, especially fairy tales and traditional narratives. Formal/literary tone; not used for everyday factual statements about the past. Often followed by setting or characters.
target_language_example: Érase una vez un castillo en lo alto de una montaña.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a castle on top of a mountain.

meaning: this one (male) + not / this is not / this one isn't
additional_notes: Éste is a demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this one' (masculine). Combined with 'no' it negates the statement: 'this one is not...' or 'this is not...'. In modern Spanish, the accent on 'éste' is optional and often omitted unless needed for clarity; many style guides recommend no accent (este). Use 'ésta' for feminine, 'éstos/estas' for plural. Context shows it refers to a specific person or thing previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Éste no es mi libro; el mío está en la mesa.
native_language_example: This one is not my book; mine is on the table.

meaning: 'this one' + reflexive/impersonal 'se' (used in different structures); literally 'this one [se ...]'.
additional_notes: Éste is a demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this one' (accent sometimes omitted in modern orthography: 'este'). When followed by 'se' it can appear in different constructions: 1) as subject + impersonal or reflexive 'se' (e.g., joking or colloquial expressions), 2) to point to a person/thing while a verb uses the impersonal/reciprocal 'se', or 3) in colloquial recounting where 'éste se' introduces an action by 'this one' (he/she/it). The exact translation depends on context — often simply 'this one (he/she/it)'.
target_language_example: Éste se pone siempre a hablar cuando llega tarde.
native_language_example: This one always starts talking when he arrives late.

meaning: last hope; final chance
additional_notes: Used to refer to a final possibility or remaining option when others have failed. Often preceded by 'la' (la última esperanza). Can be used literally (a final person/place that can help) or figuratively (a last resort).
target_language_example: La medicación fue la última esperanza para su recuperación.
native_language_example: The medication was the last hope for his recovery.

meaning: the last straw; the final small thing that makes a situation unbearable or causes someone to react.
additional_notes: Used to describe the final, often small, incident that makes someone lose patience or decide to act. Commonly appears in the phrase 'la gota que colmó el vaso' (the straw that broke the camel's back), but 'última gota' alone can emphasize the final triggering event.
target_language_example: Cuando llegó tarde otra vez, fue la última gota; renuncié.
native_language_example: When he was late yet again, it was the last straw; I quit.

meaning: breaking news; last-minute (news or update).
additional_notes: Used to refer to very recent, important news or developments. Commonly seen in headlines or TV/radio banners: '¡Última hora!' can introduce urgent updates. Can also describe last-minute changes (e.g., 'una noticia de última hora').
target_language_example: Última hora: la autopista está cerrada por un accidente.
native_language_example: Breaking news: the highway is closed due to an accident.

meaning: 'the last word' — the final remark or opinion in a conversation or argument.
additional_notes: Used to describe having the final say or making a closing comment. Often implies someone insisting on ending a discussion with their opinion; can be neutral (final remark) or negative (always needing to be right). Common in phrases like 'tener la última palabra' (to have the last word).
target_language_example: No discutas más; no voy a darte la última palabra.
native_language_example: Don't argue anymore; I'm not going to give you the last word.

meaning: the last person to (do something); the one who does something last.
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (en + infinitive) to say someone was the final person to perform an action. Can express literal order (e.g., leaving a room) or characterize someone's unlikely behavior (e.g., ‘the last person to accept a bribe’ meaning they would never do it). Often used with conditional/hypothetical verbs (sería) to show improbability.
target_language_example: María fue la última persona en salir de la oficina.
native_language_example: María was the last person to leave the office.

meaning: 'the last person who/that'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the final individual in a sequence or group who did something or has a certain quality. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Followed by a verb clause (e.g., 'última persona que llegó'). Can imply surprise or contrast (e.g., 'La última persona que esperábamos').
target_language_example: Él fue la última persona que salió de la oficina.
native_language_example: He was the last person who left the office.

meaning: 'the last time that I/he/she/they ... (to him/her)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent occasion something happened involving a person (indirect object 'le' = to/for him, her, or formal you in some regions). Commonly followed by a verb in past tense (vi, llamé) or present when warning (pregunto). English often renders it as "the last time I saw him" or "the last time I asked him." Word order: 'la última vez que' + clause; 'le' marks the person affected.
target_language_example: La última vez que le vi, llevaba una chaqueta roja.
native_language_example: The last time I saw him, he was wearing a red jacket.

meaning: 'the last time that (something/someone) it/him'
additional_notes: This phrase begins a clause referring to the most recent occasion something happened. 'Última vez' = 'last time'; 'que' introduces the clause; 'lo' is a direct object pronoun (it/him). You will often see variations depending on gender/number (la, las, los) or omitted pronoun: e.g. 'la última vez que la vi' (the last time I saw her).
target_language_example: La última vez que lo vi, estaba muy cansado.
native_language_example: The last time I saw him, he was very tired.

meaning: 'the last time that you...'/ 'the last time you...'
additional_notes: This is a common phrase starter used to talk about the most recent occasion someone did something. It is followed by a verb or clause describing the action (e.g., última vez que te vi, última vez que te llamé). Often used in questions and statements about memory or frequency: ¿Cuál fue la última vez que te vi? / La última vez que te llamé fue ayer.
target_language_example: ¿Recuerdas la última vez que te vi?
native_language_example: Do you remember the last time I saw you?

meaning: last moment; at the last minute
additional_notes: Used to refer to the final point in time before something happens. Can mean a very late or last-minute action or advice. Common in phrases like "a último momento" (at the last minute) or "con palabras de último momento" (last-minute words).
target_language_example: Lo dije todo en el último momento antes de salir.
native_language_example: I said everything at the last moment before leaving.

meaning: the last thing (I/he/she/they) want; used to say something is the thing you least want.
additional_notes: Commonly used in negative statements to emphasize that something is unwanted or undesired. Often appears as 'es lo último que quiero' or 'lo último que quiero es...'. Can refer to the speaker's wishes or someone else's (context decides subject).
target_language_example: Lo último que quiero es causarte problemas.
native_language_example: The last thing I want is to cause you problems.

meaning: last resort; final option when nothing else works
additional_notes: Used to describe the final measure taken after all other options have failed. Often preceded by 'como' (as a) or used with verbs like 'ser', 'tomar' or 'quedar'. Not literal; it means an emergency or last possibility.
target_language_example: Como último recurso, llamaremos a la policía.
native_language_example: As a last resort, we'll call the police.

meaning: the only thing; sole thing
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is a single item, fact, or concern. Can appear before or after a verb or clause: "La única cosa que quiero..." or in short answers: "La única cosa." Often interchangeable with "la única cosa que" + clause.
target_language_example: La única cosa que necesito es tiempo.
native_language_example: The only thing I need is time.

meaning: the only family (left); sole remaining family members
additional_notes: Used to say someone or a group is your only family or the only family you have left. Often expresses closeness or loss (e.g., after other relatives are gone). 'Única' agrees in gender/number with 'familia'.
target_language_example: Mi madre es mi única familia ahora.
native_language_example: My mother is my only family now.

meaning: the only one (who/in which).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is the only person/place/thing in a group or situation. Often appears with a relative clause introduced by que, en el que, en quien, or followed by a location (e.g., 'en la habitación'). Make sure gender/number agree: único (m. sing.), única (f. sing.), únicos/únicas (pl.).
target_language_example: Él es el único en quien confío.
native_language_example: He is the only one I trust.

meaning: the only thing (is that)... — used to introduce a single exception, detail, or important point.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'Lo único es que...' to point out one main issue, exception, or important piece of information. Followed by a clause explaining that one detail. Tone is neutral and common in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Lo único es que mañana tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: The only thing is that I have to work tomorrow.

meaning: 'only problem' or 'sole problem' — the single issue (often used to introduce a drawback or complication).
additional_notes: Used to point out the main or sole difficulty in a situation. Often appears as 'El único problema es que...' (The only problem is that...) or in negative form 'no es el único problema' (it's not the only problem). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: El único problema es que no tenemos suficiente tiempo.
native_language_example: The only problem is that we don't have enough time.

meaning: the only thing you do is / all you do is
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone's sole action or behavior is the one mentioned. Often appears as 'Lo único que haces es + [infinitive]'. Can be used critically or neutrally depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Lo único que haces es quejarte.
native_language_example: All you do is complain.

meaning: the only thing/person that (to) me / the only ... that I ...
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a fragment often used in sentences like "lo único que me preocupa..." or "lo único que me dijo...". It combines único (only, sole) + que (that) + me (to me / me as indirect or direct object). Common patterns: "lo único que me importa..." (the only thing that matters to me), "lo único que me falta..." (the only thing I'm missing). Remember to include the appropriate article (lo, la, el) or noun when forming a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Lo único que me preocupa es el examen.
native_language_example: The only thing that worries me is the exam.

meaning: the only one I have left / the only one remaining for me.
additional_notes: Used when referring to a single item, option, or thing that remains for the speaker. Commonly follows a noun: 'Es el único que me queda' (It's the only one I have left). Can refer to time, money, objects, choices, or people in context.
target_language_example: Este es el único que me queda, así que lo voy a conservar.
native_language_example: This is the only one I have left, so I'm going to keep it.

meaning: the only thing we have left / what's left for us
additional_notes: Used to point out the single remaining thing, option, or resource. Often appears as 'lo único que nos queda' or 'es lo único que nos queda.' Can refer to tangible things (money, food) or abstract ones (memories, options). 'Nos' indicates 'for us' or 'to us.'
target_language_example: Después del incendio, los recuerdos son lo único que nos queda.
native_language_example: After the fire, memories are the only thing we have left.

meaning: the only thing we can do
additional_notes: Used to say there is no other option or action available. Often appears as 'lo único que podemos hacer' (with the neutral article 'lo'). Followed by an infinitive or clause describing the action (e.g., 'es esperar').
target_language_example: Lo único que podemos hacer es llamar a emergencias.
native_language_example: The only thing we can do is call emergency services.

meaning: the only thing that (is/does)...
additional_notes: Used to introduce what is the sole thing that happens, exists, or can be done. Often appears as 'lo único que se...' + verb (passive/impersonal) or 'lo único que se me...' with an indirect object. 'Lo' is a neutral article meaning 'the thing'.
target_language_example: Lo único que se escucha en la noche son los grillos.
native_language_example: The only thing that is heard at night is the crickets.

meaning: 'the only thing that (to) you' — used to say what is the only thing that matters, helps, interests, etc., to someone.
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Es/Lo único que te + [verb]'. 'Lo' is often used before 'único' (lo único) to mean 'the only thing'. The verb after 'te' is conjugated for the thing that matters to the person (importa, interesa, sirve, pido, etc.). Used to emphasize exclusivity: nothing else matters or helps the person.
target_language_example: Lo único que te falta es práctica.
native_language_example: The only thing you're missing is practice.

meaning: useful for / useful in (some situation or activity).
additional_notes: Used to say that something helps or is beneficial in a particular area, situation, activity, or time. Follows the thing that is useful (e.g., 'El griego') and is followed by 'en' plus the context (e.g., 'en la ciencia', 'en el viaje'). Can be used with different pronouns (le, les, te) for indirect objects.
target_language_example: Este consejo te será útil en el trabajo.
native_language_example: This advice will be useful to you at work.
